document_context_data.document_summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot study investigated the effects of 6-month potassium citrate (K citrate) supplementation (30 mEq/day), in combination with calcium and vitamin D, on bone turnover markers and urinary metabolic profiles in 40 postmenopausal women with osteopenia. The study found that while bone turnover markers (CTX and BAP) decreased in both K citrate and placebo groups, K citrate significantly enhanced these beneficial effects, particularly in a subgroup of patients with pre-existing low-grade acidosis (low urine pH and/or low potassium and citrate excretion). K citrate also improved urinary pH, citrate, and potassium excretion. The study concluded that K citrate is beneficial for osteopenic women with documented potassium/citrate deficits and low-grade acidosis, but its indiscriminate use is not recommended without such evidence.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Potassium Citrate (K citrate) supplementation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Daily oral supplementation with 30 mEq of K citrate (in two tablets) for 6 months. This was administered in addition to daily calcium carbonate (500 mg day   ⁻¹) and vitamin D (400 IU day   ⁻¹) for all subjects (K citrate and placebo groups). The K citrate treatment showed significant benefits in subjects with evidence of low-grade acidosis (low 24h-citrate excretion or low fasting-morning urine pH) compared to the placebo, with significant changes observed as early as 3 months. No specific dose-response comparisons were reported, and adherence rates were approximately 90% for both groups.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Not reported

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: The active form of vitamin D, crucial for calcium absorption in the gut and bone mineralization.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: K citrate supplementation in postmenopausal women with osteopenia, with additional vitamin D3 supplementation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of vitamin D status and its role in calcium metabolism and bone health.

document_context_data.document_summary: This longitudinal, prospective observational study investigated whether vitamin D metabolites (25-hydroxyvitamin D, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) and Vitamin D Binding Protein (VDBP), along with their ratios, could predict preeclampsia (PE) in women with Type 1 Diabetes (T1DM). The study found that higher concentrations of 1,25(OH)2D, lower concentrations of VDBP, and elevated 1,25(OH)2D/VDBP ratios in the second and third trimesters were significantly associated with and predictive of subsequent PE, while 25(OH)D, the standard metric for vitamin D status, did not predict PE.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Longitudinal Prospective Observational Study on Preeclampsia Prediction
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational study with no therapeutic interventions or dose comparisons. Biomarker concentrations and clinical data were collected at three gestational visits: V1 (~12 weeks), V2 (~22 weeks), and V3 (~32 weeks). The study enrolled 151 women with Type 1 Diabetes (T1DM) and 24 non-diabetic controls, rigorously phenotyped and free of proteinuria and hypertension at enrolment. The primary analysis compared 23 T1DM women who developed preeclampsia (PE) with 24 matched T1DM women who remained normotensive. A secondary analysis compared normotensive T1DM women with non-diabetic controls. The cohort was largely vitamin D insufficient or deficient.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly higher concentrations (total, bioavailable, and free) observed in T1DM women who developed PE (DM+PE+) compared to normotensive T1DM women (DM+PE−) at V2 (~22 weeks, all p < 0.01) and V3 (~32 weeks for bioavailable and free, p < 0.05 and p < 0.01 respectively). Lower concentrations were noted in DM+PE− vs. non-diabetic controls at V2 (total p=0.002, bioavailable p=0.004, free p=0.018). In DM+PE+ women, total and free 1,25(OH)2D at V2 were positively correlated with uNGALcc (p < 0.05). At V2, every 1 pg/mL increase in total 1,25(OH)2D increased PE odds by 3% (OR: 1.03, p=0.012); for bioavailable 1,25(OH)2D, every 1 pg/mL increase raised odds by 28% at V2 (OR: 1.28, p=0.010) and 18% at V3 (OR: 1.18, p=0.047). Significance persisted in multivariate analyses.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: The active hormonal form of vitamin D, primarily responsible for regulating calcium and phosphate homeostasis and promoting intestinal absorption of calcium. It increases 2-3 fold during pregnancy, reflecting the calcium needs of the developing fetus and up-regulating trans-placental transport. It also has protective functions, inhibiting inflammatory cytokines and inducing anti-microbial peptide synthesis.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Preeclampsia risk prediction in women with Type 1 Diabetes during the second (~22 weeks) and third (~32 weeks) trimesters of pregnancy. Also in relation to early subclinical renal dysfunction (uNGALcc).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: May serve as a new marker for preeclampsia risk and could be implicated in its pathogenesis in women with Type 1 Diabetes. Elevated levels predict subsequent preeclampsia and may reflect early subclinical renal or placental dysfunction. Conversely, lower levels in non-diabetic PE may suggest a defeat of protective responses.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study performed an integrative multi-platform meta-analysis of gene expression profiles from Affymetrix and Illumina datasets in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) patients and healthy controls to identify novel, robust diagnostic biomarkers. The analysis revealed 5 commonly differentially expressed genes and 28 novel 'gained' genes, suggesting their significant potential for early PDAC diagnosis.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Integrative meta-analysis of gene expression data for biomarker identification and diagnostic prediction in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Gene expression data from two independent cohorts of PDAC patients (Affymetrix: 18 PDAC patients; Illumina: 36 PDAC patients) and 18 healthy controls were integrated. Profiling was performed on peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) using Affymetrix GeneChip® Human Gene ST 1.0 Arrays and Illumina HumanHT-12 v4 Expression BeadChip microarray platforms. Data were integrated using an empirical Bayesian methodology (ComBat) for batch effect removal, and differential expression was analyzed with limma software, identifying genes with p<0.01 and at least 1.5-fold differential expression. The analysis identified 5 commonly differentially expressed genes (with individual ROC curve AUC > 0.9) and 28 novel 'gained' genes, which could discriminate PDAC patients from controls with an average sensitivity of 74.8% and specificity of 73.3% for individual gained genes, 100% sensitivity and 94% specificity for combined common genes, and 91% sensitivity and 87% specificity for combined gained genes. No dose-response comparisons were applicable as it is a diagnostic biomarker identification study.

matched_biomarker_details.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC) patient samples (gene expression data).

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Overexpression; identified as a differentially expressed gene with individual ROC curve showing AUC > 0.9 for distinguishing PDAC patients from healthy controls.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Involved in adaptation to the microenvironment, regulating metabolism and hypoxia, contributing to vascular development (increasing VEGF expression), involved in mTOR pathway activation.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: PDAC patients, metastatic process in lung cancer.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Associated with the metastatic process; key in metastatic progression; potential predictor for PDAC diagnosis.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the influence of oral contraceptive (OC) use on physiological, oxidative stress, and inflammatory responses to fixed-intensity and sprint cycling in recreationally trained women, comparing them to naturally cycling women. It also examined the acute effects of N-acetylcysteine (NAC) supplementation on these responses and 1-km cycling time trial performance. Key findings showed that women using OC had elevated oxidative stress (higher MDA, lower GPx) and inflammation (higher CRP) biomarkers, as well as increased ventilation, during exercise. While NAC supplementation increased plasma thiols, it only blunted exercise-induced malondialdehyde increases in naturally cycling women, not in OC users, and did not improve cycling performance in either group. This suggests an increased strain on the endogenous antioxidant system in women using OC during exercise.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Acute N-acetylcysteine (NAC) supplementation and cycling exercise (fixed-intensity and sprint time trial).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Twenty recreationally trained women completed five exercise trials, including two double-blind crossover intervention trials where participants acutely supplemented with NAC or a placebo. NAC was administered orally in a total dose of 105 mg·kg⁻¹ of body mass, given as 70 mg·kg⁻¹ 60 minutes prior to exercise and 35 mg·kg⁻¹ 30 minutes prior. The exercise protocol involved 40 minutes of fixed-intensity cycling at 105% of the gas-exchange threshold (GET), immediately followed by an all-out 1-km cycling time trial. No dose-response comparisons for NAC were reported beyond the acute vs. placebo comparison.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Statistically equivalent between the placebo and NAC trial for WomenNC (d = 0.05) and for WomenOC (d = 0.17). There was no Group effect on the difference in completion time between the NAC and placebo trial (  [95% CI] = 0.4 s [− 3.3, 4.1]), with completion time statistically equivalent between the groups (  [90% CI] = 0.4 s [− 2.7, 3.5]), based on the equivalence bounds of 0 ± 4.8 s.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Direct measure of exercise performance in a cycling time trial.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: After NAC or placebo supplementation, following fixed-intensity cycling.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Lack of change indicates that acute NAC supplementation did not improve 1-km cycling time trial performance in either group under these conditions.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigates the molecular determinants of hemogenic endothelial cells (HECs) and hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs) by generating a GATA2w/eGFP reporter in human embryonic stem cells (hESCs). The reporter accurately marks endogenous GATA2 expression, which is critical for endothelial-to-hematopoietic transition (EHT). A key finding is the identification of ITGB3 (CD61) as a reliable novel positive surface marker that precisely labels functional HECs with superior hemogenic potential, both in hESC/hPSC differentiation in vitro and in embryonic day 10 mouse embryos in vivo. The research provides a robust platform for dissecting hematopoiesis and facilitates the generation of functional hematopoietic stem cells in vitro.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Gene targeting using TALENs, in vitro human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC) differentiation, and in vivo mouse embryo analysis.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: GATA2w/eGFP reporter was generated in H1 hESCs via gene editing (TALENs, electroporation of 1 μg linearized vector and 2.5 μg of each TALEN plasmid into 1 × 10^6 H1 cells, puromycin selection at 0.5 μg/mL, and Cre recombinase (400 ng per 1 × 10^6 cells) for cassette removal). In vitro differentiation involved hPSC blood differentiation protocols using co-culturing with OP9 stromal cells or AGM-S3 co-culture. Bone morphogenetic protein 4 (BMP4) treatment was applied for 5 days. Cell seeding used Y-27632 (10 μM). CFU assay medium contained 100 ng/mL recombinant murine stem cell factor, 10 ng/mL recombinant murine interleukin-3, 10 ng/mL recombinant human interleukin-6, and 3 U/mL human erythropoietin, with endothelial cell assays using 100 ng/mL vascular endothelial growth factor. In vivo analysis included mouse embryos at E10.0, E11, E12, E14, with fractionation of endothelial cells based on CD61 expression (CD61 high, CD61 low, and CD61 − subpopulations). No specific dose-response comparisons for differentiation conditions or therapeutic interventions were reported beyond qualitative observations of effect.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: After removal of the cassette, a 1.10-kb product was produced.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Verification of genomic DNA modification, specifically the removal of the selection cassette.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Cre recombinase-mediated removal of the loxP-flanked PGK-puromycin cassette from TALEN-targeted H1 ESCs.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Confirms successful Cre recombinase activity and removal of the PGK-puromycin selection cassette, leaving the desired gene modification.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of consuming cow's milk versus an energy-matched carbohydrate solution on recovery markers and performance in twenty female team-sport athletes following repeated simulated team games (STGs). The findings indicated that 500 mL of milk consumption attenuated losses in muscle function (peak torque for knee extension and flexion), sprint performance (5m and 10m), and perceptions of stress, and helped reduce muscle soreness and tiredness, particularly after the first STG. However, for many other physiological and performance markers (e.g., CK, hsCRP, LOOHs, PCs, CMJ, HR, RPE), the effects were mostly unclear or trivial, with milk showing no clear benefit after the second STG.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Nutritional intervention (consumption of cow's milk vs. an energy-matched carbohydrate solution) combined with a multi-stage physical activity protocol.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants consumed 500 mL of either cow's milk (910 kJ/215 kcal, 17.0 g protein, 25.5 g carbohydrate, 5.0 g fat) or an energy-matched carbohydrate solution (910 kJ/215 kcal, 0.2 g protein, 53.6 g carbohydrate, 0.0 g fat) immediately following each of two simulated team games (STG1 and STG2). The 17 g protein from milk was noted to be below the recommended 20 g threshold for maximal protein synthesis stimulation. The exercise protocol involved two ~30 minute halves of intermittent running with sprints, agility, and jumps, separated by a 10-minute half-time, with a 48-hour recovery period between STG1 and STG2. No explicit dose-response comparisons were reported for the nutritional interventions.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Benefit for MILK (likely; ES = 0.30 to 0.53) following STG1. Overall positive effect of milk on post-exercise muscle function was small to moderate, but performance remained below baseline at 96 h. For 15m sprint, a likely within-group increase was observed for both MILK and CHO from STG1 to STG2, but between-group comparisons were unclear.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Indicator of explosive power, acceleration, and short-distance speed.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Recovery from repeated simulated team games (STGs), specifically after STG1. Also includes 15m sprint context for repeated games and milk vs CHO.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Directly indicates recovery of speed and acceleration, which are vital components of team-sport performance.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of post-exercise milk consumption (500 mL) versus an energy-matched carbohydrate drink on recovery from a repeated sprinting and jumping protocol in female team-sport athletes. The strenuous protocol successfully induced muscle damage, leading to post-exercise decreases in muscle function (peak torque, countermovement jump, sprint performance, rate of force development) and increases in subjective muscle soreness and tiredness. Milk consumption attenuated losses in muscle function, particularly for peak torque (knee extension/flexion at 180°/s) and countermovement jump height, and reduced perceived stress (DALDA B) at various time points (24h, 48h, 72h) post-exercise. The study concluded that milk may be a valuable recovery intervention for female team-sport athletes following this type of exercise, although its effects on serum creatine kinase, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, reactive strength index, and some sprint performances were unclear.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Post-exercise nutritional intervention (Milk vs. Carbohydrate drink)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants immediately consumed either 500 mL of milk (910 kJ/215 kcal, 17.0 g Protein, 25.5 g Carbohydrate, 5.0 g Fat) or 500 mL of an energy-matched carbohydrate drink (910 kJ/215 kcal, 0.2 g Protein, 53.6 g Carbohydrate, 0.0 g Fat) following a whole-body sport and exercise protocol designed to induce muscle damage (15x20m maximal sprints and 8 sets of 10 plyometric jumps). The milk protein dose (17g) was noted to be potentially suboptimal for maximal protein synthesis compared to other studies. No dose-response comparisons were conducted, as a single volume of 500 mL was used for both interventions.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Measures short-distance speed.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Post-exercise recovery following exercise-induced muscle damage from sprinting and jumping.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates recovery of sprint speed.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study aimed to identify new genetic susceptibility loci for invasive epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) by performing a comprehensive meta-analysis of genome-wide association studies (GWAS). The investigation included data from general population EOC cases and controls, as well as BRCA1/2 mutation carriers. Six novel EOC susceptibility loci were discovered, and their potential functional roles were characterized through eQTL analysis, epigenetic profiling, gene expression and DNA copy number assessments, and in vitro transcriptional assays, with the ultimate goal of improving EOC risk prediction.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Genetic Risk Factor Identification and Functional Genomics Analysis (via Genome-Wide Association Studies, Meta-analysis, and In Vitro Transcriptional Assays)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study focused on identifying genetic risk factors for EOC, not a therapeutic intervention. A meta-analysis of approximately 11-11.4 million genetic variants was performed using data from 15,397-15,437 EOC cases (including 9,627 serous EOC), 30,816-30,845 controls, 15,252 BRCA1 mutation carriers (2,462 with EOC), and 8,211 BRCA2 mutation carriers (631 with EOC). Genome-wide significance for associations was set at p<5	10^-8. Functional analyses included gene expression analysis for 91 coding genes and mRNA expression for 316 complete tumors (Z-score threshold of 2), DNA copy number analysis for 481 serous EOC samples, and an in vitro luciferase reporter assay performed by co-transfecting 800 ng of luciferase constructs and 50 ng of pRL-TK Renilla into 8 	 10^4 iOSE4 normal ovarian cells. Methodological details included sample exclusion for genotyping call rate <95% and SNP exclusion based on imputation accuracy (r^2 <0.25-0.3) or minor allele frequency (MAF <0.005-0.01). Imputation utilized 90 MCMC iterations and specific buffer regions. No dose-response comparisons for a therapeutic treatment were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Associated with invasive EOC risk (p<5	10^-8). The lead SNP chr17:29181220:I showed an estimated HR for BRCA1 carriers significantly different from OCAC (p=0.005), while the association for BRCA2 carriers was consistent with OCAC (BRCA2-OCAC meta-analysis p=2.6	10^-9). A specific haplotype (rs9910051 and rs3764419) showed p=8.6	10^-8 for haplotype, and p=1.8	10^-8 for chr17:29181220:I in BRCA2-OCAC meta-analysis.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: ATAD5 acts as a tumor suppressor gene, modulating RAD9A/BCL2 interaction to induce DNA damage-related apoptosis; involved in DNA replication and repair, contributing to EOC susceptibility.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Susceptibility to invasive Epithelial Ovarian Cancer (EOC) in the general population (OCAC) and in BRCA1/BRCA2 mutation carriers, assessed via meta-analysis of GWAS data.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates an increased genetic predisposition to invasive EOC; its incorporation into risk assessment tools can improve clinical risk predictions for BRCA1/2 mutation carriers.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated a chemically defined, serum-free protocol for the in vitro transdifferentiation of pancreatic progenitor AR42J-B13 cells into functional hepatocyte-like cells (HLCs) over five days. The research examined morphological, transcriptomic, proteomic, and functional changes, concluding that successful transdifferentiation, facilitated by extracellular matrix proteins like fibronectin or laminin, is independent of serum.

treatment_details.therapy_type: In vitro pancreatic progenitor cell transdifferentiation to hepatocyte-like cells
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Clonal pancreatic progenitor AR42J-B13 cells were cultured for five days in a differentiation medium containing 100 nM Dexamethasone, 10 ng/ml Oncostatin M, 20 ng/ml HGF, 20 ng/ml FGF-2, 1% ITS+ (insulin, transferrin, selenous acid), 0.2% BSA, 4.4 mM nicotinamide, 1 µM copper sulphate, 30 µg/ml ascorbic acid, and 1 µg/ml heparin. Cells were grown on uncoated plastic, laminin-coated (2 µg/cm2), or fibronectin-coated (5 µg/cm2) substrata, with or without 5% FBS supplementation. The study primarily focused on the effectiveness of serum-free conditions facilitated by ECM proteins, rather than dose-response comparisons for individual components, finding no significant difference in transdifferentiation potential between fibronectin and laminin substrata.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Not reported as changing; used as a housekeeping gene for normalization.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Component of the small ribosomal subunit, used as a stable reference for gene expression studies.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: In vitro transdifferentiation of AR42J-B13 cells under various substratum and media conditions.

document_context_data.document_summary: This placebo-controlled, double-blind, six-arm crossover study investigated the effects of a single 60 mg Cannabidiol (CBD) supplementation versus placebo after an intensive resistance training protocol (designed to induce muscle damage) on skeletal muscle regeneration and performance in healthy, well-trained participants. The study measured muscle damage biomarkers (Creatine Kinase and Myoglobin) and neuromuscular performance (1RM Back Squat and Countermovement Jump) at 24, 48, and 72 hours post-training. While overall effects were small, CBD significantly attenuated increases in CK and Myo concentrations and aided in the recovery of 1RM Back Squat performance after 72 hours, but showed no significant effect on Countermovement Jump performance.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Cannabidiol (CBD) supplementation following an intensive strength training protocol.
treatment_details.dose_specificity:
Participants underwent an intensive strength training protocol consisting of three sets of 12 back squats at 70% of 1RM with 150 seconds rest, and three sets of 15 drop jumps from a 45 cm box landed in a deep squat with 60 seconds rest. A single dose of 60 mg CBD solubilisat or a placebo drink was consumed directly after exercise, with effects monitored at 24, 48, and 72 hours post-training. Absolute strength values and training loads averaged 118.6 
± 22.6 kg. The study did not include dose-response comparisons for CBD, nor did it investigate chronic supplementation or endurance training effects, and it was suggested that the protocol might not have induced sufficient power reduction for CMJ.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: initially decreased, then recovered and increased
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significant decrease observed after 24 h (p < 0.01) in both groups; significant group difference detected after 72 h (p < 0.05; ES = 0.371), with the CBD group recovering and slightly increasing performance. Overall, a significant increase over the course of the study (p < 0.05, ES = 0.34), representing a linear recovery trend.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Measures maximal muscular strength in a single effort, reflecting lower body muscular strength and adaptation to strength training.

matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates recovery of squat performance and muscle function post-exercise; CBD appears to support the recovery of maximal strength performance after 72 hours following intensive exercise.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated whether post-exercise branched chain amino acid and carbohydrate (BCAA-CHO) supplementation, compared to carbohydrate-only (CHO) supplementation, could mitigate performance decrements, muscle damage, and soreness, or alter immunological markers following three consecutive days of high-intensity resistance training (back squats) in resistance-trained males. The findings consistently indicated that BCAA-CHO did not significantly improve lower body strength, isometric/isokinetic torque, neuromuscular activation (EMG), perceived muscle soreness, or reduce levels of muscle damage markers like myoglobin, creatine kinase, and lactate dehydrogenase. However, BCAA-CHO supplementation did attenuate the exercise-induced increase in monocyte percentages, suggesting a modulated immune or inflammatory response.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Post-exercise nutritional supplementation (branched chain amino acids + carbohydrates vs. carbohydrates only) combined with a high-intensity, high-volume resistance training protocol.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Resistance training involved three consecutive days of 10 sets of 5 repetitions at 80% of 1RM barbell back squat, with a 5% weight reduction if repetitions could not be completed. Participants received two servings of either BCAA-CHO (3g L-leucine, 1g L-isoleucine, 2g L-valine, 2g non-sugar carbohydrates) or CHO (42g carbohydrates, predominantly sugars) immediately after each lifting bout and on a recovery day. Supplements were provided in 600 mL of tap water. The study compared these two supplementation types, reflecting a real-world application, but reported no further dose-response comparisons or standardization for overall carbohydrate or calorie content.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Similar decrements in 1RM squat strength were observed in both the BCAA-CHO and CHO groups (p=0.40 for time, p=0.16 for interaction), indicating that BCAA-CHO supplementation did not reduce performance decrements in 1RM squat strength compared to CHO.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Indicator of maximal muscular strength and neuromuscular function.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Following three consecutive high-intensity resistance training bouts (barbell back squat protocol).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of lower body strength performance and recovery from intense exercise; sustained decrements suggest incomplete recovery, not mitigated by BCAA-CHO supplementation.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study aimed to identify new genetic susceptibility loci for invasive epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) by performing a comprehensive meta-analysis of genome-wide association studies (GWAS). The investigation included data from general population EOC cases and controls, as well as BRCA1/2 mutation carriers. Six novel EOC susceptibility loci were discovered, and their potential functional roles were characterized through eQTL analysis, epigenetic profiling, gene expression and DNA copy number assessments, and in vitro transcriptional assays, with the ultimate goal of improving EOC risk prediction.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Genetic Risk Factor Identification and Functional Genomics Analysis (via Genome-Wide Association Studies, Meta-analysis, and In Vitro Transcriptional Assays)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study focused on identifying genetic risk factors for EOC, not a therapeutic intervention. A meta-analysis of approximately 11-11.4 million genetic variants was performed using data from 15,397-15,437 EOC cases (including 9,627 serous EOC), 30,816-30,845 controls, 15,252 BRCA1 mutation carriers (2,462 with EOC), and 8,211 BRCA2 mutation carriers (631 with EOC). Genome-wide significance for associations was set at p<5	10^-8. Functional analyses included gene expression analysis for 91 coding genes and mRNA expression for 316 complete tumors (Z-score threshold of 2), DNA copy number analysis for 481 serous EOC samples, and an in vitro luciferase reporter assay performed by co-transfecting 800 ng of luciferase constructs and 50 ng of pRL-TK Renilla into 8 	 10^4 iOSE4 normal ovarian cells. Methodological details included sample exclusion for genotyping call rate <95% and SNP exclusion based on imputation accuracy (r^2 <0.25-0.3) or minor allele frequency (MAF <0.005-0.01). Imputation utilized 90 MCMC iterations and specific buffer regions. No dose-response comparisons for a therapeutic treatment were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Associated with higher risk of all invasive EOC in meta-analysis (p<5	10^-8). The lead SNP rs58722170 showed stronger associations with the serous EOC subtype in OCAC (p=2.7	10^-12).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: RSPO1 encodes R-spondin 1, involved in Wnt signaling, cell proliferation, tumorigenesis, and early ovarian development, regulating WNT4 expression. This gene contributes specifically to serous EOC subtype susceptibility.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Susceptibility to all invasive EOC, particularly serous EOC, in a meta-analysis including OCAC and BRCA1/BRCA2 carriers.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates an increased genetic predisposition to invasive EOC, particularly the serous subtype, which can improve clinical risk predictions for BRCA1/2 mutation carriers when incorporated into risk assessment tools.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study employed NMR metabolomics to investigate metabolic profiles in serum and urine from COVID-19 patients across varying disease severities (Medical Ward and Intensive Care Unit) and healthy controls. The primary aim was to identify biomarkers for COVID-19 diagnosis, severity classification, and prognosis, and to explore correlations with clinical factors like hypertension, obesity, and dyslipidemia. Key findings include the development of a highly efficient diagnostic panel (isoleucine, TMAO, glucose) and a robust severity classification panel (ethanol, TMAO, tyrosine, betaine, and clinical characteristics), alongside identification of numerous individual metabolites and clinical parameters associated with infection, disease progression, hospitalization duration, and patient outcome.

treatment_details.therapy_type: NMR metabolomics-based profiling and observational study of COVID-19 infection
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This observational study analyzed 80 serum and urine samples from COVID-19 patients (34 intensive care, 46 hospitalized) and 32 from healthy controls using NMR spectroscopy. The research focused on identifying and validating metabolite-based panels for COVID-19 diagnosis and severity classification. A diagnostic panel of isoleucine, TMAO, and glucose achieved an AUC of 0.91 (86.08% sensitivity, 83.87% specificity). A severity classification panel, combining ethanol, TMAO, tyrosine, betaine, and clinical characteristics (obesity/overweight, dyslipidemia, lymphocyte count), achieved an AUC of 0.825 (84.85% sensitivity, 72.09% specificity). No therapeutic intervention or dose-response comparisons were part of the study design.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher levels observed in COVID-19 patients compared to healthy controls. Identified as a key discriminating molecule.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: COVID-19 infection vs. healthy controls.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Potential biomarker for COVID-19 infection, differentiating patients from controls.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigates the molecular determinants of hemogenic endothelial cells (HECs) and hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs) by generating a GATA2w/eGFP reporter in human embryonic stem cells (hESCs). The reporter accurately marks endogenous GATA2 expression, which is critical for endothelial-to-hematopoietic transition (EHT). A key finding is the identification of ITGB3 (CD61) as a reliable novel positive surface marker that precisely labels functional HECs with superior hemogenic potential, both in hESC/hPSC differentiation in vitro and in embryonic day 10 mouse embryos in vivo. The research provides a robust platform for dissecting hematopoiesis and facilitates the generation of functional hematopoietic stem cells in vitro.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Gene targeting using TALENs, in vitro human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC) differentiation, and in vivo mouse embryo analysis.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: GATA2w/eGFP reporter was generated in H1 hESCs via gene editing (TALENs, electroporation of 1 μg linearized vector and 2.5 μg of each TALEN plasmid into 1 × 10^6 H1 cells, puromycin selection at 0.5 μg/mL, and Cre recombinase (400 ng per 1 × 10^6 cells) for cassette removal). In vitro differentiation involved hPSC blood differentiation protocols using co-culturing with OP9 stromal cells or AGM-S3 co-culture. Bone morphogenetic protein 4 (BMP4) treatment was applied for 5 days. Cell seeding used Y-27632 (10 μM). CFU assay medium contained 100 ng/mL recombinant murine stem cell factor, 10 ng/mL recombinant murine interleukin-3, 10 ng/mL recombinant human interleukin-6, and 3 U/mL human erythropoietin, with endothelial cell assays using 100 ng/mL vascular endothelial growth factor. In vivo analysis included mouse embryos at E10.0, E11, E12, E14, with fractionation of endothelial cells based on CD61 expression (CD61 high, CD61 low, and CD61 − subpopulations). No specific dose-response comparisons for differentiation conditions or therapeutic interventions were reported beyond qualitative observations of effect.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: A 2.50-kb product was obtained from cell line with the loxP flanked PGK-puromycin cassette.

matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Confirms successful integration of the donor cassette containing the selection marker at the GATA2 locus.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of Montmorency tart cherry concentrate (MC) supplementation on recovery markers, including functional performance, muscle soreness, inflammation, muscle damage, and oxidative stress, in semi-professional male soccer players following prolonged, intermittent sprint activity. Findings suggest MC supplementation accelerates functional performance recovery (MVIC, CMJ, agility, 20m sprint), reduces muscle soreness (DOMS), and attenuates the acute inflammatory response (IL-6), but showed no significant effect on general muscle damage (CK) or oxidative stress (LOOH).

treatment_details.therapy_type: Montmorency tart cherry concentrate (MC) supplementation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants consumed 30 mL of Montmorency tart cherry concentrate (MC) or an energy-matched placebo twice per day (8:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m.) for eight consecutive days, including four days pre-trial and throughout the trial period. The MC contained 73.5 mg 7L 91 cyanidin-3-glucoside, 178.8 gallic acid equivalent 7L 91 total phenolic content, and a TEAC of 0.58 trolox equivalents 7L 91. No dose-response comparisons were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: The MC group demonstrated significantly faster 20m sprint times (4%) compared to PLA at 48 h post-exercise (p=0.043), despite both groups showing overall slower times in the 72 h post-trial period. (Time: F(1,4)=9.681, p=0.001,  72=0.409; Interaction: F(1,4)=3.145, p=0.035,  72=0.183).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Measures maximal sprint speed and anaerobic power.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Recovery following prolonged, intermittent sprint activity (adapted Loughborough Intermittent Shuttle Test) with MC supplementation vs. placebo.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates maximal running speed and fatigue levels, showing MC improves sprint recovery and accelerates functional performance in intermittent sprint sports.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated changes in cellular immune inflammation markers (NLR, PLR, SII), various blood cell counts (leucocytes and their subsets, platelets), and physical fitness parameters (VO2max, YYIRL1 performance, sprint, jump tests) in elite male soccer players over a 12-week period, including both uncongested and congested match play phases. It found that a congested match play period significantly altered immune cell counts and inflammation markers, leading to increased leucocyte, neutrophil, eosinophil, basophil, and monocyte counts, and higher NLR, PLR, and SII, with concurrent decreases in lymphocyte counts and aerobic physical fitness. These immune inflammation markers were negatively correlated with physical fitness (YYIRL1 performance, VO2max) and positively correlated with workload parameters, suggesting their utility for monitoring training intensity, competitive load, and aerobic physical fitness, and for preventing overtraining.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Elite Soccer Training and Congested Match Play
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Fifteen elite male soccer players were monitored for 12 weeks, comprising a 6-week uncongested match play period (30 training sessions, 45 hours training volume, 6 matches with 350±53.5 minutes average playing time) followed by a 6-week congested match play period (24 training sessions, 36 hours training volume, 10 matches with 629.6±133.9 minutes average playing time). Players typically trained five times per week and played one match per week, with the congested period exposing them to up to eight matches per month. Physical fitness tests (Squat Jump, Countermovement Jump, 20-meter sprint, Yo-Yo intermittent recovery test level 1) and blood samples were taken at T1 (week 1), T2 (week 7), and T3 (week 13). Workload parameters (Global load, Training load, Competitive load, Training volume, Session-Rating of Perceived Exertion) were recorded and compared. The congested period showed significantly increased total and competitive loads and decreased training load, training volume, and Session-RPE compared to the uncongested period. No explicit dose-response comparisons for varying levels of congestion beyond the two defined periods were reported.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: mixed (faster after congested period, slower after uncongested period)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significant moderate decrease (faster time) from T2 (uncongested) to T3 (congested) (ES = -0.76). Significant moderate increase (slower time) from T1 (baseline) to T2 (uncongested) (ES = 0.62). Most players (n=9) presented lower values (faster) in T3 compared to T1 and T2.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Anaerobic power, acceleration, and speed.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Competitive soccer periods (T1 to T3, including uncongested and congested periods).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates anaerobic performance and acceleration. A lower sprint time signifies improved speed, while a higher sprint time suggests fatigue or reduced explosive power.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of post-exercise milk consumption (500 mL) versus an energy-matched carbohydrate drink on recovery from a repeated sprinting and jumping protocol in female team-sport athletes. The strenuous protocol successfully induced muscle damage, leading to post-exercise decreases in muscle function (peak torque, countermovement jump, sprint performance, rate of force development) and increases in subjective muscle soreness and tiredness. Milk consumption attenuated losses in muscle function, particularly for peak torque (knee extension/flexion at 180°/s) and countermovement jump height, and reduced perceived stress (DALDA B) at various time points (24h, 48h, 72h) post-exercise. The study concluded that milk may be a valuable recovery intervention for female team-sport athletes following this type of exercise, although its effects on serum creatine kinase, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, reactive strength index, and some sprint performances were unclear.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Post-exercise nutritional intervention (Milk vs. Carbohydrate drink)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants immediately consumed either 500 mL of milk (910 kJ/215 kcal, 17.0 g Protein, 25.5 g Carbohydrate, 5.0 g Fat) or 500 mL of an energy-matched carbohydrate drink (910 kJ/215 kcal, 0.2 g Protein, 53.6 g Carbohydrate, 0.0 g Fat) following a whole-body sport and exercise protocol designed to induce muscle damage (15x20m maximal sprints and 8 sets of 10 plyometric jumps). The milk protein dose (17g) was noted to be potentially suboptimal for maximal protein synthesis compared to other studies. No dose-response comparisons were conducted, as a single volume of 500 mL was used for both interventions.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Post-exercise recovery following exercise-induced muscle damage from sprinting and jumping.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates recovery of sprint speed.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review critically evaluates wet biomarkers for Huntington's Disease (HD), covering markers in biofluids like blood, urine, saliva, and cerebrospinal fluid. It summarizes findings related to metabolic, inflammatory, oxidative stress, endocrine (melatonin, cortisol, growth hormone), and neuronal/glial degeneration pathways, including promising markers like neurofilament light chain. The document also highlights the importance of standardized protocols, independent validation, and considers pre-analytical and analytical variables (e.g., sampling time, feeding state) that influence biomarker reliability, noting the current lack of clinically validated biomarkers but expressing optimism for future discoveries.

The intervention significantly improved cardiometabolic health by reducing insulin resistance (fasting insulin, HOMA-IR), improving left ventricular systolic (LVEF) and diastolic function (LV mass index, interventricular septal thickness, E/A ratio), reducing heart rate, and lowering inflammation (CrP). While beneficial effects were observed for glucose and lipid metabolism markers, premature beats and BMI remained largely unchanged.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Dietary intervention with a specific micronutrient combination as an add-on to concomitant cardiovascular drug treatment.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: A 6-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled dietary intervention involving 54 patients. The verum group received a specific micronutrient combination (2 tablets twice daily), including 145.8 mg magnesium, 469.2 mg potassium, 3.0 µg Vitamin B12, 400.0 µg folic acid, 48.0 mg niacin, and 60.0 mg coenzyme Q10. Other micronutrients like Vitamin C, Vitamin E, and Selenium were also part of the combination. The placebo group received microcrystalline cellulose. No dose-response comparisons were reported. Minor gastric pain was noted in one verum and one placebo patient, with no serious side effects.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Elevated in the verum group (p = 0.059, ES = 0.326).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Reflects renal handling and overall body potassium balance, indicative of dietary intake and kidney function.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: After 6 weeks of dietary intervention with specific micronutrient combination in the verum group.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Suggests increased potassium turnover or elimination, which could be related to the dietary intervention's impact on electrolyte balance; indicates renal handling of potassium following supplementation.

document_context_data.document_summary: The study aimed to evaluate bone turnover and remodeling markers in children with Noonan Syndrome (NS) to understand their bone status and explore genotype-phenotype correlations. It revealed increased bone resorption in NS patients, evidenced by significantly elevated serum C-telopeptides of type I collagen (CTX) levels, and a non-significant increase in RANKL. The study also discussed the influence of RAS/MAPK signaling pathway alterations and SHP2 protein on osteoclastic activity and the effects of recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) treatment on bone parameters.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational Case-Control Study evaluating bone turnover and remodeling markers in children with Noonan Syndrome, including an analysis of recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) treatment effects.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This cross-sectional, case-control study compared 28 children with Noonan Syndrome to 35 healthy controls. No specific therapeutic intervention or dose was administered to the main cohorts. Within the NS cohort, some subjects had received or were receiving rhGH therapy, but no specific dosages, duration, or dose-response comparisons for rhGH treatment were reported, and no significant differences in bone parameters were found between treated and untreated subjects in this study.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: unchanged (relative to control group mean, though variable within NS cohort)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification:
No significant differences were found between NS patients and controls overall. However, within the NS cohort, mean values were 26.7 
	± 13.3 mg/mL, with 8 subjects having normal values (40.2 
	± 11.1 ng/mL), 11 insufficient (24.5 
	± 2.4 ng/mL), and 9 deficient (14.5 
	± 4.6 ng/mL).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Essential for calcium absorption and bone health, playing a crucial role in bone metabolism and mineralization.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Children with Noonan Syndrome (NS) population.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Not a primary factor contributing to reduced bone mineralization in NS patients when compared to controls, but high prevalence of insufficiency/deficiency noted within the NS cohort is an indicator of overall health status.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of vitamin D supplementation, sunlight exposure, home isolation during the COVID-19 pandemic, and training loads on seasonal changes in 25(OH)D concentration and various blood biomarkers in young elite soccer players over a one-year cycle. It found significant seasonal variations in 25(OH)D, Hemoglobin (HGB), Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST), and Creatine Kinase (CK). While 8-week vitamin D supplementation (5,000 IU/day) showed no sustained effect on 25(OH)D levels, possibly due to home isolation and seasonal factors, it did influence some biomarkers positively. Biomarkers related to morphology, lipid profile, and muscle damage varied more with training loads and seasonal factors than with supplementation alone.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Vitamin D supplementation and Sports Training.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Vitamin D supplementation involved 5,000 IU/day for 8 weeks (mid-January to mid-March 2020) in the supplemented group (n=11), compared to a placebo group (n=13) receiving sunflower oil. This supplementation had no sustained extended effect on 25(OH)D levels beyond the 8-week period, suggesting continuous dosing during deficiency is needed. Training encompassed typical competitive season volumes of 720 minutes/week (mainly aerobic and mixed aerobic-anaerobic drills), increasing to 810 minutes/week in pre-season. No explicit dose-response comparisons were reported for either the vitamin D or training regimen.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Higher in summer (T4, August), significantly lower in autumn-winter (T2, T3).
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly (p < 0.001, pη[1] = 0.82) higher in T4 (August 2020) for both groups compared to T2 (December 2019) and T3 (May 2020). Largest deficits (October-April) showed 25% deficiency (≤20 ng/dl) in T2. T3 levels were 26.6 ± 6.35 ng/ml (GS) and 26.2 ± 4.52 ng/ml (GP). T4 exhibited highest values, a 34.8% increase from T3, with 22/24 participants at optimal levels. 8-week supplementation had no extended effect; changes were statistically significant and dependent on sunlight radiation.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Regulation of calcium and phosphate homeostasis, bone health, immune function, and overall physiological processes, particularly during physical effort.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: One-year training cycle in young soccer players, seasonal changes in sunlight (UV radiation exposure, highest May-September), home isolation during COVID-19 pandemic, and 8-week vitamin D supplementation (5,000 IU/day).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of vitamin D status and overall health; optimal levels are crucial for immune function, preventing deficits, and avoiding post-COVID dysfunctions. Deficiency (≤20 ng/dl), widespread in autumn-winter, is highly influenced by season and sunlight and can negatively impact health and physiological functions.

document_context_data.document_summary: This 2-year prospective longitudinal study investigated changes in bone remodeling and turnover markers in children with Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) from diagnosis through chemotherapy. It revealed that ALL onset significantly slows bone remodeling, with significantly lower bone turnover markers at diagnosis compared to controls. During chemotherapy, particularly the induction phase, these markers increased, suggesting a recovery of bone turnover, and a potential balance in active bone remodeling by the end of therapy.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Risk-adapted multiagent antileukemic chemotherapy, specifically for Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL), including Glucocorticoid (GC) therapy.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The 2-year prospective longitudinal study involved chemotherapy according to international AIEOP-BFM ALL 2017 and ESPhALL 2017 protocols, with patients stratified by risk (standard, intermediate, high). The treatment included induction, reinduction/delayed intensification (two phases of high-dose glucocorticoid therapy), and a maintenance phase. Blood sampling was conducted at 5 time points (T0-T4) from diagnosis until treatment cessation. No specific numerical drug dosages were reported, but it was noted that different glucocorticoid doses did not significantly alter bone marker profiles after intensive therapy phases.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Below the normal reference range at diagnosis (T0) and showed a statistically significant drop to lower values during follow-up time points (T1-T4) throughout chemotherapy.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Crucial for calcium and phosphorus homeostasis, bone mineralization, and overall bone health.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: ALL children at diagnosis and during ALL chemotherapy from diagnosis to end of therapy.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Insufficient or deficient levels are widely reported in children with leukemia, indicating a potential risk factor for bone complications or impaired bone health during and after treatment, and warranting supplementation.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated teriparatide (TPTD) as an adjunct therapy for medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ), finding it significantly shortened treatment periods, reduced surgical interventions, improved bone mineral density in the lumbar spine and femur neck, and favorably altered bone turnover markers (CTX, OC, 25-OH-vitamin D, calcium).

treatment_details.therapy_type: Teriparatide (TPTD) administration for Medication-Related Osteonecrosis of the Jaw (MRONJ)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Teriparatide (Forsteo®) was administered as a 20 µg daily subcutaneous injection for >3 months and up to 24 months. Patients also received 1,000 IU/day of oral Vitamin D. TPTD treatment led to significantly shorter surgical recovery periods (3.89 ± 2.71 months vs 6.64 ± 6.38 months, p = 0.030) and fewer surgical procedures (average 1.26 vs 1.82, p = 0.049) in surgical patients compared to non-TPTD counterparts. The overall treatment period was also shorter in the TPTD group (5.5 months vs 6.75 months in non-TPTD), though not statistically significant.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly increased in both TPTD and non-TPTD groups post-treatment. Levels showed a slightly higher increase in the TPTD group than in the non-TPTD group. Also significantly increased only in the surgical treatment group.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Precursor to active vitamin D, crucial for calcium absorption, bone health, and overall bone metabolism.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: MRONJ treatment with or without Teriparatide (TPTD), with conservative or surgical approaches, in patients receiving 1,000 IU/day of oral Vitamin D.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates vitamin D status, essential for bone mineral density and overall bone health. Increased levels reflect supplementation and improved vitamin D status, suggesting enhanced bone metabolism and contributing to bone healing in MRONJ; deficiency is associated with increased MRONJ incidence.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of a 12-week (3-month) food-based vitamin D3 fortification intervention on serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels, bone turnover markers (Osteocalcin, Bone specific Alkaline Phosphatase, Procollagen type 1 amino-terminal propeptide, C-terminal crosslinked telopeptide of type 1 collagen), and muscle strength (handgrip, knee extension, chair-standing) in 143 women of Danish and Pakistani origin, aged 18-50 years, living in Denmark and at risk of vitamin D deficiency. Despite a significant increase in serum 25(OH)D concentrations in the fortified groups, the intervention did not result in significant changes in bone turnover markers or muscle strength. Baseline characteristics including anthropometrics and vitamin D status were also assessed.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Food-based vitamin D fortification
treatment_details.dose_specificity: A 12-week (3-month) randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled winter intervention trial. The intervention group (143 women) received 30 μg vitamin D3/day (analyzed as 29 μg/day total vitamin D content) through fortified daily foods (150g yoghurt, 60g cheese, 1 egg, 1 small crisp-bread); the placebo group received similar non-fortified products. No dose-response comparisons were reported, and the study noted potential insufficient power to detect changes in secondary endpoints.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Increased in fortified groups; no significant ethnic difference at baseline.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: At baseline, mean concentration was 49.6 (18) nmol/L for Danish women and 46.9 (22) nmol/L for Pakistani women (P = 0.8), with 9% of Danish and 24% of Pakistani participants below 30 nmol/L. After intervention, fortified groups showed significant increases: from 53.3 (17) to 77.8 (14) nmol/L in Danish women (P < 0.05) and from 44.5 (21) to 54.7 (18) nmol/L in Pakistani women (P < 0.05). Placebo groups decreased by 2.8 (9) nmol/L (Danish) and 11.2 (12) nmol/L (Pakistani).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Essential for calcium and phosphorus homeostasis, bone health, and immune function; key indicator of vitamin D status.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: 12-week intervention with vitamin D fortified foods during winter months in women of Danish and Pakistani origin (18-50 years of age), including baseline comparison.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates vitamin D status, essential for bone and muscle health. Deficiency (< 25-30 nmol/L) is associated with decreased muscle strength and poor bone health. Optimal concentration of > 50 nmol/L is suggested for maintaining health during winter.

document_context_data.document_summary: This longitudinal, prospective observational study investigated whether vitamin D metabolites (25-hydroxyvitamin D, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) and Vitamin D Binding Protein (VDBP), along with their ratios, could predict preeclampsia (PE) in women with Type 1 Diabetes (T1DM). The study found that higher concentrations of 1,25(OH)2D, lower concentrations of VDBP, and elevated 1,25(OH)2D/VDBP ratios in the second and third trimesters were significantly associated with and predictive of subsequent PE, while 25(OH)D, the standard metric for vitamin D status, did not predict PE.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Longitudinal Prospective Observational Study on Preeclampsia Prediction
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational study with no therapeutic interventions or dose comparisons. Biomarker concentrations and clinical data were collected at three gestational visits: V1 (~12 weeks), V2 (~22 weeks), and V3 (~32 weeks). The study enrolled 151 women with Type 1 Diabetes (T1DM) and 24 non-diabetic controls, rigorously phenotyped and free of proteinuria and hypertension at enrolment. The primary analysis compared 23 T1DM women who developed preeclampsia (PE) with 24 matched T1DM women who remained normotensive. A secondary analysis compared normotensive T1DM women with non-diabetic controls. The cohort was largely vitamin D insufficient or deficient.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Higher frequency of deficiency/insufficiency in diabetic women, no predictive change for PE
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher frequency of deficiency/insufficiency in diabetic women (65-73% vs. 22% in non-diabetics, p < 0.05). Total 25(OH)D was lower in normotensive T1DM women than non-diabetics at V1 (p=0.020) and V2 (p=0.034). Bioavailable and free 25(OH)D did not differ by diabetes status at any visit. No measure of 25(OH)D (total, bioavailable, or free) predicted subsequent preeclampsia. However, total, bioavailable, and free 25(OH)D were negatively correlated with eGFR (all p < 0.05) in T1DM women who developed PE at the first trimester. Deficiency defined as <20 ng/mL (<50 nmol/L) and insufficiency as <32 ng/mL (<80 nmol/L).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Prohormone and precursor of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, considered the principal metric for assessing overall vitamin D status. Essential for bone health, immune function, cell proliferation and differentiation, inflammation, insulin secretion and action, and vascular health.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Preeclampsia risk prediction in women with Type 1 Diabetes during pregnancy (assessed at ~12, ~22, and ~32 weeks' gestation). Also, early pregnancy in DM+PE+ women in relation to renal function.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates overall vitamin D status. Deficiency is common in diabetic pregnant women. While not a direct predictor of preeclampsia in this study, lower levels are associated with poor pregnancy outcomes, and a negative correlation with eGFR suggests an association with subtle, early renal abnormalities that confer PE risk.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the impact of acute preexercise calcium intake on bone turnover markers and calcium homeostasis in elite male rowers during a day with multiple strenuous, non-weight-bearing training sessions. The findings indicate that consuming a calcium-rich meal before training stabilizes ionized calcium levels, reduces the postexercise parathyroid hormone response, and attenuates the increase in bone resorption markers (e.g., β-CTX-I) over a sustained 7-hour period, thereby supporting long-term bone health and reducing the risk of bone stress injuries.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Dietary calcium supplementation (via whole foods/meals) in conjunction with repeated, strenuous, non-weight-bearing rowing exercise.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Elite male rowers (n=16) participated in two trials, one week apart, each involving two 90-min rowing ergometer sessions (EX1, EX2) separated by 150 minutes. Before each trial, participants consumed either a high calcium meal (~1000 mg, CAL) or an isocaloric low calcium meal (<10 mg, CON). Each exercise session consisted of three 30-minute sets at 90-100% of individual 2 mmol·L−1 capillary blood lactate power (mean 255-260W). Calcium was provided acutely before training sessions. No dose-response comparisons were reported beyond the high versus low intake, nor for exercise intensity.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Levels were insufficient in 30% of the study sample.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Indicator of vitamin D status, essential for calcium absorption, bone mineralization, and immune function; deficiency can secondarily affect PTH levels.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: General health status of elite male rowers during the study, coinciding with an annual seasonal nadir for vitamin D levels.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Insufficient levels highlight a common nutritional concern in athletes; however, due to the crossover design and absence of frank deficiency, it was deemed unlikely to have affected the main study findings related to acute calcium intervention.

document_context_data.document_summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial investigated the effects of 12 weeks of daily protein supplementation on lean body mass, fat mass, muscle strength, physical performance, and various biochemical markers in physically active older adults with low habitual protein intake, who were also training for a 4-day walking event. The study found that protein supplementation resulted in a larger increase in relative lean body mass and a greater reduction in fat mass compared to placebo. While both the protein and placebo groups showed improvements in physical performance and cardiorespiratory fitness due to the walking exercise, no additional between-group differences were observed in muscle strength, muscle contractile properties, or physical performance from protein supplementation. Serum urea increased in the protein group, but no adverse effects on renal function or muscle damage markers were noted, indicating protein supplementation is a safe strategy for this population.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Protein supplementation combined with walking exercise
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Physically active older adults were randomized to receive either 31 g of milk protein concentrate daily (split into 15g at breakfast and 15g post-exercise/lunch) or an iso-caloric placebo for 12 weeks. This increased the protein group's total daily protein intake from 0.86 ± 0.23 g/kg/day upon enrollment to 1.29 ± 0.28 g/kg/day at 12 weeks. Both groups concurrently participated in walking exercise training for a 4-day walking event, covering an average of 338-391 km over 12 weeks. No dose-response comparisons for protein intake were reported, only the comparison between the protein and placebo groups.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased in both groups after 12 weeks (P Time = 0.001), but no between-group differences were observed. At baseline, 79% of the protein group and 84% of the placebo group had serum levels of ">="50 nmol/L.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: The main circulating form of vitamin D, indicative of vitamin D status; crucial for bone health and immune function.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Assessed before and after the 12-week supplementation period of daily protein combined with walking exercise.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Key indicator of vitamin D sufficiency, associated with bone density, muscle function, and overall health. No between-group differences observed for vitamin D status.

document_context_data.document_summary: This cross-sectional observational study aimed to assess cognitive impairment and oxidative stress markers in vitamin D insufficient elderly patients, both with and without type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). The study found that cognitive impairment is more predominant in individuals with diabetes. While no overall significant relationship was established between T2DM, vitamin D deficiency, cognitive impairment, and oxidative stress, a significant association was found between GPx levels and 3MSE cognitive scores, and a significant negative correlation between fasting blood sugar (FBS) and 3MS scores, specifically in vitamin D insufficient non-diabetic individuals.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational Cross-Sectional Study
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational study without any therapeutic intervention. Participants were categorized based on their existing health status: diabetic vs. non-diabetic (based on medical history and HbA1c levels), and serum vitamin D levels were used to classify them as vitamin D insufficient (< 29 ng/mL) vs. vitamin D sufficient (>= 30 ng/mL). Cognitive function was assessed using the modified Mini Mental Status Examination (3MS test score < 80 out of 100 indicating impairment). No dose-response comparisons or interventions were reported.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Fat-soluble steroid hormone with roles in mineral metabolism (calcium), inflammation regulation, mitigating insulin resistance, neuroprotection (influencing neurogenesis, calcium signaling, neurotrophic factor expression, amyloid-beta clearance), and antioxidant effects.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review critically evaluates wet biomarkers for Huntington's Disease (HD), covering markers in biofluids like blood, urine, saliva, and cerebrospinal fluid. It summarizes findings related to metabolic, inflammatory, oxidative stress, endocrine (melatonin, cortisol, growth hormone), and neuronal/glial degeneration pathways, including promising markers like neurofilament light chain. The document also highlights the importance of standardized protocols, independent validation, and considers pre-analytical and analytical variables (e.g., sampling time, feeding state) that influence biomarker reliability, noting the current lack of clinically validated biomarkers but expressing optimism for future discoveries.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Review and evaluation of wet biomarkers for Huntington's Disease (HD) progression and pathology
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Not applicable, as this document is a comprehensive review of biomarkers, their changes, and factors influencing their measurement in HD, rather than an experimental study of a specific therapeutic intervention or its dose.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Reduced levels in HD patients' plasma.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Bile acid precursor.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Huntington's Disease (HD); lipid metabolism.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates altered bile acid synthesis pathway in HD.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of 2-week hemp fiber (high and low doses) or placebo supplementation on post-exercise gut permeability and plasma metabolite shifts in healthy male and female cyclists after intensive cycling. While hemp fiber did not significantly alter post-exercise gut permeability (measured by urine sugar data), untargeted metabolomics revealed that the combination of hemp fiber intake and vigorous exercise increased beneficial gut-derived metabolites and influenced pathways related to tryptophan, primary bile acid, steroid, sphingolipid, alpha-linolenic acid, arginine and proline, lipid, and amino acid metabolism.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Dietary supplementation with hemp fiber (hemp hull powder) combined with intensive cycling exercise.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants received daily supplementation for 2 weeks with either a high dose (20 g/d) or low dose (5 g/d) of hemp hull powder, or a placebo (0 g/d). Each supplementation period concluded with a 2.25-hour intensive cycling bout performed at approximately 70% VO2max. While distinct metabolomic shifts were observed between the hemp fiber and placebo groups (R2Y = 0.987 and 0.995), no significant dose-response for gut permeability was reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Numerous metabolites with significant hits within the primary bile acid biosynthesis pathway (pathway significantly influenced by hemp fiber supplementation, p < 0.05).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Oxysterol, involved in cholesterol transport and metabolism, and a precursor in bile acid synthesis.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: High-dose hemp fiber supplementation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates modulation of cholesterol and bile acid metabolism.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study employed NMR metabolomics to investigate metabolic profiles in serum and urine from COVID-19 patients across varying disease severities (Medical Ward and Intensive Care Unit) and healthy controls. The primary aim was to identify biomarkers for COVID-19 diagnosis, severity classification, and prognosis, and to explore correlations with clinical factors like hypertension, obesity, and dyslipidemia. Key findings include the development of a highly efficient diagnostic panel (isoleucine, TMAO, glucose) and a robust severity classification panel (ethanol, TMAO, tyrosine, betaine, and clinical characteristics), alongside identification of numerous individual metabolites and clinical parameters associated with infection, disease progression, hospitalization duration, and patient outcome.

treatment_details.therapy_type: NMR metabolomics-based profiling and observational study of COVID-19 infection
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This observational study analyzed 80 serum and urine samples from COVID-19 patients (34 intensive care, 46 hospitalized) and 32 from healthy controls using NMR spectroscopy. The research focused on identifying and validating metabolite-based panels for COVID-19 diagnosis and severity classification. A diagnostic panel of isoleucine, TMAO, and glucose achieved an AUC of 0.91 (86.08% sensitivity, 83.87% specificity). A severity classification panel, combining ethanol, TMAO, tyrosine, betaine, and clinical characteristics (obesity/overweight, dyslipidemia, lymphocyte count), achieved an AUC of 0.825 (84.85% sensitivity, 72.09% specificity). No therapeutic intervention or dose-response comparisons were part of the study design.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher content in ICU patients compared to Medical Ward patients in urine. In serum, it was positively correlated and statistically associated with hypertension in COVID-19 patients. Metabolic changes (unspecified direction) detected in ICU patients in urine.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the impact of two distinct heat stress modalities—exertional heating (exercise/cycling) and exogenous heating (hot water immersion)—on physiological responses, stress markers, and peripheral kynurenine pathway (KP) metabolites in 11 young healthy males. Both modalities were designed to induce a comparable increase in core body temperature up to 39°C. The study found that heat exposure transiently induced the KP, elevating several plasma KP metabolite concentrations (Kynurenic acid, Picolinic acid, 3-Hydroxykynurenine, Quinolinic acid, Kynurenine, KYN/TRP ratio) and stress markers (Cortisol, Prolactin, Adrenaline, Noradrenaline, Lactate). These changes generally returned to baseline during recovery, suggesting adaptability of KP enzymes to physiological stressors. Differential changes were observed depending on the specific heat stress protocol and the phase (heating vs. recovery), with exertional heating often showing more pronounced effects for some markers and sustained elevation for others (e.g., KYNA, PIC in EXE). The study highlights the potential of KP metabolites as disease biomarkers.

Both trials were conducted until rectal temperature (Trec) reached 39°C (with measurements taken at every 0.5°C increment up to a maximum of 39.5°C), followed by a recovery phase to a baseline temperature of 37.5°C. The time required to reach specific temperature set points was similar in both trials. No direct dose-response comparisons were explicitly reported; however, EXE induced greater increases in stress markers and sympathetic vasomotor activity compared to EXO, suggesting differential physiological loads.

document_context_data.document_summary: This observational study investigated sex-specific differences in oxi-inflammatory responses, body composition, and cardiovascular health in older adults. It aimed to assess the usefulness of serum oxi-inflammatory markers for vascular disease prediction and prevention, revealing that postmenopausal women exhibit elevated production of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (RONS) leading to increased oxidative stress (oxLDLs, 3-NitroT) but also enhanced endothelial regeneration (EPCs, HMGB1). The study identified sex-specific patterns in various inflammatory (NLR, SII, NHR) and lipid markers, notably highlighting the C-reactive-protein-to-HDL ratio (CHR) as a strong predictor of endothelial dysfunction and cardiovascular disease risk, with women generally showing reduced levels of these inflammatory indices.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational Study
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Cross-sectional assessment of physiological, hematological, lipid, and inflammatory markers in women (n=145) and men (n=50) aged 72.2  1 7.8 years; no intervention or dose comparison was reported, focusing on sex-specific differences.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: High concentration in older women, demonstrating reduced NO bioavailability. Correlated with oxLDL (r s = 0.55, p < 0.001) in men. The relation of NO/3-NitroT was r s = 0.811 (p < 0.001) in women and r s = -0.611 (p < 0.001) in men.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: A stable marker of peroxynitrite formation and protein nitration, indicating nitrosative stress and reduced nitric oxide bioavailability.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Aging, particularly in older women where it signifies compromised NO bioavailability, and in men, indicating oxidative stress and sex-specific mechanisms of endothelial dysfunction.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates reduced nitric oxide bioavailability and endothelial dysfunction, contributing to cardiovascular risk and associated with atherosclerotic endothelial dysfunction; its relationship with NO varies by sex.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the influence of oral contraceptive (OC) use on physiological, oxidative stress, and inflammatory responses to fixed-intensity and sprint cycling in recreationally trained women, comparing them to naturally cycling women. It also examined the acute effects of N-acetylcysteine (NAC) supplementation on these responses and 1-km cycling time trial performance. Key findings showed that women using OC had elevated oxidative stress (higher MDA, lower GPx) and inflammation (higher CRP) biomarkers, as well as increased ventilation, during exercise. While NAC supplementation increased plasma thiols, it only blunted exercise-induced malondialdehyde increases in naturally cycling women, not in OC users, and did not improve cycling performance in either group. This suggests an increased strain on the endogenous antioxidant system in women using OC during exercise.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Acute N-acetylcysteine (NAC) supplementation and cycling exercise (fixed-intensity and sprint time trial).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Twenty recreationally trained women completed five exercise trials, including two double-blind crossover intervention trials where participants acutely supplemented with NAC or a placebo. NAC was administered orally in a total dose of 105 mg·kg⁻¹ of body mass, given as 70 mg·kg⁻¹ 60 minutes prior to exercise and 35 mg·kg⁻¹ 30 minutes prior. The exercise protocol involved 40 minutes of fixed-intensity cycling at 105% of the gas-exchange threshold (GET), immediately followed by an all-out 1-km cycling time trial. No dose-response comparisons for NAC were reported beyond the acute vs. placebo comparison.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Showed an exercise-induced increase (Time effect   = 9.25 mol·L⁻¹ [2.78, 15.75]) after 40-min fixed-intensity cycling and 1-km cycling time trial compared to baseline in both groups. No significant differences were observed between groups at rest or during exercise, and no effect of NAC supplementation was found.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: During and after fixed-intensity cycling and 1-km cycling time trial, in naturally cycling women and women using oral contraceptives, with or without NAC supplementation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates nitroxidative stress, which increased with exercise but was not significantly affected by OC use or NAC supplementation in this context.
