document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the associations between circulating fibrocytes and left atrial (LA) fibrosis or the prevalence of recurrence after catheter ablation in patients with persistent and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (AF), compared to sinus rhythm controls. It examined fibrocyte proportion, differentiation, and migration, as well as gene expression of various molecular markers. The findings demonstrated that increased circulating fibrocytes positively correlate with LA fibrosis (low-voltage area) and are a significant predictor of 1-year recurrence after ablation in persistent AF. Fibrocytes from persistent AF patients showed enhanced differentiation into myofibroblasts and elevated expression of pro-fibrotic and inflammatory markers, with TGF-β1 promoting differentiation and SDF-1 enhancing migration.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Catheter ablation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Catheter ablation was performed as a first-time or single procedure, predominantly for persistent AF. Specifics included radiofrequency energy applied with a power limit of 35 W and a maximal temperature of 45°C, applied until a voltage of <0.1 mV was achieved or for a maximum of 30 seconds per point. A single bolus of 100 IU/kg heparin was administered to maintain activated clotting time within 250-300 seconds. Oral antiplatelet/anticoagulant drugs were stopped 3 days before ablation and restored afterward, while antiarrhythmic drugs were stopped on the day of ablation and restored the next day for up to 2 months. Electroanatomic mapping systems were used to identify fibrotic (low-voltage) areas. Patients were followed up for 1 year post-ablation.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Persistent AF: 3.24±0.51%; Paroxysmal AF: 2.58±0.16%; SR controls: 1.94±0.17%. Significantly higher in persistent AF compared to paroxysmal AF and SR controls (P<0.05). Percentage positively associated with LA low-voltage area. A percentage ≥4.05% (62% sensitivity, 96% specificity) was a significant predictor of 1-year recurrence after single ablation in persistent AF (P=0.05). A percentage ≥4.10% was a significant predictor for all AF patients. Cultured fibrocytes from persistent AF showed enhanced differentiation potential (67.58±1.54%) versus paroxysmal AF (56.67±1.52%) and SR controls (48.43±1.79%). Expression of fibroblast activation markers and cell migratory ability were elevated in differentiated fibrocytes from persistent AF.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Persistent and Paroxysmal Atrial Fibrillation (AF), associated with LA fibrosis and post-catheter ablation recurrence.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: A useful cellular marker for assessing the degree of LA fibrosis and predicting 1-year recurrence after single ablation, particularly in persistent AF patients, and indicates a hyperactivated status with enhanced capacity to differentiate into myofibroblasts.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study developed and validated the Expanded Multimodal Analysis (EMMA) framework for the ultra-early detection of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) and precancerous lesions (IENs). EMMA integrates cfDNA methylation (DMRs), copy number variations (CNVs), and fragmentation features (FSRs) derived from whole-genome bisulfite sequencing, significantly improving diagnostic accuracy and detection rates across all ESCC stages and IENs compared to single-modal approaches. The study also demonstrated the utility of cfDNA methylation markers for molecular subtyping of ESCC, revealing associations with distinct molecular subtypes, tumor microenvironments, gene expression profiles, and survival outcomes, thus offering potential for dynamic molecular monitoring and therapeutic guidance to improve patient survival.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Diagnostic Method Development and Biomarker-based Molecular Subtyping
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study focused on the development and validation of diagnostic methods for Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma (ESCC) and precancerous lesions (IENs) using multimodal cfDNA analysis. This involved Whole-Genome Bisulfite Sequencing (WGBS) of 460 cfDNA samples (230 patients with non-metastatic ESCC/precancerous lesions and 230 matched healthy controls) to identify optimal differentially methylated regions (50 DMRs), copy number variations (153 recurrent CNV regions), and fragmentation features (83 FSRs). Machine learning models (ESCC-cfMeth, DMR plus CNV, and EMMA) were developed with 10-fold cross-validation in a discovery cohort and validated in independent cohorts. The study also explored biomarker-based molecular subtyping of 155 ESCC patients into three groups based on cfDNA methylation. ESCC patients underwent surgery or endoscopic resection, and IEN patients underwent endoscopic resection for sample collection, but no therapeutic interventions or dose-response comparisons were investigated, as the study's primary aim was diagnostic and prognostic marker development.

matched_biomarker_details.biomarker_name: cfDNA Fragmentation features (Fragment Size Ratios - FSRs)
matched_biomarker_details.activity_type: DNA fragment size distribution and ratios (fragmentomic features, fragmentation pattern analysis)

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Related to late-stage ESCC, with significantly higher ratios of short fragments. Differential features identified.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: A higher proportion of shorter fragments (90–150 bp) observed in ESCC groups. 83 differential FSR features were identified (p<0.05, Student's t-test), showing significantly higher average FSRs in ESCC patients (p=0.032 and p=2.6×10−7). No significant difference observed in IEN patients (p=0.33). Optimal DMRs were located in regions with significantly high ratios of short fragment sizes. Contributed to increasing AUCs from 0.90 to 0.99 for EMMA detection.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Reflects differences in nucleosomal organization, DNA accessibility, and altered DNA degradation patterns in tumor cells versus normal cells, influencing cfDNA release patterns. Shorter fragments are often enriched with circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA).
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Used in multimodal cfDNA analysis for ESCC detection and identification of early-stage ESCC patients. FSRs specifically relate to late-stage ESCC, while short fragment sizes linked to optimal methylation markers enhance detection by indicating higher ctDNA proportions.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Linked to late-stage disease; limited discriminatory abilities as a standalone model (AUCs = 0.54 and 0.53) but improves detection when integrated into multi-modal models. Indicates potential for ESCC diagnosis, particularly distinguishing ESCC from HCs, though less effective for precancerous IEN detection. Potentially indicates a higher proportion of ctDNA.

document_context_data.document_summary: This longitudinal study systematically investigated distinct host responses, cellular injury, and tissue damage in pediatric COVID-19 and Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children (MIS-C) through next-generation sequencing of plasma cell-free RNA (cfRNA), cell-free DNA (cfDNA), and whole-blood RNA (wbRNA) from 228 patients. It revealed unique molecular signatures distinguishing MIS-C from COVID-19, including increased multiorgan involvement and pyroptosis-related gene enrichment in MIS-C, alongside shared and distinct pro-inflammatory pathways. The analysis highlighted the complementary insights provided by cfRNA and wbRNA profiling, demonstrating varying biomarker trajectories, such as persistent immune dysregulation in COVID-19 compared to MIS-C resolution.

Samples were collected at acute, 1-month, and 3-month post-hospitalization time points. While some patients received intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg), it was not a tested intervention, and its administration was found not to significantly confound observed molecular differences. No therapeutic interventions or dose-response comparisons were conducted or reported.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review identifies and recommends validated biomarkers for tracking health, performance, and recovery in athletes across multiple domains including nutritional status (macronutrients, micronutrients, food allergies), hydration, muscle status (damage, endocrine response), endurance, and injury risk (concussions, stress fractures, ACL). It advocates for a comprehensive, integrative, and individualized approach to biomarker analysis, emphasizing dynamic monitoring and contextual interpretation over single markers or universal thresholds to optimize training and minimize injury and overtraining risks.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Biomarker-guided monitoring and management of athletic training, nutrition, hydration, and injury recovery
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This review primarily focuses on the diagnostic and prognostic value of biomarkers rather than specific therapeutic doses. It emphasizes frequent, individualized monitoring (e.g., pre/post-exercise, daily, seasonally, after injury/competition) to establish personalized baseline ranges and track physiological changes in response to various training loads (e.g., acute bouts, heavy strength training, challenging training weeks). While specific nutritional intake recommendations are mentioned for protein (1.3–2.0 g/kg/day) and omega-3 fatty acids (≤3 g/day for average, 6–8 g/day for elite athletes), and iron supplementation at low-moderate doses, the document does not report dose-response comparisons for biomarker changes. Instead, it provides specific thresholds for identifying deficiencies (e.g., Vitamin D >50 ng/ml, Ferritin <12 µg/L), dehydration (e.g., >-2% body mass decrease, blood osmolality ≥295 mmol/kg, USG ≥1.020), insufficient recovery (30% decrease in T:C ratio), and overtraining (T:C ratio of 0.35 × 10⁻³). The overall approach prioritizes dynamic, contextualized assessment over universal thresholds for effective athlete management.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Shifts in cell populations occur as immune cells move between tissue and systemic circulation, measurable via CBC/diff; not quantitatively specified.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Key components of the immune system, mediating immune response, facilitating repair (e.g., phagocytosis, debris clearance), and indicating inflammation following tissue injury.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Muscle tissue injury, skeletal muscle regeneration, muscle damage-induced inflammation, exercise training, chronic inflammation (overtraining), infection, or illness.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Reflects immune response to injury/stress (e.g., muscle damage, infection, overtraining), providing context for inflammation and aiding in diagnosis of potential infection/disease; not suitable as a sole indicator of inflammation.

document_context_data.document_summary: This review comprehensively investigates the potentials, pitfalls, and practical applications of blood-based biomarkers for objective individualized monitoring of training load, recovery, and health status in elite sports. It evaluates the utility and limitations of established markers like creatine kinase (CK), lactate, C-reactive protein (CRP), urea, myoglobin, and various leukocyte populations, detailing their physiological responses to acute and chronic exercise, kinetics, and implications for muscle damage, immune function, and inflammation. The document also addresses methodological considerations, confounding variables, the need for individual reference ranges, and statistical approaches for interpreting biomarker changes, concluding with recommendations for best practices in their sport-specific use.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Blood-based biomarker monitoring in conjunction with physical exercise and training load management in elite sports.

Biomarker responses are noted to depend on exercise modality, intensity, duration, and individual factors such as ethnicity and body composition. While specific exercise regimens like 30 minutes of endurance running (65% vs 85% of VO2max) showed CRP increases, no single standardized dose-response is consistently reported or compared across all biomarkers. The document emphasizes the need for individual reference levels, standardized collection, and careful consideration of confounding variables, particularly in managing workload by adjusting training when physiological parameters exceed baseline.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the pro/anti-inflammatory status and molecular changes, including circulating microRNAs (miRs), proteasome, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), cytokines, and muscle proteomic changes, in two crewmembers after a 6-month International Space Station mission. The aim was to evaluate systemic and muscle-related stress responses and recovery patterns, comparing biomarkers at 1 day (R+1) and 15 days (R+15) post-landing with pre-flight values and age-matched controls. Findings revealed a strong spaceflight-induced stress response in muscle tissue, leading to a proinflammatory state, with inflamma-miRs and myo-miR-206 mediating systemic recovery, and significant inter-individual differences in biomarker responses were observed.

treatment_details.therapy_type: 6-month International Space Station (ISS) spaceflight exposure with in-flight countermeasure training, followed by a post-flight recovery period.

Samples were collected pre-flight (76-79 days before) and post-flight at 1 day (R+1 / 24 hours) and 15 days (R+15) after landing. Individual molecular responses varied significantly between the two crewmembers, with crewmember A generally showing more persistent changes. Specifics of in-flight countermeasure training dose were not detailed, and no dose-response comparisons for spaceflight duration were reported.

The primary aim was to identify biomarkers for COVID-19 diagnosis, severity classification, and prognosis, and to explore correlations with clinical factors like hypertension, obesity, and dyslipidemia. document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigates the metabolic reprogramming mechanisms underlying sorafenib activity and resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells and patients. It reveals that sorafenib impairs mitochondrial function, forcing a metabolic shift towards glycolysis, leading to D-lactate accumulation, which serves as a biomarker for treatment response. In resistant cells, adaptation involves rerouting dihydroxyacetone phosphate towards glycerol-3-phosphate synthesis, extensive phospholipid remodeling to evade ferroptosis, enhanced antioxidant capacity, and increased reliance on exogenous triglycerides, resulting in glycerol accumulation as a marker of resistance. The study identifies D-lactate and glycerol as potential plasma biomarkers for monitoring sorafenib efficacy and resistance in HCC patients.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Sorafenib
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The primary therapy investigated was Sorafenib, a multi-kinase inhibitor for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). In vitro studies used sorafenib at an IC50 of 8.5 µM for acute, 48-hour, or 7-day prolonged treatments, and 7 µM for sorafenib-resistant IR-Huh7 cells. Clinical treatment involved oral administration of 400 mg twice daily for HCC patients, with dose reductions permitted for adverse effects. Other interventions included adenoviral gene downregulation (50 MOI for Gpd1/1l, Gpd2; 20 MOI for Glo1) and supplementation with various fatty acids (SFAs, MUFAs, PUFAs) or lipoproteins (VLDL, LDL), and inhibition of Mgll with JZL184. No detailed dose-response comparisons were consistently reported for sorafenib, though Mgll inhibition showed dose-dependent effects.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significant reduction observed in sorafenib-treated cells.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: In sorafenib-treated cells with downregulation of key genes involved in lipid synthesis.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Suggests that sorafenib-treated cells fail to produce endogenous lipids, potentially relying on exogenous lipids for membrane turnover and remodeling to escape ferroptosis.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the role of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) in traumatic brain injury (TBI)-induced neural damage in mice, employing a controlled cortical impact model and various pharmacological and genetic manipulations. The central finding was that inhibiting NETs with Cl-amidine ameliorated neuroinflammation, neuronal apoptosis, and neurological deficits by suppressing the STING-dependent IRE1α/ASK1/JNK signaling pathway. Specifically, Cl-amidine treatment reduced cerebral lesion volume, brain edema, and restored cerebral blood flow, while also attenuating blood-brain barrier disruption, inhibiting immune cell infiltration, alleviating neuronal death, and promoting a shift from pro-inflammatory to anti-inflammatory microglia/macrophage polarization. Conversely, STING activation by 2'3'-cGAMP abolished Cl-amidine's neuroprotection, and PAD4 overexpression aggravated neuroinflammation and neuronal death via the same pathway, effects that were successfully counteracted by STING or IRE1α inhibition. The study also detailed comprehensive methodologies for establishing the TBI model and assessing various molecular and cellular changes.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Controlled Cortical Impact (CCI) model for Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI); Pharmacological interventions including Neutrophil Extracellular Trap (NET) inhibition with Cl-amidine, STING activation with 2'3'-cGAMP, STING inhibition with C-176, and IRE1α inhibition with Kira6; Genetic manipulation via adenovirus-mediated overexpression of Peptidyl arginine deiminase 4 (PAD4).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: TBI was induced using a controlled cortical impactor (3-mm flat-tip, 5 m/s velocity, 200 ms dwelling time, 2.2 mm depth, 3.5 mm craniotomy). Cl-amidine was administered at 50 mg/kg intraperitoneally (i.p.) once daily for three days, starting 1 hour post-TBI. 2'3'-cGAMP was given at 1 mg/kg intravenously 10 minutes pre-TBI, then repeated at 24 and 48 hours post-TBI. C-176 was administered at 10 mg/kg i.p. 1 hour post-TBI, daily until sacrifice. Kira6 was given at 10 mg/kg i.p. 1 hour post-TBI, once daily for three days. Ad-PAD4 or Ad-con (control) adenoviruses were stereotactically injected (4 μL total at 0.5 μL/min across two cortical locations) 1 day before CCI to overexpress PAD4. PAD4 overexpression resulted in a 2.28-fold increase in PAD4 protein and 1.73-fold increase in H3Cit at 3 days post-TBI. Effects were analyzed at 1 and 3 days post-TBI. No explicit dose-response comparisons were reported for most agents, and potential inflammatory or cytotoxic effects of the adenovirus vector were not tested.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased time-dependently, peaking at 3 days and persisting for at least 14 days after TBI (p < 0.001). Substantially decreased by Cl-amidine treatment (p < 0.01). Overexpression of PAD4 led to 1.73-fold upregulation at 3 days post-TBI (p < 0.01).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: A key component and marker of Neutrophil Extracellular Trap (NET) formation.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI); Cl-amidine treatment after TBI; PAD4 overexpression after TBI.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates NET formation which contributes to secondary brain injury after TBI. document_context_data.document_summary: This randomized, double-blind, cross-over study investigated the effects of acute cocoa flavanol (CF) intake on exercise-induced changes in antioxidant capacity, oxidative stress, inflammation, nitric oxide (NO) production, exercise performance, and recovery in well-trained male cyclists. Stable eIF3a knockout cells were selected with puromycin (5 µg/mL for 7 days, then 1 µg/mL for 7 days). For xenograft models, 2 × 10^6 stable eIF3a knockout or control SW620 cells were subcutaneously injected per mouse. document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated LL-37/CRAMP as both a potential biomarker and therapeutic agent for acute heart failure (HF) and cardiac hypertrophy. TAC surgery involved tying a 27-gauge needle parallel to the transverse aorta with 7-0 silk suture. Betulinic acid (BA) was used at 20 µM for 48 h in cardiomyocytes. Generally, no explicit dose-response comparisons were reported for the various treatments, beyond the duration of supplementation.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study utilized genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screening in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) cells, primarily Nalm6 B-ALL, to elucidate the molecular mechanisms of panobinostat resistance and action. Key findings reveal mitochondrial activity as a driver of panobinostat resistance and SIRT1 expression as a critical determinant of sensitivity. Panobinostat treatment abrogates mitochondrial activity in ALL cells, contributing to resistance, while enhancing mitochondrial function (via rosiglitazone or SIRT1 overexpression) sensitizes ALL cells to panobinostat by activating the mitochondrial apoptosis pathway. The investigation identifies the SIRT1-mitochondria-PMAIP1 pathway as central to panobinostat response and suggests that higher SIRT1 expression or mitochondrial hyperactivity could indicate patient benefit from panobinostat therapy. The study also details various methods used, including cell culture, gene modulation techniques, drug sensitivity assays, RNA sequencing, Western blotting, and flow cytometry.

treatment_details.therapy_type: The study primarily investigated Panobinostat, a pan-histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor, often in combination with genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 knockout screening or SIRT1 modulation. Other HDAC inhibitors (chidamide, vorinostat) and conventional chemotherapeutic agents (l-asparaginase, cytarabine, 6-mecaptopurine, vincristine, dexamethasone, daunorubicin) were mentioned for comparative or contextual analysis. Rosiglitazone, a PPAR   γ activator, was used to stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis and enhance panobinostat sensitivity.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Panobinostat was frequently used at 10 nM for durations of 24 hours (for RNA sequencing, combination treatments) or 14 days (for CRISPR screening), leading to 60-80% cell death and significant proliferation inhibition in Nalm6 cells. Gradient concentrations were employed for drug sensitivity assays. Rosiglitazone was administered at 31.25 µM for 24 or 48 hours. Dose-response comparisons for panobinostat sensitivity were analyzed using Sanger GDSC1 IC50 data across 576 diverse cancer cell lines. No specific doses or dose-response comparisons were consistently reported for other HDAC inhibitors or conventional chemotherapeutic agents.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: 'Cleaved PARP was expressed in the same pattern as PMAIP1 on panobinostat treatment', indicating dramatic upregulation in SIRT1 OE cells and modest effect in SIRT1 disturbed cells when treated with panobinostat.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Panobinostat-induced cell death, modulated by SIRT1 expression in ALL cells.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Higher levels indicate increased apoptosis and panobinostat sensitivity.

document_context_data.document_summary: This observational study investigated the association of circulating Advanced Glycation End-products (AGEs) and soluble RAGE (sRAGE) isoforms (cRAGE, esRAGE) and their ratios with 15-year all-cause mortality and cardiovascular complications (MACE) in type 2 diabetes patients. It explored baseline demographic and biochemical characteristics, including AGEs and sRAGE isoforms, in type 2 diabetes patients compared to healthy controls, and examined their associations with diabetic complications, aging, and metabolic parameters. The study found increased circulating AGEs and sRAGE (specifically cRAGE) in type 2 diabetes, with the AGEs/cRAGE ratio predicting all-cause mortality and sRAGE associated with MACE development. A nomogram for long-term survival probability prediction, based on age, sex, HbA1c, SBP, and the AGEs/cRAGE ratio, was developed and internally validated.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational and prognostic assessment study of circulating biomarkers.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: A retrospective cohort study with a 15-year follow-up, investigating baseline circulating levels of AGEs and soluble RAGE isoforms in 362 type 2 diabetes patients and 125 age- and gender-matched healthy controls. No therapeutic interventions, specific doses, or dose-response comparisons were administered or reported.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher (in type 2 diabetes patients), negatively correlated with age (in healthy controls)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly increased in patients with type 2 diabetes compared to healthy controls (p < 0.001), primarily responsible for the overall sRAGE increase in type 2 diabetes. A significant negative correlation between cRAGE and age was observed in healthy control subjects (p = 0.003), but not in type 2 diabetes patients. Increased levels were associated with retinopathy and atherosclerotic vascular disease, while lower levels were associated with diabetic neuropathy. Significantly reduced with insulin therapy (adjusted for age and HbA1c).

It acts as a decoy molecule, binding AGEs to restrain RAGE/ligand-induced cell activation and inflammatory processes. It is a potential biomarker of aging.

Influenced by insulin therapy.

document_context_data.document_summary: This large-scale observational study (5522 individuals across four cohorts) investigated the association and synergistic interaction between Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP) and epigenetic age acceleration, measured by multiple epigenetic clocks (e.g., Horvath, Hannum, GrimAge, PhenoAge, EEAA, IEAA), with clinical outcomes including all-cause mortality and coronary heart disease (CHD). The study found that CHIP is strongly linked to epigenetic age acceleration and reduced methylation-estimated telomere length. Critically, the combination of CHIP and significant epigenetic age acceleration (particularly AgeAccelHG, a composite of Hannum and GrimAge) identifies a high-risk population for all-cause mortality and CHD, with specific gene mutations (e.g., TET2, DNMT3A, JAK2) showing differential impacts on age acceleration and risk. While general inflammatory markers like hs-CRP and IL6R genotype were also explored, AgeAccelHG proved a superior risk discriminator in CHIP carriers.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study investigating genetic and epigenetic associations.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was a large-scale observational study across four cohorts (FHS, JHS, WHI, MESA) involving 5522 individuals. No therapeutic intervention or dose was administered. The study identified Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP) through Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS) for somatic mutations (e.g., in DNMT3A, TET2, JAK2, ASXL1, DDR genes) from whole blood DNA. Epigenetic age acceleration was quantified using DNA methylation arrays, calculating residuals from various epigenetic clocks including Horvath, Hannum, PhenoAge, SkinBloodClock, GrimAge, IEAA, and EEAA, and methylation-based telomere length (DNAmTL). A composite measure, AgeAccelHG (Hannum and GrimAge acceleration >0), was used for advanced risk stratification. The study analyzed quantitative associations between CHIP status, specific mutations, epigenetic aging metrics, and clinical outcomes.

matched_biomarker_details.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Blood (whole blood DNA from hematopoietic cells via DNA-methylation array and whole-genome sequencing)
matched_biomarker_details.activity_type: Presence/Absence of cancer-associated somatic mutations in hematopoietic stem cells (e.g., DNMT3A, TET2, JAK2, ASXL1, DDR genes)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Prevalence >20% in those over 80 years. CHIP carriers were significantly older (+7.23 	 0.61 years, p < 1.13 	 10-31). Associated with epigenetic age acceleration ranging from 1.31 years (GrimAge, p < 8.6 	 10-7) to 3.08 years (EEAA, p < 3.7 	 10-18). Specifically: Horvath (3.01 years, p < 3.0 	 10-25), IEAA (2.92 years, p < 9.3 	 10-26), Hannum (2.71 years, p < 1.8 	 10-23), PhenoAge (2.21 years, p < 1.0 	 10-8), SkinBloodClock (1.58 years, p < 2.5 	 10-13). Associated with reduced predicted age-adjusted DNAmTL (-0.06, p < 1.2 	 10-8); increasing number of mutations (2 mut. vs. 1: -0.174, p < 8.0 	 10-7; >2 mut. vs. 2: -0.404, p < 1.1 	 10-5) led to further decrease. Individually associated with all-cause mortality (HR 1.27, p < 0.077). CHIP/AgeAccelHG interaction pooled: coefficient = 0.80, p < 3.7 	 10-3; fixed-effects meta-analysis: coefficient = 0.85, p < 2.4 	 10-3.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: A pre-malignant condition characterized by clonal expansion of hematopoietic stem cells that have acquired cancer-associated somatic mutations (e.g., in epigenetic factors), contributing to accelerated aging and increased immune cell dysfunction.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Aging and genetic predisposition, assessed in a large multi-cohort observational study (5522 individuals across FHS, JHS, WHI, MESA cohorts) for association with epigenetic age acceleration and clinical outcomes (all-cause mortality, CHD).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: A significant predictor of increased risk for developing blood cancers, all-cause mortality, and coronary heart disease (CHD). When combined with epigenetic age acceleration (AgeAccelHG+), it identifies a very high-risk subgroup for all-cause mortality (HR 2.90, p < 4.1 	 10-8) and CHD (HR 3.24, p < 9.3 	 10-6). Also associated with enhanced inflammatory gene expression in mutant macrophages and reduced telomere length.

document_context_data.document_summary: This narrative review investigates the molecular mechanisms of lung injury in acute and chronic respiratory diseases, including damage from viral, bacterial, oxidative stress, and cytokine factors. It highlights established and newly identified plasma biomarkers indicative of specific lung cell (Club, AT1, AT2, pan-epithelial, endothelial) and extracellular scaffold damage across various conditions like COVID-19, ARDS, COPD, and IPF. The review also discusses the limitations of individual biomarkers in predicting outcomes, emphasizing the enhanced predictive efficacy of combined biomarkers (e.g., ferritin and KL-6) and proposes an Artificial Intelligence-driven model to integrate diverse patient data for comprehensive lung injury monitoring, severity assessment, prognosis prediction, and personalized medicine.

treatment_details.therapy_type: A narrative review of lung injury mechanisms, biomarkers, and Artificial Intelligence (AI)-directed lung injury evaluation and monitoring.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: No specific therapeutic intervention or dose was investigated; the document is a review of existing knowledge focusing on intrinsic pathological processes and biomarker responses. It proposes an AI-driven monitoring model, which involved analyzing diverse datasets including chest CT scans, biological pathways, and 13 blood biomarkers from 455 IPF patients, alongside demographic and clinical data. No specific dose comparisons for AI application were reported.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Club cell injury, ARDS, COVID-19, sarcoidosis, pulmonary fibrosis, increased permeability and leakage of the air-blood barrier, and evaluation of ARDS mortality prediction.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates club cell injury and increased permeability of the air-blood barrier; while individually suboptimal, it predicts mortality rates in patients with ARDS.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review critically evaluates wet biomarkers for Huntington's Disease (HD), covering markers in biofluids like blood, urine, saliva, and cerebrospinal fluid. document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated proteomic and histological changes in human intervertebral disc (IVD) tissue and matched plasma samples to identify biomarkers for disc degeneration progression. It compared mild and severe degenerate IVD tissues from individuals undergoing lumbar discectomy, employing mass spectrometry, immunohistochemistry, and qRT-PCR. The main finding was the identification of AEBP1 as a significant tissue marker for monitoring degeneration severity, with increased levels in severe IVD. While other matrisomal proteins (TNC, MGP, COL12A1, COL6A2, COL6A3, TGFBI) and complement system proteins (C4A, C3, CFB, CFH) were also elevated in severe IVD, and some plasma proteins (A2M, F13B, MMP2, IGF1) showed changes, plasma biomarkers exhibited a weak correlation with tissue degeneration.

No therapeutic intervention or dose-response comparisons were conducted, as the focus was on characterizing disease states and identifying associated biomarkers.

document_context_data.document_summary: This pilot study investigated the effects of a 6-week dietary intervention with a specific micronutrient combination (including magnesium, potassium, B vitamins, and Coenzyme Q10) as an add-on therapy for patients with cardiac arrhythmias, cardiovascular disorders, and metabolic syndrome components. The intervention significantly improved cardiometabolic health by reducing insulin resistance (fasting insulin, HOMA-IR), improving left ventricular systolic (LVEF) and diastolic function (LV mass index, interventricular septal thickness, E/A ratio), reducing heart rate, and lowering inflammation (CrP). While beneficial effects were observed for glucose and lipid metabolism markers, premature beats and BMI remained largely unchanged.

Other micronutrients like Vitamin C, Vitamin E, and Selenium were also part of the combination. The placebo group received microcrystalline cellulose. No dose-response comparisons were reported. Minor gastric pain was noted in one verum and one placebo patient, with no serious side effects.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive observational study utilized plasma proteomics and machine learning to develop and validate a framework for measuring organ-specific biological aging, termed 'e-ageotypes', in humans. Analyzing 4,778 proteins from 5,676 adults across five independent cohorts, the research revealed that accelerated aging in specific organs (including heart, brain, kidney, muscle, liver, adipose, pancreas, lung, and immune system) is significantly associated with higher risks of all-cause mortality and various age-related diseases, such as heart failure, Alzheimer's disease, hypertension, diabetes, and cognitive decline. The study's methodology involved defining 'extreme agers' (individuals with highly accelerated organ aging), clustering them into distinct ageotypes, and identifying key protein biomarkers (e.g., REN, KL, NPPB, TNNT2, CPLX1/2) that contribute to these aging profiles and offer prognostic utility for disease risk and progression.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational Study on Biological Aging via Plasma Proteomics and Machine Learning
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This observational study involved the quantification of approximately 4,778 plasma proteins using SomaScan assays (v.4 and v.4.1) in 5,676 adults from five independent cohorts. Machine learning models (LASSO regression-based chronological age predictors) were developed and validated to estimate biological (organ-specific) age, referred to as 'age gaps' or 'e-ageotypes', for 11 major organs (adipose tissue, artery, brain, heart, immune tissue, intestine, kidney, liver, lung, muscle, and pancreas) and the whole organism. Models were trained on 1,398 healthy participants from the Knight-ADRC cohort and tested across the full cohort. Age gaps were calculated using local regression, z-scored per model and cohort, and adjusted for age and sex. Associations with various age-related phenotypes, future mortality, heart disease, clinical biochemistry markers, and cognitive decline were assessed using linear models or Cox proportional hazards models, with multiple testing correction (Benjamini-Hochberg method, 5% false discovery rate). No therapeutic intervention or dose comparison was performed.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review systematically examines the therapeutic potential of gamma ("\u03b3") neuromodulation as a non-pharmacological strategy across a range of neurological and psychiatric disorders, including Alzheimer's Disease, Parkinson's Disease, epilepsy, Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder, schizophrenia, and depression. It investigates various neuromodulation techniques (such as rTMS, tACS, tDCS, neurofeedback, DBS, VNS, optogenetic stimulation, and rhythmic sensory stimulation) to regulate neuronal oscillations, particularly \u03b3 oscillations and cross-frequency coupling. The document highlights the role of \u03b3 neuromodulation in improving cognitive, emotional, and motor functions by addressing oscillatory imbalances, reducing pathology (e.g., amyloid-\"\u03b2" accumulation), improving seizure control, and sharpening executive functions, while also discussing the physiological mechanisms, intervention outcomes, and the need for further research into specific treatment strategies and precision medicine.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Various neuromodulation techniques are investigated, including gamma (\u03b3) neuromodulation, repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS), transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), neurofeedback (including EEG-neurofeedback and olfactory bulb-driven closed-loop neuromodulation), Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS - including responsive DBS and high-frequency DBS of the habenula, fornix, posterior cingulate cortex, subthalamic nucleus, and anterior nucleus of the thalamus), Vagus Nerve Stimulation (VNS), optogenetic neuromodulation, Rhythmic Sensory Stimulation (RSS), multisensory \u03b3 stimulation, \u03b3 Knife Surgery, \u03b3 Entrainment Using Sensory Stimulation (GENUS), and high-frequency modulation.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This review synthesizes existing literature and, as such, generally lacks specific dose-response data from new interventions. However, various dose details are mentioned for different neuromodulation techniques. Optogenetic stimulation increased cortical \u03b3 band oscillations (GBO) by entraining at approximately 40 Hz, with inhibition reducing GBO power. Multisensory \u03b3 stimulation was applied at 40 Hz, and 40 Hz \u03b3 entrainment via sensory stimulation (light flicker or sound) reduced amyloid plaques and tau pathology. rTMS is described as enhancing high-frequency oscillations (\u03b3, \u03b2) and reducing low-frequency rhythms (\u03b1, \u03b8, \u03b4), with low-frequency rTMS for epilepsy showing uncertain effectiveness. tACS synchronizes neuronal oscillations, directly entraining \u03b3 oscillations through phase-locked sinusoidal currents, sometimes targeting frontal areas. tDCS delivers low-level electrical currents to adjust cortical excitability. Neurofeedback (including EEG-neurofeedback and multisensory stimulation with operant conditioning) allowed for self-modulation of \u03b3-band synchronization, achieving up to 71% accuracy in enhancing neural synchronization in preclinical AD and older adults, with success rates for \u03b3 modulation varying (approximately 75%). DBS was applied to the fornix for AD, the posterior cingulate cortex for PD, the subthalamic nucleus (STN) for \u03b3 activity modulation, the subgenual cingulate or ventral striatum, and bilaterally to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus (ANT) for epilepsy, which reduced seizures by 40.5% at 3 months and 75.0% at 5 years. VNS aimed at desynchronizing epileptiform activity in the \u03b3 band. \u03b3 neuromodulation involved a rapid transition from an over-activated Cross-frequency coupling (CFC) pattern to an inhibited-activated state during stimulation, which remained significantly weakened post-stimulation. High-frequency modulation and high-frequency DBS of the habenula were also mentioned. The document notes a significant gap in research addressing specific, detailed treatment strategies with \u03b3 neuromodulations.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study describes a multi-round Delphi expert consensus process to identify and prioritize 14 key biomarkers of aging for use in human intervention studies. The identified biomarkers encompass physiological, inflammatory, functional, and genetic/epigenetic domains. The study outlines the methodology, discusses the suitability of biomarkers for different intervention durations, and identifies future research needs regarding biomarker standardization and early life application, concluding with a preference for composite biomarkers due to the complexity of aging.

	<=50%" leading to removal. Initially, 460 biomarkers were suggested, leading to 20 being appraised in detail. The consensus level for the 14 recommended biomarkers ranged from 70% to 98%. The identified biomarkers were deemed more suitable for medium- (3-6 months) and long-term (">=6 months") interventions, and less suitable for acute or short-term ("<3 months") interventions, as short-term changes are likely homeostatic responses with limited long-term significance for aging. No specific therapeutic doses or dose-response comparisons were investigated as this was a consensus-building study on biomarker utility.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study performed a comprehensive qualitative and quantitative proteomic analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) derived from different somatic origins (fibroblasts and peripheral blood CD34+ cells), comparing them to original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC) and human embryonic stem cells (hESC). Using ESI-MS e and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry, complemented by Western blot validation, the research aimed to characterize hiPSC proteomic profiles, identify known and novel pluripotency markers, and distinguish hiPSCs from their somatic precursors. Key findings include the identification of approximately 220 commonly up-regulated proteins in pluripotent stem cell lines, the development and confirmation of a 22-protein marker panel for hiPSC characterization, and the observation of coordinated up-regulation of proteins involved in protein synthesis, folding, RNA processing, DNA replication, DNA repair, and energy metabolism (including oxidative phosphorylation and lipogenesis) in hiPSCs. The study also identified somatic cell markers that were down-regulated upon reprogramming and highlighted specific proteomic differences between hiPSCs and hESCs, contributing to improved hiPSC quality control for therapeutic applications.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Proteomic characterization and comparative analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) and human embryonic stem cells (hESCs).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was a characterization study, not a therapeutic intervention, thus no 'dose' of therapy was administered. Quantitative and qualitative proteomic analyses were performed using electrospray ionization (ESI)-MS e (label-free quantification with internal reference standard) and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry. Two hiPSC lines (iNC-01 from CD34+ cells, SB5-MP1 from fibroblasts, both generated using loxP-flanked excisable polycistronic STEMCCA lentiviral vector) and one hESC line (H9) were analyzed at earlier and later passages. Comparisons were made against their respective original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC). Proteins were considered differentially expressed if expression changed by >=1.5-fold, with a maximum false discovery rate of 2% and >95% confidence. Western blot analysis was used for validation. The developed marker panel was further tested in 8-9 additional hiPSC lines or passages from different somatic origins and reprogramming techniques. Differentiation studies were conducted with embryoid bodies at 24 hours and 7 days to assess marker changes during spontaneous differentiation.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study protocol describes a 9-week randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind clinical trial investigating the ergogenic effects of a 6-week daily probiotic supplementation on high-intensity endurance running performance in healthy non-elite athletes (N=32). Primary objectives include assessing the impact on time-to-exhaustion, while secondary objectives involve evaluating perceived exertion, blood chemistry (glucose, lactate), immune and stress biomarkers (cortisol, alpha-amylase, sIgA), cold and flu symptoms, gastrointestinal health (symptoms, stool characteristics, microbiota composition), and body composition. The study hypothesizes increased running time-to-exhaustion and reduced gastrointestinal/cold/flu symptoms with probiotic intervention.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Probiotic supplementation (intervention) with standardized exercise testing protocols
treatment_details.dose_specificity: A 6-week intervention period involves daily oral supplementation of 5 billion colony-forming units (CFU)/day of a specific probiotic capsule taken with a meal. The study is preceded by a 2-week pre-baseline and followed by a 1-week washout period. Participants are considered compliant if they take at least 80% of the supplement. Exercise testing includes a modified Bruce V̇O2 max treadmill test and a time-to-exhaustion treadmill endurance test conducted at 85% of V̇O2 max heart rate. No dose-response comparisons are reported in this study protocol.

document_context_data.document_summary: This scientific roadmap by the Heart Failure Association comprehensively addresses the complex and heterogeneous nature of fibrosis in heart failure, aiming to improve its definition, quantification, and treatment. It reviews mechanisms of myocardial fibrosis across various etiologies like pressure overload, aging, and cardiomyopathies, emphasizing the central role of TGF-β, collagen deposition, and myofibroblast activity. The document discusses challenges in detecting fibrosis using circulating biomarkers, proposing a framework for assessment and a roadmap for future research to identify individual fibrotic mechanisms, novel therapeutic targets, and diagnostic tools. It also evaluates diverse anti-fibrotic strategies, including pharmacological agents and non-coding RNA-based treatments, highlighting the need for targeted, multi-pathway approaches given the complexity of the fibrotic process.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Anti-fibrotic therapies for heart failure, including established drugs like angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, as well as specific anti-fibrotic agents like pirfenidone. Investigational strategies include targeting the TGF-β pathway (e.g., TGF-β inhibitors, CTGF inhibitors like FG-3019), MAPK pathways (e.g., ERK inhibitors), inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1α), neuregulin-1 administration, Matrix Metalloproteinase (MMP) inhibitors, Galectin-3 inhibitors, and non-coding RNA-based treatments (microRNA and long non-coding RNAs).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This is a review document, and as such, no specific therapeutic doses, intensities, or durations are consistently reported for any intervention, nor are dose-response comparisons detailed. While some agents like Pirfenidone and non-coding RNA modulators show utility in experimental models and clinical trials (e.g., microRNA-21 inhibitor in a Phase II trial), precise quantitative dosage or detailed treatment parameters are generally absent, reflecting a discussion of general approaches and their limitations, including a noted 'lack of precision' in current therapies. For example, MMP-12i was given 3h post-MI, but without specific dosage.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Content progressively increases with advanced age, and its production increases while degradation becomes less effective. Cross-linking seems to increase with aging. Collagen formation becomes disproportionate to left ventricular mass under chronic pressure overload. Pirfenidone has been reported to decrease its expression. No specific quantitative values (e.g., fold change, absolute concentration) provided.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Aging, pressure overload, human and experimental heart failure, (genetic) cardiomyopathies, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), pirfenidone treatment in experimental models of fibrosis, pressure overload, and hypertension.

Its decrease with treatment indicates a therapeutic utility in reducing fibrosis and arrhythmogenic substrate, as accumulation is a hallmark of fibrosis.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated LL-37/CRAMP as both a potential biomarker and therapeutic agent for acute heart failure (HF) and cardiac hypertrophy. It revealed that serum LL-37/CRAMP levels are significantly decreased in acute HF patients and various preclinical models of HF. Functionally, therapeutic administration of CRAMP was found to attenuate HF and pathological hypertrophy in these models. Mechanistically, CRAMP's cardioprotective effects against hypertrophy were mediated through the inhibition of NF-κB signaling, highlighting its dual potential as a diagnostic biomarker and a protective therapeutic target for acute HF.

treatment_details.therapy_type: The primary therapeutic method involved administration of cathelicidin-related antimicrobial peptides (CRAMP, mCRAMP, rCRAMP). Heart failure and hypertrophy models were induced using Transverse Aortic Constriction (TAC) surgery, Angiotensin II (Ang II) infusion, Isoproterenol (ISO) infusion, and Phenylephrine (PE) treatment.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: CRAMP treatments included mCRAMP peptide supplementation for 2 or 4 weeks in mice, and 0.1 mg/L for 48 h in cardiomyocytes. rCRAMP was applied to neonatal rat cardiomyocytes. Inducers for HF models included Ang II (1.3 mg/kg/day for 4 weeks in mice; 1 µM for 48 h in cardiomyocytes), Isoproterenol (30 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks in mice), and PE (100 µM for 48 h in cardiomyocytes). TAC surgery involved tying a 27-gauge needle parallel to the transverse aorta with 7-0 silk suture. Betulinic acid (BA) was used at 20 µM for 48 h in cardiomyocytes. Generally, no explicit dose-response comparisons were reported for the various treatments, beyond the duration of supplementation.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Expression level was reduced in the TAC model upon mCRAMP peptide treatment.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: A major structural protein of the extracellular matrix, central to cardiac fibrosis and tissue integrity.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: TAC-induced heart failure (HF) with mCRAMP peptide supplementation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Reduced expression indicates attenuated cardiac fibrosis and improved cardiac remodeling.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the associations between circulating fibrocytes and left atrial (LA) fibrosis or the prevalence of recurrence after catheter ablation in patients with persistent and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (AF), compared to sinus rhythm controls. It examined fibrocyte proportion, differentiation, and migration, as well as gene expression of various molecular markers. The findings demonstrated that increased circulating fibrocytes positively correlate with LA fibrosis (low-voltage area) and are a significant predictor of 1-year recurrence after ablation in persistent AF. Fibrocytes from persistent AF patients showed enhanced differentiation into myofibroblasts and elevated expression of pro-fibrotic and inflammatory markers, with TGF-β1 promoting differentiation and SDF-1 enhancing migration.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Catheter ablation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Catheter ablation was performed as a first-time or single procedure, predominantly for persistent AF. Specifics included radiofrequency energy applied with a power limit of 35 W and a maximal temperature of 45°C, applied until a voltage of <0.1 mV was achieved or for a maximum of 30 seconds per point. A single bolus of 100 IU/kg heparin was administered to maintain activated clotting time within 250-300 seconds. Oral antiplatelet/anticoagulant drugs were stopped 3 days before ablation and restored afterward, while antiarrhythmic drugs were stopped on the day of ablation and restored the next day for up to 2 months. Electroanatomic mapping systems were used to identify fibrotic (low-voltage) areas. Patients were followed up for 1 year post-ablation.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Content was higher at mRNA levels in differentiated fibrocytes from AF patients compared to the paroxysmal AF group and SR controls, indicating a hyperactivated status.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: A major structural protein of the extracellular matrix, prominently involved in fibrosis and tissue stiffness.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Differentiated fibrocytes from Atrial Fibrillation patients.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Increased Collagen I mRNA levels indicate enhanced extracellular matrix production by fibrocytes from AF patients, contributing to cardiac fibrosis.

document_context_data.document_summary: The study investigated LRP1 expression, circulating soluble LRP1 (sLRP1) levels, and myocardial lipid content in idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy (IDCM) patients compared to healthy controls, and assessed the role of extracellular vesicles (EVs) in sLRP1 secretion. Key findings include increased circulating sLRP1, higher myocardial collagen and triglyceride content, and elevated LRP1 alpha chain expression in myocardial vessels of IDCM patients, with sLRP1 release found to be independent of the exosome pathway and not associated with blood lipid parameters.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study investigating disease pathogenesis and biomarker identification in Idiopathic Dilated Cardiomyopathy (IDCM)

No therapeutic intervention or dose-response comparisons were conducted.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study evaluated and compared the regenerative potential of different blood-derived products (EDTA-PRP, Citrate-PRP, and hyperacute serum [hypACT]) in a 3D osteoarthritic chondrocyte pellet model over 21 days. Key assessments included metabolic cell activity, cartilage-related gene expression (SOX9, COL2AB, COL1A1, MMP3, P21), and extracellular matrix (ECM) morphology and quality, using 1% or 5% concentrations of the products. HypACT consistently demonstrated superior and more stable results for cartilage-related gene expression and tissue quality. In contrast, Citrate-PRP showed negative effects on ECM production, chondrocyte presence, and gene expression, which was partly attributed to anticoagulants and extensive platelet accumulation. Metabolic activity generally showed no significant differences among the blood products compared to controls, though some variations were observed.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Blood-derived products: hyperacute serum (hypACT), leukocyte-poor Platelet-rich plasma prepared with EDTA (EPRP), and leukocyte-poor Platelet-rich plasma prepared with trisodium citrate (CPRP).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Blood products (hypACT, EPRP, CPRP) were prepared from whole blood (18mL for hypACT, 16mL for EPRP, 16mL for CPRP) and used as 1% or 5% (v/v) supplementation in 3D osteoarthritic chondrocyte pellet cultures for 21 days; 10% concentration was deemed unsuitable. HypACT showed stable effects across both 1% and 5% concentrations. For EPRP, 1% was favored over 5% due to better glycosaminoglycan deposition and lower platelet accumulation, with concentration influencing specific gene expressions (SOX9, MMP3, COL2AB, COL1A1). CPRP at both 1% and 5% concentrations resulted in poor tissue quality and no increase in COL2AB production, with extensive platelet accumulation observed.

matched_biomarker_details.measured_tissue_or_fluid: OA Chondrocytes (3D pellet cell culture model)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Overall increase in expression observed in most groups, with highest values in 5% FCS and 5% hypACT. Specifically upregulated in hypACT 5% (significant vs. CPRP 1%, p=0.02) and EPRP 1% (significant vs. CPRP 1%, p=0.003). Levels in 1% EPRP were similar to 5% EPRP, 1% FCS, and 1% hypACT.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: A hypertrophic differentiation marker, typically associated with fibrous tissue formation and dedifferentiated chondrocytes, rather than healthy articular cartilage.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: 21 days of 3D pellet culture of OA chondrocytes with 1% or 5% supplementation of hypACT, EPRP, CPRP, or FCS.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Upregulation indicates hypertrophic differentiation or fibrous tissue formation, generally undesirable in articular cartilage repair, suggesting a less healthy or stable cartilage phenotype.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the cytokine changes, tissue viability, and remodeling markers in an in vitro osteoarthritic knee joint explant co-culture model (comprising cartilage, subchondral bone, and synovial membrane) in response to hyperacute serum treatment. The findings demonstrate that hyperacute serum induces cell proliferation, shifts the cytokine milieu towards a less inflamed state, and improves tissue remodeling in the osteoarthritic joint model.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Hyperacute Serum Treatment and IL-1β Stimulation in an in vitro explant co-culture model
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Osteoarthritic knee joint explants (cartilage, subchondral bone, and synovial membrane) were stimulated with IL-1β as an inflammatory trigger, then treated with 10% hyperacute serum containing medium. The treatment lasted up to 5 days, with supernatants collected on days 3 and 5. Comparisons were made against human serum albumin-treated controls. No explicit dose-response comparisons were reported for either hyperacute serum or IL-1β beyond their observed effects.

matched_biomarker_details.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Co-culture supernatant of osteoarthritic knee joint explants (bone-cartilage-synovium tissues)

measured_effect.direction_of_change: lower (due to IL-1β stimulation), then higher (after hyperacute serum treatment)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: IL-1β stimulation inhibited its secretion. In response to hyperacute serum treatment, concentrations were significantly elevated, indicating enhanced production.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: A crucial structural component of collagen, primarily forming 90% of a bone's extracellular matrix, involved in tissue repair, extracellular matrix formation, and is a key tissue remodeling marker.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Inhibition by IL-1β stimulation and subsequent enhanced production during hyperacute serum treatment in an in vitro osteoarthritic knee joint explant model.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Initial inhibition by IL-1β indicates a negative effect on cartilage and bone remodeling. Enhanced production due to hyperacute serum suggests promotion of tissue repair, regeneration, and enhanced bone matrix formation, indicating a beneficial effect on OA knee joint health.

document_context_data.document_summary: The study aimed to identify and validate novel protein biomarkers for Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM), focusing on blood-based protein profiling. It successfully identified serum protein c-KIT as a novel biomarker capable of differentiating HCM patients from healthy controls. Furthermore, the investigation demonstrated c-KIT's involvement in cardiac remodeling and fibrosis-related processes, particularly in Obstructive Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HOCM), suggesting its potential role in understanding fibrotic signaling within HCM.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Biomarker discovery, identification, and functional investigation for diagnostic purposes in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational study involving 60 HCM patients (33 HOCM, 27 HNCM) and 28 healthy controls. Proteomic profiling of 92 cardiometabolic proteins in serum was conducted on a subgroup (20 HCM, 10 healthy), with c-KIT validated in the full cohort via ELISA. Myocardial c-KIT gene expression was analyzed in HOCM patient myectomies, and in vitro c-KIT silencing was performed in human cardiac fibroblasts for functional investigation. No therapeutic interventions or dose-response comparisons were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly increased in myectomies of HOCM patients compared to healthy controls.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Cardiac tissue in Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy (HOCM).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Elevated levels indicate cardiac fibrosis, which is clinically relevant for prognosis and risk assessment in HCM, particularly concerning the risk of sudden cardiac death.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated disease and target engagement biomarkers in the phase 2b RISE-SSc trial of riociguat in early diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (dcSSc) to predict treatment response. While the primary endpoint (modified Rodnan Skin Score, mRSS) did not reach statistical significance, riociguat treatment significantly increased plasma cGMP levels, indicating engagement of the NO-sGC-cGMP pathway. Additionally, serum sPECAM-1 and CXCL-4 levels decreased with riociguat. Elevated baseline sPECAM-1 and the presence of αSMA-positive cells in skin biopsies were identified as potential predictive biomarkers for greater mRSS reduction with riociguat, suggesting these markers may help identify patients who could benefit from the treatment for skin fibrosis.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Riociguat (Drug Treatment)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Patients with early treatment-naïve diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis were randomized to receive riociguat (n=60) or placebo (n=61) for 52 weeks. Riociguat was administered up to 2.5 mg, maximum three times daily. Biomarker assessments were performed at baseline (day 0) and week 14, with clinical endpoints evaluated up to week 52. Rescue therapy was permitted from week 26. While cGMP changes correlated with riociguat pharmacokinetics, no explicit dose-response comparisons for other biomarkers were formally reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant differences in mean fold-changes from baseline to week 14 between riociguat and placebo groups for Collagen 1A1 (riociguat: 1.27, placebo: 0.96), Collagen 1A2 (riociguat: 1.24, placebo: 1.11), or Collagen 3A1 (riociguat: 1.21, placebo: 1.05). Collagen 1A1 mRNA fold-change showed a modest correlation (0.339) with mRSS change in the riociguat group.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Components of the extracellular matrix, reflecting fibrotic gene expression and structural integrity of the skin.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Riociguat treatment in early diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (RISE-SSc trial) from baseline to week 14.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: No significant change suggests riociguat did not reverse advanced fibrosis at the mRNA level. Modest correlation for Collagen 1A1 mRNA with mRSS changes may indicate some association with skin fibrosis progression.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review identifies and recommends validated biomarkers for tracking health, performance, and recovery in athletes across multiple domains including nutritional status (macronutrients, micronutrients, food allergies), hydration, muscle status (damage, endocrine response), endurance, and injury risk (concussions, stress fractures, ACL). It advocates for a comprehensive, integrative, and individualized approach to biomarker analysis, emphasizing dynamic monitoring and contextual interpretation over single markers or universal thresholds to optimize training and minimize injury and overtraining risks.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Biomarker-guided monitoring and management of athletic training, nutrition, hydration, and injury recovery
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This review primarily focuses on the diagnostic and prognostic value of biomarkers rather than specific therapeutic doses. It emphasizes frequent, individualized monitoring (e.g., pre/post-exercise, daily, seasonally, after injury/competition) to establish personalized baseline ranges and track physiological changes in response to various training loads (e.g., acute bouts, heavy strength training, challenging training weeks). While specific nutritional intake recommendations are mentioned for protein (1.3–2.0 g/kg/day) and omega-3 fatty acids (≤3 g/day for average, 6–8 g/day for elite athletes), and iron supplementation at low-moderate doses, the document does not report dose-response comparisons for biomarker changes. Instead, it provides specific thresholds for identifying deficiencies (e.g., Vitamin D >50 ng/ml, Ferritin <12 µg/L), dehydration (e.g., >-2% body mass decrease, blood osmolality ≥295 mmol/kg, USG ≥1.020), insufficient recovery (30% decrease in T:C ratio), and overtraining (T:C ratio of 0.35 × 10⁻³). The overall approach prioritizes dynamic, contextualized assessment over universal thresholds for effective athlete management.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Immediately after ACL injury, serum concentration indicates an imbalance between cartilage breakdown and synthesis.

matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Could be indicative of posttraumatic changes in cartilage metabolism and signals the potential onset of posttraumatic osteoarthritis (OA).

document_context_data.document_summary: This narrative review investigates current and potential blood and urine biomarkers for osteoarthritis (OA), focusing on markers derived from type II collagen and aggrecan to reflect joint tissue turnover. The review details their molecular targets, measurement methods, and diagnostic, prognostic, and pharmacodynamic utility in assessing cartilage degradation, bone turnover, and disease progression, including responses to treatments. It highlights both established and preclinical markers, emphasizing the complexities of cleavage sites, the need for multi-protease inhibition strategies, and further biomarker validation, while noting a continued lack of operationalized in vitro diagnostics and markers for patient endotyping.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Osteoarthritis (OA) biomarker investigation, Doxycycline treatment, Oral salmon calcitonin (sCT), Cathepsin K inhibition, Collagen hydrolysate supplementation, Fibroblast growth factor 18 (FGF-18) induced remodeling
treatment_details.dose_specificity: No specific therapeutic dose or intervention protocols are primarily reported, as this is a narrative review focusing on biomarkers for Osteoarthritis and their utility in drug development and patient management. However, some treatments were mentioned: Doxycycline was investigated in a randomized controlled trial in 120 obese knee OA patients (specific dose/duration not detailed). Oral salmon calcitonin (sCT) was examined for its effect on knee OA patients (specific dose not detailed). Cathepsin K inhibition reduced CTX-I by more than 90% (specific inhibitor dose/duration not reported). Collagen hydrolysate administration led to a modest decrease in CS846 and an elevation in PIIANP (specific dose/duration not reported). No dose-response comparisons were generally reported.

matched_biomarker_details.activity_type: Type II collagen formation (synthesis) marker (mature articular cartilage variant, PIIBNP)

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Lower in OA patients; low levels associated with higher likelihood of progression. In explants, initial decrease followed by increase.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Lower in knee OA patients (KL grade 2–4, n=123) compared with healthy controls (n=22). Low serum levels were associated with 3.4-fold higher likelihood of radiographic progression than those with high levels in two independent cohorts (106 and 147 participants). In explant culture, it showed an initial decrease over three weeks, then an increase over seven weeks during FGF-18 induced remodeling.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Indicates the synthesis and formation of mature articular type II collagen, essential for maintaining the structural integrity and for dynamic anabolic restructuring of cartilage.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Osteoarthritis progression, diagnosis, assessment of cartilage repair capacity, Fibroblast growth factor 18 (FGF-18) induced biphasic remodeling process in OA cartilage explants.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review identifies and recommends validated biomarkers for tracking health, performance, and recovery in athletes across multiple domains including nutritional status (macronutrients, micronutrients, food allergies), hydration, muscle status (damage, endocrine response), endurance, and injury risk (concussions, stress fractures, ACL). It advocates for a comprehensive, integrative, and individualized approach to biomarker analysis, emphasizing dynamic monitoring and contextual interpretation over single markers or universal thresholds to optimize training and minimize injury and overtraining risks.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Biomarker-guided monitoring and management of athletic training, nutrition, hydration, and injury recovery
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This review primarily focuses on the diagnostic and prognostic value of biomarkers rather than specific therapeutic doses. It emphasizes frequent, individualized monitoring (e.g., pre/post-exercise, daily, seasonally, after injury/competition) to establish personalized baseline ranges and track physiological changes in response to various training loads (e.g., acute bouts, heavy strength training, challenging training weeks). While specific nutritional intake recommendations are mentioned for protein (1.3–2.0 g/kg/day) and omega-3 fatty acids (≤3 g/day for average, 6–8 g/day for elite athletes), and iron supplementation at low-moderate doses, the document does not report dose-response comparisons for biomarker changes. Instead, it provides specific thresholds for identifying deficiencies (e.g., Vitamin D >50 ng/ml, Ferritin <12 µg/L), dehydration (e.g., >-2% body mass decrease, blood osmolality ≥295 mmol/kg, USG ≥1.020), insufficient recovery (30% decrease in T:C ratio), and overtraining (T:C ratio of 0.35 × 10⁻³). The overall approach prioritizes dynamic, contextualized assessment over universal thresholds for effective athlete management.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the associations between circulating fibrocytes and left atrial (LA) fibrosis or the prevalence of recurrence after catheter ablation in patients with persistent and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (AF), compared to sinus rhythm controls. It examined fibrocyte proportion, differentiation, and migration, as well as gene expression of various molecular markers. The findings demonstrated that increased circulating fibrocytes positively correlate with LA fibrosis (low-voltage area) and are a significant predictor of 1-year recurrence after ablation in persistent AF. Fibrocytes from persistent AF patients showed enhanced differentiation into myofibroblasts and elevated expression of pro-fibrotic and inflammatory markers, with TGF-β1 promoting differentiation and SDF-1 enhancing migration.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Catheter ablation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Catheter ablation was performed as a first-time or single procedure, predominantly for persistent AF. Specifics included radiofrequency energy applied with a power limit of 35 W and a maximal temperature of 45°C, applied until a voltage of <0.1 mV was achieved or for a maximum of 30 seconds per point. A single bolus of 100 IU/kg heparin was administered to maintain activated clotting time within 250-300 seconds. Oral antiplatelet/anticoagulant drugs were stopped 3 days before ablation and restored afterward, while antiarrhythmic drugs were stopped on the day of ablation and restored the next day for up to 2 months. Electroanatomic mapping systems were used to identify fibrotic (low-voltage) areas. Patients were followed up for 1 year post-ablation.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive observational study utilized plasma proteomics and machine learning to develop and validate a framework for measuring organ-specific biological aging, termed 'e-ageotypes', in humans. Analyzing 4,778 proteins from 5,676 adults across five independent cohorts, the research revealed that accelerated aging in specific organs (including heart, brain, kidney, muscle, liver, adipose, pancreas, lung, and immune system) is significantly associated with higher risks of all-cause mortality and various age-related diseases, such as heart failure, Alzheimer's disease, hypertension, diabetes, and cognitive decline. The study's methodology involved defining 'extreme agers' (individuals with highly accelerated organ aging), clustering them into distinct ageotypes, and identifying key protein biomarkers (e.g., REN, KL, NPPB, TNNT2, CPLX1/2) that contribute to these aging profiles and offer prognostic utility for disease risk and progression.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational Study on Biological Aging via Plasma Proteomics and Machine Learning
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This observational study involved the quantification of approximately 4,778 plasma proteins using SomaScan assays (v.4 and v.4.1) in 5,676 adults from five independent cohorts. Machine learning models (LASSO regression-based chronological age predictors) were developed and validated to estimate biological (organ-specific) age, referred to as 'age gaps' or 'e-ageotypes', for 11 major organs (adipose tissue, artery, brain, heart, immune tissue, intestine, kidney, liver, lung, muscle, and pancreas) and the whole organism. Models were trained on 1,398 healthy participants from the Knight-ADRC cohort and tested across the full cohort. Age gaps were calculated using local regression, z-scored per model and cohort, and adjusted for age and sex. Associations with various age-related phenotypes, future mortality, heart disease, clinical biochemistry markers, and cognitive decline were assessed using linear models or Cox proportional hazards models, with multiple testing correction (Benjamini-Hochberg method, 5% false discovery rate). No therapeutic intervention or dose comparison was performed.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated proteomic and histological changes in human intervertebral disc (IVD) tissue and matched plasma samples to identify biomarkers for disc degeneration progression. It compared mild and severe degenerate IVD tissues from individuals undergoing lumbar discectomy, employing mass spectrometry, immunohistochemistry, and qRT-PCR. The main finding was the identification of AEBP1 as a significant tissue marker for monitoring degeneration severity, with increased levels in severe IVD. While other matrisomal proteins (TNC, MGP, COL12A1, COL6A2, COL6A3, TGFBI) and complement system proteins (C4A, C3, CFB, CFH) were also elevated in severe IVD, and some plasma proteins (A2M, F13B, MMP2, IGF1) showed changes, plasma biomarkers exhibited a weak correlation with tissue degeneration.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study comprehensively investigated the clinical relevance and efficacy of collagen X breakdown product (CXM) as a blood-based biomarker for endochondral long bone fracture repair in both healthy individuals and patients with tibia or femur fractures. It characterized CXM expression patterns, stability across demographics (age, sex), correlation with other bone turnover markers (P1NP, CTX, osteocalcin, leptin, sclerostin), and its utility in predicting healing prognosis (early, normal, delayed). The findings showed CXM levels are low in healthy individuals, peak around 25-35 days post-fracture, can be reliably measured via dried blood spots, and offer an earlier, quantitative indication of healing compared to traditional radiographic methods, supporting its prospective use in fracture studies.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study of natural long bone fracture repair, with a secondary analysis of a Vitamin D3 supplementation trial (VitaShock).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study primarily focused on observing biomarker changes in patients with acute closed or low-grade open tibial or femoral shaft fractures (Gustilo type I or II, AO/OTA type 42), without applying a specific therapeutic dose as an intervention. For the secondary analysis of the VitaShock trial, multiple Vitamin D3 dosing strategies were assessed, but specific dose details were not provided, and no significant difference in CXM response was found compared to placebo. Longitudinal blood samples were collected at various standard-of-care clinical visits over a period up to 48 weeks post-fracture.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: low in healthy individuals, peaks post-fracture, does not vary with age or sex in healthy, positively correlates with P1NP, CTX, and osteocalcin, negatively correlates with leptin, higher in early healers, varied by sex and fracture location, unchanged with Vitamin D3 treatment
