matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Enzyme primarily found in muscle cells; elevated levels indicate muscle damage, involved in cellular energy metabolism.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: After each of three repeated bouts of exhaustive treadmill exercise, and in baseline levels across the study period.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates the level of muscle damage and insufficient recovery between exhaustive exercise bouts, suggesting cumulative physiological stress.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review identifies and recommends validated biomarkers for tracking health, performance, and recovery in athletes across multiple domains including nutritional status (macronutrients, micronutrients, food allergies), hydration, muscle status (damage, endocrine response), endurance, and injury risk (concussions, stress fractures, ACL). It advocates for a comprehensive, integrative, and individualized approach to biomarker analysis, emphasizing dynamic monitoring and contextual interpretation over single markers or universal thresholds to optimize training and minimize injury and overtraining risks.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Biomarker-guided monitoring and management of athletic training, nutrition, hydration, and injury recovery
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This review primarily focuses on the diagnostic and prognostic value of biomarkers rather than specific therapeutic doses. It emphasizes frequent, individualized monitoring (e.g., pre/post-exercise, daily, seasonally, after injury/competition) to establish personalized baseline ranges and track physiological changes in response to various training loads (e.g., acute bouts, heavy strength training, challenging training weeks). While specific nutritional intake recommendations are mentioned for protein (1.3–2.0 g/kg/day) and omega-3 fatty acids (≤3 g/day for average, 6–8 g/day for elite athletes), and iron supplementation at low-moderate doses, the document does not report dose-response comparisons for biomarker changes. Instead, it provides specific thresholds for identifying deficiencies (e.g., Vitamin D >50 ng/ml, Ferritin <12 µg/L), dehydration (e.g., >-2% body mass decrease, blood osmolality ≥295 mmol/kg, USG ≥1.020), insufficient recovery (30% decrease in T:C ratio), and overtraining (T:C ratio of 0.35 × 10⁻³). The overall approach prioritizes dynamic, contextualized assessment over universal thresholds for effective athlete management.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Elevated after muscle-damaging exercise, peaking around 24 hours and remaining elevated up to 7 days; athletic norms: 82–1,083 U·L⁻¹ for males, 47–513 U·L⁻¹ for females. Exhibits high interindividual variability, with different ranges compared to sedentary individuals. Released from muscle cells upon damage.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Enzyme involved in cellular energy metabolism, released into circulation upon skeletal or cardiac muscle cell damage, serving as an indicator of muscle damage.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Exercise (muscle-damaging, heavy strength training), overtraining, insufficient recovery, cardiac muscle damage (myocardial infarction).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Valuable biomarker for muscle damage, indicating recovery status and potential overtraining; chronically elevated levels may signal insufficient recovery. Aids in indirect tracking of inflammation, but individual variability requires careful interpretation.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of a single 6g dose of citrulline malate (CM) supplementation on muscle recovery after a high-intensity resistance exercise (RE) session in untrained young adult men, examining functional, metabolic, anabolic, and physiological markers. The findings concluded that CM supplementation does not improve the muscle recovery process.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Citrulline Malate (CM) supplementation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: A single oral dose of 6 g of citrulline malate (CM) was administered 60 minutes pre-workout, dissolved in 200 mL water. Participants then performed a single session of high-intensity resistance exercise (RE) consisting of 3 sets of 8–12 repetitions at 90% of 10RM for leg press and hack squat exercises, with 2 min rest between sets and exercises, performed with a 1s concentric:2s eccentric cadence. No dose-response comparisons were reported, and no significant treatment × time interaction was found for any measured variables, indicating CM did not improve recovery compared to placebo.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Serum CK levels increased significantly (p < 0.001) at 24 h post-exercise and remained elevated at 48 and 72 h in both CM and placebo conditions, with no significant difference between treatments (treatment × time p = 0.632).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Enzyme primarily found in muscle cells, released into the bloodstream upon muscle fiber damage, indicating muscle injury and involved in energy transfer.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Blood samples collected pre- and post-exercise, and immediately after muscular fatigue tests (24, 48, and 72 h after RE session) during recovery from a single high-intensity resistance exercise (RE) session with CM or placebo supplementation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Metabolic indicator of muscle damage and integrity, commonly used to assess exercise-induced muscle injury and recovery, reflecting impaired muscle function.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of post-exercise milk consumption (500 mL) versus an energy-matched carbohydrate drink on recovery from a repeated sprinting and jumping protocol in female team-sport athletes. The strenuous protocol successfully induced muscle damage, leading to post-exercise decreases in muscle function (peak torque, countermovement jump, sprint performance, rate of force development) and increases in subjective muscle soreness and tiredness. Milk consumption attenuated losses in muscle function, particularly for peak torque (knee extension/flexion at 180°/s) and countermovement jump height, and reduced perceived stress (DALDA B) at various time points (24h, 48h, 72h) post-exercise. The study concluded that milk may be a valuable recovery intervention for female team-sport athletes following this type of exercise, although its effects on serum creatine kinase, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, reactive strength index, and some sprint performances were unclear.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Post-exercise nutritional intervention (Milk vs. Carbohydrate drink)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants immediately consumed either 500 mL of milk (910 kJ/215 kcal, 17.0 g Protein, 25.5 g Carbohydrate, 5.0 g Fat) or 500 mL of an energy-matched carbohydrate drink (910 kJ/215 kcal, 0.2 g Protein, 53.6 g Carbohydrate, 0.0 g Fat) following a whole-body sport and exercise protocol designed to induce muscle damage (15x20m maximal sprints and 8 sets of 10 plyometric jumps). The milk protein dose (17g) was noted to be potentially suboptimal for maximal protein synthesis compared to other studies. No dose-response comparisons were conducted, as a single volume of 500 mL was used for both interventions.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Serum CK levels increased post-exercise, peaking at 24 hours and returning to baseline by 72 hours. Peak values at 24h: MILK 246.4 "+/-" 75.8 U/L, CHO 373.9 "+/-" 157.82 U/L. Baseline: MILK 128.5 "+/-" 118.4 U/L, CHO 192.2 "+/-" 103.6 U/L. Relative changes from baseline showed unclear outcomes for milk vs. carbohydrate at B-2h (MILK 1.8x vs CHO 1.7x), B-24h (MILK 2.3x vs CHO 2.1x), B-48h (MILK 1.8x vs CHO 1.4x), and B-72h (MILK 1.4x vs CHO 1.1x).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Indicator of muscle cell damage and integrity, released into the bloodstream upon muscle cell breakdown (sarcolemma damage).
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Post-repeated sprinting and jumping exercise recovery in female team-sport athletes.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates the extent of muscle damage. Despite its role, serum CK was not a reliable indicator of muscle function recovery in this context, showing unclear intervention effects despite milk's benefits on muscle function.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of a 36-hour survival training, which included moderate to low physical activity and complete sleep deprivation, on oxidative stress and muscle damage biomarkers in young, healthy men. The training impaired enzymatic antioxidant defense (GPx, SOD), increased lipid peroxidation (LHs), and induced muscle damage (CK). A subsequent 12-hour recovery period, including overnight sleep, was found to be sufficient to normalize these markers and restore blood prooxidant-antioxidant homeostasis.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Survival Training (combined with moderate to low intensity physical activity and sleep deprivation)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: A 36-hour survival training regimen for young, healthy men, involving moderate to low physical activity such as a 12-km march, 6 hours of rowing, 4 hours of kayaking, running, swimming, climbing, solving special tasks, and navigation in wild terrain. Ambient temperatures ranged from 8°C at night to 30°C during the day. The average heart rate was 80-90 beats/min (40-45% age-predicted HR max), with individual variations from 70-80 beats/min during march to 120-130 beats/min during rowing or kayaking. Participants experienced complete sleep deprivation and consumed approximately 3800 ± 120 kcal daily. This was followed by a 12-hour recovery period, including overnight sleep. No dose-response comparisons were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased significantly at 24 h and remained elevated up to 36 h (p < 0.05, main effects for CK: time, p = 0.000001; group, p = 0.005; group × time, p = 0.000001). Peak levels were observed at 24 h. Showed significant positive correlations with plasma LHs and a weak correlation with plasma TAC. After a 12-h recovery, activity significantly decreased below pre-training levels (p < 0.05).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: An enzyme primarily found in muscle cells, involved in energy metabolism. Its release into the bloodstream indicates muscle cell membrane integrity loss or muscle damage.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: During 36-hour survival training with moderate to low physical activity and sleep deprivation; subsequent 12-hour recovery period.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: A widely used marker for exercise-induced muscle injury and damage level; initial increase indicates damage, while subsequent decrease suggests muscle recovery and integrity restoration.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of 80 mg/day oral iron supplementation on hematological parameters, muscle damage biomarkers (CK, LDH, Mb), and cortisol levels in elite male cyclists during a 3-week stage race (Vuelta a España). It concluded that iron supplementation effectively prevented declines in iron metabolism and hematological profiles (serum iron, ferritin, hemoglobin, hematocrit, TSI, TP, RBC), significantly reduced accumulated stress (cortisol), and significantly lowered Creatine Kinase (CK) levels within the supplemented group, thereby contributing to optimal recovery and performance.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Oral Iron Supplementation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: 80 mg/day of oral iron (800 mg of iron protein succinylate, e.g., Ferplex 40®), administered as two 40 mg doses per day (during breakfast and dinner). The supplementation lasted for a 4-week period, starting one week before and continuing throughout the 3-week Vuelta a España stage race. No dose-response comparisons were reported, but a control group received no oral iron.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: lower in ITG, increased in CG
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: In ITG, circulating levels significantly decreased from T1 (306.7 ± 56.12 UI/L) to T2 (260.8 ± 66.3 UI/L), representing a -53.53 ± 29.18% change (p < 0.05). In CG, an increase of 28.27 ± 100.25% was observed. The percentage change in CG was significantly greater than ITG (p < 0.05). However, no significant group-by-time interaction was observed for circulating muscle biomarkers (p > 0.05). High negative correlations observed with sFe (r = −0.915; p < 0.001), Hb (r = −0.996; p < 0.001), and FER (r = −0.701; p = 0.001).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Enzyme primarily found in muscle cells, indicating muscle damage and cellular breakdown when elevated in the blood.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Elite male cyclists during a 3-week stage race (Vuelta a España) with 80 mg/day oral iron supplementation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates muscle damage level and muscle stress; lower levels suggest reduced muscle damage or improved muscle recovery. While ITG showed a significant decrease, the overall group-by-time interaction was not significant.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of consuming cow's milk versus an energy-matched carbohydrate solution on recovery markers and performance in twenty female team-sport athletes following repeated simulated team games (STGs). The findings indicated that 500 mL of milk consumption attenuated losses in muscle function (peak torque for knee extension and flexion), sprint performance (5m and 10m), and perceptions of stress, and helped reduce muscle soreness and tiredness, particularly after the first STG. However, for many other physiological and performance markers (e.g., CK, hsCRP, LOOHs, PCs, CMJ, HR, RPE), the effects were mostly unclear or trivial, with milk showing no clear benefit after the second STG.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Nutritional intervention (consumption of cow's milk vs. an energy-matched carbohydrate solution) combined with a multi-stage physical activity protocol.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants consumed 500 mL of either cow's milk (910 kJ/215 kcal, 17.0 g protein, 25.5 g carbohydrate, 5.0 g fat) or an energy-matched carbohydrate solution (910 kJ/215 kcal, 0.2 g protein, 53.6 g carbohydrate, 0.0 g fat) immediately following each of two simulated team games (STG1 and STG2). The 17 g protein from milk was noted to be below the recommended 20 g threshold for maximal protein synthesis stimulation. The exercise protocol involved two ~30 minute halves of intermittent running with sprints, agility, and jumps, separated by a 10-minute half-time, with a 48-hour recovery period between STG1 and STG2. No explicit dose-response comparisons were reported for the nutritional interventions.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: increased (post-STG1 and STG2); unclear effect with milk
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification:
Increases observed post-STG1 activity (two-fold) and after STG2. Baseline values: MILK: 196.2  
	± 130.0 U/L, CHO: 188.6  
	± 125.0 U/L. No clear between-group effects (MILK vs CHO) at any timepoint; overall outcomes were unclear.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: An enzyme involved in cellular energy metabolism, released into the bloodstream following muscle cell damage or injury.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Post-simulated team-sport exercise recovery (STG1 and STG2) after nutritional intervention (Milk vs. CHO).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates the extent of skeletal muscle damage or injury, relevant for monitoring exercise-induced muscle stress and recovery, influencing recovery capacity.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated whether aerobic capacity predicts skeletal and cardiac muscle damage in amateur triathletes after a full-distance Ironman. It found that higher aerobic capacity was negatively associated with skeletal muscle damage biomarkers (myoglobin and creatine kinase), but no association was observed with cardiac muscle damage biomarkers (cTnT, MHC-a, NT-proBNP).

treatment_details.therapy_type: Full Distance Ironman Triathlon
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants engaged in a full distance Ironman triathlon (3.8 km swimming, 180 km cycling, 42.2 km running). These amateur athletes reported training for 11.2  1 3 hours/week and had previously completed a median of 8 ultra-endurance races. Aerobic capacity was assessed one month prior to the event using a 20m shuttle-run test. The study focused on post-race biomarker levels, and no specific dose-response comparisons for varying triathlon distances or intensities were reported, though models using absolute aerobic capacity showed slightly higher predictive power for skeletal muscle damage.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Post-race levels typically increase; however, a negative association was found with aerobic capacity. For CK, higher aerobic capacity (mLO2*kg 11*min 11) increased adjusted r2 from -0.015 to 0.267 (F: 13.778, p = 0.001), and in absolute terms (LO2*min 11), adjusted r2 increased from -0.029 to 0.281 (F: 15.215, p < 0.001). Baseline reference < 1.9  5kat/L.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Enzyme primarily found in muscle cells, involved in energy metabolism; elevated levels indicate skeletal muscle damage.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Post-full distance Ironman triathlon in amateur triathletes.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates skeletal muscle damage level; higher aerobic capacity is associated with reduced post-race skeletal muscle damage.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the associations between dietary intake in the week prior to a marathon race and post-race exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) and cardiac stress (EICS) in recreational male endurance runners. It found that consumption of meat, butter, and fatty meat was positively associated with higher EIMD and EICS markers, whereas fish, vegetables, and olive oil intake showed a negative association, suggesting a protective role.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Dietary intake assessment combined with endurance running (marathon race)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Sixty-nine male recreational runners participated in a competitive marathon (42.195 km). Dietary intake for the week prior to and on race day was collected using a seven-day weighed food record. Pre-race average daily intake was 3005.7     362.5 kcal (44.8     6.2 kcal/kg), with carbohydrates at 338.3     55.1 g, protein at 130.5     24.2 g, and fat at 121.5     19.8 g. Race-day intake included 1.8     0.7 L fluid and 597.1     394.9 kcal. Participants showed dietary imbalances with lower than recommended servings of cereals, potatoes, dairy, vegetables, and legumes, and excess in pastries, sweets, and dried fruits. The study identified associations between food group consumption (e.g., meat, butter, fatty meat, fish, vegetables, olive oil) and post-race biomarker levels, but no specific dose-response comparisons for dietary components were explicitly reported beyond these associations. The race took place in Madrid in April 2016, with a mean dry temperature of 27     3    °C and 27     2% relative humidity.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher or lower depending on diet
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Post-race mean: 453.4     268.9 U/L. Positively associated with meat intake (Standardized Coefficients (   ) = 0.643; p < 0.01). Negatively associated with vegetable intake (    = -0.482; p = 0.002) and fish intake (    = -0.272; p = 0.042).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Enzyme released from damaged muscle cells, indicative of muscle damage.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Post-competitive marathon race, with levels influenced by pre-race dietary intake of meat, vegetables, and fish.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) level. High values reflect significant muscle breakdown, while lower values suggest reduced damage.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the acute effects of a single High-Intensity Functional Training (HIFT) 'Cindy' workout session on immune parameters (leucocyte counts and subsets), muscle damage markers (creatine kinase), and stress markers (cortisol, lactate, neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio, and neutrophil-cortisol ratio). The research compared these physiological responses between novice and experienced participants, concluding that the HIFT session elicited significant acute perturbations across all measured markers. Notably, experienced participants exhibited greater lymphocyte and cortisol responses compared to novice individuals, indicating differential physiological adaptations and stress responses to the high-intensity exercise.

treatment_details.therapy_type: High-Intensity Functional Training (HIFT) / CrossFit 'Cindy' workout
treatment_details.dose_specificity: A single 'Cindy' workout session, performed as many rounds as possible (AMRAP) within 20 minutes (consisting of 5 pull-ups, 10 push-ups, and 15 squats). Participants were categorized as novice (3–8 months experience; n=10) and experienced (≥18 months experience; n=13), with responses compared between these groups. The session occurred after a 48-hour rest, between 6:00 AM and 8:00 AM, following a standardized breakfast (320-350 cal, 20% protein, 35% fat, 45% carbohydrate). Participants abstained from specific supplements (antioxidants, caffeine, creatine, beta-alanine, nitrate, bicarbonates) before the study. Mean heart rate during exercise was 172.0 ± 8.6 bpm (93.1 ± 2.3%HR max). No direct dose-response comparisons for varying workout intensity were reported, though individual work (number of rounds) varied.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased significantly at all post-exercise time points (immediately, 30 min, 24 h) from a pre-exercise level of 174.9 U.L^-1 to 226.7 U.L^-1 post-exercise (p<0.01), remaining elevated at 24 h. The highest average was 276 U/L at 24 h, with an individual maximum of 765 U/L. No significant differences in the magnitude of increase were observed between novice and experienced groups (p>0.01).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Enzyme involved in energy metabolism, released into blood upon muscle damage; marker released into circulation upon muscle cell damage.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Single 'Cindy' workout session (HIFT); acute 'Cindy' workout session. Post-exercise response.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates acute muscle tissue damage and breakdown following intense physical exertion. Observed values were well below those indicative of rhabdomyolysis (10,000–20,000 U/L), confirming that the intervention did not induce excessive muscle damage.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the correlation between lower limb skin temperature, measured by infrared thermography (IRT), and common physiological indicators (creatine kinase levels, pain, fatigue, recovery perception) and performance data in professional soccer athletes following matches. The primary finding was a lack of correlation between IRT measurements and these physiological and performance variables within a 48-hour post-match period.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Professional Soccer Matches (Physical Activity Monitoring and Post-Match Assessment)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Twenty-two professional male soccer athletes were monitored during a national championship season, participating in 19 matches with a 7-day interval over five months. Performance data was collected via GPS during matches (athletes played >60% of the match). Infrared thermography was applied, and physiological/biochemical markers (CK, pain, fatigue, recovery perception) were collected 48 hours after each match. No dose-response comparisons for IRT application timing were reported.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Higher (post-exercise peak); unchanged (in terms of correlation with skin temperature)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Peak typically between 48-72 hours post-exercise. No correlation observed between blood CK levels and mean skin temperature (r <0.2, p>0.05).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Indicator of muscle damage, exertion, and strenuous physical activity.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Quantified 48 hours after professional soccer matches, in relation to infrared thermography readings.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates muscle damage level following physical activity. The study found no correlation between CK levels and skin temperature changes, suggesting IRT may not be a reliable tool for indicating muscle damage or recovery status based on CK levels within the 48-hour post-match window for injury prevention.

document_context_data.document_summary: This double-blind, randomized controlled trial investigated the efficacy of post-exercise dairy-based protein supplementation versus an iso-caloric carbohydrate placebo in attenuating muscle soreness and other muscle damage markers in 323 recreational athletes following a 15-km road race. The study concluded that protein supplementation was not superior to carbohydrate supplementation for reducing muscle soreness or damage markers, and, notably, per-protocol analysis indicated higher perceived and objective lower extremity muscle soreness in the protein group 24 hours post-race, with no significant differences observed in blood markers like Creatine Kinase and Lactate Dehydrogenase between groups.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Nutritional Supplementation (Protein vs. Carbohydrate)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants received either milk protein (20% whey, 80% casein) or an iso-caloric maltodextrin carbohydrate placebo for three consecutive days post-race. The protein protocol involved 20 g immediately post-exercise and with breakfast, and 40 g prior to sleep. Compliant participants in the protein group consumed an average of 1.94-1.97 g/kg/d protein on race day and 1-2 days post-race, compared to 1.09-1.12 g/kg/d in the placebo group. The study focused on comparing protein versus carbohydrate effects, with no dose-response comparisons reported within the protein group itself.

matched_biomarker_details.activity_type: Enzyme concentration / Protein Level / Enzyme activity

measured_effect.direction_of_change: unchanged / Similar levels observed between protein and placebo groups
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant differences were found in concentrations of CK post-race between groups (p = 0.26). Protein group: 265 (171–495) U/L; Placebo group: 366 (196–508) U/L (ITT analysis). Observed levels one day post-race: placebo group 346 U/L, protein group 285 U/L. Baseline pre-exercise levels were assumed similar.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Enzyme primarily found in muscle cells; elevated levels in blood typically indicate muscle cell damage or breakdown.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Following a 15-km road race, with post-race protein or carbohydrate supplementation, measured 1-2 days post-race.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates the extent of muscle damage at a cellular level; no difference suggests similar muscle cell membrane integrity between groups.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the regulation of 23 blood-based biomarkers (including CK, IL-6, IL-17A, S100A8, BDNF, CD163, IL-1ß, and LDH) in 35 male elite athletes (badminton and soccer players) across different recovery-stress states. The primary aim was to identify markers responsive to habitual loading microcycles compared to recovered states. Key findings indicated that Creatine Kinase (CK), Interleukin-6 (IL-6), and Interleukin-17A (IL-17A) were generally higher in non-recovered states. S100A8 levels were significantly lower in non-recovered badminton players, while Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (BDNF) levels were lower in non-recovered soccer players. Statistical trends were also observed for CD163 and Interleukin-1 beta (IL-1ß). The study concludes that these discipline-specific biomarker responses are potentially useful for monitoring exercise and recovery to prevent overtraining and injury, though further validation is needed.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Exercise Training / Habitual Loading Microcycles
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study compared blood biomarker levels in elite male athletes (badminton and soccer players) during two states: 'recovered' (REC, after at least one day of rest from exercise) and 'non-recovered' (NOR, after a habitual loading microcycle). The habitual loading involved intensive, sport-specific training. For badminton players, this included four consecutive days with up to two sessions per day (50-310 min of moderate to intensive exercise daily). For soccer players, it involved high-intensity sessions with strenuous small-sided games, with at least two sessions within 48 hours. Blood samples for the NOR state were taken 12-16 hours after the last training session. The specific training content within microcycles varied and was not precisely controlled, reflecting real-world conditions. No explicit dose-response comparisons for varying training loads were reported within the context of the main findings, although external references to other exercise bouts (e.g., marathon, duathlon, interval training) were used to characterize biomarker behavior generally.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Overall, significantly higher in non-recovered (NOR) state compared to recovered (REC) (p < 0.001), with REC at 152.6  1 102.4 U/L and NOR at 693.1  1 435.5 U/L (mean difference 540.6 U/L, 95% CI [399.2, 681.9]). Similar significant increases observed in badminton (REC 117.4  1 26.4 U/L vs NOR 776.9  1 585.4 U/L; p < 0.001) and soccer players (REC 173.4  1 124 U/L vs NOR 643.6  1 323.1 U/L; p < 0.001).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Indicates exercise-induced muscle damage; an intramuscular enzyme that floods into the blood upon loss of muscular integrity.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Non-recovered state following intensive, sport-dependent habitual loading microcycles (badminton and soccer training) involving high mechanical stress and eccentric force production.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates levels of muscle damage due to exercise stress and reflects exercise-sensitive muscular integrity, useful for monitoring recovery and stress levels in athletes.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of broad-spectrum polyphenol supplementation from powdered tart cherry extract on markers of recovery, oxidative stress, and muscle damage following intense resistance exercise in men. It concluded that tart cherry extract significantly reduced oxidative stress (protein carbonyls), skeletal muscle damage (creatine kinase), and cardiac/type I muscle fiber damage (creatine kinase MB), while also preventing a decrease in handgrip strength compared to placebo.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Broad-spectrum polyphenol supplementation using powdered tart cherry extract combined with an acute resistance exercise protocol (AREP).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants received 500 mg of powdered NordicCherry® tart cherry extract (with minimal calorie content, 1.3 kcal) daily for 7 days prior to an Acute Resistance Exercise Protocol (AREP), compared to a rice flour placebo. The AREP involved 6 sets of 10 repetitions of barbell back squat at 80% of 1-repetition maximum, with load reduction to 75% 1RM if 10 repetitions were not completed in a set. No dose-response comparisons for the supplement or exercise intensity were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly lower activity in Tart Cherry (TC) group compared to Placebo (PL) group: Immediate Post (IP) (PL: 491.1 	 280 vs. TC: 296.3 	 178 U	L	-1; p = 0.008) and 3 h (PL: -87 	 123 vs. TC: 43.1 	 105.3 U	L	-1; p = 0.006). Reference values for CK are 38-174 U	L	-1. This showed a significant main effect for supplement (p = 0.036), time (p < 0.001), and supplement*time interaction (p = 0.003), attenuating the exercise-induced increase in CK.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: An enzyme involved in energy metabolism, released into circulation following skeletal muscle damage, reflecting structural disruption of muscle fibers.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Following an Acute Resistance Exercise Protocol (AREP) (6 sets of 10 repetitions of barbell back squat at 80% 1RM) after a 7-day supplementation period with tart cherry extract.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates reduced skeletal muscle damage and a mitigating effect of tart cherry supplementation on exercise-induced muscle injury, enhancing recovery.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of New Zealand Blackcurrant (NZBC) extract supplementation on markers of exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) and recovery following strenuous isokinetic resistance exercise in healthy, non-resistance trained men and women. The findings indicate that NZBC extract consumption leads to faster recovery of muscle function, significantly attenuates muscle soreness, and reduces serum creatine kinase (CK) levels, collectively demonstrating improved functional recovery and mitigated muscle damage.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Dietary supplementation with New Zealand Blackcurrant (NZBC) extract, combined with strenuous eccentric isokinetic resistance exercise.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants consumed either 3 g·day−1 NZBC extract (containing 105 mg anthocyanins) or a placebo (microcrystalline cellulose M102) once daily for a total of 12 days (8 days prior to and 4 days following strenuous exercise). The exercise protocol involved 60 strenuous concentric and eccentric contractions of the biceps brachii muscle on an isokinetic dynamometer (4 sets of 15 maximal contractions at 45°/s concentric and 60°/s eccentric, with 1-min recovery). The supplement was consumed 1 hour before exercise on day 8. No dose-response comparisons for NZBC extract were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Serum CK concentration was significantly lower in the NZBC group at 96 h (NZBC: 635 ± 921 UL vs. PLA: 4021 ± 4319 UL, p = 0.04). CK significantly increased after the muscle damage protocol in the PLA group (p = 0.008) but remained unchanged in the NZBC group (p = 0.798). CK was significantly elevated above baseline in the PLA group at 96 h post-exercise (p = 0.003). A trend toward being lower at 72 h in NZBC (NZBC: 542 ± 818 UL vs. PLA: 3977 ± 5392 UL, p = 0.080) was also observed.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Enzyme involved in cellular energy metabolism, primarily found in muscle cells; its leakage into the bloodstream signifies muscle cell membrane damage.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Following 60 strenuous concentric and eccentric contractions of the biceps brachii muscle (Exercise-Induced Muscle Damage, EIMD).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Commonly used biomarker to quantify the extent of muscle damage and assess the integrity of muscle cell membranes; lower or unchanged levels after exercise suggest reduced muscle injury or enhanced recovery, indicating NZBC supplementation mitigates damage.

document_context_data.document_summary: This placebo-controlled, double-blind, six-arm crossover study investigated the effects of a single 60 mg Cannabidiol (CBD) supplementation versus placebo after an intensive resistance training protocol (designed to induce muscle damage) on skeletal muscle regeneration and performance in healthy, well-trained participants. The study measured muscle damage biomarkers (Creatine Kinase and Myoglobin) and neuromuscular performance (1RM Back Squat and Countermovement Jump) at 24, 48, and 72 hours post-training. While overall effects were small, CBD significantly attenuated increases in CK and Myo concentrations and aided in the recovery of 1RM Back Squat performance after 72 hours, but showed no significant effect on Countermovement Jump performance.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Cannabidiol (CBD) supplementation following an intensive strength training protocol.
treatment_details.dose_specificity:
Participants underwent an intensive strength training protocol consisting of three sets of 12 back squats at 70% of 1RM with 150 seconds rest, and three sets of 15 drop jumps from a 45 cm box landed in a deep squat with 60 seconds rest. A single dose of 60 mg CBD solubilisat or a placebo drink was consumed directly after exercise, with effects monitored at 24, 48, and 72 hours post-training. Absolute strength values and training loads averaged 118.6 
± 22.6 kg. The study did not include dose-response comparisons for CBD, nor did it investigate chronic supplementation or endurance training effects, and it was suggested that the protocol might not have induced sufficient power reduction for CMJ.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Initially elevated, then decreased over study course; CBD attenuated the increase and showed lower levels.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased significantly after 24 h (p < 0.001), 48 h (p < 0.001), and 72 h (p < 0.001) in both groups. CBD attenuated the increase after 72 h, resulting in a significant group difference (p < 0.05; ES = -0.24). Significant negative population trends were observed with an effect size of -0.29; comparably small. The CBD group largely recovered after 72 hours.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Enzyme primarily found in muscle cells, involved in energy metabolism. Elevated levels in serum are a marker of skeletal muscle damage and breakdown.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Following an intensive resistance training protocol and single CBD supplementation, measured at 24, 48, and 72 hours post-training, compared to placebo.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates the level of muscle damage or injury. Higher levels suggest greater exercise-induced muscle damage. CBD may aid in the recovery from muscle damage after 72 hours by attenuating the increase.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated whether pre-sleep casein protein supplementation, following an acute bout of evening resistance exercise, improved next-day recovery biomarkers (Creatine Kinase, C-reactive protein), maximal strength performance (1RM squat and bench press), or perceived hunger in resistance-trained men. The study concluded that pre-sleep protein did not significantly improve muscle damage biomarkers or strength performance, though a trend for lower perceived hunger was observed in the protein group. It was also noted that the exercise protocol might not have been strenuous enough to induce significant muscle damage in the trained participants.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Pre-sleep casein protein supplementation combined with an acute bout of evening resistance exercise.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants performed a single bout of evening resistance exercise (eight sets of eight repetitions for weighted barbell back squats and chest press, including sets at 55%, 65%, and 75% 1RM). They then received either 40g of casein protein mixed with 450 mL water (PRO group) or a non-caloric, flavor-matched placebo (PLA group) 30 minutes before sleep. A standard recovery drink was given immediately post-exercise to both groups. A 40g bolus was chosen as the minimum required dose to improve overnight myofibrillar protein synthesis. No dose-response comparisons were reported for the protein supplementation, and the resistance exercise protocol was suggested to be insufficient to induce significant muscle damage in the trained participants.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher (in all groups post-exercise) but unchanged (between PRO and PLA groups)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly greater at +12-h compared to pre-RE (p = 0.003) for both groups combined. No significant differences between the pre-sleep protein and placebo groups in next morning muscle damage biomarkers (no time 	 treatment interaction or main effect of group observed), indicating no attenuation of the rise by protein supplementation. Values >1500 IU/l were diluted and re-analyzed.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: An enzyme associated with energy metabolism and an indirect marker of muscle cell damage and breakdown or physiological/metabolic load.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Following an acute bout of evening resistance exercise, with or without pre-sleep casein protein supplementation (measured at pre-RE and 12-h post-RE).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates muscle disturbance or metabolic load from exercise; elevated levels are often associated with muscle damage, but in well-trained individuals, it may reflect metabolic stress rather than damage if performance is sustained. Pre-sleep protein supplementation did not improve this marker of muscle damage.

document_context_data.document_summary: This observational study evaluated the usefulness of a panel of biochemical and hematological variables for assessing training loads and recovery effectiveness in young professional long-distance and sprint swimmers over a 10-week preparatory training period. It identified an optimal panel including creatine kinase (CK), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), urea (U), total bilirubin (TB), direct bilirubin (DB), and ferritin concentrations, which collectively provide crucial information for monitoring post-training effort and recovery, regardless of sex or competitive distance. The study also highlighted the importance of ferritin, iron, and blood morphology in preventing deficiencies, anemia, and inflammatory states.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study monitoring biochemical and hematological recovery variables in young professional swimmers during a training program
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Data was collected over a 10-week preparatory training stage involving 27 male and female swimmers, aged 15-18 years, categorized by competitive distance (sprint: 50-100m; long-distance: 400-800m). Measurements included enzyme activities (ALT, AST, LDH, ALP, CK), metabolite concentrations (Cr, CRP, ferritin, TB, DB, urea, iron), and various capillary blood morphology parameters. The study primarily focused on observing responses to ongoing training loads and recovery, rather than comparing specific training "doses."

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Fluctuated based on competitive distance and sex; high individual variability
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Values were within athlete-specific reference ranges (males: 82–1083 U/L; females: 47–513 U/L) but exceeded general population ranges. Maximum plasma activity may appear 24–36 hours post-training. Correlated with AST activity (male groups, FS group) and urea concentration. No significant differences between female sprint and long-distance groups, nor in male groups for CK activity over 10 weeks.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Enzyme primarily found in muscle cells, indicating muscle damage or stress and monitoring energy cost.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Long-lasting high-intensity training, post-training recovery, and during a 10-week preparatory training stage in professional long-distance and sprint swimmers.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Most common enzymatic marker in sport diagnostics, indicating muscle damage level, release of muscle cell content, and assessing training effort. High individual variability can make interpretation difficult. Considered useful as part of an effective recovery monitoring panel.

document_context_data.document_summary: This randomized, single-blind, placebo-controlled trial investigated the effects of 6-week Tribulus terrestris L. (TT) supplementation (770 mg/day) on muscle metabolism, inflammation, and antioxidant biomarkers in trained male CrossFit® athletes. The study concluded that TT supplementation could attenuate CrossFit® training-induced oxidative stress, muscle damage, and inflammation by modulating levels of LDH, CRP, and TAS, while other muscle damage and inflammatory markers remained unchanged.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Tribulus terrestris L. (TT) supplementation combined with a structured CrossFit training program
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Tribulus terrestris (TT) was supplemented orally at 770 mg/day (2 capsules of 385 mg, 72.64% TT extract at 40% saponins) for 6 weeks, taken daily after workouts. The CrossFit training program involved 3 high-intensity sessions per week on alternate weekdays (4.5 hours/week total), including specific warm-ups, Workouts of the Day (WODs) like 'Grace' and 'Fran', and cool-downs. The TT dose was within the reported safety range of 250-9000 mg, and no dose-response comparisons were reported in this study.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant differences (p > 0.05) between time points (T1, T2, T3) nor between control and intervention groups.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Enzyme indicative of muscle damage and energy metabolism.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: 6 weeks of CrossFit® exercise with/without Tribulus Terrestris supplementation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Muscle damage biomarker; TT supplementation had no significant impact on this specific marker of muscle damage.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the time-course alterations of early and late phases of the rate of voluntary force development (RVFD) and traditional muscle damage markers following a 30-minute downhill running session in recreational runners. It concluded that downhill running impairs the RVFD late phase, maximal voluntary isometric force (MVIC), serum creatine kinase (CK), quadriceps swelling, and muscle soreness for up to 72 hours, with full recovery generally observed within 4 days, while the early phase of RVFD remains unaffected. The RVFD late phase is suggested as an additional sensitive marker of eccentric-induced muscle damage in trail running.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Downhill Running (eccentric exercise)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: A single 30-minute downhill run was performed at 10 km/h with a -20% (-11.3°) decline on a motorized treadmill. Effects were monitored for up to 4 days, with full recovery generally observed by day 4. No dose-response comparisons were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased significantly (p < 0.05), peaking at POST24 (613   ± 394% of PRE values), remaining elevated at POST48 (232   ± 118% of PRE values), and fully resolved after 4 days (p > 0.05).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: An enzyme released into the bloodstream from damaged muscle cells, indicating muscle fiber damage and disruption of myonuclei.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Post-downhill running session (peaked at 24 hours, elevated up to 48 hours post-bout).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: A traditional and classic biochemical indicator confirming muscle fiber damage due to eccentric exercise.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the time course of cell-free DNA (cfDNA) and conventional muscle damage markers in response to mechanically demanding muscle-damaging drop jump exercise without significant metabolic stress in healthy males. It found that cfDNA levels increased acutely and with a delayed response up to 72 hours post-exercise, correlating strongly with primary muscle damage indicators (low-frequency fatigue, MVIC torque, P20/P100 torque) and delayed-onset muscle soreness. This suggests cfDNA is a sensitive marker for acute loss of muscle function after mechanical stress, offering insights into primary and secondary muscle damage responses.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Muscle-damaging exercise (Drop Jumps)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Fourteen participants performed 50 intermittent drop jumps once, from heights of approximately 0.5 m (ranging from 30.37 ± 5.55 cm to 36.39 ± 6.83 cm) with 20-second rest intervals between each jump. This protocol was designed to be mechanically demanding, inducing sufficient primary and secondary muscle damage, without placing the organism under significant metabolic stress. No dose-response comparisons were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased from 2.22 ± 0.29 to 2.31 ± 0.24 IU/L (log10 scale) at 90 min post-exercise (P < 0.05), to 2.62 ± 0.26 IU/L at 6 h post-exercise (P < 0.001), and peaked at 12 h post-exercise (2.77 ± 0.28 IU/L, log10 scale, P < 0.001). Levels did not return to baseline by the end of the experiment (96 hours).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: An enzyme involved in energy metabolism within muscle cells; its presence in plasma indicates muscle cell membrane integrity disruption, typically linked to secondary muscle damage (structural changes to muscle fibers).
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: After muscle-damaging drop jump exercise, peaking at 12 hours post-exercise.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: A widely accepted marker of muscle damage, but showed no significant correlation with cfDNA or LFF in this study, suggesting a poor relationship with functional outcomes. It represents secondary muscle damage.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated sex differences in biomarkers of end-organ damage (Creatinine (CR), estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate (eGFR), Creatine Kinase (CK), Alanine-Transaminase (ALT), and Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST)) and their time course following exertional heat stroke (EHS) in 62 active-duty service members. Findings indicate that women exhibited significantly lower peak values for kidney (CR) and muscle (CK) damage biomarkers compared to men, with ALT and AST also being similar or lower in women during recovery, suggesting women may be less susceptible to organ injury from EHS despite similar recorded core temperatures or potential higher actual peak temperatures due to pre-measurement cooling.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Exertional Heat Stroke (EHS) and subsequent active cooling interventions
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study focused on Exertional Heat Stroke (EHS) events where individuals received active cooling interventions (ice sheets, cold-water immersion, chilled saline) prehospital and en route to the emergency department. While recorded peak body core temperatures were similar between sexes (women: 41.11°C (40.06, 41.67); men: 41.11°C (40.28, 41.72), P = 0.57), active cooling was initiated prior to temperature recording more frequently in women (91%) than men (57%), suggesting actual peak temperatures might have been higher for women. No specific dose-response comparisons for EHS severity or cooling interventions were reported.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: lower at peak, but sex effect disappears with control for variables
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Women had significantly lower peak CK (584 U·L−1) compared to men (2,183 U·L−1, P = 0.02). However, this sex difference became non-significant when controlling for age, height, and weight, suggesting it may be related to muscle mass. No sex differences observed in time points or mean difference from upper limit when controlling for variables; only men statistically exceeded their upper limit.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Enzyme primarily found in muscle cells, involved in energy production, and indicates muscle damage when elevated in blood.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Post-exertional heat stroke (EHS) in otherwise healthy humans (military personnel) during acute phase and recovery.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates severity of muscle damage; lower peak levels in women, potentially due to lower muscle mass, suggest less severe muscle injury post-EHS, contributing to shorter hospitalization.

document_context_data.document_summary: This systematic review aimed to synthesize and analyze scientific evidence on biomarkers used for monitoring chronic fatigue and physiological responses to training and competition loads in professional male team sport athletes. It synthesizes evidence across 28 studies, covering muscle damage markers, anabolic/catabolic hormones, inflammatory markers, immunological markers, and oxidative stress markers. The review concluded that professional team sports induce significant alterations in these biomarkers, reflecting physiological strain, muscle damage, oxidative stress, inflammation, and immunosuppression, with effects generally larger and more prolonged after official matches than training. It emphasizes that a comprehensive analysis of these biomarkers provides a holistic understanding crucial for managing athlete fatigue, optimizing performance, and mitigating risks of overtraining, injury, or disease. The review also highlights the importance of establishing sex-specific reference ranges and monitoring strategies for biomarkers.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Physiological loads from intensive training and competition in professional male team sports.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The systematic review analyzed responses to varying physiological loads experienced by professional male team sport athletes during official matches and training sessions across competitive seasons (e.g., 4-week intensive training, 6-month seasons, 12-week periods, consecutive matches over 1-week). Biomarker data was collected from sports including basketball, soccer, handball, futsal, rugby, Australian football, volleyball, netball, and water-polo. Responses were generally larger and more prolonged after official matches compared to training, with recovery times ranging from 24 hours to several days post-exercise. The review also considered the impact of congested fixture schedules, high-intensity efforts, and sports with high eccentric loads, noting variability based on playing position, game time, and specific sporting discipline, but did not provide specific quantitative doses for training or matches.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher, with significant sustained elevations post-exercise, peaking at 24-48 hours. Increases were 26-27% with a smallest worthwhile change of 8.6%, and significant changes of 266 μ/L during preseason with higher training load (p<0.05). Changes vary by exercise type, intensity, duration, and evaluation time, and evidence for chronic load changes is moderate. Responses may differ in females.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Enzyme released from damaged muscle cells, indicating muscle cell damage and breakdown and is an enzyme indicative of muscle damage.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Physiological loads from intensive training and competition (official matches, training sessions, preseason with higher loads, congested schedules, high eccentric loads) in professional male team sport athletes. Acute (24-72h post-activity) and chronic training load, exercise-induced muscle damage, and chronic fatigue monitoring.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Sensitive tool for detecting acute muscle damage and physiological load, quantifying biochemical responses to training load changes. Useful for monitoring physical state, training-related stress, strain, recovery, and wellness to identify early fatigue and potential overtraining, and to adjust training/recovery programs. Less reliable for chronic load monitoring due to variability, and interpretation requires consideration of sex differences.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of 2-week hemp fiber (high and low doses) or placebo supplementation on post-exercise gut permeability and plasma metabolite shifts in healthy male and female cyclists after intensive cycling. While hemp fiber did not significantly alter post-exercise gut permeability (measured by urine sugar data), untargeted metabolomics revealed that the combination of hemp fiber intake and vigorous exercise increased beneficial gut-derived metabolites and influenced pathways related to tryptophan, primary bile acid, steroid, sphingolipid, alpha-linolenic acid, arginine and proline, lipid, and amino acid metabolism.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Dietary supplementation with hemp fiber (hemp hull powder) combined with intensive cycling exercise.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants received daily supplementation for 2 weeks with either a high dose (20 g/d) or low dose (5 g/d) of hemp hull powder, or a placebo (0 g/d). Each supplementation period concluded with a 2.25-hour intensive cycling bout performed at approximately 70% VO2max. While distinct metabolomic shifts were observed between the hemp fiber and placebo groups (R2Y = 0.987 and 0.995), no significant dose-response for gut permeability was reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased post-exercise in all groups (p < 0.001), but no significant trial differences were found between supplementation groups.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Enzyme involved in muscle energy metabolism and cellular energy; elevated levels typically indicate muscle damage.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Post-2.25 h intensive cycling, following 2-week hemp fiber (high/low dose) or placebo supplementation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of muscle damage level; the increase reflects exercise-induced muscle damage, but hemp fiber had no effect on post-exercise muscle damage differences.

document_context_data.document_summary: This sportomics study investigated the metabolic, immune, hormonal, and amino acid responses, alongside muscle and liver injury markers, in two elite female Olympic beach volleyball athletes during a simulated competition day involving two matches. Key findings revealed significant acute physiological impacts, including electrolyte disturbances (notably hypokalemia), 20-60% increases in muscle injury markers and up to 50% for liver enzymes, elevated stress hormones (ACTH up to 4-fold, cortisol up to 3-fold), and altered energy metabolism and amino acid profiles indicative of central fatigue risk (e.g., Fischer ratio and tryptophan decreased by 60%, serotonin increased by 180%). The study emphasized distinct individual recovery kinetics, highlighted the inadequacy of short recovery sessions, and advocated for personalized monitoring due to varied biomarker responses despite similar external loads.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Simulated Beach Volleyball Competition
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Two world-class female athletes participated in a simulated competition day involving two high-intensity beach volleyball matches (a two-set match in the morning and a three-set match in the afternoon), under identical environmental conditions. Blood and urine samples were collected at seven time points: pre-match, post-match, 60 minutes after each match (short recovery), and after a 15-hour long recovery. The protocol included 15-minute warm-ups. No dose-response comparisons were explicitly reported; however, individual responses to the same protocol were highlighted, and short recovery sessions were found to be inadequate for full physiological recovery, with the second match demonstrating cumulative strain.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased significantly post-exercise, with 20-45% increases after the first match and 35-60% increases after the second match. Levels remained elevated by ~20% at the end of the protocol, showing incomplete normalization during short recovery sessions; increased to concentrations above post-match 1 after the second match.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Enzyme found in muscle; elevated levels indicate myocyte damage and muscle integrity.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Simulated beach volleyball competition (post-match, recovery), cumulative strain from consecutive matches.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates muscle microinjury and damage, and incomplete recovery from exercise loads; associated with low exercise tolerance, pre-clinical injury, and overtraining syndrome.

document_context_data.document_summary: This literature review comprehensively investigates the various factors contributing to creatine kinase (CK) variability following different exercise modalities. It highlights the significant influence of exercise type, intensity, gender differences, body composition, individual characteristics (e.g., fitness level, training history, genetic predispositions), and recovery strategies on CK levels. The study emphasizes understanding these variations for optimizing training, enhancing recovery, preventing overuse injuries and overtraining, and the necessity of individualized CK reference values for accurate interpretation of muscle damage.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Exercise
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The review examines creatine kinase variability across a wide range of exercise modalities, including high-intensity and low-intensity activities, eccentric and concentric contractions, varying velocities, and different rest intervals. Specific exercise types discussed include resistance training (high-intensity, high-volume, eccentric), aerobic exercises (endurance running), high-intensity interval training (HIIT), maximal eccentric knee extensions, downhill running, Ironman-distance triathlon, active skiing, and workloads in team sports. Higher intensities and eccentric contractions generally induce greater CK elevations, while moderate intensities and aerobic exercise result in lower variability. The document notes that specific quantitative dose-response comparisons for defined exercise protocols are not consistently reported, but it discusses how these factors influence CK response variability. Repeated bouts of eccentric exercise were observed to attenuate subsequent CK elevations.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Highly variable; generally higher following intense or unaccustomed exercise, higher in males than females, and higher with greater muscle mass or BMI; lower with moderate intensity exercise, aerobic exercise, and higher fitness levels, or with repeated bouts of eccentric exercise. Females show a faster return to baseline compared to males.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Exhibits substantial elevations, peaking 2-6 days post-insult, with increases up to 100% baseline, or prolonged increases ranging from 300-6000 IU/L (high-intensity/high-volume resistance exercise), up to 5.5 times baseline or 900 U/L (typical gym exercises), and potentially reaching 33-fold baseline in untrained individuals after acute exercise. Males exhibit significantly higher post-exercise CK activities (e.g., baseline 139 U/L) compared to females (baseline 81 U/L), though females may show a greater relative increase. Variability can be substantial (e.g., 50-58% intra-individual, up to 75% between teammates). Resting CK values are higher in trained individuals; a decrease in CK variability was observed after 3 weeks of training.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Creatine Kinase (CK) is an enzyme primarily found in muscle cells, serving as the most sensitive indicator of muscle damage, stress, and fiber disruption. Its presence and levels in the bloodstream reflect muscle function, damage, and repair. It is influenced by physiological sex differences (muscle mass, estrogen), individual adaptive capacities, fitness level, training history, and recovery mechanisms. Nearly all CK activity in normal plasma is derived from skeletal muscle, making it important in the diagnosis of muscle disease.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Post-exercise, particularly following high-intensity, high-volume, or unaccustomed exercise involving eccentric muscle contractions (Exercise-Induced Muscle Damage - EIMD). This includes various modalities such as resistance training, high-intensity interval training (HIIT), endurance activities (e.g., Ironman-distance triathlon, downhill running, endurance running), maximal eccentric knee extensions, active skiing, youth soccer, early-season boxing training, and general workloads in team sports. Its response is modulated by training status, genetic predisposition, prior exposure to eccentric exercise, and individual body composition (muscle mass, BMI, body fat percentage).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Creatine Kinase (CK) levels indicate the extent of muscle damage, stress, and microtrauma, with higher levels suggesting greater damage. Understanding CK variability is crucial for optimizing training programs, enhancing recovery strategies, preventing overuse injuries, overtraining, and guiding personalized recovery. It is associated with impairments in athletic performance and an increased risk of injury. It helps in developing gender-specific training and recovery protocols, considering physiological sex differences and body composition. Furthermore, individualized CK reference values are critical for accurate assessment of muscle damage and recovery, and higher fitness levels are linked to better management of exercise-induced muscle damage. CK also aids in the diagnosis of muscle disease.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the impact of 4 weeks of Urolithin A (UA) supplementation on running performance, recovery, and mitochondrial biomarkers in highly trained male distance runners during an altitude training camp. Findings showed that UA supplementation significantly lowered post-exercise muscle damage (Creatine Kinase tAUC after a 3000 m time trial) and ratings of perceived exertion, while also showing a large within-group increase in VO2max. Proteomic analysis revealed UA upregulated mitochondrial pathways and downregulating inflammatory pathways in skeletal muscle. However, UA did not significantly improve 3000 m running performance directly. The study also assessed physiological adaptations including running economy, body composition, and hemoglobin mass.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Urolithin A (UA) supplementation combined with altitude training and structured exercise challenges.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Competitive male distance runners received 1000 mg/day of Urolithin A or placebo for 4 weeks, concurrent with an intensified altitude training camp (~1700–2200 m). The regimen included weekly downhill running bouts and 3000 m time trials. No dose-response comparisons for UA were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: UA supplementation significantly reduced the 24-hour total area under the curve (tAUC) for CK after a 3000 m time trial compared with placebo (p < 0.0001). However, no significant treatment effect was observed for the total CK response after downhill running (p = 0.137).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Indirect marker of muscle damage and integrity, released into blood upon muscle damage.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Post-exercise muscle damage following a 3000m time trial and downhill running bouts during an altitude training camp, after 4 weeks of UA supplementation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates level of muscle damage; associated with facilitated recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage.

document_context_data.document_summary: A longitudinal study investigated hematological responses and hydration status in NCAA Division I American football players with sickle cell trait (SCT) compared to controls (CON) over a two-year period, encompassing an entire athletic season and pre-season training. The study found that SCT players exhibited altered hematological profiles, including higher red cell distribution width (RDW), elevated serum uric acid, and greater creatine kinase (CPK) levels at pre-camp and throughout the season. Furthermore, SCT players showed altered hydration status with lower pre- and post-practice urine electrolytes and specific gravity, but higher sweat sodium, potassium, and chloride concentrations, indicating differences in fluid balance and electrolyte regulation during intensive training. These findings suggest potential implications for kidney function and muscle damage in SCT players during long-term conditioning and highlight the importance of careful hydration management.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Collegiate American Football Training and Competition (Observational Study)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This longitudinal study observed NCAA Division I American football players over two consecutive years, encompassing an entire athletic season. This involved 17 consecutive practices in year 1 and 16 practices in year 2 between pre-camp and post-camp, followed by 13 weekly in-season competitions between post-camp and post-season. Hydration status was specifically assessed during pre-season training camp practices conducted under hot and humid environmental conditions (average 26.8            1.9 °C WBGT and 68.9            11.1% relative humidity). The study focused on the physiological responses to sustained physical activity and environmental exposure inherent to standard collegiate football regimens, with no explicit dose-response comparisons for varying training intensities.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly greater in SCT players (1617.0            1034.8 IU/L) at pre-camp compared to CON (1037.4            602.8 IU/L; p = 0.03). Overall mean levels were SCT: 955.2            797.2 IU/L vs. CON: 718.1            510.2 IU/L (p = 0.03). Both groups exhibited levels 3-5 times higher than upper reference limits at all visits, especially at pre-camp.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Enzyme primarily found in muscle cells; elevated levels typically indicate muscle damage or breakdown.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: NCAA Division I American football players with sickle cell trait throughout the collegiate athletic season, particularly at pre-camp coinciding with heavy resistance training.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: May serve as an early indicator of muscle damage in SCT players, potentially increasing their risk for exertional rhabdomyolysis during intensive athletic activity. High levels are likely associated with large body weight and muscle mass in these athletes.

document_context_data.document_summary: This descriptive, cross-sectional study investigated serum biochemical markers of muscle damage, including C-Reactive Protein (CRP), Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH), total Creatine Kinase (CK), Creatine Kinase-MB (CK-MB), and the CK-MB/CK ratio, in 326 adolescent athletes (aged 13-18 years, primarily soccer players) from sports centers in Tacna, Peru. The study aimed to evaluate muscle damage and inflammation related to intense physical activity, concluding that alterations in these markers are present, with specific ranges identified for elevated markers and notable correlations (e.g., a strong positive correlation between LDH and CK-MB) among the adolescent cohort.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study of physical training and activity, specifically soccer training
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational, cross-sectional study of adolescent athletes (aged 13-18 years, including soccer players) engaging in regular, intense physical activity and competitive training for at least three months. No specific training interventions or dose-response comparisons were applied or controlled by the researchers; the study analyzed pre-existing biomarker levels influenced by the athletes' own training regimes, which involve macro and microcycles and varying intensity/duration. The study notes 'different stages of training' and 'adjustment of physical load' as influencing factors.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: 25.2% of adolescents had elevated serum values (>195 U/L, ranging from 190 to 270 U/L), while 74.8% were within normal limits (24-195 U/L); no low values were reported. Normal values are significantly elevated during physical exercise, increasing proportionally with intensity and duration. Pre-game mean values for soccer players were around 330-347 U/L, rising to 632-702 U/L post-game. Moderate correlation with LDH (r = 0.260), weak positive correlation with CRP (r = 0.237), and weak negative correlation with CK-MB (r = -0.143) were observed.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: A cytosolic enzyme primarily found in skeletal muscles and heart, also in brain. It catalyzes phosphocreatine formation and is the most common marker for muscle damage, released upon muscle cell injury.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Intense physical exercise and athletic activity in adolescent athletes, including pre-game and post-game soccer activity, leading to rupture of striated muscle fibers. Elevated values can persist at rest, with peak values typically 24-72 hours post-exercise.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Considered the primary and key indicator of muscle damage, trauma, or overtraining from intense physical activity. Useful for diagnosing injuries and monitoring recovery. Persistently elevated levels may also indicate degenerative muscle processes or neuromuscular disorders.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of various post-exercise recovery strategies (active recovery, cold water immersion, massage, and passive recovery) on subjective and objective fatigue markers in 46 recreational male runners after a competitive half-marathon. The findings indicate that cold water immersion and massage were effective in improving subjective fatigue measures, such as muscle soreness and perceived recovery/stress, compared to passive recovery. However, active recovery was largely ineffective or even detrimental, worsening subjective recovery and negatively impacting certain objective markers (creatine kinase, free-testosterone). Overall, none of the recovery interventions demonstrated beneficial effects on objective physiological markers of fatigue.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Post-exercise recovery interventions (Active Recovery (ACT), Cold Water Immersion (CWI), Massage (MAS), and Passive Recovery (PAS)) following a half-marathon race.
treatment_details.dose_specificity:
46 recreational male runners completed a competitive half-marathon (average time 107-116 min, 86.2%-92.9% of anaerobic threshold, 450 m altitude climb). Within 15 minutes post-race, a single application of one of four recovery protocols was performed: Passive Recovery (PAS) was 15 min sitting at rest; Active Recovery (ACT) was 15 min sub-maximal jogging at 60% anaerobic threshold; Cold Water Immersion (CWI) involved 15 min of lower limb immersion up to the iliac crest in 15 
	1
	C water, with circular leg motions every 2 min; and Massage (MAS) consisted of 20 min of classical sports massage (effleurage, petrissage, friction), split into 5 min per leg in prone and supine positions, performed by certified sports scientists. No dose-response comparisons for the overall half-marathon intensity or the recovery interventions were explicitly reported, though the CWI protocol was chosen based on existing dose-response evidence.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: The half-marathon itself increased CK levels. Active recovery (ACT) significantly increased CK levels compared to passive recovery (PAS) immediately post-recovery (ES = 0.42) and at 24 hours post-race (ES = 0.84), indicating a harmful effect. Cold water immersion (CWI) and massage (MAS) showed no beneficial effect on CK levels.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: An enzyme released from muscle cells into the bloodstream, serving as a primary indicator of muscle damage and metabolic stress.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Following a half-marathon race and various recovery strategies (active, cold water immersion, massage, or passive).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates the level of muscle damage and breakdown; higher levels suggest increased muscle soreness, reduced performance, and impaired physiological muscle recovery, particularly exacerbated by active recovery.

document_context_data.document_summary: This double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled study evaluated the effect of oral palmitoylethanolamide (PEA, Levagen+™) on recovery from muscle-damaging leg press exercise in 28 healthy young males. The study found that while PEA supplementation did not significantly reduce perceived muscle soreness, thigh circumference, or most inflammatory and phosphoprotein markers (Creatine Kinase, Lactate Dehydrogenase, IL-6, IL-10, hs-CRP, TNF-α, CREB, ERK1/2, JNK, NF-κB, p38 MAPK, S6K1, STAT3, STAT5), it did significantly reduce blood myoglobin and lactate concentrations. Furthermore, PEA increased Protein Kinase B phosphorylation immediately post-exercise, suggesting aid in muscle recovery through improved metabolic efficiency and activation of anabolic/repair signaling pathways from repeat bouts of exercise.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Oral Supplementation with Palmitoylethanolamide (Levagen+™) combined with Resistance Exercise
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants were randomized to consume either liquid PEA (167.5 mg Levagen+™ containing 150 mg PEA and 17.5 mg excipients, with 832.5 mg maltodextrin) or a matched placebo (1 g maltodextrin). Treatments were administered pre-exercise, immediately post-exercise, 24 h post-exercise, and 48 h post-exercise. The muscle-damaging exercise consisted of four sets of leg press at 80% of one-repetition maximum (1-RM) to volitional exhaustion, with 60s rest between sets, followed by a performance set at 70% 1-RM to maximal repetitions. No dose-response comparisons for PEA were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Peaked +24 h after leg press exercise and decreased thereafter (p < 0.05); no significant effect of PEA supplementation.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Enzyme involved in energy production in muscle; released into circulation upon muscle damage.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Leg press exercise to volitional exhaustion, with/without PEA supplementation.
