matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: A primary indicator of muscle damage.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of short-term powdered Montmorency tart cherry supplementation on markers of muscle damage, inflammation, oxidative stress, and muscle soreness in aerobically trained individuals undergoing a half-marathon run. Findings indicate that supplementation attenuated muscle catabolism (creatinine, urea/BUN, total protein), reduced physiological stress (cortisol), lessened immune and inflammatory stress (IL-2, IL-6, IL-13), better maintained redox balance (antioxidant activity, TAS), and reduced muscle soreness, ultimately enhancing endurance performance and recovery.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Powdered Montmorency tart cherry supplementation and endurance running (half-marathon race)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Subjects ingested capsules containing 480 mg of powdered Montmorency tart cherries (CherryPURE®) once daily for 10 days (7 days pre-race, race day, and 2 days post-race), compared to a 480 mg rice flour placebo. This 480 mg supplement is equivalent to 51.3 mL (17.4 fl oz) of tart cherry juice, providing 991 mg of phenolic compounds and 66 mg of anthocyanins. The intervention was evaluated in the context of a stressful endurance challenge: a half-marathon run (21.1 km). No dose-response comparisons were reported, but the supplementation significantly affected physiological responses and race performance compared to placebo.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No differences in the CK response between tart cherry supplementation and placebo were reported in the current study.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Enzyme primarily found in muscle cells, involved in energy production, and indicates muscle damage or injury when elevated in blood.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Acute endurance exercise recovery with tart cherry supplementation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates muscle damage level (though no significant change was observed with tart cherry in this specific study).

document_context_data.document_summary: This case report investigates the association between high-intensity, short-duration exercise and elevated cardiac troponin I (cTnI) levels in a 29-year-old recreationally active female with chronic energy restriction. Clinically significant cTnI elevations, indicative of myocardial stress or damage, were observed, while creatine kinase levels did not suggest significant skeletal muscle damage. The findings suggest that individuals with habitually low energy availability may be more susceptible to exercise-induced cardiac stress, highlighting the importance of considering energy balance for risk stratification.

treatment_details.therapy_type: High-intensity Interval Training (HIIT) / Repeated sprint anaerobic exercise
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The therapy involved short-duration, high-intensity repeated sprint protocols (8 x 8-s Wingate Anaerobic Test) performed on a cycle ergometer across two trials. Braking force was applied relative to total body mass (Trial 1) or relative to fat-free mass (Trial 2). No explicit dose-response comparisons for different braking forces were reported regarding biomarker changes, with the focus being on the response to this specific type of exercise in the context of low energy availability.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: unchanged; lower (in females compared to males)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: CK serum concentrations did not change through time (P = .984) in response to high-intensity cycling exercise; the adjusted R2 value for the model was 21.72%. Females had lower mean serum CK levels than males (95% CI -0.256 to -0.139 IU/L [transformed units]; P < .001).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Indicator of muscle damage (skeletal or cardiac); helps differentiate between skeletal and cardiac damage.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: High-intensity cycling exercise; gender comparison of resting levels.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates no significant level of skeletal muscle damage had occurred in response to the high-intensity cycling exercise. Lower resting CK levels in females compared to males are commonly observed, potentially due to differences in muscle mass and general physical activity levels.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the relationship between routine plasma biomarker levels and recovery efficiency in elite professional soccer players over an entire eleven-month competitive match season, including seasonal variations and differences based on player position and cumulative match time. It concluded that a panel of AST, CK, LDH, and creatinine can effectively monitor recovery, adaptation, and overtraining risk, particularly in active positions like midfielders who may also be prone to iron and magnesium deficiencies.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Competitive professional soccer matches and regular intense training
treatment_details.dose_specificity: An eleven-month competitive season, comprising 44 league and cup matches (23 autumn, 21 spring), typically one to two matches per week. Fasting capillary blood samples were collected 17-24 hours after each match. The study compared player positions (midfielder/defender vs. goalie/substitute, and individual midfielder/defender subgroups), noting significant differences in cumulative match time and physical demands. No explicit dose-response comparisons were reported for training intensity, but adaptation to increasing training load was observed.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: increased significantly over time, higher in spring vs. autumn, decreased in goalie/substitutes
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: While no significant differences were found between player groups, CK activity generally increased significantly over time, especially in the spring round for midfielder/defender groups and midfielders. It showed a slight but significant positive correlation with cumulative match-time in midfielder/defender groups (R=0.14-0.17, P<=0.05) and for midfielders (R=0.30, P<=0.05) and defenders (R=0.23, P<=0.05) over the entire season. In contrast, it decreased with time in the goalie/substitute group (R=-0.22 to -0.23, P<=0.05). It is generally expected to be permanently elevated in professional soccer players and usually increases after 24-36 hours of strenuous exercise.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: An enzyme involved in energy metabolism and production in muscle cells, serving as a primary marker of muscle damage, cellular necrosis, and tissue integrity following acute and chronic muscle injuries. It also indicates metabolic stress.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Throughout an eleven-month professional competitive soccer match season, encompassing daily training, strenuous exercise, and post-match recovery (17-24 hours post-match). Observations were made across different player positions (midfielder/defender, goalie/substitute, individual midfielder and defender subgroups), considering cumulative game time and seasonal variations (autumn vs. spring rounds).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: A valuable and useful marker for monitoring recovery periods, reflecting muscle damage levels, cumulative muscle damage, and physiological stress from intense muscular effort. However, due to its large interindividual variability and constant elevation in professional soccer players, it might be unsuitable as a sole parameter for monitoring the recovery process. It contributes to assessing recovery efficiency, adaptation, and diminishing the risk of overreaching or injury.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the changes in biochemical markers of oxidative stress and muscle damage, along with psychomotor abilities (divided attention, handgrip strength, and strength differentiation), in 15 special unit soldiers undergoing a 48-hour military survival training program combined with sleep deprivation. The findings indicated that the training did not cause oxidative stress or muscle tissue damage, improved divided attention, but suggested a potential deterioration in motor control.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Military survival training (SERE training)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: 15 special unit soldiers underwent 48 hours of military survival training (SERE) combined with significant sleep deprivation (no sleep for the first 24h, 3h total for the subsequent 24h), psychological burden, and carrying 15kg equipment over an average of 6km, performed at 4-11°C. Measurements (biochemical markers, divided attention, maximal handgrip strength, and strength differentiation) were taken at baseline (P1), after 24 hours (P2), and after 48 hours (P3). No dose-response comparisons were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Initial low level at baseline; no significant changes observed throughout the 48-hour survival training (p > 0.05).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: An enzyme primarily found in muscle cells; elevated levels in blood typically indicate muscle damage or injury.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: 48-hour military survival training combined with sleep deprivation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Absence of increase indicates no significant muscle tissue damage or injury occurred during the training period.

document_context_data.document_summary: The study investigated the test-retest reliability and suitability of various subjective, muscle force, and blood-based physiological markers (including oxidative stress markers, hormones, cytokines, and haematological parameters) for monitoring exercise response and recovery processes in endurance athletes after strenuous endurance exercise bouts, concluding that TBARS and IL-1RA exhibited the best reliability and suitability.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Continuous Endurance Running Field Tests (RFTs)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Two identical 60-minute continuous endurance running field tests (RFTs) were performed, separated by a four-week recovery period. The exercise protocol involved 40 minutes of running at an intensity corresponding to 95% of Heart Rate (HR) at Individual Anaerobic Threshold (IAT), followed by 20 minutes at 110% of HR at IAT to ensure exhaustion. Biomarkers were measured before, immediately after, 3 hours after, and 24 hours after each bout. No dose-response comparisons for varying exercise intensities or durations were reported, but reliability was compared between trained and untrained subgroups.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: increased, delayed peak, lower reliability in trained
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased immediately after exercise, further increased 3 hours after, and continued to increase 24 hours after compared to pre-exercise levels (F1.44 = 153.09; p < 0.001). Peak of CK values was somewhat delayed at 24 h after RFTs. Demonstrated moderate reliability (ICC = 0.64), with poor reliability in trained individuals (ICC = 0.49) and good in untrained (ICC = 0.84). Correlated with MVC knee extension and flexion (r values between 0.27 and 0.40, p < 0.05). Significant associations to MVC were also found generally.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Enzyme primarily found in muscle, elevated levels indicate muscle fiber damage; diagnostic marker for detecting exercise-induced muscle disruption or increased cell permeability; marker for determination of muscular damage.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: After 60-min continuous endurance exercise bouts; released in response to muscle fiber damage; endurance running field tests (RFTs) and subsequent recovery phases; after eccentric or unaccustomed exercise.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates muscle damage level and is exercise-sensitive, highly correlated to MVC values. However, its moderate reliability (especially poor in trained individuals), high interindividual variability, and delayed peak complicate its practical use and association with muscular fatigue and recovery processes.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effect of D-ribose supplementation on delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) induced by plyometric exercise in untrained male college students. Findings indicate that oral administration of 15g D-ribose reduced muscle soreness, improved knee extensor function by mitigating strength reduction, lowered muscle damage markers (Creatine Kinase, Lactate Dehydrogenase, Myoglobin), and inhibited lipid peroxidation (Malondialdehyde), thereby accelerating DOMS recovery. However, D-ribose showed no significant effect on overall isokinetic muscle strength (flexor peak torque and total work) and modulated the time-course of antioxidant enzymes (Superoxide Dismutase) and total antioxidant capacity (TAC) without consistently showing a superior antioxidant effect compared to placebo after 48 hours.

treatment_details.therapy_type: D-ribose supplementation combined with plyometric exercise
treatment_details.dose_specificity: D-ribose was orally administered at 15g per dose, 1-hour before, and 1-hour, 12-hours, 24-hours, and 36-hours after exercise. A calorically equivalent placebo containing sorbitol and β-cyclodextrin was given at the same dose and times. The plyometric exercise protocol consisted of 7 sets of 20 consecutive frog hops with 90-second rest intervals between sets, performed twice with a 14-day washout period. No dose-response comparisons for D-ribose were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased significantly in both groups after 24-h (p < 0.01) and 48-h (p < 0.01). CK was significantly lower in the DRIB group after 24-h compared to the PLAC group (p < 0.01), with PLAC levels not returning to baseline within 48-h.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Enzyme primarily found in skeletal muscle, its leakage into blood indicates muscle cell membrane damage and sarcolemma integrity compromise.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Post-plyometric exercise muscle damage and D-ribose supplementation effect on recovery.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Lower levels in DRIB indicate reduced muscle cell damage and accelerated restoration of membrane integrity, signifying faster muscle recovery.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of 4-week oral garlic supplementation on 40-km cycling time trial performance, whole-body energy metabolism, exercise-induced oxidative stress, inflammation, and muscle damage in healthy adult males. Findings indicate that garlic supplementation significantly enhanced total antioxidant capacity and attenuated oxidative stress (MDA), inflammatory response (TNF-α), and some markers of muscle damage (LDH and UA at specific time points), but it did not improve cycling performance or overall whole-body energy metabolism.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Oral garlic extract supplementation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: 1000 mg/day for 4 weeks (28 consecutive days) in a single-blind crossover design. No dose-response comparisons were reported, as a single dose was used.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant differences between garlic and placebo groups (p > 0.05), though levels increased post-exercise in both groups.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: An enzyme released from skeletal muscle cells, serving as a blood marker indicative of muscle damage.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: 4-wk garlic supplementation during a 40-km cycling challenge
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: No observed attenuation of exercise-induced muscle damage by garlic supplementation, despite its role as a key indicator for muscle fiber damage and high-intensity endurance performance.

document_context_data.document_summary: This review comprehensively investigates the potentials, pitfalls, and practical applications of blood-based biomarkers for objective individualized monitoring of training load, recovery, and health status in elite sports. It evaluates the utility and limitations of established markers like creatine kinase (CK), lactate, C-reactive protein (CRP), urea, myoglobin, and various leukocyte populations, detailing their physiological responses to acute and chronic exercise, kinetics, and implications for muscle damage, immune function, and inflammation. The document also addresses methodological considerations, confounding variables, the need for individual reference ranges, and statistical approaches for interpreting biomarker changes, concluding with recommendations for best practices in their sport-specific use.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Blood-based biomarker monitoring in conjunction with physical exercise and training load management in elite sports.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This review focuses on the application and interpretation of blood-based biomarkers for athlete monitoring across various exercise loads, including strenuous, resistance, high-intensity, submaximal, acute physical stress, soccer matches, ultradistance races, and long-term intensive endurance exercise. Biomarker responses are noted to depend on exercise modality, intensity, duration, and individual factors such as ethnicity and body composition. While specific exercise regimens like 30 minutes of endurance running (65% vs 85% of VO2max) showed CRP increases, no single standardized dose-response is consistently reported or compared across all biomarkers. The document emphasizes the need for individual reference levels, standardized collection, and careful consideration of confounding variables, particularly in managing workload by adjusting training when physiological parameters exceed baseline.

matched_biomarker_details.activity_type: Enzyme catalytic activity, Protein Level (Damage Marker)

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher, delayed and diminished, accelerated decrease, blunted, increased, drastically increase, peak (24-120h post-exercise), significant change
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher levels are commonly observed after unaccustomed exercises, peaking between 24-120 hours post-exercise, with reported levels exceeding 3000 U·L−1 after maximal resistance training (clinical abnormality is 3000-5000 U·L−1). A 23-h bedrest or lymphatic drainage can delay/diminish or accelerate its decrease, respectively. Blunted responses are seen after repeated eccentric contractions. Ethnicity and impact trauma also influence levels. Changes of at least 50 U·L−1 are considered meaningful (typical error 25 U·L−1). CK levels correlate with performance changes (e.g., sprint distance) during acute intermittent exercise and indirectly reflect tissue-specific muscle damage.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Catalyzes the reversible reaction of phosphocreatine to re-phosphorylate ADP to ATP, serving as an indicator of muscle stress and damage, particularly after exercise.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Unaccustomed exercises (especially eccentric contractions), strenuous exercise, acute intermittent exercise, maximal resistance exercise training, long runs (e.g., 18-km cross-country), bedrest, lymphatic drainage, impact trauma, and workload management in elite athletes, typically monitored during and days following exercise.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Frequently used as an indirect marker of muscle damage, estimating retrospective internal load, reflecting recovery, or indicating readiness for new loads. Levels >3000 U·L−1 may indicate acute kidney injury risk. Its utility for load management and as a validated surrogate for fatigue or injury risk is limited by enzyme inactivation, influencing factors (ethnicity, body composition), and a poor relationship with functional outcomes. However, it can detect meaningful changes beyond measurement error and is relevant for understanding muscle soreness.

document_context_data.document_summary: This systematic review evaluates the effects of soy protein (SP) supplementation on muscle adaptations, metabolic and antioxidant status, hormonal response, and exercise performance in active individuals and athletes, often comparing it to whey protein or placebo. The review encompasses studies on protein synthesis, amino acid transport, and signaling pathways, highlighting that while some anabolic markers might be less favorable with soy, it can provide similar increases in lean mass to whey protein, especially at optimal protein intakes. SP is shown to reduce exercise-induced metabolic/blood circulating biomarkers (triglycerides, uric acid, lactate) and improve antioxidant capacity, reducing oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation. However, its effects on hormonal responses, such as testosterone and cortisol, are inconsistent or contradictory across studies. SP supplementation also demonstrates potential benefits in improving various exercise performance indicators, including high-intensity running, maximal cardiac output, delaying fatigue, improving isometric strength, running velocity, and muscle recovery after damage. The review concludes that SP can be a viable alternative to conventional protein supplements, but emphasizes the need for further research addressing methodological limitations and consistent dosing.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Soy Protein and Soy Peptide Supplementation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The review encompassed a wide range of soy protein (SP) and soy peptide supplementation protocols, from acute doses (e.g., 15-20g SP, 18g SP beverage, 10g essential amino acids from soy) to chronic daily intakes varying from 0.5 g/kg BW/day to 90 g/day (e.g., 33-40 g/day, 1 g/kg BW/day, 53.3 g/day). Doses were often combined with carbohydrates (e.g., 10g soy peptide + 30g sugar, 15g SP + 52.5g CHO) or matched for nitrogen/leucine content for comparison with whey protein. Durations ranged from single acute sessions to long-term interventions of 2 weeks, 4 weeks, 6 weeks, 9 weeks, 4 months, or even "12 weeks. Comparisons were consistently made against whey protein, soy-dairy blends, isoenergetic placebos, or control (exercise-only) groups. While some studies aimed for optimal protein intakes ("  1.6 g/kg BW/day), there was a notable lack of consistent dosing or explicit dose-response comparisons across the reviewed literature, indicating significant variability in intervention designs.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Reduced serum levels after a month of soy peptides supplementation and lower in SP+sugar group after 4 weeks of strenuous training compared to placebo. However, it stayed elevated after speed endurance training (no significant mitigation by acute SP or whey) and showed no meaningful differences during a 60 min stress test. Improved recovery profile (faster return to baseline) after exercise-induced muscle damage.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: An enzyme released into the blood when muscle is damaged, serving as a marker for muscle injury.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Soy peptides/protein supplementation (acute to 4 weeks/1 month) following various exercises (moderate resistance, speed-endurance, strenuous training, EIMD); 60 min stress test.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates reduced exercise-induced muscle damage and faster recovery in some contexts, but also situations where SP had no significant protective effect on acute muscle damage.

document_context_data.document_summary: The study identified a robust signature of 40 novel and reproducible plasma and serum protein biomarkers associated with Spinal and Bulbar Muscular Atrophy (SBMA) in multiple human cohorts and AR113Q mouse models. These proteins, many of which are muscle-enriched, correlated with clinical severity and functional traits, outperformed existing clinical markers like CK, and showed mechanistic links to androgen receptor gene regulation and muscle pathology, indicating their potential as early predictors of treatment effects and for tracking disease progression.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Biomarker Discovery and Disease Characterization (Observational Study)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was primarily an observational study focused on biomarker identification and disease characterization in Spinal and Bulbar Muscular Atrophy (SBMA) across human patient cohorts and AR113Q mouse models. No therapeutic interventions or dose comparisons were conducted. Plasma and serum samples were collected from SBMA patients and healthy controls, with protein levels measured using targeted proteomic approaches (Olink platforms). Longitudinal plasma samples were also collected from male AR113Q mice (12-28 weeks of age), and secondary mechanistic analyses included public data from female mice treated with Dihydrotestosterone (DHT) to investigate AR links.

matched_biomarker_details.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Plasma, Serum (Fluid from clinical laboratory test)
matched_biomarker_details.activity_type: Enzyme Activity / Protein Level (Clinical Laboratory Test)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly different between SBMA and controls (P_adj < 0.05). However, exhibited variability across patient cohorts and inconsistent associations with clinical characteristics; generally failed to track disease progression. Did not correlate with any functional readout in patients with SBMA.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Enzyme involved in energy metabolism within muscle cells. Common clinical marker, typically indicative of muscle damage.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Existing fluid biomarker used in SBMA clinical studies. Assessed in adult male patients with SBMA compared to age-matched healthy controls (NIH cohort).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Clinical biomarker for neuromuscular disorders; indicates muscle damage but has lower sensitivity, higher variability, and limited utility for tracking disease progression or correlating with functional outcomes in SBMA compared to novel biomarkers.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of pre- versus post-exercise branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) supplementation on muscle recovery, delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS), inflammatory markers (IL-6, CRP), muscle damage indicators (CK), and neuromuscular performance (CMJ) after resistance training in healthy untrained males. Resistance training induced DOMS and elevated inflammatory factors and muscle proteins. Post-exercise BCAA supplementation was generally more effective than pre-exercise supplementation in alleviating DOMS symptoms and reducing inflammatory factors (IL-6, CRP). While some findings indicated BCAA supplementation, particularly post-exercise, could reduce muscle soreness and inflammation markers, other analyses noted no significant effect on neuromuscular recovery (CMJ) or blood lactate levels, and mixed findings for CK between specific timing comparisons.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) supplementation combined with resistance training
treatment_details.dose_specificity: BCAA capsules at 40 mg/kg with a leucine:isoleucine:valine ratio of 2:1:1. Supplementation was administered either 30 minutes before resistance training or immediately after. The resistance training program, lasting one hour, included 90% 10RM weighted knee extensions, vertical jumps, and continuous frog jumps, designed to induce delayed-onset muscle soreness. The study focused on comparing the timing of BCAA intake (pre- vs. post-exercise) rather than varying the BCAA dosage.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: lower (overall BCAA vs. placebo), but unchanged (between BCAA timing groups)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Resistance training induced elevated CK levels, peaking at 30 min to 24 hr. Serum CK was significantly lower in the BCAA group overall compared to the placebo group at 30 min (p < .05), 24 hr (p < .001), and 48 hr (p < .001) of recovery. However, no significant difference was found specifically between pre- and post-exercise BCAA supplementation timings for CK levels.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: An enzyme primarily found in muscle tissue; elevated levels in the bloodstream indicate muscle damage and sarcolemma integrity compromise.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Recovery after resistance training (including deep squats) with BCAA supplementation, comparing overall BCAA effect to placebo and specific timing (pre/post).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates muscle damage level and injury; overall BCAA supplementation may mitigate this, but timing (pre/post) did not show differential effects on CK in this study.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of acute and long-term (16 weeks) heavy resistance exercise, with and without angiotensin II type I receptor blocker (losartan) supplementation, on serum C-terminal agrin fragment (CAF) levels in healthy older men. The findings indicate that 16 weeks of exercise alone did not affect CAF, but losartan supplementation led to an increase in CAF levels. Conversely, a single bout of heavy resistance exercise acutely lowered serum CAF. The study emphasizes drug interaction and the timing of blood sampling relative to exercise as crucial factors influencing CAF turnover and interpretation in neuromuscular research.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Heavy resistance exercise and Angiotensin II Type I Receptor Blocker (Losartan)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Acute exercise (1EX) consisted of a single bout of unilateral heavy resistance exercise targeting the quadriceps muscles (5 sets of 12 concentric repetitions at 70% 1RM followed by 4 sets of 6 eccentric repetitions at 110% 1RM). Losartan (100 mg daily) or placebo was administered from Day -10 to Day 7 for 1EX. Long-term exercise (48EX) involved 48 sessions over 16 weeks (3 sessions/week) of progressive heavy resistance exercise, with loads gradually increasing from 67% to 86% of 1RM, 3 to 5 sets, and 15 to 6 repetitions. Losartan for 48EX was 50 mg/day for the first week, then 100 mg/day for the remaining 15 weeks. No dose-response comparisons were reported for either exercise or medication regarding biomarker outcomes.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Higher post-acute exercise; unchanged relative to CAF 1 day post-exercise.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased significantly by 4.5 h (p < 0.05) and 1 day (p < 0.0005) after acute exercise, peaked by Day 4 (p < 0.05), and remained elevated until Day 7 (p < 0.05). No correlation to CAF levels 1 day post-exercise (p > 0.05).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Enzyme crucial for cellular energy metabolism, released into the bloodstream as a marker of muscle fiber damage or injury.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Acute heavy resistance exercise bout (1EX), up to 7 days post-exercise.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Serves as a surrogate marker of muscle damage and injury, indicating the level of tissue injury, subsequent recovery processes, and substantial activation of thigh muscles following acute heavy resistance exercise.

document_context_data.document_summary: This randomized controlled trial investigated the effects of 8 weeks of daily 5g Cistanche deserticola (CD) extract supplementation, combined with progressive high-intensity resistance training, on muscle strength and recovery in both untrained and resistance-trained male participants. The study found that CD supplementation significantly enhanced muscle strength (1RM bench press and squat, MVIC) and endurance (RTF in untrained), and facilitated post-exercise recovery by modulating hormonal responses (increased testosterone, reduced cortisol) and decreasing markers of stress and inflammation (reduced CRP and CK levels) in both cohorts. Mechanistic insights suggest CD's role in improving energy metabolism, reducing muscle degradation, enhancing antioxidant defense, modulating neurotransmission, and regulating endocrine axes.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Cistanche deserticola (CD) supplementation combined with a progressive resistance training program.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants received 5 g of CD extract daily, administered in two sachets (after breakfast and lunch) for 8 consecutive weeks, alongside a placebo group. A standardized resistance training program was completed three times per week for eight weeks. This program involved 4 sets of 10-12 repetitions at 65-70% of 1RM for weeks 1-4, and 4 sets of 6-8 repetitions at 80% of 1RM for weeks 5-8. Maximal strength (1RM bench press/squat, MVIC) and endurance (RTF bench press) were assessed. No dose-response comparisons for CD were reported, only comparison to placebo.

matched_biomarker_details.activity_type: Enzyme Activity / Protein Level / Gene expression

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly reduced in untrained CD group (78.33 	 16.32 U/L vs. PLAC 100.39 	 19.86 U/L; p < 0.01) and in trained CD group (71.46 	 10.68 U/L vs. PLAC 86.67 	 13.48 U/L; p < 0.01). Overall, statistically significant improvements and reduced levels.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Enzyme primarily found in muscle cells, released into the bloodstream upon muscle damage; acts as an indicator of muscle injury and plays a role in energy buffering.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Cistanche deserticola (CD) supplementation (5g daily for 8 weeks) combined with progressive resistance training; post-resistance training recovery and muscle damage.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates reduced muscle damage, enhanced muscle repair, and improved recovery status following resistance exercise.

document_context_data.document_summary: This document describes the protocol for an exploratory, multicenter, open-label, randomized controlled trial (CAME COVID-19 study) evaluating the efficacy of clarithromycin (400 mg/day or 800 mg/day) as an oral treatment for Japanese adult patients with mild COVID-19 pneumonia who do not require oxygen administration. The study aims to identify a new treatment strategy for mild COVID-19 and determine the number of days required to achieve a 50% or more improvement in clinical symptoms.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Clarithromycin
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Oral administration of clarithromycin is investigated in two dosage groups (800 mg/day, given as 400 mg twice daily, and 400 mg/day, given as 200 mg twice daily for 7 days) compared to a standard treatment control group. Patients are randomized in a 1:1:1 ratio, allowing for dose comparisons. Dose adjustment based on patient age, weight, and symptoms is possible. The doses are approved for other bacterial respiratory infections in Japan, and their safety is confirmed, but this is an exploratory trial as no prior dose-response data for COVID-19 pneumonia were available.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: To be determined by study outcomes; this is a protocol.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Not applicable as this is a study protocol outlining planned measurements; no results are reported.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: An enzyme primarily found in muscle (skeletal and cardiac) and brain; elevated levels indicate muscle damage.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Clarithromycin treatment for mild COVID-19 pneumonia.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of muscle damage, including cardiac injury.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the acute and delayed effects of the 5-m Shuttle Run Test (5mSRT) on biomarkers of muscle damage (creatinine kinase, lactate dehydrogenase, aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase), inflammation (C-reactive protein), and subjective perceptions of fatigue, recovery, and muscle soreness (DOMS, RPE, PRS) in healthy male amateur team sports players. Findings indicate that the 5mSRT significantly increased muscle damage and inflammation markers, as well as DOMS and RPE, while reducing PRS. The study concluded that a 72-hour recovery period was generally sufficient for fatigue recovery, with biomarker levels returning towards baseline.

treatment_details.therapy_type: 5-m Shuttle Run Test (5mSRT)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The 5mSRT consisted of 6 repetitions of 30-second maximal shuttle sprints, with 35-second recovery periods between each sprint. Participants ran the greatest possible distance within 30 seconds by shuttling between cones at increasing distances (5m, 10m, 15m, 20m, etc.). Blood samples and perceptual scores were taken at rest, 5 minutes post-exercise, and 72 hours post-exercise. No dose-response comparisons for varying test intensities or durations were reported within the protocol.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Increased acutely post-exercise, then returned towards baseline.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased from pre-5mSRT (190.6  1 109.1 IU/L) to post-5mSRT (234.6  1 113.7 IU/L), a 21.3% increase (p < 0.001). Levels decreased to 125.3  1 80.5 IU/L at 72 h post-5mSRT, returning towards baseline (p < 0.001 compared to post-5mSRT).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Enzyme involved in cellular energy metabolism, serving as a key marker of muscle damage and necrosis; its presence in circulation indicates leakage from damaged muscle cells due to strenuous activity.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Acute effect of 5-m Shuttle Run Test (5mSRT)-induced muscle damage and fatigue, with assessment at 5 minutes and 72 hours post-exercise.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates the level of exercise-induced muscle damage and fatigue. It is a tool for coaches/clinicians, where elevated levels alongside decreased performance may signal overtraining. Return to baseline within 72 hours suggests recovery in trained individuals.

document_context_data.document_summary: The study investigated the response of circulating miR-21, miR-378, and miR-940 to an acute exhaustive exercise in chronic heart failure (CHF) patients. It found that serum levels of miR-21, miR-378, and miR-940 were significantly up-regulated immediately after exercise, along with increases in CK, LDH, and NT-ProBNP. Conversely, several other miRNAs (miR-1, miR-133a, miR-133b, miR-499, miR-208a, miR-208b, miR-486, miR-328, miR-126, miR-221, miR-146a, miR-155, miR-210), CK-MB, Tn-T, and hs-CRP remained unchanged. Crucially, no robust correlation was identified between changes in the circulating miRNAs and exercise capacity, muscle damage, inflammation, or cardiac function.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Acute exhaustive exercise / Symptom-limited incremental cardiopulmonary exercise test
treatment_details.dose_specificity: A single session of acute exhaustive exercise was performed by 28 male chronic heart failure (CHF) participants (mean age 59.07  1 1.79 years). The standardized exercise protocol used revised Ramp10 programs on a bicycle ergometer where patients cycled at 60 rpm, with work increasing from 20 J/s for 2 minutes, then by 5 J/s every 30 seconds until exhaustion. No dose-response comparisons were reported for any biomarker changes.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Not affected (Table 3).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Indicator of cardiac or muscle damage.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Acute exhaustive exercise in CHF patients.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Not affected by acute exhaustive exercise in CHF patients.

document_context_data.document_summary: This randomized, single-blind, placebo-controlled trial investigated the effects of 6-week Tribulus terrestris L. (TT) supplementation (770 mg/day) on muscle metabolism, inflammation, and antioxidant biomarkers in trained male CrossFit® athletes. The study concluded that TT supplementation could attenuate CrossFit® training-induced oxidative stress, muscle damage, and inflammation by modulating levels of LDH, CRP, and TAS, while other muscle damage and inflammatory markers remained unchanged.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Tribulus terrestris L. (TT) supplementation combined with a structured CrossFit training program
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Tribulus terrestris (TT) was supplemented orally at 770 mg/day (2 capsules of 385 mg, 72.64% TT extract at 40% saponins) for 6 weeks, taken daily after workouts. The CrossFit training program involved 3 high-intensity sessions per week on alternate weekdays (4.5 hours/week total), including specific warm-ups, Workouts of the Day (WODs) like 'Grace' and 'Fran', and cool-downs. The TT dose was within the reported safety range of 250-9000 mg, and no dose-response comparisons were reported in this study.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant differences (p > 0.05) between time points (T1, T2, T3) nor between control and intervention groups.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Isoenzyme primarily indicative of myocardial damage, also present in skeletal muscle.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: 6 weeks of CrossFit® exercise with/without Tribulus Terrestris supplementation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Primarily indicates myocardial damage; TT supplementation had no significant impact on this marker of myocardial or muscle damage.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated novel protein-based subphenotypes in Heart Failure with reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF) patients using unsupervised machine learning on 4210 repeatedly measured circulating proteins over a median 2.1-year follow-up in 382 patients. It identified four distinct subphenotypes with varying protein profiles, clinical characteristics (e.g., age, EF, chronic renal failure), and prognosis. These subphenotypes were driven by specific protein subsets associated with various biological mechanisms, including oxidative stress, inflammation, extracellular matrix organization, myocardial stretch/stress, injury, and renal dysfunction. Subphenotypes 2 and 3 demonstrated significantly worse clinical outcomes compared to subphenotype 1, highlighting the value of dynamic proteomic profiling for gaining pathophysiological insights and exploring personalized treatment opportunities in complex diagnoses like HFrEF.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Proteomic profiling and subphenotyping in Heart Failure with reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF) patients.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational study involving trimonthly blood sampling over a median follow-up of 2.1 years (IQR: 1.1–2.6 years) in 382 HFrEF patients, totaling 1066 blood samples. An aptamer-based multiplex proteomic approach (SOMAscan assay) was used to measure 4210 circulating proteins, yielding relative fluorescence units (RFUs) for comparative analysis rather than absolute concentrations. No specific intervention, treatment, or dose-response comparisons were conducted, as the study focused on characterizing disease subphenotypes and biomarker patterns over time. Repeated proteomic measurements (incorporating both intercept and slope coefficients) demonstrated improved accuracy for survival models (c-index 0.73, BIC 1023) compared to single time-point assessments.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Levels highest in subphenotypes 3 and 4; lowest in subphenotype 1. Precise quantification not provided.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Associated with myocyte injury.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Patient subphenotype classification in a cardiac cohort, particularly defining Subphenotypes 1, 3, and 4.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Higher levels are associated with subphenotypes 3 and 4, where subphenotype 3 is linked to worse patient outcomes (HR 2.88 (1.37–6.03) compared to subphenotype 1).

document_context_data.document_summary: This descriptive, cross-sectional study investigated serum biochemical markers of muscle damage, including C-Reactive Protein (CRP), Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH), total Creatine Kinase (CK), Creatine Kinase-MB (CK-MB), and the CK-MB/CK ratio, in 326 adolescent athletes (aged 13-18 years, primarily soccer players) from sports centers in Tacna, Peru. The study aimed to evaluate muscle damage and inflammation related to intense physical activity, concluding that alterations in these markers are present, with specific ranges identified for elevated markers and notable correlations (e.g., a strong positive correlation between LDH and CK-MB) among the adolescent cohort.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study of physical training and activity, specifically soccer training
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational, cross-sectional study of adolescent athletes (aged 13-18 years, including soccer players) engaging in regular, intense physical activity and competitive training for at least three months. No specific training interventions or dose-response comparisons were applied or controlled by the researchers; the study analyzed pre-existing biomarker levels influenced by the athletes' own training regimes, which involve macro and microcycles and varying intensity/duration. The study notes 'different stages of training' and 'adjustment of physical load' as influencing factors.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: 7.1% of adolescents exhibited a CK-MB/CK ratio below 4%, suggesting potential muscle injury. 92.9% fell within the range of 4% to 25%, which, according to literature, could indicate possible ischemic cardiopathy; no participants had an index exceeding 25%.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: A diagnostic ratio used to differentiate the source of elevated total CK, aiding in distinguishing between skeletal muscle injury and potential ischemic cardiopathy.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Evaluation of muscle damage and potential cardiac involvement in adolescent athletes undergoing athletic activity and sports training, particularly when CK levels are elevated.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: An index less than 4% suggests potential skeletal muscle injury, while an index between 4% and 25% suggests possible ischemic cardiopathy, warranting further clinical investigation. This ratio is critical for identifying the probable source of muscle damage and distinguishing it from cardiac involvement in athletes.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of 4 weeks of inspiratory muscle training (IMT) on biomarkers of muscle damage, respiratory function, and functional capacity in COVID-19 recovered patients after weaning from mechanical ventilation. The findings showed that IMT significantly reduced muscle damage biomarkers (CKM and slow sTnI), improved pulmonary function and inspiratory muscle strength, and enhanced hand grip strength and quality of life compared to a control group.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Inspiratory Muscle Training (IMT)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The 4-week intervention involved an IMT group performing 30 dynamic inspiratory efforts twice daily, starting at 50% of maximal inspiratory mouth pressure (P Mmax), with periodic load increases to ensure completion of 30 maneuvers. The control group performed 60 inspiratory efforts once daily, 5 days/week, at a fixed intensity of 10% P Mmax. Compliance with IMT sessions was 78    ± 4%. No explicit dose-response comparisons were reported beyond individual load adjustments for the IMT group.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly lower for the IMT group compared to the control group at week two (p=0.001) and week four (p=0.020) during the 4-week intervention, with observed time    × group interaction effects.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: A biomarker indicating skeletal and respiratory muscle damage.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: 4 weeks of inspiratory muscle training (IMT) in COVID-19 recovered patients after weaning from mechanical ventilation, where baseline levels were elevated.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates levels of muscle damage, with a reduction post-IMT suggesting beneficial effects on muscle recovery, reduced damage, and improved respiratory function in recovered COVID-19 patients.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of 10-minute volitional hyperpnea, equivalent to 85% of maximal minute ventilation, on respiratory muscle damage biomarkers (CKM, fast sTnI, and slow sTnI) in healthy young men. The main finding indicated that only slow sTnI was significantly elevated 24 hours post-hyperpnea compared to a control, suggesting a small amount of respiratory muscle damage, while CKM and fast sTnI showed no significant changes.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Volitional Hyperpnea
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants underwent 10-minute trials of volitional hyperpnea at rest, mimicking breathing patterns (tidal volume, breathing frequency, duty cycle, transdiaphragmatic pressure) equivalent to 85% of their maximal minute ventilation (V̇Emax) produced during an incremental cycling test. A control trial involved resting. Serum was collected before and at 1, 24, and 48 hours post-intervention. No dose-response comparisons beyond this specific intensity were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant time × trial interaction effects for CKM (p = 0.072); levels did not increase after volitional hyperpnea compared with the control trial. Detection limit: 30 U/mL.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: An enzyme critical for energy metabolism in muscle cells, primarily used as a general biomarker for muscle damage or injury.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Volitional hyperpnea (equivalent to 85% of maximum minute ventilation).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Did not show significant changes, suggesting it may not be a sufficiently sensitive indicator for low-grade respiratory muscle damage caused by volitional hyperpnea under these conditions.

document_context_data.document_summary:
This study investigated sex differences in inflammatory response, lipid peroxidation, and muscle damage in men and women athletes following an acute resistance exercise, specifically a maximal incremental half-squat test. Results showed men exhibited a larger pro-inflammatory response (IL6) and increased lipid peroxidation (HPX) at 24 hours post-exercise compared to women at equivalent workloads, while no significant sex-based differences were observed in other muscle damage markers (CK-MB, LDH, 
	-actin).

treatment_details.therapy_type: Acute Resistance Exercise (Maximal Incremental Half-Squat)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants performed half-squat exercises with five incremental intensities (20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, and 100% of one-repetition maximum, 1RM). Repetitions varied: 5 at 20-60% 1RM, 2 at 80% 1RM, and 1 at 100% 1RM. Rest periods between sets were 3-5 minutes. Equivalent workloads were used for men and women, but men achieved larger net loads due to greater muscle mass. No specific dose-response comparisons for biomarkers were reported across different intensities.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant differences between different time points nor between both sexes were found.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Isoenzyme of Creatine Kinase, primarily used as a marker of muscle damage, particularly cardiac.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Acute resistance exercise (half-squat).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: No significant difference in muscle damage between sexes or at different time points after acute resistance exercise.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated whether pre-exercise ascorbic acid supplementation influenced antioxidant defenses, glucose metabolism, inflammation, and muscle damage in untrained healthy adults following a single bout of moderate-intensity cycling. Findings indicated that ascorbic acid supplementation reduced plasma Malondialdehyde (MDA) and increased Ferric Reducing Ability of Plasma (FRAP), while also modulating glucose levels and attenuating exercise-induced changes in albumin and total protein. While moderate-intensity cycling led to an increase in red blood cell Superoxide Dismutase (SOD) activity and low-grade muscle damage (Total Creatine Kinase), it did not induce systemic inflammation or lipid peroxidation. Ascorbic acid supplementation appeared to mitigate the exercise-induced increase in SOD activity but did not significantly prevent muscle damage or affect other inflammatory/damage markers such as hsCRP, LDH, CK-MB, GPx, or Catalase.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Oral ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) supplementation combined with a single bout of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Subjects received 1000 mg of ascorbic acid (or placebo) orally 5 minutes prior to a 30-minute indoor cycling session. Exercise intensity was set at 65–75% of maximum heart rate, which was predicted by an age-based equation. No dose-response comparisons were reported for either ascorbic acid or exercise intensity.

matched_biomarker_details.biomarker_name: Creatine Kinase Muscle and Brain Isoenzymes (CK-MB)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Concentrations remained unchanged in subjects with or without vitamin C supplement post-exercise (p>0.05, implied).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: An isoenzyme of creatine kinase predominantly found in cardiac muscle, used as a marker for cardiac injury, but also present in skeletal muscle.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Acute aerobic exercise (indoor cycling) in untrained healthy adults, with or without ascorbic acid supplementation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: No significant change suggests that this specific exercise bout, with or without ascorbic acid, did not induce significant acute cardiac-related muscle damage detectable by CK-MB.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of broad-spectrum polyphenol supplementation from powdered tart cherry extract on markers of recovery, oxidative stress, and muscle damage following intense resistance exercise in men. It concluded that tart cherry extract significantly reduced oxidative stress (protein carbonyls), skeletal muscle damage (creatine kinase), and cardiac/type I muscle fiber damage (creatine kinase MB), while also preventing a decrease in handgrip strength compared to placebo.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Broad-spectrum polyphenol supplementation using powdered tart cherry extract combined with an acute resistance exercise protocol (AREP).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants received 500 mg of powdered NordicCherry® tart cherry extract (with minimal calorie content, 1.3 kcal) daily for 7 days prior to an Acute Resistance Exercise Protocol (AREP), compared to a rice flour placebo. The AREP involved 6 sets of 10 repetitions of barbell back squat at 80% of 1-repetition maximum, with load reduction to 75% 1RM if 10 repetitions were not completed in a set. No dose-response comparisons for the supplement or exercise intensity were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly lower concentration in Tart Cherry (TC) group compared to Placebo (PL) group at 1 h post exercise (PL: 21.6 	 12.4 vs. TC: -0.3 	 11.8 ng	ml	-1; p = 0.006). Reference values for CKMB are 0-10 ng	ml	-1. This showed a significant main effect for time (p < 0.001) and supplement*time interaction (p = 0.001).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: An isoenzyme primarily associated with cardiac muscle damage, but also indicative of type I skeletal muscle fiber damage; elevated serum levels reflect muscle tissue damage.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Following an Acute Resistance Exercise Protocol (AREP) (6 sets of 10 repetitions of barbell back squat at 80% 1RM) after a 7-day supplementation period with tart cherry extract.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates reduced cardiac muscle and potentially type I muscle fiber damage, suggesting a protective effect of tart cherry supplementation following intense resistance exercise.

document_context_data.document_summary: This descriptive, cross-sectional study investigated serum biochemical markers of muscle damage, including C-Reactive Protein (CRP), Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH), total Creatine Kinase (CK), Creatine Kinase-MB (CK-MB), and the CK-MB/CK ratio, in 326 adolescent athletes (aged 13-18 years, primarily soccer players) from sports centers in Tacna, Peru. The study aimed to evaluate muscle damage and inflammation related to intense physical activity, concluding that alterations in these markers are present, with specific ranges identified for elevated markers and notable correlations (e.g., a strong positive correlation between LDH and CK-MB) among the adolescent cohort.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study of physical training and activity, specifically soccer training
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational, cross-sectional study of adolescent athletes (aged 13-18 years, including soccer players) engaging in regular, intense physical activity and competitive training for at least three months. No specific training interventions or dose-response comparisons were applied or controlled by the researchers; the study analyzed pre-existing biomarker levels influenced by the athletes' own training regimes, which involve macro and microcycles and varying intensity/duration. The study notes 'different stages of training' and 'adjustment of physical load' as influencing factors.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: 99.1% of adolescents had normal serum levels (0-25 U/L), while 0.9% had elevated values (>25 U/L), specifically ranging from 19 to 24 U/L in affected cases. A weak negative correlation with CK (r = -0.143) and a strong positive correlation with LDH (r = 0.780) were observed.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: An isoenzyme of Creatine Kinase primarily found in cardiac muscle, but also present in skeletal muscle. Elevated levels indicate muscle damage, potentially cardiac or severe skeletal.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Muscle damage assessment in adolescent athletes engaged in physical activity and sports training, where it is evaluated for muscle impact and potential cardiac involvement.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Elevated levels, especially when interpreted with total CK and the CK-MB/CK ratio, are crucial for distinguishing between severe skeletal muscle injury and potential cardiac involvement. Normal values generally suggest no significant cardiac damage related to activity, while elevated levels, though rare, indicate muscle damage and correlate strongly with LDH levels.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the associations between dietary intake in the week prior to a marathon race and post-race exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) and cardiac stress (EICS) in recreational male endurance runners. It found that consumption of meat, butter, and fatty meat was positively associated with higher EIMD and EICS markers, whereas fish, vegetables, and olive oil intake showed a negative association, suggesting a protective role.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Dietary intake assessment combined with endurance running (marathon race)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Sixty-nine male recreational runners participated in a competitive marathon (42.195 km). Dietary intake for the week prior to and on race day was collected using a seven-day weighed food record. Pre-race average daily intake was 3005.7     362.5 kcal (44.8     6.2 kcal/kg), with carbohydrates at 338.3     55.1 g, protein at 130.5     24.2 g, and fat at 121.5     19.8 g. Race-day intake included 1.8     0.7 L fluid and 597.1     394.9 kcal. Participants showed dietary imbalances with lower than recommended servings of cereals, potatoes, dairy, vegetables, and legumes, and excess in pastries, sweets, and dried fruits. The study identified associations between food group consumption (e.g., meat, butter, fatty meat, fish, vegetables, olive oil) and post-race biomarker levels, but no specific dose-response comparisons for dietary components were explicitly reported beyond these associations. The race took place in Madrid in April 2016, with a mean dry temperature of 27     3    °C and 27     2% relative humidity.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Post-race mean: 17.45     14.04 U/L.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Cardiac specific isoenzyme of creatine kinase, indicating cardiac muscle damage or stress.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Post-competitive marathon race.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates exercise-induced cardiac stress (EICS).

document_context_data.document_summary: This sportomics study investigated the metabolic, immune, hormonal, and amino acid responses, alongside muscle and liver injury markers, in two elite female Olympic beach volleyball athletes during a simulated competition day involving two matches. Key findings revealed significant acute physiological impacts, including electrolyte disturbances (notably hypokalemia), 20-60% increases in muscle injury markers and up to 50% for liver enzymes, elevated stress hormones (ACTH up to 4-fold, cortisol up to 3-fold), and altered energy metabolism and amino acid profiles indicative of central fatigue risk (e.g., Fischer ratio and tryptophan decreased by 60%, serotonin increased by 180%). The study emphasized distinct individual recovery kinetics, highlighted the inadequacy of short recovery sessions, and advocated for personalized monitoring due to varied biomarker responses despite similar external loads.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Simulated Beach Volleyball Competition
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Two world-class female athletes participated in a simulated competition day involving two high-intensity beach volleyball matches (a two-set match in the morning and a three-set match in the afternoon), under identical environmental conditions. Blood and urine samples were collected at seven time points: pre-match, post-match, 60 minutes after each match (short recovery), and after a 15-hour long recovery. The protocol included 15-minute warm-ups. No dose-response comparisons were explicitly reported; however, individual responses to the same protocol were highlighted, and short recovery sessions were found to be inadequate for full physiological recovery, with the second match demonstrating cumulative strain.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased significantly post-exercise (20-45% after first match, ~20% after second match). Recovered to initial levels before the second match.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Isoenzyme of creatine kinase, primarily found in heart muscle; also present in skeletal muscle.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Simulated beach volleyball competition (post-match, recovery).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Highlights potential for inducing muscle microinjury from exercise loads.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of anserine supplementation on exercise-induced oxidative stress, cellular damage, and haematological biomarkers in ten healthy men. Anserine, at both low and high doses, enhanced antioxidant activity by significantly increasing superoxide dismutase (SOD) and preserving catalase (CAT) activity, while elevating glutathione disulfide (GSSG) and consequently lowering the GSH/GSSG ratio. Although anserine had no significant effect on glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase (GOT), myoglobin, or thiobarbituric acid reactive substances (TBARS), the high dose transiently elevated glutamate pyruvate transaminase (GPT) and creatine kinase isoenzyme (CKMB). Furthermore, high-dose anserine increased mean cell volume (MCV) and decreased mean corpuscular haemoglobin concentration (MCHC), indicating altered red blood cell parameters. The findings suggest anserine preserves cellular homeostasis and protects cell integrity through enhanced antioxidant activity, potentially augmenting exercise-induced adaptive responses and recovery in healthy men.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Anserine supplementation (oral intake)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Ten healthy men were administered anserine orally 1 hour prior to an exercise challenge (running time trials to volitional exhaustion, approximately 40 minutes at 50% V̇O2peak). Participants received either a low dose (ANS-LD) of 15 mg·kg⁻¹·bw⁻¹, a high dose (ANS-HD) of 30 mg·kg⁻¹·bw⁻¹, or a placebo (PLA, corn starch) on three separate occasions in a randomized, placebo-controlled, repeated-measures design. Blood samples were collected at rest, 5 minutes, 60 minutes, and 24 hours post-exercise. Exercise performance (Time-to-Exhaustion) showed no significant difference between conditions. While both doses conferred antioxidant benefits, some dose-dependent effects were observed, particularly for cell damage markers (GPT, CKMB) and haematological parameters (MCV, MCHC) which were more pronounced with the high dose.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Anserine induced significant increases in CKMB (p < 0.05, main treatment effects). ANS-HD induced significantly higher CKMB than PLA (p < 0.05), and ANS-LD showed a trend towards being higher than PLA (p = 0.056). CKMB levels remained within the normal range (0.9–6.1 ng/mL), with 'transient increased CKMB levels' noted.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Muscle damage biomarker, primarily indicating cardiac muscle damage but also elevated in skeletal muscle injury.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: High-dose anserine supplementation following an exercise challenge (time to exhaustion).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Elevations suggest anserine (at high dose) might be associated with an augmented exercise-induced adaptive response and recovery, rather than detrimental damage.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study utilized a sportomics approach to investigate the physiological, biochemical, hemodynamic, metabolic, and hydration parameters in elite athletes undergoing a 40-minute high-intensity functional Cross Combat (CCombat) exercise protocol. The main aim was to evaluate the effects of this intensive training on hydration and kidney function, ultimately suggesting albuminuria as a sensitive biomarker for assessing hydration status changes during strenuous activity and mitigating chronic renal impairment.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Cross Combat (CCombat), a high-intensity functional exercise protocol inspired by CrossFit
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The protocol involved a 40-minute high-intensity functional Cross Combat (CCombat) session, characterized as a 'cyclic exercise' with high-ATP demand, an intensity level of 70% repetition maximum, and 12 different exercises combined into six modules, designed to induce metabolic stress. Sixteen elite-level professional male athletes were engaged in training sessions over a 96-hour protocol, with blood samples collected. The study was observational, and athletes had free access to hydration post-protocol. No specific dose-response comparisons were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Induced a highly correlated increase (up to 20%) during the first 24 hours of recovery after the CCombat protocol, decreasing to pre-exercise levels during long recovery (LRecover1d). Showed a strong correlation with myoglobin during short recovery (SRecover) until long recovery (LRecover) at 24 h (r s 0.66 10.86).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Enzyme released into the blood as a marker of cardiac or skeletal muscle damage, indicating muscle integrity.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: During and post-CCombat protocol, specifically observed during recovery periods (up to 24 hours).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Consensus biomarker of muscle microinjuries and damage.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated alterations in serum levels of tumor, cardiac, liver, and renal function markers, alongside the IL-18 rs1946518 polymorphism, in patients with breast, colorectal, and prostate cancers (BC, CRC, PCa), and myocardial infarction (MI), compared to healthy controls. It revealed significantly elevated tumor markers (CA 15-3, CA 19-9, CEA, TPSA) in cancer patients, which serve as efficient early detection biomarkers. Cardiac markers (hs-cTnT, CK-MB) were specific to MI and largely unchanged in cancer. Liver and renal markers (ALP, AST, ALT, urea, creatinine) showed varied elevations, particularly in CRC and PCa, suggesting their utility as alternative diagnostic indicators. The IL-18 -607 C/A polymorphism was identified as a risk factor for PCa (AA genotype and A allele), and also showed an Odds Ratio of 1.75 for BC, while A/C heterozygotes were linked to increased CRC risk and C allele homozygotes offered protection against CRC.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Diagnostic Biomarker and Genetic Polymorphism Study
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This observational study focused on assessing diagnostic biomarker levels and genetic polymorphisms in various patient groups and healthy controls, without any therapeutic intervention or dose comparisons.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher in MI, unchanged in cancer
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Notably elevated in Myocardial Infarction (MI) patients compared with healthy controls, BC, CRC, and PCa patients (P<0.001). No statistically significant difference observed between BC, CRC, PCa patients, and healthy volunteers. Reduced levels are noted to indicate no significant risk of cardiac failure in BC patients or healthy individuals.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Cardiac marker, indicator of cardiac muscle injury.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Myocardial Infarction (MI) patients compared to healthy controls and various cancer patients (BC, CRC, PCa); also referenced in context of cardiac failure in BC patients or healthy individuals.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates myocardial infarction. Not a significant indicator for BC, CRC, or PCa; reduced levels imply no significant cardiac failure risk.

document_context_data.document_summary: The study investigated the release patterns, time course, and predictive value of circulating microRNAs (miR-499, miR-133a, miR-133b) and cardiac troponin I (cTnI) for perioperative myocardial infarction (PMI) in Coronary Artery Bypass Graft (CABG) patients. It concluded that circulating miR-499 is a novel and early biomarker for identifying PMI in cardiac surgery, demonstrating earlier elevation and superior diagnostic accuracy (higher sensitivity and specificity) compared to cTnI, particularly following on-pump CABG surgery.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Coronary Artery Bypass Graft (CABG) surgery
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Patients underwent either on-pump (n=30 in initial phase, n=120 in prospective cohort) or off-pump (n=30) CABG surgery. Serial plasma samples were collected at seven perioperative time points: preoperatively, and 1, 3, 6, 12, 24, and 48 hours after aortic declamping. While no dose-response comparisons for the surgery itself were reported, comparisons were made between on-pump (involving whole heart ischemia-reperfusion) and off-pump (beating heart) procedures, revealing higher miR release in on-pump cases attributed to increased myocardial stress.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Commonly measured due to release of intracellular components into the blood. Time delay between the detection of circulating protein and ischemic damage remains a major problem.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Intracellular enzyme released into the blood following myocardial ischemia.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Myocardial ischemia during cardiac surgery.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of myocardial damage, but limited by time delay in detection.
