document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the impact of a 12-week cardiac rehabilitation program, involving moderate-intensity aerobic and resistance training, and omega-3 fatty acid supplementation, on gut barrier integrity and inflammatory biomarkers in older adults with Coronary Artery Disease. The key finding was that an increase in cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2peak   5 mL/kg/min) was significantly associated with a reduction in serum FABP2, indicating improved gut barrier integrity, while zonulin and inflammatory markers (CRP, IL-6, TNF) did not show significant changes or associations.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Cardiac Rehabilitation (Aerobic and Resistance Exercise Training, and Omega-3 Fatty Acid Supplementation)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: A 12-week moderate-intensity cardiac rehabilitation program, involving 5 days/week exercise (1 supervised in-class session, 4 at-home sessions). Supervised sessions were approximately 60 minutes, progressing from 60% to 80% of VO2peak. Omega-3 PUFA supplementation consisted of 1.9 g daily (1.2 g EPA, 0.6 g DHA) for 12 weeks, compared to a placebo. While the program had a progressive exercise intensity, no explicit dose-response comparisons between different exercise regimens or omega-3 doses were reported. The study focused on the impact of achieving a significant increase in cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2peak   5 mL/kg/min).

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: At baseline, higher VO2peak was associated with lower FABP2 (B = -0.363, p = 0.029 unadjusted; B = -0.337, p = 0.009 adjusted for metformin). Metformin use was associated with higher FABP2 (B = 0.325, p = 0.028). Overall, FABP2 levels did not significantly change with the intervention (t = 0.201, p = 0.842) or omega-3 supplementation (F(1, 36), p = 0.814). However, a significant VO2peak improvement (  5 mL/kg/min) was consistently associated with a relative reduction in FABP2 (B = -0.45, p = 0.018; B = 0.530, p = 0.013; B = -0.446, p = 0.018 after adjustment). Participants with   5 mL/kg/min VO2peak improvement had significantly lower mean termination FABP2 levels (378.61   86.82 ng/ml) compared to those without (607.02   284.47 ng/ml; t = 3.191, p = 0.004).

document_context_data.document_summary: This study employed NMR metabolomics to investigate metabolic profiles in serum and urine from COVID-19 patients across varying disease severities (Medical Ward and Intensive Care Unit) and healthy controls. The primary aim was to identify biomarkers for COVID-19 diagnosis, severity classification, and prognosis, and to explore correlations with clinical factors like hypertension, obesity, and dyslipidemia. Key findings include the development of a highly efficient diagnostic panel (isoleucine, TMAO, glucose) and a robust severity classification panel (ethanol, TMAO, tyrosine, betaine, and clinical characteristics), alongside identification of numerous individual metabolites and clinical parameters associated with infection, disease progression, hospitalization duration, and patient outcome.

treatment_details.therapy_type: NMR metabolomics-based profiling and observational study of COVID-19 infection
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This observational study analyzed 80 serum and urine samples from COVID-19 patients (34 intensive care, 46 hospitalized) and 32 from healthy controls using NMR spectroscopy. The research focused on identifying and validating metabolite-based panels for COVID-19 diagnosis and severity classification. A diagnostic panel of isoleucine, TMAO, and glucose achieved an AUC of 0.91 (86.08% sensitivity, 83.87% specificity). A severity classification panel, combining ethanol, TMAO, tyrosine, betaine, and clinical characteristics (obesity/overweight, dyslipidemia, lymphocyte count), achieved an AUC of 0.825 (84.85% sensitivity, 72.09% specificity). No therapeutic intervention or dose-response comparisons were part of the study design.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher levels (especially unsaturated fatty acids - UFA) observed in COVID-19 patients compared to healthy controls. Identified as a key discriminating molecule.

document_context_data.document_summary: This multi-phase, multi-center study developed and validated a machine learning-enabled blood-derived exosomal RNA profiling platform (ETR.sig) for noninvasive multi-cancer detection and localization, demonstrating its robust potential for accurate diagnosis, tumor origin classification, and prognostic assessment across eight primary cancer types.

Filtering criteria for differential gene expression included |log2FC|>1 and P<0.05 for bulk RNA-seq, and P<0.01 with FC ≥1.4 or ≤−1.6 for multi-cancer exoRNA-seq. document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated whether pre-exercise ascorbic acid supplementation influenced antioxidant defenses, glucose metabolism, inflammation, and muscle damage in untrained healthy adults following a single bout of moderate-intensity cycling. Findings indicated that ascorbic acid supplementation reduced plasma Malondialdehyde (MDA) and increased Ferric Reducing Ability of Plasma (FRAP), while also modulating glucose levels and attenuating exercise-induced changes in albumin and total protein. While moderate-intensity cycling led to an increase in red blood cell Superoxide Dismutase (SOD) activity and low-grade muscle damage (Total Creatine Kinase), it did not induce systemic inflammation or lipid peroxidation. Ascorbic acid supplementation appeared to mitigate the exercise-induced increase in SOD activity but did not significantly prevent muscle damage or affect other inflammatory/damage markers such as hsCRP, LDH, CK-MB, GPx, or Catalase.

Exercise intensity was set at 65–75% of maximum heart rate, which was predicted by an age-based equation. No dose-response comparisons were reported for either ascorbic acid or exercise intensity.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant differences in placebo subjects. A significant interaction between the effects of exercise and supplements was found (p < 0.05).

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of 6-week cranberry (Vaccinium macrocarpon) extract supplementation on antioxidant capacity, inflammatory markers, and iron metabolism in rowers subjected to exhaustive exercise. Findings indicate that supplementation significantly strengthened antioxidant potential (TAC) and mitigated exercise-induced increases in pro-inflammatory markers (TNF-alpha), muscle damage indicators (myoglobin), and iron regulatory hormones (hepcidin) in the supplemented group. However, IL-6, ferritin, sTfR, iron, TIBC, and UIBC remained largely unaffected by supplementation or showed exercise-induced changes independent of it.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Cranberry (Vaccinium macrocarpon) extract supplementation combined with strenuous physical exercise
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Athletes received 720 mg of highly-concentrated large cranberry extract daily (two 360-mg capsules, containing 36 mg proanthocyanidins per capsule) for 6 weeks. The control group received dyed gelatin placebo capsules containing flour. Participants performed a 2000-m rowing ergometer test at maximal effort on day 1 (pre-supplementation) and at the end of the 6-week training camp (post-supplementation), with blood samples taken pre-exercise, 1 minute post-exercise, and after a 24-hour recovery. No dose-response comparisons for cranberry extract were reported within the study.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Neither strenuous physical exercise nor cranberry intake exerted statistically significant effects on ferritin levels (main effect, p=0.086).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Main intracellular iron storage protein, reflecting total body iron stores.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: 6-week cranberry supplementation combined with strenuous physical exercise.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of iron status; cranberry supplementation had no discernible effect on its levels.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review identifies and recommends validated biomarkers for tracking health, performance, and recovery in athletes across multiple domains including nutritional status (macronutrients, micronutrients, food allergies), hydration, muscle status (damage, endocrine response), endurance, and injury risk (concussions, stress fractures, ACL). It advocates for a comprehensive, integrative, and individualized approach to biomarker analysis, emphasizing dynamic monitoring and contextual interpretation over single markers or universal thresholds to optimize training and minimize injury and overtraining risks.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Biomarker-guided monitoring and management of athletic training, nutrition, hydration, and injury recovery
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This review primarily focuses on the diagnostic and prognostic value of biomarkers rather than specific therapeutic doses. It emphasizes frequent, individualized monitoring (e.g., pre/post-exercise, daily, seasonally, after injury/competition) to establish personalized baseline ranges and track physiological changes in response to various training loads (e.g., acute bouts, heavy strength training, challenging training weeks). While specific nutritional intake recommendations are mentioned for protein (1.3–2.0 g/kg/day) and omega-3 fatty acids (≤3 g/day for average, 6–8 g/day for elite athletes), and iron supplementation at low-moderate doses, the document does not report dose-response comparisons for biomarker changes. Instead, it provides specific thresholds for identifying deficiencies (e.g., Vitamin D >50 ng/ml, Ferritin <12 µg/L), dehydration (e.g., >-2% body mass decrease, blood osmolality ≥295 mmol/kg, USG ≥1.020), insufficient recovery (30% decrease in T:C ratio), and overtraining (T:C ratio of 0.35 × 10⁻³). The overall approach prioritizes dynamic, contextualized assessment over universal thresholds for effective athlete management.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Depleted when <12 µg·L⁻¹; functional iron deficiency often defined as <35 µg·L⁻¹ (or 12–20 µg·L⁻¹ by some). Can be falsely elevated in inflammatory states.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Primary iron storage protein, serving as an indicator of iron stores.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Assessment of iron deficiency in athletes, inflammatory states (e.g., post-exercise, infection).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Useful biomarker for assessing iron deficiency; low levels (even without anemia) indicate depleted iron stores and can impair endurance performance, which may be improved with supplementation. Interpretation must consider potential false elevation during inflammation.

document_context_data.document_summary: This retrospective cohort study investigated the association between iron status and renal outcomes, specifically progression to End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD), in 111 pre-dialysis patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) and biopsy-proven Diabetic Nephropathy (DN). It found that reduced serum transferrin is an independent predictor of ESRD, and identified increased iron and transferrin deposition in renal tubular epithelial cells of DN patients, suggesting a pathological role for altered iron metabolism in disease progression.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study investigating the prognostic value of iron status and related biomarkers in Diabetic Nephropathy (DN) progression.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This retrospective observational cohort study analyzed baseline serum iron status markers (serum iron, ferritin, TIBC, transferrin, TSAT) and their association with progression to End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) in 111 Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) patients with biopsy-proven DN. Serum markers were measured using chemiluminescence immunoassay, immunoradiometric assay, and colorimetric methods. Additionally, histological analysis involved immunohistochemical staining for transferrin and Perl's blue staining for iron in kidney biopsy specimens from DN patients and healthy controls. No therapeutic interventions, dose comparisons, or active treatments were investigated; the study focused on correlation and predictive value.

matched_biomarker_details.activity_type: Protein Level / Iron Storage Marker / Concentration

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Lower (in ESRD patients), Higher (associated with diabetes/DN, potentially confounded by inflammation)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Lower baseline concentrations in ESRD patients (median 311.0 ng/mL, IQR 168.9-555.1) compared to non-ESRD patients. Higher levels were observed in patients with lower serum transferrin quartiles. No direct relationship with renal outcomes found in this cohort, possibly due to confounding by chronic inflammation, infection, liver disease, or malignancies, which can increase ferritin concentration.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Primary intracellular iron storage protein; indicates body iron stores. Also an acute-phase reactant. Primary parameter for diagnosing absolute iron deficiency. Increased iron stores contribute to inflammation, reactive oxygen species production, and lipid peroxidation.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Development and progression of Diabetic Nephropathy (DN) in T2DM patients; associated with mortality in hemodialysis patients; T2DM with biopsy-proven DN.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of increased iron stores, associated with inflammation, oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation, and increased mortality risk in CKD/dialysis patients. Potential indicator for DN progression, but its utility for predicting ESRD in DN is limited due to confounding factors like inflammation, hindering accurate assessment of iron status. Lower levels are associated with ESRD, but not an independent significant predictor; high levels in patients with low transferrin may indicate altered iron metabolism.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the relationship between serum S100B protein levels and disease severity in hospitalized Covid-19 (SARS-CoV-2 infected) patients. It revealed that increased S100B serum concentrations significantly correlate with Covid-19 disease severity, intensity of care, inflammatory processes, and several inflammatory and organ damage markers, suggesting S100B as a novel biomarker for monitoring disease course and prognosis.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study on the progression of SARS-CoV-2 infection (Covid-19) in hospitalized patients.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Patients received standard care following WHO guidelines. Disease severity was quantified using a Covid-score and categorization into High Intensity Care (HIC) or Low Intensity Care (LIC) wards. No specific intervention doses or therapeutic dose-response comparisons were investigated, as this was an observational study.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Positive and significant correlation observed with S100B concentrations (p < 0.01, 74 Observations).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Inflammation marker.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: SARS-CoV-2 infection (Covid-19 patients).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Associated with inflammatory status and Covid-19 severity.

document_context_data.document_summary: This document describes the protocol for an exploratory, multicenter, open-label, randomized controlled trial (CAME COVID-19 study) evaluating the efficacy of clarithromycin (400 mg/day or 800 mg/day) as an oral treatment for Japanese adult patients with mild COVID-19 pneumonia who do not require oxygen administration. The study aims to identify a new treatment strategy for mild COVID-19 and determine the number of days required to achieve a 50% or more improvement in clinical symptoms.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Clarithromycin
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Oral administration of clarithromycin is investigated in two dosage groups (800 mg/day, given as 400 mg twice daily, and 400 mg/day, given as 200 mg twice daily for 7 days) compared to a standard treatment control group. Patients are randomized in a 1:1:1 ratio, allowing for dose comparisons. Dose adjustment based on patient age, weight, and symptoms is possible. The doses are approved for other bacterial respiratory infections in Japan, and their safety is confirmed, but this is an exploratory trial as no prior dose-response data for COVID-19 pneumonia were available.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: To be determined by study outcomes; this is a protocol.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Not applicable as this is a study protocol outlining planned measurements; no results are reported.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: An iron storage protein and an acute phase reactant.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Clarithromycin treatment for mild COVID-19 pneumonia.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of iron status, inflammation, and severity of hyperinflammatory syndromes like cytokine storm in COVID-19.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the changes in blood biochemical and hematological parameters and physical fitness outcomes in professional male soccer players following a pre-season (PS) training phase. It also analyzed the associations between these blood markers and various physical fitness measures, including sprint performance, VAMEVAL, and Countermovement Jump (CMJ) tests. Key findings revealed significant increases in platelets, creatinine, alkaline phosphatase, C-reactive protein, cortisol, and testosterone, as well as significant decreases in albumin and corrected calcium after the PS phase. Overall physical fitness measures improved, and several blood biomarkers showed moderate to large correlations with specific physical performance indicators.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Professional soccer pre-season (PS) training and specific physical fitness testing
treatment_details.dose_specificity:
The study involved 25 professional male soccer players (28.1 
D7 4.6 years old) undergoing a regular pre-season training phase (June to October 2019) characterized by high training loads in both soccer practice and strength training, described as "intense physical exercise" and "intensification of training demands." Biological markers were assessed at baseline (June 02, 2019) and post-PS (September 19, 2019), following a 48-hour rest, with an additional acute exercise component 12 hours prior to the second blood draw. Physical fitness was assessed using standardized tests: VAMEVAL (incremental running to exhaustion), 30-15 Intermittent Fitness Test (30-seconds intense running interspersed by 15-seconds rest until failure), linear sprints (5m, 10m, 15m, 20m split times), and Countermovement Jump (CMJ with hands on hips and free hands). No specific dose-response comparisons for the training or physical tests were reported as these were standardized maximal efforts.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Not reported

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: An intracellular protein that stores iron and releases it in a controlled fashion; serves as a buffer against iron deficiency and iron overload.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Pre-Season (PS) training phase in professional soccer players, assessed at baseline and post-PS.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Not reported in this study, but generally indicates iron status, important for oxygen transport and energy metabolism.

document_context_data.document_summary: This observational study evaluated the usefulness of a panel of biochemical and hematological variables for assessing training loads and recovery effectiveness in young professional long-distance and sprint swimmers over a 10-week preparatory training period. It identified an optimal panel including creatine kinase (CK), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), urea (U), total bilirubin (TB), direct bilirubin (DB), and ferritin concentrations, which collectively provide crucial information for monitoring post-training effort and recovery, regardless of sex or competitive distance. The study also highlighted the importance of ferritin, iron, and blood morphology in preventing deficiencies, anemia, and inflammatory states.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study monitoring biochemical and hematological recovery variables in young professional swimmers during a training program
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Data was collected over a 10-week preparatory training stage involving 27 male and female swimmers, aged 15-18 years, categorized by competitive distance (sprint: 50-100m; long-distance: 400-800m). Measurements included enzyme activities (ALT, AST, LDH, ALP, CK), metabolite concentrations (Cr, CRP, ferritin, TB, DB, urea, iron), and various capillary blood morphology parameters. The study primarily focused on observing responses to ongoing training loads and recovery, rather than comparing specific training "doses."

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Decreased as a function of time during recovery; differed significantly in male groups
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Decreased as a function of time during recovery in both sexes, regardless of competitive distance. Differed significantly in male groups. Can be nonspecifically elevated in inflammatory conditions and linked with relative iron deficiency, restricting serum iron utilization.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Protein that stores iron, recognized as an acute phase reactant, and a pro-inflammatory marker, indicating inflammation status.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Post-training effort, recovery profiles during training programs, inflammatory states, and in the context of avoiding iron deficiencies, anemia, and adverse inflammatory states in swimmers.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Provides a good overview of post-training effort, helps assess recovery, and reflects basic inflammation status. Combined with iron and blood morphology, it helps avoid iron deficiencies, anemia, and adverse inflammatory states. Appears more informative than CRP and is recommended for an optimal monitoring panel.

document_context_data.document_summary:
This study investigated the predictive impact of free and complexed forms of urokinase-type plasminogen activator (uPA), tissue-type plasminogen activator (tPA), and plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1), along with other inflammatory and coagulation biomarkers, for COVID-19 severity and the development of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) in Japanese adults. It revealed that elevated free, non-complexed PAI-1 antigen, and low circulating uPA and uPA/PAI-1 complex levels were associated with increased COVID-19 severity and ARDS, particularly in the complicated phase. These fibrinolytic changes correlated with heightened inflammation (e.g., TNF
Gα, IL1
Gβ, IL6, CRP), endothelial dysfunction (suPAR, sVCAM1), and clinical outcomes like lymphopenia, suggesting a "fibrinolysis-sleeper/shutdown" state in severe COVID-19.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational Study on COVID-19 Disease Progression
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was a retrospective observational study involving 69 hospitalized Japanese adults with COVID-19 and 20 healthy donors, comparing biomarker levels across uncomplicated, complicated, and critical disease phases. No therapeutic intervention or dose comparisons were reported, focusing instead on naturally occurring changes during disease progression and noting ethnic differences in biomarker profiles.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher levels in patients in the complicated phase compared to the uncomplicated phase.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Iron storage protein; acute phase reactant.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: COVID-19 complicated phase vs uncomplicated phase.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Associated with increased inflammation and COVID-19 severity.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study employed NMR metabolomics to investigate metabolic profiles in serum and urine from COVID-19 patients across varying disease severities (Medical Ward and Intensive Care Unit) and healthy controls. The primary aim was to identify biomarkers for COVID-19 diagnosis, severity classification, and prognosis, and to explore correlations with clinical factors like hypertension, obesity, and dyslipidemia. Key findings include the development of a highly efficient diagnostic panel (isoleucine, TMAO, glucose) and a robust severity classification panel (ethanol, TMAO, tyrosine, betaine, and clinical characteristics), alongside identification of numerous individual metabolites and clinical parameters associated with infection, disease progression, hospitalization duration, and patient outcome.

treatment_details.therapy_type: NMR metabolomics-based profiling and observational study of COVID-19 infection
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This observational study analyzed 80 serum and urine samples from COVID-19 patients (34 intensive care, 46 hospitalized) and 32 from healthy controls using NMR spectroscopy. The research focused on identifying and validating metabolite-based panels for COVID-19 diagnosis and severity classification. A diagnostic panel of isoleucine, TMAO, and glucose achieved an AUC of 0.91 (86.08% sensitivity, 83.87% specificity). A severity classification panel, combining ethanol, TMAO, tyrosine, betaine, and clinical characteristics (obesity/overweight, dyslipidemia, lymphocyte count), achieved an AUC of 0.825 (84.85% sensitivity, 72.09% specificity). No therapeutic intervention or dose-response comparisons were part of the study design.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: High levels associated with longer ICU stay (32.50 vs. 16.17 days, p = 0.021) and longer hospitalization in both Medical Ward (27.55 vs. 10.25 days, p = 0.023) and ICU (47.64 vs. 25.83 days, p = 0.03) patients.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Iron storage protein, also an acute phase reactant.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: COVID-19 disease severity and prognosis (hospital stay).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Associated with longer ICU stay, longer hospitalization, critical disease, unfavorable evolution, and increased mortality due to COVID-19.

document_context_data.document_summary: This narrative review investigates the molecular mechanisms of lung injury in acute and chronic respiratory diseases, including damage from viral, bacterial, oxidative stress, and cytokine factors. It highlights established and newly identified plasma biomarkers indicative of specific lung cell (Club, AT1, AT2, pan-epithelial, endothelial) and extracellular scaffold damage across various conditions like COVID-19, ARDS, COPD, and IPF. The review also discusses the limitations of individual biomarkers in predicting outcomes, emphasizing the enhanced predictive efficacy of combined biomarkers (e.g., ferritin and KL-6) and proposes an Artificial Intelligence-driven model to integrate diverse patient data for comprehensive lung injury monitoring, severity assessment, prognosis prediction, and personalized medicine.

treatment_details.therapy_type: A narrative review of lung injury mechanisms, biomarkers, and Artificial Intelligence (AI)-directed lung injury evaluation and monitoring.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: No specific therapeutic intervention or dose was investigated; the document is a review of existing knowledge focusing on intrinsic pathological processes and biomarker responses. It proposes an AI-driven monitoring model, which involved analyzing diverse datasets including chest CT scans, biological pathways, and 13 blood biomarkers from 455 IPF patients, alongside demographic and clinical data. No specific dose comparisons for AI application were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: The combination of ferritin and KL-6 as biomarkers showed significantly greater predictive efficacy for the progression to severe ARDS compared to any individual biomarker.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Not explicitly stated in the text.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Prediction of progression to severe ARDS when combined with KL-6.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Associated with significantly greater predictive efficacy for severe ARDS progression when used in combination with KL-6.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of 80 mg/day oral iron supplementation on hematological parameters, muscle damage biomarkers (CK, LDH, Mb), and cortisol levels in elite male cyclists during a 3-week stage race (Vuelta a España). It concluded that iron supplementation effectively prevented declines in iron metabolism and hematological profiles (serum iron, ferritin, hemoglobin, hematocrit, TSI, TP, RBC), significantly reduced accumulated stress (cortisol), and significantly lowered Creatine Kinase (CK) levels within the supplemented group, thereby contributing to optimal recovery and performance.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Oral Iron Supplementation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: 80 mg/day of oral iron (800 mg of iron protein succinylate, e.g., Ferplex 40®), administered as two 40 mg doses per day (during breakfast and dinner). The supplementation lasted for a 4-week period, starting one week before and continuing throughout the 3-week Vuelta a España stage race. No dose-response comparisons were reported, but a control group received no oral iron.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher in ITG (prevented decline in CG)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: ITG showed significant increases, from T1: 153.3 ± 68.8 ng/mL to T2: 231.0 ± 62.0 ng/mL, representing a 91.08 ± 118.30% increase (p < 0.05). CG showed a decline from T1: 128.3 ± 55.7 ng/mL to T2: 104.7 ± 41.2 ng/mL, representing a -13.88 ± 23.53% change. Group-by-time interaction was significant (p = 0.004).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Primary intracellular iron storage protein, reflecting total body iron stores.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Elite male cyclists during a 3-week stage race (Vuelta a España) with 80 mg/day oral iron supplementation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates optimal iron stores, preventing iron deficiency which can lead to fatigue; contributes to optimal recovery levels and enhanced endurance capacity.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the safety and efficacy of human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cell (UC-MSC) transplantation in patients with severe COVID-19 and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), focusing on clinical outcomes, lung functional status, hematological parameters, cytokine levels, and miRNA expression profiles. The findings demonstrated that UC-MSC therapy was safe, improved lung lesions over a one-year follow-up by reducing fibrosis and markers of lung damage (CT score, Surfactant D, sRAGE), hastened lymphocyte recovery, and modulated inflammation (decreased ESR, CRP, banded neutrophils). The treatment also showed complex immunomodulatory effects, including altered levels of several cytokines (e.g., increased IP-10, MIP-1α, G-CSF, IL-10, while IL-6, MCP-1, and RAGE remained mostly unchanged in vivo but exhibited changes in vitro) and specific miRNAs, as well as influencing PBMC activation and proliferation in vitro.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Human Umbilical Cord Mesenchymal Stem Cell (UC-MSC) transplantation combined with conventional anti-viral treatment (antibiotic therapy, dexamethasone).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Triple intravenous infusion of UC-MSC at a concentration of 1 × 10^6 cells/kg, administered on days 0, 3, and 6. The average cell viability was 87.8% ± 5.1% before infusion. This was combined with conventional anti-viral treatment including dexamethasone and antibiotic therapy. No explicit dose-response comparisons were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased expression observed.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Involved in a form of regulated cell death.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: PBMC co-cultured with UC-MSC in vitro.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: May have a positive impact, as increased expression was reported in the acute phase of COVID-19 and decreased in recovery.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigates the metabolic reprogramming mechanisms underlying sorafenib activity and resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells and patients. It reveals that sorafenib impairs mitochondrial function, forcing a metabolic shift towards glycolysis, leading to D-lactate accumulation, which serves as a biomarker for treatment response. In resistant cells, adaptation involves rerouting dihydroxyacetone phosphate towards glycerol-3-phosphate synthesis, extensive phospholipid remodeling to evade ferroptosis, enhanced antioxidant capacity, and increased reliance on exogenous triglycerides, resulting in glycerol accumulation as a marker of resistance. The study identifies D-lactate and glycerol as potential plasma biomarkers for monitoring sorafenib efficacy and resistance in HCC patients.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Sorafenib
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The primary therapy investigated was Sorafenib, a multi-kinase inhibitor for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). In vitro studies used sorafenib at an IC50 of 8.5 µM for acute, 48-hour, or 7-day prolonged treatments, and 7 µM for sorafenib-resistant IR-Huh7 cells. Clinical treatment involved oral administration of 400 mg twice daily for HCC patients, with dose reductions permitted for adverse effects. Other interventions included adenoviral gene downregulation (50 MOI for Gpd1/1l, Gpd2; 20 MOI for Glo1) and supplementation with various fatty acids (SFAs, MUFAs, PUFAs) or lipoproteins (VLDL, LDL), and inhibition of Mgll with JZL184. No detailed dose-response comparisons were consistently reported for sorafenib, though Mgll inhibition showed dose-dependent effects.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Upregulation observed after 48 hours of sorafenib treatment.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Genes that suppress ferroptosis.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: After 48 hours of sorafenib treatment.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates a cellular mechanism to resist sorafenib-induced ferroptosis.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study protocol describes a 9-week randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind clinical trial investigating the ergogenic effects of a 6-week daily probiotic supplementation on high-intensity endurance running performance in healthy non-elite athletes (N=32). Primary objectives include assessing the impact on time-to-exhaustion, while secondary objectives involve evaluating perceived exertion, blood chemistry (glucose, lactate), immune and stress biomarkers (cortisol, alpha-amylase, sIgA), cold and flu symptoms, gastrointestinal health (symptoms, stool characteristics, microbiota composition), and body composition. The study hypothesizes increased running time-to-exhaustion and reduced gastrointestinal/cold/flu symptoms with probiotic intervention.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Probiotic supplementation (intervention) with standardized exercise testing protocols
treatment_details.dose_specificity: A 6-week intervention period involves daily oral supplementation of 5 billion colony-forming units (CFU)/day of a specific probiotic capsule taken with a meal. The study is preceded by a 2-week pre-baseline and followed by a 1-week washout period. Participants are considered compliant if they take at least 80% of the supplement. Exercise testing includes a modified Bruce V̇O2 max treadmill test and a time-to-exhaustion treadmill endurance test conducted at 85% of V̇O2 max heart rate. No dose-response comparisons are reported in this study protocol.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Not applicable, measurement described without reported change (in current study protocol).
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Fiber Screener administered.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study is a multidisciplinary randomized trial investigating the feasibility and effects of a Psychodynamic Motivation and Training program (PMT) for secondary prevention in 90 physically inactive patients with stable coronary heart disease. It compares PMT with a single session of exercise training advice (EX) and treatment as usual (TAU). The primary outcome is the change in individual anaerobic threshold, with secondary endpoints including endothelial function, biomarkers of inflammation and oxidative stress, and various psychological measures. The study hypothesizes that PMT will lead to greater improvements in physical fitness than EX and TAU, and EX will be superior to TAU, particularly benefiting patients with mental or psychosocial distress.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Psychodynamic Motivation and Training program (PMT), individualized advice in exercise training (EX), and treatment as usual (TAU) for lifestyle modification and psychological support in patients with coronary heart disease.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study randomizes 90 patients into three groups (n=30 each) over a six-month follow-up. Treatment as Usual (TAU) involves standard recommendations. Exercise Training (EX) consists of one session of individualized exercise advice (ACSM/AHA guidelines, individualized heart rate zones) aiming for 300 minutes moderate or 150 minutes vigorous training/week. The Psychodynamic Motivation and Training (PMT) program includes 2-8 sessions of individual psychodynamic psychotherapy (max 400 minutes/patient over six months), tailored to individual needs, in addition to the EX advice, also aiming for 300/150 minutes training/week. Home-based exercise training is unsupervised. The study aims to explore optimal dosage but no formal dose-response comparisons between interventions are reported.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Assessment of oxidative and inflammatory stress, general health monitoring in patients with stable coronary heart disease.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of inflammation, coagulation status, and cardiovascular risk.

It emphasizes frequent, individualized monitoring (e.g., pre/post-exercise, daily, seasonally, after injury/competition) to establish personalized baseline ranges and track physiological changes in response to various training loads (e.g., acute bouts, heavy strength training, challenging training weeks). While specific nutritional intake recommendations are mentioned for protein (1.3–2.0 g/kg/day) and omega-3 fatty acids (≤3 g/day for average, 6–8 g/day for elite athletes), and iron supplementation at low-moderate doses, the document does not report dose-response comparisons for biomarker changes. Instead, it provides specific thresholds for identifying deficiencies (e.g., Vitamin D >50 ng/ml, Ferritin <12 µg/L), dehydration (e.g., >-2% body mass decrease, blood osmolality ≥295 mmol/kg, USG ≥1.020), insufficient recovery (30% decrease in T:C ratio), and overtraining (T:C ratio of 0.35 × 10⁻³). The overall approach prioritizes dynamic, contextualized assessment over universal thresholds for effective athlete management.

document_context_data.document_summary:
This study investigated the predictive impact of free and complexed forms of urokinase-type plasminogen activator (uPA), tissue-type plasminogen activator (tPA), and plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1), along with other inflammatory and coagulation biomarkers, for COVID-19 severity and the development of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) in Japanese adults. It revealed that elevated free, non-complexed PAI-1 antigen, and low circulating uPA and uPA/PAI-1 complex levels were associated with increased COVID-19 severity and ARDS, particularly in the complicated phase. These fibrinolytic changes correlated with heightened inflammation (e.g., TNF
Gα, IL1
Gβ, IL6, CRP), endothelial dysfunction (suPAR, sVCAM1), and clinical outcomes like lymphopenia, suggesting a "fibrinolysis-sleeper/shutdown" state in severe COVID-19.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study developed and optimized a portable, economical, and sensitive biosensor for rapid thrombin activity detection, leveraging a blood coagulation-inspired fibrin hydrogel system with a personal glucometer readout; the principle involves thrombin-mediated fibrinogen cleavage and invertase immobilization, and the method's analytical performance, selectivity, and reliability in serum samples were thoroughly evaluated.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Development and optimization of a portable biosensor and in vitro enzymatic assay for thrombin activity
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The biosensor was optimized for thrombin detection, achieving a linear range of 0–0.8 U/mL with an LOD of 0.04 U/mL. Optimal conditions included a fibrinogen concentration of 10.0 mg/mL, thrombin-fibrinogen incubation for 5.0 min, invertase concentration of 1.0 mg/mL, sucrose concentration of 7.5 mg/mL, and invertase-sucrose incubation for 5.0 min at an enzymatic reaction temperature of 40–50 °C. Recovery rates in serum samples ranged from 92.8% to 107.7%, and repeatability was 7.0% RSD. The study focused on diagnostic method development, so no therapeutic dose-response comparisons were reported.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study employed NMR metabolomics to investigate metabolic profiles in serum and urine from COVID-19 patients across varying disease severities (Medical Ward and Intensive Care Unit) and healthy controls. The primary aim was to identify biomarkers for COVID-19 diagnosis, severity classification, and prognosis, and to explore correlations with clinical factors like hypertension, obesity, and dyslipidemia. Key findings include the development of a highly efficient diagnostic panel (isoleucine, TMAO, glucose) and a robust severity classification panel (ethanol, TMAO, tyrosine, betaine, and clinical characteristics), alongside identification of numerous individual metabolites and clinical parameters associated with infection, disease progression, hospitalization duration, and patient outcome.

treatment_details.therapy_type: NMR metabolomics-based profiling and observational study of COVID-19 infection
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This observational study analyzed 80 serum and urine samples from COVID-19 patients (34 intensive care, 46 hospitalized) and 32 from healthy controls using NMR spectroscopy. The research focused on identifying and validating metabolite-based panels for COVID-19 diagnosis and severity classification. A diagnostic panel of isoleucine, TMAO, and glucose achieved an AUC of 0.91 (86.08% sensitivity, 83.87% specificity). A severity classification panel, combining ethanol, TMAO, tyrosine, betaine, and clinical characteristics (obesity/overweight, dyslipidemia, lymphocyte count), achieved an AUC of 0.825 (84.85% sensitivity, 72.09% specificity). No therapeutic intervention or dose-response comparisons were part of the study design.

document_context_data.document_summary: This retrospective single-center cohort study investigated sex-specific long-term alterations in metabolic, endocrine, renal, cardiovascular, and inflammatory biomarkers among 426 vaccinated COVID-19 survivors (PCR-confirmed, symptomatic, at least two vaccine doses) over a 30-month follow-up period. The study revealed distinct physiological recovery patterns, with males exhibiting earlier metabolic and cardiac alterations and females showing more persistent endocrine and inflammatory shifts, underscoring the need for sex-tailored monitoring strategies.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study aimed to identify serum proteomic biomarkers for predicting the effectiveness and diagnosing complications (acute rejection (AR) and ischemic-type biliary lesion (ITBL)) in liver transplant patients. Using MALDI-TOF MS, LC-MS, ELISA, and Western blot, the study found that ACLY, FGA, and APOA1 protein levels were significantly lower in pre-transplant, AR, and ITBL patients compared to healthy controls, showing modest recovery post-transplantation. These dysregulated proteins, implicated in glucolipid metabolism and the clotting cascade, are proposed as novel non-invasive and early diagnostic and prognostic indicators for liver transplantation outcomes and complications. Additionally, the study noted changes in clinical parameters such as blood cell counts, liver synthesis markers (CHO, ALB, FIB), and liver damage markers (GGT, TBIL, PT, ALT, AST) in transplant patients and those with complications.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Liver Transplantation (Orthotopic)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This study focuses on orthotopic liver transplantation, investigating outcomes and complications (acute rejection, ischemic-type biliary lesion) in patients. While no specific dose-response comparisons for the transplantation procedure were reported, the study did note that the anhepatic phase was significantly longer in ITBL patients (57.60 ± 7.28 minutes vs 45.88 ± 8.43 minutes for excellent patients, p = 0.0377) and warm ischemia time was longer in AR patients (14.57 ± 7.28 minutes vs 9.63 ± 0.86 minutes for healthy transplant patients, p = 0.0996). Samples were collected pre-transplant, 14 days post-transplant, and within 48 hours of complication onset, including grafts from extended criteria, donation after death, and partial/suboptimal donors.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: lower liver synthesis function markers (fibrinogen (FIB))

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Post-liver transplantation in transplant, acute rejection (AR), and ischemic-type biliary lesion (ITBL) patients compared to healthy controls.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates impaired liver synthesis function and potential coagulation disorder.

document_context_data.document_summary: This scientific roadmap by the Heart Failure Association comprehensively addresses the complex and heterogeneous nature of fibrosis in heart failure, aiming to improve its definition, quantification, and treatment. It reviews mechanisms of myocardial fibrosis across various etiologies like pressure overload, aging, and cardiomyopathies, emphasizing the central role of TGF-β, collagen deposition, and myofibroblast activity. The document discusses challenges in detecting fibrosis using circulating biomarkers, proposing a framework for assessment and a roadmap for future research to identify individual fibrotic mechanisms, novel therapeutic targets, and diagnostic tools. It also evaluates diverse anti-fibrotic strategies, including pharmacological agents and non-coding RNA-based treatments, highlighting the need for targeted, multi-pathway approaches given the complexity of the fibrotic process.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Anti-fibrotic therapies for heart failure, including established drugs like angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, as well as specific anti-fibrotic agents like pirfenidone. Investigational strategies include targeting the TGF-β pathway (e.g., TGF-β inhibitors, CTGF inhibitors like FG-3019), MAPK pathways (e.g., ERK inhibitors), inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1α), neuregulin-1 administration, Matrix Metalloproteinase (MMP) inhibitors, Galectin-3 inhibitors, and non-coding RNA-based treatments (microRNA and long non-coding RNAs).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This is a review document, and as such, no specific therapeutic doses, intensities, or durations are consistently reported for any intervention, nor are dose-response comparisons detailed. While some agents like Pirfenidone and non-coding RNA modulators show utility in experimental models and clinical trials (e.g., microRNA-21 inhibitor in a Phase II trial), precise quantitative dosage or detailed treatment parameters are generally absent, reflecting a discussion of general approaches and their limitations, including a noted 'lack of precision' in current therapies. For example, MMP-12i was given 3h post-MI, but without specific dosage.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Identified as a rather specific marker of activated, collagen-synthesizing fibroblasts; not expressed by inactive fibroblasts or fully differentiated myofibroblasts and non-fibroblast cells. No quantitative data provided.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Marker for fibroblast activation and collagen synthesis, crucial for wound healing and scar formation.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Post-myocardial infarction fibroblast activity and collagen synthesis.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates the presence of activated, collagen-synthesizing fibroblasts, which are key players in infarct scar formation and the fibrotic response to cardiac injury.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study comprehensively investigated the functional implications of heterogeneity in human embryonic stem cells (hESCs), focusing on an endodermally biased pluripotent substate. Using a GATA6-GFP reporter line and single-cell functional/transcriptomic analyses, the research identified distinct, interconvertible hESC substates defined by differential expression of GATA6 and SSEA3. GATA6-positive hESCs, while retaining long-term self-renewal and pluripotency (often alongside OCT4 and SOX2 co-expression), exhibited a higher propensity and bias towards spontaneous endoderm and mesoderm differentiation, with downregulation of ectodermal genes. SOX17 was identified as a potential driver for this endoderm-biased substate.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Human Embryonic Stem Cell (hESC) Substate Characterization and Differentiation Study
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study utilized the Shef4 hESC line, which was genetically modified with a GATA6-GFP reporter via Zinc Finger Nuclease-mediated homologous recombination. Cells were cultured in KO/SR on MEF feeders or E8 medium. hESC substates, defined by differential GATA6 and SSEA3 expression (e.g., 3+/6-, 3+/6L, 3+/6H, 3-/6+), were isolated by Fluorescence Activated Cell Sorting (FACS). These sorted cells were subjected to single-cell cloning, gene expression analysis (qPCR, single-cell RNA sequencing), high-content clonogenic assays, and differentiation protocols, including a spin-embryoid body (EB) system, without external therapeutic interventions or dose-response comparisons for differentiation-inducing factors. The focus was on intrinsic marker expression and resultant lineage bias.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated systemic and synovial Pentraxin-3 (PTX3) levels in early, treatment-naïve rheumatoid arthritis (RA) patients, both at baseline and after 6 months of conventional-synthetic Disease-Modifying-Anti-Rheumatic-Drugs (cs-DMARDs) treatment. It found that circulating PTX3 is a reliable marker of RA activity and predicts structural damage, remaining high post-treatment regardless of clinical response. Synovial PTX3 gene and protein expression correlated with local inflammation, disease activity, immune cell infiltration, ectopic lymphoid structures, and specific synovial pathotypes. While synovial PTX3 protein levels significantly decreased after cs-DMARD treatment, reflecting reduced local inflammation, this change was independent of clinical response.

treatment_details.dose_specificity: Patients received cs-DMARDs for 6 months; 94.1% received cs-DMARDs and 47.9% received adjunctive corticosteroid treatment. Treatment effects on PTX3 levels were assessed at 6 months and were independent of clinical response status; no specific dosages or dose-response comparisons were reported.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated novel protein-based subphenotypes in Heart Failure with reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF) patients using unsupervised machine learning on 4210 repeatedly measured circulating proteins over a median 2.1-year follow-up in 382 patients. It identified four distinct subphenotypes with varying protein profiles, clinical characteristics (e.g., age, EF, chronic renal failure), and prognosis. These subphenotypes were driven by specific protein subsets associated with various biological mechanisms, including oxidative stress, inflammation, extracellular matrix organization, myocardial stretch/stress, injury, and renal dysfunction. Subphenotypes 2 and 3 demonstrated significantly worse clinical outcomes compared to subphenotype 1, highlighting the value of dynamic proteomic profiling for gaining pathophysiological insights and exploring personalized treatment opportunities in complex diagnoses like HFrEF.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Proteomic profiling and subphenotyping in Heart Failure with reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF) patients.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational study involving trimonthly blood sampling over a median follow-up of 2.1 years (IQR: 1.1–2.6 years) in 382 HFrEF patients, totaling 1066 blood samples. An aptamer-based multiplex proteomic approach (SOMAscan assay) was used to measure 4210 circulating proteins, yielding relative fluorescence units (RFUs) for comparative analysis rather than absolute concentrations. No specific intervention, treatment, or dose-response comparisons were conducted, as the study focused on characterizing disease subphenotypes and biomarker patterns over time. Repeated proteomic measurements (incorporating both intercept and slope coefficients) demonstrated improved accuracy for survival models (c-index 0.73, BIC 1023) compared to single time-point assessments.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Levels highest in subphenotype 2. Precise quantification not provided.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Indicates myocardial stretch/stress and fibrosis.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Patient subphenotype classification in a cardiac cohort, particularly defining Subphenotype 2.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Higher levels are associated with subphenotype 2, which is linked to significantly worse patient outcomes (HR 3.43 (1.76–6.69) compared to subphenotype 1).

document_context_data.document_summary: This study comprehensively investigated the clinical relevance and efficacy of collagen X breakdown product (CXM) as a blood-based biomarker for endochondral long bone fracture repair in both healthy individuals and patients with tibia or femur fractures. It characterized CXM expression patterns, stability across demographics (age, sex), correlation with other bone turnover markers (P1NP, CTX, osteocalcin, leptin, sclerostin), and its utility in predicting healing prognosis (early, normal, delayed). The findings showed CXM levels are low in healthy individuals, peak around 25-35 days post-fracture, can be reliably measured via dried blood spots, and offer an earlier, quantitative indication of healing compared to traditional radiographic methods, supporting its prospective use in fracture studies.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study of natural long bone fracture repair, with a secondary analysis of a Vitamin D3 supplementation trial (VitaShock).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study primarily focused on observing biomarker changes in patients with acute closed or low-grade open tibial or femoral shaft fractures (Gustilo type I or II, AO/OTA type 42), without applying a specific therapeutic dose as an intervention. For the secondary analysis of the VitaShock trial, multiple Vitamin D3 dosing strategies were assessed, but specific dose details were not provided, and no significant difference in CXM response was found compared to placebo. Longitudinal blood samples were collected at various standard-of-care clinical visits over a period up to 48 weeks post-fracture.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Not detectable above reliability threshold of 80%.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Phosphate homeostasis.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Fracture healing.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Not a viable biomarker for analysis in this study due to detection limits.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study clinically validated C12FDG as a flow cytometry-based biomarker for detecting senescent peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and T cells in humans. It investigated the association of C12FDG+ cells with chronological age, sex, and various serum senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) biomarkers. Findings revealed that C12FDG++ PBMCs and T cells increase with age, are elevated in males and patients with mild to moderate osteoarthritis, and decrease following fisetin treatment. The C12FDG platform shows promise as a quantifiable clinical tool for assessing healthy aging, age-related orthopedic decline, and the efficacy of senolytic therapies.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Senolytic therapy using the flavonoid fisetin
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Fisetin was administered at 100 mg/day to a small subgroup of 10 participants, with longitudinal analysis performed. While dose consistency was self-reported, specific duration details or comprehensive dose-response comparisons were not systematically reported in this study, though future controlled trials are acknowledged as necessary to determine the optimum senolytic dosing regimen.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Positively correlated with increasing C12FDG++ signal (r=0.2018; p=0.0537).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: A biomarker related to senescence and the Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype (SASP).
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Healthy human participants (age range 20–82 years), association with peripheral senescence (C12FDG++ PBMCs).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Biomarker of senescence.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study performed a comprehensive qualitative and quantitative proteomic analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) derived from different somatic origins (fibroblasts and peripheral blood CD34+ cells), comparing them to original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC) and human embryonic stem cells (hESC). Using ESI-MS e and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry, complemented by Western blot validation, the research aimed to characterize hiPSC proteomic profiles, identify known and novel pluripotency markers, and distinguish hiPSCs from their somatic precursors. Key findings include the identification of approximately 220 commonly up-regulated proteins in pluripotent stem cell lines, the development and confirmation of a 22-protein marker panel for hiPSC characterization, and the observation of coordinated up-regulation of proteins involved in protein synthesis, folding, RNA processing, DNA replication, DNA repair, and energy metabolism (including oxidative phosphorylation and lipogenesis) in hiPSCs. The study also identified somatic cell markers that were down-regulated upon reprogramming and highlighted specific proteomic differences between hiPSCs and hESCs, contributing to improved hiPSC quality control for therapeutic applications.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Proteomic characterization and comparative analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) and human embryonic stem cells (hESCs).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was a characterization study, not a therapeutic intervention, thus no 'dose' of therapy was administered. Quantitative and qualitative proteomic analyses were performed using electrospray ionization (ESI)-MS e (label-free quantification with internal reference standard) and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry. Two hiPSC lines (iNC-01 from CD34+ cells, SB5-MP1 from fibroblasts, both generated using loxP-flanked excisable polycistronic STEMCCA lentiviral vector) and one hESC line (H9) were analyzed at earlier and later passages. Comparisons were made against their respective original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC). Proteins were considered differentially expressed if expression changed by >=1.5-fold, with a maximum false discovery rate of 2% and >95% confidence. Western blot analysis was used for validation. The developed marker panel was further tested in 8-9 additional hiPSC lines or passages from different somatic origins and reprogramming techniques. Differentiation studies were conducted with embryoid bodies at 24 hours and 7 days to assess marker changes during spontaneous differentiation.

matched_biomarker_details.measured_tissue_or_fluid: human embryonic stem cells (hESC), human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs), Peripheral Blood Mononuclear Cells (PBMC), fibroblasts

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Detected by Western blot analysis in hESC, both hiPSCs, and PBMC. Also expressed in fibroblasts. Not reliably identified by MS. Expression in PBMC has not been previously reported.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Well-known marker of pluripotency
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Characterization of hESC and hiPSCs, and expression in somatic cells; investigation of MS compatibility.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Essential pluripotency marker; challenging to detect by standard MS methods. Novel finding of expression in PBMC.

document_context_data.document_summary: This document outlines the protocol for the PROSAP-A randomized controlled trial, investigating the effects of preoperative insomnia treatment (Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia or Sleep Education Therapy) on acute and long-term postoperative pain control, brain health, and physical recovery in patients undergoing total knee or hip arthroplasty. The study aims to assess various patient-reported outcomes (e.g., opioid use, quality of recovery, sleep, mood, quality of life), objective measures (e.g., actigraphic sleep, quantitative sensory testing for pain, neurocognitive function), and blood biomarkers (e.g., inflammatory, monoamine, genetic mediators) across preoperative and postoperative phases to determine the impact on pain intensity, opioid use, sleep quality, mental health, and functional recovery. The document also details the recruitment, randomization, blinding, and data collection plans for this prehabilitation approach.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Preoperative Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) and Sleep Education Therapy (SET) as an active comparator.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Both interventions are delivered over 4 weeks in a hybrid format, comprising a digital self-guided platform and weekly telehealth video sessions (up to 60 minutes). CBT-I sessions are conducted with a psychologist and include sleep restriction and stimulus control, while SET sessions are with a research nurse. A video-assisted booster session is provided 1-2 weeks postoperatively. No dose-response comparisons are reported as these are fixed intervention protocols.

matched_biomarker_details.biomarker_name: Fibromyalgia Severity Score (FS) (derived from ACR 2016 fibromyalgia criteria)
matched_biomarker_details.activity_type: Assessment of the degree of 'fibromyalgianess' or nociplastic pain components

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Not specified in this study protocol.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Consists of two subscales: Widespread Pain Index and Symptom Severity Scale. The sum of these is the FS score. Identified as a robust predictor of poorer outcome following TKA and THA and a predictor of higher opioid consumption following surgery, also in individuals who do not fulfil the criteria for fibromyalgia.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Quantifies the severity of fibromyalgia symptoms and nociplastic pain components.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Fibromyalgia symptom assessment, particularly in the context of TKA/THA surgery.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Predicts poorer outcomes and higher opioid consumption post-surgery, indicating risk for adverse recovery in surgical patients, even in individuals not fulfilling full fibromyalgia criteria.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the associations between circulating fibrocytes and left atrial (LA) fibrosis or the prevalence of recurrence after catheter ablation in patients with persistent and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (AF), compared to sinus rhythm controls. It examined fibrocyte proportion, differentiation, and migration, as well as gene expression of various molecular markers. The findings demonstrated that increased circulating fibrocytes positively correlate with LA fibrosis (low-voltage area) and are a significant predictor of 1-year recurrence after ablation in persistent AF. Fibrocytes from persistent AF patients showed enhanced differentiation into myofibroblasts and elevated expression of pro-fibrotic and inflammatory markers, with TGF-β1 promoting differentiation and SDF-1 enhancing migration.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Catheter ablation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Catheter ablation was performed as a first-time or single procedure, predominantly for persistent AF. Specifics included radiofrequency energy applied with a power limit of 35 W and a maximal temperature of 45°C, applied until a voltage of <0.1 mV was achieved or for a maximum of 30 seconds per point. A single bolus of 100 IU/kg heparin was administered to maintain activated clotting time within 250-300 seconds. Oral antiplatelet/anticoagulant drugs were stopped 3 days before ablation and restored afterward, while antiarrhythmic drugs were stopped on the day of ablation and restored the next day for up to 2 months. Electroanatomic mapping systems were used to identify fibrotic (low-voltage) areas. Patients were followed up for 1 year post-ablation.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Content was higher at mRNA levels in differentiated fibrocytes from AF patients compared to the paroxysmal AF group and SR controls, indicating a hyperactivated status.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: An extracellular matrix glycoprotein involved in cell adhesion, migration, and wound healing, often elevated in fibrotic conditions.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Differentiated fibrocytes from Atrial Fibrillation patients.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Increased Fibronectin mRNA levels indicate enhanced extracellular matrix production and altered cell-matrix interactions by fibrocytes from AF patients, contributing to cardiac fibrosis.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated disease and target engagement biomarkers in the phase 2b RISE-SSc trial of riociguat in early diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (dcSSc) to predict treatment response. While the primary endpoint (modified Rodnan Skin Score, mRSS) did not reach statistical significance, riociguat treatment significantly increased plasma cGMP levels, indicating engagement of the NO-sGC-cGMP pathway. Additionally, serum sPECAM-1 and CXCL-4 levels decreased with riociguat. Elevated baseline sPECAM-1 and the presence of αSMA-positive cells in skin biopsies were identified as potential predictive biomarkers for greater mRSS reduction with riociguat, suggesting these markers may help identify patients who could benefit from the treatment for skin fibrosis.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Riociguat (Drug Treatment)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Patients with early treatment-naïve diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis were randomized to receive riociguat (n=60) or placebo (n=61) for 52 weeks. Riociguat was administered up to 2.5 mg, maximum three times daily. Biomarker assessments were performed at baseline (day 0) and week 14, with clinical endpoints evaluated up to week 52. Rescue therapy was permitted from week 26. While cGMP changes correlated with riociguat pharmacokinetics, no explicit dose-response comparisons for other biomarkers were formally reported.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: unchanged (between groups); fold-change correlated with mRSS change
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Changes in mRNA levels did not differ significantly between riociguat and placebo groups from baseline to week 14. However, fold-changes showed a modest correlation (0.358) with change in mRSS from baseline to week 52 in the riociguat group, but no clear predictive value for mRSS at week 52 (interaction P > 0.05).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Extracellular matrix glycoprotein involved in cell adhesion, migration, tissue repair, and key in fibrotic processes.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Riociguat treatment in dcSSc patients from baseline to week 14/52.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: No significant change in mRNA levels due to treatment, but a modest correlation with mRSS changes suggests it could be a potential indicator of skin fibrosis progression.

document_context_data.document_summary: This document synthesizes the proceedings of the Tau2024 Global Conference, showcasing interdisciplinary advancements in tau-associated brain disorders. Key areas covered include the pathophysiology, molecular mechanisms, and brain microenvironments of tauopathies, as well as global perspectives highlighting genetic, socioeconomic, and linguistic diversity's impact on conditions like Frontotemporal Lobe Dementia and Primary Progressive Aphasia. The conference reviewed cellular mechanisms, advanced tau-PET, CSF, and blood-based biomarkers for diagnosis and monitoring of Alzheimer's Disease and other tauopathies, alongside discussions on therapeutic strategies such as antisense oligonucleotides, immunotherapy, senolytics, OGA inhibitors, and novel intrabody approaches aimed at reducing tau levels and aggregates.

treatment_details.therapy_type: The conference proceedings discussed a range of therapeutic advancements for tauopathies, including antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) therapy, tau immunotherapy (e.g., bepranemab), anti-tau-PEST intrabody therapy, pharmacological inhibition of PERK, senolytics (dasatinib plus quercetin), and O-GlcNAcase (OGA) inhibition (e.g., FNP-223).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Specific dose details varied by therapy: BIIB080 (ASO) demonstrated a dose-dependent reduction of approximately 60% in CSF tau. Anti-tau-PEST intrabodies reduced eGFP-tau by 70-78% in cellular models and endogenous tau by 38-58% in organoids over 21 days. A PERK inhibitor and nanobody constructs were effective in animal models without specific dose reporting. Bepranemab, senolytics (dasatinib plus quercetin), and FNP-223 (OGA inhibitor) were evaluated in early-phase human trials with various administration routes (IV, oral) and were generally well-tolerated, but detailed dose-response comparisons were not consistently reported across all interventions.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Dysregulation reported

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Tissue repair and extracellular matrix remodeling; dysregulation can lead to pathological scarring.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Cerebral Autosomal Dominant Arteriopathy with Subcortical Infarcts and Leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Contributes to molecular pathologies in cerebral small vessel diseases (cSVDs) and development/progression of neuro-glial tauopathies; molecular measures of fibrosis are associated with enlarged perivascular space and white matter injury.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the efficacy and fate of intravenously administered human kidney-derived CD133+ and CD133- cells in ameliorating cisplatin-induced nephropathy in immunodeficient rats. Both cell types similarly improved renal function and promoted regeneration, reducing acute kidney injury and histological damage. Crucially, therapeutic effects were not due to renal engraftment; instead, cells were entrapped in the lungs, underwent cell death within 24 hours, and likely mediated repair through paracrine or endocrine factors, potentially involving macrophage infiltration and IL10 secretion in the lungs.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Cisplatin-induced acute kidney injury model in rats, followed by intravenous administration of human kidney-derived CD133+ or CD133- cells.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Cisplatin was administered intraperitoneally at 7 mg/100 g body weight to induce injury. Cell therapy consisted of two intravenous injections of 10^6 GFP-expressing CD133+ or CD133- cells (in 500 µl sterile PBS) via tail vein on days 2 and 7 post-cisplatin. Control groups received saline or PBS. Cells were at passage 5. A second cell injection after day 7 did not provide additional benefits. No dose-response comparisons for cell therapy were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Minimal fibrotic lesions observed. No significant differences in fibrosis were observed between the cisplatin-injured and cell-treated groups at day 14. Attributed to the nude rat model lacking T cells, which play a role in renal fibrosis development.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Indicator of renal fibrosis (scarring).
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Assessment of renal fibrosis at day 14 following cisplatin injury and cell therapy in nude rats.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Minimal fibrosis suggests lack of progression of scarring, possibly due to model characteristics rather than treatment effect.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated novel post-exercise oxygen uptake recovery (VO2Rec) measures, especially VO2T12.5% (time to recover 12.5% of peak VO2), in patients with dyspnea on exertion (DOE) and obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (oHCM). The research established VO2T12.5% as an easily derived, reliable, non-invasive biomarker that reflects cardiac performance, predicts heart failure hospitalization and all-cause death, and tracks with invasive hemodynamic indices. document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated brain and blood biomarker signatures in both rat models exposed to repetitive low-level blast and human veterans exposed to IED blasts, aiming to identify antemortem evidence of tauopathy and neuronal injury related to neurobehavioral syndromes. Key findings include chronic increases in hyperphosphorylated tau (p-tau) immunoreactivity and abnormal perivascular p-tau accumulation in specific brain regions of blast-exposed rats from 6 weeks to 12 months post-injury. In human veterans, a significant subset (50%) with multiple blast exposures exhibited excessive cortical [18F]AV1451 tau ligand retention, indicating tauopathy, which correlated with higher circulating plasma neurofilament light (NfL) levels, suggesting neuronal injury. The study also explored cortical diffusivity analysis and [18F]AV45 amyloid PET imaging, finding no significant amyloid pathology but identifying microstructural cortical disruption linked to tau pathology. Additionally, increases in stathmin 1 in the amygdala of blast-exposed animals were associated with increased anxiety. The findings collectively suggest a link between blast injury, tauopathy, neuronal injury, and associated neurobehavioral complaints, highlighting potential biomarkers for diagnosing long-term neuropsychiatric sequelae of mTBI.

treatment_details.dose_specificity: Rats received three repetitive low-level blast exposures (74.5 kPa/10.8 psi, 4.8 ms duration, 175.8 kPa ms impulse) administered one per day for 3 consecutive days using a shock tube. Human veterans reported histories of multiple blast exposures from improvised explosive devices (IEDs), ranging from 1 to 50 or more, all associated with at least one mTBI. The study primarily focused on the effects of these exposures rather than varying doses, and no dose-response comparisons were reported. Diagnostic procedures included MRI (3-Tesla Siemens Biograph MR system) and PET imaging (370 MBq [18F]AV45 and 370 MBq [18F]AV1451 injected, with image acquisition approximately 60-80 min post-injection for 20 min durations).
