document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigates the metabolic reprogramming mechanisms underlying sorafenib activity and resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells and patients. It reveals that sorafenib impairs mitochondrial function, forcing a metabolic shift towards glycolysis, leading to D-lactate accumulation, which serves as a biomarker for treatment response. In resistant cells, adaptation involves rerouting dihydroxyacetone phosphate towards glycerol-3-phosphate synthesis, extensive phospholipid remodeling to evade ferroptosis, enhanced antioxidant capacity, and increased reliance on exogenous triglycerides, resulting in glycerol accumulation as a marker of resistance. The study identifies D-lactate and glycerol as potential plasma biomarkers for monitoring sorafenib efficacy and resistance in HCC patients.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Sorafenib
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The primary therapy investigated was Sorafenib, a multi-kinase inhibitor for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). In vitro studies used sorafenib at an IC50 of 8.5 µM for acute, 48-hour, or 7-day prolonged treatments, and 7 µM for sorafenib-resistant IR-Huh7 cells. Clinical treatment involved oral administration of 400 mg twice daily for HCC patients, with dose reductions permitted for adverse effects. Other interventions included adenoviral gene downregulation (50 MOI for Gpd1/1l, Gpd2; 20 MOI for Glo1) and supplementation with various fatty acids (SFAs, MUFAs, PUFAs) or lipoproteins (VLDL, LDL), and inhibition of Mgll with JZL184. No detailed dose-response comparisons were consistently reported for sorafenib, though Mgll inhibition showed dose-dependent effects.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Accumulation of these glycolytic intermediates.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Glycolytic intermediates.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Sorafenib treatment, impaired OxPhos, increased glycolysis.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Contributes to metabolic imbalance and accumulation of toxic byproducts like methylglyoxal (MG).

document_context_data.document_summary: This study employed NMR metabolomics to investigate metabolic profiles in serum and urine from COVID-19 patients across varying disease severities (Medical Ward and Intensive Care Unit) and healthy controls. The primary aim was to identify biomarkers for COVID-19 diagnosis, severity classification, and prognosis, and to explore correlations with clinical factors like hypertension, obesity, and dyslipidemia. Key findings include the development of a highly efficient diagnostic panel (isoleucine, TMAO, glucose) and a robust severity classification panel (ethanol, TMAO, tyrosine, betaine, and clinical characteristics), alongside identification of numerous individual metabolites and clinical parameters associated with infection, disease progression, hospitalization duration, and patient outcome.

treatment_details.therapy_type: NMR metabolomics-based profiling and observational study of COVID-19 infection
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This observational study analyzed 80 serum and urine samples from COVID-19 patients (34 intensive care, 46 hospitalized) and 32 from healthy controls using NMR spectroscopy. The research focused on identifying and validating metabolite-based panels for COVID-19 diagnosis and severity classification. A diagnostic panel of isoleucine, TMAO, and glucose achieved an AUC of 0.91 (86.08% sensitivity, 83.87% specificity). A severity classification panel, combining ethanol, TMAO, tyrosine, betaine, and clinical characteristics (obesity/overweight, dyslipidemia, lymphocyte count), achieved an AUC of 0.825 (84.85% sensitivity, 72.09% specificity). No therapeutic intervention or dose-response comparisons were part of the study design.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher levels ranked among the top positive correlates to arterial hypertension and obesity/overweight; increased levels significantly associated with cardiovascular risk comorbidities.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Involved in arginine and proline, galactose, and glycerolipid metabolisms; general metabolism.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: COVID-19 patients admitted to medical ward with arterial hypertension, obesity/overweight, and cardiovascular risk comorbidities.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Associated with arterial hypertension, obesity/overweight, and cardiovascular risk comorbidities in COVID-19 patients.

document_context_data.document_summary: This review provides updated guidelines and a consensus for standardizing pre-analytical variables in salivary biomarker studies for Alzheimer's disease (AD) research. It critically appraises current methodologies, identifies inconsistencies, and proposes a standardized protocol for saliva collection, processing, and storage to improve reliability for diagnostic biomarker detection and quantification. The document investigates various protein and metabolomic biomarkers in saliva, assessing their diagnostic potential for AD and Mild Cognitive Impairment, and highlights the importance of controlling factors like collection methods, centrifugation, and storage conditions for accurate measurement.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Salivary Biomarker Research and Standardization for Alzheimer's Disease Diagnosis
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This is a comprehensive review article focusing on standardizing pre-analytical variables for salivary Alzheimer's Disease (AD) biomarker studies, rather than a therapeutic intervention or dose-response investigation. It critically discusses how inconsistent methodologies and pre-analytical factors (e.g., collection kits like Salivette vs. passive drooling, acute food intake, physical activity, stress, diurnal variations, dental restorations, freezing/thawing protocols, centrifugation speeds) influence biomarker detection and quantification, leading to conflicting findings for analytes like Aβ42, Aβ40, and AChE activity. The document proposes a standardized pre-analytical protocol, including pre-collection instructions (e.g., abstinence from food, drinks, smoking, alcohol, exercise), passive drool collection (e.g., 2 mL after 5 min pooling), and post-collection processing (e.g., immediate freezing, visual inspection, two-step centrifugation, aliquoting 100-250 µL). Various analytical methods (ELISA, Western blot, SIMOA, MS-based methods, NMR) were discussed for diagnostic marker identification, emphasizing that a universal protocol might not suit all biomarkers due to their diverse physiological roles.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significant concentration changes identified in MCI and AD patients compared to controls. Statistically significant multivariate models identified it as a discriminator.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) and Alzheimer's Disease (AD) patients compared to controls.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Identified as a discriminator for distinguishing AD patients from control subjects.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review identifies and recommends validated biomarkers for tracking health, performance, and recovery in athletes across multiple domains including nutritional status (macronutrients, micronutrients, food allergies), hydration, muscle status (damage, endocrine response), endurance, and injury risk (concussions, stress fractures, ACL). It advocates for a comprehensive, integrative, and individualized approach to biomarker analysis, emphasizing dynamic monitoring and contextual interpretation over single markers or universal thresholds to optimize training and minimize injury and overtraining risks.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Biomarker-guided monitoring and management of athletic training, nutrition, hydration, and injury recovery
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This review primarily focuses on the diagnostic and prognostic value of biomarkers rather than specific therapeutic doses. It emphasizes frequent, individualized monitoring (e.g., pre/post-exercise, daily, seasonally, after injury/competition) to establish personalized baseline ranges and track physiological changes in response to various training loads (e.g., acute bouts, heavy strength training, challenging training weeks). While specific nutritional intake recommendations are mentioned for protein (1.3–2.0 g/kg/day) and omega-3 fatty acids (≤3 g/day for average, 6–8 g/day for elite athletes), and iron supplementation at low-moderate doses, the document does not report dose-response comparisons for biomarker changes. Instead, it provides specific thresholds for identifying deficiencies (e.g., Vitamin D >50 ng/ml, Ferritin <12 µg/L), dehydration (e.g., >-2% body mass decrease, blood osmolality ≥295 mmol/kg, USG ≥1.020), insufficient recovery (30% decrease in T:C ratio), and overtraining (T:C ratio of 0.35 × 10⁻³). The overall approach prioritizes dynamic, contextualized assessment over universal thresholds for effective athlete management.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study aimed to develop and validate a female-focused predictive atherosclerosis risk signature based on serum metabolites in patients with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), addressing the inadequacy of established cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk scores. It investigated metabolomic and clinical features associated with subclinical plaque status, developing and validating a 35-metabolite/5-clinical trait signature (UCLH-40) and a refined 5-feature panel (including age, glycine, M-LDL-C, IDL-C, and omega-6/omega-3 ratio) that accurately classifies SLE patients with/without subclinical atherosclerosis, predicts atherosclerosis progression, and identifies elevated CVD risk, thereby outperforming existing risk assessment tools.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Diagnostic/Prognostic Biomarker Discovery and Validation for Atherosclerosis Risk Stratification (via Metabolomics and Machine Learning)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational, diagnostic study that did not involve therapeutic interventions or dose comparisons for treatments. Its primary focus was on developing and validating predictive biomarker signatures. Serum metabolomic analysis was performed using a high-throughput nuclear magnetic resonance platform (≥250 metabolites). Various machine learning models (e.g., univariate logistic regression, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator LR, random forest, neural network, support vector machine, and eXtreme gradient boost) with 10-fold cross-validation were used to analyze metabolomic data and clinical traits. Model performance was assessed by AUROC (>0.7 for inclusion), sensitivity, specificity, and F1 score. Vascular ultrasound was used for carotid/femoral intima-media thickness assessment of subclinical atherosclerosis. The study discusses the implications for guiding statin therapy or lifestyle modifications but does not directly test them, noting that standard statin prescriptions may be insufficient due to normal lipid ranges in SLE patients.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly lower in patients with SLE-P compared with patients with SLE-NP (P <0.05). Low glycine concentration (part of a 5-panel atherosclerosis risk signature); noted as 'glycine deficiency'. Inversely associated with risk of acute myocardial infarction; higher plasma glycine was associated with a more favorable baseline lipid profile and lower prevalence of obesity, hypertension, and diabetes; genetically associated with lower CHD risk.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Nonessential amino acid involved in protein synthesis and various metabolic pathways. Used in the synthesis of purines and glucose; exerts anti-inflammatory and antioxidative effects; its deficiency can lead to diminished capacity for triglyceride-rich very-low-density lipoprotein uptake by macrophages, resulting in elevated triglyceride content; central to cell metabolism, lipid metabolism, and the de novo production of sphingolipids.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Subclinical plaque status in adult Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) patients (SLE-P vs. SLE-NP) and atherosclerosis progression in Juvenile Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (JSLE) patients; Subclinical atherosclerosis risk in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) patients; Acute myocardial infarction, traditional cardiovascular risk factors (obesity, hypertension, diabetes), CHD risk, metabolic syndrome.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Associated with subclinical plaque status and increased cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk. It is a key feature in the simplified 5-feature predictive panel for plaque status and CVD risk. Also shows potential utility in non-SLE populations for MI, stroke, and peripheral vascular disease. Associated with elevated CVD risk and subclinical atherosclerosis in SLE; inversely associated with traditional cardiovascular risk factors, including obesity, hypertension, and diabetes. Indicates protection against cardiovascular risk factors and acute myocardial infarction; associated with lower CHD risk.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of 2-week hemp fiber (high and low doses) or placebo supplementation on post-exercise gut permeability and plasma metabolite shifts in healthy male and female cyclists after intensive cycling. While hemp fiber did not significantly alter post-exercise gut permeability (measured by urine sugar data), untargeted metabolomics revealed that the combination of hemp fiber intake and vigorous exercise increased beneficial gut-derived metabolites and influenced pathways related to tryptophan, primary bile acid, steroid, sphingolipid, alpha-linolenic acid, arginine and proline, lipid, and amino acid metabolism.

Each supplementation period concluded with a 2.25-hour intensive cycling bout performed at approximately 70% VO2max. While distinct metabolomic shifts were observed between the hemp fiber and placebo groups (R2Y = 0.987 and 0.995), no significant dose-response for gut permeability was reported.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated a chemically defined, serum-free protocol for the in vitro transdifferentiation of pancreatic progenitor AR42J-B13 cells into functional hepatocyte-like cells (HLCs) over five days. The research examined morphological, transcriptomic, proteomic, and functional changes, concluding that successful transdifferentiation, facilitated by extracellular matrix proteins like fibronectin or laminin, is independent of serum.

treatment_details.therapy_type: In vitro pancreatic progenitor cell transdifferentiation to hepatocyte-like cells
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Clonal pancreatic progenitor AR42J-B13 cells were cultured for five days in a differentiation medium containing 100 nM Dexamethasone, 10 ng/ml Oncostatin M, 20 ng/ml HGF, 20 ng/ml FGF-2, 1% ITS+ (insulin, transferrin, selenous acid), 0.2% BSA, 4.4 mM nicotinamide, 1 µM copper sulphate, 30 µg/ml ascorbic acid, and 1 µg/ml heparin. Cells were grown on uncoated plastic, laminin-coated (2 µg/cm2), or fibronectin-coated (5 µg/cm2) substrata, with or without 5% FBS supplementation. The study primarily focused on the effectiveness of serum-free conditions facilitated by ECM proteins, rather than dose-response comparisons for individual components, finding no significant difference in transdifferentiation potential between fibronectin and laminin substrata.

document_context_data.document_summary: This randomized controlled trial investigated the effects of 8 weeks of daily 5g Cistanche deserticola (CD) extract supplementation, combined with progressive high-intensity resistance training, on muscle strength and recovery in both untrained and resistance-trained male participants. The study found that CD supplementation significantly enhanced muscle strength (1RM bench press and squat, MVIC) and endurance (RTF in untrained), and facilitated post-exercise recovery by modulating hormonal responses (increased testosterone, reduced cortisol) and decreasing markers of stress and inflammation (reduced CRP and CK levels) in both cohorts. Mechanistic insights suggest CD's role in improving energy metabolism, reducing muscle degradation, enhancing antioxidant defense, modulating neurotransmission, and regulating endocrine axes.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Cistanche deserticola (CD) supplementation combined with a progressive resistance training program.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants received 5 g of CD extract daily, administered in two sachets (after breakfast and lunch) for 8 consecutive weeks, alongside a placebo group. A standardized resistance training program was completed three times per week for eight weeks. This program involved 4 sets of 10-12 repetitions at 65-70% of 1RM for weeks 1-4, and 4 sets of 6-8 repetitions at 80% of 1RM for weeks 5-8. Maximal strength (1RM bench press/squat, MVIC) and endurance (RTF bench press) were assessed. No dose-response comparisons for CD were reported, only comparison to placebo.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigates the metabolic reprogramming mechanisms underlying sorafenib activity and resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells and patients. It reveals that sorafenib impairs mitochondrial function, forcing a metabolic shift towards glycolysis, leading to D-lactate accumulation, which serves as a biomarker for treatment response. In resistant cells, adaptation involves rerouting dihydroxyacetone phosphate towards glycerol-3-phosphate synthesis, extensive phospholipid remodeling to evade ferroptosis, enhanced antioxidant capacity, and increased reliance on exogenous triglycerides, resulting in glycerol accumulation as a marker of resistance. The study identifies D-lactate and glycerol as potential plasma biomarkers for monitoring sorafenib efficacy and resistance in HCC patients.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Sorafenib
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The primary therapy investigated was Sorafenib, a multi-kinase inhibitor for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). In vitro studies used sorafenib at an IC50 of 8.5 µM for acute, 48-hour, or 7-day prolonged treatments, and 7 µM for sorafenib-resistant IR-Huh7 cells. Clinical treatment involved oral administration of 400 mg twice daily for HCC patients, with dose reductions permitted for adverse effects. Other interventions included adenoviral gene downregulation (50 MOI for Gpd1/1l, Gpd2; 20 MOI for Glo1) and supplementation with various fatty acids (SFAs, MUFAs, PUFAs) or lipoproteins (VLDL, LDL), and inhibition of Mgll with JZL184. No detailed dose-response comparisons were consistently reported for sorafenib, though Mgll inhibition showed dose-dependent effects.

document_context_data.document_summary: This scoping review synthesizes existing literature on the frequency, function, and dynamics of regulatory T cells (Tregs) and their subsets in convalescent COVID-19 patients, including those with Long COVID, comparing them to acutely ill patients and seronegative controls. The review concludes that while Treg populations can quantitatively and functionally reconstitute during recovery, an infection-induced dysregulation often persists for several months. Findings reveal varied outcomes for total Treg frequencies, but distinct patterns for specific Treg subsets, FoxP3 expression, and cytokine production. Long COVID patients consistently exhibit significantly altered proportions of Tregs, indicating persistent immune dysregulation potentially contributing to the syndrome's pathophysiology and viral persistence, despite methodological heterogeneity across studies.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Scoping Review of Regulatory T Cell Dynamics in COVID-19 Convalescence and Long COVID
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This scoping review systematically investigated the frequency (e.g., absolute counts, relative frequency) and functionality (e.g., cytokine secretion, ex vivo suppressive capacity) of regulatory T cells (Tregs) and their subsets in convalescent COVID-19 patients, including those with Long COVID. Studies included comparisons across different initial disease severities (asymptomatic, mild, severe, fatal), hospitalization statuses, and various stages of convalescence (ranging from 4 weeks to ~1 year post-infection), and against acute COVID-19 cases or seronegative controls. The literature search was conducted on MEDLINE (via Pubmed) and Web of Science up to July 23, 2022. No therapeutic interventions or dose-response comparisons were directly reported as this is a review of observational studies. The reviewed studies showed methodological heterogeneity in subject recruitment and Treg phenotyping strategies, and most subjects were likely unvaccinated and contracted wild-type SARS-CoV-2.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study performed a comprehensive qualitative and quantitative proteomic analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) derived from different somatic origins (fibroblasts and peripheral blood CD34+ cells), comparing them to original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC) and human embryonic stem cells (hESC). Using ESI-MS e and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry, complemented by Western blot validation, the research aimed to characterize hiPSC proteomic profiles, identify known and novel pluripotency markers, and distinguish hiPSCs from their somatic precursors. Key findings include the identification of approximately 220 commonly up-regulated proteins in pluripotent stem cell lines, the development and confirmation of a 22-protein marker panel for hiPSC characterization, and the observation of coordinated up-regulation of proteins involved in protein synthesis, folding, RNA processing, DNA replication, DNA repair, and energy metabolism (including oxidative phosphorylation and lipogenesis) in hiPSCs. The study also identified somatic cell markers that were down-regulated upon reprogramming and highlighted specific proteomic differences between hiPSCs and hESCs, contributing to improved hiPSC quality control for therapeutic applications.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Proteomic characterization and comparative analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) and human embryonic stem cells (hESCs).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was a characterization study, not a therapeutic intervention, thus no 'dose' of therapy was administered. Quantitative and qualitative proteomic analyses were performed using electrospray ionization (ESI)-MS e (label-free quantification with internal reference standard) and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry. Two hiPSC lines (iNC-01 from CD34+ cells, SB5-MP1 from fibroblasts, both generated using loxP-flanked excisable polycistronic STEMCCA lentiviral vector) and one hESC line (H9) were analyzed at earlier and later passages. Comparisons were made against their respective original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC). Proteins were considered differentially expressed if expression changed by >=1.5-fold, with a maximum false discovery rate of 2% and >95% confidence. Western blot analysis was used for validation. The developed marker panel was further tested in 8-9 additional hiPSC lines or passages from different somatic origins and reprogramming techniques. Differentiation studies were conducted with embryoid bodies at 24 hours and 7 days to assess marker changes during spontaneous differentiation.

document_context_data.document_summary: This retrospective cross-sectional study investigated plasma glycoprotein non-metastatic melanoma protein B (gpNMB) and glucosylsphingosine (GlcSph) concentrations in a cohort of patients with Gaucher disease (GD1, GD3, GD1-PD), idiopathic Parkinson's disease (IPD), and GBA heterozygous PD, alongside healthy controls. The primary aim was to explore gpNMB's relationship to Gaucher disease severity, clinical phenotypes (neurological, pulmonary, liver disease, monoclonal gammopathy), and treatment status. Findings revealed significantly elevated plasma gpNMB levels in Gaucher disease patients compared to controls (mean: 200.9 vs. 35.1 ng/ml), which remained high even after prolonged enzyme replacement therapy. Higher gpNMB concentrations were notably associated with splenectomy, pulmonary disease, liver disease (including fibrosis and cirrhosis), and monoclonal gammopathy. Additionally, gpNMB levels were elevated in Parkinsonism patients with type 1 GD compared to GBA1 heterozygotes or IPD (p=0.0001). The study also highlighted gpNMB's good diagnostic performance for GD (AUC 0.894), and its significant positive correlations with other established GD biomarkers (GlcSph, Chitotriosidase, CCL18, ACE), suggesting its potential as a supportive biomarker for residual disease activity, disease complications, and clinical stratification, although it does not differentiate between neuronopathic GD subtypes or idiopathic PD. The study also reviewed other diagnostic markers like acid β-glucosidase activity and GBA1 mutation analysis, noting their utility and limitations.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Enzyme Replacement Therapy (ERT) and Substrate Reduction Therapy (SRT), including macrophage-targeted enzyme therapy.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Gaucher disease patients received ERT or SRT for varying durations: mean 14.6 ± 6.9 years (range: 1–29 years) for ERT, and 10.1 ± 7.5 years (range: 6 months–23 years) for SRT. Plasma gpNMB concentrations showed an inverse correlation with treatment duration during the first 5 years of specific therapy (rho= -0.470, p= 0.024) but no correlation after 10 years. gpNMB levels remained elevated in GD1 patients on ERT for over 5 years, and no statistical difference was observed between treated GD1 and GD3 patients. Glucosylsphingosine concentrations declined with ERT or SRT. No explicit dose-response comparisons for ERT or SRT were reported, though it was noted that therapeutic response may vary across Gaucher disease subtypes.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: High concentrations described in three GD3 patients and GD3 mice.

matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Proposed as a new useful biomarker for quantifying neuropathology in Gaucher disease due to expression in activated microglia.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher; elevated; lower; inversely correlated; correlated
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly higher in Gaucher disease patients (mean: 200.9 ng/ml; range: 9.8-1643 ng/ml) compared with healthy controls (mean: 35.1 ng/ml; range: 10.1- 125 ng/ml). Median (CI) in males [125 (53.2-290 ng/ml)] vs. females [105.5 (60.3-226.4 ng/ml)], with no significant gender or age-group difference. Elevated 15-fold in treatment-naive Gaucher patients and 10-fold in treated Gaucher patients compared to healthy controls, averaging a 5.6-fold (4.7-6.7) increase in treated patients. No significant difference in plasma levels between treated GD1 and GD3 patients, nor between Gaucher patients with or without Parkinsonism on average. Lower in IPD and GBA heterozygous IPD compared to GD1, GD3, and GD1-PD (p < 0.001 for all comparisons). Among Parkinsonism patients, levels were higher in type 1 GD than GBA1 heterozygotes or idiopathic PD (p=0.0001). Concentrations remained elevated in GD1 patients receiving ERT for over 5 years. Levels were increased 7-fold in splenectomized patients (p=0.0012), 7-fold with pulmonary disease (p=0.038), 15-fold with monoclonal gammopathy (p=0.0004), and 17-fold with liver disease (p<0.05) compared to healthy subjects. Diagnostic performance for GD was good (AUC 0.894; sensitivity 63.0%; specificity 93.9%), with measurements > 125 ng/ml suggesting GD diagnosis with >98% probability. Inversely correlated with treatment duration during the first 5 years of specific therapy (rho= -0.470, p= 0.024), but no correlation after 10 years. Correlated with IgG (rho: 0.408, p < 0.001) and IgA (rho: 0.369, p < 0.001), but not with BMI.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Potential biomarker of inflammation and neurodegeneration; directly stimulates lipogenesis in white adipocytes; expressed by melanocytes, osteoclasts, macrophages, and dendritic cells. Highly correlated with the accumulation of bioactive lipid substrates (e.g., glucosylsphingosine) and implicated in lysosomal stress via macroautophagy. It reflects the presence of pathological macrophages undergoing alternative-type activation (M2 activation) and is expressed in disease-associated microglia (DAMs), potentially playing an inflammatory role in the CNS. Considered a putative regulator of inflammatory responses, a lysosomal protein involved in cell differentiation and immune response, and a secreted product of macrophages involved in chronic inflammation. High circulating or local gpNMB release might be responsible for pathological changes in the extracellular matrix and the development of tissue fibrosis. It is considered a potent angiogenic factor in gammopathies and multiple myeloma, and is reported to play a crucial role during obesity in white adipose tissue inflammation (in mouse models).
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Gaucher disease (Type 1 and Type 3, treatment-naive or treated with ERT/SRT), Parkinson's disease (idiopathic, GBA-related, and co-occurring with GD), GBA1 heterozygotes, patients who had been splenectomized, and those with known pulmonary disease, liver disease (including fibrosis and cirrhosis), or monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS). Also relevant to lysosomal stress, chronic inflammation despite treatment, and long-term stabilization of disease. Used for differentiation from Isolated Parkinson's Disease (IPD) and in relation to body mass index.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates inflammation in individuals with Gaucher disease and serves as a supportive biomarker for evaluating and clinically monitoring residual disease activity. Associated with liver cirrhosis, gammopathy, pulmonary disease, and specific organ involvement/complications in GD patients. Good diagnostic marker for Gaucher Disease (values >125 ng/ml suggest >98% probability), indicating increased probability of GD diagnosis and disease severity. Potential new useful biomarker for quantifying neuropathology in Gaucher disease and associated with late-stage Parkinson's disease. Its potential as a biomarker for predicting PD risk in the GD1 population remains speculative. Reflects the impact of long-term stabilization of disease and the secretion of protein from pathological macrophages/cognate cells sequestered at peripheral sanctuary sites. Associated with the distribution of gpNMB-expressing macrophages/monocytes, especially after splenectomy. Shows potential for detecting fibrotic pulmonary and liver disease, and MGUS in Gaucher patients, aiding in clinical stratification. Consistent with chronic inflammation in Gaucher disease even with ongoing treatment. Indicates no direct association between gpNMB and BMI in this specific cohort of Gaucher patients, despite its known role in obesity-related metabolic disorders in animal models.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study evaluated and compared the regenerative potential of different blood-derived products (EDTA-PRP, Citrate-PRP, and hyperacute serum [hypACT]) in a 3D osteoarthritic chondrocyte pellet model over 21 days. Key assessments included metabolic cell activity, cartilage-related gene expression (SOX9, COL2AB, COL1A1, MMP3, P21), and extracellular matrix (ECM) morphology and quality, using 1% or 5% concentrations of the products. HypACT consistently demonstrated superior and more stable results for cartilage-related gene expression and tissue quality. In contrast, Citrate-PRP showed negative effects on ECM production, chondrocyte presence, and gene expression, which was partly attributed to anticoagulants and extensive platelet accumulation. Metabolic activity generally showed no significant differences among the blood products compared to controls, though some variations were observed.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Blood-derived products: hyperacute serum (hypACT), leukocyte-poor Platelet-rich plasma prepared with EDTA (EPRP), and leukocyte-poor Platelet-rich plasma prepared with trisodium citrate (CPRP).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Blood products (hypACT, EPRP, CPRP) were prepared from whole blood (18mL for hypACT, 16mL for EPRP, 16mL for CPRP) and used as 1% or 5% (v/v) supplementation in 3D osteoarthritic chondrocyte pellet cultures for 21 days; 10% concentration was deemed unsuitable. HypACT showed stable effects across both 1% and 5% concentrations. For EPRP, 1% was favored over 5% due to better glycosaminoglycan deposition and lower platelet accumulation, with concentration influencing specific gene expressions (SOX9, MMP3, COL2AB, COL1A1). CPRP at both 1% and 5% concentrations resulted in poor tissue quality and no increase in COL2AB production, with extensive platelet accumulation observed.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: 1% EPRP favored deposition over 5% EPRP. HypACT supplementation resulted in superior deposition.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Major components of the extracellular matrix of cartilage, providing structural support, hydration, and biomechanical properties.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: 1% and 5% EPRP, and hypACT supplementation in chondrocyte pellet culture.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Higher deposition indicates improved cartilage matrix production, essential for the structural integrity and functional health of cartilage.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study utilized discovery metabolomics and lipidomics to investigate plasma glycosphingolipids and other lipid metabolites as potential biomarkers for distinguishing aggressive from indolent prostate cancer (PCa) in treatment-naïve African-American and European-American men. The findings indicate that specific glycosphingolipid species, particularly trihexosylceramide and tetrahexosylceramide, along with other sphingolipids and triglycerides, are significantly associated with PCa aggressiveness. A five-sphingolipid signature demonstrated promising diagnostic accuracy comparable to or exceeding PSA, suggesting their utility as novel diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers and highlighting their role in related metabolic networks and genetic alterations.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Diagnostic biomarker discovery via metabolomics and lipidomics
treatment_details.dose_specificity: An observational study conducted on plasma samples from 159 men with treatment-naïve prostate cancer, utilizing ultra-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS). The study focused on identifying biomarkers for PCa aggressiveness (Grade Group 1 vs. Grade Groups 2-5, low vs. intermediate/high aggressive PCa), without administering or comparing any therapeutic interventions or doses.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Most associated with PCa aggressiveness, demonstrating different relative abundance between low, intermediate, and high aggressive PCa (Grade Group 1 vs. 2-5). Increases observed in plasma from castration-resistant PCa patients.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Prostate Cancer (PCa) aggressiveness (low, intermediate, high aggressive, Grade Group 1 vs. 2-5) in treatment-naïve patients, including correlation with castration-resistant PCa.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Potential biomarker for Prostate Cancer (PCa) status and aggressiveness, including novel diagnostic/prognostic utility and correlation with castration-resistant forms, potentially improving PCa management.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigates the metabolic reprogramming mechanisms underlying sorafenib activity and resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells and patients. It reveals that sorafenib impairs mitochondrial function, forcing a metabolic shift towards glycolysis, leading to D-lactate accumulation, which serves as a biomarker for treatment response. In resistant cells, adaptation involves rerouting dihydroxyacetone phosphate towards glycerol-3-phosphate synthesis, extensive phospholipid remodeling to evade ferroptosis, enhanced antioxidant capacity, and increased reliance on exogenous triglycerides, resulting in glycerol accumulation as a marker of resistance. The study identifies D-lactate and glycerol as potential plasma biomarkers for monitoring sorafenib efficacy and resistance in HCC patients.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Sorafenib
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The primary therapy investigated was Sorafenib, a multi-kinase inhibitor for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). In vitro studies used sorafenib at an IC50 of 8.5 µM for acute, 48-hour, or 7-day prolonged treatments, and 7 µM for sorafenib-resistant IR-Huh7 cells. Clinical treatment involved oral administration of 400 mg twice daily for HCC patients, with dose reductions permitted for adverse effects. Other interventions included adenoviral gene downregulation (50 MOI for Gpd1/1l, Gpd2; 20 MOI for Glo1) and supplementation with various fatty acids (SFAs, MUFAs, PUFAs) or lipoproteins (VLDL, LDL), and inhibition of Mgll with JZL184. No detailed dose-response comparisons were consistently reported for sorafenib, though Mgll inhibition showed dose-dependent effects.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Decreased protein levels and reduced gene expression after 7 days of sorafenib treatment, characterizing the sorafenib-resistant phenotype.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: GLO1 converts methylglyoxal (MG) into S-lactoylglutathione for detoxification. LDHD converts D-lactate into pyruvate, involved in D-lactate metabolism.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Sorafenib treatment, particularly in sorafenib-resistant cells (7 days treatment and resistant phenotype).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Low levels may indicate resistant cells avoiding MG toxicity and minimizing D-lactate conversion to prevent cell death; reduced expression characterizes sorafenib resistance, indicating impaired detoxification.

document_context_data.document_summary: This narrative literature review investigates biosensor approaches for continuous, real-time in vivo monitoring of molecular markers relevant to performance and health status. It highlights the limitations of current technologies and proposes electrochemical aptamer-based (EAB) sensors as a generalizable, minimally invasive solution. The review details the development, validation, and attributes (generalizability, selectivity, reversibility, stability) of EAB sensors for detecting diverse targets (drugs, metabolites, hormones, proteins) in complex biological fluids and tissues. It also addresses the technological hurdles for subcutaneous placement, the correlation between interstitial fluid and systemic concentrations, and their potential for monitoring stress indicators (e.g., cortisol) and HPA/HPG axis hormones to assess overtraining syndromes.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Electrochemical Aptamer-Based (EAB) Sensor Technology for Real-time In Vivo Molecular Monitoring
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This narrative literature review discusses the development and application of Electrochemical Aptamer-Based (EAB) sensors for continuous, real-time in vivo molecular monitoring, without an applied 'dose' in the traditional sense as it is a review of technology. EAB sensors, including 75-µm-diameter, 3-mm-long versions, have been tested in live rats for plasma monitoring (jugular vein) for up to 12 hours with few-second to sub-second resolution and clinically relevant precision. They are also adapted for minimally invasive subcutaneous placements (microneedles, indwelling needles) for interstitial fluid monitoring (e.g., brain, tumor, dermal ISF). The review highlights the importance of seconds-resolved time resolution and nanomolar limits of detection for hormones (achieved for LH and NGAL, micromolar for others). Time delays between subcutaneous ISF and plasma concentrations (e.g., 5-12 min for glucose, ~17 min for vancomycin) and correlations (strong for cortisol, <6% error for glucose) are noted, influenced by target properties. No dose-response comparisons for sensor parameters or monitoring duration were explicitly reported.

matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Governs the synthesis and secretion of LH and FSH; indicator of HPG axis function and integrity.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated inflammatory, epigenetic, and molecular changes in women with unexplained euploid embryo transfer failure (UEETF) and suspected endometriosis. It evaluated the predictive value of endometrial BCL6 and SIRT1, compared GnRH agonist treatment to controls, and conducted a pilot randomized controlled trial comparing GnRH antagonist (elagolix) to oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) for two months. The findings characterized changes in inflammatory gene and miRNA expression in blood following treatments and suggested that medical suppression of suspected endometriosis could improve implantation success rates by addressing underlying inflammatory and epigenetic factors.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Medical suppression, including GnRH agonist, orally active GnRH antagonist (elagolix), and Oral Contraceptive Pills (OCPs).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: GnRH agonist was administered for two months prior to embryo transfer and compared to a no-treatment control, showing significantly improved ongoing pregnancy/live birth rates (68.1% vs. 35.7%, p=0.02). In a pilot randomized controlled trial, elagolix (200 mg BID) and OCPs (Orthocyclin) were each administered for 2 months before embryo transfer. Elagolix treatment was associated with a trend toward higher pregnancy and live birth rates (100% pregnancy, 60% live birth) compared to OCPs (60% pregnancy, 20% ongoing/delivered), though statistical significance was not reached due to small numbers. Elagolix also dramatically altered the inflammatory milieu in blood compared to OCP suppression. No specific dose-response comparisons were reported within the treatments.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased after elagolix treatment (part of 42 DETs with similar significance levels)

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Growth factor.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: After elagolix treatment in women with unexplained euploid embryo transfer failure and suspected endometriosis.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Previously shown higher in peritoneal fluid of women with endometriosis; gene associated with a receptive endometrium.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the lipid metabolic profile and its correlation with immune/cytokine indexes in COVID-19 patients to predict disease progression, severity, and clinical outcomes. It identified several differential lipid metabolites, particularly lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) 20:0, as potential biomarkers for discriminating between mild/severe disease, acute/recovery stages, and survival/fatal outcomes, suggesting their role in immune/inflammatory responses and as potential therapeutic targets.

Patients were stratified by disease severity (mild, severe), clinical stage (acute, recovery), and outcome (fatal, survival). No therapeutic interventions or dose comparisons were involved.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated serum levels of various biomarkers, including matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs), cytokines (SDF-1α, SCGF-β, SCF-1, G-CSF, MCP-1), hormones (leptin, ghrelin), and liver enzymes (ALT, AST, γ-GTP), in patients with histologically proven nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). The aim was to determine if these biomarkers reflect disease activity, steatosis, inflammation, and fibrosis progression across early and advanced NASH stages. The study also evaluated the impact of pharmacological interventions, specifically pioglitazone and ezetimibe, and lifestyle modifications on these biomarkers and the clinical course of NASH. Key findings identified serum MMP-1 as significantly higher in early-stage NASH (stage 1 fibrosis) and reflective of disease activity, while SDF-1α strongly correlated with fibrosis, steatosis, and inflammation across various stages. Pioglitazone treatment was observed to improve histological features and modulate biomarker levels, decreasing MMP-1 and increasing SDF-1α.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study of Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) disease progression and correlation with biomarkers, supplemented by pharmacological interventions and lifestyle modifications.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study involved both observational components, comparing serum biomarker levels in patients with histologically proven early (n=24) and advanced (n=9) NASH against healthy controls (n=14), with subgroup analysis based on histological characteristics. Pharmacological interventions included pioglitazone, administered at 15 mg daily for durations ranging from over two months to two or more years, and in some cases for 14 months concurrently with ezetimibe. Ezetimibe was also administered alone for 10 months. Other unspecified lipid-lowering and anti-diabetic agents, along with diet and physical activity, were also utilized. While changes before and after treatment were observed, comprehensive dose-response comparisons were not consistently reported, focusing more on the outcomes of specific treatment regimens.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly increased in NASH with stage 1 fibrosis. Statistically higher in early NASH patients. Statistically higher than in healthy controls in grade 2 of inflammation and F3 group. Higher serum levels observed (no statistical difference) in all grades of steatosis, grades 1 and 3 of inflammation, grades 1 and 2 of ballooning, and F1 and F2 groups. The F3 group showed the highest levels, while the F4 group showed the same levels as healthy controls. No correlation with histological findings was observed. May cause increased levels of SDF-1 (based on an acute liver failure model, not directly quantified in NASH patients in this study).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Colony-stimulating factor for granulocytes; involved in hematopoiesis, immune cell mobilization, immune response, inflammation, and cell proliferation. Reported to prevent development of hepatic steatosis (in rat NASH models); enhances SDF-1 gradient inducing chemo-attraction of CD34+ cells from bone marrow to injured liver; reported to activate HSCs, KCs, and ECs in NASH progression.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Early Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), NASH with stage 1 fibrosis, grade 2 inflammation, fibrosis stage 3 (F3), and various other histological grades (all grades steatosis, inflammation grades 1-3, ballooning grades 1-2, fibrosis stages F1-F4). Acute liver failure models and NASH models.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Associated with early stage NASH and specific inflammatory and fibrotic stages (elevated in F3, normal in F4). Its lack of direct correlation with histological findings suggests it may not be a direct progression marker, but it may indicate inflammatory or fibrotic activity in NASH. Potentially has a protective role against hepatic steatosis.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated plasma protein biomarkers (including cytokines, chemokines, growth factors, and cell death markers) to identify unique expression patterns associated with the severity and duration of Primary Graft Dysfunction (PGD) after lung transplantation. It identified several strong biomarker candidates, such as IP-10, MIP-1B, RANTES, M30, M65, IL-1Ra, PDGF-BB, G-CSF, IL-4, MIP-1A, IL-17, IL-9, IL-1B, IL-10, IL-6, TNF-alpha, sRAGE, and PAI-1, which are informative for early detection, predicting clinical course, and monitoring treatment efficacy of PGD.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Lung transplantation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study included 40 consecutive lung transplant patients (February 2018 – May 2019). Blood samples were collected immediately pretransplant (T0) and at 6, 24, 48, and 72 hours post-transplant/reperfusion, with PGD severity scored using 2016 ISHLT guidelines. Biomarker analysis involved a bead-based multiplex assay for 27 plasma proteins (cytokines, growth factors, chemokines) and enzyme-linked immunoassay for cell injury markers (M30, M65, sRAGE, PAI-1). Statistical methods included pairwise comparisons, sensitivity, and temporal analyses. An immunosuppression regimen of basiliximab, solumedrol, and mycophenolate (induction) and tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil (maintenance) was used. Intraoperative extracorporeal life support (ECLS), ex vivo lung perfusion (EVLP), and postoperative extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) were considered for severe PGD (PGD3). No specific dose-response comparisons for transplantation or immunosuppression were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Differential perioperative expression correlated with PGD3 development at T48–72 h (FDR < 0.1 and p < 0.05). Upregulated at 72 h post-transplant, associated with PGD3 at T48–72h (p < 0.05).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Growth factor; stimulates production and differentiation of granulocytes and mediates inflammation.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Post-lung transplant reperfusion (72h, T48–72h), associated with PGD severity, particularly PGD3.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates severe primary graft dysfunction (PGD3) and is informative of PGD severity and duration. Higher levels post-transplant are associated with severe PGD, potentially indicating a heightened systemic inflammatory or recovery response.

document_context_data.document_summary: This review investigates immune dysregulation in COVID-19 patients with comorbidities, identifying key pro-inflammatory cytokines and immune markers associated with increased mortality. It proposes immune-enhancement strategies, particularly focusing on the immune-modulating properties of Aureobasidium pullulans strain (AFO-202) beta 1,3-1,6 glucan, which stimulates various immune cells and beneficial cytokines while reducing inflammatory markers to counter hyper-inflammation and immune dysregulation characteristic of severe COVID-19.

treatment_details.dose_specificity: The AFO-202 beta 1,3-1,6 glucan is a soluble exopolysaccharide derived from Aureobasidium pullulans strain AFO-202, composed of both high and low molecular weight components. It is investigated as a nutritional supplement with proven safety over two decades. No specific quantitative dosage (e.g., mg/kg), regimen details, or dose-response comparisons are reported across the analyzed texts.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Characteristic feature of COVID-19 infection, especially in critically ill patients requiring ICU.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates pro-inflammatory status in COVID-19.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the safety and efficacy of human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cell (UC-MSC) transplantation in patients with severe COVID-19 and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), focusing on clinical outcomes, lung functional status, hematological parameters, cytokine levels, and miRNA expression profiles. The findings demonstrated that UC-MSC therapy was safe, improved lung lesions over a one-year follow-up by reducing fibrosis and markers of lung damage (CT score, Surfactant D, sRAGE), hastened lymphocyte recovery, and modulated inflammation (decreased ESR, CRP, banded neutrophils). The treatment also showed complex immunomodulatory effects, including altered levels of several cytokines (e.g., increased IP-10, MIP-1α, G-CSF, IL-10, while IL-6, MCP-1, and RAGE remained mostly unchanged in vivo but exhibited changes in vitro) and specific miRNAs, as well as influencing PBMC activation and proliferation in vitro.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Human Umbilical Cord Mesenchymal Stem Cell (UC-MSC) transplantation combined with conventional anti-viral treatment (antibiotic therapy, dexamethasone).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Triple intravenous infusion of UC-MSC at a concentration of 1 × 10^6 cells/kg, administered on days 0, 3, and 6. The average cell viability was 87.8% ± 5.1% before infusion. This was combined with conventional anti-viral treatment including dexamethasone and antibiotic therapy. No explicit dose-response comparisons were reported.

matched_biomarker_details.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Plasma/Serum; conditioned media from PBMC and UC-MSC/PBMC cultures (in vitro)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Led to elevation of plasma levels. Gradually decreased in the Control group, in contrast to the MSC group, where it increased consistently throughout the observation period, reaching a significant difference between groups on days 14 and 28. In vitro, a significant increase was observed.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Stimulates neutrophil production, maturation, and release from bone marrow, involved in immune response and inflammation.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Severe COVID-19 patients after MSC transplantation; PBMC co-cultured with UC-MSC in vitro.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Potentially indicates modulation of immune response by MSCs, possibly promoting leukocyte recovery and immune system support without worsening inflammation.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated immune subphenotypes and biomarker differences in critically ill adult COVID-19 patients from the REMAP-CAP trial. It identified three distinct subphenotypes based on biomarker patterns, revealing differential treatment effects of ABO-compatible convalescent plasma therapy on hospital mortality and organ support free days (OSFD-21). Seronegative patients showed significantly higher hospital mortality, with specific biomarker profiles varying by serostatus within subphenotypes. The findings suggest that convalescent plasma therapy should be avoided in subphenotypes 2 and 3 and emphasize the importance of patient selection based on host immune response for COVID-19 immunotherapy.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Convalescent Plasma Therapy
treatment_details.dose_specificity:
Critically ill COVID-19 patients were randomized to receive two units of high-titer, ABO-compatible convalescent plasma (total volume approximately 550 mL 
G
 150 mL) administered within 48 hours of randomization, or usual care. While no overall benefit was found (OSFD-21 OR 0.91 (0.74

1.11), mortality OR 1.01 (0.80

1.29)), differential treatment effects were observed across identified subphenotypes: subphenotype-1 showed lower hospital mortality with plasma (37.6% vs 40.5% in usual care), whereas subphenotypes-2 and -3 showed higher mortality with plasma (35.4% vs 24.1% for subphenotype-2; 34.1% vs 29.7% for subphenotype-3). No specific dose-response comparisons for plasma were reported.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: High, defining subphenotype-2 (with elevated type i/ii effector immune responses). Used to characterize subphenotypes.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: 'high GM-CSF levels'; not quantified in relation to treatment effect on biomarker levels; used to define subphenotype patterns.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Stimulates the production of granulocytes and monocytes, and regulates their function; central role in endothelial injury, Th17 T cell response, neutrophil recruitment, and thrombosis.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Characterization of COVID-19 subphenotypes in critically ill adults for differential treatment response to convalescent plasma therapy; defining biomarker for subphenotype-2.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates a patient's immunological subphenotype which predicts differential response to convalescent plasma therapy and clinical outcomes; associated with endothelial injury, Th17 response, neutrophil recruitment, and thrombosis seen in COVID-19. Subphenotype patterns (2 and 3) associated with worse outcomes/poorer plasma response.

document_context_data.document_summary: This observational study aimed to identify biomarkers for predicting severe dengue disease progression and cytokine release syndrome (CRS) by evaluating an integrated multiplex panel of cytokines/chemokines and clinical parameters in adult dengue patients. Researchers compared various severity groups (mild, severe without/with comorbidities, and healthy controls) across acute and convalescent phases. Key findings highlighted how specific markers like IL-18, IL-8, IL-6, and IFN-γ are altered in severe dengue, particularly with comorbidities, and their correlation with clinical indicators such as platelet counts and NS1. The study also characterized demographic and clinical parameters across patient groups, confirming the utility of a 24-plex cytokine/chemokine panel designed based on extensive literature review.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study on biomarker identification and monitoring for dengue disease progression and severity
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational study on 30 adult dengue patients (mean age 61.6 years, 17 male, 13 female) categorized into three severity groups based on WHO criteria (1997 and 2009): Mild Dengue Fever (MDF, n=10), Severe Dengue Disease without comorbidities (SDD-C, n=10), and Severe Dengue Disease with comorbidities (SDD+C, n=10). Six healthy controls were also included. A 24-plex panel of cytokines/chemokines was used to measure plasma levels, along with clinical blood parameters. Blood samples were collected during the acute febrile phase (before 6 days from disease onset) and the convalescent phase (9-18 days from disease onset). No therapeutic interventions or dose-response comparisons were reported, as the study focused on natural disease progression and biomarker correlation with severity.

It proposes immune-enhancement strategies, particularly focusing on the immune-modulating properties of Aureobasidium pullulans strain (AFO-202) beta 1,3-1,6 glucan, which stimulates various immune cells and beneficial cytokines while reducing inflammatory markers to counter hyper-inflammation and immune dysregulation characteristic of severe COVID-19.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the acute and cumulative effects of three repeated bouts of exhaustive treadmill exercise on circulating cell-free nuclear DNA (cf n-DNA), cell-free mitochondrial DNA (cf mt-DNA), muscle damage, and metabolic markers in healthy, average-trained men. Participants were allowed to drink mineral water. The intensity of each bout was comparable to a half-marathon in terms of cf n-DNA response. document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated inflammatory, epigenetic, and molecular changes in women with unexplained euploid embryo transfer failure (UEETF) and suspected endometriosis. document_context_data.document_summary: This review comprehensively investigates the potentials, pitfalls, and practical applications of blood-based biomarkers for objective individualized monitoring of training load, recovery, and health status in elite sports. It evaluates the utility and limitations of established markers like creatine kinase (CK), lactate, C-reactive protein (CRP), urea, myoglobin, and various leukocyte populations, detailing their physiological responses to acute and chronic exercise, kinetics, and implications for muscle damage, immune function, and inflammation. The document also addresses methodological considerations, confounding variables, the need for individual reference ranges, and statistical approaches for interpreting biomarker changes, concluding with recommendations for best practices in their sport-specific use.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Blood-based biomarker monitoring in conjunction with physical exercise and training load management in elite sports.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This review focuses on the application and interpretation of blood-based biomarkers for athlete monitoring across various exercise loads, including strenuous, resistance, high-intensity, submaximal, acute physical stress, soccer matches, ultradistance races, and long-term intensive endurance exercise. Biomarker responses are noted to depend on exercise modality, intensity, duration, and individual factors such as ethnicity and body composition. While specific exercise regimens like 30 minutes of endurance running (65% vs 85% of VO2max) showed CRP increases, no single standardized dose-response is consistently reported or compared across all biomarkers. The document emphasizes the need for individual reference levels, standardized collection, and careful consideration of confounding variables, particularly in managing workload by adjusting training when physiological parameters exceed baseline.

document_context_data.document_summary: This observational study evaluated the usefulness of a panel of biochemical and hematological variables for assessing training loads and recovery effectiveness in young professional long-distance and sprint swimmers over a 10-week preparatory training period. It identified an optimal panel including creatine kinase (CK), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), urea (U), total bilirubin (TB), direct bilirubin (DB), and ferritin concentrations, which collectively provide crucial information for monitoring post-training effort and recovery, regardless of sex or competitive distance. The study also highlighted the importance of ferritin, iron, and blood morphology in preventing deficiencies, anemia, and inflammatory states.

Measurements included enzyme activities (ALT, AST, LDH, ALP, CK), metabolite concentrations (Cr, CRP, ferritin, TB, DB, urea, iron), and various capillary blood morphology parameters. The study primarily focused on observing responses to ongoing training loads and recovery, rather than comparing specific training "doses."

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the safety and efficacy of human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cell (UC-MSC) transplantation in patients with severe COVID-19 and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), focusing on clinical outcomes, lung functional status, hematological parameters, cytokine levels, and miRNA expression profiles. The findings demonstrated that UC-MSC therapy was safe, improved lung lesions over a one-year follow-up by reducing fibrosis and markers of lung damage (CT score, Surfactant D, sRAGE), hastened lymphocyte recovery, and modulated inflammation (decreased ESR, CRP, banded neutrophils). The treatment also showed complex immunomodulatory effects, including altered levels of several cytokines (e.g., increased IP-10, MIP-1α, G-CSF, IL-10, while IL-6, MCP-1, and RAGE remained mostly unchanged in vivo but exhibited changes in vitro) and specific miRNAs, as well as influencing PBMC activation and proliferation in vitro.

treatment_details.dose_specificity: Triple intravenous infusion of UC-MSC at a concentration of 1 × 10^6 cells/kg, administered on days 0, 3, and 6. The average cell viability was 87.8% ± 5.1% before infusion. This was combined with conventional anti-viral treatment including dexamethasone and antibiotic therapy. No explicit dose-response comparisons were reported.

document_context_data.document_summary: This document provides comprehensive guidelines for establishing and managing immune monitoring programs in patients undergoing allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation and cellular therapies (TCT/HCT). It highlights the critical need for standardized protocols for assay, flow cytometric, and data analysis to ensure consistent, scalable, and comparable results across multiple centers. The aim is to enhance prognosis prediction, enable early relapse detection, and improve clinical decision-making by evaluating immune reconstitution and functional recovery, as well as by identifying predictive cellular and secreted biomarkers for complications like graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), infections, viral reactivation, and relapse.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Allogeneic Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation (HCT), Transplant and Cellular Therapy (TCT), and related immune effector cell (IEC) therapies, including Genetically Modified Hematopoietic Stem Cell Therapies (GMHSCT) and CAR T-cell therapy.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The document primarily focuses on immune monitoring protocols post-transplantation rather than specific therapeutic dose-response comparisons for HCT/TCT itself. It highlights the variability in transplant platforms (e.g., T-cell depletion techniques, add backs, T-replete) and conditioning regimens (e.g., lymphocyte ablation, total body irradiation). Monitoring thresholds are mentioned for specific immune cells, such as >50 CD4+ T cells/μL within 100 days and >150 NK cells/mL at day 30 post-HCT, to indicate timely immune recovery. Recommended longitudinal sampling schedules are provided (e.g., biweekly for 3 months, then monthly/quarterly) post-HCT/GMHSCT, along with typical blood volumes (8-20 mL), but lack specific dose details for primary therapies or dose-response observations.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Granulocytes and monocytes are among the first immune cells to reconstitute post-TCT, showing rapid recovery. Monocytes have a half-life of 24–48 hours in unprocessed samples, while neutrophils (a type of granulocyte) have a half-life of 6-8 hours, indicating significant loss if not processed promptly.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study performed an integrative multi-platform meta-analysis of gene expression profiles from Affymetrix and Illumina datasets in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) patients and healthy controls to identify novel, robust diagnostic biomarkers. The analysis revealed 5 commonly differentially expressed genes and 28 novel 'gained' genes, suggesting their significant potential for early PDAC diagnosis.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Integrative meta-analysis of gene expression data for biomarker identification and diagnostic prediction in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Gene expression data from two independent cohorts of PDAC patients (Affymetrix: 18 PDAC patients; Illumina: 36 PDAC patients) and 18 healthy controls were integrated. Profiling was performed on peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) using Affymetrix GeneChip® Human Gene ST 1.0 Arrays and Illumina HumanHT-12 v4 Expression BeadChip microarray platforms. Data were integrated using an empirical Bayesian methodology (ComBat) for batch effect removal, and differential expression was analyzed with limma software, identifying genes with p<0.01 and at least 1.5-fold differential expression. The analysis identified 5 commonly differentially expressed genes (with individual ROC curve AUC > 0.9) and 28 novel 'gained' genes, which could discriminate PDAC patients from controls with an average sensitivity of 74.8% and specificity of 73.3% for individual gained genes, 100% sensitivity and 94% specificity for combined common genes, and 91% sensitivity and 87% specificity for combined gained genes. No dose-response comparisons were applicable as it is a diagnostic biomarker identification study.

document_context_data.document_summary: This proteogenomic study investigated Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) samples from adult and pediatric patients at diagnosis, relapse, and primary resistance to identify underlying molecular characteristics. It revealed that AML relapse is consistently associated with reprogrammed energy metabolism, marked by increased mitochondrial ribosomal proteins and respiratory chain complex subunits, and a distinctive pro-inflammatory proteomic signature with higher granzymes and lower CR1/CD35. The analysis also identified increased levels of RNA splicing-related proteins, novel peptides, single amino acid alterations, and fusion peptides, highlighting potential new biomarkers and immunotherapeutic targets for improving AML treatment and patient survival.

treatment_details.dose_specificity: This study is an observational proteogenomic analysis that investigated molecular changes associated with disease progression and resistance to current AML treatment strategies. document_context_data.document_summary: This multicentre longitudinal GENFI study investigated the disease-modifying effects of common variants within TMEM106B (specifically the rs1990622 G allele dosage) on disease endophenotypes in genetic Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD) caused by GRN, C9orf72, or MAPT mutations. The study aimed to longitudinally examine the interactive effects between the TMEM106B-rs1990622 genetic polymorphism, FTD mutations, clinical status (presymptomatic/symptomatic), and time on brain imaging (grey matter volume), serum biomarkers (NfL), and cognitive/behavioural measures. Findings consistently demonstrate that the TMEM106B-rs1990622 G allele confers protective effects, likely in an additive manner, on multiple endophenotypes, including reduced grey matter atrophy, lower serum neurofilament light chain (NfL) levels, and better cognitive and behavioural outcomes, predominantly in GRN and C9orf72 mutation carriers, and reduces the risk of conversion to clinical FTD in GRN carriers.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Genetic modifier investigation; Observational longitudinal study
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This study is observational and investigates an intrinsic genetic factor, not an active therapeutic intervention. The 'dose' refers to the additive effects of the TMEM106B-rs1990622 G allele dosage (0, 1, or 2 G alleles), which was modeled as a continuous variable. The protective effects varied across genetic FTD groups (GRN, C9orf72, MAPT mutations), specific biomarkers, disease stage (presymptomatic vs. symptomatic), and over time (baseline vs. longitudinal). No deviations from an additive effect were observed (heterozygosity indicator P > 0.05), and no traditional dose-response comparisons for a therapeutic agent were reported.

matched_biomarker_details.activity_type: Imaging Biomarker (Voxel-based analysis of grey matter volume)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: In C9orf72 presymptomatic carriers: less atrophy in the right occipital region at baseline and in the right calcarine cortex. In C9orf72 symptomatic carriers longitudinally: reduced atrophy rate (0.006 to 0.012 ΔpGM per G allele/year reduction) in putamen, caudate nucleus, insular cortex, fronto-temporal cortices, and cingulate cortex. In GRN presymptomatic carriers longitudinally: reduced atrophy rate (0.004 to 0.006 ΔpGM per G allele/year reduction) within the right temporal and occipital regions. In GRN symptomatic carriers longitudinally: reduced atrophy rate (0.013 to 0.02 ΔpGM per G allele/year reduction) in the right frontal cortex, insula, left anterior cingulate cortex, superior frontal gyrus, and bilateral putamen. In MAPT symptomatic carriers longitudinally: reduced atrophy rate in the right inferior frontal gyrus. Overall, reduced atrophy rate in the right frontal region observed in all three gene groups (strongest in GRN). In C9orf72 and GRN groups past EASO: Less atrophy over time compared to converter counterparts in left insular volume. Lower cortical volumes were associated with rs1990622 AA genotype compared to AG/GG in frontal (P=0.009), temporal (P=0.029), cingulate (P=0.014), and insular (P=0.018) lobes. Reduced grey matter volume of left-sided temporal brain regions (β = −88.8 μl per risk allele, P = 7.64 × 10−5) was associated with the rs1990622 A allele in a population-based study.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Reflects neurodegeneration, neuronal loss, and brain structural integrity. Indicator of brain atrophy and neuronal health.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Genetic Frontotemporal Dementia (C9orf72, GRN, MAPT mutations) in presymptomatic and symptomatic carriers, modified by TMEM106B-rs1990622 G allele dosage. Also observed in clinically diagnosed FTD cohort and population-based Rotterdam Study.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates progression of neurodegeneration and brain structural health in FTD; reduced atrophy suggests a protective effect against disease progression and better preservation of brain tissue.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the associations between critically short telomeres (%CST) and various brain and blood markers related to aging and Alzheimer's disease (AD) in 129 cognitively healthy older adults from the Age-Well trial. The research specifically examined the influence of the APOE ε4 genotype on these relationships. Key findings indicate that while %CST is linked to age-related alterations in white matter integrity and specific hippocampal subfield volumes (subiculum, DG, CA1), it does not show a direct association with AD pathophysiological processes in the general healthy older adult population. However, higher %CST significantly increases AD susceptibility in APOE4 carriers, likely due to enhanced vulnerability to age-related effects.

document_context_data.document_summary: This large-scale observational study (5522 individuals across four cohorts) investigated the association and synergistic interaction between Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP) and epigenetic age acceleration, measured by multiple epigenetic clocks (e.g., Horvath, Hannum, GrimAge, PhenoAge, EEAA, IEAA), with clinical outcomes including all-cause mortality and coronary heart disease (CHD). The study found that CHIP is strongly linked to epigenetic age acceleration and reduced methylation-estimated telomere length. Critically, the combination of CHIP and significant epigenetic age acceleration (particularly AgeAccelHG, a composite of Hannum and GrimAge) identifies a high-risk population for all-cause mortality and CHD, with specific gene mutations (e.g., TET2, DNMT3A, JAK2) showing differential impacts on age acceleration and risk. While general inflammatory markers like hs-CRP and IL6R genotype were also explored, AgeAccelHG proved a superior risk discriminator in CHIP carriers.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study investigating genetic and epigenetic associations.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was a large-scale observational study across four cohorts (FHS, JHS, WHI, MESA) involving 5522 individuals. No therapeutic intervention or dose was administered. The study identified Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP) through Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS) for somatic mutations (e.g., in DNMT3A, TET2, JAK2, ASXL1, DDR genes) from whole blood DNA. Epigenetic age acceleration was quantified using DNA methylation arrays, calculating residuals from various epigenetic clocks including Horvath, Hannum, PhenoAge, SkinBloodClock, GrimAge, IEAA, and EEAA, and methylation-based telomere length (DNAmTL). A composite measure, AgeAccelHG (Hannum and GrimAge acceleration >0), was used for advanced risk stratification. The study analyzed quantitative associations between CHIP status, specific mutations, epigenetic aging metrics, and clinical outcomes.

matched_biomarker_details.activity_type: Epigenetic clock used to calculate age acceleration; methylation age estimate

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: CHIP was associated with 1.31 years of age acceleration (p < 8.6 	 10-7) as measured by GrimAge. Predictive of time to death or CHD in previous studies. Interaction with CHIP was significant, though not Bonferroni-corrected significant. Incorporated into AgeAccelHG for better stratification.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: An epigenetic clock that predicts biological age and various health outcomes based on specific DNA methylation patterns, trained on time to death, contributing orthogonal information to Hannum in assessing biological aging and mortality risk.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Used to assess epigenetic age acceleration in individuals with Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP), and as a component of the AgeAccelHG composite measure for risk stratification.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of biological age and risk of mortality/CHD; its acceleration contributes to increased risk, especially as part of AgeAccelHG. When combined with Hannum (AgeAccelHG+), it identifies CHIP carriers at high risk for all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 2.90, p < 4.1 	 10-8) and coronary heart disease (hazard ratio 3.24, p < 9.3 	 10-6).

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the influence of oral contraceptive (OC) use on physiological, oxidative stress, and inflammatory responses to fixed-intensity and sprint cycling in recreationally trained women, comparing them to naturally cycling women. It also examined the acute effects of N-acetylcysteine (NAC) supplementation on these responses and 1-km cycling time trial performance. Key findings showed that women using OC had elevated oxidative stress (higher MDA, lower GPx) and inflammation (higher CRP) biomarkers, as well as increased ventilation, during exercise. While NAC supplementation increased plasma thiols, it only blunted exercise-induced malondialdehyde increases in naturally cycling women, not in OC users, and did not improve cycling performance in either group. This suggests an increased strain on the endogenous antioxidant system in women using OC during exercise.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Acute N-acetylcysteine (NAC) supplementation and cycling exercise (fixed-intensity and sprint time trial).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Twenty recreationally trained women completed five exercise trials, including two double-blind crossover intervention trials where participants acutely supplemented with NAC or a placebo. NAC was administered orally in a total dose of 105 mg·kg⁻¹ of body mass, given as 70 mg·kg⁻¹ 60 minutes prior to exercise and 35 mg·kg⁻¹ 30 minutes prior. The exercise protocol involved 40 minutes of fixed-intensity cycling at 105% of the gas-exchange threshold (GET), immediately followed by an all-out 1-km cycling time trial. No dose-response comparisons for NAC were reported beyond the acute vs. placebo comparison.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Decreased over time (  = − 0.03% [− 0.04, − 0.02]). There may also have been a Time by Supplement effect on efficiency (  = 0.012% [− 0.001, 0.026]), with efficiency possibly preserved over time in the NAC compared to placebo trial, irrespective of group.
