matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: During fixed-intensity cycling.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Preservation of efficiency with NAC suggests a potential benefit in sustaining performance during prolonged exercise, though the effect was marginal.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive observational study utilized plasma proteomics and machine learning to develop and validate a framework for measuring organ-specific biological aging, termed 'e-ageotypes', in humans. Analyzing 4,778 proteins from 5,676 adults across five independent cohorts, the research revealed that accelerated aging in specific organs (including heart, brain, kidney, muscle, liver, adipose, pancreas, lung, and immune system) is significantly associated with higher risks of all-cause mortality and various age-related diseases, such as heart failure, Alzheimer's disease, hypertension, diabetes, and cognitive decline. The study's methodology involved defining 'extreme agers' (individuals with highly accelerated organ aging), clustering them into distinct ageotypes, and identifying key protein biomarkers (e.g., REN, KL, NPPB, TNNT2, CPLX1/2) that contribute to these aging profiles and offer prognostic utility for disease risk and progression.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational Study on Biological Aging via Plasma Proteomics and Machine Learning
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This observational study involved the quantification of approximately 4,778 plasma proteins using SomaScan assays (v.4 and v.4.1) in 5,676 adults from five independent cohorts. Machine learning models (LASSO regression-based chronological age predictors) were developed and validated to estimate biological (organ-specific) age, referred to as 'age gaps' or 'e-ageotypes', for 11 major organs (adipose tissue, artery, brain, heart, immune tissue, intestine, kidney, liver, lung, muscle, and pancreas) and the whole organism. Models were trained on 1,398 healthy participants from the Knight-ADRC cohort and tested across the full cohort. Age gaps were calculated using local regression, z-scored per model and cohort, and adjusted for age and sex. Associations with various age-related phenotypes, future mortality, heart disease, clinical biochemistry markers, and cognitive decline were assessed using linear models or Cox proportional hazards models, with multiple testing correction (Benjamini-Hochberg method, 5% false discovery rate). No therapeutic intervention or dose comparison was performed.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Part of a protein network involved in extracellular matrix, cartilage development, and osteoblast signaling pathways, implicated in vascular calcification and early cognitive decline.

matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Component of a protein network indicating vascular calcification and extracellular matrix alterations as a major component of aging that underlies early cognitive decline.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study clinically validated C12FDG as a flow cytometry-based biomarker for detecting senescent peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and T cells in humans. It investigated the association of C12FDG+ cells with chronological age, sex, and various serum senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) biomarkers. Findings revealed that C12FDG++ PBMCs and T cells increase with age, are elevated in males and patients with mild to moderate osteoarthritis, and decrease following fisetin treatment. The C12FDG platform shows promise as a quantifiable clinical tool for assessing healthy aging, age-related orthopedic decline, and the efficacy of senolytic therapies.

treatment_details.dose_specificity: Fisetin was administered at 100 mg/day to a small subgroup of 10 participants, with longitudinal analysis performed. While dose consistency was self-reported, specific duration details or comprehensive dose-response comparisons were not systematically reported in this study, though future controlled trials are acknowledged as necessary to determine the optimum senolytic dosing regimen.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated novel protein-based subphenotypes in Heart Failure with reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF) patients using unsupervised machine learning on 4210 repeatedly measured circulating proteins over a median 2.1-year follow-up in 382 patients. It identified four distinct subphenotypes with varying protein profiles, clinical characteristics (e.g., age, EF, chronic renal failure), and prognosis. These subphenotypes were driven by specific protein subsets associated with various biological mechanisms, including oxidative stress, inflammation, extracellular matrix organization, myocardial stretch/stress, injury, and renal dysfunction. Subphenotypes 2 and 3 demonstrated significantly worse clinical outcomes compared to subphenotype 1, highlighting the value of dynamic proteomic profiling for gaining pathophysiological insights and exploring personalized treatment opportunities in complex diagnoses like HFrEF.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Proteomic profiling and subphenotyping in Heart Failure with reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF) patients.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational study involving trimonthly blood sampling over a median follow-up of 2.1 years (IQR: 1.1–2.6 years) in 382 HFrEF patients, totaling 1066 blood samples. An aptamer-based multiplex proteomic approach (SOMAscan assay) was used to measure 4210 circulating proteins, yielding relative fluorescence units (RFUs) for comparative analysis rather than absolute concentrations. No specific intervention, treatment, or dose-response comparisons were conducted, as the study focused on characterizing disease subphenotypes and biomarker patterns over time. Repeated proteomic measurements (incorporating both intercept and slope coefficients) demonstrated improved accuracy for survival models (c-index 0.73, BIC 1023) compared to single time-point assessments.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Levels highest in subphenotype 2 and elevated as part of Subset D. Precise quantification not provided.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Indicates myocardial stretch/stress, fibrosis, and is involved in stress response and inflammation.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Patient subphenotype classification in HFrEF, particularly defining Subphenotype 2 (older patients, lower SBP, more comorbidities, and worse clinical outcomes).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Higher levels are associated with significantly worse patient outcomes (HR 3.43 (1.76–6.69) for Subphenotype 2 vs. Subphenotype 1) and is a known heart failure biomarker.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study comprehensively investigated the clinical relevance and efficacy of collagen X breakdown product (CXM) as a blood-based biomarker for endochondral long bone fracture repair in both healthy individuals and patients with tibia or femur fractures. It characterized CXM expression patterns, stability across demographics (age, sex), correlation with other bone turnover markers (P1NP, CTX, osteocalcin, leptin, sclerostin), and its utility in predicting healing prognosis (early, normal, delayed). The findings showed CXM levels are low in healthy individuals, peak around 25-35 days post-fracture, can be reliably measured via dried blood spots, and offer an earlier, quantitative indication of healing compared to traditional radiographic methods, supporting its prospective use in fracture studies.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study of natural long bone fracture repair, with a secondary analysis of a Vitamin D3 supplementation trial (VitaShock).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study primarily focused on observing biomarker changes in patients with acute closed or low-grade open tibial or femoral shaft fractures (Gustilo type I or II, AO/OTA type 42), without applying a specific therapeutic dose as an intervention. For the secondary analysis of the VitaShock trial, multiple Vitamin D3 dosing strategies were assessed, but specific dose details were not provided, and no significant difference in CXM response was found compared to placebo. Longitudinal blood samples were collected at various standard-of-care clinical visits over a period up to 48 weeks post-fracture.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant correlations were seen with CXM at 0 weeks, 6 weeks, or when all timepoints were clustered together (S3 Fig). No significant relationship was seen between CXM and GDF-15.

document_context_data.document_summary: This scientific roadmap by the Heart Failure Association comprehensively addresses the complex and heterogeneous nature of fibrosis in heart failure, aiming to improve its definition, quantification, and treatment. It reviews mechanisms of myocardial fibrosis across various etiologies like pressure overload, aging, and cardiomyopathies, emphasizing the central role of TGF-β, collagen deposition, and myofibroblast activity. The document discusses challenges in detecting fibrosis using circulating biomarkers, proposing a framework for assessment and a roadmap for future research to identify individual fibrotic mechanisms, novel therapeutic targets, and diagnostic tools. It also evaluates diverse anti-fibrotic strategies, including pharmacological agents and non-coding RNA-based treatments, highlighting the need for targeted, multi-pathway approaches given the complexity of the fibrotic process.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Anti-fibrotic therapies for heart failure, including established drugs like angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, as well as specific anti-fibrotic agents like pirfenidone. Investigational strategies include targeting the TGF-β pathway (e.g., TGF-β inhibitors, CTGF inhibitors like FG-3019), MAPK pathways (e.g., ERK inhibitors), inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1α), neuregulin-1 administration, Matrix Metalloproteinase (MMP) inhibitors, Galectin-3 inhibitors, and non-coding RNA-based treatments (microRNA and long non-coding RNAs).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This is a review document, and as such, no specific therapeutic doses, intensities, or durations are consistently reported for any intervention, nor are dose-response comparisons detailed. While some agents like Pirfenidone and non-coding RNA modulators show utility in experimental models and clinical trials (e.g., microRNA-21 inhibitor in a Phase II trial), precise quantitative dosage or detailed treatment parameters are generally absent, reflecting a discussion of general approaches and their limitations, including a noted 'lack of precision' in current therapies. For example, MMP-12i was given 3h post-MI, but without specific dosage.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Plasma levels do not reflect myocardial fibrosis; production in extracardiac tissues (fatty and lung tissue) had greater impact (Du and colleagues)

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Involved in various forms of fibrosis and stress responses
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Mouse models of post-MI heart failure, hypertensive heart failure, and HFpEF
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Not a reliable surrogate for myocardial fibrosis in mouse models; its plasma levels are more influenced by extracardiac tissue production.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study describes a multi-round Delphi expert consensus process to identify and prioritize 14 key biomarkers of aging for use in human intervention studies. The identified biomarkers encompass physiological, inflammatory, functional, and genetic/epigenetic domains. The study outlines the methodology, discusses the suitability of biomarkers for different intervention durations, and identifies future research needs regarding biomarker standardization and early life application, concluding with a preference for composite biomarkers due to the complexity of aging.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Expert consensus methodology (Delphi method) for identifying biomarkers of aging for use in human intervention studies (nutritional, lifestyle, or pharmacological).
treatment_details.dose_specificity:
The study utilized a 3-round online Delphi method, starting with 116 experts in Round 1 and concluding with 60 experts in Round 3, out of 460 invited international panel members. Consensus for statements was defined as ">=70%" agreement, with "51-69%" indicating moderate agreement and "

	<=50%" leading to removal. Initially, 460 biomarkers were suggested, leading to 20 being appraised in detail. The consensus level for the 14 recommended biomarkers ranged from 70% to 98%. The identified biomarkers were deemed more suitable for medium- (3-6 months) and long-term (">=6 months") interventions, and less suitable for acute or short-term ("<3 months") interventions, as short-term changes are likely homeostatic responses with limited long-term significance for aging. No specific therapeutic doses or dose-response comparisons were investigated as this was a consensus-building study on biomarker utility.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Achieved ">=70%" agreement in expert panel consensus and classified as minimal burden.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Involved in mitochondrial dysfunction, stress responses, inflammation, and general physiological processes related to aging.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Identified by expert consensus via Delphi method for use in human intervention studies on aging and for assessment of the aging process.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Potential outcome measure for longevity-promoting interventions, indicator of biological age, ease of assessment, and for harmonizing outcome measures in future intervention studies.

document_context_data.document_summary: This document describes the protocol for an observational cross-sectional study. Its primary objective is to assess the reliability of systemic inflammatory biomarkers (CRP, TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β) and immune cell reactivity, alongside perceived pain and pressure pain thresholds, through nine repeated measurements in workers exposed to constant real-life occupational workloads. Secondary aims include assessing correlations between these biomarkers and pain measures, and comparing levels between groups with higher and lower upper-extremity physical workloads. The study also details screening for metabolic parameters to ensure participant eligibility and ultimately aims to clarify the predictive role of these biomarkers in the development of work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) and to inform work-related stress-recovery concepts.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Exposure to real-life occupational workloads
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This observational study compares two groups: an 'exposed group' with higher upper-extremity physical workloads (exceeding the Action Limit of TLV for HAL, with daily repetitive strain for >=4 days/week and >=20 hours/week) and an 'unexposed group' (office workers) with lower upper-extremity physical workloads (not exceeding TLV for HAL). Participants will undergo nine repeated measurements of blood samples and pain assessments once every two weeks. The study assesses reliability and compares biomarker levels between these workload groups, rather than evaluating a therapeutic dose-response.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study evaluated and compared the regenerative potential of different blood-derived products (EDTA-PRP, Citrate-PRP, and hyperacute serum [hypACT]) in a 3D osteoarthritic chondrocyte pellet model over 21 days. Key assessments included metabolic cell activity, cartilage-related gene expression (SOX9, COL2AB, COL1A1, MMP3, P21), and extracellular matrix (ECM) morphology and quality, using 1% or 5% concentrations of the products. HypACT consistently demonstrated superior and more stable results for cartilage-related gene expression and tissue quality. In contrast, Citrate-PRP showed negative effects on ECM production, chondrocyte presence, and gene expression, which was partly attributed to anticoagulants and extensive platelet accumulation. Metabolic activity generally showed no significant differences among the blood products compared to controls, though some variations were observed.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Blood-derived products: hyperacute serum (hypACT), leukocyte-poor Platelet-rich plasma prepared with EDTA (EPRP), and leukocyte-poor Platelet-rich plasma prepared with trisodium citrate (CPRP).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Blood products (hypACT, EPRP, CPRP) were prepared from whole blood (18mL for hypACT, 16mL for EPRP, 16mL for CPRP) and used as 1% or 5% (v/v) supplementation in 3D osteoarthritic chondrocyte pellet cultures for 21 days; 10% concentration was deemed unsuitable. HypACT showed stable effects across both 1% and 5% concentrations. For EPRP, 1% was favored over 5% due to better glycosaminoglycan deposition and lower platelet accumulation, with concentration influencing specific gene expressions (SOX9, MMP3, COL2AB, COL1A1). CPRP at both 1% and 5% concentrations resulted in poor tissue quality and no increase in COL2AB production, with extensive platelet accumulation observed.

matched_biomarker_details.activity_type: Conceptual/Theoretical (based on known properties of PRPs)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: High, non-physiological concentration of growth factors present in PRPs.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Regulate cell growth, proliferation, differentiation, and matrix synthesis.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Implied comparison of chondrocyte behavior between EPRP and CPRP vs. hypACT and FCS, where high growth factor concentrations in PRPs might contribute to observed discrepancies or negative effects.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Non-physiological concentrations of growth factors can lead to unpredictable or detrimental cellular responses, potentially explaining observed negative effects or discrepancies in PRP treatments.

document_context_data.document_summary: This prospective single-center study investigated the relationship between an impaired Growth Hormone (GH)-Insulin-like Growth Factor I (IGF-I) axis and cardiac wasting (reduced left ventricular mass) in 307 advanced cancer patients. The findings reveal that reduced LV mass is associated with an imbalance in the GH-IGF-I axis, characterized by higher plasma GH levels and a lower IGF-I/GH ratio, suggesting acquired GH resistance. This resistance is particularly evident in patients with wasting syndrome with unintentional weight loss, and higher baseline IGF-I was associated with a subsequent decline in relative LV mass.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study investigating GH-IGF-I axis dysregulation in advanced cancer patients; no therapeutic intervention.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational, cross-sectional, and longitudinal study (with follow-up for 85 patients) assessing baseline characteristics and follow-up changes in GH-IGF-I axis parameters. No intervention or dose was administered. Patient stratification involved grouping by echocardiographic left ventricular mass/height^2 tertiles (women: <50, 50–61, >61 g/m^2; men: <60, 60–74, >74 g/m^2) and by the presence of wasting syndrome (BMI <24 kg/m^2 and ≥5% weight loss in the prior 12 months).

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly higher in patients in the lowest LVmass/height^2 tertile (women, median (IQR) 1.8 (0.9–4.2) ng/mL vs. 0.8 (0.2–2.2) and 0.5 (0.3–1.6) ng/mL in higher tertiles (p=0.029); men, median (IQR) 2.1 (0.8–3.2) ng/mL vs. 0.6 (0.1–1.7) and 0.7 (0.2–1.9) ng/mL in higher tertiles (p=0.003)). Levels were also significantly higher in men and women with wasting syndrome with unintentional weight loss compared to those without. An inverse relationship was observed between GH and LV mass.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Regulates growth, cellular reproduction, and metabolism; acts as an anabolic hormone that activates lipolysis and mediates cardiometabolic processes, requiring adequate IGF-I response.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Advanced cancer patients (mostly stage III/IV) with reduced left ventricular mass (cardiac wasting) or presence of wasting syndrome with unintentional weight loss.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Increased levels indicate acquired GH resistance and a catabolic state, contributing to cardiac wasting-associated cardiomyopathy and independent loss of left ventricular mass in advanced cancer patients, especially those with wasting syndrome.

document_context_data.document_summary: This review comprehensively investigates the potentials, pitfalls, and practical applications of blood-based biomarkers for objective individualized monitoring of training load, recovery, and health status in elite sports. It evaluates the utility and limitations of established markers like creatine kinase (CK), lactate, C-reactive protein (CRP), urea, myoglobin, and various leukocyte populations, detailing their physiological responses to acute and chronic exercise, kinetics, and implications for muscle damage, immune function, and inflammation. The document also addresses methodological considerations, confounding variables, the need for individual reference ranges, and statistical approaches for interpreting biomarker changes, concluding with recommendations for best practices in their sport-specific use.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Blood-based biomarker monitoring in conjunction with physical exercise and training load management in elite sports.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This review focuses on the application and interpretation of blood-based biomarkers for athlete monitoring across various exercise loads, including strenuous, resistance, high-intensity, submaximal, acute physical stress, soccer matches, ultradistance races, and long-term intensive endurance exercise. Biomarker responses are noted to depend on exercise modality, intensity, duration, and individual factors such as ethnicity and body composition. While specific exercise regimens like 30 minutes of endurance running (65% vs 85% of VO2max) showed CRP increases, no single standardized dose-response is consistently reported or compared across all biomarkers. The document emphasizes the need for individual reference levels, standardized collection, and careful consideration of confounding variables, particularly in managing workload by adjusting training when physiological parameters exceed baseline.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Blunted during maximal exercise; resting levels are generally within expected ranges.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Hormone involved in growth, cell reproduction, and regeneration.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Maximal exercise, overreaching, and overtraining. Resting conditions.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: A blunted response during maximal exercise indicates potential overreaching or overtraining. Resting levels are not a reliable indicator for these conditions.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review identifies and recommends validated biomarkers for tracking health, performance, and recovery in athletes across multiple domains including nutritional status (macronutrients, micronutrients, food allergies), hydration, muscle status (damage, endocrine response), endurance, and injury risk (concussions, stress fractures, ACL). It advocates for a comprehensive, integrative, and individualized approach to biomarker analysis, emphasizing dynamic monitoring and contextual interpretation over single markers or universal thresholds to optimize training and minimize injury and overtraining risks.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Biomarker-guided monitoring and management of athletic training, nutrition, hydration, and injury recovery
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This review primarily focuses on the diagnostic and prognostic value of biomarkers rather than specific therapeutic doses. It emphasizes frequent, individualized monitoring (e.g., pre/post-exercise, daily, seasonally, after injury/competition) to establish personalized baseline ranges and track physiological changes in response to various training loads (e.g., acute bouts, heavy strength training, challenging training weeks). While specific nutritional intake recommendations are mentioned for protein (1.3–2.0 g/kg/day) and omega-3 fatty acids (≤3 g/day for average, 6–8 g/day for elite athletes), and iron supplementation at low-moderate doses, the document does not report dose-response comparisons for biomarker changes. Instead, it provides specific thresholds for identifying deficiencies (e.g., Vitamin D >50 ng/ml, Ferritin <12 µg/L), dehydration (e.g., >-2% body mass decrease, blood osmolality ≥295 mmol/kg, USG ≥1.020), insufficient recovery (30% decrease in T:C ratio), and overtraining (T:C ratio of 0.35 × 10⁻³). The overall approach prioritizes dynamic, contextualized assessment over universal thresholds for effective athlete management.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Concentrations have been correlated to exercise volume and intensity.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Stimulates anabolism by promoting muscle protein synthesis and inhibiting protein breakdown.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Training adaptations and muscle mass regulation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Together with IGF-1, GH is potentially a useful biomarker for monitoring muscle mass regulation and training adaptations.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review critically evaluates wet biomarkers for Huntington's Disease (HD), covering markers in biofluids like blood, urine, saliva, and cerebrospinal fluid. It summarizes findings related to metabolic, inflammatory, oxidative stress, endocrine (melatonin, cortisol, growth hormone), and neuronal/glial degeneration pathways, including promising markers like neurofilament light chain. The document also highlights the importance of standardized protocols, independent validation, and considers pre-analytical and analytical variables (e.g., sampling time, feeding state) that influence biomarker reliability, noting the current lack of clinically validated biomarkers but expressing optimism for future discoveries.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Review and evaluation of wet biomarkers for Huntington's Disease (HD) progression and pathology
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Not applicable, as this document is a comprehensive review of biomarkers, their changes, and factors influencing their measurement in HD, rather than an experimental study of a specific therapeutic intervention or its dose.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Morning fasting levels were reported higher in stage I/II HD in some studies (3 studies showed increase, 5 showed no difference). Levels show circadian rhythmicity and are influenced by feeding status.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Hormone of the somatotropic axis, regulating growth, cell reproduction, and whole-body metabolism.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Huntington's Disease (stage I/II HD); circadian rhythm; feeding status.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Suggests early dysfunction of the somatotropic axis in HD, with increased activity associated with disease severity. Its levels are highly variable due to circadian rhythm and feeding status, requiring standardized sampling.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study clinically validated C12FDG as a flow cytometry-based biomarker for detecting senescent peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and T cells in humans. It investigated the association of C12FDG+ cells with chronological age, sex, and various serum senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) biomarkers. Findings revealed that C12FDG++ PBMCs and T cells increase with age, are elevated in males and patients with mild to moderate osteoarthritis, and decrease following fisetin treatment. The C12FDG platform shows promise as a quantifiable clinical tool for assessing healthy aging, age-related orthopedic decline, and the efficacy of senolytic therapies.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Senolytic therapy using the flavonoid fisetin
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Fisetin was administered at 100 mg/day to a small subgroup of 10 participants, with longitudinal analysis performed. While dose consistency was self-reported, specific duration details or comprehensive dose-response comparisons were not systematically reported in this study, though future controlled trials are acknowledged as necessary to determine the optimum senolytic dosing regimen.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Negatively correlated with C12FDG++ TCs in males only (r=-0.2655; p=0.0015).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: A biomarker related to the Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype (SASP).
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Healthy human participants (age range 20–82 years), association with peripheral senescence (C12FDG++ T cells) with sexually dimorphic correlations.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Biomarker of senescence.

document_context_data.document_summary: This scoping review systematically evaluates the application of systems biology-driven precision sports nutrition, incorporating 'omics' platforms (e.g., nutrigenetics, metabolomics, metagenomics, proteomics, epigenomics, lipidomics, multi-omics) and wearable technologies, particularly Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM), for endurance athletes. It maps existing literature, summarizes key findings, identifies research gaps, and investigates the impact of various nutritional interventions (e.g., polyphenols, astaxanthin, nitrates, carbohydrate-protein blends, probiotics) on immune function, inflammation, metabolism, gut microbiome composition, and glycemic responses during and after exercise. The review concludes that while these technologies offer insights into individual variability and physiological responses, current evidence is often insufficient to robustly link identified biomarkers to enhanced performance, recovery, and long-term health outcomes, noting methodological limitations.

treatment_details.therapy_type: This scoping review investigates precision sports nutrition strategies for endurance athletes, focusing on systems biology approaches (including various 'omics' platforms and wearable technologies like Continuous Glucose Monitoring) and a wide range of nutritional interventions. These interventions include specific foods (e.g., banana, blueberry, mango), supplements (e.g., soy protein, astaxanthin, beet-based nitrates, cranberry beverage, prebiotics, probiotics, cocoa flavanols), macronutrient manipulations (e.g., carbohydrate-protein blends, oligopeptides, specific protein amounts, dietary fat, low-carbohydrate high-fat diets, low/high FODMAP diets), and their interactions with diverse exercise regimens (e.g., cycling trials, marathons, ultra-endurance events, submaximal and prolonged exercise, exercise under heat stress).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This scoping review synthesizes findings from various studies on nutritional interventions, which include specific food consumptions (e.g., banana, mango) often compared against controls or other carbohydrate sources, and supplementations (e.g., astaxanthin, beet-based nitrates, cranberry beverage, specific probiotics) with durations ranging from acute intake to 2-week periods. It also examines the effects of different macronutrient strategies (e.g., low-carbohydrate high-fat diets, carbohydrate-protein blends) and genetic variations on caffeine metabolism. The review notes that while specific interventions are detailed, it generally reports on rather than conducts dose-response comparisons, highlighting that existing studies often compare interventions against controls. A key emphasis is on the need for tailored, individual-specific strategies, robust randomized controlled trials, and better reporting of training status, dose-response relationships, and demographic stratifications in future research, as current evidence often lacks detailed dose-response comparisons.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Varied: mostly unchanged, decreased, or increased depending on intervention.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Without alteration following cranberry beverage supplementation. Mostly non-significant differences following nutritional/probiotic interventions or physical activity. Significant decrease following prebiotic supplementation with dietary fibers. Increased bacterial diversity associated with exercise and dietary fiber consumption.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: The variety of microbial species in the gut, crucial for gut health, overall well-being, metabolic functions, and immune modulation.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Response to cranberry beverage, nutritional/probiotic interventions, physical activity, prebiotic supplementation with dietary fibers, and exercise in endurance athletes.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates overall gut ecosystem health and potential for immune modulation. While mostly unchanged with some interventions, significant decreases highlight complex responses. Higher diversity is generally associated with a healthier gut microbiome, potentially mitigating gut perturbations and supporting overall health in athletes.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the role of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) in traumatic brain injury (TBI)-induced neural damage in mice, employing a controlled cortical impact model and various pharmacological and genetic manipulations. The central finding was that inhibiting NETs with Cl-amidine ameliorated neuroinflammation, neuronal apoptosis, and neurological deficits by suppressing the STING-dependent IRE1α/ASK1/JNK signaling pathway. Specifically, Cl-amidine treatment reduced cerebral lesion volume, brain edema, and restored cerebral blood flow, while also attenuating blood-brain barrier disruption, inhibiting immune cell infiltration, alleviating neuronal death, and promoting a shift from pro-inflammatory to anti-inflammatory microglia/macrophage polarization. Conversely, STING activation by 2'3'-cGAMP abolished Cl-amidine's neuroprotection, and PAD4 overexpression aggravated neuroinflammation and neuronal death via the same pathway, effects that were successfully counteracted by STING or IRE1α inhibition. The study also detailed comprehensive methodologies for establishing the TBI model and assessing various molecular and cellular changes.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Controlled Cortical Impact (CCI) model for Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI); Pharmacological interventions including Neutrophil Extracellular Trap (NET) inhibition with Cl-amidine, STING activation with 2'3'-cGAMP, STING inhibition with C-176, and IRE1α inhibition with Kira6; Genetic manipulation via adenovirus-mediated overexpression of Peptidyl arginine deiminase 4 (PAD4).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: TBI was induced using a controlled cortical impactor (3-mm flat-tip, 5 m/s velocity, 200 ms dwelling time, 2.2 mm depth, 3.5 mm craniotomy). Cl-amidine was administered at 50 mg/kg intraperitoneally (i.p.) once daily for three days, starting 1 hour post-TBI. 2'3'-cGAMP was given at 1 mg/kg intravenously 10 minutes pre-TBI, then repeated at 24 and 48 hours post-TBI. C-176 was administered at 10 mg/kg i.p. 1 hour post-TBI, daily until sacrifice. Kira6 was given at 10 mg/kg i.p. 1 hour post-TBI, once daily for three days. Ad-PAD4 or Ad-con (control) adenoviruses were stereotactically injected (4 μL total at 0.5 μL/min across two cortical locations) 1 day before CCI to overexpress PAD4. PAD4 overexpression resulted in a 2.28-fold increase in PAD4 protein and 1.73-fold increase in H3Cit at 3 days post-TBI. Effects were analyzed at 1 and 3 days post-TBI. No explicit dose-response comparisons were reported for most agents, and potential inflammatory or cytotoxic effects of the adenovirus vector were not tested.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly increased at 1 day and 3 days after TBI (p < 0.001). Substantially reduced by Cl-amidine treatment (p < 0.01). Significantly increased by PAD4 overexpression (p < 0.01) at 3 days post-TBI.

document_context_data.document_summary: This systematic review aimed to critically examine the effects of melatonin supplementation on sports performance and a range of circulating health biomarkers in highly trained athletes, drawing from randomized controlled trials. The review concluded that melatonin supplementation is safe and demonstrates benefits in improving antioxidant status, reducing inflammatory responses, and reversing exercise-induced liver and muscle damage. Moderate modulating effects were observed on glycemia, total cholesterol, triglycerides, and creatinine. While promising data suggest potential benefits for hematological biomarkers and hormonal responses, the direct efficiency of melatonin in improving sports performance needs further assessment; however, indirect benefits via health biomarker improvements are suggested. Melatonin was also found to counteract oxidative stress, modulate immune function, and show hepatoprotective and renoprotective properties after intense exercise.

Specific dose-response observations were mixed; for instance, 5 mg melatonin showed modest strength improvements, while 8 mg led to significant decreases, and 10 mg improved jumping performance. High heterogeneity in dosages prevented a complete meta-analysis and the establishment of a single efficient dose, though 8 mg melatonin was noted to cause significant harmful effects on strength and power compared to 5 mg and control.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study developed and characterized a responsive human triple-culture model of the air-blood barrier, integrating distinct macrophage phenotypes (M1, M2 wound-healing, M2 regulatory) derived from THP-1 monocytes to mimic in vivo alveolar macrophage features. The research investigated their immunological impact, particularly on epithelial barrier function and inflammatory responses in both A549/ISO-HAS-1 and H441/ISO-HAS-1 co-culture systems. It demonstrated that the M1 macrophage model induced a severe inflammatory-like response, characterized by impaired epithelial barrier integrity and increased pro-inflammatory markers, making it suitable for modeling inflammatory lung diseases. Conversely, the M2 models (M2wh and M2reg) exhibited a non-inflammatory or pro-regenerative profile, maintaining barrier integrity and thus providing a foundation for establishing a quiescent, physiological air-blood barrier model. The study also detailed the specific biomarker profiles of these differentiated macrophage subtypes and their varied responses to Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) stimulation within the triple-culture system, highlighting cell line-specific differences in inflammatory outcomes.

treatment_details.therapy_type: In vitro differentiation of human monocytic leukemia cell line THP-1 into M1 (classically activated), M2wh (wound-healing), and M2reg (regulatory) macrophage phenotypes, followed by their integration into a human triple-culture air-blood barrier model. The model consisted of alveolar epithelial cells (A549 or NCI H441) and microvascular endothelial cells (ISO-HAS-1) cultured on Transwell filter membranes. Immunological impact was subsequently assessed via Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) stimulation.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: THP-1 cells were differentiated for 48h using specific cytokine cocktails: for M1 macrophages, 50 nM PMA, 100 ng/ml GM-CSF, and 25 ng/ml TNFα; for M2wh macrophages, 8 nM PMA, 100 ng/ml GM-CSF, 35 ng/ml IL-4, and 20 ng/ml IL-13; for M2reg macrophages, 8 nM PMA, 100 ng/ml GM-CSF, and 20 ng/ml IL-10. Dexamethasone (1 µM) was also used in some contexts. The differentiated macrophages were seeded onto the epithelial layer of the co-culture system. Cell culture media contained 10% Fetal Calf Serum (FCS), which was reduced to 5% for the triple cultures. The triple cultures were stimulated apically with 1 µg/ml LPS (end concentration) and incubated for 24h. No explicit dose-response comparisons for LPS or macrophage cell numbers were reported; the focus was on comparing responses across macrophage phenotypes and with/without LPS stimulation.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated genomic variants associated with thiazide-like diuretic (chlorthalidone and hydrochlorothiazide)-induced glucose changes in hypertensive patients, specifically focusing on genetic predictors in Black and White participants from PEAR and PEAR-2 studies. It identified and replicated the intronic single-nucleotide polymorphism (rs9943291) in the HMGCS2 gene as strongly associated with increased glucose levels following both chlorthalidone and hydrochlorothiazide treatment. The analysis noted a more potent effect of chlorthalidone on glucose increase, particularly in white participants, indicating a genetic predisposition to thiazide-induced hyperglycemia.

Chlorthalidone demonstrated a more potent effect on adverse glucose response and induced higher mean glucose changes compared to hydrochlorothiazide, with adverse metabolic events observed within 9 weeks. The difference in glucose change between the two diuretics was statistically significant in white participants (P=0.0002) but not in black participants. No specific mg/dose details were provided, and no dose-response comparisons for the drugs themselves were reported, as the study focused on genetic variants influencing treatment response.

This was replicated in hydrochlorothiazide-treated participants (ß=5.54; P=0.023 in PEAR, with G-allele carriers showing +7.31±2.61 mg/dL mean change vs +1.79±0.88 mg/dL for T/T). It is also an eQTL for PHGDH, an enzyme important for L-serine synthesis.

document_context_data.document_summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial investigated the effects of 12 weeks of daily protein supplementation on lean body mass, fat mass, muscle strength, physical performance, and various biochemical markers in physically active older adults with low habitual protein intake, who were also training for a 4-day walking event. The study found that protein supplementation resulted in a larger increase in relative lean body mass and a greater reduction in fat mass compared to placebo. While both the protein and placebo groups showed improvements in physical performance and cardiorespiratory fitness due to the walking exercise, no additional between-group differences were observed in muscle strength, muscle contractile properties, or physical performance from protein supplementation. Serum urea increased in the protein group, but no adverse effects on renal function or muscle damage markers were noted, indicating protein supplementation is a safe strategy for this population.

treatment_details.dose_specificity: Physically active older adults were randomized to receive either 31 g of milk protein concentrate daily (split into 15g at breakfast and 15g post-exercise/lunch) or an iso-caloric placebo for 12 weeks. This increased the protein group's total daily protein intake from 0.86 ± 0.23 g/kg/day upon enrollment to 1.29 ± 0.28 g/kg/day at 12 weeks. Both groups concurrently participated in walking exercise training for a 4-day walking event, covering an average of 338-391 km over 12 weeks. No dose-response comparisons for protein intake were reported, only the comparison between the protein and placebo groups.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study conducted a secondary analysis of data from the European First-Episode Schizophrenia Trial (EUFEST) and Recovery After an Initial Schizophrenia Episode Early Treatment Program (RAISE-ETP) trials. It utilized machine learning models (support vector regressors and classifiers) to predict depressive symptom trajectories (changes in CDSS scores) and the occurrence of post-psychotic depressive episodes (PPD) at 6 and 12 months in first-episode psychosis (FEP) patients with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders. The models leveraged various baseline variables including sociodemographic information, clinical assessments (e.g., PANSS, CDSS scores), neurocognitive performance, quality of life, and blood-based biomarkers, demonstrating accurate prediction and geographical generalizability across populations. The study also analyzed how factors like treatment assignment (e.g., NAVIGATE program) and antidepressant prescription influenced model misclassification and patient outcomes.

The NAVIGATE program was associated with a sharper decline in depressive symptoms, especially among patients prescribed antidepressants at baseline. document_context_data.document_summary: This longitudinal study investigated the impact of sleep quality improvement, specifically through treatment for sleep-disordered breathing (SDB), on neuropsychological symptoms and Alzheimer's disease biomarkers in patients with mild-to-moderate cognitive impairment (MCI) due to Alzheimer's. document_context_data.document_summary: This pilot study aimed to investigate the effects of allogeneic stem-cell transplantation (alloSCT) on physical condition, muscle function, and inflammation in patients during inpatient time. It describes methods for assessing cardiopulmonary performance, body composition, muscle strength, motor skills, and various blood biomarkers (inflammatory, muscular, cardiovascular, and red blood cell parameters) at pre-transplantation, engraftment, and discharge time points. The main findings include a significant decline in grip strength and muscle function, increased levels of hsCRP and Kynurenine at engraftment, and changes in TNF-alpha, Musclin, and Galectin-3, suggesting their utility as novel biomarkers for monitoring acute inflammation, myopathy, sarcopenia, and cardiovascular health in alloSCT patients. It also noted a decline in patient physical activity adherence during the inpatient stay, without a direct correlation between steroid dosage and grip strength decline.

Patients underwent allogenic stem-cell transplantation (alloSCT), with conditioning regimens consisting of 76.9% myeloablative and 23.0% dose-reduced approaches; no non-myeloablative. The study did not report specific dose-response comparisons for alloSCT itself. Glucocorticoids were administered at an average dose of 4.5 
	3.9 mg/kg body weight per week, totaling a mean of 27.9 
	27.7 mg/kg per patient during the inpatient stay, aligning with guideline recommendations. Daily physical activity was documented and declined significantly, with endurance training decreasing from an average of 14.0 
	8.2 min/day before engraftment to 7.2 
	7.0 min/day post-engraftment, and strength training decreasing from 12.11 
	7.0 min/day pre-engraftment to 9.6 
	6.3 min/day post-engraftment. Supervised physiotherapy was offered approximately every three days. No correlation was observed between administered steroid dosage and the decline in grip strength within this study's cohort.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study describes a multi-round Delphi expert consensus process to identify and prioritize 14 key biomarkers of aging for use in human intervention studies. The identified biomarkers encompass physiological, inflammatory, functional, and genetic/epigenetic domains. The study outlines the methodology, discusses the suitability of biomarkers for different intervention durations, and identifies future research needs regarding biomarker standardization and early life application, concluding with a preference for composite biomarkers due to the complexity of aging.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Expert consensus methodology (Delphi method) for identifying biomarkers of aging for use in human intervention studies (nutritional, lifestyle, or pharmacological).
treatment_details.dose_specificity:
The study utilized a 3-round online Delphi method, starting with 116 experts in Round 1 and concluding with 60 experts in Round 3, out of 460 invited international panel members. Consensus for statements was defined as ">=70%" agreement, with "51-69%" indicating moderate agreement and "

	<=50%" leading to removal. Initially, 460 biomarkers were suggested, leading to 20 being appraised in detail. The consensus level for the 14 recommended biomarkers ranged from 70% to 98%. The identified biomarkers were deemed more suitable for medium- (3-6 months) and long-term (">=6 months") interventions, and less suitable for acute or short-term ("<3 months") interventions, as short-term changes are likely homeostatic responses with limited long-term significance for aging. No specific therapeutic doses or dose-response comparisons were investigated as this was a consensus-building study on biomarker utility.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Achieved ">=70%" agreement in expert panel consensus.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Common measure of overall muscle strength, functional capacity, and a key indicator within the functional domain.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Identified by expert consensus via Delphi method for use in human intervention studies on aging and for assessment of the aging process.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Potential outcome measure for longevity-promoting interventions and indicators of biological age, indicating overall physical frailty and predicting adverse health outcomes in aging. Recommended for harmonizing outcome measures.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of broad-spectrum polyphenol supplementation from powdered tart cherry extract on markers of recovery, oxidative stress, and muscle damage following intense resistance exercise in men. It concluded that tart cherry extract significantly reduced oxidative stress (protein carbonyls), skeletal muscle damage (creatine kinase), and cardiac/type I muscle fiber damage (creatine kinase MB), while also preventing a decrease in handgrip strength compared to placebo.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Broad-spectrum polyphenol supplementation using powdered tart cherry extract combined with an acute resistance exercise protocol (AREP).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants received 500 mg of powdered NordicCherry® tart cherry extract (with minimal calorie content, 1.3 kcal) daily for 7 days prior to an Acute Resistance Exercise Protocol (AREP), compared to a rice flour placebo. The AREP involved 6 sets of 10 repetitions of barbell back squat at 80% of 1-repetition maximum, with load reduction to 75% 1RM if 10 repetitions were not completed in a set. No dose-response comparisons for the supplement or exercise intensity were reported.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Following Acute Resistance Exercise Protocol (AREP) at 24 hours and 48 hours post-protocol, after 7-day tart cherry supplementation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates preserved functional performance, enhanced recovery, and a potential reduction in central fatigue.

document_context_data.document_summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial investigated the effects of 12 weeks of daily protein supplementation on lean body mass, fat mass, muscle strength, physical performance, and various biochemical markers in physically active older adults with low habitual protein intake, who were also training for a 4-day walking event. The study found that protein supplementation resulted in a larger increase in relative lean body mass and a greater reduction in fat mass compared to placebo. While both the protein and placebo groups showed improvements in physical performance and cardiorespiratory fitness due to the walking exercise, no additional between-group differences were observed in muscle strength, muscle contractile properties, or physical performance from protein supplementation. Serum urea increased in the protein group, but no adverse effects on renal function or muscle damage markers were noted, indicating protein supplementation is a safe strategy for this population.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Protein supplementation combined with walking exercise
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Physically active older adults were randomized to receive either 31 g of milk protein concentrate daily (split into 15g at breakfast and 15g post-exercise/lunch) or an iso-caloric placebo for 12 weeks. This increased the protein group's total daily protein intake from 0.86 ± 0.23 g/kg/day upon enrollment to 1.29 ± 0.28 g/kg/day at 12 weeks. Both groups concurrently participated in walking exercise training for a 4-day walking event, covering an average of 338-391 km over 12 weeks. No dose-response comparisons for protein intake were reported, only the comparison between the protein and placebo groups.

document_context_data.document_summary: This large-scale observational study (5522 individuals across four cohorts) investigated the association and synergistic interaction between Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP) and epigenetic age acceleration, measured by multiple epigenetic clocks (e.g., Horvath, Hannum, GrimAge, PhenoAge, EEAA, IEAA), with clinical outcomes including all-cause mortality and coronary heart disease (CHD). The study found that CHIP is strongly linked to epigenetic age acceleration and reduced methylation-estimated telomere length. Critically, the combination of CHIP and significant epigenetic age acceleration (particularly AgeAccelHG, a composite of Hannum and GrimAge) identifies a high-risk population for all-cause mortality and CHD, with specific gene mutations (e.g., TET2, DNMT3A, JAK2) showing differential impacts on age acceleration and risk. While general inflammatory markers like hs-CRP and IL6R genotype were also explored, AgeAccelHG proved a superior risk discriminator in CHIP carriers.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study investigating genetic and epigenetic associations.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was a large-scale observational study across four cohorts (FHS, JHS, WHI, MESA) involving 5522 individuals. No therapeutic intervention or dose was administered. The study identified Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP) through Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS) for somatic mutations (e.g., in DNMT3A, TET2, JAK2, ASXL1, DDR genes) from whole blood DNA. Epigenetic age acceleration was quantified using DNA methylation arrays, calculating residuals from various epigenetic clocks including Horvath, Hannum, PhenoAge, SkinBloodClock, GrimAge, IEAA, and EEAA, and methylation-based telomere length (DNAmTL). A composite measure, AgeAccelHG (Hannum and GrimAge acceleration >0), was used for advanced risk stratification. The study analyzed quantitative associations between CHIP status, specific mutations, epigenetic aging metrics, and clinical outcomes.

matched_biomarker_details.activity_type: Epigenetic clock used to calculate age acceleration; methylation age estimate

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Approximately 40% of CHIP carriers showed age acceleration >0 in Hannum when combined with GrimAge (AgeAccelHG+). Predictive of time to death or CHD in previous studies. Interaction with CHIP was significant, though not Bonferroni-corrected significant. Incorporated into AgeAccelHG for better stratification.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: An epigenetic clock that estimates biological age based on DNA methylation patterns, trained on chronological age, contributing orthogonal information to GrimAge in assessing biological aging.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Used to assess epigenetic age acceleration in individuals with Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP), and as a component of the AgeAccelHG composite measure for risk stratification.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of biological age; its acceleration contributes to increased risk of mortality and CHD, especially as part of AgeAccelHG. When combined with GrimAge (AgeAccelHG+), it identifies CHIP carriers at high risk for all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 2.90, p < 4.1 	 10-8) and coronary heart disease (hazard ratio 3.24, p < 9.3 	 10-6).

document_context_data.document_summary: This review provides updated guidelines and a consensus for standardizing pre-analytical variables in salivary biomarker studies for Alzheimer's disease (AD) research. It critically appraises current methodologies, identifies inconsistencies, and proposes a standardized protocol for saliva collection, processing, and storage to improve reliability for diagnostic biomarker detection and quantification. The document investigates various protein and metabolomic biomarkers in saliva, assessing their diagnostic potential for AD and Mild Cognitive Impairment, and highlights the importance of controlling factors like collection methods, centrifugation, and storage conditions for accurate measurement.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Salivary Biomarker Research and Standardization for Alzheimer's Disease Diagnosis
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This is a comprehensive review article focusing on standardizing pre-analytical variables for salivary Alzheimer's Disease (AD) biomarker studies, rather than a therapeutic intervention or dose-response investigation. It critically discusses how inconsistent methodologies and pre-analytical factors (e.g., collection kits like Salivette vs. passive drooling, acute food intake, physical activity, stress, diurnal variations, dental restorations, freezing/thawing protocols, centrifugation speeds) influence biomarker detection and quantification, leading to conflicting findings for analytes like Aβ42, Aβ40, and AChE activity. The document proposes a standardized pre-analytical protocol, including pre-collection instructions (e.g., abstinence from food, drinks, smoking, alcohol, exercise), passive drool collection (e.g., 2 mL after 5 min pooling), and post-collection processing (e.g., immediate freezing, visual inspection, two-step centrifugation, aliquoting 100-250 µL). Various analytical methods (ELISA, Western blot, SIMOA, MS-based methods, NMR) were discussed for diagnostic marker identification, emphasizing that a universal protocol might not suit all biomarkers due to their diverse physiological roles.

document_context_data.document_summary: This cross-sectional study investigated the relationship between dietary vitamin intake, specific blood biomarkers, and muscle activation in 61 Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) patients. It found that albumin consistently predicted muscle activation in both arm and leg muscles. Vitamin B9 positively predicted leg muscle activation, while vitamin A negatively predicted it, with potential toxicity at higher intakes. The B6/protein ratio showed inconsistent effects, negatively predicting arm muscle activation but positively predicting leg activation. Among other blood biomarkers, PON1 positively predicted arm muscle activation, whereas BuChE and haptoglobin negatively predicted leg muscle activation. CRP, Vitamin C, and Vitamin D were not found to be significant predictors of muscle activation in this cohort.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational cross-sectional study investigating dietary habits and biomarkers in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) patients.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational study with no specific therapeutic interventions or experimental doses administered. Dietary intake of B vitamins (B1, B2, B6, B12, folate, niacin), vitamins C, A, D, and E, and the B6/protein ratio were assessed using a seven-day dietary record, Food Frequency Questionnaire, and 24-hour recalls in 61 ALS patients. Blood concentrations of butyrylcholinesterase (BuChE), albumin, haptoglobin, C-reactive protein (CRP), and paraoxonase 1 (PON1) were determined. Basal muscle activation was measured using surface electromyography. Patients were under riluzole treatment as an inclusion criterion, not an intervention. No dose-response comparisons were made for treatments, but effects of estimated vitamin intake levels and ratios (e.g., B6/protein) on muscle activation were analyzed.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Leg muscle activation:   = -0.15. Negatively associated with muscle activation.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Clinical assessment of muscle function alterations or disease progression, and prediction of leg muscle activation in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) patients.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Negative predictor of muscle activation in ALS patients, indicating muscle injury and inflammatory response.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study performed an integrative multi-platform meta-analysis of gene expression profiles from Affymetrix and Illumina datasets in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) patients and healthy controls to identify novel, robust diagnostic biomarkers. The analysis revealed 5 commonly differentially expressed genes and 28 novel 'gained' genes, suggesting their significant potential for early PDAC diagnosis.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Integrative meta-analysis of gene expression data for biomarker identification and diagnostic prediction in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Gene expression data from two independent cohorts of PDAC patients (Affymetrix: 18 PDAC patients; Illumina: 36 PDAC patients) and 18 healthy controls were integrated. Profiling was performed on peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) using Affymetrix GeneChip® Human Gene ST 1.0 Arrays and Illumina HumanHT-12 v4 Expression BeadChip microarray platforms. Data were integrated using an empirical Bayesian methodology (ComBat) for batch effect removal, and differential expression was analyzed with limma software, identifying genes with p<0.01 and at least 1.5-fold differential expression. The analysis identified 5 commonly differentially expressed genes (with individual ROC curve AUC > 0.9) and 28 novel 'gained' genes, which could discriminate PDAC patients from controls with an average sensitivity of 74.8% and specificity of 73.3% for individual gained genes, 100% sensitivity and 94% specificity for combined common genes, and 91% sensitivity and 87% specificity for combined gained genes. No dose-response comparisons were applicable as it is a diagnostic biomarker identification study.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Upregulated; identified as a novel gained gene, differentially expressed and capable of discriminating between PDAC patients and healthy controls (individual ROC curves showed average sensitivity 74.8% and specificity 73.3%).

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review investigates the potential of extracellular vesicle (EV)-enclosed non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs), including microRNAs (miRNAs), long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), piRNAs, circRNAs, and tsRNAs, along with N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA modifications, as stable, non-invasive diagnostic, prognostic, and monitoring biomarkers for a wide range of chronic liver diseases (CLDs). These include metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), metabolic-dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), Alcoholic Liver Disease (ALD), Autoimmune Hepatitis (AIH), Chronic Viral Hepatitis (HBV/HCV), cholestatic liver diseases, liver fibrosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), cholangiocarcinoma (CCA), and gallbladder carcinoma (GBC). The document also touches upon the therapeutic potential of engineered EVs for targeted cargo delivery in preclinical models to modulate inflammation and fibrosis pathways, highlighting their utility and associated challenges in clinical application.

treatment_details.therapy_type: This document primarily functions as a review investigating biomarkers for the diagnosis, prognosis, and monitoring of chronic liver diseases (CLDs). While the main focus is on biomarker identification, the review also touches upon the therapeutic potential of Extracellular Vesicle (EV) therapy, including engineered EVs for targeted cargo delivery, and mentions pharmacological inhibition of miR-34a as a potential therapeutic strategy.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study does not report specific therapeutic doses or dose-response comparisons for most interventions, as its primary focus is on biomarker evaluation. However, preclinical models utilized various EV-based interventions, such as native and engineered EVs derived from mesenchymal/stromal stem cells (MSCs) or human liver stem cells in models of liver fibrosis, NASH, and cancer, without detailed quantitative dosing. In biomarker contexts, some observations included a dose-dependent increase in serum miR-122 and miR-192 levels in induced liver injury mouse models. Disease states and exposures examined for biomarker changes included acute and chronic alcohol consumption, autoimmune inflammation, viral infections, cholestasis, CCl4-induced liver fibrosis, lipotoxic palmitic acid treatment of hepatocytes, arsenite-induced liver fibrosis, and various human liver conditions including biliary cholangitis, biliary atresia, liver fibrosis, HCC, CCA, and GBC.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly enriched in the circulating EVs of cholestatic mice with respect to non-cholestatic ones.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Cholestasis-induced liver fibrosis (murine model).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Correlated with the development of cholestasis-induced liver fibrosis; potential biomarker for detecting early fibrosis.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study protocol describes a two-arm, prospective, randomized controlled trial designed to investigate the cardioprotective effects of a structured exercise program in adult women with early breast cancer undergoing anthracycline-containing chemotherapy. The primary aim is to mitigate anthracycline-related cardiotoxicity (ARC) by assessing changes in circulating biomarkers (NT-proBNP) and cardiac function endpoints (LV global longitudinal strain, LVEF). Secondary objectives include evaluating other cardiac health parameters (blood pressure, HR, HRV, recovery HR), physical function, self-reported physical activity, health-related quality of life, and fatigue. The protocol also details the planned methodology for assessing these outcomes and administrative aspects of the study.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Structured Exercise Program (Aerobic and Resistance Training)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The intervention group will perform a supervised exercise program three times per week, during anthracycline-containing chemotherapy (ACT). Each 70-minute session includes a 5-minute warm-up, 60 minutes of training, and a 5-minute cooldown. Aerobic training, progressively increasing from 20 to 30 minutes at light to moderate-to-high intensity (50-80% HR reserve), combines treadmill, stationary bike, and stepping. Resistance training involves 2-3 sets of 10-12 maximal repetitions (12-RM) for upper and lower body, with progressive intensity. The program starts 1-2 days after the first chemotherapy session and continues throughout treatment. The control group receives standard breast cancer care without specific physical activity advice. No dose-response comparisons are reported.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated everolimus (an mTORC1 inhibitor) as a treatment for progressive NF2-related vestibular schwannomas (VS), evaluating its impact on tumor volume, growth rate, hearing outcomes, and quality of life over 52 weeks. The findings indicate that 3-month volumetric imaging can serve as an early biomarker to predict long-term sensitivity to everolimus, which demonstrated a cytostatic effect by decreasing VS growth rates, stabilizing tumors, and improving time to progression, while generally maintaining hearing and quality of life, despite not achieving significant tumor shrinkage in all cases.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Everolimus (mTORC1 inhibitor), with some cases also involving Bevacizumab as a subsequent or alternative treatment.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Oral everolimus was administered daily for 52 weeks (12 months) to NF2 patients with progressive VS. Adult participants (18+) received 10 mg/day, and adolescents (16-17) received 3 mg/day. Doses could be reduced (e.g., to 5 mg/day for adults) due to toxicity, such as grade 3+ or grade 2 oral ulcers. While no formal dose-response comparisons were reported, the treatment period was continuous for 52 weeks, with some patients re-challenged with everolimus after discontinuation, and others receiving bevacizumab if everolimus failed to control growth.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Stable or improved for most; decline for some.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: PTA remained stable or improved in all target ears of the 8 participants who completed the 12-month study. Participant 8 showed PTA improvement from 60dB at baseline to 52.5dB at 12-month follow-up. WRS remained stable or improved for 7 of 8 participants, with Participant 9's WRS improving from 96% to 100% at month 15 after resuming everolimus. However, Participant 7 experienced marked WRS deterioration from 58% to 20% over drug treatment, decreasing to 0% after drug withdrawal. Participant 1 experienced rapid decreased hearing in the contralateral ear one month after everolimus discontinuation, while Participant 8 had concurrent hearing recovery in the associated ear with a 6.2% reduction in non-target VS.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study comprehensively investigated the functional implications of heterogeneity in human embryonic stem cells (hESCs), focusing on an endodermally biased pluripotent substate. Using a GATA6-GFP reporter line and single-cell functional/transcriptomic analyses, the research identified distinct, interconvertible hESC substates defined by differential expression of GATA6 and SSEA3. GATA6-positive hESCs, while retaining long-term self-renewal and pluripotency (often alongside OCT4 and SOX2 co-expression), exhibited a higher propensity and bias towards spontaneous endoderm and mesoderm differentiation, with downregulation of ectodermal genes. SOX17 was identified as a potential driver for this endoderm-biased substate.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Human Embryonic Stem Cell (hESC) Substate Characterization and Differentiation Study
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study utilized the Shef4 hESC line, which was genetically modified with a GATA6-GFP reporter via Zinc Finger Nuclease-mediated homologous recombination. Cells were cultured in KO/SR on MEF feeders or E8 medium. hESC substates, defined by differential GATA6 and SSEA3 expression (e.g., 3+/6-, 3+/6L, 3+/6H, 3-/6+), were isolated by Fluorescence Activated Cell Sorting (FACS). These sorted cells were subjected to single-cell cloning, gene expression analysis (qPCR, single-cell RNA sequencing), high-content clonogenic assays, and differentiation protocols, including a spin-embryoid body (EB) system, without external therapeutic interventions or dose-response comparisons for differentiation-inducing factors. The focus was on intrinsic marker expression and resultant lineage bias.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study developed and validated blood-derived DNA methylation-based prediction models, including epigenetic scores (epi-LIBRA, epi-CAIDE) and a Multivariate Methylation Risk Score (MMRS), to assess and predict cognitive impairment and dementia (including AD and MCI) in various independent cohorts. The MMRS showed notable predictive capacity for MCI and prospective cognitive decline in AD and Parkinson's disease, and enhanced prediction when combined with traditional biomarkers, though individual epi-CAIDE and epi-LIBRA models performed poorly for AD and MCI status prediction. The study also detailed data preprocessing for various dementia risk factors, CSF biomarkers (amyloid- , tau, p-tau), whole blood DNA methylation profiling, and polygenic scores, aiming to investigate cognitive status and dementia.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Diagnostic/Prognostic Model Development and Validation using Epigenetic Markers
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This observational study involved the development and validation of DNA methylation-based predictive models (including MMRS, epi-CAIDE, epi-LIBRA) for cognitive impairment and dementia. Whole blood genome-wide DNA methylation data, genotyping, and CSF biomarkers were utilized from various cohorts (EXTEND, EMIF-AD MBD, PPMI, ADNI, BASE-II) with different age ranges (40-75,  60 years). Models were constructed using machine learning techniques (e.g., ElasticNet, Random Forest, sPLS-DA, RF-RFE) with hyperparameter optimization via cross-validation. The study focused on predictive modeling and model performance comparisons, rather than therapeutic interventions or traditional dose-response relationships.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of rehabilitation training (RT) and cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) on coronary artery disease (CAD) patients following percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). It found that RT, particularly aerobic exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation, significantly improved patients' exercise ability, cardiopulmonary function, lipid profiles, quantitative load indexes, and reduced anxiety and depression, ultimately enhancing overall quality of life and health status.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Rehabilitation training (RT) or Exercise Therapy (ET) combined with routine health education and standard pharmacological treatment, for Coronary Artery Disease (CAD) patients post-Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Fifty CHD patients post-PCI were randomized into a control group (routine health education) and an intervention group (routine health education combined with RT/ET). ET consisted of a 5-10 minute warm-up, followed by 30-60 minutes of formal aerobic exercise (treadmill or upper body fluid resistance) performed 3-4 times per week with 1-day intervals. Exercise intensity was assessed using the Berg Balance Scale (13-16 score required), and CPET involved a progressive workload increase on a stationary bike every minute for 8-12 minutes. PCI details included stenosis >80% with residual stenosis <20% post-stent deployment. Specifics for pharmacological treatment were standard. Although some dose parameters were provided for ET, detailed FITT parameters were not fully available in the provided text, and no explicit dose-response comparisons were reported for any aspect of the intervention.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: significantly decreased (P < 0.05) during quantitative load exercise in the intervention group compared to baseline and control, and showed a significant decrease following aerobic exercise training.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Indicator of cardiac workload, efficiency, and autonomic nervous system activity.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: During quantitative load exercise and following rehabilitation training/aerobic exercise therapy in CAD patients after PCI.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Lower heart rate indicates improved cardiac efficiency, reduced cardiovascular strain, enhanced ventricular adaptation, and improved fitness.
