document_context_data.document_summary: The study investigated the effect of Montmorency cherry concentrate (MC) supplementation on oxidative stress, inflammation, and muscle damage in trained cyclists undergoing three consecutive days of high-intensity simulated road cycle racing. Findings consistently showed that MC attenuated post-exercise oxidative stress, indicated by lower lipid hydroperoxides (LOOH), and inflammatory responses, evidenced by reduced interleukin-6 (IL-6) and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP), compared to a placebo. No significant effect was found on muscle damage markers (creatine kinase) or other cytokines (TNF-α, IL-8, and IL-1-β). This suggests that MC is effective in combating oxidative and inflammatory cascades induced by metabolically strenuous exercise.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Montmorency Tart Cherry Concentrate (MC) Supplementation in conjunction with a high-intensity, simulated road cycling exercise protocol.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Trained cyclists consumed 30 mL of Montmorency cherry concentrate or a placebo twice daily (8 am, 6 pm) for seven consecutive days (4 days pre-trial and throughout the 3-day trial period). The exercise protocol involved three consecutive days (days 5, 6, and 7 of supplementation) of a 109-minute simulated road cycling race, which included 66 sprints (5, 10, or 15 seconds) and specific time trials (2x2 min, 1x5 min). No dose-response comparisons for the MC supplement or exercise intensity were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: LOOH responses to trials were significantly lower in the MC group versus PLA (p < 0.01). Specifically, LOOH was 29.8% lower in the MC group following trial 3 compared to PLA, and did not rise above baseline at any time point in the MC group, unlike the PLA group where it remained elevated. Average increases from pre-to-post trial were 5% in MC vs. 11% in PLA.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Indicates oxidative stress via lipid peroxidation and cell membrane phospholipid damage.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Post-exercise responses to repeated days high-intensity stochastic cycling following Montmorency cherry concentrate supplementation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates attenuated oxidative stress and reduced lipid peroxidation, suggesting a protective effect against exercise-induced cellular disruption and improved redox balance.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of Montmorency tart cherry concentrate (MC) supplementation on recovery markers, including functional performance, muscle soreness, inflammation, muscle damage, and oxidative stress, in semi-professional male soccer players following prolonged, intermittent sprint activity. Findings suggest MC supplementation accelerates functional performance recovery (MVIC, CMJ, agility, 20m sprint), reduces muscle soreness (DOMS), and attenuates the acute inflammatory response (IL-6), but showed no significant effect on general muscle damage (CK) or oxidative stress (LOOH).

treatment_details.therapy_type: Montmorency tart cherry concentrate (MC) supplementation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants consumed 30 mL of Montmorency tart cherry concentrate (MC) or an energy-matched placebo twice per day (8:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m.) for eight consecutive days, including four days pre-trial and throughout the trial period. The MC contained 73.5 mg 7L 91 cyanidin-3-glucoside, 178.8 gallic acid equivalent 7L 91 total phenolic content, and a TEAC of 0.58 trolox equivalents 7L 91. No dose-response comparisons were reported.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: increased overall, but unchanged between groups
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: LOOH increased in both groups in the 72 h post-exercise period (Time: F(1,8)=5.973, p<0.001,  72=0.289), with peak increases of 35% above baseline at 5 h. No significant group or interaction effects were found, indicating no protective effect of MC.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Products of lipid peroxidation, indicating oxidative stress and cellular membrane damage by reactive oxygen species.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Oxidative stress markers following prolonged, intermittent sprint activity (adapted Loughborough Intermittent Shuttle Test) with MC supplementation vs. placebo.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates oxidative stress induced by exercise; lack of group difference suggests MC supplementation did not significantly alter oxidative stress levels in this context.

document_context_data.document_summary: This scoping review systematically evaluates the application of systems biology-driven precision sports nutrition, incorporating 'omics' platforms (e.g., nutrigenetics, metabolomics, metagenomics, proteomics, epigenomics, lipidomics, multi-omics) and wearable technologies, particularly Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM), for endurance athletes. It maps existing literature, summarizes key findings, identifies research gaps, and investigates the impact of various nutritional interventions (e.g., polyphenols, astaxanthin, nitrates, carbohydrate-protein blends, probiotics) on immune function, inflammation, metabolism, gut microbiome composition, and glycemic responses during and after exercise. The review concludes that while these technologies offer insights into individual variability and physiological responses, current evidence is often insufficient to robustly link identified biomarkers to enhanced performance, recovery, and long-term health outcomes, noting methodological limitations.

treatment_details.therapy_type: This scoping review investigates precision sports nutrition strategies for endurance athletes, focusing on systems biology approaches (including various 'omics' platforms and wearable technologies like Continuous Glucose Monitoring) and a wide range of nutritional interventions. These interventions include specific foods (e.g., banana, blueberry, mango), supplements (e.g., soy protein, astaxanthin, beet-based nitrates, cranberry beverage, prebiotics, probiotics, cocoa flavanols), macronutrient manipulations (e.g., carbohydrate-protein blends, oligopeptides, specific protein amounts, dietary fat, low-carbohydrate high-fat diets, low/high FODMAP diets), and their interactions with diverse exercise regimens (e.g., cycling trials, marathons, ultra-endurance events, submaximal and prolonged exercise, exercise under heat stress).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This scoping review synthesizes findings from various studies on nutritional interventions, which include specific food consumptions (e.g., banana, mango) often compared against controls or other carbohydrate sources, and supplementations (e.g., astaxanthin, beet-based nitrates, cranberry beverage, specific probiotics) with durations ranging from acute intake to 2-week periods. It also examines the effects of different macronutrient strategies (e.g., low-carbohydrate high-fat diets, carbohydrate-protein blends) and genetic variations on caffeine metabolism. The review notes that while specific interventions are detailed, it generally reports on rather than conducts dose-response comparisons, highlighting that existing studies often compare interventions against controls. A key emphasis is on the need for tailored, individual-specific strategies, robust randomized controlled trials, and better reporting of training status, dose-response relationships, and demographic stratifications in future research, as current evidence often lacks detailed dose-response comparisons.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study comprehensively investigated the role of PPARγ1, specifically its K154/155 acetylation site, as a molecular switch in oncogenic ErbB2- and Ha-Ras-driven mammary adenocarcinoma tumor growth, stem cell expansion, and metastasis. Using in vitro cell models, in vivo mouse xenograft models, and human breast cancer patient datasets, the research demonstrated that K154/155 acetylation is essential for promoting tumor growth, de novo lipogenesis, and cancer stem cell characteristics, while also regulating cellular apoptosis and autophagy. The acetylation status was found to determine genome-wide DNA binding site selection, shifting from canonical to non-canonical (C/EBP) binding, and influencing transcriptional programs for growth factor signaling. Furthermore, gene signatures reflecting acetylation-dependent genomic occupancy in lipogenesis (PASS1 and PASS2) showed predictive value for survival outcomes and distant metastasis-free survival in various breast cancer subtypes.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Molecular mechanism investigation focusing on PPARγ1 post-translational modification (acetylation) and the functional consequences of genetic variants (wild-type vs. acetylation-defective mutants)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study primarily involved comparing wild-type PPARγ1 with specific genetic variants (acetylation-defective mutants K154/155Q, K154/155A, an acetylation mimic K154/155R, and a sumoylation site mutant K77R) expressed in various breast cancer cell lines (MCF10A-NeuT, MCF10A-Ha-Ras, MCF10A-Src) and in vivo in mouse xenograft models and transgenic mice with inducible Pparγ1 deletion. Experiments often involved subcutaneous injection of 1 x 10^6 cells. No dose-response comparisons of external therapeutic agents were reported; the focus was on the impact of specific molecular modifications and genetic manipulations, with the K154/155Q mutant demonstrating a significant ~90% reduction in tumor growth.

K154/155Q mutant tumors demonstrated less robust lipogenesis. Reduced binding of PPARγ1 K154/155Q compared with WT at regulatory regions of FABP4, SCD, SREBF2, ADIPOQ. SREBP1/2 were previously shown to correlate with poor prognosis in breast cancer.

document_context_data.document_summary: This scoping review systematically evaluates the application of systems biology-driven precision sports nutrition, incorporating 'omics' platforms (e.g., nutrigenetics, metabolomics, metagenomics, proteomics, epigenomics, lipidomics, multi-omics) and wearable technologies, particularly Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM), for endurance athletes. It maps existing literature, summarizes key findings, identifies research gaps, and investigates the impact of various nutritional interventions (e.g., polyphenols, astaxanthin, nitrates, carbohydrate-protein blends, probiotics) on immune function, inflammation, metabolism, gut microbiome composition, and glycemic responses during and after exercise. The review concludes that while these technologies offer insights into individual variability and physiological responses, current evidence is often insufficient to robustly link identified biomarkers to enhanced performance, recovery, and long-term health outcomes, noting methodological limitations.

treatment_details.therapy_type: This scoping review investigates precision sports nutrition strategies for endurance athletes, focusing on systems biology approaches (including various 'omics' platforms and wearable technologies like Continuous Glucose Monitoring) and a wide range of nutritional interventions. These interventions include specific foods (e.g., banana, blueberry, mango), supplements (e.g., soy protein, astaxanthin, beet-based nitrates, cranberry beverage, prebiotics, probiotics, cocoa flavanols), macronutrient manipulations (e.g., carbohydrate-protein blends, oligopeptides, specific protein amounts, dietary fat, low-carbohydrate high-fat diets, low/high FODMAP diets), and their interactions with diverse exercise regimens (e.g., cycling trials, marathons, ultra-endurance events, submaximal and prolonged exercise, exercise under heat stress).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This scoping review synthesizes findings from various studies on nutritional interventions, which include specific food consumptions (e.g., banana, mango) often compared against controls or other carbohydrate sources, and supplementations (e.g., astaxanthin, beet-based nitrates, cranberry beverage, specific probiotics) with durations ranging from acute intake to 2-week periods. It also examines the effects of different macronutrient strategies (e.g., low-carbohydrate high-fat diets, carbohydrate-protein blends) and genetic variations on caffeine metabolism. The review notes that while specific interventions are detailed, it generally reports on rather than conducts dose-response comparisons, highlighting that existing studies often compare interventions against controls. A key emphasis is on the need for tailored, individual-specific strategies, robust randomized controlled trials, and better reporting of training status, dose-response relationships, and demographic stratifications in future research, as current evidence often lacks detailed dose-response comparisons.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Elevated by intense exercise; effectively reduced by peri-workout carbohydrate intake.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated whether pre-exercise ascorbic acid supplementation influenced antioxidant defenses, glucose metabolism, inflammation, and muscle damage in untrained healthy adults following a single bout of moderate-intensity cycling. Findings indicated that ascorbic acid supplementation reduced plasma Malondialdehyde (MDA) and increased Ferric Reducing Ability of Plasma (FRAP), while also modulating glucose levels and attenuating exercise-induced changes in albumin and total protein. While moderate-intensity cycling led to an increase in red blood cell Superoxide Dismutase (SOD) activity and low-grade muscle damage (Total Creatine Kinase), it did not induce systemic inflammation or lipid peroxidation. Ascorbic acid supplementation appeared to mitigate the exercise-induced increase in SOD activity but did not significantly prevent muscle damage or affect other inflammatory/damage markers such as hsCRP, LDH, CK-MB, GPx, or Catalase.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Oral ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) supplementation combined with a single bout of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Subjects received 1000 mg of ascorbic acid (or placebo) orally 5 minutes prior to a 30-minute indoor cycling session. Exercise intensity was set at 65–75% of maximum heart rate, which was predicted by an age-based equation. No dose-response comparisons were reported for either ascorbic acid or exercise intensity.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Decreased plasma lipid hydroperoxides with ascorbic acid supplementation (P-value not specified, inferred from main text as a finding).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Primary products of lipid peroxidation, indicative of oxidative damage to cell membranes.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Post-moderate-intensity cycling exercise with pre-workout ascorbic acid supplementation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates reduced oxidative damage and lipid peroxidation.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of a 36-hour survival training, which included moderate to low physical activity and complete sleep deprivation, on oxidative stress and muscle damage biomarkers in young, healthy men. The training impaired enzymatic antioxidant defense (GPx, SOD), increased lipid peroxidation (LHs), and induced muscle damage (CK). A subsequent 12-hour recovery period, including overnight sleep, was found to be sufficient to normalize these markers and restore blood prooxidant-antioxidant homeostasis.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Survival Training (combined with moderate to low intensity physical activity and sleep deprivation)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: A 36-hour survival training regimen for young, healthy men, involving moderate to low physical activity such as a 12-km march, 6 hours of rowing, 4 hours of kayaking, running, swimming, climbing, solving special tasks, and navigation in wild terrain. Ambient temperatures ranged from 8°C at night to 30°C during the day. The average heart rate was 80-90 beats/min (40-45% age-predicted HR max), with individual variations from 70-80 beats/min during march to 120-130 beats/min during rowing or kayaking. Participants experienced complete sleep deprivation and consumed approximately 3800 ± 120 kcal daily. This was followed by a 12-hour recovery period, including overnight sleep. No dose-response comparisons were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased significantly at 24 h and remained elevated up to 36 h (p < 0.05, main effects for LHs: time, p = 0.006; group × time, p = 0.00008). Peak levels were observed at 24 h. Following a 12-h recovery, levels normalized and significantly decreased below pre-training levels (p < 0.05) and were below control group levels.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Primary products of lipid peroxidation, indicating oxidative damage to cell membranes and a key process in oxidative stress.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: During 36-hour survival training with moderate to low physical activity and sleep deprivation; subsequent 12-hour recovery period.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Serves as a direct marker of oxidative stress and cellular damage; its normalization indicates restoration of oxidative balance and tissue repair.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of consuming cow's milk versus an energy-matched carbohydrate solution on recovery markers and performance in twenty female team-sport athletes following repeated simulated team games (STGs). The findings indicated that 500 mL of milk consumption attenuated losses in muscle function (peak torque for knee extension and flexion), sprint performance (5m and 10m), and perceptions of stress, and helped reduce muscle soreness and tiredness, particularly after the first STG. However, for many other physiological and performance markers (e.g., CK, hsCRP, LOOHs, PCs, CMJ, HR, RPE), the effects were mostly unclear or trivial, with milk showing no clear benefit after the second STG.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Nutritional intervention (consumption of cow's milk vs. an energy-matched carbohydrate solution) combined with a multi-stage physical activity protocol.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants consumed 500 mL of either cow's milk (910 kJ/215 kcal, 17.0 g protein, 25.5 g carbohydrate, 5.0 g fat) or an energy-matched carbohydrate solution (910 kJ/215 kcal, 0.2 g protein, 53.6 g carbohydrate, 0.0 g fat) immediately following each of two simulated team games (STG1 and STG2). The 17 g protein from milk was noted to be below the recommended 20 g threshold for maximal protein synthesis stimulation. The exercise protocol involved two ~30 minute halves of intermittent running with sprints, agility, and jumps, separated by a 10-minute half-time, with a 48-hour recovery period between STG1 and STG2. No explicit dose-response comparisons were reported for the nutritional interventions.

document_context_data.document_summary: This systematic review aimed to critically examine the effects of melatonin supplementation on sports performance and a range of circulating health biomarkers in highly trained athletes, drawing from randomized controlled trials. The review concluded that melatonin supplementation is safe and demonstrates benefits in improving antioxidant status, reducing inflammatory responses, and reversing exercise-induced liver and muscle damage. Moderate modulating effects were observed on glycemia, total cholesterol, triglycerides, and creatinine. While promising data suggest potential benefits for hematological biomarkers and hormonal responses, the direct efficiency of melatonin in improving sports performance needs further assessment; however, indirect benefits via health biomarker improvements are suggested. Melatonin was also found to counteract oxidative stress, modulate immune function, and show hepatoprotective and renoprotective properties after intense exercise.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Melatonin Supplementation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Melatonin supplementation was investigated with doses ranging from 5 mg to 100 mg, administered acutely (1 day) or continuously for 3 to 30 days. Timing varied from 15-60 minutes before exercise to 2 hours post-exercise, 6 days post-training, 3 days before exercise, or before rest/sleep. Specific dose-response observations were mixed; for instance, 5 mg melatonin showed modest strength improvements, while 8 mg led to significant decreases, and 10 mg improved jumping performance. High heterogeneity in dosages prevented a complete meta-analysis and the establishment of a single efficient dose, though 8 mg melatonin was noted to cause significant harmful effects on strength and power compared to 5 mg and control.

matched_biomarker_details.activity_type: Level of oxidative damage / General oxidative damage marker

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly reduces (p < 0.05) levels of oxidative damage.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Markers of lipid oxidative damage, causing cell membrane damage by free radicals.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Melatonin supplementation, demonstrating direct antioxidant action against lipid oxidative damage and protecting against muscle damage and inflammatory response.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Reduced levels indicate decreased lipid oxidative damage, suggesting improved protection against oxidative stress and cellular integrity.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the changes in biochemical markers of oxidative stress and muscle damage, along with psychomotor abilities (divided attention, handgrip strength, and strength differentiation), in 15 special unit soldiers undergoing a 48-hour military survival training program combined with sleep deprivation. The findings indicated that the training did not cause oxidative stress or muscle tissue damage, improved divided attention, but suggested a potential deterioration in motor control.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Military survival training (SERE training)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: 15 special unit soldiers underwent 48 hours of military survival training (SERE) combined with significant sleep deprivation (no sleep for the first 24h, 3h total for the subsequent 24h), psychological burden, and carrying 15kg equipment over an average of 6km, performed at 4-11°C. Measurements (biochemical markers, divided attention, maximal handgrip strength, and strength differentiation) were taken at baseline (P1), after 24 hours (P2), and after 48 hours (P3). No dose-response comparisons were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Initial low level at baseline; no significant changes observed throughout the 48-hour survival training (p > 0.05).

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: 48-hour military survival training combined with sleep deprivation.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigates the metabolic reprogramming mechanisms underlying sorafenib activity and resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells and patients. It reveals that sorafenib impairs mitochondrial function, forcing a metabolic shift towards glycolysis, leading to D-lactate accumulation, which serves as a biomarker for treatment response. In resistant cells, adaptation involves rerouting dihydroxyacetone phosphate towards glycerol-3-phosphate synthesis, extensive phospholipid remodeling to evade ferroptosis, enhanced antioxidant capacity, and increased reliance on exogenous triglycerides, resulting in glycerol accumulation as a marker of resistance. The study identifies D-lactate and glycerol as potential plasma biomarkers for monitoring sorafenib efficacy and resistance in HCC patients.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Sorafenib
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The primary therapy investigated was Sorafenib, a multi-kinase inhibitor for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). In vitro studies used sorafenib at an IC50 of 8.5 µM for acute, 48-hour, or 7-day prolonged treatments, and 7 µM for sorafenib-resistant IR-Huh7 cells. Clinical treatment involved oral administration of 400 mg twice daily for HCC patients, with dose reductions permitted for adverse effects. Other interventions included adenoviral gene downregulation (50 MOI for Gpd1/1l, Gpd2; 20 MOI for Glo1) and supplementation with various fatty acids (SFAs, MUFAs, PUFAs) or lipoproteins (VLDL, LDL), and inhibition of Mgll with JZL184. No detailed dose-response comparisons were consistently reported for sorafenib, though Mgll inhibition showed dose-dependent effects.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly increased following 48 hours of sorafenib exposure.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Central biochemical hallmark of ferroptotic cell death, indicating oxidative stress and oxidative damage to lipids.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Following 48 hours of sorafenib exposure.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates that sorafenib promotes oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation, a characteristic of ferroptosis, and is relevant in disease pathology and drug toxicity.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review critically evaluates wet biomarkers for Huntington's Disease (HD), covering markers in biofluids like blood, urine, saliva, and cerebrospinal fluid. It summarizes findings related to metabolic, inflammatory, oxidative stress, endocrine (melatonin, cortisol, growth hormone), and neuronal/glial degeneration pathways, including promising markers like neurofilament light chain. The document also highlights the importance of standardized protocols, independent validation, and considers pre-analytical and analytical variables (e.g., sampling time, feeding state) that influence biomarker reliability, noting the current lack of clinically validated biomarkers but expressing optimism for future discoveries.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Review and evaluation of wet biomarkers for Huntington's Disease (HD) progression and pathology
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Not applicable, as this document is a comprehensive review of biomarkers, their changes, and factors influencing their measurement in HD, rather than an experimental study of a specific therapeutic intervention or its dose.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Enhanced or increased levels of lipid peroxidation products have been consistently reported in individuals with HD, with plasma levels correlating with the degree of disease severity.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: By-products of oxidative damage to lipids, indicating cell membrane damage and oxidative stress resulting from reactive oxygen species activity.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Huntington's Disease (HD), correlated with disease severity.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates increased oxidative stress and cellular damage, associated with the severity of Huntington's Disease.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated early blood lipidome signatures using a prospective approach within the Three-City cohort, identifying a robust serum lipid profile and a composite score associated with subsequent cognitive decline over 12 years in non-demented elderly individuals.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational population-based study of cognitive aging and lipidomics.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was a longitudinal observational study with no therapeutic intervention or dose comparisons. Fasting serum samples were collected at baseline from non-demented older persons, measuring 189 serum lipids, and cognitive decline was assessed repeatedly over a 12-year period in discovery (n=418) and validation (n=314) cohorts.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Associated with greater cognitive decline (OR for 1SD- increase in score = 3.39 (discovery) and 1.39 [95% CI 1.08–1.78] (validation)). In APOE-ε4 carriers in validation sample: OR for 1SD-increase in score = 2.51 [95% CI 1.32–4.78].

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Represents a composite measure of multiple lipid levels (17 lipids), indicative of systemic lipid metabolism and membrane health.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Association with subsequent cognitive decline in an aging population.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Strongly associated with greater cognitive decline, particularly in APOE-ε4 carriers, suggesting its utility as a predictive biomarker.

document_context_data.document_summary: This document outlines the protocol for the PROSAP-A randomized controlled trial, investigating the effects of preoperative insomnia treatment (Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia or Sleep Education Therapy) on acute and long-term postoperative pain control, brain health, and physical recovery in patients undergoing total knee or hip arthroplasty. The study aims to assess various patient-reported outcomes (e.g., opioid use, quality of recovery, sleep, mood, quality of life), objective measures (e.g., actigraphic sleep, quantitative sensory testing for pain, neurocognitive function), and blood biomarkers (e.g., inflammatory, monoamine, genetic mediators) across preoperative and postoperative phases to determine the impact on pain intensity, opioid use, sleep quality, mental health, and functional recovery. The document also details the recruitment, randomization, blinding, and data collection plans for this prehabilitation approach.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Preoperative Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) and Sleep Education Therapy (SET) as an active comparator.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Both interventions are delivered over 4 weeks in a hybrid format, comprising a digital self-guided platform and weekly telehealth video sessions (up to 60 minutes). CBT-I sessions are conducted with a psychologist and include sleep restriction and stimulus control, while SET sessions are with a research nurse. A video-assisted booster session is provided 1-2 weeks postoperatively. No dose-response comparisons are reported as these are fixed intervention protocols.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study performed an integrative multi-platform meta-analysis of gene expression profiles from Affymetrix and Illumina datasets in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) patients and healthy controls to identify novel, robust diagnostic biomarkers. The analysis revealed 5 commonly differentially expressed genes and 28 novel 'gained' genes, suggesting their significant potential for early PDAC diagnosis.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Integrative meta-analysis of gene expression data for biomarker identification and diagnostic prediction in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Gene expression data from two independent cohorts of PDAC patients (Affymetrix: 18 PDAC patients; Illumina: 36 PDAC patients) and 18 healthy controls were integrated. Profiling was performed on peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) using Affymetrix GeneChip® Human Gene ST 1.0 Arrays and Illumina HumanHT-12 v4 Expression BeadChip microarray platforms. Data were integrated using an empirical Bayesian methodology (ComBat) for batch effect removal, and differential expression was analyzed with limma software, identifying genes with p<0.01 and at least 1.5-fold differential expression. The analysis identified 5 commonly differentially expressed genes (with individual ROC curve AUC > 0.9) and 28 novel 'gained' genes, which could discriminate PDAC patients from controls with an average sensitivity of 74.8% and specificity of 73.3% for individual gained genes, 100% sensitivity and 94% specificity for combined common genes, and 91% sensitivity and 87% specificity for combined gained genes. No dose-response comparisons were applicable as it is a diagnostic biomarker identification study.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study performed a comprehensive qualitative and quantitative proteomic analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) derived from different somatic origins (fibroblasts and peripheral blood CD34+ cells), comparing them to original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC) and human embryonic stem cells (hESC). Using ESI-MS e and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry, complemented by Western blot validation, the research aimed to characterize hiPSC proteomic profiles, identify known and novel pluripotency markers, and distinguish hiPSCs from their somatic precursors. Key findings include the identification of approximately 220 commonly up-regulated proteins in pluripotent stem cell lines, the development and confirmation of a 22-protein marker panel for hiPSC characterization, and the observation of coordinated up-regulation of proteins involved in protein synthesis, folding, RNA processing, DNA replication, DNA repair, and energy metabolism (including oxidative phosphorylation and lipogenesis) in hiPSCs. The study also identified somatic cell markers that were down-regulated upon reprogramming and highlighted specific proteomic differences between hiPSCs and hESCs, contributing to improved hiPSC quality control for therapeutic applications.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Proteomic characterization and comparative analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) and human embryonic stem cells (hESCs).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was a characterization study, not a therapeutic intervention, thus no 'dose' of therapy was administered. Quantitative and qualitative proteomic analyses were performed using electrospray ionization (ESI)-MS e (label-free quantification with internal reference standard) and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry. Two hiPSC lines (iNC-01 from CD34+ cells, SB5-MP1 from fibroblasts, both generated using loxP-flanked excisable polycistronic STEMCCA lentiviral vector) and one hESC line (H9) were analyzed at earlier and later passages. Comparisons were made against their respective original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC). Proteins were considered differentially expressed if expression changed by >=1.5-fold, with a maximum false discovery rate of 2% and >95% confidence. Western blot analysis was used for validation. The developed marker panel was further tested in 8-9 additional hiPSC lines or passages from different somatic origins and reprogramming techniques. Differentiation studies were conducted with embryoid bodies at 24 hours and 7 days to assess marker changes during spontaneous differentiation.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the physiological and biochemical responses, including oxygen uptake, power output, and arterial lactate concentrations, during two maximal incremental cycle ergometer tests performed 24 hours apart in female Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS) patients compared to healthy controls. The findings revealed that previous exercise deteriorates physical performance and increases lactate accumulation in ME/CFS patients, while it improves lactate handling in healthy subjects, indicating a disturbed metabolic response to exertion in ME/CFS.

treatment_details.dose_specificity: Two maximal incremental ramp tests (CPET 1 and CPET 2) were performed 24 hours apart on a cycle ergometer. Each test included a 2-min resting phase and 2 min of unloaded pedaling, followed by a linear increase in power output until volitional exhaustion. Increment rates were individually set (10-24 W/min for ME/CFS patients; 15-30 W/min for controls) to reach VO2peak within 8-12 min. Arterial lactate concentrations were measured every 30 seconds during exercise. Blood sampling during CPET 1 amounted to approximately 150–200 mL. No specific dose-response comparisons for different fixed exercise intensities were reported beyond the comparisons between the two repeated tests.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the predictive power of Neuroimmune Guidance Cue (NGC) gene expression profiles from peripheral blood monocytes for classifying cardiovascular disease (CVD) patients versus healthy individuals. Utilizing various machine learning methods, including Linear Discriminant Analysis, Naïve Bayesian, and Stochastic Gradient Boosting, the research aimed to identify key biomarkers for CVD prediction. The findings indicated that expression levels of SEMA6B, SEMA6D, and EPHA2 in circulating monocytes were predictive of CVD outcomes, with machine learning models demonstrating high accuracy and sensitivity in discriminating between healthy individuals and CVD patients.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Predictive modeling for cardiovascular disease diagnosis and risk prediction using machine learning on biomarker expression profiles.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study involved profiling transcriptomes of purified CD14+ monocytes from 368 subjects in the CIRCULATING CELLS study cohort, utilizing 60 mL EDTA blood samples with stringent RNA quality control (RIN > 9) and Illumina BeadStation for hybridization. Various machine-learning methods (including Linear Discriminant Analysis, Naïve Bayesian, Stochastic Gradient Boosting, Logistic Regression, Partial Least Square, Bagged CART, and Random Forest) were applied to gene expression data to classify CVD patients and healthy individuals. Model performances were compared, with linear discriminant analysis, Naïve Bayesian, and stochastic gradient boost models yielding perfect or near-perfect sensibility and specificity, and some models achieving up to 100% accuracy in classification. No therapeutic interventions or dose-response comparisons were reported, as the focus was on predictive modeling and biomarker analysis.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the association between markers of gut damage, permeability, and microbial translocation (I-FABP, REG3α, LPS, BDG) and cognitive function (performance-based B-CAM and self-reported PDQ) in a cohort of 80 ART-treated men living with HIV. The findings indicate that bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) translocation and higher regenerating islet-derived protein 3 α (REG3α) levels are significantly associated with increased self-reported cognitive difficulties, while fungal translocation (BDG) and intestinal fatty acid binding protein (I-FABP) did not show consistent or significant associations with cognitive outcomes. The study concluded that bacterial but not fungal translocation was associated with cognitive difficulties in ART-treated men living with HIV.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Antiretroviral Therapy (ART)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants were men living with HIV, receiving ART for an average of 12 years (range 6.6–17.8 years), with HIV viral load below or equal to 50 copies/mL. The study focused on biomarker associations within this ART-treated cohort and did not report specific ART dose, intensity, or duration details, nor were dose-response comparisons investigated.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher levels (median 39.0 vs. 54.6 pg/mL, p=0.01) were observed in participants with self-reported cognitive difficulties (PDQ scores higher than the median 26.25). This association with PDQ was independent of age and education in multivariable analyses. Splines analysis showed a strong link with worse self-reported cognition (PDQ) between 20 and 70 pg/mL, though an unexpected positive association with performance-based cognition (B-CAM) was also noted in this range. Daily plasma levels vary and systemic levels induce inflammation.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Men living with HIV receiving antiretroviral therapy, specifically in relation to self-reported and performance-based cognitive difficulties, and chronic stimulation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Strongly associated with increased self-reported cognitive difficulties (higher PDQ scores) in ART-treated men living with HIV, independent of age and education, indicating detrimental effects of bacterial microbial translocation on cognitive health, brain inflammation, and neuronal network disorganization. Also linked to increased risk of non-AIDS comorbidities and dementia in AIDS patients.

document_context_data.document_summary: This scoping review systematically evaluates the application of systems biology-driven precision sports nutrition, incorporating 'omics' platforms (e.g., nutrigenetics, metabolomics, metagenomics, proteomics, epigenomics, lipidomics, multi-omics) and wearable technologies, particularly Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM), for endurance athletes. It maps existing literature, summarizes key findings, identifies research gaps, and investigates the impact of various nutritional interventions (e.g., polyphenols, astaxanthin, nitrates, carbohydrate-protein blends, probiotics) on immune function, inflammation, metabolism, gut microbiome composition, and glycemic responses during and after exercise. The review concludes that while these technologies offer insights into individual variability and physiological responses, current evidence is often insufficient to robustly link identified biomarkers to enhanced performance, recovery, and long-term health outcomes, noting methodological limitations.

treatment_details.therapy_type: This scoping review investigates precision sports nutrition strategies for endurance athletes, focusing on systems biology approaches (including various 'omics' platforms and wearable technologies like Continuous Glucose Monitoring) and a wide range of nutritional interventions. These interventions include specific foods (e.g., banana, blueberry, mango), supplements (e.g., soy protein, astaxanthin, beet-based nitrates, cranberry beverage, prebiotics, probiotics, cocoa flavanols), macronutrient manipulations (e.g., carbohydrate-protein blends, oligopeptides, specific protein amounts, dietary fat, low-carbohydrate high-fat diets, low/high FODMAP diets), and their interactions with diverse exercise regimens (e.g., cycling trials, marathons, ultra-endurance events, submaximal and prolonged exercise, exercise under heat stress).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This scoping review synthesizes findings from various studies on nutritional interventions, which include specific food consumptions (e.g., banana, mango) often compared against controls or other carbohydrate sources, and supplementations (e.g., astaxanthin, beet-based nitrates, cranberry beverage, specific probiotics) with durations ranging from acute intake to 2-week periods. It also examines the effects of different macronutrient strategies (e.g., low-carbohydrate high-fat diets, carbohydrate-protein blends) and genetic variations on caffeine metabolism. The review notes that while specific interventions are detailed, it generally reports on rather than conducts dose-response comparisons, highlighting that existing studies often compare interventions against controls. A key emphasis is on the need for tailored, individual-specific strategies, robust randomized controlled trials, and better reporting of training status, dose-response relationships, and demographic stratifications in future research, as current evidence often lacks detailed dose-response comparisons.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated novel protein-based subphenotypes in Heart Failure with reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF) patients using unsupervised machine learning on 4210 repeatedly measured circulating proteins over a median 2.1-year follow-up in 382 patients. It identified four distinct subphenotypes with varying protein profiles, clinical characteristics (e.g., age, EF, chronic renal failure), and prognosis. These subphenotypes were driven by specific protein subsets associated with various biological mechanisms, including oxidative stress, inflammation, extracellular matrix organization, myocardial stretch/stress, injury, and renal dysfunction. Subphenotypes 2 and 3 demonstrated significantly worse clinical outcomes compared to subphenotype 1, highlighting the value of dynamic proteomic profiling for gaining pathophysiological insights and exploring personalized treatment opportunities in complex diagnoses like HFrEF.

treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational study involving trimonthly blood sampling over a median follow-up of 2.1 years (IQR: 1.1–2.6 years) in 382 HFrEF patients, totaling 1066 blood samples. An aptamer-based multiplex proteomic approach (SOMAscan assay) was used to measure 4210 circulating proteins, yielding relative fluorescence units (RFUs) for comparative analysis rather than absolute concentrations. No specific intervention, treatment, or dose-response comparisons were conducted, as the study focused on characterizing disease subphenotypes and biomarker patterns over time. Repeated proteomic measurements (incorporating both intercept and slope coefficients) demonstrated improved accuracy for survival models (c-index 0.73, BIC 1023) compared to single time-point assessments.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive observational study utilized plasma proteomics and machine learning to develop and validate a framework for measuring organ-specific biological aging, termed 'e-ageotypes', in humans. Analyzing 4,778 proteins from 5,676 adults across five independent cohorts, the research revealed that accelerated aging in specific organs (including heart, brain, kidney, muscle, liver, adipose, pancreas, lung, and immune system) is significantly associated with higher risks of all-cause mortality and various age-related diseases, such as heart failure, Alzheimer's disease, hypertension, diabetes, and cognitive decline. The study's methodology involved defining 'extreme agers' (individuals with highly accelerated organ aging), clustering them into distinct ageotypes, and identifying key protein biomarkers (e.g., REN, KL, NPPB, TNNT2, CPLX1/2) that contribute to these aging profiles and offer prognostic utility for disease risk and progression.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational Study on Biological Aging via Plasma Proteomics and Machine Learning
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This observational study involved the quantification of approximately 4,778 plasma proteins using SomaScan assays (v.4 and v.4.1) in 5,676 adults from five independent cohorts. Machine learning models (LASSO regression-based chronological age predictors) were developed and validated to estimate biological (organ-specific) age, referred to as 'age gaps' or 'e-ageotypes', for 11 major organs (adipose tissue, artery, brain, heart, immune tissue, intestine, kidney, liver, lung, muscle, and pancreas) and the whole organism. Models were trained on 1,398 healthy participants from the Knight-ADRC cohort and tested across the full cohort. Age gaps were calculated using local regression, z-scored per model and cohort, and adjusted for age and sex. Associations with various age-related phenotypes, future mortality, heart disease, clinical biochemistry markers, and cognitive decline were assessed using linear models or Cox proportional hazards models, with multiple testing correction (Benjamini-Hochberg method, 5% false discovery rate). No therapeutic intervention or dose comparison was performed.

document_context_data.document_summary: This randomized controlled crossover trial investigated the impact of continuous multi-food-derived oligopeptide supplementation (FOPS) on intraday lipid metabolism in young male cyclists. The study found that FOPS accelerated total body triglyceride breakdown, non-esterified fatty acid (NEFA) uptake, and fat oxidation during both sedentary and exercise states. It also increased plasma free amino acids (FAAs) and post-exercise blood glucose, suggesting a modulation of metabolic substrate selection for improved endurance performance and cardiometabolic health.

The total dosage was 0.5 g/kg body weight, administered in multiple servings (0.05 g/kg body weight each) throughout a one-day exercise protocol. Specifically, approximately 7g of oligopeptides were ingested 20 minutes pre-exercise, followed by continuous ingestion totaling approximately 31.5g to 35g during the 24-hour trial. The protocol included intraday fasting, 30 minutes of sitting still, 85 minutes of prolonged exercise plus a 5-minute sprint, a 60-minute recovery, and a 20-minute time trial. No dose-response comparisons for varying oligopeptide amounts were reported.

document_context_data.document_summary: This randomized controlled trial investigated the effects of 8 weeks of daily 5g Cistanche deserticola (CD) extract supplementation, combined with progressive high-intensity resistance training, on muscle strength and recovery in both untrained and resistance-trained male participants. The study found that CD supplementation significantly enhanced muscle strength (1RM bench press and squat, MVIC) and endurance (RTF in untrained), and facilitated post-exercise recovery by modulating hormonal responses (increased testosterone, reduced cortisol) and decreasing markers of stress and inflammation (reduced CRP and CK levels) in both cohorts. Mechanistic insights suggest CD's role in improving energy metabolism, reducing muscle degradation, enhancing antioxidant defense, modulating neurotransmission, and regulating endocrine axes.

document_context_data.document_summary: This longitudinal study systematically investigated distinct host responses, cellular injury, and tissue damage in pediatric COVID-19 and Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children (MIS-C) through next-generation sequencing of plasma cell-free RNA (cfRNA), cell-free DNA (cfDNA), and whole-blood RNA (wbRNA) from 228 patients. It revealed unique molecular signatures distinguishing MIS-C from COVID-19, including increased multiorgan involvement and pyroptosis-related gene enrichment in MIS-C, alongside shared and distinct pro-inflammatory pathways. The analysis highlighted the complementary insights provided by cfRNA and wbRNA profiling, demonstrating varying biomarker trajectories, such as persistent immune dysregulation in COVID-19 compared to MIS-C resolution.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study characterizing and differentiating disease states of pediatric COVID-19 and Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children (MIS-C) through comprehensive molecular profiling.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This study involved longitudinal analysis of 402 blood samples from 228 pediatric patients (MIS-C, COVID-19) and controls, utilizing next-generation sequencing of plasma cell-free RNA (cfRNA), cell-free DNA (cfDNA), and whole-blood RNA (wbRNA). Samples were collected at acute, 1-month, and 3-month post-hospitalization time points. While some patients received intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg), it was not a tested intervention, and its administration was found not to significantly confound observed molecular differences. No therapeutic interventions or dose-response comparisons were conducted or reported.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated a chemically defined, serum-free protocol for the in vitro transdifferentiation of pancreatic progenitor AR42J-B13 cells into functional hepatocyte-like cells (HLCs) over five days. The research examined morphological, transcriptomic, proteomic, and functional changes, concluding that successful transdifferentiation, facilitated by extracellular matrix proteins like fibronectin or laminin, is independent of serum.

treatment_details.therapy_type: In vitro pancreatic progenitor cell transdifferentiation to hepatocyte-like cells
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Clonal pancreatic progenitor AR42J-B13 cells were cultured for five days in a differentiation medium containing 100 nM Dexamethasone, 10 ng/ml Oncostatin M, 20 ng/ml HGF, 20 ng/ml FGF-2, 1% ITS+ (insulin, transferrin, selenous acid), 0.2% BSA, 4.4 mM nicotinamide, 1 µM copper sulphate, 30 µg/ml ascorbic acid, and 1 µg/ml heparin. Cells were grown on uncoated plastic, laminin-coated (2 µg/cm2), or fibronectin-coated (5 µg/cm2) substrata, with or without 5% FBS supplementation. The study primarily focused on the effectiveness of serum-free conditions facilitated by ECM proteins, rather than dose-response comparisons for individual components, finding no significant difference in transdifferentiation potential between fibronectin and laminin substrata.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the tissue origins of cell-free DNA (cfDNA) in healthy mice using tissue-specific knockout models and its utility as a biomarker following paracetamol (APAP) overdose in both mice and humans. It found that cfDNA predominantly originates from blood cell lineages in healthy mice. Following APAP overdose, total and hepatocyte-derived cfDNA, as well as ALT and AST levels, significantly increased in mice (peaking at 8 hours), while albumin and bilirubin remained unaffected. In human APAP overdose patients, total cfDNA and liver-specific cfDNA (via methylation analysis) also significantly increased, especially in those with biochemical evidence of liver injury, demonstrating cfDNA's potential as a clinical biomarker for distinguishing overdose patients, assessing liver injury severity, and monitoring treatment efficacy.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Paracetamol (APAP) Overdose; N-acetylcysteine (NAC) treatment
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Mice received intraperitoneal (IP) APAP at 350 mg/kg body weight, with samples collected at 8, 24, and 48 hours post-dosing (optimal cfDNA peak at 8 hours, liver damage most severe at 24 hours). Human patients presented with APAP overdose, with a subset receiving N-acetylcysteine (NAC) at 500-900 mg/kg body weight 20-40 hours after initial overdose. Patient groups were stratified by liver injury severity (normal vs. raised ALT); no specific APAP dose comparisons were performed in humans.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Hepatocyte contribution increased to 77.9% (from 4.2% baseline) in APAP-dosed mice at 8 hours post-dosing, representing a ~19-fold increase in percentage fraction.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Indicates cell death specifically originating from liver cells (hepatocytes).
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: APAP-induced acute liver injury in hepatocyte-specific knockout mice.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Specific indicator of liver cell damage, demonstrating the utility of tissue-specific knockout models.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study conducted a secondary analysis of data from the European First-Episode Schizophrenia Trial (EUFEST) and Recovery After an Initial Schizophrenia Episode Early Treatment Program (RAISE-ETP) trials. It utilized machine learning models (support vector regressors and classifiers) to predict depressive symptom trajectories (changes in CDSS scores) and the occurrence of post-psychotic depressive episodes (PPD) at 6 and 12 months in first-episode psychosis (FEP) patients with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders. The models leveraged various baseline variables including sociodemographic information, clinical assessments (e.g., PANSS, CDSS scores), neurocognitive performance, quality of life, and blood-based biomarkers, demonstrating accurate prediction and geographical generalizability across populations. The study also analyzed how factors like treatment assignment (e.g., NAVIGATE program) and antidepressant prescription influenced model misclassification and patient outcomes.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Antipsychotic medication, NAVIGATE program (psychosocial intervention), Antidepressant coadministration, and Usual community care.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants in the EUFEST trial received 1 year of antipsychotic treatment (described as "minimally antipsychotic-treated"), while RAISE-ETP participants were allocated to either usual community care or the NAVIGATE program. Antidepressant prescriptions were observed, with RAISE-ETP patients showing a higher rate (33.33%) compared to EUFEST (2.18%). The NAVIGATE program was associated with a sharper decline in depressive symptoms, especially among patients prescribed antidepressants at baseline. However, no specific doses, intensities, or durations for antipsychotics, the NAVIGATE program, or antidepressants were detailed, nor were dose-response comparisons reported for any treatment; their influence on predictive model performance and patient characteristics was primarily analyzed.

document_context_data.document_summary: This review comprehensively investigates the potentials, pitfalls, and practical applications of blood-based biomarkers for objective individualized monitoring of training load, recovery, and health status in elite sports. It evaluates the utility and limitations of established markers like creatine kinase (CK), lactate, C-reactive protein (CRP), urea, myoglobin, and various leukocyte populations, detailing their physiological responses to acute and chronic exercise, kinetics, and implications for muscle damage, immune function, and inflammation. The document also addresses methodological considerations, confounding variables, the need for individual reference ranges, and statistical approaches for interpreting biomarker changes, concluding with recommendations for best practices in their sport-specific use.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Blood-based biomarker monitoring in conjunction with physical exercise and training load management in elite sports.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This review focuses on the application and interpretation of blood-based biomarkers for athlete monitoring across various exercise loads, including strenuous, resistance, high-intensity, submaximal, acute physical stress, soccer matches, ultradistance races, and long-term intensive endurance exercise. Biomarker responses are noted to depend on exercise modality, intensity, duration, and individual factors such as ethnicity and body composition. While specific exercise regimens like 30 minutes of endurance running (65% vs 85% of VO2max) showed CRP increases, no single standardized dose-response is consistently reported or compared across all biomarkers. The document emphasizes the need for individual reference levels, standardized collection, and careful consideration of confounding variables, particularly in managing workload by adjusting training when physiological parameters exceed baseline.

document_context_data.document_summary: This prospective single-center study investigated the relationship between an impaired Growth Hormone (GH)-Insulin-like Growth Factor I (IGF-I) axis and cardiac wasting (reduced left ventricular mass) in 307 advanced cancer patients. The findings reveal that reduced LV mass is associated with an imbalance in the GH-IGF-I axis, characterized by higher plasma GH levels and a lower IGF-I/GH ratio, suggesting acquired GH resistance. This resistance is particularly evident in patients with wasting syndrome with unintentional weight loss, and higher baseline IGF-I was associated with a subsequent decline in relative LV mass.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study investigating GH-IGF-I axis dysregulation in advanced cancer patients; no therapeutic intervention.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational, cross-sectional, and longitudinal study (with follow-up for 85 patients) assessing baseline characteristics and follow-up changes in GH-IGF-I axis parameters. No intervention or dose was administered. Patient stratification involved grouping by echocardiographic left ventricular mass/height^2 tertiles (women: <50, 50–61, >61 g/m^2; men: <60, 60–74, >74 g/m^2) and by the presence of wasting syndrome (BMI <24 kg/m^2 and ≥5% weight loss in the prior 12 months).

matched_biomarker_details.biomarker_name: log Insulin-like Growth Factor-I (IGF-I)/Growth Hormone (GH) ratio

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly lower in patients with lower LVmass/height^2 (women, 1.60 ± 0.09 vs. 2.02 ± 0.09 and 1.88 ± 0.09 in higher tertiles, p=0.004; men, 1.64 ± 0.09 vs. 2.14 ± 0.11 and 2.04 ± 0.11 in higher tertiles, p=0.002). Also significantly lower in men and women with wasting syndrome with unintentional weight loss. An inverse relationship was observed with LV mass (Pearson r=0.203, p<0.001).

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Advanced cancer patients (mostly stage III/IV) with reduced left ventricular mass (cardiac wasting) or presence of wasting syndrome with unintentional weight loss.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: A lower ratio indicates acquired GH resistance, which is strongly associated with cardiac wasting and the progression of wasting syndrome in advanced cancer patients.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review investigates the potential of extracellular vesicle (EV)-enclosed non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs), including microRNAs (miRNAs), long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), piRNAs, circRNAs, and tsRNAs, along with N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA modifications, as stable, non-invasive diagnostic, prognostic, and monitoring biomarkers for a wide range of chronic liver diseases (CLDs). These include metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), metabolic-dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), Alcoholic Liver Disease (ALD), Autoimmune Hepatitis (AIH), Chronic Viral Hepatitis (HBV/HCV), cholestatic liver diseases, liver fibrosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), cholangiocarcinoma (CCA), and gallbladder carcinoma (GBC). The document also touches upon the therapeutic potential of engineered EVs for targeted cargo delivery in preclinical models to modulate inflammation and fibrosis pathways, highlighting their utility and associated challenges in clinical application.

treatment_details.therapy_type: This document primarily functions as a review investigating biomarkers for the diagnosis, prognosis, and monitoring of chronic liver diseases (CLDs). While the main focus is on biomarker identification, the review also touches upon the therapeutic potential of Extracellular Vesicle (EV) therapy, including engineered EVs for targeted cargo delivery, and mentions pharmacological inhibition of miR-34a as a potential therapeutic strategy.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study does not report specific therapeutic doses or dose-response comparisons for most interventions, as its primary focus is on biomarker evaluation. However, preclinical models utilized various EV-based interventions, such as native and engineered EVs derived from mesenchymal/stromal stem cells (MSCs) or human liver stem cells in models of liver fibrosis, NASH, and cancer, without detailed quantitative dosing. In biomarker contexts, some observations included a dose-dependent increase in serum miR-122 and miR-192 levels in induced liver injury mouse models. Disease states and exposures examined for biomarker changes included acute and chronic alcohol consumption, autoimmune inflammation, viral infections, cholestasis, CCl4-induced liver fibrosis, lipotoxic palmitic acid treatment of hepatocytes, arsenite-induced liver fibrosis, and various human liver conditions including biliary cholangitis, biliary atresia, liver fibrosis, HCC, CCA, and GBC.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Upregulated in patients with MASLD (among 15 lncRNAs).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Long non-coding RNA; involved in gene expression regulation.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: MASLD diagnosis.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Implied biomarker for MASLD diagnosis.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigates the metabolic reprogramming mechanisms underlying sorafenib activity and resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells and patients. It reveals that sorafenib impairs mitochondrial function, forcing a metabolic shift towards glycolysis, leading to D-lactate accumulation, which serves as a biomarker for treatment response. In resistant cells, adaptation involves rerouting dihydroxyacetone phosphate towards glycerol-3-phosphate synthesis, extensive phospholipid remodeling to evade ferroptosis, enhanced antioxidant capacity, and increased reliance on exogenous triglycerides, resulting in glycerol accumulation as a marker of resistance. The study identifies D-lactate and glycerol as potential plasma biomarkers for monitoring sorafenib efficacy and resistance in HCC patients.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Sorafenib
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The primary therapy investigated was Sorafenib, a multi-kinase inhibitor for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). In vitro studies used sorafenib at an IC50 of 8.5 µM for acute, 48-hour, or 7-day prolonged treatments, and 7 µM for sorafenib-resistant IR-Huh7 cells. Clinical treatment involved oral administration of 400 mg twice daily for HCC patients, with dose reductions permitted for adverse effects. Other interventions included adenoviral gene downregulation (50 MOI for Gpd1/1l, Gpd2; 20 MOI for Glo1) and supplementation with various fatty acids (SFAs, MUFAs, PUFAs) or lipoproteins (VLDL, LDL), and inhibition of Mgll with JZL184. No detailed dose-response comparisons were consistently reported for sorafenib, though Mgll inhibition showed dose-dependent effects.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study developed and validated a multilayer perceptron (MLP) machine learning model for the early postnatal differential diagnosis of choledochal cysts (CC) and cystic biliary atresia (CBA). The model utilized routinely available clinical parameters, including biochemical markers (Total bile acid, Total bilirubin, γ-glutamyl transferase, Aspartate aminotransferase, Alanine aminotransferase, Direct bilirubin, and Taurodeoxycholate) and ultrasonographic measurements (Longitudinal and Transverse diameters of cysts), from a retrospective cohort of 319 patients. The MLP model achieved high diagnostic performance (95.8% accuracy, 92.9% sensitivity, 96.3% specificity, and AUC of 0.990 for differentiating CBA from CC), aiming to facilitate timely surgical intervention for CBA and improve patient outcomes.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Diagnostic Model Development (Machine Learning)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This retrospective study involved the analysis of clinical features from 319 patients (< 60 days old at surgery) with hepatic hilar cysts (274 CC, 45 CBA) treated between 2011 and 2022. It focused on developing a diagnostic model rather than a therapeutic intervention. Biochemical markers and ultrasonographic measurements were compared, and key diagnostic features were identified using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression. Eleven machine learning models were developed and compared, with a multilayer perceptron (MLP) model showing optimal performance: 95.8% accuracy, 92.9% sensitivity, 96.3% specificity, and an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.990. The model utilized seven routine clinical parameters (GGT, TBA, DBIL, TBIL, ALT, LDC, and TDC) as input variables. No therapeutic dose-response comparisons were reported.

Shin et al. proposed postnatal cyst diameter ≤ 2.2 cm without a visible distal common bile duct to differentiate CC from CBA. Guan et al. found an initial postnatal ultrasound and first prenatal ultrasound difference < 7.5 mm suggests a higher likelihood of CBA diagnosis. Demonstrated the highest absolute coefficient magnitude among negative contributors in the LASSO model.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study developed and validated blood-derived DNA methylation-based prediction models, including epigenetic scores (epi-LIBRA, epi-CAIDE) and a Multivariate Methylation Risk Score (MMRS), to assess and predict cognitive impairment and dementia (including AD and MCI) in various independent cohorts.
