document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated inflammatory, epigenetic, and molecular changes in women with unexplained euploid embryo transfer failure (UEETF) and suspected endometriosis. It evaluated the predictive value of endometrial BCL6 and SIRT1, compared GnRH agonist treatment to controls, and conducted a pilot randomized controlled trial comparing GnRH antagonist (elagolix) to oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) for two months. The findings characterized changes in inflammatory gene and miRNA expression in blood following treatments and suggested that medical suppression of suspected endometriosis could improve implantation success rates by addressing underlying inflammatory and epigenetic factors.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Medical suppression, including GnRH agonist, orally active GnRH antagonist (elagolix), and Oral Contraceptive Pills (OCPs).

Elagolix treatment was associated with a trend toward higher pregnancy and live birth rates (100% pregnancy, 60% live birth) compared to OCPs (60% pregnancy, 20% ongoing/delivered), though statistical significance was not reached due to small numbers. Elagolix also dramatically altered the inflammatory milieu in blood compared to OCP suppression. No specific dose-response comparisons were reported within the treatments.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study performed a comprehensive qualitative and quantitative proteomic analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) derived from different somatic origins (fibroblasts and peripheral blood CD34+ cells), comparing them to original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC) and human embryonic stem cells (hESC). Using ESI-MS e and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry, complemented by Western blot validation, the research aimed to characterize hiPSC proteomic profiles, identify known and novel pluripotency markers, and distinguish hiPSCs from their somatic precursors. Key findings include the identification of approximately 220 commonly up-regulated proteins in pluripotent stem cell lines, the development and confirmation of a 22-protein marker panel for hiPSC characterization, and the observation of coordinated up-regulation of proteins involved in protein synthesis, folding, RNA processing, DNA replication, DNA repair, and energy metabolism (including oxidative phosphorylation and lipogenesis) in hiPSCs. The study also identified somatic cell markers that were down-regulated upon reprogramming and highlighted specific proteomic differences between hiPSCs and hESCs, contributing to improved hiPSC quality control for therapeutic applications.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Proteomic characterization and comparative analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) and human embryonic stem cells (hESCs).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was a characterization study, not a therapeutic intervention, thus no 'dose' of therapy was administered. Quantitative and qualitative proteomic analyses were performed using electrospray ionization (ESI)-MS e (label-free quantification with internal reference standard) and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry. Two hiPSC lines (iNC-01 from CD34+ cells, SB5-MP1 from fibroblasts, both generated using loxP-flanked excisable polycistronic STEMCCA lentiviral vector) and one hESC line (H9) were analyzed at earlier and later passages. Comparisons were made against their respective original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC). Proteins were considered differentially expressed if expression changed by >=1.5-fold, with a maximum false discovery rate of 2% and >95% confidence. Western blot analysis was used for validation. The developed marker panel was further tested in 8-9 additional hiPSC lines or passages from different somatic origins and reprogramming techniques. Differentiation studies were conducted with embryoid bodies at 24 hours and 7 days to assess marker changes during spontaneous differentiation.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated inflammatory clusters in sepsis based on plasma cytokine protein abundance and their relationship with leucocyte transcriptomic subphenotypes, utilizing data from three cohorts (UK GAinS, VANISH, and LeoPARDS). It identified two or three inflammatory clusters across these datasets, with a 'high cytokine' cluster exhibiting elevated levels of both pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory cytokines, which was consistently associated with worse organ dysfunction, increased disease severity, and higher mortality. The study also explored the overlap between inflammatory clusters and previously described transcriptomic subphenotypes (SRS1/SRS2) and ARDS subphenotypes, suggesting that combining cytokine protein abundance and transcriptomic data could provide complementary information for optimal sepsis patient stratification. document_context_data.document_summary: This study performed a comprehensive qualitative and quantitative proteomic analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) derived from different somatic origins (fibroblasts and peripheral blood CD34+ cells), comparing them to original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC) and human embryonic stem cells (hESC). Using ESI-MS e and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry, complemented by Western blot validation, the research aimed to characterize hiPSC proteomic profiles, identify known and novel pluripotency markers, and distinguish hiPSCs from their somatic precursors. Key findings include the identification of approximately 220 commonly up-regulated proteins in pluripotent stem cell lines, the development and confirmation of a 22-protein marker panel for hiPSC characterization, and the observation of coordinated up-regulation of proteins involved in protein synthesis, folding, RNA processing, DNA replication, DNA repair, and energy metabolism (including oxidative phosphorylation and lipogenesis) in hiPSCs. The study also identified somatic cell markers that were down-regulated upon reprogramming and highlighted specific proteomic differences between hiPSCs and hESCs, contributing to improved hiPSC quality control for therapeutic applications.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Proteomic characterization and comparative analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) and human embryonic stem cells (hESCs).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was a characterization study, not a therapeutic intervention, thus no 'dose' of therapy was administered. Quantitative and qualitative proteomic analyses were performed using electrospray ionization (ESI)-MS e (label-free quantification with internal reference standard) and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry. Two hiPSC lines (iNC-01 from CD34+ cells, SB5-MP1 from fibroblasts, both generated using loxP-flanked excisable polycistronic STEMCCA lentiviral vector) and one hESC line (H9) were analyzed at earlier and later passages. Comparisons were made against their respective original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC). Proteins were considered differentially expressed if expression changed by >=1.5-fold, with a maximum false discovery rate of 2% and >95% confidence. Western blot analysis was used for validation. The developed marker panel was further tested in 8-9 additional hiPSC lines or passages from different somatic origins and reprogramming techniques. Differentiation studies were conducted with embryoid bodies at 24 hours and 7 days to assess marker changes during spontaneous differentiation.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the impact of 4 weeks of Urolithin A (UA) supplementation on running performance, recovery, and mitochondrial biomarkers in highly trained male distance runners during an altitude training camp. document_context_data.document_summary: This study comprehensively investigated the functional implications of heterogeneity in human embryonic stem cells (hESCs), focusing on an endodermally biased pluripotent substate. Using a GATA6-GFP reporter line and single-cell functional/transcriptomic analyses, the research identified distinct, interconvertible hESC substates defined by differential expression of GATA6 and SSEA3. GATA6-positive hESCs, while retaining long-term self-renewal and pluripotency (often alongside OCT4 and SOX2 co-expression), exhibited a higher propensity and bias towards spontaneous endoderm and mesoderm differentiation, with downregulation of ectodermal genes. SOX17 was identified as a potential driver for this endoderm-biased substate.

These sorted cells were subjected to single-cell cloning, gene expression analysis (qPCR, single-cell RNA sequencing), high-content clonogenic assays, and differentiation protocols, including a spin-embryoid body (EB) system, without external therapeutic interventions or dose-response comparisons for differentiation-inducing factors. The focus was on intrinsic marker expression and resultant lineage bias.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigates the molecular determinants of hemogenic endothelial cells (HECs) and hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs) by generating a GATA2w/eGFP reporter in human embryonic stem cells (hESCs). The reporter accurately marks endogenous GATA2 expression, which is critical for endothelial-to-hematopoietic transition (EHT). A key finding is the identification of ITGB3 (CD61) as a reliable novel positive surface marker that precisely labels functional HECs with superior hemogenic potential, both in hESC/hPSC differentiation in vitro and in embryonic day 10 mouse embryos in vivo. The research provides a robust platform for dissecting hematopoiesis and facilitates the generation of functional hematopoietic stem cells in vitro.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Gene targeting using TALENs, in vitro human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC) differentiation, and in vivo mouse embryo analysis.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: GATA2w/eGFP reporter was generated in H1 hESCs via gene editing (TALENs, electroporation of 1 μg linearized vector and 2.5 μg of each TALEN plasmid into 1 × 10^6 H1 cells, puromycin selection at 0.5 μg/mL, and Cre recombinase (400 ng per 1 × 10^6 cells) for cassette removal). In vitro differentiation involved hPSC blood differentiation protocols using co-culturing with OP9 stromal cells or AGM-S3 co-culture. Bone morphogenetic protein 4 (BMP4) treatment was applied for 5 days. Cell seeding used Y-27632 (10 μM). CFU assay medium contained 100 ng/mL recombinant murine stem cell factor, 10 ng/mL recombinant murine interleukin-3, 10 ng/mL recombinant human interleukin-6, and 3 U/mL human erythropoietin, with endothelial cell assays using 100 ng/mL vascular endothelial growth factor. In vivo analysis included mouse embryos at E10.0, E11, E12, E14, with fractionation of endothelial cells based on CD61 expression (CD61 high, CD61 low, and CD61 − subpopulations). No specific dose-response comparisons for differentiation conditions or therapeutic interventions were reported beyond qualitative observations of effect.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Enriched in the eGFP+ cells and highly expressed in GATA2/eGFP+ HECs.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Critical transcription factor for normal function of HSC or HSC niche, and for EHT or HPC function.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Transcriptome analysis of GATA2/eGFP+ HECs during hESC blood differentiation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates active EHT, HPC function, and HSC niche characteristics in GATA2/eGFP+ HECs.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated large-scale plasma proteomic changes in 75 middle-aged adults during acute treadmill exercise and up to 1-hour post-exercise, identifying 765 proteins changed at peak and 128 at 1-hour post-exercise. It further characterized 56 proteins with sustained changes, linking them to cardiometabolic traits and responses to a 20-week aerobic exercise training program. The research aimed to biochemically characterize acute exercise protein kinetics, finding enrichment for coagulation-related proteins post-exercise and MYC targets, and noting both concordant and discordant protein responses between acute and chronic exercise.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Acute treadmill exercise and chronic aerobic exercise training.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Acute exercise consisted of symptom-limited treadmill stress testing in 75 middle-aged adults, following a standard Bruce protocol with plasma protein quantification at baseline, peak exercise (mean 90% predicted peak heart rate, 9.6 METs), and 1-hour post-exercise. Chronic exercise involved a 20-week aerobic training program with three sessions per week, with intensity and duration gradually increased based on individual VO2max. Acute exercise intensity and duration varied, making it difficult to effectively analyze specific exertion thresholds or dose-response comparisons for the acute protocol.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Peak acute exercise; 1-h post-acute exercise
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of metabolic adaptation and gene expression modulation in response to exercise.

These proteins, many of which are muscle-enriched, correlated with clinical severity and functional traits, outperformed existing clinical markers like CK, and showed mechanistic links to androgen receptor gene regulation and muscle pathology, indicating their potential as early predictors of treatment effects and for tracking disease progression.

Plasma and serum samples were collected from SBMA patients and healthy controls, with protein levels measured using targeted proteomic approaches (Olink platforms). document_context_data.document_summary: This study aimed to establish comprehensive reference intervals for novel circulating biomarkers of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) and hepatic regeneration in healthy human volunteers. It investigated intra- and interindividual variability, as well as diurnal variation, to provide robust data for interpreting exploratory clinical DILI studies and assisting biomarker qualification by regulatory authorities.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study for establishing reference intervals of circulating biomarkers
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study involved serum sample collection from 227 healthy volunteers in a cross-sectional study (single sample). Additionally, 25 subjects underwent weekly serial sampling over 3 weeks, and 23 subjects had intensive 24-hour blood sampling every 3 hours after a 10-h overnight fast and standardized meals. No therapeutic interventions or dose comparisons were involved, as the focus was on establishing reference intervals and assessing natural variability in healthy subjects.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Reference intervals established; levels not significantly influenced by demographic factors; intra-individual variability non-significant; higher mean level than previously reported, potentially due to sample collection methods.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Reference intervals based on the 97.5% quantile (90% CI). No significant fixed effects of sex, age, height, weight, BMI, or ethnicity were observed. Intra-individual variability found to be non-significant, with no significant impact of diurnal variation. Mean serum level was 12.18 ng/mL, significantly higher than previously reported (0.251 ng/mL), suggesting potential loss during clotting.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Promotes hepatic regeneration; diagnostic marker for certain cancers.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Establishing reference ranges in healthy human volunteers, characterizing natural variability, diurnal variation, and assessing its stability across demographic factors, also noting potential issues with sample collection.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Potential to improve DILI prediction and hepatic regeneration assessment. Supports universal reference intervals due to stable levels across demographics. Also a sensitive diagnostic marker for pancreatic and ampullary cancer. Awareness of potential loss during serum clotting is crucial for accurate measurement.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated serum levels of various biomarkers, including matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs), cytokines (SDF-1α, SCGF-β, SCF-1, G-CSF, MCP-1), hormones (leptin, ghrelin), and liver enzymes (ALT, AST, γ-GTP), in patients with histologically proven nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). The aim was to determine if these biomarkers reflect disease activity, steatosis, inflammation, and fibrosis progression across early and advanced NASH stages. The study also evaluated the impact of pharmacological interventions, specifically pioglitazone and ezetimibe, and lifestyle modifications on these biomarkers and the clinical course of NASH. Key findings identified serum MMP-1 as significantly higher in early-stage NASH (stage 1 fibrosis) and reflective of disease activity, while SDF-1α strongly correlated with fibrosis, steatosis, and inflammation across various stages. Pioglitazone treatment was observed to improve histological features and modulate biomarker levels, decreasing MMP-1 and increasing SDF-1α.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study of Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) disease progression and correlation with biomarkers, supplemented by pharmacological interventions and lifestyle modifications.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study involved both observational components, comparing serum biomarker levels in patients with histologically proven early (n=24) and advanced (n=9) NASH against healthy controls (n=14), with subgroup analysis based on histological characteristics. Pharmacological interventions included pioglitazone, administered at 15 mg daily for durations ranging from over two months to two or more years, and in some cases for 14 months concurrently with ezetimibe. Ezetimibe was also administered alone for 10 months. Other unspecified lipid-lowering and anti-diabetic agents, along with diet and physical activity, were also utilized. While changes before and after treatment were observed, comprehensive dose-response comparisons were not consistently reported, focusing more on the outcomes of specific treatment regimens.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Tendency to be higher in grade 1 steatosis, grades 1 and 3 inflammation, grade 1 ballooning, and F1, F3 and F4 groups. Grade 2 steatosis, grades 1 and 3 inflammation, and F1, F3 and F4 groups showed a slightly higher tendency. No correlation between serum SCF-1 level and grade of histological finding observed. Serum levels appeared related to inflammation; levels were similar to MCP-1, G-CSF, and leptin, and reflected the beginning of steatosis with inflammation.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Cytokine reported to activate HSCs, KCs, and ECs in NASH progression; involved in proliferation and migration of stem cells and HPCs.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: NASH with various histological grades (steatosis grades 1-2, inflammation grades 1-3, ballooning grade 1, fibrosis stages F1, F3, F4). Progression of NASH, inflammation, beginning of steatosis.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Potential indicator across various NASH stages, but without strong statistical correlation with histological findings reported. Related to inflammation and the onset of steatosis in NASH.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of acute and long-term (16 weeks) heavy resistance exercise, with and without angiotensin II type I receptor blocker (losartan) supplementation, on serum C-terminal agrin fragment (CAF) levels in healthy older men. The findings indicate that 16 weeks of exercise alone did not affect CAF, but losartan supplementation led to an increase in CAF levels. Conversely, a single bout of heavy resistance exercise acutely lowered serum CAF. The study emphasizes drug interaction and the timing of blood sampling relative to exercise as crucial factors influencing CAF turnover and interpretation in neuromuscular research.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Heavy resistance exercise and Angiotensin II Type I Receptor Blocker (Losartan)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Acute exercise (1EX) consisted of a single bout of unilateral heavy resistance exercise targeting the quadriceps muscles (5 sets of 12 concentric repetitions at 70% 1RM followed by 4 sets of 6 eccentric repetitions at 110% 1RM). Losartan (100 mg daily) or placebo was administered from Day -10 to Day 7 for 1EX. Long-term exercise (48EX) involved 48 sessions over 16 weeks (3 sessions/week) of progressive heavy resistance exercise, with loads gradually increasing from 67% to 86% of 1RM, 3 to 5 sets, and 15 to 6 repetitions. Losartan for 48EX was 50 mg/day for the first week, then 100 mg/day for the remaining 15 weeks. No dose-response comparisons were reported for either exercise or medication regarding biomarker outcomes.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Involved in immune response, inflammation, and tissue repair after injury.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Single bout of unaccustomed heavy resistance exercise (unilateral leg extensions).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates a substantial activation of the thigh muscles and an immune response associated with muscle damage and repair.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated plasma protein biomarkers (including cytokines, chemokines, growth factors, and cell death markers) to identify unique expression patterns associated with the severity and duration of Primary Graft Dysfunction (PGD) after lung transplantation. It identified several strong biomarker candidates, such as IP-10, MIP-1B, RANTES, M30, M65, IL-1Ra, PDGF-BB, G-CSF, IL-4, MIP-1A, IL-17, IL-9, IL-1B, IL-10, IL-6, TNF-alpha, sRAGE, and PAI-1, which are informative for early detection, predicting clinical course, and monitoring treatment efficacy of PGD.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Lung transplantation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study included 40 consecutive lung transplant patients (February 2018 – May 2019). Blood samples were collected immediately pretransplant (T0) and at 6, 24, 48, and 72 hours post-transplant/reperfusion, with PGD severity scored using 2016 ISHLT guidelines. Biomarker analysis involved a bead-based multiplex assay for 27 plasma proteins (cytokines, growth factors, chemokines) and enzyme-linked immunoassay for cell injury markers (M30, M65, sRAGE, PAI-1). Statistical methods included pairwise comparisons, sensitivity, and temporal analyses. An immunosuppression regimen of basiliximab, solumedrol, and mycophenolate (induction) and tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil (maintenance) was used. Intraoperative extracorporeal life support (ECLS), ex vivo lung perfusion (EVLP), and postoperative extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) were considered for severe PGD (PGD3). No specific dose-response comparisons for transplantation or immunosuppression were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Downregulated before transplant, associated with PGD3 at T48–72h (FDR-adjusted p < 0.1).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Chemokine; involved in acute inflammation and recruitment of monocytes and neutrophils.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Pre-transplant, associated with development of severe PGD (PGD3 at T48–72h).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Lower pre-transplant levels are associated with a higher risk of developing severe PGD, indicating a potential predictive biomarker.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study comprehensively investigates the distinct roles of myeloperoxidase (MPO) in gastric health and gastric adenocarcinoma. It reveals an inverse and non-linear association between MPO and gastric mucosal injury markers (PGI, PGR) in a large healthy population, with a significant MPO threshold of 24 ng/ml. Furthermore, high MPO expression is identified as an independent predictor of poor prognosis in gastric adenocarcinoma, correlating with immune dysregulation, specific immune cell infiltration (macrophages, dendritic cells), and pathways involved in cell proliferation and invasion. The study also examined associations between pepsinogen ratio quartiles and various health indicators including blood pressure, diabetes, H. pylori infection, and lipid profiles.

document_context_data.document_summary: This scientific roadmap by the Heart Failure Association comprehensively addresses the complex and heterogeneous nature of fibrosis in heart failure, aiming to improve its definition, quantification, and treatment. It reviews mechanisms of myocardial fibrosis across various etiologies like pressure overload, aging, and cardiomyopathies, emphasizing the central role of TGF-β, collagen deposition, and myofibroblast activity. The document discusses challenges in detecting fibrosis using circulating biomarkers, proposing a framework for assessment and a roadmap for future research to identify individual fibrotic mechanisms, novel therapeutic targets, and diagnostic tools. It also evaluates diverse anti-fibrotic strategies, including pharmacological agents and non-coding RNA-based treatments, highlighting the need for targeted, multi-pathway approaches given the complexity of the fibrotic process.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Anti-fibrotic therapies for heart failure, including established drugs like angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, as well as specific anti-fibrotic agents like pirfenidone. Investigational strategies include targeting the TGF-β pathway (e.g., TGF-β inhibitors, CTGF inhibitors like FG-3019), MAPK pathways (e.g., ERK inhibitors), inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1α), neuregulin-1 administration, Matrix Metalloproteinase (MMP) inhibitors, Galectin-3 inhibitors, and non-coding RNA-based treatments (microRNA and long non-coding RNAs).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This is a review document, and as such, no specific therapeutic doses, intensities, or durations are consistently reported for any intervention, nor are dose-response comparisons detailed. While some agents like Pirfenidone and non-coding RNA modulators show utility in experimental models and clinical trials (e.g., microRNA-21 inhibitor in a Phase II trial), precise quantitative dosage or detailed treatment parameters are generally absent, reflecting a discussion of general approaches and their limitations, including a noted 'lack of precision' in current therapies. For example, MMP-12i was given 3h post-MI, but without specific dosage.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: TGF-β 'may polarize macrophages and neutrophils towards a M2 phenotype', which then 'produces large quantities of inflammatory cytokines'. No specific quantification of the increase in M2 macrophages provided.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Immunomodulatory cells that produce large quantities of inflammatory cytokines, involved in fibrosis.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Low-grade, persistent systemic inflammation in heart failure, MI-related remodelling.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Contributes to chronic inflammation and drives fibrosis, suggesting regulating the inflammatory response as a therapeutic target.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review identifies and recommends validated biomarkers for tracking health, performance, and recovery in athletes across multiple domains including nutritional status (macronutrients, micronutrients, food allergies), hydration, muscle status (damage, endocrine response), endurance, and injury risk (concussions, stress fractures, ACL). It advocates for a comprehensive, integrative, and individualized approach to biomarker analysis, emphasizing dynamic monitoring and contextual interpretation over single markers or universal thresholds to optimize training and minimize injury and overtraining risks.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Biomarker-guided monitoring and management of athletic training, nutrition, hydration, and injury recovery
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This review primarily focuses on the diagnostic and prognostic value of biomarkers rather than specific therapeutic doses. It emphasizes frequent, individualized monitoring (e.g., pre/post-exercise, daily, seasonally, after injury/competition) to establish personalized baseline ranges and track physiological changes in response to various training loads (e.g., acute bouts, heavy strength training, challenging training weeks). While specific nutritional intake recommendations are mentioned for protein (1.3–2.0 g/kg/day) and omega-3 fatty acids (≤3 g/day for average, 6–8 g/day for elite athletes), and iron supplementation at low-moderate doses, the document does not report dose-response comparisons for biomarker changes. Instead, it provides specific thresholds for identifying deficiencies (e.g., Vitamin D >50 ng/ml, Ferritin <12 µg/L), dehydration (e.g., >-2% body mass decrease, blood osmolality ≥295 mmol/kg, USG ≥1.020), insufficient recovery (30% decrease in T:C ratio), and overtraining (T:C ratio of 0.35 × 10⁻³). The overall approach prioritizes dynamic, contextualized assessment over universal thresholds for effective athlete management.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Deficiency may result in reduced endurance work performance and muscle function, and can lead to muscle weakness, spasms, and altered CK and lactate response to exercise.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Essential mineral important for energy metabolism, muscle function, and nerve transmission.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Athletes with nutritional deficiencies, physical performance.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates nutritional deficiency; deficiencies can reduce endurance work performance, muscle function, and lead to muscle weakness, spasms, and altered CK and lactate response to exercise.

document_context_data.document_summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot study investigated the effects of 6-month potassium citrate (K citrate) supplementation (30 mEq/day), in combination with calcium and vitamin D, on bone turnover markers and urinary metabolic profiles in 40 postmenopausal women with osteopenia. The study found that while bone turnover markers (CTX and BAP) decreased in both K citrate and placebo groups, K citrate significantly enhanced these beneficial effects, particularly in a subgroup of patients with pre-existing low-grade acidosis (low urine pH and/or low potassium and citrate excretion). K citrate also improved urinary pH, citrate, and potassium excretion. The study concluded that K citrate is beneficial for osteopenic women with documented potassium/citrate deficits and low-grade acidosis, but its indiscriminate use is not recommended without such evidence.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Potassium Citrate (K citrate) supplementation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Daily oral supplementation with 30 mEq of K citrate (in two tablets) for 6 months. This was administered in addition to daily calcium carbonate (500 mg day   ⁻¹) and vitamin D (400 IU day   ⁻¹) for all subjects (K citrate and placebo groups). The K citrate treatment showed significant benefits in subjects with evidence of low-grade acidosis (low 24h-citrate excretion or low fasting-morning urine pH) compared to the placebo, with significant changes observed as early as 3 months. No specific dose-response comparisons were reported, and adherence rates were approximately 90% for both groups.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Not reported

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Essential for numerous enzymatic reactions, nerve and muscle function, and bone structure.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: K citrate supplementation in postmenopausal women with osteopenia.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of magnesium metabolism and renal handling.

document_context_data.document_summary: This sportomics study investigated the metabolic, immune, hormonal, and amino acid responses, alongside muscle and liver injury markers, in two elite female Olympic beach volleyball athletes during a simulated competition day involving two matches. Key findings revealed significant acute physiological impacts, including electrolyte disturbances (notably hypokalemia), 20-60% increases in muscle injury markers and up to 50% for liver enzymes, elevated stress hormones (ACTH up to 4-fold, cortisol up to 3-fold), and altered energy metabolism and amino acid profiles indicative of central fatigue risk (e.g., Fischer ratio and tryptophan decreased by 60%, serotonin increased by 180%). The study emphasized distinct individual recovery kinetics, highlighted the inadequacy of short recovery sessions, and advocated for personalized monitoring due to varied biomarker responses despite similar external loads.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Simulated Beach Volleyball Competition
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Two world-class female athletes participated in a simulated competition day involving two high-intensity beach volleyball matches (a two-set match in the morning and a three-set match in the afternoon), under identical environmental conditions. Blood and urine samples were collected at seven time points: pre-match, post-match, 60 minutes after each match (short recovery), and after a 15-hour long recovery. The protocol included 15-minute warm-ups. No dose-response comparisons were explicitly reported; however, individual responses to the same protocol were highlighted, and short recovery sessions were found to be inadequate for full physiological recovery, with the second match demonstrating cumulative strain.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: For Athlete 1, magnesium decreased during matches and then increased ~70% at long recovery. For Athlete 2, it remained stable during matches and then increased 10% at long recovery. Identified as one of the most impacted electrolytes.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Cofactor for numerous enzymatic reactions, muscle and nerve function, blood glucose control, blood pressure regulation
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Simulated beach volleyball competition (during matches and long recovery), beach sports conditions.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates electrolyte balance and potential impact on muscle performance and recovery; suggests potential electrolyte disturbance in beach sports players.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the relationship between routine plasma biomarker levels and recovery efficiency in elite professional soccer players over an entire eleven-month competitive match season, including seasonal variations and differences based on player position and cumulative match time. It concluded that a panel of AST, CK, LDH, and creatinine can effectively monitor recovery, adaptation, and overtraining risk, particularly in active positions like midfielders who may also be prone to iron and magnesium deficiencies.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Competitive professional soccer matches and regular intense training
treatment_details.dose_specificity: An eleven-month competitive season, comprising 44 league and cup matches (23 autumn, 21 spring), typically one to two matches per week. Fasting capillary blood samples were collected 17-24 hours after each match. The study compared player positions (midfielder/defender vs. goalie/substitute, and individual midfielder/defender subgroups), noting significant differences in cumulative match time and physical demands. No explicit dose-response comparisons were reported for training intensity, but adaptation to increasing training load was observed.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: generally lower with cumulative time, higher in spring vs. autumn for midfielders, and increased in spring for midfielders
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant differences in baseline levels were found between player subgroups. However, magnesium levels generally decreased significantly over time and showed a negative correlation with cumulative match time in the midfielder/defender group (R=-0.16 to -0.30, P<=0.05 for various phases), midfielders (R=-0.19 to -0.30, P<=0.05), and defenders (R=-0.32, P<=0.05). Conversely, midfielders exhibited significantly higher plasma magnesium levels in the spring round compared to the autumn round, and also increased significantly with time in spring.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: An essential mineral and cofactor for over 325 enzymatic reactions, crucial for anaerobic performance, muscle contraction and relaxation, nerve function, blood glucose control, and energy production. It is involved in regulating troponin expression via calcium ion gradients and plays a role in glucose availability and lactate clearance in muscles during exercise.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Throughout an eleven-month professional competitive soccer match season, including post-match recovery, conditions of insufficient recovery time, and mineral deficiency. Observations were made across various player positions (midfielder/defender, individual midfielder and defender subgroups), considering cumulative game time and seasonal variations (autumn vs. spring rounds).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Measurement can be an additional tool for monitoring recovery efficiency, as it reflects electrolyte balance, physiological stress, and potential depletion or increased utilization due to intense activity. It may suggest altered mineral balance, cellular shifts, or the need for supplementation, especially for active players like midfielders who are prone to deficiencies, particularly in the spring season. It can impact enhancing muscle strength and indicates progressive electrolyte depletion with increased playing time.

document_context_data.document_summary: This pilot study investigated the effects of a 6-week dietary intervention with a specific micronutrient combination (including magnesium, potassium, B vitamins, and Coenzyme Q10) as an add-on therapy for patients with cardiac arrhythmias, cardiovascular disorders, and metabolic syndrome components. The intervention significantly improved cardiometabolic health by reducing insulin resistance (fasting insulin, HOMA-IR), improving left ventricular systolic (LVEF) and diastolic function (LV mass index, interventricular septal thickness, E/A ratio), reducing heart rate, and lowering inflammation (CrP). While beneficial effects were observed for glucose and lipid metabolism markers, premature beats and BMI remained largely unchanged.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Dietary intervention with a specific micronutrient combination as an add-on to concomitant cardiovascular drug treatment.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: A 6-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled dietary intervention involving 54 patients. The verum group received a specific micronutrient combination (2 tablets twice daily), including 145.8 mg magnesium, 469.2 mg potassium, 3.0 µg Vitamin B12, 400.0 µg folic acid, 48.0 mg niacin, and 60.0 mg coenzyme Q10. Other micronutrients like Vitamin C, Vitamin E, and Selenium were also part of the combination. The placebo group received microcrystalline cellulose. No dose-response comparisons were reported. Minor gastric pain was noted in one verum and one placebo patient, with no serious side effects.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly higher in the verum group compared to placebo after intervention (p = 0.005, ES = 0.708; and p = 0.034, ES = 0.512), remaining within the normal range.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Essential mineral involved in over 300 enzymatic reactions, muscle and nerve function, blood glucose control, and blood pressure regulation. Plays an important role in glucose metabolism and leads to economization of cardiac pump function.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: After 6 weeks of dietary intervention with specific micronutrient combination in patients. LVMI was shown to depend on serum magnesium concentration.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates improved magnesium status, which can positively impact cardiovascular health, metabolic function, and cardiac structure, connected with significantly decreased HOMA-IR, suggesting improved insulin sensitivity.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive study investigated alpha-synuclein (αSN) as a potential diagnostic and monitoring biomarker for Inclusion Body Myositis (IBM). It evaluated αSN immunoreactivity in muscle biopsies and its concentration in serum and muscle homogenates, comparing IBM patients to other myopathies and healthy controls. The findings suggest αSN immunoreactivity in muscle is a promising diagnostic marker, while serum αSN levels could serve as a monitoring biomarker, correlating with disease duration and clinical severity in IBM. The study also explored the diagnostic utility of other established and emerging biomarkers in IBM.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational/Diagnostic Biomarker Investigation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This observational study involved a multimodal assessment of alpha-synuclein (αSN) levels and immunoreactivity in muscle biopsies, muscle tissue homogenates, and serum samples from various cohorts. Muscle biopsies (N=63, including 19 IBM, 21 other inflammatory myopathies, 20 other myopathies, 3 healthy controls) were analyzed by immunohistochemical staining. Serum samples (N=156, including 11 IBM, 25 other inflammatory myopathies, 53 hereditary myopathies, 30 mitochondriopathies, 37 healthy controls) were assessed by ELISA. Muscle homogenates were also examined (N=17 IBM, N=19 other inflammatory myopathies, N=5 hereditary myopathies, N=2 healthy controls). IBM patients were stratified by disease severity (IBMFRS) and disease duration for serum αSN analysis. No interventional dose or therapeutic comparisons were reported, as the study focused on diagnostic and monitoring biomarker evaluation.

matched_biomarker_details.biomarker_name: MHC Classes I and II proteins

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Upregulation reported; no quantitative data provided.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Major histocompatibility complex proteins, involved in immune response and antigen presentation.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Autoimmune features and diagnostic histological feature of Inclusion body myositis (IBM).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of immune activation and a useful diagnostic histological feature for IBM.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the expression characteristics of cuproptosis markers, oxidative stress indexes, copper metabolism, and hepatic fibrosis in Wilson disease patients, concluding that conventional chelation therapy significantly improves these abnormal markers and may reverse hepatic fibrosis progression.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Conventional chelation therapy using sodium dimercaptosulphonate (DMPS)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Sodium dimercaptosulphonate (DMPS) at 20 mg 7kg 7−1 was administered intravenously once daily for 6 days per course, dissolved in 5% glucose or 0.9% sodium chloride solution, with calcium gluconate (20 mL) given intravenously once daily for 2 days during intervals. This regimen consisted of four 8-day courses of treatment, totaling 32 days; no dose-response comparisons were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Before treatment: 10.53  1 4.76 nmol 7mL 7−1 (WD patients) vs control 4.92  1 1.81 nmol 7mL 7−1 (P < .001, up-regulated); After treatment: decreased from 10.53  1 4.76 nmol 7mL 7−1 to 7.65  1 3.65 nmol 7mL 7−1 (P < .001), but remained up-regulated compared to control.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Lipid peroxidation product, commonly used as a marker of oxidative stress and cellular damage.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Wilson's disease patients (compared to control) and after conventional chelation therapy.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Higher levels before treatment indicate significant oxidative damage in WD. Reduction after treatment suggests alleviation of oxidative stress, though still elevated compared to control.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study primarily investigated the effects of physical exercise combined with whole-body cryotherapy (WBC) on oxidant/antioxidant balance and other physiological parameters in 16 high-level kayakers. It found an initial decrease and subsequent recovery in GPx activity, decreased TBARS, and variable urea levels, with no significant changes in MDA, CD, protein carbonyls, vitamin E, cortisol, testosterone, total antioxidant capacity (TAC), or hematological parameters. The document also reviews findings from other studies, indicating that WBC generally increases overall antioxidant capacity, helps normalize oxidant/antioxidant balance during intensive exercise, and exhibits anti-inflammatory effects, potentially enhancing recovery and performance during training.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Physical Exercise Combined with Whole-Body Cryotherapy (WBC)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: In the primary study, 16 kayakers underwent specialized physical training twice daily for 19 days. For the first 10 days, this was combined with Whole-Body Cryotherapy (WBC) sessions administered twice daily (morning pre-exercise stimulation and afternoon post-exercise recovery). Each WBC session lasted 3 minutes (excluding a 30-second adaptive vestibule at -60°C) with chamber temperatures gradually decreasing from -120°C to -145°C. The document also refers to other studies using varying WBC protocols, including 10 sessions at -130°C for 3 minutes (once daily), 5 sessions/week at -110°C for 2 minutes, and single sessions at -130°C for 2 or 3 minutes, either with or without exercise.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No statistically significant changes (P > 0.05) were found throughout the experiment.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Lipid peroxidation product, an indicator of oxidative stress.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: During a training cycle involving combined physical exercise and WBC, followed by exercise-only in kayakers.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: No significant change observed, suggesting no statistically significant impact on this specific marker of oxidative damage under the study conditions.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Negatively correlated with vitamin E on Day 5 (r = -0.645, P < 0.05); negatively correlated with TAC on Day 19 (r = -0.634, P < 0.05).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Biomarker for oxidative stress; its relationship with antioxidant defenses.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Kayakers during a training cycle involving intensive exercise and WBC sessions (Day 5 and Day 19).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Negative correlations indicate a healthy balance between oxidative stress (MDA) and antioxidant capacity (Vitamin E, TAC), reflecting proper physiological functions.

document_context_data.document_summary: This randomized, double-blind, cross-over study investigated the effects of acute cocoa flavanol (CF) intake on exercise-induced changes in antioxidant capacity, oxidative stress, inflammation, nitric oxide (NO) production, exercise performance, and recovery in well-trained male cyclists. Findings showed acute CF intake increased systemic epicatechin levels and total antioxidant capacity (TEAC/UA and UA), but did not significantly affect exercise-induced lipid peroxidation (MDA), inflammation (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α), or NO production markers (L-arginine/ADMA, citrulline). While CF intake showed a tendency for improved late-stage performance in the first time trial, overall exercise performance and recovery were not significantly enhanced.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Acute cocoa flavanol (CF) intake and cycling exercise
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants received an acute dose of either 903.75 mg of cocoa flavanols (CF) or a placebo (15 mg CF) in chocolate milk prior to exercise. The exercise protocol involved two 30-minute time trials (TT1 and TT2) performed at a workload equivalent to 75% of peak power output, separated by a 100-minute passive recovery. No explicit dose-response comparisons were conducted beyond the high-CF vs. placebo design.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher (due to exercise), unchanged (by CF intake)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Plasma concentrations significantly increased after TT1 compared to before TT1 and before TT2 (main effect of time: F(4) = 2.98; p = 0.029). However, these exercise-induced increases were not affected by acute CF intake.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: A reactive aldehyde and an end-product of lipid peroxidation, serving as a biomarker for oxidative damage to lipids and cellular membranes.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: During exhaustive exercise (primarily after TT1) following acute cocoa flavanol intake in well-trained cyclists.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates acute oxidative stress and cell damage in response to intense exercise; suggests no protective effect of acute CF intake against exercise-induced lipid peroxidation.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effect of varying intensities of a single session of aerobic exercise on serum markers of lipid peroxidation (MDA) and muscle damage (CK) in sedentary males, concluding that moderate to high-intensity exercise significantly increases MDA and CK levels, while low-intensity exercise is suggested for adaptation and damage prevention.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Single-session aerobic exercise
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants performed 20 minutes of aerobic treadmill running at low (40% VO2 max), moderate (60% VO2 max), or high (80% VO2 max) intensities. Intensity levels significantly affected both MDA (P=0.001) and CK (P=0.003) post-test, with increasing intensity leading to increased amounts of both markers. Specifically, MDA levels significantly differed between control and all intensity levels, but not among the intensity levels themselves. CK levels significantly differed between control and moderate/high intensity levels, but not between control and low intensity, and no significant differences were observed among the intensity levels themselves.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly affected by aerobic exercise intensity [F(3, 45) = 27.210, P = 0.001] post-test. Amounts increased with increasing intensity. Significant differences were observed between the control group (M = 2.69, SD = 1.32 µmol/L) and each intensity level (P ≤ 0.05). The highest amount was detected in the high intensity level (M = 9.09, SD = 2.08 µmol/L), though no significant differences were observed among the three intensity levels themselves.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: End-product marker of lipid peroxidation, indicating oxidative damage caused by free radicals.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Post-test after a single session of aerobic exercise with varying intensities (low, moderate, high) in sedentary males.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates increased oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation, and potential cell/muscle damage; higher levels are associated with high-intensity exercise, while low intensity is recommended for prevention.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the oxidative stress and genotoxicity in gas station refueling workers exposed to long-term, low levels of atmospheric BTEX in Nanning, China, comparing them to office workers. It found significantly higher BTEX levels in refueling areas, which, despite being generally below occupational limits, were associated with reduced antioxidant capacity (lower T-SOD and GSH) and increased oxidative stress (higher MDA and 8-OHdG) and DNA damage (higher micronucleus rate, tail moment, and Olive tail moment) in refueling workers.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Long-term occupational exposure to BTEX (Benzene, Toluene, Ethylbenzene, Xylenes) compounds in gas station refueling workers, compared to office workers
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Long-term occupational exposure to low levels of atmospheric BTEX, with refueling workers exposed for an average of 8.7 years. BTEX concentrations in refueling areas were significantly higher than in office areas (p < 0.001), with mean ambient air concentrations including Benzene (60.03 vs 16.86 µg/m3), Toluene (317.76 vs 89.93 µg/m3), Ethylbenzene (113.85 vs 12.09 µg/m3), m-xylene (40.91 vs 28.44 µg/m3), p-xylene (57.51 vs 10.62 µg/m3), and o-xylene (37.18 vs 15.67 µg/m3). These levels were generally below current occupational exposure limits, but fixed environmental monitoring may underestimate actual exposure. No specific dose-response analysis for individual BTEX compounds was reported in human subjects.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly higher in refueling workers compared to office workers (p < 0.001 to z = -5.864, p < 0.001); however, after controlling for confounding factors (age, gender, years of exposure, smoking, and drinking habits), MDA levels were significantly lower in refueling workers than in office workers.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Product of lipid peroxidation, serving as a biomarker of oxidative stress and cellular damage; formed during oxidative stress and can react with DNA bases.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Long-term occupational exposure to low levels of BTEX in gas station refueling workers compared to office workers.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates increased oxidative damage, specifically lipid peroxidation, potentially linked to cellular injury and oxidative stress.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated whether pre-exercise ascorbic acid supplementation influenced antioxidant defenses, glucose metabolism, inflammation, and muscle damage in untrained healthy adults following a single bout of moderate-intensity cycling. Findings indicated that ascorbic acid supplementation reduced plasma Malondialdehyde (MDA) and increased Ferric Reducing Ability of Plasma (FRAP), while also modulating glucose levels and attenuating exercise-induced changes in albumin and total protein. While moderate-intensity cycling led to an increase in red blood cell Superoxide Dismutase (SOD) activity and low-grade muscle damage (Total Creatine Kinase), it did not induce systemic inflammation or lipid peroxidation. Ascorbic acid supplementation appeared to mitigate the exercise-induced increase in SOD activity but did not significantly prevent muscle damage or affect other inflammatory/damage markers such as hsCRP, LDH, CK-MB, GPx, or Catalase.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Oral ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) supplementation combined with a single bout of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Subjects received 1000 mg of ascorbic acid (or placebo) orally 5 minutes prior to a 30-minute indoor cycling session. Exercise intensity was set at 65–75% of maximum heart rate, which was predicted by an age-based equation. No dose-response comparisons were reported for either ascorbic acid or exercise intensity.

matched_biomarker_details.activity_type: Level (as TBARS, indicator of lipid peroxidation)

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Unchanged in placebo; significantly lower immediately and 30 minutes post-exercise with ascorbic acid supplementation
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant changes in plasma MDA levels in placebo. The ascorbic acid group showed a significant reduction in MDA immediately (p=0.048) and 30 min post-exercise (p=0.034). A main effect of supplement (p < 0.05) was observed, indicating that moderate-intensity exercise did not induce systemic lipid peroxidation without supplementation.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: A common product of lipid peroxidation, serving as an indicator of oxidative stress and cell damage.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Acute aerobic exercise (indoor cycling) in untrained healthy adults, with ascorbic acid supplementation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates reduced oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation with ascorbic acid supplementation following acute exercise.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effect of D-ribose supplementation on delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) induced by plyometric exercise in untrained male college students. Findings indicate that oral administration of 15g D-ribose reduced muscle soreness, improved knee extensor function by mitigating strength reduction, lowered muscle damage markers (Creatine Kinase, Lactate Dehydrogenase, Myoglobin), and inhibited lipid peroxidation (Malondialdehyde), thereby accelerating DOMS recovery. However, D-ribose showed no significant effect on overall isokinetic muscle strength (flexor peak torque and total work) and modulated the time-course of antioxidant enzymes (Superoxide Dismutase) and total antioxidant capacity (TAC) without consistently showing a superior antioxidant effect compared to placebo after 48 hours.

treatment_details.therapy_type: D-ribose supplementation combined with plyometric exercise
treatment_details.dose_specificity: D-ribose was orally administered at 15g per dose, 1-hour before, and 1-hour, 12-hours, 24-hours, and 36-hours after exercise. A calorically equivalent placebo containing sorbitol and β-cyclodextrin was given at the same dose and times. The plyometric exercise protocol consisted of 7 sets of 20 consecutive frog hops with 90-second rest intervals between sets, performed twice with a 14-day washout period. No dose-response comparisons for D-ribose were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased significantly in PLAC after 24-h (p < 0.01) and 48-h (p < 0.01), but not in DRIB (p > 0.05). MDA was significantly lower in the DRIB group compared to the PLAC group after 24-h (p < 0.05) and 48-h (p < 0.01).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: End-product of lipid peroxidation, serving as a marker for oxidative stress and cellular membrane damage.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Post-plyometric exercise oxidative stress and D-ribose supplementation effect on recovery.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Lower levels in DRIB indicate inhibited Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS) production and reduced lipid peroxidation, contributing to less muscle damage and faster DOMS recovery.

document_context_data.document_summary: This randomized, double-blinded, crossover study investigated the comparative effects of 1-week supplementation with tomato powder, isolated lycopene, or placebo on total antioxidant capacity (TAC) and exercise-induced lipid peroxidation biomarkers (MDA, 8-isoprostane) in well-trained male athletes. The study concluded that tomato powder was significantly more effective than pure lycopene in enhancing resting TAC and reducing the post-exercise elevation of lipid peroxidation biomarkers, suggesting that tomato powder's benefits are due to the synergistic interaction of lycopene with other bioactive components.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Nutritional supplementation (Tomato powder, Lycopene supplement, Placebo) combined with exhaustive exercise.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants received 1-week supplementation with either tomato powder (containing 30 mg lycopene, 5.38 mg beta-carotene, 22.32 mg phytoene, 9.84 mg phytofluene, and implied vitamin C and E per serving), pure lycopene (30 mg), or a placebo (dextrose and 3g tomato powder). Each subject underwent three exhaustive exercise tests (incremental treadmill protocol until failure) after each 1-week supplementation period. No explicit dose-response comparisons for the supplements were reported; the study focused on comparisons between the different supplement types and the placebo.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: lower extent of increase compared to placebo after exhaustive exercise
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Exhaustive exercise increased MDA levels (P < 0.001). Following exhaustive exercise, MDA elevated 20% in the tomato powder group versus 51% in the placebo group (p = 0.009), indicating a significantly lower elevation with tomato powder. Pure lycopene did not show similar beneficial outcomes compared to placebo (p > 0.05).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: A product and biomarker of lipid peroxidation, indicating oxidative damage to cell membranes and other lipid-containing molecules due to free radical activity.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Following exhaustive exercise after 1-week supplementation with tomato powder, lycopene, or placebo in well-trained male athletes.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates levels of lipid peroxidation and oxidative stress. Lower levels suggest reduced exercise-induced oxidative stress and cellular damage, implying a protective effect and better recovery for athletes.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of 4-week oral garlic supplementation on 40-km cycling time trial performance, whole-body energy metabolism, exercise-induced oxidative stress, inflammation, and muscle damage in healthy adult males. Findings indicate that garlic supplementation significantly enhanced total antioxidant capacity and attenuated oxidative stress (MDA), inflammatory response (TNF-α), and some markers of muscle damage (LDH and UA at specific time points), but it did not improve cycling performance or overall whole-body energy metabolism.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Oral garlic extract supplementation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: 1000 mg/day for 4 weeks (28 consecutive days) in a single-blind crossover design. No dose-response comparisons were reported, as a single dose was used.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly attenuated/reduced (p < 0.05) before exercise (0-km), and throughout the 20-km and 40-km cycling exercise periods compared to placebo.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: A lipid peroxidation product and free radical marker, indicating systemic oxidative stress.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: 4-wk garlic supplementation during a 40-km cycling challenge
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates reduced oxidative stress, leading to decreased oxidative damage in muscle cells, potentially improving recovery and endurance performance by delaying damage from redox imbalance.

document_context_data.document_summary: This systematic review evaluates the effects of soy protein (SP) supplementation on muscle adaptations, metabolic and antioxidant status, hormonal response, and exercise performance in active individuals and athletes, often comparing it to whey protein or placebo. The review encompasses studies on protein synthesis, amino acid transport, and signaling pathways, highlighting that while some anabolic markers might be less favorable with soy, it can provide similar increases in lean mass to whey protein, especially at optimal protein intakes. SP is shown to reduce exercise-induced metabolic/blood circulating biomarkers (triglycerides, uric acid, lactate) and improve antioxidant capacity, reducing oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation. However, its effects on hormonal responses, such as testosterone and cortisol, are inconsistent or contradictory across studies. SP supplementation also demonstrates potential benefits in improving various exercise performance indicators, including high-intensity running, maximal cardiac output, delaying fatigue, improving isometric strength, running velocity, and muscle recovery after damage. The review concludes that SP can be a viable alternative to conventional protein supplements, but emphasizes the need for further research addressing methodological limitations and consistent dosing.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Soy Protein and Soy Peptide Supplementation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The review encompassed a wide range of soy protein (SP) and soy peptide supplementation protocols, from acute doses (e.g., 15-20g SP, 18g SP beverage, 10g essential amino acids from soy) to chronic daily intakes varying from 0.5 g/kg BW/day to 90 g/day (e.g., 33-40 g/day, 1 g/kg BW/day, 53.3 g/day). Doses were often combined with carbohydrates (e.g., 10g soy peptide + 30g sugar, 15g SP + 52.5g CHO) or matched for nitrogen/leucine content for comparison with whey protein. Durations ranged from single acute sessions to long-term interventions of 2 weeks, 4 weeks, 6 weeks, 9 weeks, 4 months, or even "12 weeks. Comparisons were consistently made against whey protein, soy-dairy blends, isoenergetic placebos, or control (exercise-only) groups. While some studies aimed for optimal protein intakes ("  1.6 g/kg BW/day), there was a notable lack of consistent dosing or explicit dose-response comparisons across the reviewed literature, indicating significant variability in intervention designs.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly decreased malondialdehyde and lipid peroxidation. Lower serum lipid peroxides from 5 min to 24 h post-workout and decreased after moderate weight exercise training compared with whey. Chronic SP (40 g/day) lowered lipid peroxidation, with antioxidant effects superior to whey.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: A lipid peroxidation product, serving as a well-known biomarker of oxidative stress and cellular damage.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Soy isoflavones consumption; after moderate weight resistance workout; chronic soy protein supplementation during resistance training.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Reduced oxidative stress and cellular damage, indicating improved antioxidant defense and cellular health, potentially reducing the risk of chronic diseases.

document_context_data.document_summary: This systematic review aimed to critically examine the effects of melatonin supplementation on sports performance and a range of circulating health biomarkers in highly trained athletes, drawing from randomized controlled trials. The review concluded that melatonin supplementation is safe and demonstrates benefits in improving antioxidant status, reducing inflammatory responses, and reversing exercise-induced liver and muscle damage. Moderate modulating effects were observed on glycemia, total cholesterol, triglycerides, and creatinine. While promising data suggest potential benefits for hematological biomarkers and hormonal responses, the direct efficiency of melatonin in improving sports performance needs further assessment; however, indirect benefits via health biomarker improvements are suggested. Melatonin was also found to counteract oxidative stress, modulate immune function, and show hepatoprotective and renoprotective properties after intense exercise.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Melatonin Supplementation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Melatonin supplementation was investigated with doses ranging from 5 mg to 100 mg, administered acutely (1 day) or continuously for 3 to 30 days. Timing varied from 15-60 minutes before exercise to 2 hours post-exercise, 6 days post-training, 3 days before exercise, or before rest/sleep. Specific dose-response observations were mixed; for instance, 5 mg melatonin showed modest strength improvements, while 8 mg led to significant decreases, and 10 mg improved jumping performance. High heterogeneity in dosages prevented a complete meta-analysis and the establishment of a single efficient dose, though 8 mg melatonin was noted to cause significant harmful effects on strength and power compared to 5 mg and control.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significant decreases (p < 0.05) in plasma levels.

document_context_data.document_summary: This randomized controlled trial investigated the effects of 8 weeks of daily 5g Cistanche deserticola (CD) extract supplementation, combined with progressive high-intensity resistance training, on muscle strength and recovery in both untrained and resistance-trained male participants. The study found that CD supplementation significantly enhanced muscle strength (1RM bench press and squat, MVIC) and endurance (RTF in untrained), and facilitated post-exercise recovery by modulating hormonal responses (increased testosterone, reduced cortisol) and decreasing markers of stress and inflammation (reduced CRP and CK levels) in both cohorts. Mechanistic insights suggest CD's role in improving energy metabolism, reducing muscle degradation, enhancing antioxidant defense, modulating neurotransmission, and regulating endocrine axes.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Cistanche deserticola (CD) supplementation combined with a progressive resistance training program.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants received 5 g of CD extract daily, administered in two sachets (after breakfast and lunch) for 8 consecutive weeks, alongside a placebo group. A standardized resistance training program was completed three times per week for eight weeks. This program involved 4 sets of 10-12 repetitions at 65-70% of 1RM for weeks 1-4, and 4 sets of 6-8 repetitions at 80% of 1RM for weeks 5-8. Maximal strength (1RM bench press/squat, MVIC) and endurance (RTF bench press) were assessed. No dose-response comparisons for CD were reported, only comparison to placebo.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of a 10-week protein blend supplementation on the gut microbiota, fecal metabolites, and oxidative stress markers in endurance athletes. While no significant changes were observed in fecal pH, water content, ammonia, short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), or plasma/urine malondialdehyde levels, the supplementation led to an increased abundance of the Bacteroidetes phylum and a decrease in health-related gut bacteria such as Roseburia, Blautia, and Bifidobacterium longum, suggesting a potentially negative impact on gut microbiota balance.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the influence of oral contraceptive (OC) use on physiological, oxidative stress, and inflammatory responses to fixed-intensity and sprint cycling in recreationally trained women, comparing them to naturally cycling women. It also examined the acute effects of N-acetylcysteine (NAC) supplementation on these responses and 1-km cycling time trial performance. Key findings showed that women using OC had elevated oxidative stress (higher MDA, lower GPx) and inflammation (higher CRP) biomarkers, as well as increased ventilation, during exercise. While NAC supplementation increased plasma thiols, it only blunted exercise-induced malondialdehyde increases in naturally cycling women, not in OC users, and did not improve cycling performance in either group. This suggests an increased strain on the endogenous antioxidant system in women using OC during exercise.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Acute N-acetylcysteine (NAC) supplementation and cycling exercise (fixed-intensity and sprint time trial).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Twenty recreationally trained women completed five exercise trials, including two double-blind crossover intervention trials where participants acutely supplemented with NAC or a placebo. NAC was administered orally in a total dose of 105 mg·kg⁻¹ of body mass, given as 70 mg·kg⁻¹ 60 minutes prior to exercise and 35 mg·kg⁻¹ 30 minutes prior. The exercise protocol involved 40 minutes of fixed-intensity cycling at 105% of the gas-exchange threshold (GET), immediately followed by an all-out 1-km cycling time trial. No dose-response comparisons for NAC were reported beyond the acute vs. placebo comparison.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Resting levels were significantly higher in WomenOC compared to WomenNC (  = 12.00 mmol·L⁻¹ [6.82, 17.17]). Exercise induced an increase in MDA (Time effect   = 13.47 mmol·L⁻¹ [4.10, 22.84]). In the placebo trial, MDA increased after 1-km cycling TT by +2.86 mmol·L⁻¹ (p = 0.036; d = 0.32) in WomenNC and +5.22 mmol·L⁻¹ (p < 0.001; d = 0.55) in WomenOC. Acute NAC supplementation attenuated this increase in WomenNC (lower by -3.28 mmol·L⁻¹ after 40-min cycling, p = 0.018; d = -0.73, and -3.69 mmol·L⁻¹ after 1-km TT, p = 0.017; d = -0.50) but had no attenuating effect on exercise-associated MDA increase in WomenOC.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Resting levels, during fixed-intensity cycling, and after 1-km cycling time trial, in naturally cycling women (WomenNC) and women using oral contraceptives (WomenOC), with or without acute N-acetylcysteine (NAC) supplementation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Higher MDA indicates increased oxidative stress and cellular damage, particularly noted in WomenOC at rest and during exercise, suggesting a greater challenge for redox homeostasis. While NAC attenuated exercise-induced MDA increases in WomenNC, it had no such protective effect in WomenOC, potentially indicating OC-induced depletion of endogenous antioxidant capacity or a different redox status.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of short-term powdered Montmorency tart cherry supplementation on markers of muscle damage, inflammation, oxidative stress, and muscle soreness in aerobically trained individuals undergoing a half-marathon run. Findings indicate that supplementation attenuated muscle catabolism (creatinine, urea/BUN, total protein), reduced physiological stress (cortisol), lessened immune and inflammatory stress (IL-2, IL-6, IL-13), better maintained redox balance (antioxidant activity, TAS), and reduced muscle soreness, ultimately enhancing endurance performance and recovery.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Powdered Montmorency tart cherry supplementation and endurance running (half-marathon race)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Subjects ingested capsules containing 480 mg of powdered Montmorency tart cherries (CherryPURE®) once daily for 10 days (7 days pre-race, race day, and 2 days post-race), compared to a 480 mg rice flour placebo. This 480 mg supplement is equivalent to 51.3 mL (17.4 fl oz) of tart cherry juice, providing 991 mg of phenolic compounds and 66 mg of anthocyanins. The intervention was evaluated in the context of a stressful endurance challenge: a half-marathon run (21.1 km). No dose-response comparisons were reported, but the supplementation significantly affected physiological responses and race performance compared to placebo.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Not reported.
