document_context_data.document_summary: This study performed a comprehensive qualitative and quantitative proteomic analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) derived from different somatic origins (fibroblasts and peripheral blood CD34+ cells), comparing them to original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC) and human embryonic stem cells (hESC). Using ESI-MS e and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry, complemented by Western blot validation, the research aimed to characterize hiPSC proteomic profiles, identify known and novel pluripotency markers, and distinguish hiPSCs from their somatic precursors. Key findings include the identification of approximately 220 commonly up-regulated proteins in pluripotent stem cell lines, the development and confirmation of a 22-protein marker panel for hiPSC characterization, and the observation of coordinated up-regulation of proteins involved in protein synthesis, folding, RNA processing, DNA replication, DNA repair, and energy metabolism (including oxidative phosphorylation and lipogenesis) in hiPSCs. The study also identified somatic cell markers that were down-regulated upon reprogramming and highlighted specific proteomic differences between hiPSCs and hESCs, contributing to improved hiPSC quality control for therapeutic applications.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Proteomic characterization and comparative analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) and human embryonic stem cells (hESCs).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was a characterization study, not a therapeutic intervention, thus no 'dose' of therapy was administered. Quantitative and qualitative proteomic analyses were performed using electrospray ionization (ESI)-MS e (label-free quantification with internal reference standard) and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry. Two hiPSC lines (iNC-01 from CD34+ cells, SB5-MP1 from fibroblasts, both generated using loxP-flanked excisable polycistronic STEMCCA lentiviral vector) and one hESC line (H9) were analyzed at earlier and later passages. Comparisons were made against their respective original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC). Proteins were considered differentially expressed if expression changed by >=1.5-fold, with a maximum false discovery rate of 2% and >95% confidence. Western blot analysis was used for validation. The developed marker panel was further tested in 8-9 additional hiPSC lines or passages from different somatic origins and reprogramming techniques. Differentiation studies were conducted with embryoid bodies at 24 hours and 7 days to assess marker changes during spontaneous differentiation.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigates the discovery of novel traumatic brain injury (TBI) biomarkers using autoimmune profiling in both rat models and human patients. It details methodologies for sample preparation, protein analysis via 2D gel electrophoresis, immunoprofiling, and the development of an immunosorbent electrochemiluminescence assay (IEA) for peroxiredoxin 6 (PRDX6). The main findings establish PRDX6 as a candidate TBI biomarker, showing its astrocytic expression, TBI-induced autoantibody reactivity in rats, gender differences in baseline human plasma levels, and a significant, persistent approximately fourfold elevation of circulating PRDX6 in humans following mild-to-moderate TBI, which is proportional to injury severity and independent of imaging findings. The study also acknowledges S100B and GFAP as other relevant TBI indicators.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) and Controlled Cortical Impact (CCI) injury model
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Human TBI was observed as mild-to-moderate (median GCS 15), with plasma collected at 4-24 hours and 2-7 days post-injury; no direct manipulation or controlled dose was applied, though PRDX6 response correlated with injury severity. In rat models, severe CCI injury was induced using a stereotaxic impactor with a 5 mm impactor at a 20-degree angle to a depth of 2 mm at 5 m/sec with a dwell time of 500 msec to maximize autoimmune response. No specific dose-response comparisons were explicitly reported for either human TBI or rat CCI, beyond PRDX6 response proportionality in humans.

matched_biomarker_details.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Human plasma, human serum, human cerebral cortex, human platelets, rat cerebral cortex, rat serum/plasma
matched_biomarker_details.activity_type: Protein Level, Protein Expression (Immunohistochemistry), Protein Concentration (IEA), Autoantibody reactivity

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: PRDX6 is highly expressed in rat brain astrocytes (perivascular space) and human cerebral cortex (approx. 940 ng/mg soluble protein), and human platelets (approx. 500 ng/mg soluble protein). Autoantibodies against PRDX6 are enhanced in rat serum following CCI. In humans, basal plasma levels are significantly higher in females (141-178 ng/mL) than males (43-65 ng/mL, p<0.001). Coagulation significantly reduces measured PRDX6 levels in serum compared to plasma, especially in females. Following mild-to-moderate TBI, circulating human plasma PRDX6 is elevated approximately fourfold over control values (from 93±18 ng/mL to 322±15 ng/mL at admission), persisting up to seven days (372±15 ng/mL, p>0.01). While absolute elevated levels post-TBI did not differ by gender (males: 351±17 ng/mL vs. females: 312±25 ng/mL), fold increases were approximately sevenfold in males and twofold in females. No difference was observed between image-positive and image-negative TBI patients. The assay has a lower limit of detection of 0.7 ng/mL and quantitation of 1 ng/mL.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: A crucial antioxidant enzyme involved in hydrolyzing hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) during injury and disease. It is highly expressed in astrocytes, particularly in the perivascular space, and acts as an autoantigen target following TBI, with oxidative stress potentially influencing its antigenicity. It also functions as a circulating protein whose levels are influenced by gender and sample preparation.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Mild-to-moderate Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) in humans (acute phase at 4-24 hours post-injury, persisting up to seven days), Controlled Cortical Impact (CCI) in rats, and basal physiological conditions including gender differences and sample preparation effects (plasma vs. serum).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: A promising candidate biomarker for the diagnosis and assessment of Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI), particularly mild TBI. Its acute plasma response is proportional to injury severity, making it useful as an injury severity marker. It indicates a TBI-induced autoimmune response, highlights the importance of gender and sample type (plasma vs. serum) for accurate measurement, and can indicate injury presence and persistence for at least seven days, though it doesn't distinguish TBI with visible imaging abnormalities.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated systemic metabolic alterations in early Parkinson's disease (PD), focusing on the thyroid-liver axis, dysautonomia, and fatty acid beta-oxidation. It utilized nuclear medicine techniques (MIBG scintigraphy, DaT-SPECT) in 1,158 PD patients, combined with trans-omic analyses (serum exosome miRNA transcriptome and plasma metabolome) in de novo PD patients, and in vitro cell experiments. Key findings include sympathetic denervation of the thyroid and heart correlating with disease severity, decreased thyroxine levels, insufficient fatty acid β-oxidation, and enrichment of the PPARα axis. The research identified significantly altered exosomal miRNAs and demonstrated the association of thyroid hormone with PPARα-dependent β-oxidation regulation and enhanced mitochondrial function in muscle cells, suggesting disorganized interorgan communication as a sensitive diagnostic biomarker.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational and Diagnostic Study of Parkinson's Disease Pathophysiology; In vitro Hormonal Stimulation and RNA-interference.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study primarily involved observational investigation and diagnostic imaging (MIBG scintigraphy, 123I-ioflupane-dopamine transporter (DaT)-SPECT) on Parkinson's disease patients; no therapeutic intervention or dose comparisons were conducted on human subjects. For mechanistic insights, in vitro experiments were performed on cultured HepG2 and primary human skeletal myotubular cells, stimulated with 100 nM 3,3′,5-triiodo-L-thyronine (T3). siRNA oligonucleotides were transfected into HepG2 cells and myotubes, with experiments conducted 48 hours post-transfection. While T3 treatment showed an 'almost dose-dependent' effect on CPT1A expression in HepG2 cells, specific concentrations for siRNA knockdown were not provided, and no dose-response comparisons were reported for the overall observational study or the siRNA interventions.

Reducing PPARα signaling is associated with inducing systemic insults.

matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Implicated in disorganized interorgan communications (thyroid-PPARα-liver axis) and suppressed FA beta-oxidation in early PD; dysregulation contributes to systemic metabolic insults.

It aimed to develop a miRNA-based 'fitness score' to assess individual responses to diet, metabolism, and exercise, identifying significantly altered miRNAs and anthropometric data, and their correlations with genetic polymorphisms (ACE, ACTN3, FTO), dietary intake, fluid intake, and stress levels, ultimately providing information for assessing individual health, performance, and recovery.

The training involved both endurance and strength exercises, with observations extending to 10 months post-intervention. No specific intensity levels, frequencies, or detailed exercise modalities were provided, and no dose-response comparisons were reported. A healthy, age- and sex-matched control group (n=20) received no intervention.

document_context_data.document_summary: This large-scale observational study (5522 individuals across four cohorts) investigated the association and synergistic interaction between Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP) and epigenetic age acceleration, measured by multiple epigenetic clocks (e.g., Horvath, Hannum, GrimAge, PhenoAge, EEAA, IEAA), with clinical outcomes including all-cause mortality and coronary heart disease (CHD). The study found that CHIP is strongly linked to epigenetic age acceleration and reduced methylation-estimated telomere length. Critically, the combination of CHIP and significant epigenetic age acceleration (particularly AgeAccelHG, a composite of Hannum and GrimAge) identifies a high-risk population for all-cause mortality and CHD, with specific gene mutations (e.g., TET2, DNMT3A, JAK2) showing differential impacts on age acceleration and risk. While general inflammatory markers like hs-CRP and IL6R genotype were also explored, AgeAccelHG proved a superior risk discriminator in CHIP carriers.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study investigating genetic and epigenetic associations.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was a large-scale observational study across four cohorts (FHS, JHS, WHI, MESA) involving 5522 individuals. No therapeutic intervention or dose was administered. The study identified Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP) through Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS) for somatic mutations (e.g., in DNMT3A, TET2, JAK2, ASXL1, DDR genes) from whole blood DNA. Epigenetic age acceleration was quantified using DNA methylation arrays, calculating residuals from various epigenetic clocks including Horvath, Hannum, PhenoAge, SkinBloodClock, GrimAge, IEAA, and EEAA, and methylation-based telomere length (DNAmTL). A composite measure, AgeAccelHG (Hannum and GrimAge acceleration >0), was used for advanced risk stratification. The study analyzed quantitative associations between CHIP status, specific mutations, epigenetic aging metrics, and clinical outcomes.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: CHIP was associated with 2.21 years of age acceleration (p < 1.0 	 10-8) as measured by PhenoAge. JAK2 mutations showed an exceptionally strong association with PhenoAge acceleration (10.01 years, p < 9.7 	 10-6).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: An epigenetic clock used for estimating biological age, which integrates chronological age and clinical biomarkers, thus predicting health outcomes.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Analysis of epidemiological cohort data for associations with CHIP and clinical outcomes, particularly sensitive to specific CHIP mutations like JAK2.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Serves as an indicator of biological aging and is used to predict clinical outcomes; its acceleration is a predictor of mortality risk, especially strongly influenced by JAK2 mutations, suggesting a link to myeloproliferative neoplasm and related hematological abnormalities.

document_context_data.document_summary: This scoping review systematically evaluates the application of systems biology-driven precision sports nutrition, incorporating 'omics' platforms (e.g., nutrigenetics, metabolomics, metagenomics, proteomics, epigenomics, lipidomics, multi-omics) and wearable technologies, particularly Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM), for endurance athletes. It maps existing literature, summarizes key findings, identifies research gaps, and investigates the impact of various nutritional interventions (e.g., polyphenols, astaxanthin, nitrates, carbohydrate-protein blends, probiotics) on immune function, inflammation, metabolism, gut microbiome composition, and glycemic responses during and after exercise. The review concludes that while these technologies offer insights into individual variability and physiological responses, current evidence is often insufficient to robustly link identified biomarkers to enhanced performance, recovery, and long-term health outcomes, noting methodological limitations.

treatment_details.therapy_type: This scoping review investigates precision sports nutrition strategies for endurance athletes, focusing on systems biology approaches (including various 'omics' platforms and wearable technologies like Continuous Glucose Monitoring) and a wide range of nutritional interventions. These interventions include specific foods (e.g., banana, blueberry, mango), supplements (e.g., soy protein, astaxanthin, beet-based nitrates, cranberry beverage, prebiotics, probiotics, cocoa flavanols), macronutrient manipulations (e.g., carbohydrate-protein blends, oligopeptides, specific protein amounts, dietary fat, low-carbohydrate high-fat diets, low/high FODMAP diets), and their interactions with diverse exercise regimens (e.g., cycling trials, marathons, ultra-endurance events, submaximal and prolonged exercise, exercise under heat stress).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This scoping review synthesizes findings from various studies on nutritional interventions, which include specific food consumptions (e.g., banana, mango) often compared against controls or other carbohydrate sources, and supplementations (e.g., astaxanthin, beet-based nitrates, cranberry beverage, specific probiotics) with durations ranging from acute intake to 2-week periods. It also examines the effects of different macronutrient strategies (e.g., low-carbohydrate high-fat diets, carbohydrate-protein blends) and genetic variations on caffeine metabolism. The review notes that while specific interventions are detailed, it generally reports on rather than conducts dose-response comparisons, highlighting that existing studies often compare interventions against controls. A key emphasis is on the need for tailored, individual-specific strategies, robust randomized controlled trials, and better reporting of training status, dose-response relationships, and demographic stratifications in future research, as current evidence often lacks detailed dose-response comparisons.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive observational study utilized plasma proteomics and machine learning to develop and validate a framework for measuring organ-specific biological aging, termed 'e-ageotypes', in humans. Analyzing 4,778 proteins from 5,676 adults across five independent cohorts, the research revealed that accelerated aging in specific organs (including heart, brain, kidney, muscle, liver, adipose, pancreas, lung, and immune system) is significantly associated with higher risks of all-cause mortality and various age-related diseases, such as heart failure, Alzheimer's disease, hypertension, diabetes, and cognitive decline. The study's methodology involved defining 'extreme agers' (individuals with highly accelerated organ aging), clustering them into distinct ageotypes, and identifying key protein biomarkers (e.g., REN, KL, NPPB, TNNT2, CPLX1/2) that contribute to these aging profiles and offer prognostic utility for disease risk and progression.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational Study on Biological Aging via Plasma Proteomics and Machine Learning
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This observational study involved the quantification of approximately 4,778 plasma proteins using SomaScan assays (v.4 and v.4.1) in 5,676 adults from five independent cohorts. Machine learning models (LASSO regression-based chronological age predictors) were developed and validated to estimate biological (organ-specific) age, referred to as 'age gaps' or 'e-ageotypes', for 11 major organs (adipose tissue, artery, brain, heart, immune tissue, intestine, kidney, liver, lung, muscle, and pancreas) and the whole organism. Models were trained on 1,398 healthy participants from the Knight-ADRC cohort and tested across the full cohort. Age gaps were calculated using local regression, z-scored per model and cohort, and adjusted for age and sex. Associations with various age-related phenotypes, future mortality, heart disease, clinical biochemistry markers, and cognitive decline were assessed using linear models or Cox proportional hazards models, with multiple testing correction (Benjamini-Hochberg method, 5% false discovery rate). No therapeutic intervention or dose comparison was performed.

matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of physiological age-related dysfunction and potential predictor of future health status.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study developed predictive models using a novel machine learning pipeline to identify viable intrauterine pregnancies (Live Normally Sited Pregnancies, LNSP) in symptomatic women, differentiating them from combined adverse outcomes (CAO) such as miscarriage, pregnancy of unknown location (PUL), and tubal ectopic pregnancy (tEP). The models integrate serum metabolite levels (untargeted 1H NMR profiling) with plasma hormone concentrations (β-hCG and progesterone) and clinicodemographic data, finding that a composite biomarker provides superior predictive accuracy (0.79). The aim is to offer a rapid, non-invasive diagnostic test to reduce diagnostic burden and improve outcomes in early gestation by accurately identifying LNSP and excluding conditions associated with maternal morbidity and mortality.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Diagnostic biomarker identification and predictive model development using machine learning, untargeted 1H NMR metabolomics, and hormone assays.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational study involving 370 symptomatic pregnant women (≤10 weeks gestation), presenting with abdominal pain and/or vaginal bleeding. A single blood sample was collected upon first emergency presentation; plasma was used for β-hCG and progesterone concentration measurements, and serum for untargeted metabolomic profiling. Nine key metabolite signals were identified. Random forest models were constructed and compared: a model using metabolite signals alone yielded 0.68 accuracy, β-hCG and progesterone alone yielded 0.71 accuracy, and the combined model achieved the best predictive accuracy of 0.79. Model performance was assessed using an independent validation cohort. No therapeutic intervention or dose-response comparisons were reported, as the study focused on diagnostic accuracy for pregnancy outcomes.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly higher in Live Normally Sited Pregnancies (LNSP) compared with combined adverse outcomes (CAO). Also observed to increase in early pregnancy relative to non-pregnant women.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Essential amino acid, a precursor for tyrosine and other neurotransmitters, involved in protein metabolism.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Early pregnancy outcomes (LNSP vs. combined adverse outcomes (CAO)), reflecting abnormal progression of failed LNSPs and ectopically located pregnancies.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Identified as a key metabolite in a composite biomarker for discriminating viable intrauterine pregnancies from adverse pregnancy outcomes; promising biomarker to differentiate normal pregnancy.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study employed NMR metabolomics to investigate metabolic profiles in serum and urine from COVID-19 patients across varying disease severities (Medical Ward and Intensive Care Unit) and healthy controls. The primary aim was to identify biomarkers for COVID-19 diagnosis, severity classification, and prognosis, and to explore correlations with clinical factors like hypertension, obesity, and dyslipidemia. Key findings include the development of a highly efficient diagnostic panel (isoleucine, TMAO, glucose) and a robust severity classification panel (ethanol, TMAO, tyrosine, betaine, and clinical characteristics), alongside identification of numerous individual metabolites and clinical parameters associated with infection, disease progression, hospitalization duration, and patient outcome.

treatment_details.therapy_type: NMR metabolomics-based profiling and observational study of COVID-19 infection
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This observational study analyzed 80 serum and urine samples from COVID-19 patients (34 intensive care, 46 hospitalized) and 32 from healthy controls using NMR spectroscopy. The research focused on identifying and validating metabolite-based panels for COVID-19 diagnosis and severity classification. A diagnostic panel of isoleucine, TMAO, and glucose achieved an AUC of 0.91 (86.08% sensitivity, 83.87% specificity). A severity classification panel, combining ethanol, TMAO, tyrosine, betaine, and clinical characteristics (obesity/overweight, dyslipidemia, lymphocyte count), achieved an AUC of 0.825 (84.85% sensitivity, 72.09% specificity). No therapeutic intervention or dose-response comparisons were part of the study design.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher levels observed in COVID-19 patients compared to healthy controls; elevated levels associated with obesity/overweight in COVID-19 patients. Identified as a key discriminating molecule.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Essential amino acid, involved in protein synthesis, 'Phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan biosynthesis', 'Phenylalanine metabolism', and related to inflammation.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: COVID-19 infection vs. healthy controls, and association with obesity/overweight.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Potential biomarker for COVID-19 infection, indicates perturbation in metabolic routes, and is associated with inflammation and obesity/overweight.

document_context_data.document_summary: This sportomics study investigated the metabolic, immune, hormonal, and amino acid responses, alongside muscle and liver injury markers, in two elite female Olympic beach volleyball athletes during a simulated competition day involving two matches. Key findings revealed significant acute physiological impacts, including electrolyte disturbances (notably hypokalemia), 20-60% increases in muscle injury markers and up to 50% for liver enzymes, elevated stress hormones (ACTH up to 4-fold, cortisol up to 3-fold), and altered energy metabolism and amino acid profiles indicative of central fatigue risk (e.g., Fischer ratio and tryptophan decreased by 60%, serotonin increased by 180%). The study emphasized distinct individual recovery kinetics, highlighted the inadequacy of short recovery sessions, and advocated for personalized monitoring due to varied biomarker responses despite similar external loads.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Simulated Beach Volleyball Competition
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Two world-class female athletes participated in a simulated competition day involving two high-intensity beach volleyball matches (a two-set match in the morning and a three-set match in the afternoon), under identical environmental conditions. Blood and urine samples were collected at seven time points: pre-match, post-match, 60 minutes after each match (short recovery), and after a 15-hour long recovery. The protocol included 15-minute warm-ups. No dose-response comparisons were explicitly reported; however, individual responses to the same protocol were highlighted, and short recovery sessions were found to be inadequate for full physiological recovery, with the second match demonstrating cumulative strain.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Athlete 1 remained unchanged during the protocol. Athlete 2’s concentration rose ~60% during the second match.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: An essential aromatic amino acid, precursor for neurotransmitters like tyrosine, dopamine, and norepinephrine.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Simulated beach volleyball competition (during protocol, second match).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates altered aromatic amino acid metabolism during exercise, potentially affecting neurotransmitter synthesis.

document_context_data.document_summary: This systematic review evaluates the effects of soy protein (SP) supplementation on muscle adaptations, metabolic and antioxidant status, hormonal response, and exercise performance in active individuals and athletes, often comparing it to whey protein or placebo. The review encompasses studies on protein synthesis, amino acid transport, and signaling pathways, highlighting that while some anabolic markers might be less favorable with soy, it can provide similar increases in lean mass to whey protein, especially at optimal protein intakes. SP is shown to reduce exercise-induced metabolic/blood circulating biomarkers (triglycerides, uric acid, lactate) and improve antioxidant capacity, reducing oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation. However, its effects on hormonal responses, such as testosterone and cortisol, are inconsistent or contradictory across studies. SP supplementation also demonstrates potential benefits in improving various exercise performance indicators, including high-intensity running, maximal cardiac output, delaying fatigue, improving isometric strength, running velocity, and muscle recovery after damage. The review concludes that SP can be a viable alternative to conventional protein supplements, but emphasizes the need for further research addressing methodological limitations and consistent dosing.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Soy Protein and Soy Peptide Supplementation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The review encompassed a wide range of soy protein (SP) and soy peptide supplementation protocols, from acute doses (e.g., 15-20g SP, 18g SP beverage, 10g essential amino acids from soy) to chronic daily intakes varying from 0.5 g/kg BW/day to 90 g/day (e.g., 33-40 g/day, 1 g/kg BW/day, 53.3 g/day). Doses were often combined with carbohydrates (e.g., 10g soy peptide + 30g sugar, 15g SP + 52.5g CHO) or matched for nitrogen/leucine content for comparison with whey protein. Durations ranged from single acute sessions to long-term interventions of 2 weeks, 4 weeks, 6 weeks, 9 weeks, 4 months, or even "12 weeks. Comparisons were consistently made against whey protein, soy-dairy blends, isoenergetic placebos, or control (exercise-only) groups. While some studies aimed for optimal protein intakes ("  1.6 g/kg BW/day), there was a notable lack of consistent dosing or explicit dose-response comparisons across the reviewed literature, indicating significant variability in intervention designs.

matched_biomarker_details.biomarker_name: Phenylalanine transport and amino acid transporters mRNA

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Phenylalanine transport into muscle was significantly higher with a soy  ffd   dairy protein blend compared to whey protein (p < 0.05). Similarly, mRNA expression of various amino acid transporters (System L amino acid transporter 1 (SLC7A5), CD98/SLC3A2, System A amino acid transporter 2, Proton-assisted amino acid transporter 1, Cationic amino acid transporter 1) was significantly higher (p < 0.05) following a soy  ffd   dairy protein blend, with both soy  ffd   dairy and whey groups experiencing an increase in general amino acid transporter mRNA expression.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Post-exercise acute supplementation with Soy-Dairy Protein Blend versus Whey Isolate; one hour after acute resistance exercise and ingestion of soy  ffd   dairy protein blend or whey protein.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates enhanced availability and increased capacity for amino acid and peptide uptake into muscle cells, potentially promoting anabolism and muscle growth.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study utilized genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screening in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) cells, primarily Nalm6 B-ALL, to elucidate the molecular mechanisms of panobinostat resistance and action. Key findings reveal mitochondrial activity as a driver of panobinostat resistance and SIRT1 expression as a critical determinant of sensitivity. Panobinostat treatment abrogates mitochondrial activity in ALL cells, contributing to resistance, while enhancing mitochondrial function (via rosiglitazone or SIRT1 overexpression) sensitizes ALL cells to panobinostat by activating the mitochondrial apoptosis pathway. The investigation identifies the SIRT1-mitochondria-PMAIP1 pathway as central to panobinostat response and suggests that higher SIRT1 expression or mitochondrial hyperactivity could indicate patient benefit from panobinostat therapy. The study also details various methods used, including cell culture, gene modulation techniques, drug sensitivity assays, RNA sequencing, Western blotting, and flow cytometry.

treatment_details.therapy_type: The study primarily investigated Panobinostat, a pan-histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor, often in combination with genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 knockout screening or SIRT1 modulation. Other HDAC inhibitors (chidamide, vorinostat) and conventional chemotherapeutic agents (l-asparaginase, cytarabine, 6-mecaptopurine, vincristine, dexamethasone, daunorubicin) were mentioned for comparative or contextual analysis. Rosiglitazone, a PPAR   γ activator, was used to stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis and enhance panobinostat sensitivity.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Panobinostat was frequently used at 10 nM for durations of 24 hours (for RNA sequencing, combination treatments) or 14 days (for CRISPR screening), leading to 60-80% cell death and significant proliferation inhibition in Nalm6 cells. Gradient concentrations were employed for drug sensitivity assays. Rosiglitazone was administered at 31.25 µM for 24 or 48 hours. Dose-response comparisons for panobinostat sensitivity were analyzed using Sanger GDSC1 IC50 data across 576 diverse cancer cell lines. No specific doses or dose-response comparisons were consistently reported for other HDAC inhibitors or conventional chemotherapeutic agents.

Western blot showed panobinostat had a 'modest effect on PMAIP1 in SIRT1 disturbed cells' and led to a 'dramatic upregulation' in SIRT1 overexpression cells. Knockout of PMAIP1 'conferred panobinostat resistance'. Identified as a determinant of ALL response to panobinostat as part of the SIRT1-mitochondria-PMAIP1 pathway. 'More significant elevation of PMAIP1 in SIRT1-overexpressed cells than SIRT1 knockout cells on panobinostat exposure'.

document_context_data.document_summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot study investigated the effects of 6-month potassium citrate (K citrate) supplementation (30 mEq/day), in combination with calcium and vitamin D, on bone turnover markers and urinary metabolic profiles in 40 postmenopausal women with osteopenia. The study found that while bone turnover markers (CTX and BAP) decreased in both K citrate and placebo groups, K citrate significantly enhanced these beneficial effects, particularly in a subgroup of patients with pre-existing low-grade acidosis (low urine pH and/or low potassium and citrate excretion). K citrate also improved urinary pH, citrate, and potassium excretion. The study concluded that K citrate is beneficial for osteopenic women with documented potassium/citrate deficits and low-grade acidosis, but its indiscriminate use is not recommended without such evidence.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Potassium Citrate (K citrate) supplementation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Daily oral supplementation with 30 mEq of K citrate (in two tablets) for 6 months. This was administered in addition to daily calcium carbonate (500 mg day   ⁻¹) and vitamin D (400 IU day   ⁻¹) for all subjects (K citrate and placebo groups). The K citrate treatment showed significant benefits in subjects with evidence of low-grade acidosis (low 24h-citrate excretion or low fasting-morning urine pH) compared to the placebo, with significant changes observed as early as 3 months. No specific dose-response comparisons were reported, and adherence rates were approximately 90% for both groups.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Low daily excretion (baseline).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Excretion of excess phosphate; plays a role in bone health and energy metabolism. Nutritional marker.

matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of renal phosphate handling and bone metabolism. Low excretion proved scarce dietary acid load.

document_context_data.document_summary: The study aimed to evaluate bone turnover and remodeling markers in children with Noonan Syndrome (NS) to understand their bone status and explore genotype-phenotype correlations. It revealed increased bone resorption in NS patients, evidenced by significantly elevated serum C-telopeptides of type I collagen (CTX) levels, and a non-significant increase in RANKL. The study also discussed the influence of RAS/MAPK signaling pathway alterations and SHP2 protein on osteoclastic activity and the effects of recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) treatment on bone parameters.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational Case-Control Study evaluating bone turnover and remodeling markers in children with Noonan Syndrome, including an analysis of recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) treatment effects.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This cross-sectional, case-control study compared 28 children with Noonan Syndrome to 35 healthy controls. No specific therapeutic intervention or dose was administered to the main cohorts. Within the NS cohort, some subjects had received or were receiving rhGH therapy, but no specific dosages, duration, or dose-response comparisons for rhGH treatment were reported, and no significant differences in bone parameters were found between treated and untreated subjects in this study.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification:
No significant differences were found between NS patients and controls; levels were within the normal range. However, lower levels were observed in GH-treated NS children (4.33 
	± 0.5 mg/dL) compared to untreated NS children (4.80 
	± 0.38 mg/dL, p = 0.02).

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Children with Noonan Syndrome (NS), including analysis of rhGH treatment effects.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the immediate and short-term bone metabolic responses to carbohydrate (CHO) feeding during prolonged treadmill running (120-min at 70% V̇o2max) in healthy men. It found that CHO feeding during exercise acutely attenuated the post-exercise increases in bone resorption (β-CTX) and bone formation (P1NP) markers, as well as reduced Interleukin-6 (IL-6) elevation, in the hours immediately following exercise, but these effects did not persist in the subsequent days, suggesting a potential strategy to minimize acute exercise-induced bone resorption and influence bone turnover.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Carbohydrate (CHO) feeding during prolonged treadmill running
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Ten men completed two 7-day trials, one with CHO feeding and one with placebo (PBO). On day 4, participants completed a 120-min treadmill run at 70% of maximal oxygen consumption (V̇o2max). In the CHO trial, an 8% glucose solution was ingested immediately before, every 20 minutes during, and immediately after exercise, at a rate of 0.7 g CHO·kg body mass−1·h−1 (approximately 50 g/h), totaling 102.1 ± 10.6 g glucose in 1,276 ± 132 ml solution. The PBO trial involved equal volumes of a taste-matched flavored water. No dose-response comparisons were reported.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: increased then returned to baseline (PBO trial), unchanged (with CHO)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: In the PBO trial, phosphate increased significantly (P < 0.001) by 21% immediately after exercise (1.4 ± 0.1 mmol/l vs BASE 1.1 ± 0.1 mmol/l), then returned to baseline values by R1 (1.1 ± 0.2 mmol/l). No immediate or short-term effects of CHO feeding observed.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Essential for bone mineralization, energy metabolism (ATP), and cell function. Phosphate is an essential mineral for bone health and numerous physiological processes.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: During and after strenuous exercise (120-min treadmill run at 70% V̇o2max) with PBO or CHO feeding.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Reflects electrolyte and metabolic shifts during exercise. Unlikely to be a mediator of the effects of CHO supplementation on bone turnover, as no alterations due to CHO were observed in phosphate metabolism.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study aimed to develop and validate a female-focused predictive atherosclerosis risk signature based on serum metabolites in patients with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), addressing the inadequacy of established cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk scores. It investigated metabolomic and clinical features associated with subclinical plaque status, developing and validating a 35-metabolite/5-clinical trait signature (UCLH-40) and a refined 5-feature panel (including age, glycine, M-LDL-C, IDL-C, and omega-6/omega-3 ratio) that accurately classifies SLE patients with/without subclinical atherosclerosis, predicts atherosclerosis progression, and identifies elevated CVD risk, thereby outperforming existing risk assessment tools.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Diagnostic/Prognostic Biomarker Discovery and Validation for Atherosclerosis Risk Stratification (via Metabolomics and Machine Learning)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational, diagnostic study that did not involve therapeutic interventions or dose comparisons for treatments. Its primary focus was on developing and validating predictive biomarker signatures. Serum metabolomic analysis was performed using a high-throughput nuclear magnetic resonance platform (≥250 metabolites). Various machine learning models (e.g., univariate logistic regression, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator LR, random forest, neural network, support vector machine, and eXtreme gradient boost) with 10-fold cross-validation were used to analyze metabolomic data and clinical traits. Model performance was assessed by AUROC (>0.7 for inclusion), sensitivity, specificity, and F1 score. Vascular ultrasound was used for carotid/femoral intima-media thickness assessment of subclinical atherosclerosis. The study discusses the implications for guiding statin therapy or lifestyle modifications but does not directly test them, noting that standard statin prescriptions may be insufficient due to normal lipid ranges in SLE patients.

document_context_data.document_summary: This review provides updated guidelines and a consensus for standardizing pre-analytical variables in salivary biomarker studies for Alzheimer's disease (AD) research. It critically appraises current methodologies, identifies inconsistencies, and proposes a standardized protocol for saliva collection, processing, and storage to improve reliability for diagnostic biomarker detection and quantification. The document investigates various protein and metabolomic biomarkers in saliva, assessing their diagnostic potential for AD and Mild Cognitive Impairment, and highlights the importance of controlling factors like collection methods, centrifugation, and storage conditions for accurate measurement.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Salivary Biomarker Research and Standardization for Alzheimer's Disease Diagnosis
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This is a comprehensive review article focusing on standardizing pre-analytical variables for salivary Alzheimer's Disease (AD) biomarker studies, rather than a therapeutic intervention or dose-response investigation. It critically discusses how inconsistent methodologies and pre-analytical factors (e.g., collection kits like Salivette vs. passive drooling, acute food intake, physical activity, stress, diurnal variations, dental restorations, freezing/thawing protocols, centrifugation speeds) influence biomarker detection and quantification, leading to conflicting findings for analytes like Aβ42, Aβ40, and AChE activity. The document proposes a standardized pre-analytical protocol, including pre-collection instructions (e.g., abstinence from food, drinks, smoking, alcohol, exercise), passive drool collection (e.g., 2 mL after 5 min pooling), and post-collection processing (e.g., immediate freezing, visual inspection, two-step centrifugation, aliquoting 100-250 µL). Various analytical methods (ELISA, Western blot, SIMOA, MS-based methods, NMR) were discussed for diagnostic marker identification, emphasizing that a universal protocol might not suit all biomarkers due to their diverse physiological roles.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Reduced concentrations; significant differences observed when comparing AD patients with healthy individuals.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Involved in metabolism, specific role as a lipid (acyl-alkyl-phosphatidylcholine).
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) vs. healthy individuals.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Potential biomarker to distinguish AD patients from healthy individuals.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigates the metabolic reprogramming mechanisms underlying sorafenib activity and resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells and patients. It reveals that sorafenib impairs mitochondrial function, forcing a metabolic shift towards glycolysis, leading to D-lactate accumulation, which serves as a biomarker for treatment response. In resistant cells, adaptation involves rerouting dihydroxyacetone phosphate towards glycerol-3-phosphate synthesis, extensive phospholipid remodeling to evade ferroptosis, enhanced antioxidant capacity, and increased reliance on exogenous triglycerides, resulting in glycerol accumulation as a marker of resistance. The study identifies D-lactate and glycerol as potential plasma biomarkers for monitoring sorafenib efficacy and resistance in HCC patients.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Sorafenib
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The primary therapy investigated was Sorafenib, a multi-kinase inhibitor for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). In vitro studies used sorafenib at an IC50 of 8.5 µM for acute, 48-hour, or 7-day prolonged treatments, and 7 µM for sorafenib-resistant IR-Huh7 cells. Clinical treatment involved oral administration of 400 mg twice daily for HCC patients, with dose reductions permitted for adverse effects. Other interventions included adenoviral gene downregulation (50 MOI for Gpd1/1l, Gpd2; 20 MOI for Glo1) and supplementation with various fatty acids (SFAs, MUFAs, PUFAs) or lipoproteins (VLDL, LDL), and inhibition of Mgll with JZL184. No detailed dose-response comparisons were consistently reported for sorafenib, though Mgll inhibition showed dose-dependent effects.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Reduced upon sorafenib treatment.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Indicator of membrane phospholipid composition, affecting membrane fluidity and curvature.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Upon sorafenib treatment.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Suggests that cells actively remodel their membranes to adapt to stress, potentially facilitating resistance to sorafenib.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study aimed to evaluate and verify the diagnostic value of serum exosomal miRNAs, particularly miR-193b-5p and miR-511-5p, in sepsis and septic shock. It identified miR-193b-5p as a potential diagnostic biomarker, associated with inflammation and immune regulation, and a protective factor against sepsis and septic shock progression.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Diagnostic Biomarker Identification and Disease State Analysis (Observational Study)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study involved an initial screening cohort of serum exosomal miRNA sequencing on patients with sepsis (n=6), septic shock (n=6), and healthy controls (n=3). This was followed by validation using qRT-PCR in a larger cohort of 90 participants, comprising 30 patients with sepsis, 30 with septic shock, and 30 general surgery patients serving as controls. Blood samples were collected within 24 hours of ICU admission. Comparisons were made between disease groups and controls to identify diagnostic biomarkers and understand disease progression; no specific therapeutic dose or dose-response comparisons were reported.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study introduces MiSL (Mining Synthetic Lethals), a novel computational algorithm that identifies mutation-specific synthetic lethal (SL) partners and predictive genetic biomarkers by mining pan-cancer human primary tumor data. MiSL was applied to 12 different cancers, predicting numerous SL partners and demonstrating its utility in precision oncology. Key validations include the identification of ACACA as a novel druggable SL partner for the IDH1 mutation in AML and glioma, and PIK3CA mutation as a predictive biomarker for AKT1 inhibitors in breast cancer. The algorithm also integrates functional screens like shRNA data to rank gene essentiality and detect genomic alterations and differentially expressed genes, aiding in the discovery of novel therapeutic targets.

treatment_details.therapy_type: The study focuses on developing and validating MiSL, a computational algorithm for identifying mutation-specific synthetic lethal partners and predictive genetic biomarkers in cancer. This involves synthetic lethality-based targeted therapy approaches, computational analysis (MiSL pipeline), and various experimental validation methods including gene knockdown (shRNA, siRNA), CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, pharmacological inhibition (e.g., ACACA inhibitors, AKT1-inhibitor MK-2206), and xenograft models.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The MiSL algorithm analyzed approximately 3,000 primary tumor samples from 12 TCGA cancer datasets, predicting 145,891 synthetic lethal partners for 3,120 mutations, utilizing specific criteria for genomic alterations and statistical thresholds (e.g., Fisher's exact test P value <0.05). Experimental validation involved shRNA screens (54,020 shRNAs targeting 11,194 genes, >20% reduction in reads for SL hits, 16 population doublings), doxycycline induction (1 µg ml⁻¹ for 3-12 days), siRNA (25 nM siGLS), and drug treatments with dose-response IC50 curves (e.g., 2 µM TOFA for ACACA inhibition; IDH1 R132-mutated AML blasts IC50 1.1 µM vs 6 µM for wild-type; MK-2206 for AKT1 inhibition with PIK3CA mutated breast cancer cell lines sensitive at IC50 <1 µM). Specific shRNA knockdown efficiencies were assessed, but general dose-response comparisons for all therapeutic interventions were not explicitly detailed.

matched_biomarker_details.activity_type: Genetic mutation presence, Drug sensitivity (IC50), Cell viability, Colony formation, Protein phosphorylation

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher (sensitivity), increased (cleaved PARP), decreased (phospho-PRAS40, S6K, 4EBP1, BAD)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: All four PIK3CA mutated breast cancer cell lines were sensitive to MK-2206 (IC50 <1 µM) versus >15 µM for PIK3CA wild-type (P value=0.003) in viability and colony assays. Increased cleaved PARP and decreased phospho-PRAS40, S6K, 4EBP1 and BAD.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: A genetic alteration in the PI3K catalytic subunit alpha, commonly found in breast cancer, influencing the PIK3CA-AKT1 signaling pathway, and acting as a driver mutation forming a synthetic lethal interaction with AKT1.

matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Predictive biomarker for sensitivity and responsiveness to AKT1 inhibitors (like MK-2206) in breast cancer, identifying patients who might benefit from this therapy.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigates the metabolic reprogramming mechanisms underlying sorafenib activity and resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells and patients. It reveals that sorafenib impairs mitochondrial function, forcing a metabolic shift towards glycolysis, leading to D-lactate accumulation, which serves as a biomarker for treatment response. In resistant cells, adaptation involves rerouting dihydroxyacetone phosphate towards glycerol-3-phosphate synthesis, extensive phospholipid remodeling to evade ferroptosis, enhanced antioxidant capacity, and increased reliance on exogenous triglycerides, resulting in glycerol accumulation as a marker of resistance. The study identifies D-lactate and glycerol as potential plasma biomarkers for monitoring sorafenib efficacy and resistance in HCC patients.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Sorafenib
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The primary therapy investigated was Sorafenib, a multi-kinase inhibitor for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). In vitro studies used sorafenib at an IC50 of 8.5 µM for acute, 48-hour, or 7-day prolonged treatments, and 7 µM for sorafenib-resistant IR-Huh7 cells. Clinical treatment involved oral administration of 400 mg twice daily for HCC patients, with dose reductions permitted for adverse effects. Other interventions included adenoviral gene downregulation (50 MOI for Gpd1/1l, Gpd2; 20 MOI for Glo1) and supplementation with various fatty acids (SFAs, MUFAs, PUFAs) or lipoproteins (VLDL, LDL), and inhibition of Mgll with JZL184. No detailed dose-response comparisons were consistently reported for sorafenib, though Mgll inhibition showed dose-dependent effects.

document_context_data.document_summary: This randomized controlled trial investigated the effects of 8 weeks of daily 5g Cistanche deserticola (CD) extract supplementation, combined with progressive high-intensity resistance training, on muscle strength and recovery in both untrained and resistance-trained male participants. The study found that CD supplementation significantly enhanced muscle strength (1RM bench press and squat, MVIC) and endurance (RTF in untrained), and facilitated post-exercise recovery by modulating hormonal responses (increased testosterone, reduced cortisol) and decreasing markers of stress and inflammation (reduced CRP and CK levels) in both cohorts. Mechanistic insights suggest CD's role in improving energy metabolism, reducing muscle degradation, enhancing antioxidant defense, modulating neurotransmission, and regulating endocrine axes.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Cistanche deserticola (CD) supplementation combined with a progressive resistance training program.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants received 5 g of CD extract daily, administered in two sachets (after breakfast and lunch) for 8 consecutive weeks, alongside a placebo group. A standardized resistance training program was completed three times per week for eight weeks. This program involved 4 sets of 10-12 repetitions at 65-70% of 1RM for weeks 1-4, and 4 sets of 6-8 repetitions at 80% of 1RM for weeks 5-8. Maximal strength (1RM bench press/squat, MVIC) and endurance (RTF bench press) were assessed. No dose-response comparisons for CD were reported, only comparison to placebo.

document_context_data.document_summary: The study developed and applied a Nano-omics integrative workflow, utilizing nanoparticle protein coronas, to link systemic (plasma) and localized (tumor tissue) protein changes associated with glioblastoma (GB) progression. This comprehensive proteomic investigation in GL261 murine models and human high-grade glioma patients aimed to identify GB-specific molecular pathways and peripheral blood biomarkers for early detection and disease monitoring. The methodology included inducing murine GB models, preparing and administering liposome nanoparticles in vivo or incubating them ex vivo with plasma, and subsequent proteomic analysis via mass spectrometry to identify differentially abundant proteins. The findings revealed significant plasma protein alterations, even at low tumor burden, with over 30% overlap between GB-specific plasma and tumor tissue proteomes, leading to the identification of 48 potential GB biomarker candidates across various biological pathways.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Biomarker Discovery Method: Nano-omics integrative proteomics workflow utilizing nanoparticle protein coronas for glioblastoma (GB).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study involved inducing murine glioblastoma by stereotactic injection of 50,000 GL261 cells into the striatum of C57BL/6 J mice. Liposomes (HSPC:Chol:DSPE-PEG2000) were prepared at a final lipid concentration of 25 mM and administered intravenously at a lipid dose of 0.125 mM/g body weight (equivalent to 5 mg/kg doxorubicin-loaded liposomes) 10 minutes prior to blood collection in mice. In human validation, ex vivo nanoparticle corona analysis was performed on pre-operative plasma samples from 10 high-grade glioma patients. Matched blood and tumor tissue samples were collected from mice at D7, D14, and D18 post-tumor inoculation, representing low, medium, and large tumor volumes. Matched resected tumor tissue from human patients was analyzed by LCM-coupled LC:MS/MS. No specific dose-response comparisons for nanoparticle application or tumor cell inoculation were reported for therapeutic purposes, as the focus was on biomarker discovery.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Log2 fold change > 10, ranked among top 5 most significant plasma differentially abundant proteins (DAPs) between Glioblastoma (GB) patients and healthy controls.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review investigates the potential of extracellular vesicle (EV)-enclosed non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs), including microRNAs (miRNAs), long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), piRNAs, circRNAs, and tsRNAs, along with N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA modifications, as stable, non-invasive diagnostic, prognostic, and monitoring biomarkers for a wide range of chronic liver diseases (CLDs). These include metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), metabolic-dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), Alcoholic Liver Disease (ALD), Autoimmune Hepatitis (AIH), Chronic Viral Hepatitis (HBV/HCV), cholestatic liver diseases, liver fibrosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), cholangiocarcinoma (CCA), and gallbladder carcinoma (GBC). The document also touches upon the therapeutic potential of engineered EVs for targeted cargo delivery in preclinical models to modulate inflammation and fibrosis pathways, highlighting their utility and associated challenges in clinical application.

treatment_details.therapy_type: This document primarily functions as a review investigating biomarkers for the diagnosis, prognosis, and monitoring of chronic liver diseases (CLDs). While the main focus is on biomarker identification, the review also touches upon the therapeutic potential of Extracellular Vesicle (EV) therapy, including engineered EVs for targeted cargo delivery, and mentions pharmacological inhibition of miR-34a as a potential therapeutic strategy.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study does not report specific therapeutic doses or dose-response comparisons for most interventions, as its primary focus is on biomarker evaluation. However, preclinical models utilized various EV-based interventions, such as native and engineered EVs derived from mesenchymal/stromal stem cells (MSCs) or human liver stem cells in models of liver fibrosis, NASH, and cancer, without detailed quantitative dosing. In biomarker contexts, some observations included a dose-dependent increase in serum miR-122 and miR-192 levels in induced liver injury mouse models. Disease states and exposures examined for biomarker changes included acute and chronic alcohol consumption, autoimmune inflammation, viral infections, cholestasis, CCl4-induced liver fibrosis, lipotoxic palmitic acid treatment of hepatocytes, arsenite-induced liver fibrosis, and various human liver conditions including biliary cholangitis, biliary atresia, liver fibrosis, HCC, CCA, and GBC.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study performed an integrative multi-platform meta-analysis of gene expression profiles from Affymetrix and Illumina datasets in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) patients and healthy controls to identify novel, robust diagnostic biomarkers. The analysis revealed 5 commonly differentially expressed genes and 28 novel 'gained' genes, suggesting their significant potential for early PDAC diagnosis.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Integrative meta-analysis of gene expression data for biomarker identification and diagnostic prediction in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Gene expression data from two independent cohorts of PDAC patients (Affymetrix: 18 PDAC patients; Illumina: 36 PDAC patients) and 18 healthy controls were integrated. Profiling was performed on peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) using Affymetrix GeneChip® Human Gene ST 1.0 Arrays and Illumina HumanHT-12 v4 Expression BeadChip microarray platforms. Data were integrated using an empirical Bayesian methodology (ComBat) for batch effect removal, and differential expression was analyzed with limma software, identifying genes with p<0.01 and at least 1.5-fold differential expression. The analysis identified 5 commonly differentially expressed genes (with individual ROC curve AUC > 0.9) and 28 novel 'gained' genes, which could discriminate PDAC patients from controls with an average sensitivity of 74.8% and specificity of 73.3% for individual gained genes, 100% sensitivity and 94% specificity for combined common genes, and 91% sensitivity and 87% specificity for combined gained genes. No dose-response comparisons were applicable as it is a diagnostic biomarker identification study.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Elevated expression; identified as a differentially expressed gene with individual ROC curve showing AUC > 0.9 for distinguishing PDAC patients from healthy controls.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigates the metabolic reprogramming mechanisms underlying sorafenib activity and resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells and patients. It reveals that sorafenib impairs mitochondrial function, forcing a metabolic shift towards glycolysis, leading to D-lactate accumulation, which serves as a biomarker for treatment response. In resistant cells, adaptation involves rerouting dihydroxyacetone phosphate towards glycerol-3-phosphate synthesis, extensive phospholipid remodeling to evade ferroptosis, enhanced antioxidant capacity, and increased reliance on exogenous triglycerides, resulting in glycerol accumulation as a marker of resistance. The study identifies D-lactate and glycerol as potential plasma biomarkers for monitoring sorafenib efficacy and resistance in HCC patients.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Sorafenib
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The primary therapy investigated was Sorafenib, a multi-kinase inhibitor for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). In vitro studies used sorafenib at an IC50 of 8.5 µM for acute, 48-hour, or 7-day prolonged treatments, and 7 µM for sorafenib-resistant IR-Huh7 cells. Clinical treatment involved oral administration of 400 mg twice daily for HCC patients, with dose reductions permitted for adverse effects. Other interventions included adenoviral gene downregulation (50 MOI for Gpd1/1l, Gpd2; 20 MOI for Glo1) and supplementation with various fatty acids (SFAs, MUFAs, PUFAs) or lipoproteins (VLDL, LDL), and inhibition of Mgll with JZL184. No detailed dose-response comparisons were consistently reported for sorafenib, though Mgll inhibition showed dose-dependent effects.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study performed an integrative multi-platform meta-analysis of gene expression profiles from Affymetrix and Illumina datasets in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) patients and healthy controls to identify novel, robust diagnostic biomarkers. The analysis revealed 5 commonly differentially expressed genes and 28 novel 'gained' genes, suggesting their significant potential for early PDAC diagnosis.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Integrative meta-analysis of gene expression data for biomarker identification and diagnostic prediction in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Gene expression data from two independent cohorts of PDAC patients (Affymetrix: 18 PDAC patients; Illumina: 36 PDAC patients) and 18 healthy controls were integrated. Profiling was performed on peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) using Affymetrix GeneChip® Human Gene ST 1.0 Arrays and Illumina HumanHT-12 v4 Expression BeadChip microarray platforms. Data were integrated using an empirical Bayesian methodology (ComBat) for batch effect removal, and differential expression was analyzed with limma software, identifying genes with p<0.01 and at least 1.5-fold differential expression. The analysis identified 5 commonly differentially expressed genes (with individual ROC curve AUC > 0.9) and 28 novel 'gained' genes, which could discriminate PDAC patients from controls with an average sensitivity of 74.8% and specificity of 73.3% for individual gained genes, 100% sensitivity and 94% specificity for combined common genes, and 91% sensitivity and 87% specificity for combined gained genes. No dose-response comparisons were applicable as it is a diagnostic biomarker identification study.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Upregulation; identified as a novel gained gene, differentially expressed and capable of discriminating between PDAC patients and healthy controls (individual ROC curves showed average sensitivity 74.8% and specificity 73.3%).

document_context_data.document_summary: This systematic review aimed to critically examine the effects of melatonin supplementation on sports performance and a range of circulating health biomarkers in highly trained athletes, drawing from randomized controlled trials. The review concluded that melatonin supplementation is safe and demonstrates benefits in improving antioxidant status, reducing inflammatory responses, and reversing exercise-induced liver and muscle damage. Moderate modulating effects were observed on glycemia, total cholesterol, triglycerides, and creatinine. While promising data suggest potential benefits for hematological biomarkers and hormonal responses, the direct efficiency of melatonin in improving sports performance needs further assessment; however, indirect benefits via health biomarker improvements are suggested. Melatonin was also found to counteract oxidative stress, modulate immune function, and show hepatoprotective and renoprotective properties after intense exercise.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Melatonin Supplementation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Melatonin supplementation was investigated with doses ranging from 5 mg to 100 mg, administered acutely (1 day) or continuously for 3 to 30 days. Timing varied from 15-60 minutes before exercise to 2 hours post-exercise, 6 days post-training, 3 days before exercise, or before rest/sleep. Specific dose-response observations were mixed; for instance, 5 mg melatonin showed modest strength improvements, while 8 mg led to significant decreases, and 10 mg improved jumping performance. High heterogeneity in dosages prevented a complete meta-analysis and the establishment of a single efficient dose, though 8 mg melatonin was noted to cause significant harmful effects on strength and power compared to 5 mg and control.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: tendency to decrease (p > 0.05) in the melatonin group

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the role of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) in traumatic brain injury (TBI)-induced neural damage in mice, employing a controlled cortical impact model and various pharmacological and genetic manipulations. The central finding was that inhibiting NETs with Cl-amidine ameliorated neuroinflammation, neuronal apoptosis, and neurological deficits by suppressing the STING-dependent IRE1α/ASK1/JNK signaling pathway. Specifically, Cl-amidine treatment reduced cerebral lesion volume, brain edema, and restored cerebral blood flow, while also attenuating blood-brain barrier disruption, inhibiting immune cell infiltration, alleviating neuronal death, and promoting a shift from pro-inflammatory to anti-inflammatory microglia/macrophage polarization. Conversely, STING activation by 2'3'-cGAMP abolished Cl-amidine's neuroprotection, and PAD4 overexpression aggravated neuroinflammation and neuronal death via the same pathway, effects that were successfully counteracted by STING or IRE1α inhibition. The study also detailed comprehensive methodologies for establishing the TBI model and assessing various molecular and cellular changes.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Controlled Cortical Impact (CCI) model for Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI); Pharmacological interventions including Neutrophil Extracellular Trap (NET) inhibition with Cl-amidine, STING activation with 2'3'-cGAMP, STING inhibition with C-176, and IRE1α inhibition with Kira6; Genetic manipulation via adenovirus-mediated overexpression of Peptidyl arginine deiminase 4 (PAD4).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: TBI was induced using a controlled cortical impactor (3-mm flat-tip, 5 m/s velocity, 200 ms dwelling time, 2.2 mm depth, 3.5 mm craniotomy). Cl-amidine was administered at 50 mg/kg intraperitoneally (i.p.) once daily for three days, starting 1 hour post-TBI. 2'3'-cGAMP was given at 1 mg/kg intravenously 10 minutes pre-TBI, then repeated at 24 and 48 hours post-TBI. C-176 was administered at 10 mg/kg i.p. 1 hour post-TBI, daily until sacrifice. Kira6 was given at 10 mg/kg i.p. 1 hour post-TBI, once daily for three days. Ad-PAD4 or Ad-con (control) adenoviruses were stereotactically injected (4 μL total at 0.5 μL/min across two cortical locations) 1 day before CCI to overexpress PAD4. PAD4 overexpression resulted in a 2.28-fold increase in PAD4 protein and 1.73-fold increase in H3Cit at 3 days post-TBI. Effects were analyzed at 1 and 3 days post-TBI. No explicit dose-response comparisons were reported for most agents, and potential inflammatory or cytotoxic effects of the adenovirus vector were not tested.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher (after TBI, with STING activation), lower (with Cl-amidine, with STING/IRE1α inhibition)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly increased at 3 days after TBI (p < 0.05). Significantly decreased by Cl-amidine treatment (p < 0.01). Remarkably increased by 2'3'-cGAMP pretreatment (p < 0.01). Significantly downregulated by STING antagonist C-176 (p < 0.01) and IRE1α inhibitor Kira6 (p < 0.001).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: The activated form of ASK1, a component of the IRE1α/ASK1/JNK signaling pathway involved in stress responses and apoptosis.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI); modulated by Cl-amidine treatment, STING activation (2'3'-cGAMP), STING inhibition (C-176), or IRE1α inhibition (Kira6).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Increased phosphorylation indicates activation of the ASK1 pathway, correlating with neuroinflammation and neuronal damage. Decreased phosphorylation indicates inhibition of this pathway, contributing to neuroprotective effects.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated disease and target engagement biomarkers in the phase 2b RISE-SSc trial of riociguat in early diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (dcSSc) to predict treatment response. While the primary endpoint (modified Rodnan Skin Score, mRSS) did not reach statistical significance, riociguat treatment significantly increased plasma cGMP levels, indicating engagement of the NO-sGC-cGMP pathway. Additionally, serum sPECAM-1 and CXCL-4 levels decreased with riociguat. Elevated baseline sPECAM-1 and the presence of αSMA-positive cells in skin biopsies were identified as potential predictive biomarkers for greater mRSS reduction with riociguat, suggesting these markers may help identify patients who could benefit from the treatment for skin fibrosis.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Riociguat (Drug Treatment)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Patients with early treatment-naïve diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis were randomized to receive riociguat (n=60) or placebo (n=61) for 52 weeks. Riociguat was administered up to 2.5 mg, maximum three times daily. Biomarker assessments were performed at baseline (day 0) and week 14, with clinical endpoints evaluated up to week 52. Rescue therapy was permitted from week 26. While cGMP changes correlated with riociguat pharmacokinetics, no explicit dose-response comparisons for other biomarkers were formally reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant differences in changes from baseline to week 14 between riociguat and placebo groups (assessed by immunohistochemistry).

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Riociguat treatment in dcSSc patients from baseline to week 14.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Assessed as an indicator of NO–sGC–cGMP pathway activation and TGF-β signalling; no change observed with riociguat treatment.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated whether baseline myocardial and systemic inflammatory burden could predict cardiac structural and functional improvement in advanced heart failure patients undergoing durable Left Ventricular Assist Device (LVAD) support. It found that lower levels of circulating inflammatory cytokines (TNF alpha, IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, IL-7, IL-13, and Interferon gamma) and less activated myocardial STAT-3 inversely correlated with cardiac improvement. A two-cytokine model based on low circulating Interferon gamma and TNF alpha was identified as an effective predictor of significant reverse remodeling and post-LVAD cardiac recovery.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Durable continuous-flow Left Ventricular Assist Device (LVAD) support, used as mechanical circulatory support and combined with standard guideline-directed heart failure medications.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: LVAD implantation was performed on 93 patients with advanced heart failure. Device speed was adjusted under echocardiographic guidance to optimize flow and left ventricular decompression, targeting a midline septum position and minimal mitral regurgitation. Cardiac improvement, defined as significant reverse remodeling (e.g., final LVEF >=40% or 35-40% with >=50% relative improvement), was assessed via serial echocardiography, with 11% of patients showing such improvement (responders). No explicit dose-response comparisons for LVAD speed or medication regimens were reported; the study primarily compared biomarker levels between responders and non-responders to the intervention.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Levels of phosphorylated p65 were similar between responders and non-responders, with no significant difference between the two study groups.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: The activated subunit of NFkB, a transcription factor with a central role in cellular inflammatory processes, activated by cytokines (e.g., TNFα) that regulates genes involved in inflammation, fibrosis, and hypertrophy.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Pre-LVAD intervention in advanced chronic heart failure patients, in the context of subsequent mechanical unloading and circulatory support by LVAD, comparing responders to non-responders.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: No significant association found with response to LVAD therapy or as a differing factor between responders and non-responders to LVAD unloading in this study.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigates the role of fatty acid-binding protein 4 (FABP4), particularly adipocyte-released e-FABP4, in clear cell Renal Cell Carcinoma (ccRCC) progression and its correlation with peri-renal adipose tissue. It demonstrates that FABP4 serum levels and e-FABP4 in adipocyte conditioned media are significantly higher in ccRCC patients. In vitro experiments showed that recombinant FABP4 significantly promotes ccRCC cell migration and ERK phosphorylation, while adipocyte-released factors (other than FABP4) also enhance ACHN cell proliferation. These findings highlight FABP4 as a driver of ccRCC progression and a potential noninvasive biomarker and therapeutic target.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Investigation of FABP4's role in renal cancer progression through in vitro studies using recombinant FABP4, adipocyte-conditioned media (Ad-CM) from ccRCC patients and healthy donors, and the FABP4 inhibitor BMS309403, alongside analysis of patient serum biomarkers.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: In vitro experiments involved recombinant FABP4 (specifically at 10000 pg/mL), Adipocyte-Conditioned Medium (Ad-CM) from ccRCC patients and healthy donors, and the FABP4 inhibitor BMS309403. Cells were treated for proliferation and migration assays, with Mitomycin C (10 µg/mL) used to halt proliferation in scratch assays. While specific concentrations were provided for some reagents, comprehensive dose-response comparisons were generally not reported. Patient serum FABP4 levels were also compared between ccRCC patients and healthy donors.

document_context_data.document_summary: This multicentre longitudinal GENFI study investigated the disease-modifying effects of common variants within TMEM106B (specifically the rs1990622 G allele dosage) on disease endophenotypes in genetic Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD) caused by GRN, C9orf72, or MAPT mutations. The study aimed to longitudinally examine the interactive effects between the TMEM106B-rs1990622 genetic polymorphism, FTD mutations, clinical status (presymptomatic/symptomatic), and time on brain imaging (grey matter volume), serum biomarkers (NfL), and cognitive/behavioural measures. Findings consistently demonstrate that the TMEM106B-rs1990622 G allele confers protective effects, likely in an additive manner, on multiple endophenotypes, including reduced grey matter atrophy, lower serum neurofilament light chain (NfL) levels, and better cognitive and behavioural outcomes, predominantly in GRN and C9orf72 mutation carriers, and reduces the risk of conversion to clinical FTD in GRN carriers.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Genetic modifier investigation; Observational longitudinal study
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This study is observational and investigates an intrinsic genetic factor, not an active therapeutic intervention. The 'dose' refers to the additive effects of the TMEM106B-rs1990622 G allele dosage (0, 1, or 2 G alleles), which was modeled as a continuous variable. The protective effects varied across genetic FTD groups (GRN, C9orf72, MAPT mutations), specific biomarkers, disease stage (presymptomatic vs. symptomatic), and over time (baseline vs. longitudinal). No deviations from an additive effect were observed (heterozygosity indicator P > 0.05), and no traditional dose-response comparisons for a therapeutic agent were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Disease pathology was exacerbated along with accumulation of phosphorylated TDP-43 in an age-dependent manner in double knock-out models of Tmem106b − / − and Grn − / − mice. An increase in TDP-43 cytoplasmic aggregates was reported in Tmem106b knock-out mice in a cellular model for TDP-43.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Double knock-out models of Tmem106b − / − and Grn − / − mice; Tmem106b knock-out mice in a cellular model; GRN haploinsufficiency.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Serves as a marker of exacerbated disease pathology and neurodegeneration, particularly in contexts of Tmem106b and Grn deficiencies.
