document_context_data.document_summary: This document provides comprehensive guidelines for establishing and managing immune monitoring programs in patients undergoing allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation and cellular therapies (TCT/HCT). It highlights the critical need for standardized protocols for assay, flow cytometric, and data analysis to ensure consistent, scalable, and comparable results across multiple centers. The aim is to enhance prognosis prediction, enable early relapse detection, and improve clinical decision-making by evaluating immune reconstitution and functional recovery, as well as by identifying predictive cellular and secreted biomarkers for complications like graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), infections, viral reactivation, and relapse.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Allogeneic Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation (HCT), Transplant and Cellular Therapy (TCT), and related immune effector cell (IEC) therapies, including Genetically Modified Hematopoietic Stem Cell Therapies (GMHSCT) and CAR T-cell therapy.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The document primarily focuses on immune monitoring protocols post-transplantation rather than specific therapeutic dose-response comparisons for HCT/TCT itself. It highlights the variability in transplant platforms (e.g., T-cell depletion techniques, add backs, T-replete) and conditioning regimens (e.g., lymphocyte ablation, total body irradiation). Monitoring thresholds are mentioned for specific immune cells, such as >50 CD4+ T cells/μL within 100 days and >150 NK cells/mL at day 30 post-HCT, to indicate timely immune recovery. Recommended longitudinal sampling schedules are provided (e.g., biweekly for 3 months, then monthly/quarterly) post-HCT/GMHSCT, along with typical blood volumes (8-20 mL), but lack specific dose details for primary therapies or dose-response observations.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Upregulation correlates with relapse. Exhibits contrasting effects on GVHD.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Post-transplant (TCT)
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Upregulation correlates with relapse; its influence on GVHD/GVL balance requires further study.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the safety and efficacy of human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cell (UC-MSC) transplantation in patients with severe COVID-19 and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), focusing on clinical outcomes, lung functional status, hematological parameters, cytokine levels, and miRNA expression profiles. The findings demonstrated that UC-MSC therapy was safe, improved lung lesions over a one-year follow-up by reducing fibrosis and markers of lung damage (CT score, Surfactant D, sRAGE), hastened lymphocyte recovery, and modulated inflammation (decreased ESR, CRP, banded neutrophils). The treatment also showed complex immunomodulatory effects, including altered levels of several cytokines (e.g., increased IP-10, MIP-1α, G-CSF, IL-10, while IL-6, MCP-1, and RAGE remained mostly unchanged in vivo but exhibited changes in vitro) and specific miRNAs, as well as influencing PBMC activation and proliferation in vitro.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Human Umbilical Cord Mesenchymal Stem Cell (UC-MSC) transplantation combined with conventional anti-viral treatment (antibiotic therapy, dexamethasone).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Triple intravenous infusion of UC-MSC at a concentration of 1 × 10^6 cells/kg, administered on days 0, 3, and 6. The average cell viability was 87.8% ± 5.1% before infusion. This was combined with conventional anti-viral treatment including dexamethasone and antibiotic therapy. No explicit dose-response comparisons were reported.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Immunoregulatory protein, ligand for PD-1, involved in T-cell inhibition.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: PBMC co-cultured with UC-MSC in vitro.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Suggests an immunosuppressive mechanism via T-cell inactivation, indicating the immunomodulatory role of MSC.

document_context_data.document_summary: This multi-center cross-sectional study investigated the association between different dietary protein sources (animal vs. plant) and circulating levels of pentraxin 3 (PTX3) in 227 adult patients undergoing maintenance hemodialysis (HD) for end-stage renal disease (ESRD). The study aimed to clarify the role of dietary protein in inflammation given its importance in cardiovascular disease pathogenesis, the main cause of mortality in HD patients. The main finding was that higher animal protein intake was directly and significantly associated with elevated PTX3 concentrations, an indicator of dialysis-related inflammation and cardiovascular disease risk, while total and plant protein intake showed no such significant association.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Dietary Intake Analysis in End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) patients undergoing Maintenance Hemodialysis (HD)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational, multi-center cross-sectional study; no specific dietary intervention or dose-response comparisons were performed. Patients were already undergoing maintenance hemodialysis for a minimum of 90 days, with dialysis adequacy assessed by Kt/V and Urea Reduction Ratio (URR). Dietary intake was assessed using a validated 168-item food frequency questionnaire. Patients with higher PTX3 levels (≥ 3.75 ng/mL) had a significantly greater animal protein intake (mean 0.54 g/kg dry weight) compared to those with lower PTX3 levels (< 3.75 ng/mL, mean 0.46 g/kg dry weight; P=0.035). A one-unit increase in animal protein intake per kilogram dry weight was directly associated with an increased chance of elevated PTX3 concentration (Model 1: OR=3.123; 95% CI 1.077, 9.053; P=0.036; Model 2: OR=4.524; 95% CI 1.247, 16.417; P=0.022). No significant association was found for plant protein intake with PTX3. A marginal association for a one-unit increase in total protein intake was also observed in Model 2 (OR=3.114; 95% CI 0.943, 10.283; P=0.062).

document_context_data.document_summary: This study performed a comprehensive qualitative and quantitative proteomic analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) derived from different somatic origins (fibroblasts and peripheral blood CD34+ cells), comparing them to original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC) and human embryonic stem cells (hESC). Using ESI-MS e and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry, complemented by Western blot validation, the research aimed to characterize hiPSC proteomic profiles, identify known and novel pluripotency markers, and distinguish hiPSCs from their somatic precursors. Key findings include the identification of approximately 220 commonly up-regulated proteins in pluripotent stem cell lines, the development and confirmation of a 22-protein marker panel for hiPSC characterization, and the observation of coordinated up-regulation of proteins involved in protein synthesis, folding, RNA processing, DNA replication, DNA repair, and energy metabolism (including oxidative phosphorylation and lipogenesis) in hiPSCs. The study also identified somatic cell markers that were down-regulated upon reprogramming and highlighted specific proteomic differences between hiPSCs and hESCs, contributing to improved hiPSC quality control for therapeutic applications.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Proteomic characterization and comparative analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) and human embryonic stem cells (hESCs).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was a characterization study, not a therapeutic intervention, thus no 'dose' of therapy was administered. Quantitative and qualitative proteomic analyses were performed using electrospray ionization (ESI)-MS e (label-free quantification with internal reference standard) and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry. Two hiPSC lines (iNC-01 from CD34+ cells, SB5-MP1 from fibroblasts, both generated using loxP-flanked excisable polycistronic STEMCCA lentiviral vector) and one hESC line (H9) were analyzed at earlier and later passages. Comparisons were made against their respective original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC). Proteins were considered differentially expressed if expression changed by >=1.5-fold, with a maximum false discovery rate of 2% and >95% confidence. Western blot analysis was used for validation. The developed marker panel was further tested in 8-9 additional hiPSC lines or passages from different somatic origins and reprogramming techniques. Differentiation studies were conducted with embryoid bodies at 24 hours and 7 days to assess marker changes during spontaneous differentiation.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Consistently up-regulated in early and late passage cells of both hiPSC lines (by ESI-MS e) and confirmed by Western blot analysis. All selected proteins were confirmed to be up-regulated in hiPSC and hESC compared to somatic cells.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Not explicitly stated, inferred as related to cell maintenance and potentially pluripotency.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Proposed novel pluripotency marker identification and validation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Candidate novel pluripotency marker for hiPSCs/hESCs.

document_context_data.document_summary: This systematic review evaluates the effects of soy protein (SP) supplementation on muscle adaptations, metabolic and antioxidant status, hormonal response, and exercise performance in active individuals and athletes, often comparing it to whey protein or placebo. The review encompasses studies on protein synthesis, amino acid transport, and signaling pathways, highlighting that while some anabolic markers might be less favorable with soy, it can provide similar increases in lean mass to whey protein, especially at optimal protein intakes. SP is shown to reduce exercise-induced metabolic/blood circulating biomarkers (triglycerides, uric acid, lactate) and improve antioxidant capacity, reducing oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation. However, its effects on hormonal responses, such as testosterone and cortisol, are inconsistent or contradictory across studies. SP supplementation also demonstrates potential benefits in improving various exercise performance indicators, including high-intensity running, maximal cardiac output, delaying fatigue, improving isometric strength, running velocity, and muscle recovery after damage. The review concludes that SP can be a viable alternative to conventional protein supplements, but emphasizes the need for further research addressing methodological limitations and consistent dosing.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Soy Protein and Soy Peptide Supplementation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The review encompassed a wide range of soy protein (SP) and soy peptide supplementation protocols, from acute doses (e.g., 15-20g SP, 18g SP beverage, 10g essential amino acids from soy) to chronic daily intakes varying from 0.5 g/kg BW/day to 90 g/day (e.g., 33-40 g/day, 1 g/kg BW/day, 53.3 g/day). Doses were often combined with carbohydrates (e.g., 10g soy peptide + 30g sugar, 15g SP + 52.5g CHO) or matched for nitrogen/leucine content for comparison with whey protein. Durations ranged from single acute sessions to long-term interventions of 2 weeks, 4 weeks, 6 weeks, 9 weeks, 4 months, or even "12 weeks. Comparisons were consistently made against whey protein, soy-dairy blends, isoenergetic placebos, or control (exercise-only) groups. While some studies aimed for optimal protein intakes ("  1.6 g/kg BW/day), there was a notable lack of consistent dosing or explicit dose-response comparisons across the reviewed literature, indicating significant variability in intervention designs.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased in the supplemented group after 4 months of 1 g/kg BW/day SP supplementation in Olympic female gymnasts.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: A hormone involved in various physiological functions, including stress response and metabolism.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Female athletes supplemented with Soy Protein (SP) for 4 months.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates a hormonal response to chronic SP supplementation.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study conducted a secondary analysis of data from the European First-Episode Schizophrenia Trial (EUFEST) and Recovery After an Initial Schizophrenia Episode Early Treatment Program (RAISE-ETP) trials. It utilized machine learning models (support vector regressors and classifiers) to predict depressive symptom trajectories (changes in CDSS scores) and the occurrence of post-psychotic depressive episodes (PPD) at 6 and 12 months in first-episode psychosis (FEP) patients with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders. The models leveraged various baseline variables including sociodemographic information, clinical assessments (e.g., PANSS, CDSS scores), neurocognitive performance, quality of life, and blood-based biomarkers, demonstrating accurate prediction and geographical generalizability across populations. The study also analyzed how factors like treatment assignment (e.g., NAVIGATE program) and antidepressant prescription influenced model misclassification and patient outcomes.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Antipsychotic medication, NAVIGATE program (psychosocial intervention), Antidepressant coadministration, and Usual community care.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants in the EUFEST trial received 1 year of antipsychotic treatment (described as "minimally antipsychotic-treated"), while RAISE-ETP participants were allocated to either usual community care or the NAVIGATE program. Antidepressant prescriptions were observed, with RAISE-ETP patients showing a higher rate (33.33%) compared to EUFEST (2.18%). The NAVIGATE program was associated with a sharper decline in depressive symptoms, especially among patients prescribed antidepressants at baseline. However, no specific doses, intensities, or durations for antipsychotics, the NAVIGATE program, or antidepressants were detailed, nor were dose-response comparisons reported for any treatment; their influence on predictive model performance and patient characteristics was primarily analyzed.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Not specified as a change; its baseline level served as a predictor.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Identified as a key predictor in EUFEST dataset models for depressive symptoms and episodes. Its exclusion increased model bias, suggesting its importance for unbiased detection of symptom changes. Specific quantitative changes or thresholds were not provided.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Metabolic hormone; associated with affective symptoms, metabolic regulation, immuno-metabolic dysfunction, and metabolic comorbidity in psychiatric disorders.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Prediction of depressive symptoms and episodes in First-Episode Psychosis (FEP) patients, specifically identified as a key baseline predictor within the EUFEST dataset.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Valuable biomarker for predicting and managing depressive symptoms in FEP patients, helping to ensure unbiased detection of symptom changes.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the impact of two distinct heat stress modalities—exertional heating (exercise/cycling) and exogenous heating (hot water immersion)—on physiological responses, stress markers, and peripheral kynurenine pathway (KP) metabolites in 11 young healthy males. Both modalities were designed to induce a comparable increase in core body temperature up to 39°C. The study found that heat exposure transiently induced the KP, elevating several plasma KP metabolite concentrations (Kynurenic acid, Picolinic acid, 3-Hydroxykynurenine, Quinolinic acid, Kynurenine, KYN/TRP ratio) and stress markers (Cortisol, Prolactin, Adrenaline, Noradrenaline, Lactate). These changes generally returned to baseline during recovery, suggesting adaptability of KP enzymes to physiological stressors. Differential changes were observed depending on the specific heat stress protocol and the phase (heating vs. recovery), with exertional heating often showing more pronounced effects for some markers and sustained elevation for others (e.g., KYNA, PIC in EXE). The study highlights the potential of KP metabolites as disease biomarkers.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Induced Hyperthermia / Heat Stress (Exertional heating and Exogenous heating)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants underwent two distinct heat stress modalities: exertional heating (EXE) via cycling exercise at an intensity eliciting 60% VO2max in a 30°C room, and exogenous heating (EXO) via hot water immersion up to the waistline in a 44°C bath. Both trials were conducted until rectal temperature (Trec) reached 39°C (with measurements taken at every 0.5°C increment up to a maximum of 39.5°C), followed by a recovery phase to a baseline temperature of 37.5°C. The time required to reach specific temperature set points was similar in both trials. No direct dose-response comparisons were explicitly reported; however, EXE induced greater increases in stress markers and sympathetic vasomotor activity compared to EXO, suggesting differential physiological loads.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased upon both EXE and EXO, peaking at 39°C (p < 0.01) and returning to baseline. The greatest increase was observed during the EXO trial.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Stress hormone involved in various physiological processes, including immune modulation and osmoregulation.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Heat stress (EXE and EXO trials) induced by core temperature increases, with samples collected at 0.5°C rectal temperature increments up to 39°C and subsequent decrease until 37.5°C.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates a physiological stress response to thermal load. Expected to be more responsive in EXO due to sensitivity to skin temperature.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated novel protein-based subphenotypes in Heart Failure with reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF) patients using unsupervised machine learning on 4210 repeatedly measured circulating proteins over a median 2.1-year follow-up in 382 patients. It identified four distinct subphenotypes with varying protein profiles, clinical characteristics (e.g., age, EF, chronic renal failure), and prognosis. These subphenotypes were driven by specific protein subsets associated with various biological mechanisms, including oxidative stress, inflammation, extracellular matrix organization, myocardial stretch/stress, injury, and renal dysfunction. Subphenotypes 2 and 3 demonstrated significantly worse clinical outcomes compared to subphenotype 1, highlighting the value of dynamic proteomic profiling for gaining pathophysiological insights and exploring personalized treatment opportunities in complex diagnoses like HFrEF.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Proteomic profiling and subphenotyping in Heart Failure with reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF) patients.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational study involving trimonthly blood sampling over a median follow-up of 2.1 years (IQR: 1.1–2.6 years) in 382 HFrEF patients, totaling 1066 blood samples. An aptamer-based multiplex proteomic approach (SOMAscan assay) was used to measure 4210 circulating proteins, yielding relative fluorescence units (RFUs) for comparative analysis rather than absolute concentrations. No specific intervention, treatment, or dose-response comparisons were conducted, as the study focused on characterizing disease subphenotypes and biomarker patterns over time. Repeated proteomic measurements (incorporating both intercept and slope coefficients) demonstrated improved accuracy for survival models (c-index 0.73, BIC 1023) compared to single time-point assessments.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Levels highest in subphenotype 2. Precise quantification not provided.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Implicated in inflammation.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Patient subphenotype classification in a cardiac cohort, particularly defining Subphenotype 2.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Higher levels are associated with subphenotype 2, which is linked to significantly worse patient outcomes (HR 3.43 (1.76–6.69) compared to subphenotype 1).

document_context_data.document_summary: This study employed NMR metabolomics to investigate metabolic profiles in serum and urine from COVID-19 patients across varying disease severities (Medical Ward and Intensive Care Unit) and healthy controls. The primary aim was to identify biomarkers for COVID-19 diagnosis, severity classification, and prognosis, and to explore correlations with clinical factors like hypertension, obesity, and dyslipidemia. Key findings include the development of a highly efficient diagnostic panel (isoleucine, TMAO, glucose) and a robust severity classification panel (ethanol, TMAO, tyrosine, betaine, and clinical characteristics), alongside identification of numerous individual metabolites and clinical parameters associated with infection, disease progression, hospitalization duration, and patient outcome.

treatment_details.therapy_type: NMR metabolomics-based profiling and observational study of COVID-19 infection
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This observational study analyzed 80 serum and urine samples from COVID-19 patients (34 intensive care, 46 hospitalized) and 32 from healthy controls using NMR spectroscopy. The research focused on identifying and validating metabolite-based panels for COVID-19 diagnosis and severity classification. A diagnostic panel of isoleucine, TMAO, and glucose achieved an AUC of 0.91 (86.08% sensitivity, 83.87% specificity). A severity classification panel, combining ethanol, TMAO, tyrosine, betaine, and clinical characteristics (obesity/overweight, dyslipidemia, lymphocyte count), achieved an AUC of 0.825 (84.85% sensitivity, 72.09% specificity). No therapeutic intervention or dose-response comparisons were part of the study design.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher levels observed in COVID-19 patients compared to healthy controls, and also a top positive correlate to obesity/overweight.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Amino acid, involved in protein synthesis, collagen structure, wound healing, and arginine and proline metabolism.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: COVID-19 infection vs. healthy controls, and association with obesity/overweight.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Potential biomarker for COVID-19 infection, indicates perturbation in metabolic routes, and differentiates patients from controls.

document_context_data.document_summary: This clinical trial investigated the impact of two distinct dietary interventions, Protein Fat (PF) and Protein Fat and Fiber (PFF), on plasma amino acid and amine profiles in a Mediterranean female cohort (cloistered nuns). The study found that combining macronutrients significantly reduced plasma levels of amino acids and amines, particularly in the PFF group, with some recovery post-intervention. Metabolic profile analysis showed significant differences between groups at 55 and 98 days, identifying leucine, asparagine, alanine, cysteine, and creatine as key differentiating metabolites, and also observed significant alterations in EAA/NEAA and Kyn/Trp ratios.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Dietary Intervention (Combined Macronutrient Diet)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: A 132-day dietary intervention with 41 participants assigned to two groups: Protein Fat (PF) and Protein Fat and Fiber (PFF). The PF group consumed 150g of pork belly (standardized to approximately 20g protein and 40g fat per 100g product) with other menu items. The PFF group consumed 200g of vegetables (cardoon or borage) along with 150g pork belly (twice a week) and other daily menu items. Total menu and physical activity were identical between groups. No dose-response comparisons beyond the defined dietary groups were reported, but effects were monitored at 55, 98, and 132 days.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Notable differences between groups at 98 days (p < 0.002).

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Dietary intervention at 98 days.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Identified as a differentiating metabolite indicating the impact of the dietary intervention.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive observational study utilized plasma proteomics and machine learning to develop and validate a framework for measuring organ-specific biological aging, termed 'e-ageotypes', in humans. Analyzing 4,778 proteins from 5,676 adults across five independent cohorts, the research revealed that accelerated aging in specific organs (including heart, brain, kidney, muscle, liver, adipose, pancreas, lung, and immune system) is significantly associated with higher risks of all-cause mortality and various age-related diseases, such as heart failure, Alzheimer's disease, hypertension, diabetes, and cognitive decline. The study's methodology involved defining 'extreme agers' (individuals with highly accelerated organ aging), clustering them into distinct ageotypes, and identifying key protein biomarkers (e.g., REN, KL, NPPB, TNNT2, CPLX1/2) that contribute to these aging profiles and offer prognostic utility for disease risk and progression.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational Study on Biological Aging via Plasma Proteomics and Machine Learning
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This observational study involved the quantification of approximately 4,778 plasma proteins using SomaScan assays (v.4 and v.4.1) in 5,676 adults from five independent cohorts. Machine learning models (LASSO regression-based chronological age predictors) were developed and validated to estimate biological (organ-specific) age, referred to as 'age gaps' or 'e-ageotypes', for 11 major organs (adipose tissue, artery, brain, heart, immune tissue, intestine, kidney, liver, lung, muscle, and pancreas) and the whole organism. Models were trained on 1,398 healthy participants from the Knight-ADRC cohort and tested across the full cohort. Age gaps were calculated using local regression, z-scored per model and cohort, and adjusted for age and sex. Associations with various age-related phenotypes, future mortality, heart disease, clinical biochemistry markers, and cognitive decline were assessed using linear models or Cox proportional hazards models, with multiple testing correction (Benjamini-Hochberg method, 5% false discovery rate). No therapeutic intervention or dose comparison was performed.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Part of a protein network involved in extracellular matrix, cartilage development, and osteoblast signaling pathways, implicated in vascular calcification and early cognitive decline.

matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Component of a protein network indicating vascular calcification and extracellular matrix alterations as a major component of aging that underlies early cognitive decline.

document_context_data.document_summary: This review provides updated guidelines and a consensus for standardizing pre-analytical variables in salivary biomarker studies for Alzheimer's disease (AD) research. It critically appraises current methodologies, identifies inconsistencies, and proposes a standardized protocol for saliva collection, processing, and storage to improve reliability for diagnostic biomarker detection and quantification. The document investigates various protein and metabolomic biomarkers in saliva, assessing their diagnostic potential for AD and Mild Cognitive Impairment, and highlights the importance of controlling factors like collection methods, centrifugation, and storage conditions for accurate measurement.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Salivary Biomarker Research and Standardization for Alzheimer's Disease Diagnosis
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This is a comprehensive review article focusing on standardizing pre-analytical variables for salivary Alzheimer's Disease (AD) biomarker studies, rather than a therapeutic intervention or dose-response investigation. It critically discusses how inconsistent methodologies and pre-analytical factors (e.g., collection kits like Salivette vs. passive drooling, acute food intake, physical activity, stress, diurnal variations, dental restorations, freezing/thawing protocols, centrifugation speeds) influence biomarker detection and quantification, leading to conflicting findings for analytes like Aβ42, Aβ40, and AChE activity. The document proposes a standardized pre-analytical protocol, including pre-collection instructions (e.g., abstinence from food, drinks, smoking, alcohol, exercise), passive drool collection (e.g., 2 mL after 5 min pooling), and post-collection processing (e.g., immediate freezing, visual inspection, two-step centrifugation, aliquoting 100-250 µL). Various analytical methods (ELISA, Western blot, SIMOA, MS-based methods, NMR) were discussed for diagnostic marker identification, emphasizing that a universal protocol might not suit all biomarkers due to their diverse physiological roles.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significant concentration changes identified in MCI and AD patients compared to controls. Statistically significant multivariate models identified it as a discriminator.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study primarily investigated the effects of physical exercise combined with whole-body cryotherapy (WBC) on oxidant/antioxidant balance and other physiological parameters in 16 high-level kayakers. It found an initial decrease and subsequent recovery in GPx activity, decreased TBARS, and variable urea levels, with no significant changes in MDA, CD, protein carbonyls, vitamin E, cortisol, testosterone, total antioxidant capacity (TAC), or hematological parameters. The document also reviews findings from other studies, indicating that WBC generally increases overall antioxidant capacity, helps normalize oxidant/antioxidant balance during intensive exercise, and exhibits anti-inflammatory effects, potentially enhancing recovery and performance during training.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Physical Exercise Combined with Whole-Body Cryotherapy (WBC)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: In the primary study, 16 kayakers underwent specialized physical training twice daily for 19 days. For the first 10 days, this was combined with Whole-Body Cryotherapy (WBC) sessions administered twice daily (morning pre-exercise stimulation and afternoon post-exercise recovery). Each WBC session lasted 3 minutes (excluding a 30-second adaptive vestibule at -60°C) with chamber temperatures gradually decreasing from -120°C to -145°C. The document also refers to other studies using varying WBC protocols, including 10 sessions at -130°C for 3 minutes (once daily), 5 sessions/week at -110°C for 2 minutes, and single sessions at -130°C for 2 or 3 minutes, either with or without exercise.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the pathological landscape, subclonal evolution, and dynamics of gene fusions, specifically KMT2A/AFDN and a novel CCDC32/CBX3, along with chimeric RNA variants, in 16 adult Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) patients undergoing treatment. It aimed to understand treatment resistance and relapse mechanisms by monitoring cytogenetic, RNA-seq, and genome-wide changes from diagnosis to relapse. The research identified the CCDC32/CBX3 fusion as a new therapeutic vulnerability that promotes cell cycle progression and contributes to AML pathogenesis and treatment resistance, highlighting its prognostic significance and the necessity of advanced molecular profiling for cryptic gene fusion detection.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study utilized discovery metabolomics and lipidomics to investigate plasma glycosphingolipids and other lipid metabolites as potential biomarkers for distinguishing aggressive from indolent prostate cancer (PCa) in treatment-naïve African-American and European-American men. The findings indicate that specific glycosphingolipid species, particularly trihexosylceramide and tetrahexosylceramide, along with other sphingolipids and triglycerides, are significantly associated with PCa aggressiveness. A five-sphingolipid signature demonstrated promising diagnostic accuracy comparable to or exceeding PSA, suggesting their utility as novel diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers and highlighting their role in related metabolic networks and genetic alterations.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Diagnostic biomarker discovery via metabolomics and lipidomics
treatment_details.dose_specificity: An observational study conducted on plasma samples from 159 men with treatment-naïve prostate cancer, utilizing ultra-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS). The study focused on identifying biomarkers for PCa aggressiveness (Grade Group 1 vs. Grade Groups 2-5, low vs. intermediate/high aggressive PCa), without administering or comparing any therapeutic interventions or doses.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Standard test for PCa early detection, a protease involved in seminal coagulum liquefaction, and commonly used as a tumor marker and component of aggressiveness scores.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Early detection and differentiation of aggressive vs. indolent Prostate Cancer (PCa), and association with PCa aggressiveness in treatment-naïve, clinically localized PCa.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Established marker for PCa, but often insufficient for distinguishing aggressive from indolent PCa, warranting better biomarkers. A five-sphingolipid signature may be as accurate or slightly more accurate than PSA for aggressive PCa.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated inflammatory clusters in sepsis based on plasma cytokine protein abundance and their relationship with leucocyte transcriptomic subphenotypes, utilizing data from three cohorts (UK GAinS, VANISH, and LeoPARDS). It identified two or three inflammatory clusters across these datasets, with a 'high cytokine' cluster exhibiting elevated levels of both pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory cytokines, which was consistently associated with worse organ dysfunction, increased disease severity, and higher mortality. The study also explored the overlap between inflammatory clusters and previously described transcriptomic subphenotypes (SRS1/SRS2) and ARDS subphenotypes, suggesting that combining cytokine protein abundance and transcriptomic data could provide complementary information for optimal sepsis patient stratification. No significant interaction between inflammatory clusters and trial treatment response for therapies like norepinephrine, vasopressin, or levosimendan was found.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Patient stratification using plasma cytokine profiling; evaluation of trial therapies including Vasopressin, Norepinephrine, Hydrocortisone, and Levosimendan in septic shock.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study primarily focused on patient stratification using hierarchical clustering and latent class analysis based on plasma protein abundance of 11 to 65 circulating cytokines, cytokine receptors, and regulators across three cohorts (UK GAinS: n=124, VANISH: n=155, LeoPARDS: n=484). For trial therapies, the VANISH trial compared vasopressin with norepinephrine and hydrocortisone with placebo, while LeoPARDS compared levosimendan with placebo. No specific doses or durations for these trial treatments are detailed, and the study found no detectable heterogeneity in treatment effect for norepinephrine, vasopressin, or levosimendan, noting they had no or minimal effect on circulating cytokines.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of broad-spectrum polyphenol supplementation from powdered tart cherry extract on markers of recovery, oxidative stress, and muscle damage following intense resistance exercise in men. It concluded that tart cherry extract significantly reduced oxidative stress (protein carbonyls), skeletal muscle damage (creatine kinase), and cardiac/type I muscle fiber damage (creatine kinase MB), while also preventing a decrease in handgrip strength compared to placebo.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Broad-spectrum polyphenol supplementation using powdered tart cherry extract combined with an acute resistance exercise protocol (AREP).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants received 500 mg of powdered NordicCherry® tart cherry extract (with minimal calorie content, 1.3 kcal) daily for 7 days prior to an Acute Resistance Exercise Protocol (AREP), compared to a rice flour placebo. The AREP involved 6 sets of 10 repetitions of barbell back squat at 80% of 1-repetition maximum, with load reduction to 75% 1RM if 10 repetitions were not completed in a set. No dose-response comparisons for the supplement or exercise intensity were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly lower in Tart Cherry (TC) group compared to Placebo (PL) group across time points: Immediate Post (IP) (PL: 0.4 	 0.3 vs. TC: -0.4 	 0.2 nmol	mg	-1; p < 0.001), 1 h (PL: 0.3 	 0.3 vs. TC: -0.7 	 0.3 nmol	mg	-1; p < 0.001), and 24 h (PL: 0.1 	 0.4 vs. TC: -0.3 	 0.5 nmol	mg	-1; p = 0.010). This represented a statistically significant main effect for supplement (p = 0.019) and supplement*time interaction (p < 0.001), effectively nullifying the increase seen in the placebo group.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Indicator of oxidative stress and damage to proteins.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Following an Acute Resistance Exercise Protocol (AREP) (6 sets of 10 repetitions of barbell back squat at 80% 1RM) after a 7-day supplementation period with tart cherry extract.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates reduced oxidative stress and potentially less cellular damage, suggesting a protective effect of tart cherry supplementation against exercise-induced oxidative stress.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study primarily investigated the effects of physical exercise combined with whole-body cryotherapy (WBC) on oxidant/antioxidant balance and other physiological parameters in 16 high-level kayakers. It found an initial decrease and subsequent recovery in GPx activity, decreased TBARS, and variable urea levels, with no significant changes in MDA, CD, protein carbonyls, vitamin E, cortisol, testosterone, total antioxidant capacity (TAC), or hematological parameters. The document also reviews findings from other studies, indicating that WBC generally increases overall antioxidant capacity, helps normalize oxidant/antioxidant balance during intensive exercise, and exhibits anti-inflammatory effects, potentially enhancing recovery and performance during training.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Physical Exercise Combined with Whole-Body Cryotherapy (WBC)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: In the primary study, 16 kayakers underwent specialized physical training twice daily for 19 days. For the first 10 days, this was combined with Whole-Body Cryotherapy (WBC) sessions administered twice daily (morning pre-exercise stimulation and afternoon post-exercise recovery). Each WBC session lasted 3 minutes (excluding a 30-second adaptive vestibule at -60°C) with chamber temperatures gradually decreasing from -120°C to -145°C. The document also refers to other studies using varying WBC protocols, including 10 sessions at -130°C for 3 minutes (once daily), 5 sessions/week at -110°C for 2 minutes, and single sessions at -130°C for 2 or 3 minutes, either with or without exercise.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No statistically significant changes (P > 0.05) were found throughout the experiment.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Marker of protein oxidative damage.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: During a training cycle involving combined physical exercise and WBC, followed by exercise-only in kayakers.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: No significant change observed, indicating no statistically significant protein oxidative damage under the study conditions.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of consuming cow's milk versus an energy-matched carbohydrate solution on recovery markers and performance in twenty female team-sport athletes following repeated simulated team games (STGs). The findings indicated that 500 mL of milk consumption attenuated losses in muscle function (peak torque for knee extension and flexion), sprint performance (5m and 10m), and perceptions of stress, and helped reduce muscle soreness and tiredness, particularly after the first STG. However, for many other physiological and performance markers (e.g., CK, hsCRP, LOOHs, PCs, CMJ, HR, RPE), the effects were mostly unclear or trivial, with milk showing no clear benefit after the second STG.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Nutritional intervention (consumption of cow's milk vs. an energy-matched carbohydrate solution) combined with a multi-stage physical activity protocol.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants consumed 500 mL of either cow's milk (910 kJ/215 kcal, 17.0 g protein, 25.5 g carbohydrate, 5.0 g fat) or an energy-matched carbohydrate solution (910 kJ/215 kcal, 0.2 g protein, 53.6 g carbohydrate, 0.0 g fat) immediately following each of two simulated team games (STG1 and STG2). The 17 g protein from milk was noted to be below the recommended 20 g threshold for maximal protein synthesis stimulation. The exercise protocol involved two ~30 minute halves of intermittent running with sprints, agility, and jumps, separated by a 10-minute half-time, with a 48-hour recovery period between STG1 and STG2. No explicit dose-response comparisons were reported for the nutritional interventions.

document_context_data.document_summary: This systematic review evaluates the effects of soy protein (SP) supplementation on muscle adaptations, metabolic and antioxidant status, hormonal response, and exercise performance in active individuals and athletes, often comparing it to whey protein or placebo. The review encompasses studies on protein synthesis, amino acid transport, and signaling pathways, highlighting that while some anabolic markers might be less favorable with soy, it can provide similar increases in lean mass to whey protein, especially at optimal protein intakes. SP is shown to reduce exercise-induced metabolic/blood circulating biomarkers (triglycerides, uric acid, lactate) and improve antioxidant capacity, reducing oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation. However, its effects on hormonal responses, such as testosterone and cortisol, are inconsistent or contradictory across studies. SP supplementation also demonstrates potential benefits in improving various exercise performance indicators, including high-intensity running, maximal cardiac output, delaying fatigue, improving isometric strength, running velocity, and muscle recovery after damage. The review concludes that SP can be a viable alternative to conventional protein supplements, but emphasizes the need for further research addressing methodological limitations and consistent dosing.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Soy Protein and Soy Peptide Supplementation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The review encompassed a wide range of soy protein (SP) and soy peptide supplementation protocols, from acute doses (e.g., 15-20g SP, 18g SP beverage, 10g essential amino acids from soy) to chronic daily intakes varying from 0.5 g/kg BW/day to 90 g/day (e.g., 33-40 g/day, 1 g/kg BW/day, 53.3 g/day). Doses were often combined with carbohydrates (e.g., 10g soy peptide + 30g sugar, 15g SP + 52.5g CHO) or matched for nitrogen/leucine content for comparison with whey protein. Durations ranged from single acute sessions to long-term interventions of 2 weeks, 4 weeks, 6 weeks, 9 weeks, 4 months, or even "12 weeks. Comparisons were consistently made against whey protein, soy-dairy blends, isoenergetic placebos, or control (exercise-only) groups. While some studies aimed for optimal protein intakes ("  1.6 g/kg BW/day), there was a notable lack of consistent dosing or explicit dose-response comparisons across the reviewed literature, indicating significant variability in intervention designs.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Tended to be recovered faster with SP supplementation rather than with whey protein or isoenergetic placebo 48 h after speed-endurance exercise. Lower in the soy group (p < 0.004) and tended to be lower in the whey protein group (p < 0.061) compared with the placebo group after speed endurance training.

matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates a faster recovery from oxidative stress and reduced protein oxidative damage, suggesting protective effects of soy and potentially whey protein.

document_context_data.document_summary: This article updates the redox theory of aging, proposing that aging results from a decline in gene-exposome interaction plasticity due to cumulative exposure memory. It emphasizes the critical role of redox networks, particularly thiol/disulfide balance (e.g., plasma cystine to glutathione ratio), as an interface between an individual and the environment, influencing health, disease etiology, and resilience. The theory links compromised redox networks to increased oxidative stress biomarkers like hydroxynonenal and reactive carbonyls, and discusses the predictive power of the plasma CySS/GSH ratio for all-cause mortality in conditions like coronary artery disease, while also exploring implications for regenerative medicine, multimorbidity, and personalized health management.

treatment_details.therapy_type: This document is a comprehensive review and theoretical discussion of the redox theory of aging, its mechanisms, and implications, including the prognostic utility of specific biomarkers. No direct therapeutic interventions were investigated.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Not applicable, as this is a review article and theoretical discussion; it does not report on experimental studies involving specific therapeutic doses, intensities, durations, or dose-response comparisons for any intervention. document_context_data.document_summary: This double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled study evaluated the effect of oral palmitoylethanolamide (PEA, Levagen+™) on recovery from muscle-damaging leg press exercise in 28 healthy young males. The study found that while PEA supplementation did not significantly reduce perceived muscle soreness, thigh circumference, or most inflammatory and phosphoprotein markers (Creatine Kinase, Lactate Dehydrogenase, IL-6, IL-10, hs-CRP, TNF-α, CREB, ERK1/2, JNK, NF-κB, p38 MAPK, S6K1, STAT3, STAT5), it did significantly reduce blood myoglobin and lactate concentrations. Furthermore, PEA increased Protein Kinase B phosphorylation immediately post-exercise, suggesting aid in muscle recovery through improved metabolic efficiency and activation of anabolic/repair signaling pathways from repeat bouts of exercise.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Oral Supplementation with Palmitoylethanolamide (Levagen+™) combined with Resistance Exercise
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants were randomized to consume either liquid PEA (167.5 mg Levagen+™ containing 150 mg PEA and 17.5 mg excipients, with 832.5 mg maltodextrin) or a matched placebo (1 g maltodextrin). Treatments were administered pre-exercise, immediately post-exercise, 24 h post-exercise, and 48 h post-exercise. The muscle-damaging exercise consisted of four sets of leg press at 80% of one-repetition maximum (1-RM) to volitional exhaustion, with 60s rest between sets, followed by a performance set at 70% 1-RM to maximal repetitions. No dose-response comparisons for PEA were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased/peaked immediately post-exercise in the PEA group only (p < 0.05), returning to baseline within 1 h post-exercise.

document_context_data.document_summary: This document synthesizes the proceedings of the Tau2024 Global Conference, showcasing interdisciplinary advancements in tau-associated brain disorders. Key areas covered include the pathophysiology, molecular mechanisms, and brain microenvironments of tauopathies, as well as global perspectives highlighting genetic, socioeconomic, and linguistic diversity's impact on conditions like Frontotemporal Lobe Dementia and Primary Progressive Aphasia. The conference reviewed cellular mechanisms, advanced tau-PET, CSF, and blood-based biomarkers for diagnosis and monitoring of Alzheimer's Disease and other tauopathies, alongside discussions on therapeutic strategies such as antisense oligonucleotides, immunotherapy, senolytics, OGA inhibitors, and novel intrabody approaches aimed at reducing tau levels and aggregates.

treatment_details.therapy_type: The conference proceedings discussed a range of therapeutic advancements for tauopathies, including antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) therapy, tau immunotherapy (e.g., bepranemab), anti-tau-PEST intrabody therapy, pharmacological inhibition of PERK, senolytics (dasatinib plus quercetin), and O-GlcNAcase (OGA) inhibition (e.g., FNP-223).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Specific dose details varied by therapy: BIIB080 (ASO) demonstrated a dose-dependent reduction of approximately 60% in CSF tau. Anti-tau-PEST intrabodies reduced eGFP-tau by 70-78% in cellular models and endogenous tau by 38-58% in organoids over 21 days. A PERK inhibitor and nanobody constructs were effective in animal models without specific dose reporting. Bepranemab, senolytics (dasatinib plus quercetin), and FNP-223 (OGA inhibitor) were evaluated in early-phase human trials with various administration routes (IV, oral) and were generally well-tolerated, but detailed dose-response comparisons were not consistently reported across all interventions.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Pathological tau activates PERK; administration of a PERK inhibitor protected the brains of tau transgenic mice from deleterious effects of tauopathies.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Kinase promoting translational repression as part of cellular stress responses; pathological activation contributes to maladaptive cellular responses in tauopathies.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Pathological tau activation in tauopathies.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Its activation indicates maladaptive stress response and deleterious effects in tauopathies; its inhibition protected brains from these effects, suggesting therapeutic potential for restoring brain function.

document_context_data.document_summary: This review investigates the utility of T cell Receptor Excision Circles (TRECs) and other markers (TCR diversity, CD31, PTK7) for monitoring thymic output and T-cell reconstitution after allogeneic Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation (HSCT). It examines TRECs as a predictive marker for post-HSCT complications like infections, relapse, and Graft-versus-Host Disease (GVHD), and for clinical outcomes including overall survival. The study also explores clinical factors influencing TREC levels, such as recipient age, conditioning regimen, stem cell source and dose, and pre-transplant thymic activity, and discusses TREC's broader diagnostic utility in congenital immunodeficiencies, HIV infection, and autoimmune diseases, advocating for its inclusion in post-HSCT follow-up.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Allogeneic Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation (HSCT)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This review primarily discusses various conditioning regimens employed in Allogeneic Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation (HSCT), including total body irradiation, cyclophosphamide, busulfan, non-myeloablative or reduced-intensity conditioning (RIC), and anti-T cell serotherapy, aimed at preventing graft rejection and reducing relapse risk. It notes that a higher dose of CD34+ peripheral blood stem cells (e.g., >10^7 per kg body weight) has been associated with higher TREC levels, suggesting a dose threshold. Immunosuppressive drugs like corticosteroids and cyclosporine are mentioned in the context of GVHD prevention and treatment. However, specific dose-response relationships for HSCT or its components are not consistently reported, and the findings are often contradictory across studies due to variations in protocols and lack of randomized trials. The document focuses on monitoring applications rather than detailing specific therapeutic intervention doses.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: PTK7+ naive T cells contain higher levels of TRECs. PTK7+ cells produce less IL-2 and IFN gamma compared to the PTK7- subset.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigates the potential of extracellular vesicles (EVs) and EV-encapsulated microRNAs, specifically miR-451a, as circulating biomarkers for breast cancer, addressing challenges in their quantification. It details the methods for establishing murine breast cancer models and collecting human and murine serum, followed by the isolation and characterization of EVs using techniques such as transmission electron microscopy (TEM), Western blot, and nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA). Key findings include significantly higher total and small EV numbers, and increased miR-451a copies per EV, in human breast cancer patient sera compared to healthy controls, as well as a correlation between serum EV number and tumor burden in murine models. The research highlights the critical importance of direct EV quantification over protein yield for accurate biomarker assessment.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review investigates the potential of extracellular vesicle (EV)-enclosed non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs), including microRNAs (miRNAs), long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), piRNAs, circRNAs, and tsRNAs, along with N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA modifications, as stable, non-invasive diagnostic, prognostic, and monitoring biomarkers for a wide range of chronic liver diseases (CLDs). These include metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), metabolic-dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), Alcoholic Liver Disease (ALD), Autoimmune Hepatitis (AIH), Chronic Viral Hepatitis (HBV/HCV), cholestatic liver diseases, liver fibrosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), cholangiocarcinoma (CCA), and gallbladder carcinoma (GBC). The document also touches upon the therapeutic potential of engineered EVs for targeted cargo delivery in preclinical models to modulate inflammation and fibrosis pathways, highlighting their utility and associated challenges in clinical application.

treatment_details.therapy_type: This document primarily functions as a review investigating biomarkers for the diagnosis, prognosis, and monitoring of chronic liver diseases (CLDs). While the main focus is on biomarker identification, the review also touches upon the therapeutic potential of Extracellular Vesicle (EV) therapy, including engineered EVs for targeted cargo delivery, and mentions pharmacological inhibition of miR-34a as a potential therapeutic strategy.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study does not report specific therapeutic doses or dose-response comparisons for most interventions, as its primary focus is on biomarker evaluation. However, preclinical models utilized various EV-based interventions, such as native and engineered EVs derived from mesenchymal/stromal stem cells (MSCs) or human liver stem cells in models of liver fibrosis, NASH, and cancer, without detailed quantitative dosing. In biomarker contexts, some observations included a dose-dependent increase in serum miR-122 and miR-192 levels in induced liver injury mouse models. Disease states and exposures examined for biomarker changes included acute and chronic alcohol consumption, autoimmune inflammation, viral infections, cholestasis, CCl4-induced liver fibrosis, lipotoxic palmitic acid treatment of hepatocytes, arsenite-induced liver fibrosis, and various human liver conditions including biliary cholangitis, biliary atresia, liver fibrosis, HCC, CCA, and GBC.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the pro/anti-inflammatory status and molecular changes, including circulating microRNAs (miRs), proteasome, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), cytokines, and muscle proteomic changes, in two crewmembers after a 6-month International Space Station mission. document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated novel protein-based subphenotypes in Heart Failure with reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF) patients using unsupervised machine learning on 4210 repeatedly measured circulating proteins over a median 2.1-year follow-up in 382 patients. It identified four distinct subphenotypes with varying protein profiles, clinical characteristics (e.g., age, EF, chronic renal failure), and prognosis. These subphenotypes were driven by specific protein subsets associated with various biological mechanisms, including oxidative stress, inflammation, extracellular matrix organization, myocardial stretch/stress, injury, and renal dysfunction. Subphenotypes 2 and 3 demonstrated significantly worse clinical outcomes compared to subphenotype 1, highlighting the value of dynamic proteomic profiling for gaining pathophysiological insights and exploring personalized treatment opportunities in complex diagnoses like HFrEF.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Proteomic profiling and subphenotyping in Heart Failure with reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF) patients.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational study involving trimonthly blood sampling over a median follow-up of 2.1 years (IQR: 1.1–2.6 years) in 382 HFrEF patients, totaling 1066 blood samples. An aptamer-based multiplex proteomic approach (SOMAscan assay) was used to measure 4210 circulating proteins, yielding relative fluorescence units (RFUs) for comparative analysis rather than absolute concentrations. No specific intervention, treatment, or dose-response comparisons were conducted, as the study focused on characterizing disease subphenotypes and biomarker patterns over time. Repeated proteomic measurements (incorporating both intercept and slope coefficients) demonstrated improved accuracy for survival models (c-index 0.73, BIC 1023) compared to single time-point assessments.

document_context_data.document_summary: This scoping review systematically evaluates the application of systems biology-driven precision sports nutrition, incorporating 'omics' platforms (e.g., nutrigenetics, metabolomics, metagenomics, proteomics, epigenomics, lipidomics, multi-omics) and wearable technologies, particularly Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM), for endurance athletes. It maps existing literature, summarizes key findings, identifies research gaps, and investigates the impact of various nutritional interventions (e.g., polyphenols, astaxanthin, nitrates, carbohydrate-protein blends, probiotics) on immune function, inflammation, metabolism, gut microbiome composition, and glycemic responses during and after exercise. The review concludes that while these technologies offer insights into individual variability and physiological responses, current evidence is often insufficient to robustly link identified biomarkers to enhanced performance, recovery, and long-term health outcomes, noting methodological limitations.

treatment_details.therapy_type: This scoping review investigates precision sports nutrition strategies for endurance athletes, focusing on systems biology approaches (including various 'omics' platforms and wearable technologies like Continuous Glucose Monitoring) and a wide range of nutritional interventions. These interventions include specific foods (e.g., banana, blueberry, mango), supplements (e.g., soy protein, astaxanthin, beet-based nitrates, cranberry beverage, prebiotics, probiotics, cocoa flavanols), macronutrient manipulations (e.g., carbohydrate-protein blends, oligopeptides, specific protein amounts, dietary fat, low-carbohydrate high-fat diets, low/high FODMAP diets), and their interactions with diverse exercise regimens (e.g., cycling trials, marathons, ultra-endurance events, submaximal and prolonged exercise, exercise under heat stress).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This scoping review synthesizes findings from various studies on nutritional interventions, which include specific food consumptions (e.g., banana, mango) often compared against controls or other carbohydrate sources, and supplementations (e.g., astaxanthin, beet-based nitrates, cranberry beverage, specific probiotics) with durations ranging from acute intake to 2-week periods. It also examines the effects of different macronutrient strategies (e.g., low-carbohydrate high-fat diets, carbohydrate-protein blends) and genetic variations on caffeine metabolism. The review notes that while specific interventions are detailed, it generally reports on rather than conducts dose-response comparisons, highlighting that existing studies often compare interventions against controls. A key emphasis is on the need for tailored, individual-specific strategies, robust randomized controlled trials, and better reporting of training status, dose-response relationships, and demographic stratifications in future research, as current evidence often lacks detailed dose-response comparisons.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study performed a comprehensive qualitative and quantitative proteomic analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) derived from different somatic origins (fibroblasts and peripheral blood CD34+ cells), comparing them to original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC) and human embryonic stem cells (hESC). Using ESI-MS e and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry, complemented by Western blot validation, the research aimed to characterize hiPSC proteomic profiles, identify known and novel pluripotency markers, and distinguish hiPSCs from their somatic precursors. Key findings include the identification of approximately 220 commonly up-regulated proteins in pluripotent stem cell lines, the development and confirmation of a 22-protein marker panel for hiPSC characterization, and the observation of coordinated up-regulation of proteins involved in protein synthesis, folding, RNA processing, DNA replication, DNA repair, and energy metabolism (including oxidative phosphorylation and lipogenesis) in hiPSCs. The study also identified somatic cell markers that were down-regulated upon reprogramming and highlighted specific proteomic differences between hiPSCs and hESCs, contributing to improved hiPSC quality control for therapeutic applications.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Proteomic characterization and comparative analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) and human embryonic stem cells (hESCs).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was a characterization study, not a therapeutic intervention, thus no 'dose' of therapy was administered. Quantitative and qualitative proteomic analyses were performed using electrospray ionization (ESI)-MS e (label-free quantification with internal reference standard) and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry. Two hiPSC lines (iNC-01 from CD34+ cells, SB5-MP1 from fibroblasts, both generated using loxP-flanked excisable polycistronic STEMCCA lentiviral vector) and one hESC line (H9) were analyzed at earlier and later passages. Comparisons were made against their respective original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC). Proteins were considered differentially expressed if expression changed by >=1.5-fold, with a maximum false discovery rate of 2% and >95% confidence. Western blot analysis was used for validation. The developed marker panel was further tested in 8-9 additional hiPSC lines or passages from different somatic origins and reprogramming techniques. Differentiation studies were conducted with embryoid bodies at 24 hours and 7 days to assess marker changes during spontaneous differentiation.

document_context_data.document_summary: This document provides comprehensive guidelines for establishing and managing immune monitoring programs in patients undergoing allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation and cellular therapies (TCT/HCT). It highlights the critical need for standardized protocols for assay, flow cytometric, and data analysis to ensure consistent, scalable, and comparable results across multiple centers. The aim is to enhance prognosis prediction, enable early relapse detection, and improve clinical decision-making by evaluating immune reconstitution and functional recovery, as well as by identifying predictive cellular and secreted biomarkers for complications like graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), infections, viral reactivation, and relapse.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Allogeneic Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation (HCT), Transplant and Cellular Therapy (TCT), and related immune effector cell (IEC) therapies, including Genetically Modified Hematopoietic Stem Cell Therapies (GMHSCT) and CAR T-cell therapy.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The document primarily focuses on immune monitoring protocols post-transplantation rather than specific therapeutic dose-response comparisons for HCT/TCT itself. It highlights the variability in transplant platforms (e.g., T-cell depletion techniques, add backs, T-replete) and conditioning regimens (e.g., lymphocyte ablation, total body irradiation). Monitoring thresholds are mentioned for specific immune cells, such as >50 CD4+ T cells/μL within 100 days and >150 NK cells/mL at day 30 post-HCT, to indicate timely immune recovery. Recommended longitudinal sampling schedules are provided (e.g., biweekly for 3 months, then monthly/quarterly) post-HCT/GMHSCT, along with typical blood volumes (8-20 mL), but lack specific dose details for primary therapies or dose-response observations.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Some proteomic assays are flexible and accommodate both serum (from anticoagulant-free red-top tubes) and plasma (from sodium heparin or EDTA) for analysis.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Involved in a wide range of biological processes, including immune response, disease pathology, and cellular signaling.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Planning for future proteomic analyses within an immune monitoring program, specifically regarding sample type selection (serum vs. plasma).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Informs sample collection and processing strategies to ensure compatibility with planned proteomic assays for comprehensive immune monitoring.

document_context_data.document_summary: This review provides updated guidelines and a consensus for standardizing pre-analytical variables in salivary biomarker studies for Alzheimer's disease (AD) research. It critically appraises current methodologies, identifies inconsistencies, and proposes a standardized protocol for saliva collection, processing, and storage to improve reliability for diagnostic biomarker detection and quantification. The document investigates various protein and metabolomic biomarkers in saliva, assessing their diagnostic potential for AD and Mild Cognitive Impairment, and highlights the importance of controlling factors like collection methods, centrifugation, and storage conditions for accurate measurement.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Salivary Biomarker Research and Standardization for Alzheimer's Disease Diagnosis
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This is a comprehensive review article focusing on standardizing pre-analytical variables for salivary Alzheimer's Disease (AD) biomarker studies, rather than a therapeutic intervention or dose-response investigation. It critically discusses how inconsistent methodologies and pre-analytical factors (e.g., collection kits like Salivette vs. passive drooling, acute food intake, physical activity, stress, diurnal variations, dental restorations, freezing/thawing protocols, centrifugation speeds) influence biomarker detection and quantification, leading to conflicting findings for analytes like Aβ42, Aβ40, and AChE activity. The document proposes a standardized pre-analytical protocol, including pre-collection instructions (e.g., abstinence from food, drinks, smoking, alcohol, exercise), passive drool collection (e.g., 2 mL after 5 min pooling), and post-collection processing (e.g., immediate freezing, visual inspection, two-step centrifugation, aliquoting 100-250 µL). Various analytical methods (ELISA, Western blot, SIMOA, MS-based methods, NMR) were discussed for diagnostic marker identification, emphasizing that a universal protocol might not suit all biomarkers due to their diverse physiological roles.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Degradation occurs due to slow freezing, repeated freeze-thaw cycles (maximum of three cycles recommended, preferably two), and extended storage time. Storage at -20°C may lead to spectral changes and significant protein concentration decrease beyond 3 months, even with inhibitors.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Various fundamental biological roles, crucial for physiological and pathological insights.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Post-processing and storage of saliva samples (freezing, thawing, storage temperature, duration).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Compromised sample integrity and inaccurate quantification if proper freezing, storage protocols, and freeze-thaw cycle limitations are not strictly followed, impacting the reliability of assays.

document_context_data.document_summary: This document outlines the protocol for the PROSAP-A randomized controlled trial, investigating the effects of preoperative insomnia treatment (Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia or Sleep Education Therapy) on acute and long-term postoperative pain control, brain health, and physical recovery in patients undergoing total knee or hip arthroplasty. The study aims to assess various patient-reported outcomes (e.g., opioid use, quality of recovery, sleep, mood, quality of life), objective measures (e.g., actigraphic sleep, quantitative sensory testing for pain, neurocognitive function), and blood biomarkers (e.g., inflammatory, monoamine, genetic mediators) across preoperative and postoperative phases to determine the impact on pain intensity, opioid use, sleep quality, mental health, and functional recovery. The document also details the recruitment, randomization, blinding, and data collection plans for this prehabilitation approach.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Preoperative Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) and Sleep Education Therapy (SET) as an active comparator.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Both interventions are delivered over 4 weeks in a hybrid format, comprising a digital self-guided platform and weekly telehealth video sessions (up to 60 minutes). CBT-I sessions are conducted with a psychologist and include sleep restriction and stimulus control, while SET sessions are with a research nurse. A video-assisted booster session is provided 1-2 weeks postoperatively. No dose-response comparisons are reported as these are fixed intervention protocols.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Not yet quantified; subject of future study.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Diverse biological roles, involved in virtually all cellular processes and bodily functions.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Relevant to pathways involved in pain and sleep processes.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Broad indicator of various biological processes and pathways, potentially revealing insights into pain and sleep mechanisms.

document_context_data.document_summary: This document synthesizes the proceedings of the Tau2024 Global Conference, showcasing interdisciplinary advancements in tau-associated brain disorders. Key areas covered include the pathophysiology, molecular mechanisms, and brain microenvironments of tauopathies, as well as global perspectives highlighting genetic, socioeconomic, and linguistic diversity's impact on conditions like Frontotemporal Lobe Dementia and Primary Progressive Aphasia. The conference reviewed cellular mechanisms, advanced tau-PET, CSF, and blood-based biomarkers for diagnosis and monitoring of Alzheimer's Disease and other tauopathies, alongside discussions on therapeutic strategies such as antisense oligonucleotides, immunotherapy, senolytics, OGA inhibitors, and novel intrabody approaches aimed at reducing tau levels and aggregates.

treatment_details.therapy_type: The conference proceedings discussed a range of therapeutic advancements for tauopathies, including antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) therapy, tau immunotherapy (e.g., bepranemab), anti-tau-PEST intrabody therapy, pharmacological inhibition of PERK, senolytics (dasatinib plus quercetin), and O-GlcNAcase (OGA) inhibition (e.g., FNP-223).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Specific dose details varied by therapy: BIIB080 (ASO) demonstrated a dose-dependent reduction of approximately 60% in CSF tau. Anti-tau-PEST intrabodies reduced eGFP-tau by 70-78% in cellular models and endogenous tau by 38-58% in organoids over 21 days. A PERK inhibitor and nanobody constructs were effective in animal models without specific dose reporting. Bepranemab, senolytics (dasatinib plus quercetin), and FNP-223 (OGA inhibitor) were evaluated in early-phase human trials with various administration routes (IV, oral) and were generally well-tolerated, but detailed dose-response comparisons were not consistently reported across all interventions.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Individuals with lower Thal phase (limited amyloid beta deposition).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Suggests better degradation of misfolded/aggregated proteins, potentially conferring resistance to widespread amyloid beta deposition.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated novel protein-based subphenotypes in Heart Failure with reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF) patients using unsupervised machine learning on 4210 repeatedly measured circulating proteins over a median 2.1-year follow-up in 382 patients. It identified four distinct subphenotypes with varying protein profiles, clinical characteristics (e.g., age, EF, chronic renal failure), and prognosis. These subphenotypes were driven by specific protein subsets associated with various biological mechanisms, including oxidative stress, inflammation, extracellular matrix organization, myocardial stretch/stress, injury, and renal dysfunction. Subphenotypes 2 and 3 demonstrated significantly worse clinical outcomes compared to subphenotype 1, highlighting the value of dynamic proteomic profiling for gaining pathophysiological insights and exploring personalized treatment opportunities in complex diagnoses like HFrEF.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Proteomic profiling and subphenotyping in Heart Failure with reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF) patients.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational study involving trimonthly blood sampling over a median follow-up of 2.1 years (IQR: 1.1–2.6 years) in 382 HFrEF patients, totaling 1066 blood samples. An aptamer-based multiplex proteomic approach (SOMAscan assay) was used to measure 4210 circulating proteins, yielding relative fluorescence units (RFUs) for comparative analysis rather than absolute concentrations. No specific intervention, treatment, or dose-response comparisons were conducted, as the study focused on characterizing disease subphenotypes and biomarker patterns over time. Repeated proteomic measurements (incorporating both intercept and slope coefficients) demonstrated improved accuracy for survival models (c-index 0.73, BIC 1023) compared to single time-point assessments.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Low levels for slope coefficients, indicating less change or decreasing levels over time. Precise quantification not provided.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Contains many proteins found in intercept Subset A, thus related to oxidative stress, ataxia, intracellular components, translational processes, intracellular protein transport, actin cytoskeleton organization, post-transcriptional regulation of gene expression, platelet activation, and G-protein-coupled receptor signalling pathway.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: HFrEF Subphenotype 4 (characterized by higher SBP and higher EF with seemingly better clinical outcomes, where these proteins showed less change or decreasing levels over time).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Similar to Subset A, these changes over time may reflect prognostic implications, though for subphenotype 4 clinical outcomes seemed better than subphenotype 3.

document_context_data.document_summary: This multi-country feasibility study, part of the ISN 0by25 trial, investigated the implementation of a comprehensive program for recognizing and managing community-acquired acute kidney injury (AKI) and acute kidney disease (AKD) in low-resource settings (Bolivia, Nepal, Malawi). document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigates the metabolic reprogramming mechanisms underlying sorafenib activity and resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells and patients. It reveals that sorafenib impairs mitochondrial function, forcing a metabolic shift towards glycolysis, leading to D-lactate accumulation, which serves as a biomarker for treatment response. In resistant cells, adaptation involves rerouting dihydroxyacetone phosphate towards glycerol-3-phosphate synthesis, extensive phospholipid remodeling to evade ferroptosis, enhanced antioxidant capacity, and increased reliance on exogenous triglycerides, resulting in glycerol accumulation as a marker of resistance. The study identifies D-lactate and glycerol as potential plasma biomarkers for monitoring sorafenib efficacy and resistance in HCC patients.

Clinical treatment involved oral administration of 400 mg twice daily for HCC patients, with dose reductions permitted for adverse effects. Other interventions included adenoviral gene downregulation (50 MOI for Gpd1/1l, Gpd2; 20 MOI for Glo1) and supplementation with various fatty acids (SFAs, MUFAs, PUFAs) or lipoproteins (VLDL, LDL), and inhibition of Mgll with JZL184.
