document_context_data.document_summary: This document describes the protocol for an exploratory, multicenter, open-label, randomized controlled trial (CAME COVID-19 study) evaluating the efficacy of clarithromycin (400 mg/day or 800 mg/day) as an oral treatment for Japanese adult patients with mild COVID-19 pneumonia who do not require oxygen administration. The study aims to identify a new treatment strategy for mild COVID-19 and determine the number of days required to achieve a 50% or more improvement in clinical symptoms.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Clarithromycin
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Oral administration of clarithromycin is investigated in two dosage groups (800 mg/day, given as 400 mg twice daily, and 400 mg/day, given as 200 mg twice daily for 7 days) compared to a standard treatment control group. Patients are randomized in a 1:1:1 ratio, allowing for dose comparisons. Dose adjustment based on patient age, weight, and symptoms is possible. The doses are approved for other bacterial respiratory infections in Japan, and their safety is confirmed, but this is an exploratory trial as no prior dose-response data for COVID-19 pneumonia were available.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study conducted a secondary analysis of data from the European First-Episode Schizophrenia Trial (EUFEST) and Recovery After an Initial Schizophrenia Episode Early Treatment Program (RAISE-ETP) trials. It utilized machine learning models (support vector regressors and classifiers) to predict depressive symptom trajectories (changes in CDSS scores) and the occurrence of post-psychotic depressive episodes (PPD) at 6 and 12 months in first-episode psychosis (FEP) patients with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders. The models leveraged various baseline variables including sociodemographic information, clinical assessments (e.g., PANSS, CDSS scores), neurocognitive performance, quality of life, and blood-based biomarkers, demonstrating accurate prediction and geographical generalizability across populations. The study also analyzed how factors like treatment assignment (e.g., NAVIGATE program) and antidepressant prescription influenced model misclassification and patient outcomes.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Antipsychotic medication, NAVIGATE program (psychosocial intervention), Antidepressant coadministration, and Usual community care.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants in the EUFEST trial received 1 year of antipsychotic treatment (described as "minimally antipsychotic-treated"), while RAISE-ETP participants were allocated to either usual community care or the NAVIGATE program. Antidepressant prescriptions were observed, with RAISE-ETP patients showing a higher rate (33.33%) compared to EUFEST (2.18%). The NAVIGATE program was associated with a sharper decline in depressive symptoms, especially among patients prescribed antidepressants at baseline. However, no specific doses, intensities, or durations for antipsychotics, the NAVIGATE program, or antidepressants were detailed, nor were dose-response comparisons reported for any treatment; their influence on predictive model performance and patient characteristics was primarily analyzed.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the impact of low (LV-HIIT) and high (HV-HIIT) volumes of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) on vascular-endothelial function, oxidative stress, and atherosclerosis markers in patients after an acute myocardial infarction (AMI). The 16-week supervised HIIT programs, regardless of volume, led to a volume-dependent enhancement in endothelial function (FMD) and a decrease in oxidative stress (ox-LDL). A reduction in vascular wall thickness (cIMT) was also observed, with LV-HIIT proving sufficient to initiate favorable adaptations and reduce cardiovascular risk. The study also assessed anthropometric and other cardiovascular markers, comparing HIIT groups to an active control.

treatment_details.therapy_type: High-intensity Interval Training (HIIT) and Unsupervised Physical Activity Recommendations (Active Control, AC)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study investigated High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) with two volumes: Low Volume (LV-HIIT) and High Volume (HV-HIIT), and an Active Control (AC) group. LV-HIIT involved 8 minutes of high-intensity exercise (R3) within a 20-minute total session. HV-HIIT involved 16 minutes of high-intensity exercise (R3) within a 20-40 minute total session. Both supervised HIIT groups exercised 2 non-consecutive days per week for 16 weeks (32 sessions) on treadmills and cycle ergometers, with intensity individualized based on cardiorespiratory fitness, ventilatory thresholds, beat-to-beat HR, and the Böarg scale. The AC group received individualized recommendations for unsupervised physical activity, advised to perform at least 30 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity 5–7 days per week for 16 weeks. FMD and ox-LDL changes were volume-dependent (HV-HIIT showing greater effects), while cIMT reduction was similar between LV-HIIT and HV-HIIT, indicating a volume-independent effect for cIMT and confirming LV-HIIT's effectiveness.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased by 10.4 ± 5.5% (p = 0.0219) in the AC group.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: 16-week Active Control (AC) physical activity.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Increased pulse pressure is associated with heightened arterial stiffness and a higher risk of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality.

The study found UHR to be a significant independent predictor and risk factor for increased cIMT and carotid intima-media thickening, with this association being particularly pronounced in older men. document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigates the metabolic reprogramming mechanisms underlying sorafenib activity and resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells and patients. It reveals that sorafenib impairs mitochondrial function, forcing a metabolic shift towards glycolysis, leading to D-lactate accumulation, which serves as a biomarker for treatment response. In resistant cells, adaptation involves rerouting dihydroxyacetone phosphate towards glycerol-3-phosphate synthesis, extensive phospholipid remodeling to evade ferroptosis, enhanced antioxidant capacity, and increased reliance on exogenous triglycerides, resulting in glycerol accumulation as a marker of resistance. The study identifies D-lactate and glycerol as potential plasma biomarkers for monitoring sorafenib efficacy and resistance in HCC patients.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Sorafenib
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The primary therapy investigated was Sorafenib, a multi-kinase inhibitor for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). In vitro studies used sorafenib at an IC50 of 8.5 µM for acute, 48-hour, or 7-day prolonged treatments, and 7 µM for sorafenib-resistant IR-Huh7 cells. Clinical treatment involved oral administration of 400 mg twice daily for HCC patients, with dose reductions permitted for adverse effects. Other interventions included adenoviral gene downregulation (50 MOI for Gpd1/1l, Gpd2; 20 MOI for Glo1) and supplementation with various fatty acids (SFAs, MUFAs, PUFAs) or lipoproteins (VLDL, LDL), and inhibition of Mgll with JZL184. No detailed dose-response comparisons were consistently reported for sorafenib, though Mgll inhibition showed dose-dependent effects.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly increased in sorafenib-treated cells.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the association between thalamic volume and heart rate recovery following an orthostatic challenge in older adults from The Irish Longitudinal Study on Aging (TILDA). It consistently found that smaller thalamic volume is associated with slower heart rate recovery, suggesting that thalamic structural integrity is a potential risk marker for autonomic dysfunction, cardiovascular events, and sudden cardiac death, while also differentiating its contribution from other subcortical brain regions.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Orthostatic Challenge (Active Standing Test)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants in this observational study underwent an active stand protocol where they lay supine for 10 minutes, then stood quickly and remained standing for 3 minutes. Beat-to-beat heart rate and blood pressure were monitored, with heart rate recovery (HRR) specifically measured between 10 and 30 seconds post-standing (HRR 10|30s). This study focused on correlating brain volume with physiological response, thus no therapeutic intervention or dose-response comparisons were reported.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Interaction with HRR 10|30s was significantly different from the thalamus x HRR 10|30s interaction.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: B = 0.02; CI 95 0.01–0.04; p < .001 when compared to thalamus interaction.

document_context_data.document_summary: This surveillance report details malaria cases in the United States in 2018, reporting a 15.6% decrease in confirmed cases from 2017 while noting an overall increase since 1972, with 98.1% being imported cases predominantly from Africa and P. falciparum as the most common species. It describes comprehensive surveillance methodologies, diagnostic tests, and molecular analyses for antimalarial drug resistance markers, particularly for P. falciparum against pyrimethamine, sulfadoxine, chloroquine, and mefloquine, with no resistance markers for atovaquone or artemisinin. The report also investigates chemoprophylaxis adherence (found to be poor), treatment patterns for uncomplicated and severe malaria, and emphasizes the critical importance of prompt diagnosis, appropriate treatment with CDC guidelines, and continuous surveillance to prevent local transmission.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Malaria prevention (chemoprophylaxis, including Tafenoquine), diagnosis (microscopy, PCR, RDTs), and treatment for both uncomplicated and severe malaria (oral antimalarials like atovaquone-proguanil, artemether-lumefantrine, quinine; parenteral IV artesunate for severe malaria), alongside molecular surveillance for antimalarial drug resistance.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Chemoprophylaxis adherence was poor among U.S. residents with imported malaria in 2018, with 24.5% reporting use and 95.0% demonstrating non-adherence or inconsistent regimens, often due to forgetting or prematurely stopping. Tafenoquine offers an abbreviated schedule for eligible adults. For treatment, IV artesunate became the first-line for severe malaria in April 2019, replacing IV quinidine gluconate, though 52.1% of severe cases in 2018 did not receive guideline-appropriate treatment. Uncomplicated malaria treatments varied, with 91.7% receiving appropriate care, and primaquine was often used for P. vivax/P. ovale relapse prevention, though sometimes inappropriately. No explicit dose-response comparisons were reported, but treatment choice was emphasized based on species, severity, patient factors (e.g., pregnancy), and CDC guidelines.

matched_biomarker_details.activity_type: Antimalarial drug resistance marker testing (identification of genetic polymorphisms); Gene sequence polymorphisms; Amplification and analysis of resistance mutations

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Found in 99 (98.0%) of 106 P. falciparum-positive specimens analyzed. Identified at codons A16V, C50R, N51I, C59R, S108T/N, and I164L. Out of 101 specimens analyzed for five loci, 93 (92.1%) had three or more resistance markers.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Molecular surveillance of P. falciparum positive malaria cases in the United States, 2018; Detection of antimalarial drug resistance in imported P. falciparum malaria cases.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Guides treatment decisions; indicates potential treatment failure with pyrimethamine and pyrimethamine-containing drugs, which are not recommended by CDC for malaria treatment in the United States due to widespread resistance.

document_context_data.document_summary: This longitudinal study systematically investigated distinct host responses, cellular injury, and tissue damage in pediatric COVID-19 and Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children (MIS-C) through next-generation sequencing of plasma cell-free RNA (cfRNA), cell-free DNA (cfDNA), and whole-blood RNA (wbRNA) from 228 patients. It revealed unique molecular signatures distinguishing MIS-C from COVID-19, including increased multiorgan involvement and pyroptosis-related gene enrichment in MIS-C, alongside shared and distinct pro-inflammatory pathways. The analysis highlighted the complementary insights provided by cfRNA and wbRNA profiling, demonstrating varying biomarker trajectories, such as persistent immune dysregulation in COVID-19 compared to MIS-C resolution.

Samples were collected at acute, 1-month, and 3-month post-hospitalization time points. While some patients received intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg), it was not a tested intervention, and its administration was found not to significantly confound observed molecular differences. No therapeutic interventions or dose-response comparisons were conducted or reported.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the physiological and biochemical responses, including oxygen uptake, power output, and arterial lactate concentrations, during two maximal incremental cycle ergometer tests performed 24 hours apart in female Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS) patients compared to healthy controls. The findings revealed that previous exercise deteriorates physical performance and increases lactate accumulation in ME/CFS patients, while it improves lactate handling in healthy subjects, indicating a disturbed metabolic response to exertion in ME/CFS.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Repeated Cardiopulmonary Exercise Testing (CPET), specifically maximal incremental ramp tests.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Two maximal incremental ramp tests (CPET 1 and CPET 2) were performed 24 hours apart on a cycle ergometer. Each test included a 2-min resting phase and 2 min of unloaded pedaling, followed by a linear increase in power output until volitional exhaustion. Increment rates were individually set (10-24 W/min for ME/CFS patients; 15-30 W/min for controls) to reach VO2peak within 8-12 min. Arterial lactate concentrations were measured every 30 seconds during exercise. Blood sampling during CPET 1 amounted to approximately 150–200 mL. No specific dose-response comparisons for different fixed exercise intensities were reported beyond the comparisons between the two repeated tests.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Upregulated expression in PBMCs from ME/CFS patients.

matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Proposes a disturbed PDK regulation in ME/CFS patients, potentially limiting pyruvate flux and affecting lactate clearance through oxidation, contributing to disturbed energy metabolism.

document_context_data.document_summary: This randomized controlled trial investigated the effects of 8 weeks of daily 5g Cistanche deserticola (CD) extract supplementation, combined with progressive high-intensity resistance training, on muscle strength and recovery in both untrained and resistance-trained male participants. The study found that CD supplementation significantly enhanced muscle strength (1RM bench press and squat, MVIC) and endurance (RTF in untrained), and facilitated post-exercise recovery by modulating hormonal responses (increased testosterone, reduced cortisol) and decreasing markers of stress and inflammation (reduced CRP and CK levels) in both cohorts. Mechanistic insights suggest CD's role in improving energy metabolism, reducing muscle degradation, enhancing antioxidant defense, modulating neurotransmission, and regulating endocrine axes.

treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants received 5 g of CD extract daily, administered in two sachets (after breakfast and lunch) for 8 consecutive weeks, alongside a placebo group. A standardized resistance training program was completed three times per week for eight weeks. This program involved 4 sets of 10-12 repetitions at 65-70% of 1RM for weeks 1-4, and 4 sets of 6-8 repetitions at 80% of 1RM for weeks 5-8. Maximal strength (1RM bench press/squat, MVIC) and endurance (RTF bench press) were assessed. No dose-response comparisons for CD were reported, only comparison to placebo.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study employed NMR metabolomics to investigate metabolic profiles in serum and urine from COVID-19 patients across varying disease severities (Medical Ward and Intensive Care Unit) and healthy controls. The primary aim was to identify biomarkers for COVID-19 diagnosis, severity classification, and prognosis, and to explore correlations with clinical factors like hypertension, obesity, and dyslipidemia. Key findings include the development of a highly efficient diagnostic panel (isoleucine, TMAO, glucose) and a robust severity classification panel (ethanol, TMAO, tyrosine, betaine, and clinical characteristics), alongside identification of numerous individual metabolites and clinical parameters associated with infection, disease progression, hospitalization duration, and patient outcome.

treatment_details.therapy_type: NMR metabolomics-based profiling and observational study of COVID-19 infection
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This observational study analyzed 80 serum and urine samples from COVID-19 patients (34 intensive care, 46 hospitalized) and 32 from healthy controls using NMR spectroscopy. The research focused on identifying and validating metabolite-based panels for COVID-19 diagnosis and severity classification. A diagnostic panel of isoleucine, TMAO, and glucose achieved an AUC of 0.91 (86.08% sensitivity, 83.87% specificity). A severity classification panel, combining ethanol, TMAO, tyrosine, betaine, and clinical characteristics (obesity/overweight, dyslipidemia, lymphocyte count), achieved an AUC of 0.825 (84.85% sensitivity, 72.09% specificity). No therapeutic intervention or dose-response comparisons were part of the study design.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Contributed to a panel (AUC increased from 0.947 to 0.971 with addition of sex and neutrophil percentage) to discriminate COVID-19 positive individuals from non-COVID-19 (reported by López-Hernández et al.).

document_context_data.document_summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial investigated the effects of 12 weeks of daily protein supplementation on lean body mass, fat mass, muscle strength, physical performance, and various biochemical markers in physically active older adults with low habitual protein intake, who were also training for a 4-day walking event. The study found that protein supplementation resulted in a larger increase in relative lean body mass and a greater reduction in fat mass compared to placebo. While both the protein and placebo groups showed improvements in physical performance and cardiorespiratory fitness due to the walking exercise, no additional between-group differences were observed in muscle strength, muscle contractile properties, or physical performance from protein supplementation. Serum urea increased in the protein group, but no adverse effects on renal function or muscle damage markers were noted, indicating protein supplementation is a safe strategy for this population.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Protein supplementation combined with walking exercise
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Physically active older adults were randomized to receive either 31 g of milk protein concentrate daily (split into 15g at breakfast and 15g post-exercise/lunch) or an iso-caloric placebo for 12 weeks. This increased the protein group's total daily protein intake from 0.86 ± 0.23 g/kg/day upon enrollment to 1.29 ± 0.28 g/kg/day at 12 weeks. Both groups concurrently participated in walking exercise training for a 4-day walking event, covering an average of 338-391 km over 12 weeks. No dose-response comparisons for protein intake were reported, only the comparison between the protein and placebo groups.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: The significant decline in force of the quadriceps muscle during 2 min of electrical stimulation did not differ between groups at baseline and after the supplementation period.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the impact of two distinct heat stress modalities—exertional heating (exercise/cycling) and exogenous heating (hot water immersion)—on physiological responses, stress markers, and peripheral kynurenine pathway (KP) metabolites in 11 young healthy males. Both modalities were designed to induce a comparable increase in core body temperature up to 39°C. The study found that heat exposure transiently induced the KP, elevating several plasma KP metabolite concentrations (Kynurenic acid, Picolinic acid, 3-Hydroxykynurenine, Quinolinic acid, Kynurenine, KYN/TRP ratio) and stress markers (Cortisol, Prolactin, Adrenaline, Noradrenaline, Lactate). These changes generally returned to baseline during recovery, suggesting adaptability of KP enzymes to physiological stressors. Differential changes were observed depending on the specific heat stress protocol and the phase (heating vs. recovery), with exertional heating often showing more pronounced effects for some markers and sustained elevation for others (e.g., KYNA, PIC in EXE). The study highlights the potential of KP metabolites as disease biomarkers.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Induced Hyperthermia / Heat Stress (Exertional heating and Exogenous heating)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants underwent two distinct heat stress modalities: exertional heating (EXE) via cycling exercise at an intensity eliciting 60% VO2max in a 30°C room, and exogenous heating (EXO) via hot water immersion up to the waistline in a 44°C bath. Both trials were conducted until rectal temperature (Trec) reached 39°C (with measurements taken at every 0.5°C increment up to a maximum of 39.5°C), followed by a recovery phase to a baseline temperature of 37.5°C. The time required to reach specific temperature set points was similar in both trials. No direct dose-response comparisons were explicitly reported; however, EXE induced greater increases in stress markers and sympathetic vasomotor activity compared to EXO, suggesting differential physiological loads.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased during both EXE and EXO trials, peaking at 39°C (EXE) and 38.5°C during the recovery phase (EXO) (p < 0.05). Concentrations steadily increased during the heating phase of the EXE trial and reached their peak during the recovery phase. Reverted to baseline levels upon returning to homeostatic temperatures. Concentrations were detected higher than the LLOQ of 50 nM.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Neurotoxic metabolite of the kynurenine pathway, involved in tryptophan degradation, neurological and psychiatric disorders, immune responses, cardiovascular function, and energy metabolism. Acts as an N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor agonist, contributing to excitotoxicity.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Core temperature increases induced by exogenous heating (hot water immersion, 44°C) or exertional heating (exercise/cycling at 60% VO2max in a 30°C room), until rectal temperature reached 39°C, followed by a recovery phase. Samples collected at 0.5°C rectal temperature increments.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Potential disease biomarker. Indicates the induction and activity of the kynurenine pathway due to physiological stress, as well as potential neuroinflammatory processes and neurotoxic risk under thermal stress. The transient increase and return to baseline suggest adaptability of KP enzymes to physiological stressors. Implicated in neurological, psychiatric, cardiovascular disorders, and cancer.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study aimed to identify novel diagnostic plasma biomarkers for sport-related concussion (SRC) by investigating proteomic changes in collegiate athletes. The study focused on biomarker discovery for diagnosis rather than a therapeutic intervention, thus no specific dose comparisons for a therapeutic agent were reported, nor was a 'dose' of concussion administered or compared.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review investigates the potential of extracellular vesicle (EV)-enclosed non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs), including microRNAs (miRNAs), long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), piRNAs, circRNAs, and tsRNAs, along with N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA modifications, as stable, non-invasive diagnostic, prognostic, and monitoring biomarkers for a wide range of chronic liver diseases (CLDs). These include metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), metabolic-dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), Alcoholic Liver Disease (ALD), Autoimmune Hepatitis (AIH), Chronic Viral Hepatitis (HBV/HCV), cholestatic liver diseases, liver fibrosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), cholangiocarcinoma (CCA), and gallbladder carcinoma (GBC). The document also touches upon the therapeutic potential of engineered EVs for targeted cargo delivery in preclinical models to modulate inflammation and fibrosis pathways, highlighting their utility and associated challenges in clinical application.

treatment_details.therapy_type: This document primarily functions as a review investigating biomarkers for the diagnosis, prognosis, and monitoring of chronic liver diseases (CLDs). While the main focus is on biomarker identification, the review also touches upon the therapeutic potential of Extracellular Vesicle (EV) therapy, including engineered EVs for targeted cargo delivery, and mentions pharmacological inhibition of miR-34a as a potential therapeutic strategy.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study does not report specific therapeutic doses or dose-response comparisons for most interventions, as its primary focus is on biomarker evaluation. However, preclinical models utilized various EV-based interventions, such as native and engineered EVs derived from mesenchymal/stromal stem cells (MSCs) or human liver stem cells in models of liver fibrosis, NASH, and cancer, without detailed quantitative dosing. In biomarker contexts, some observations included a dose-dependent increase in serum miR-122 and miR-192 levels in induced liver injury mouse models. Disease states and exposures examined for biomarker changes included acute and chronic alcohol consumption, autoimmune inflammation, viral infections, cholestasis, CCl4-induced liver fibrosis, lipotoxic palmitic acid treatment of hepatocytes, arsenite-induced liver fibrosis, and various human liver conditions including biliary cholangitis, biliary atresia, liver fibrosis, HCC, CCA, and GBC.

Filtering criteria for differential gene expression included |log2FC|>1 and P<0.05 for bulk RNA-seq, and P<0.01 with FC ≥1.4 or ≤−1.6 for multi-cancer exoRNA-seq. document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated plasma protein biomarkers (including cytokines, chemokines, growth factors, and cell death markers) to identify unique expression patterns associated with the severity and duration of Primary Graft Dysfunction (PGD) after lung transplantation. It identified several strong biomarker candidates, such as IP-10, MIP-1B, RANTES, M30, M65, IL-1Ra, PDGF-BB, G-CSF, IL-4, MIP-1A, IL-17, IL-9, IL-1B, IL-10, IL-6, TNF-alpha, sRAGE, and PAI-1, which are informative for early detection, predicting clinical course, and monitoring treatment efficacy of PGD.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Lung transplantation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study included 40 consecutive lung transplant patients (February 2018 – May 2019). Blood samples were collected immediately pretransplant (T0) and at 6, 24, 48, and 72 hours post-transplant/reperfusion, with PGD severity scored using 2016 ISHLT guidelines. Biomarker analysis involved a bead-based multiplex assay for 27 plasma proteins (cytokines, growth factors, chemokines) and enzyme-linked immunoassay for cell injury markers (M30, M65, sRAGE, PAI-1). Statistical methods included pairwise comparisons, sensitivity, and temporal analyses. An immunosuppression regimen of basiliximab, solumedrol, and mycophenolate (induction) and tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil (maintenance) was used. Intraoperative extracorporeal life support (ECLS), ex vivo lung perfusion (EVLP), and postoperative extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) were considered for severe PGD (PGD3). No specific dose-response comparisons for transplantation or immunosuppression were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Lower levels pre-transplant were associated with PGD3 at T48–72h (p < 0.05). Differential perioperative expression correlated with PGD3 development at T48–72 h (FDR < 0.1 and p < 0.05). Correlated with PGD severity in paired analysis and with the duration of PGD in sensitivity analysis.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study clinically validated C12FDG as a flow cytometry-based biomarker for detecting senescent peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and T cells in humans. It investigated the association of C12FDG+ cells with chronological age, sex, and various serum senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) biomarkers. Findings revealed that C12FDG++ PBMCs and T cells increase with age, are elevated in males and patients with mild to moderate osteoarthritis, and decrease following fisetin treatment. The C12FDG platform shows promise as a quantifiable clinical tool for assessing healthy aging, age-related orthopedic decline, and the efficacy of senolytic therapies.

document_context_data.document_summary: This observational study aimed to identify biomarkers for predicting severe dengue disease progression and cytokine release syndrome (CRS) by evaluating an integrated multiplex panel of cytokines/chemokines and clinical parameters in adult dengue patients. Researchers compared various severity groups (mild, severe without/with comorbidities, and healthy controls) across acute and convalescent phases. Key findings highlighted how specific markers like IL-18, IL-8, IL-6, and IFN-γ are altered in severe dengue, particularly with comorbidities, and their correlation with clinical indicators such as platelet counts and NS1. The study also characterized demographic and clinical parameters across patient groups, confirming the utility of a 24-plex cytokine/chemokine panel designed based on extensive literature review.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study on biomarker identification and monitoring for dengue disease progression and severity
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational study on 30 adult dengue patients (mean age 61.6 years, 17 male, 13 female) categorized into three severity groups based on WHO criteria (1997 and 2009): Mild Dengue Fever (MDF, n=10), Severe Dengue Disease without comorbidities (SDD-C, n=10), and Severe Dengue Disease with comorbidities (SDD+C, n=10). Six healthy controls were also included. A 24-plex panel of cytokines/chemokines was used to measure plasma levels, along with clinical blood parameters. Blood samples were collected during the acute febrile phase (before 6 days from disease onset) and the convalescent phase (9-18 days from disease onset). No therapeutic interventions or dose-response comparisons were reported, as the study focused on natural disease progression and biomarker correlation with severity.

matched_biomarker_details.activity_type: Protein Level; Protein Concentration; Chemokine Level; Cytokine/Chemokine Panel (Protein Level)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Decreased in SDD compared to MDF (decreasing trend, not statistically significant: P = 0.071; x® = 6515.1 pg/mL in SDD vs x® = 12021.6 pg/mL in MDF). Increased in all dengue cases compared with healthy subjects, but showed an overall reduction in SDD. Higher in the acute febrile phase of dengue patients compared to healthy controls (P < 0.05), showing a borderline significant increase in acute dengue compared with healthy. document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review investigates the potential of extracellular vesicle (EV)-enclosed non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs), including microRNAs (miRNAs), long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), piRNAs, circRNAs, and tsRNAs, along with N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA modifications, as stable, non-invasive diagnostic, prognostic, and monitoring biomarkers for a wide range of chronic liver diseases (CLDs). These include metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), metabolic-dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), Alcoholic Liver Disease (ALD), Autoimmune Hepatitis (AIH), Chronic Viral Hepatitis (HBV/HCV), cholestatic liver diseases, liver fibrosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), cholangiocarcinoma (CCA), and gallbladder carcinoma (GBC). The document also touches upon the therapeutic potential of engineered EVs for targeted cargo delivery in preclinical models to modulate inflammation and fibrosis pathways, highlighting their utility and associated challenges in clinical application.

treatment_details.therapy_type: This document primarily functions as a review investigating biomarkers for the diagnosis, prognosis, and monitoring of chronic liver diseases (CLDs). treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study does not report specific therapeutic doses or dose-response comparisons for most interventions, as its primary focus is on biomarker evaluation. document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the impact of 4 weeks of Urolithin A (UA) supplementation on running performance, recovery, and mitochondrial biomarkers in highly trained male distance runners during an altitude training camp. document_context_data.document_summary: This study performed a comprehensive qualitative and quantitative proteomic analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) derived from different somatic origins (fibroblasts and peripheral blood CD34+ cells), comparing them to original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC) and human embryonic stem cells (hESC). Using ESI-MS e and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry, complemented by Western blot validation, the research aimed to characterize hiPSC proteomic profiles, identify known and novel pluripotency markers, and distinguish hiPSCs from their somatic precursors. Key findings include the identification of approximately 220 commonly up-regulated proteins in pluripotent stem cell lines, the development and confirmation of a 22-protein marker panel for hiPSC characterization, and the observation of coordinated up-regulation of proteins involved in protein synthesis, folding, RNA processing, DNA replication, DNA repair, and energy metabolism (including oxidative phosphorylation and lipogenesis) in hiPSCs. The study also identified somatic cell markers that were down-regulated upon reprogramming and highlighted specific proteomic differences between hiPSCs and hESCs, contributing to improved hiPSC quality control for therapeutic applications.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Proteomic characterization and comparative analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) and human embryonic stem cells (hESCs).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was a characterization study, not a therapeutic intervention, thus no 'dose' of therapy was administered. Quantitative and qualitative proteomic analyses were performed using electrospray ionization (ESI)-MS e (label-free quantification with internal reference standard) and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry. Two hiPSC lines (iNC-01 from CD34+ cells, SB5-MP1 from fibroblasts, both generated using loxP-flanked excisable polycistronic STEMCCA lentiviral vector) and one hESC line (H9) were analyzed at earlier and later passages. Comparisons were made against their respective original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC). Proteins were considered differentially expressed if expression changed by >=1.5-fold, with a maximum false discovery rate of 2% and >95% confidence. Western blot analysis was used for validation. The developed marker panel was further tested in 8-9 additional hiPSC lines or passages from different somatic origins and reprogramming techniques. Differentiation studies were conducted with embryoid bodies at 24 hours and 7 days to assess marker changes during spontaneous differentiation.

document_context_data.document_summary: This proteogenomic study investigated Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) samples from adult and pediatric patients at diagnosis, relapse, and primary resistance to identify underlying molecular characteristics. It revealed that AML relapse is consistently associated with reprogrammed energy metabolism, marked by increased mitochondrial ribosomal proteins and respiratory chain complex subunits, and a distinctive pro-inflammatory proteomic signature with higher granzymes and lower CR1/CD35. The analysis also identified increased levels of RNA splicing-related proteins, novel peptides, single amino acid alterations, and fusion peptides, highlighting potential new biomarkers and immunotherapeutic targets for improving AML treatment and patient survival.

Comparisons were made between different disease states (diagnosis vs. relapse/primary resistance), but no specific therapeutic interventions or dose-response relationships for a particular therapy were evaluated or reported.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigates the molecular determinants of hemogenic endothelial cells (HECs) and hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs) by generating a GATA2w/eGFP reporter in human embryonic stem cells (hESCs). The reporter accurately marks endogenous GATA2 expression, which is critical for endothelial-to-hematopoietic transition (EHT). A key finding is the identification of ITGB3 (CD61) as a reliable novel positive surface marker that precisely labels functional HECs with superior hemogenic potential, both in hESC/hPSC differentiation in vitro and in embryonic day 10 mouse embryos in vivo. The research provides a robust platform for dissecting hematopoiesis and facilitates the generation of functional hematopoietic stem cells in vitro.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Gene targeting using TALENs, in vitro human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC) differentiation, and in vivo mouse embryo analysis.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: GATA2w/eGFP reporter was generated in H1 hESCs via gene editing (TALENs, electroporation of 1 μg linearized vector and 2.5 μg of each TALEN plasmid into 1 × 10^6 H1 cells, puromycin selection at 0.5 μg/mL, and Cre recombinase (400 ng per 1 × 10^6 cells) for cassette removal). In vitro differentiation involved hPSC blood differentiation protocols using co-culturing with OP9 stromal cells or AGM-S3 co-culture. Bone morphogenetic protein 4 (BMP4) treatment was applied for 5 days. Cell seeding used Y-27632 (10 μM). CFU assay medium contained 100 ng/mL recombinant murine stem cell factor, 10 ng/mL recombinant murine interleukin-3, 10 ng/mL recombinant human interleukin-6, and 3 U/mL human erythropoietin, with endothelial cell assays using 100 ng/mL vascular endothelial growth factor. In vivo analysis included mouse embryos at E10.0, E11, E12, E14, with fractionation of endothelial cells based on CD61 expression (CD61 high, CD61 low, and CD61 − subpopulations). No specific dose-response comparisons for differentiation conditions or therapeutic interventions were reported beyond qualitative observations of effect.

matched_biomarker_details.activity_type: Gene transcript (RNA sequencing); Transcription Factor activity.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Highly expressed in GATA2/eGFP+ HECs.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Critical transcription factor for EHT or HPC function.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Transcriptome analysis of GATA2/eGFP+ HECs during hESC blood differentiation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates its important role in promoting EHT and HPC function within GATA2/eGFP+ HECs.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of New Zealand Blackcurrant (NZBC) extract supplementation on markers of exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) and recovery following strenuous isokinetic resistance exercise in healthy, non-resistance trained men and women. The findings indicate that NZBC extract consumption leads to faster recovery of muscle function, significantly attenuates muscle soreness, and reduces serum creatine kinase (CK) levels, collectively demonstrating improved functional recovery and mitigated muscle damage.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Dietary supplementation with New Zealand Blackcurrant (NZBC) extract, combined with strenuous eccentric isokinetic resistance exercise.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants consumed either 3 g·day−1 NZBC extract (containing 105 mg anthocyanins) or a placebo (microcrystalline cellulose M102) once daily for a total of 12 days (8 days prior to and 4 days following strenuous exercise). The exercise protocol involved 60 strenuous concentric and eccentric contractions of the biceps brachii muscle on an isokinetic dynamometer (4 sets of 15 maximal contractions at 45°/s concentric and 60°/s eccentric, with 1-min recovery). The supplement was consumed 1 hour before exercise on day 8. No dose-response comparisons for NZBC extract were reported.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: recovered in NZBC, suppressed in PLA
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: While there was a significant change over time in ROM in both NZBC and placebo groups (Friedman test, p < 0.01), there was no statistically significant difference between groups (Mann–Whitney U tests, p > 0.05). At 96 h post-exercise, ROM had recovered in the NZBC group but remained suppressed in the PLA group compared to baseline.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Measures joint flexibility and functional integrity, often impacted by muscle swelling or stiffness.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Post-strenuous eccentric isokinetic resistance exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) and NZBC extract supplementation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Recovery of elbow ROM indicates improved functional recovery, while suppressed ROM suggests continued stiffness or functional impairment. Despite no statistically significant difference between groups across all time points, the NZBC group showed recovered ROM at 96h post-exercise, unlike the placebo group.

document_context_data.document_summary: The study developed and applied a Nano-omics integrative workflow, utilizing nanoparticle protein coronas, to link systemic (plasma) and localized (tumor tissue) protein changes associated with glioblastoma (GB) progression. This comprehensive proteomic investigation in GL261 murine models and human high-grade glioma patients aimed to identify GB-specific molecular pathways and peripheral blood biomarkers for early detection and disease monitoring. The methodology included inducing murine GB models, preparing and administering liposome nanoparticles in vivo or incubating them ex vivo with plasma, and subsequent proteomic analysis via mass spectrometry to identify differentially abundant proteins. The findings revealed significant plasma protein alterations, even at low tumor burden, with over 30% overlap between GB-specific plasma and tumor tissue proteomes, leading to the identification of 48 potential GB biomarker candidates across various biological pathways.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Biomarker Discovery Method: Nano-omics integrative proteomics workflow utilizing nanoparticle protein coronas for glioblastoma (GB).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study involved inducing murine glioblastoma by stereotactic injection of 50,000 GL261 cells into the striatum of C57BL/6 J mice. Liposomes (HSPC:Chol:DSPE-PEG2000) were prepared at a final lipid concentration of 25 mM and administered intravenously at a lipid dose of 0.125 mM/g body weight (equivalent to 5 mg/kg doxorubicin-loaded liposomes) 10 minutes prior to blood collection in mice. In human validation, ex vivo nanoparticle corona analysis was performed on pre-operative plasma samples from 10 high-grade glioma patients. Matched blood and tumor tissue samples were collected from mice at D7, D14, and D18 post-tumor inoculation, representing low, medium, and large tumor volumes. Matched resected tumor tissue from human patients was analyzed by LCM-coupled LC:MS/MS. No specific dose-response comparisons for nanoparticle application or tumor cell inoculation were reported for therapeutic purposes, as the focus was on biomarker discovery.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Progressively upregulated with increasing disease burden; upregulated in tumour tissue; upregulated in human plasma (Supplementary Fig 6)

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Linked to the regulation of actin cytoskeleton pathway.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Increasing Glioblastoma (GB) disease burden in mice and human patients.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Potential biomarker for Glioblastoma (GB) progression.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the impact of 4 weeks of Urolithin A (UA) supplementation on running performance, recovery, and mitochondrial biomarkers in highly trained male distance runners during an altitude training camp. Findings showed that UA supplementation significantly lowered post-exercise muscle damage (Creatine Kinase tAUC after a 3000 m time trial) and ratings of perceived exertion, while also showing a large within-group increase in VO2max. However, UA did not significantly improve 3000 m running performance directly. The study also assessed physiological adaptations including running economy, body composition, and hemoglobin mass.

The regimen included weekly downhill running bouts and 3000 m time trials. No dose-response comparisons for UA were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly downregulated (absolute log2 fold change > 0.25 and nominal p < 0.05) following UA supplementation when normalized relative to placebo.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Following 4-week UA supplementation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Part of proteomic changes induced by UA supplementation.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of consuming cow's milk versus an energy-matched carbohydrate solution on recovery markers and performance in twenty female team-sport athletes following repeated simulated team games (STGs). The findings indicated that 500 mL of milk consumption attenuated losses in muscle function (peak torque for knee extension and flexion), sprint performance (5m and 10m), and perceptions of stress, and helped reduce muscle soreness and tiredness, particularly after the first STG. However, for many other physiological and performance markers (e.g., CK, hsCRP, LOOHs, PCs, CMJ, HR, RPE), the effects were mostly unclear or trivial, with milk showing no clear benefit after the second STG.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Nutritional intervention (consumption of cow's milk vs. an energy-matched carbohydrate solution) combined with a multi-stage physical activity protocol.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants consumed 500 mL of either cow's milk (910 kJ/215 kcal, 17.0 g protein, 25.5 g carbohydrate, 5.0 g fat) or an energy-matched carbohydrate solution (910 kJ/215 kcal, 0.2 g protein, 53.6 g carbohydrate, 0.0 g fat) immediately following each of two simulated team games (STG1 and STG2). The 17 g protein from milk was noted to be below the recommended 20 g threshold for maximal protein synthesis stimulation. The exercise protocol involved two ~30 minute halves of intermittent running with sprints, agility, and jumps, separated by a 10-minute half-time, with a 48-hour recovery period between STG1 and STG2. No explicit dose-response comparisons were reported for the nutritional interventions.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Comparisons of MILK vs. CHO revealed unclear outcomes with considerable variability.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Measure of how quickly muscle can generate force, reflecting explosive strength.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Recovery from simulated team-sport games (STG1 and STG2) after cow's milk consumption.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates muscle power and neuromuscular function, crucial for explosive athletic movements.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of post-exercise milk consumption (500 mL) versus an energy-matched carbohydrate drink on recovery from a repeated sprinting and jumping protocol in female team-sport athletes. The strenuous protocol successfully induced muscle damage, leading to post-exercise decreases in muscle function (peak torque, countermovement jump, sprint performance, rate of force development) and increases in subjective muscle soreness and tiredness. Milk consumption attenuated losses in muscle function, particularly for peak torque (knee extension/flexion at 180°/s) and countermovement jump height, and reduced perceived stress (DALDA B) at various time points (24h, 48h, 72h) post-exercise. The study concluded that milk may be a valuable recovery intervention for female team-sport athletes following this type of exercise, although its effects on serum creatine kinase, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, reactive strength index, and some sprint performances were unclear.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Post-exercise nutritional intervention (Milk vs. Carbohydrate drink)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants immediately consumed either 500 mL of milk (910 kJ/215 kcal, 17.0 g Protein, 25.5 g Carbohydrate, 5.0 g Fat) or 500 mL of an energy-matched carbohydrate drink (910 kJ/215 kcal, 0.2 g Protein, 53.6 g Carbohydrate, 0.0 g Fat) following a whole-body sport and exercise protocol designed to induce muscle damage (15x20m maximal sprints and 8 sets of 10 plyometric jumps). The milk protein dose (17g) was noted to be potentially suboptimal for maximal protein synthesis compared to other studies. No dose-response comparisons were conducted, as a single volume of 500 mL was used for both interventions.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the acute and delayed effects of the 5-m Shuttle Run Test (5mSRT) on biomarkers of muscle damage (creatinine kinase, lactate dehydrogenase, aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase), inflammation (C-reactive protein), and subjective perceptions of fatigue, recovery, and muscle soreness (DOMS, RPE, PRS) in healthy male amateur team sports players. Findings indicate that the 5mSRT significantly increased muscle damage and inflammation markers, as well as DOMS and RPE, while reducing PRS. The study concluded that a 72-hour recovery period was generally sufficient for fatigue recovery, with biomarker levels returning towards baseline.

treatment_details.therapy_type: 5-m Shuttle Run Test (5mSRT)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The 5mSRT consisted of 6 repetitions of 30-second maximal shuttle sprints, with 35-second recovery periods between each sprint. Participants ran the greatest possible distance within 30 seconds by shuttling between cones at increasing distances (5m, 10m, 15m, 20m, etc.). Blood samples and perceptual scores were taken at rest, 5 minutes post-exercise, and 72 hours post-exercise. No dose-response comparisons for varying test intensities or durations were reported within the protocol.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Increased acutely post-exercise, then decreased towards baseline.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Scores significantly increased from pre-5mSRT (2.1  1 0.6 UA) to 5 min post-5mSRT (8.1  1 0.6 UA, p < 0.001), representing a 62.4% increase during and 74.4% at the end. Scores decreased to 1.5  1 0.6 UA at 72 h post-5mSRT (p < 0.001 compared to post-5mSRT).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Subjective assessment of overall physical effort and fatigue experienced during physical activity.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: During and after the 5-m Shuttle Run Test (5mSRT), a maximal physical exercise.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates perceived exercise intensity, training load, and psychological stress, valuable for monitoring fatigue and readiness for subsequent activity.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the influence of oral contraceptive (OC) use on physiological, oxidative stress, and inflammatory responses to fixed-intensity and sprint cycling in recreationally trained women, comparing them to naturally cycling women. It also examined the acute effects of N-acetylcysteine (NAC) supplementation on these responses and 1-km cycling time trial performance. Key findings showed that women using OC had elevated oxidative stress (higher MDA, lower GPx) and inflammation (higher CRP) biomarkers, as well as increased ventilation, during exercise. While NAC supplementation increased plasma thiols, it only blunted exercise-induced malondialdehyde increases in naturally cycling women, not in OC users, and did not improve cycling performance in either group. This suggests an increased strain on the endogenous antioxidant system in women using OC during exercise.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Acute N-acetylcysteine (NAC) supplementation and cycling exercise (fixed-intensity and sprint time trial).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Twenty recreationally trained women completed five exercise trials, including two double-blind crossover intervention trials where participants acutely supplemented with NAC or a placebo. NAC was administered orally in a total dose of 105 mg·kg⁻¹ of body mass, given as 70 mg·kg⁻¹ 60 minutes prior to exercise and 35 mg·kg⁻¹ 30 minutes prior. The exercise protocol involved 40 minutes of fixed-intensity cycling at 105% of the gas-exchange threshold (GET), immediately followed by an all-out 1-km cycling time trial. No dose-response comparisons for NAC were reported beyond the acute vs. placebo comparison.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased during cycling (logit   = 0.017 [0.011, 0.023]). Not different between Group or Supplement.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Subjective perception of effort.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: During fixed-intensity cycling and immediately post-exercise 1-km TT.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates the perceived intensity of exercise, with no significant differences observed between groups or with NAC supplementation.

document_context_data.document_summary: This randomized, double-blind, cross-over study investigated the effects of acute cocoa flavanol (CF) intake on exercise-induced changes in antioxidant capacity, oxidative stress, inflammation, nitric oxide (NO) production, exercise performance, and recovery in well-trained male cyclists. Findings showed acute CF intake increased systemic epicatechin levels and total antioxidant capacity (TEAC/UA and UA), but did not significantly affect exercise-induced lipid peroxidation (MDA), inflammation (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α), or NO production markers (L-arginine/ADMA, citrulline). While CF intake showed a tendency for improved late-stage performance in the first time trial, overall exercise performance and recovery were not significantly enhanced.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Acute cocoa flavanol (CF) intake and cycling exercise
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants received an acute dose of either 903.75 mg of cocoa flavanols (CF) or a placebo (15 mg CF) in chocolate milk prior to exercise. The exercise protocol involved two 30-minute time trials (TT1 and TT2) performed at a workload equivalent to 75% of peak power output, separated by a 100-minute passive recovery. No explicit dose-response comparisons were conducted beyond the high-CF vs. placebo design.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher (due to exercise), unchanged (by CF intake)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly increased during both TT1 and TT2 (main effect of time, p < 0.001). Acute CF intake had no effect on RPE (no main effect of trial or interaction effect).

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: During exhaustive exercise (two 30-min time trials) following acute cocoa flavanol intake in well-trained cyclists.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Reflects the individual's subjective experience of exertion during exercise; suggests no impact of CF on perceived effort.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of total dietary antioxidant intake and capacity on body antioxidant mechanisms and exhaustive exercise-induced oxidative damage in ultra-endurance athletes. It examined physiological responses, including oxidative stress biomarkers (8-iso PGF2a, TOS, TAS, OSI) and lactate levels, during and after a combined cycling and treadmill exhaustive exercise protocol. Key findings indicated that higher dietary antioxidant intake was negatively correlated with pre-exercise total oxidant status and post-exercise increases in 8-iso PGF2a, while positively correlating with post-exercise increases in total antioxidant status and blood lactate concentrations. A higher dietary antioxidant capacity also positively influenced antioxidant defense and blood lactate removal (in both sexes) and running time to exhaustion (in males), but did not affect post-exercise heart rate recovery or perceived exertion.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Exhaustive Exercise and Dietary Antioxidant Intake Assessment
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Ultra-endurance athletes underwent an acute exhaustive exercise protocol comprising 45 minutes on a cycle ergometer at 65% VO2max, immediately followed by a treadmill test at 75% VO2max to volitional exhaustion (median running time ~26-27 min, RPE 19). Dietary antioxidant intake was assessed using the Ferric Reducing Ability of Plasma (FRAP) assay, with a median intake of 16.6-17.2 mmol/day, categorized as moderate-to-high. The study focused on correlation analysis between habitual dietary intake and exercise responses, rather than controlled dietary intervention or dose-response comparisons for exercise intensity.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant interaction between the FRAP and RPE scores. Self-perceived fatigue during exercise was almost similar in all subjects (median 19 for both sexes) and therefore not related to dietary antioxidant consumption.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Subjective assessment of exercise intensity and effort level.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: During exhaustive exercise, relation to dietary antioxidant consumption.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Common indicator to describe perceived exercise intensity and effort.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the time-of-day-dependent physiological, physical, and psychological responses of higher-weight men to a Walking Football Match (WFM). Findings revealed that evening WFM led to significantly lower glycemia, mean blood pressure (MBP), and heart rate recovery after 1 minute (HRR60s) compared to morning sessions, suggesting potential safety and metabolic benefits for higher-weight individuals when exercising in the evening. Most other parameters, including HRV, lactate, SpO2, and various physical performance metrics, showed no significant diurnal variation.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Walking Football Match (WFM)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants engaged in a single session of 5 vs. 5 Walking Football Matches (WFM) on artificial turf fields. Each session lasted approximately one hour, comprising a 10-min warm-up, two 20-min playing periods separated by a 10-min passive recovery, and a 5-min cool-down. Matches were performed in randomized order, either in the morning (6:30 a.m. - 8:30 a.m.) or in the evening (5:00 p.m. - 7:00 p.m.), with 7 days between sessions. The activity was classified as moderate intensity (4.85-4.9 METs), with participants averaging around 2500-2600 steps per session and a cadence of approximately 63.8 steps/min. The study primarily focused on time-of-day effects, with no explicit dose-response comparisons regarding WFM intensity or duration.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Higher in the evening compared to the morning
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly higher in the evening than in the morning (p = 0.04; d = 0.47). Values obtained during WFM indicated moderate (≥4) to very hard intensity (≥7).

matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates that the same walking football activity is perceived as more strenuous when performed in the evening, and can guide appropriate exercise levels for cardiorespiratory and musculoskeletal capacity.

document_context_data.document_summary: The study investigated the test-retest reliability and suitability of various subjective, muscle force, and blood-based physiological markers (including oxidative stress markers, hormones, cytokines, and haematological parameters) for monitoring exercise response and recovery processes in endurance athletes after strenuous endurance exercise bouts, concluding that TBARS and IL-1RA exhibited the best reliability and suitability.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Continuous Endurance Running Field Tests (RFTs)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Two identical 60-minute continuous endurance running field tests (RFTs) were performed, separated by a four-week recovery period. The exercise protocol involved 40 minutes of running at an intensity corresponding to 95% of Heart Rate (HR) at Individual Anaerobic Threshold (IAT), followed by 20 minutes at 110% of HR at IAT to ensure exhaustion. Biomarkers were measured before, immediately after, 3 hours after, and 24 hours after each bout. No dose-response comparisons for varying exercise intensities or durations were reported, but reliability was compared between trained and untrained subgroups.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significant changes over time (p < 0.05). Showed lower reliability compared to MDMQ, with moderate reliability (ICC < 0.75).

matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates physiological exercise response and is a valid parameter of internal training load, but its moderate reliability limits its suitability for monitoring athletes' load management.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of rehabilitation training (RT) and cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) on coronary artery disease (CAD) patients following percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). It found that RT, particularly aerobic exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation, significantly improved patients' exercise ability, cardiopulmonary function, lipid profiles, quantitative load indexes, and reduced anxiety and depression, ultimately enhancing overall quality of life and health status.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Rehabilitation training (RT) or Exercise Therapy (ET) combined with routine health education and standard pharmacological treatment, for Coronary Artery Disease (CAD) patients post-Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Fifty CHD patients post-PCI were randomized into a control group (routine health education) and an intervention group (routine health education combined with RT/ET). ET consisted of a 5-10 minute warm-up, followed by 30-60 minutes of formal aerobic exercise (treadmill or upper body fluid resistance) performed 3-4 times per week with 1-day intervals. Exercise intensity was assessed using the Berg Balance Scale (13-16 score required), and CPET involved a progressive workload increase on a stationary bike every minute for 8-12 minutes. PCI details included stenosis >80% with residual stenosis <20% post-stent deployment. Specifics for pharmacological treatment were standard. Although some dose parameters were provided for ET, detailed FITT parameters were not fully available in the provided text, and no explicit dose-response comparisons were reported for any aspect of the intervention.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: significantly decreased (P < 0.05) post-intervention in the intervention group compared to baseline and control.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: During quantitative load assessment, CPET, and following rehabilitation training/aerobic exercise therapy in CAD patients.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Lower RPE indicates improved fitness, reduced perceived effort, enhanced exercise tolerance, and reduced fatigue, contributing to mental health and quality of life.

document_context_data.document_summary: This longitudinal study investigated the physiological and psychological impacts of intense competition preparation, involving rigorous energy restriction and physical training, on male and female physique athletes. Across a 46-week period including a 21-23 week preparation phase and a recovery phase, the study assessed hormonal changes (e.g., IGF-1, IGFBP-3, testosterone, SHBG, insulin, cortisol, FSH, ACTH, estradiol), energy dynamics (energy intake, energy availability), body composition (body mass, fat mass, muscle size, lean mass, fat-free mass), muscle strength (isometric and concentric force, fatigue profiles), bone health (Z-scores), mood states (POMS), and reproductive function. Key findings revealed significant reductions in anabolic hormones (IGF-1, IGFBP-3, testosterone, free testosterone), increased catabolic markers (SHBG, cortisol), and decreased energy availability and muscle strength in both sexes, with males often showing more pronounced hormonal and psychological stress responses (e.g., increased fatigue and tension, decreased T/C ratio). While bone mineral density remained stable, many adverse changes largely reversed during the post-competition recovery phase with increased energy availability. The study suggests IGF-1 and IGFBP-3 as potential biomarkers for monitoring physiological stress and provides insights for optimizing training and nutritional strategies to minimize adverse effects.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Competition preparation in physique athletes, involving intense energy restriction, physical training, and self-managed diet and exercise regimens.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study involved a longitudinal assessment over 46 weeks, including an average 21-23 week competition preparation phase (PRE to MID) characterized by intense energy restriction and physical training, followed by a 3-5 month recovery phase (MID to POST) with increased energy availability. Participants self-managed their diet and exercise, with resistance training quantified as total weekly sets and aerobic training as total minutes per week, and average training load by metabolic equivalents (METs). Measurements were taken at PRE, MID (one week before competition), and POST (23 weeks after competition). While strategies like adequate energy availability and individualized nutrition were discussed, no specific intervention doses were administered by researchers, and no explicit dose-response comparisons for training or diet components were reported.

matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: A decrease suggests reduced muscle quality or intrinsic force-generating capacity in female participants. Stability in males suggests maintenance of muscle quality during the study period.

document_context_data.document_summary: This article updates the redox theory of aging, proposing that aging results from a decline in gene-exposome interaction plasticity due to cumulative exposure memory. It emphasizes the critical role of redox networks, particularly thiol/disulfide balance (e.g., plasma cystine to glutathione ratio), as an interface between an individual and the environment, influencing health, disease etiology, and resilience. The theory links compromised redox networks to increased oxidative stress biomarkers like hydroxynonenal and reactive carbonyls, and discusses the predictive power of the plasma CySS/GSH ratio for all-cause mortality in conditions like coronary artery disease, while also exploring implications for regenerative medicine, multimorbidity, and personalized health management.

treatment_details.therapy_type: This document is a comprehensive review and theoretical discussion of the redox theory of aging, its mechanisms, and implications, including the prognostic utility of specific biomarkers. No direct therapeutic interventions were investigated.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Not applicable, as this is a review article and theoretical discussion; it does not report on experimental studies involving specific therapeutic doses, intensities, durations, or dose-response comparisons for any intervention. It discusses observational findings and the predictive power of naturally occurring biomarkers.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study utilized genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screening in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) cells, primarily Nalm6 B-ALL, to elucidate the molecular mechanisms of panobinostat resistance and action. Key findings reveal mitochondrial activity as a driver of panobinostat resistance and SIRT1 expression as a critical determinant of sensitivity. Panobinostat treatment abrogates mitochondrial activity in ALL cells, contributing to resistance, while enhancing mitochondrial function (via rosiglitazone or SIRT1 overexpression) sensitizes ALL cells to panobinostat by activating the mitochondrial apoptosis pathway. The investigation identifies the SIRT1-mitochondria-PMAIP1 pathway as central to panobinostat response and suggests that higher SIRT1 expression or mitochondrial hyperactivity could indicate patient benefit from panobinostat therapy. The study also details various methods used, including cell culture, gene modulation techniques, drug sensitivity assays, RNA sequencing, Western blotting, and flow cytometry.

treatment_details.therapy_type: The study primarily investigated Panobinostat, a pan-histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor, often in combination with genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 knockout screening or SIRT1 modulation. Other HDAC inhibitors (chidamide, vorinostat) and conventional chemotherapeutic agents (l-asparaginase, cytarabine, 6-mecaptopurine, vincristine, dexamethasone, daunorubicin) were mentioned for comparative or contextual analysis. Rosiglitazone, a PPAR   γ activator, was used to stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis and enhance panobinostat sensitivity.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Panobinostat was frequently used at 10 nM for durations of 24 hours (for RNA sequencing, combination treatments) or 14 days (for CRISPR screening), leading to 60-80% cell death and significant proliferation inhibition in Nalm6 cells. Gradient concentrations were employed for drug sensitivity assays. Rosiglitazone was administered at 31.25 µM for 24 or 48 hours. Dose-response comparisons for panobinostat sensitivity were analyzed using Sanger GDSC1 IC50 data across 576 diverse cancer cell lines. No specific doses or dose-response comparisons were consistently reported for other HDAC inhibitors or conventional chemotherapeutic agents.

matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of mitochondrial OXPHOS activity; lower levels confirm reduced OXPHOS under panobinostat treatment, while elevated levels confirm activation by rosiglitazone.

document_context_data.document_summary: This narrative review investigates the molecular mechanisms of lung injury in acute and chronic respiratory diseases, including damage from viral, bacterial, oxidative stress, and cytokine factors. It highlights established and newly identified plasma biomarkers indicative of specific lung cell (Club, AT1, AT2, pan-epithelial, endothelial) and extracellular scaffold damage across various conditions like COVID-19, ARDS, COPD, and IPF. The review also discusses the limitations of individual biomarkers in predicting outcomes, emphasizing the enhanced predictive efficacy of combined biomarkers (e.g., ferritin and KL-6) and proposes an Artificial Intelligence-driven model to integrate diverse patient data for comprehensive lung injury monitoring, severity assessment, prognosis prediction, and personalized medicine.

It proposes an AI-driven monitoring model, which involved analyzing diverse datasets including chest CT scans, biological pathways, and 13 blood biomarkers from 455 IPF patients, alongside demographic and clinical data. No specific dose comparisons for AI application were reported.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of consuming cow's milk versus an energy-matched carbohydrate solution on recovery markers and performance in twenty female team-sport athletes following repeated simulated team games (STGs). The findings indicated that 500 mL of milk consumption attenuated losses in muscle function (peak torque for knee extension and flexion), sprint performance (5m and 10m), and perceptions of stress, and helped reduce muscle soreness and tiredness, particularly after the first STG. However, for many other physiological and performance markers (e.g., CK, hsCRP, LOOHs, PCs, CMJ, HR, RPE), the effects were mostly unclear or trivial, with milk showing no clear benefit after the second STG.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Nutritional intervention (consumption of cow's milk vs. an energy-matched carbohydrate solution) combined with a multi-stage physical activity protocol.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants consumed 500 mL of either cow's milk (910 kJ/215 kcal, 17.0 g protein, 25.5 g carbohydrate, 5.0 g fat) or an energy-matched carbohydrate solution (910 kJ/215 kcal, 0.2 g protein, 53.6 g carbohydrate, 0.0 g fat) immediately following each of two simulated team games (STG1 and STG2). The 17 g protein from milk was noted to be below the recommended 20 g threshold for maximal protein synthesis stimulation. The exercise protocol involved two ~30 minute halves of intermittent running with sprints, agility, and jumps, separated by a 10-minute half-time, with a 48-hour recovery period between STG1 and STG2. No explicit dose-response comparisons were reported for the nutritional interventions.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Comparisons of MILK vs. CHO revealed unclear outcomes with MILK possibly harmful for RSI from B-72 h and B-96 h. There was considerable variability in these variables.

matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates plyometric ability and muscle elasticity, important for jumping and rapid changes of direction in sports.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of post-exercise milk consumption (500 mL) versus an energy-matched carbohydrate drink on recovery from a repeated sprinting and jumping protocol in female team-sport athletes. The strenuous protocol successfully induced muscle damage, leading to post-exercise decreases in muscle function (peak torque, countermovement jump, sprint performance, rate of force development) and increases in subjective muscle soreness and tiredness. Milk consumption attenuated losses in muscle function, particularly for peak torque (knee extension/flexion at 180°/s) and countermovement jump height, and reduced perceived stress (DALDA B) at various time points (24h, 48h, 72h) post-exercise. The study concluded that milk may be a valuable recovery intervention for female team-sport athletes following this type of exercise, although its effects on serum creatine kinase, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, reactive strength index, and some sprint performances were unclear.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Post-exercise nutritional intervention (Milk vs. Carbohydrate drink)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants immediately consumed either 500 mL of milk (910 kJ/215 kcal, 17.0 g Protein, 25.5 g Carbohydrate, 5.0 g Fat) or 500 mL of an energy-matched carbohydrate drink (910 kJ/215 kcal, 0.2 g Protein, 53.6 g Carbohydrate, 0.0 g Fat) following a whole-body sport and exercise protocol designed to induce muscle damage (15x20m maximal sprints and 8 sets of 10 plyometric jumps). The milk protein dose (17g) was noted to be potentially suboptimal for maximal protein synthesis compared to other studies. No dose-response comparisons were conducted, as a single volume of 500 mL was used for both interventions.

document_context_data.document_summary: The study aimed to evaluate bone turnover and remodeling markers in children with Noonan Syndrome (NS) to understand their bone status and explore genotype-phenotype correlations. It revealed increased bone resorption in NS patients, evidenced by significantly elevated serum C-telopeptides of type I collagen (CTX) levels, and a non-significant increase in RANKL. The study also discussed the influence of RAS/MAPK signaling pathway alterations and SHP2 protein on osteoclastic activity and the effects of recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) treatment on bone parameters.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational Case-Control Study evaluating bone turnover and remodeling markers in children with Noonan Syndrome, including an analysis of recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) treatment effects.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This cross-sectional, case-control study compared 28 children with Noonan Syndrome to 35 healthy controls. No specific therapeutic intervention or dose was administered to the main cohorts. Within the NS cohort, some subjects had received or were receiving rhGH therapy, but no specific dosages, duration, or dose-response comparisons for rhGH treatment were reported, and no significant differences in bone parameters were found between treated and untreated subjects in this study.
