document_context_data.document_summary: This study developed and characterized a responsive human triple-culture model of the air-blood barrier, integrating distinct macrophage phenotypes (M1, M2 wound-healing, M2 regulatory) derived from THP-1 monocytes to mimic in vivo alveolar macrophage features. The research investigated their immunological impact, particularly on epithelial barrier function and inflammatory responses in both A549/ISO-HAS-1 and H441/ISO-HAS-1 co-culture systems. It demonstrated that the M1 macrophage model induced a severe inflammatory-like response, characterized by impaired epithelial barrier integrity and increased pro-inflammatory markers, making it suitable for modeling inflammatory lung diseases. Conversely, the M2 models (M2wh and M2reg) exhibited a non-inflammatory or pro-regenerative profile, maintaining barrier integrity and thus providing a foundation for establishing a quiescent, physiological air-blood barrier model. The study also detailed the specific biomarker profiles of these differentiated macrophage subtypes and their varied responses to Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) stimulation within the triple-culture system, highlighting cell line-specific differences in inflammatory outcomes.

treatment_details.therapy_type: In vitro differentiation of human monocytic leukemia cell line THP-1 into M1 (classically activated), M2wh (wound-healing), and M2reg (regulatory) macrophage phenotypes, followed by their integration into a human triple-culture air-blood barrier model. The model consisted of alveolar epithelial cells (A549 or NCI H441) and microvascular endothelial cells (ISO-HAS-1) cultured on Transwell filter membranes. Immunological impact was subsequently assessed via Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) stimulation.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: THP-1 cells were differentiated for 48h using specific cytokine cocktails: for M1 macrophages, 50 nM PMA, 100 ng/ml GM-CSF, and 25 ng/ml TNFα; for M2wh macrophages, 8 nM PMA, 100 ng/ml GM-CSF, 35 ng/ml IL-4, and 20 ng/ml IL-13; for M2reg macrophages, 8 nM PMA, 100 ng/ml GM-CSF, and 20 ng/ml IL-10. Dexamethasone (1 µM) was also used in some contexts. The differentiated macrophages were seeded onto the epithelial layer of the co-culture system. Cell culture media contained 10% Fetal Calf Serum (FCS), which was reduced to 5% for the triple cultures. The triple cultures were stimulated apically with 1 µg/ml LPS (end concentration) and incubated for 24h. No explicit dose-response comparisons for LPS or macrophage cell numbers were reported; the focus was on comparing responses across macrophage phenotypes and with/without LPS stimulation.

matched_biomarker_details.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Air-blood barrier co-culture supernatant; macrophage culture supernatant; apical and basolateral compartments of triple-culture systems

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Macrophage culture: M1 showed a marked increase of 4.7 ± 0.48-fold, while M2wh and M2reg showed significant increases of 2.2 ± 0.2-fold and 2.4 ± 0.6-fold, respectively, compared to unstimulated THP-1. M1 triple culture (tric) with A549 induced a marked 3.9 ± 1-fold apical release, but no significant basolateral elevation, which was instead significantly elevated (2.1 ± 0.2-fold) after LPS stimulation. M2wh/M2reg tric A549 without LPS showed no significant alterations. A549/ISO-HAS-1 co-culture + LPS showed significant basolateral elevation but no apical alteration. M2wh tric A549 + LPS resulted in massive sICAM production in both compartments (apical, 4.1 ± 1.3-fold; basolateral, 1.9 ± 0.1-fold), comparable to LPS-stimulated M1 tric with A549. M2reg tric A549 + LPS showed a clear but not significant apical increase and significant basolateral increase. H441/ISO-HAS-1 systems generally showed no changes in sICAM release with macrophage addition or LPS treatment, despite unstimulated H441 cells having high and inconsistent baseline production (24-fold apical, 2-fold basolateral) compared to A549.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: A soluble form of Intercellular Adhesion Molecule 1, reflecting the shedding of cell adhesion molecules and indicative of inflammation, endothelial activation, and cell adhesion processes.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: In vitro differentiation of THP-1 cells into M1, M2wh, and M2reg macrophages; their integration into air-blood barrier triple-culture models (A549/ISO-HAS-1 or H441/ISO-HAS-1) and subsequent stimulation with Lipopolysaccharide (LPS).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Signifies inflammatory activation and changes in cell-cell interactions. M1 macrophages show the most potent direct effect, with LPS treatment further modulating its release, particularly in the basolateral compartment. The lack of response in H441 cells indicates cell line-specific effects on sICAM release and inflammatory signaling. Elevated levels indicate a pro-inflammatory state.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated disease and target engagement biomarkers in the phase 2b RISE-SSc trial of riociguat in early diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (dcSSc) to predict treatment response. While the primary endpoint (modified Rodnan Skin Score, mRSS) did not reach statistical significance, riociguat treatment significantly increased plasma cGMP levels, indicating engagement of the NO-sGC-cGMP pathway. Additionally, serum sPECAM-1 and CXCL-4 levels decreased with riociguat. Elevated baseline sPECAM-1 and the presence of αSMA-positive cells in skin biopsies were identified as potential predictive biomarkers for greater mRSS reduction with riociguat, suggesting these markers may help identify patients who could benefit from the treatment for skin fibrosis.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Riociguat (Drug Treatment)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Patients with early treatment-naïve diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis were randomized to receive riociguat (n=60) or placebo (n=61) for 52 weeks. Riociguat was administered up to 2.5 mg, maximum three times daily. Biomarker assessments were performed at baseline (day 0) and week 14, with clinical endpoints evaluated up to week 52. Rescue therapy was permitted from week 26. While cGMP changes correlated with riociguat pharmacokinetics, no explicit dose-response comparisons for other biomarkers were formally reported.

Higher baseline serum sPECAM-1 was associated with greater mRSS reduction at week 52 with riociguat (interaction P = 0.004), while in the placebo group, higher baseline levels correlated with mRSS increase.

document_context_data.document_summary: This observational study investigated the association of circulating Advanced Glycation End-products (AGEs) and soluble RAGE (sRAGE) isoforms (cRAGE, esRAGE) and their ratios with 15-year all-cause mortality and cardiovascular complications (MACE) in type 2 diabetes patients. It explored baseline demographic and biochemical characteristics, including AGEs and sRAGE isoforms, in type 2 diabetes patients compared to healthy controls, and examined their associations with diabetic complications, aging, and metabolic parameters. The study found increased circulating AGEs and sRAGE (specifically cRAGE) in type 2 diabetes, with the AGEs/cRAGE ratio predicting all-cause mortality and sRAGE associated with MACE development. A nomogram for long-term survival probability prediction, based on age, sex, HbA1c, SBP, and the AGEs/cRAGE ratio, was developed and internally validated.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational and prognostic assessment study of circulating biomarkers.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: A retrospective cohort study with a 15-year follow-up, investigating baseline circulating levels of AGEs and soluble RAGE isoforms in 362 type 2 diabetes patients and 125 age- and gender-matched healthy controls. No therapeutic interventions, specific doses, or dose-response comparisons were administered or reported.

matched_biomarker_details.biomarker_name: Soluble Receptor for Advanced Glycation End-products (sRAGE)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly increased in patients with type 2 diabetes compared to healthy controls (p < 0.001). Each SD-increase in plasma sRAGE was independently associated with the development of MACE during a > 15-year follow-up (OR: 1.48, 95% CI 1.11–1.98). Decreased levels were associated with nephropathy and significantly reduced with insulin therapy (both adjusted for age and HbA1c). Lower levels also observed in diabetic neuropathy.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Soluble forms of RAGE (cRAGE and esRAGE) act as decoy receptors, binding AGEs and other ligands to restrain RAGE/ligand-induced cell activation and inflammatory processes, thereby potentially mitigating harmful effects and reflecting the extent of RAGE overexpression.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Type 2 diabetes diagnosis and progression; development of Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events (MACE) over long-term follow-up; diabetic complications (nephropathy, neuropathy); insulin therapy.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Associated with the development of MACE and all-cause mortality in type 2 diabetes, serving as an independent predictor. Increased levels may indicate new-onset or worsening renal disease and incident coronary heart disease. Lower levels are associated with diabetic neuropathy and influenced by insulin therapy.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated plasma protein biomarkers (including cytokines, chemokines, growth factors, and cell death markers) to identify unique expression patterns associated with the severity and duration of Primary Graft Dysfunction (PGD) after lung transplantation. It identified several strong biomarker candidates, such as IP-10, MIP-1B, RANTES, M30, M65, IL-1Ra, PDGF-BB, G-CSF, IL-4, MIP-1A, IL-17, IL-9, IL-1B, IL-10, IL-6, TNF-alpha, sRAGE, and PAI-1, which are informative for early detection, predicting clinical course, and monitoring treatment efficacy of PGD.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Lung transplantation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study included 40 consecutive lung transplant patients (February 2018 – May 2019). Blood samples were collected immediately pretransplant (T0) and at 6, 24, 48, and 72 hours post-transplant/reperfusion, with PGD severity scored using 2016 ISHLT guidelines. Biomarker analysis involved a bead-based multiplex assay for 27 plasma proteins (cytokines, growth factors, chemokines) and enzyme-linked immunoassay for cell injury markers (M30, M65, sRAGE, PAI-1). Statistical methods included pairwise comparisons, sensitivity, and temporal analyses. An immunosuppression regimen of basiliximab, solumedrol, and mycophenolate (induction) and tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil (maintenance) was used. Intraoperative extracorporeal life support (ECLS), ex vivo lung perfusion (EVLP), and postoperative extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) were considered for severe PGD (PGD3). No specific dose-response comparisons for transplantation or immunosuppression were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Lower levels in pre-transplant samples in patients with greater PGD severity. Increased in postoperative samples at T24–72 h. Correlation between sRAGE levels and PGD severity in one of 12 pairwise comparisons.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Marker of lung epithelial cell injury.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Pre-transplant and post-operative (T24–72 h) lung transplant, associated with PGD severity.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates lung epithelial cell injury and correlates with PGD severity, with varied temporal expression across pre- and post-transplant phases.

document_context_data.document_summary: This substudy of the REST trial investigated the effects of lower tidal volume ventilation facilitated by veno-venous extracorporeal CO2 removal (vv-ECCO2R) compared to standard care in patients with moderate-to-severe acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (AHRF). The study aimed to evaluate plasma biomarkers of systemic inflammation and lung injury, such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and interleukin-18 (IL-18), and potential heterogeneity of treatment effect based on inflammatory phenotypes. Key findings indicated no overall difference in day 3 plasma CRP, but a greater increase in plasma IL-18 in the intervention group. Notably, baseline IL-18 levels and inflammatory phenotypes were found to identify subgroups of patients who may benefit from lower tidal volume ventilation facilitated by vv-ECCO2R, demonstrating differential treatment responses and outcomes like ventilator-free days and 90-day mortality.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Lower tidal volume ventilation facilitated by veno-venous extracorporeal CO2 removal (vv-ECCO2R)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The intervention group received vv-ECCO2R via percutaneous central venous catheter with IV heparin and sweep gas flow of 10 L/min, targeting a tidal volume of 3 mL/kg predicted body weight (PBW). The intervention was applied for at least 48 hours and up to 7 days. Standard care involved mechanical ventilation with a tidal volume of 6 mL/kg PBW and PEEP titrated per the ARDSNet protocol. Plasma samples were collected at baseline and day 3 for biomarker analysis. No explicit dose-response comparisons for different levels of the intervention were reported; however, treatment responses were observed to vary based on patient phenotypes (baseline interleukin-18 levels and inflammatory status).

matched_biomarker_details.biomarker_name: sRAGE (soluble Receptor for Advanced Glycation End-products)

measured_effect.direction_of_change: overall unchanged; lower in specific subgroups
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Overall, no statistically significant difference reported between intervention and standard care groups at day 3. However, in patients with high baseline IL-18, a greater reduction was observed (Δ -99 [-235, -11] pg/mL; p < 0.01), particularly under standard care (Δ -104 [-255.8, -36.4] pg/mL; p = 0.005). Hyperinflammatory patients also showed a greater reduction (Δ -126 [-429, -26] pg/mL; p = 0.01), particularly under standard care (Δ -236.0 [-784.2, -110.5] pg/mL; p = 0.03).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Marker of lung epithelial injury and inflammation, associated with alveolar damage and representing type 1 alveolar epithelial cell injury.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Changes from baseline to day 3 following lower tidal volume ventilation facilitated by vv-ECCO2R versus standard care mechanical ventilation, with subgroup analysis by baseline IL-18 levels and inflammatory phenotypes in moderate-to-severe AHRF.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Associated with inflammatory response/resolution and increased mortality. Greater reductions in sRAGE indicate a positive modulation of type 1 alveolar epithelial cell injury, particularly noted in patients with high baseline IL-18 or a hyperinflammatory phenotype, especially under standard care.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the safety and efficacy of human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cell (UC-MSC) transplantation in patients with severe COVID-19 and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), focusing on clinical outcomes, lung functional status, hematological parameters, cytokine levels, and miRNA expression profiles. The findings demonstrated that UC-MSC therapy was safe, improved lung lesions over a one-year follow-up by reducing fibrosis and markers of lung damage (CT score, Surfactant D, sRAGE), hastened lymphocyte recovery, and modulated inflammation (decreased ESR, CRP, banded neutrophils). The treatment also showed complex immunomodulatory effects, including altered levels of several cytokines (e.g., increased IP-10, MIP-1α, G-CSF, IL-10, while IL-6, MCP-1, and RAGE remained mostly unchanged in vivo but exhibited changes in vitro) and specific miRNAs, as well as influencing PBMC activation and proliferation in vitro.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Human Umbilical Cord Mesenchymal Stem Cell (UC-MSC) transplantation combined with conventional anti-viral treatment (antibiotic therapy, dexamethasone).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Triple intravenous infusion of UC-MSC at a concentration of 1 × 10^6 cells/kg, administered on days 0, 3, and 6. The average cell viability was 87.8% ± 5.1% before infusion. This was combined with conventional anti-viral treatment including dexamethasone and antibiotic therapy. No explicit dose-response comparisons were reported.

matched_biomarker_details.biomarker_name: sRAGE (soluble form of the Receptor for Advanced Glycation End-products)

measured_effect.direction_of_change: slightly lower in MSC, complex in Control
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Plasma levels did not differ between groups. Levels positively correlated with CT scores on weeks 2 (r = 0.437, p ≤ 0.005), 8 (r = 0.436, p ≤ 0.01), 24 (r = 0.420, p ≤ 0.01), and 48 (r = 0.510, p ≤ 0.005). Positively correlated with plasma levels of MCP-1, MIP-1α, and total CT score. In the MSC group, there was a slight decrease over the entire period of hospitalization, whereas in Control patients, it significantly reduced after 7 days and increased on days 14 and 28.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Cell surface receptor involved in inflammation and immune responses; sRAGE is a lung injury marker specific for type I alveolar epithelium.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Severe COVID-19 patients after MSC transplantation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Prognostic biomarker of ARDS and severe COVID-19 development; a sustained slight decrease in the MSC group suggests potential reduction in lung inflammation and injury over time, indicating a positive effect on pulmonary health.

document_context_data.document_summary: This narrative review investigates the molecular mechanisms of lung injury in acute and chronic respiratory diseases, including damage from viral, bacterial, oxidative stress, and cytokine factors. It highlights established and newly identified plasma biomarkers indicative of specific lung cell (Club, AT1, AT2, pan-epithelial, endothelial) and extracellular scaffold damage across various conditions like COVID-19, ARDS, COPD, and IPF. The review also discusses the limitations of individual biomarkers in predicting outcomes, emphasizing the enhanced predictive efficacy of combined biomarkers (e.g., ferritin and KL-6) and proposes an Artificial Intelligence-driven model to integrate diverse patient data for comprehensive lung injury monitoring, severity assessment, prognosis prediction, and personalized medicine.

treatment_details.therapy_type: A narrative review of lung injury mechanisms, biomarkers, and Artificial Intelligence (AI)-directed lung injury evaluation and monitoring.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: No specific therapeutic intervention or dose was investigated; the document is a review of existing knowledge focusing on intrinsic pathological processes and biomarker responses. It proposes an AI-driven monitoring model, which involved analyzing diverse datasets including chest CT scans, biological pathways, and 13 blood biomarkers from 455 IPF patients, alongside demographic and clinical data. No specific dose comparisons for AI application were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Elevated plasma sRAGE is evident in pediatric and adult ARDS; Increased sRAGE correlates with enhanced pulmonary MMP-9 activity during ARDS; Lower sRAGE levels observed in ILD and IPF.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Cleaved from RAGE, which is predominantly expressed on AT1 cells and triggers pro-inflammatory responses, causing alveolar epithelial cell death. sRAGE is a cleaved/secreted form.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: AT1 cell injury, ARDS (pediatric and adult), air-blood barrier integrity loss, ILD, IPF.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates AT1 cell injury; indicates air-blood barrier integrity loss; serves as a disease-specific marker for AT1 cell injury (lower levels indicate cell loss in ILD and IPF).

document_context_data.document_summary: This observational study investigated sex-specific plasma microRNAs (miR-34a, miR-224, miR-452) and Angiopoietin-2 (Ang-2) in women with diabetes and Left Ventricular Diastolic Dysfunction (LVDD) or Heart Failure with preserved Ejection Fraction (HFpEF), including cohorts with impaired renal function or a history of preeclampsia. The study found distinct patterns of miR expression and Ang-2 levels associated with microvascular injury in these conditions, highlighting their relevance, particularly in women. Methodologies included echocardiography, standard blood testing, RNA isolation for microRNA profiling, and ELISA for specific plasma proteins.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study, diagnostic assessment
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational study primarily focused on diagnostic assessment and biomarker identification for naturally occurring cardiovascular conditions (LVDD and HFpEF) in the context of diabetes. No therapeutic interventions or dose administrations were performed or compared; the study examined existing biomarker levels in patient cohorts.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: No significant difference reported as compared to healthy controls
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Not significantly different compared to healthy controls; Associated with miR-125a (R = − 0.38, FDR adjusted p = 0.01), -126 (R = − 0.30, FDR adjusted p = 0.04) and miR-143 (R = − 0.39, FDR adjusted p = 0.01).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Endothelial cell-surface glycoprotein involved in the anticoagulant pathway and anti-inflammatory processes; implied marker of microvascular injury.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Women with a previous history of pre-eclampsia and asymptomatic LVDD.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: A marker of microvascular injury; not significantly altered in this specific cohort against controls, but shows inverse associations with certain miRs.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of 6-week cranberry (Vaccinium macrocarpon) extract supplementation on antioxidant capacity, inflammatory markers, and iron metabolism in rowers subjected to exhaustive exercise. Findings indicate that supplementation significantly strengthened antioxidant potential (TAC) and mitigated exercise-induced increases in pro-inflammatory markers (TNF-alpha), muscle damage indicators (myoglobin), and iron regulatory hormones (hepcidin) in the supplemented group. However, IL-6, ferritin, sTfR, iron, TIBC, and UIBC remained largely unaffected by supplementation or showed exercise-induced changes independent of it.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Cranberry (Vaccinium macrocarpon) extract supplementation combined with strenuous physical exercise
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Athletes received 720 mg of highly-concentrated large cranberry extract daily (two 360-mg capsules, containing 36 mg proanthocyanidins per capsule) for 6 weeks. The control group received dyed gelatin placebo capsules containing flour. Participants performed a 2000-m rowing ergometer test at maximal effort on day 1 (pre-supplementation) and at the end of the 6-week training camp (post-supplementation), with blood samples taken pre-exercise, 1 minute post-exercise, and after a 24-hour recovery. No dose-response comparisons for cranberry extract were reported within the study.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Neither cranberry supplementation nor physical exercise exerted statistically significant effects on this parameter (main effect, p=0.741).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Reflects cellular iron demand and erythropoietic activity, especially useful in diagnosing iron deficiency when inflammation is present.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: 6-week cranberry supplementation combined with strenuous physical exercise.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of iron status and erythropoiesis; cranberry supplementation had no discernible effect on its levels. Lack of change suggests stable cellular iron demand.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review identifies and recommends validated biomarkers for tracking health, performance, and recovery in athletes across multiple domains including nutritional status (macronutrients, micronutrients, food allergies), hydration, muscle status (damage, endocrine response), endurance, and injury risk (concussions, stress fractures, ACL). It advocates for a comprehensive, integrative, and individualized approach to biomarker analysis, emphasizing dynamic monitoring and contextual interpretation over single markers or universal thresholds to optimize training and minimize injury and overtraining risks.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Biomarker-guided monitoring and management of athletic training, nutrition, hydration, and injury recovery
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This review primarily focuses on the diagnostic and prognostic value of biomarkers rather than specific therapeutic doses. It emphasizes frequent, individualized monitoring (e.g., pre/post-exercise, daily, seasonally, after injury/competition) to establish personalized baseline ranges and track physiological changes in response to various training loads (e.g., acute bouts, heavy strength training, challenging training weeks). While specific nutritional intake recommendations are mentioned for protein (1.3–2.0 g/kg/day) and omega-3 fatty acids (≤3 g/day for average, 6–8 g/day for elite athletes), and iron supplementation at low-moderate doses, the document does not report dose-response comparisons for biomarker changes. Instead, it provides specific thresholds for identifying deficiencies (e.g., Vitamin D >50 ng/ml, Ferritin <12 µg/L), dehydration (e.g., >-2% body mass decrease, blood osmolality ≥295 mmol/kg, USG ≥1.020), insufficient recovery (30% decrease in T:C ratio), and overtraining (T:C ratio of 0.35 × 10⁻³). The overall approach prioritizes dynamic, contextualized assessment over universal thresholds for effective athlete management.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Elevated before training (>8 mg·L⁻¹) compared to adequate iron status (<8 mg·L⁻¹).

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Reflects iron deficiency at the tissue level; believed to be a more sensitive measure of functional iron deficiency than ferritin.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Aerobic training adaptation in females; iron deficiency at tissue level; not affected by inflammation; athletes undergoing training.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Elevated levels before training (>8 mg·L⁻¹) predict improvements with iron supplementation during aerobic training; sensitive measure of functional iron deficiency; increases confidence in iron status diagnosis.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated immune subphenotypes and biomarker differences in critically ill adult COVID-19 patients from the REMAP-CAP trial. It identified three distinct subphenotypes based on biomarker patterns, revealing differential treatment effects of ABO-compatible convalescent plasma therapy on hospital mortality and organ support free days (OSFD-21). Seronegative patients showed significantly higher hospital mortality, with specific biomarker profiles varying by serostatus within subphenotypes. The findings suggest that convalescent plasma therapy should be avoided in subphenotypes 2 and 3 and emphasize the importance of patient selection based on host immune response for COVID-19 immunotherapy.

No specific dose-response comparisons for plasma were reported.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated inflammatory clusters in sepsis based on plasma cytokine protein abundance and their relationship with leucocyte transcriptomic subphenotypes, utilizing data from three cohorts (UK GAinS, VANISH, and LeoPARDS). It identified two or three inflammatory clusters across these datasets, with a 'high cytokine' cluster exhibiting elevated levels of both pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory cytokines, which was consistently associated with worse organ dysfunction, increased disease severity, and higher mortality. The study also explored the overlap between inflammatory clusters and previously described transcriptomic subphenotypes (SRS1/SRS2) and ARDS subphenotypes, suggesting that combining cytokine protein abundance and transcriptomic data could provide complementary information for optimal sepsis patient stratification. No significant interaction between inflammatory clusters and trial treatment response for therapies like norepinephrine, vasopressin, or levosimendan was found.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Patient stratification using plasma cytokine profiling; evaluation of trial therapies including Vasopressin, Norepinephrine, Hydrocortisone, and Levosimendan in septic shock.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study primarily focused on patient stratification using hierarchical clustering and latent class analysis based on plasma protein abundance of 11 to 65 circulating cytokines, cytokine receptors, and regulators across three cohorts (UK GAinS: n=124, VANISH: n=155, LeoPARDS: n=484). For trial therapies, the VANISH trial compared vasopressin with norepinephrine and hydrocortisone with placebo, while LeoPARDS compared levosimendan with placebo. No specific doses or durations for these trial treatments are detailed, and the study found no detectable heterogeneity in treatment effect for norepinephrine, vasopressin, or levosimendan, noting they had no or minimal effect on circulating cytokines.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher concentrations observed in the 'high cytokine' cluster compared to the 'low cytokine' cluster. Used in ARDS models for classification. High levels.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Soluble receptor for TNF, can act as an anti-inflammatory modulator; modulates TNF-alpha signaling, involved in inflammation.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Sepsis patient classification via hierarchical cluster analysis in GAinS, VANISH, and LeoPARDS cohorts; used in ARDS models for classifying hyperinflamed states and in evaluating inflammatory groups in sepsis.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Elevation in the 'high cytokine' cluster is associated with features of more severe disease (higher heart rates, lower PaO2:FiO2 ratios, higher fluid and norepinephrine requirements) and higher 28-day mortality in sepsis patients. Indicates a hyperinflamed state when classified by ARDS models and is linked to worse survival and higher levels of shock in ARDS and heightened disease severity in hyperinflamed sepsis patients.

document_context_data.document_summary: This multi-phase, multi-center study developed and validated a machine learning-enabled blood-derived exosomal RNA profiling platform (ETR.sig) for noninvasive multi-cancer detection and localization, demonstrating its robust potential for accurate diagnosis, tumor origin classification, and prognostic assessment across eight primary cancer types.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Diagnostic biomarker discovery and validation for multi-cancer detection and prognosis using exosomal RNA signatures.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This multi-phase, multi-center study involved a discovery phase (818 participants, 8 cancer types, 194 healthy controls, exoRNA-seq), a screening phase (245 participants, TaqMan qPCR), and a validation phase (1,385 participants). Machine learning (Random Forest and LASSO algorithms) was applied to refine 33 initial candidate biomarkers down to 12 exosomal tumor RNA signatures (ETR.sig). Diagnostic models were built with stratified random sampling (7:3 or 8:2 training/validation splits, tenfold cross-validation). Filtering criteria for differential gene expression included |log2FC|>1 and P<0.05 for bulk RNA-seq, and P<0.01 with FC ≥1.4 or ≤−1.6 for multi-cancer exoRNA-seq. The study focused on diagnostic development and biomarker identification, thus no therapeutic dose-response comparisons were reported.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study performed a comprehensive qualitative and quantitative proteomic analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) derived from different somatic origins (fibroblasts and peripheral blood CD34+ cells), comparing them to original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC) and human embryonic stem cells (hESC). Using ESI-MS e and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry, complemented by Western blot validation, the research aimed to characterize hiPSC proteomic profiles, identify known and novel pluripotency markers, and distinguish hiPSCs from their somatic precursors. Key findings include the identification of approximately 220 commonly up-regulated proteins in pluripotent stem cell lines, the development and confirmation of a 22-protein marker panel for hiPSC characterization, and the observation of coordinated up-regulation of proteins involved in protein synthesis, folding, RNA processing, DNA replication, DNA repair, and energy metabolism (including oxidative phosphorylation and lipogenesis) in hiPSCs. The study also identified somatic cell markers that were down-regulated upon reprogramming and highlighted specific proteomic differences between hiPSCs and hESCs, contributing to improved hiPSC quality control for therapeutic applications.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Proteomic characterization and comparative analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) and human embryonic stem cells (hESCs).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was a characterization study, not a therapeutic intervention, thus no 'dose' of therapy was administered. Quantitative and qualitative proteomic analyses were performed using electrospray ionization (ESI)-MS e (label-free quantification with internal reference standard) and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry. Two hiPSC lines (iNC-01 from CD34+ cells, SB5-MP1 from fibroblasts, both generated using loxP-flanked excisable polycistronic STEMCCA lentiviral vector) and one hESC line (H9) were analyzed at earlier and later passages. Comparisons were made against their respective original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC). Proteins were considered differentially expressed if expression changed by >=1.5-fold, with a maximum false discovery rate of 2% and >95% confidence. Western blot analysis was used for validation. The developed marker panel was further tested in 8-9 additional hiPSC lines or passages from different somatic origins and reprogramming techniques. Differentiation studies were conducted with embryoid bodies at 24 hours and 7 days to assess marker changes during spontaneous differentiation.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the functional heterogeneity of mesenchymal and neural stem cells (MSC and NSC) to identify highly migrating subpopulations (sMSC and sNSC) and evaluate their therapeutic efficacy. The research found that sMSC and sNSC exhibited superior motility and migratory potential compared to their parental non-selected cells, with podoplanin (PDPN) identified as a major regulator of this enhanced migration. In mouse models, sMSC demonstrated improved targeted migration to glioblastoma tumor sites and significantly reduced Alzheimer's disease hallmarks, including amyloid-beta pathology, cortical hyperactivity, and memory deficits, while promoting neurogenesis, neuronal survival, and synaptic integrity. PDPN overexpression in NSC also enhanced oncolytic activity against glioblastoma cells. The findings suggest that stem cell motility and migration potential are key determinants of their therapeutic efficacy, with implications for developing customized cell-based therapies for neurodegenerative and oncological brain disorders.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Stem Cell Therapy (using Mesenchymal Stem Cells (MSC) and Neural Stem Cells (NSC) or their highly migrating subpopulations (sMSC, sNSC)), Gene Engineering (siRNA knockdown or overexpression of podoplanin (PDPN)), and Oncolytic Virotherapy (using Oncolytic Adenovirus Ad-Delo3-RGD).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Highly migrating subpopulations (sMSC and sNSC) were selected based on their superior intrinsic migration capacity. Treatments included intranasal administration (1x10^6 MSC in 40 µL PBS, applied on day 1 and 3 after pre-treatment with 100 U hyaluronidase) of oMSC or sMSC in transgenic Alzheimer's disease mouse models (APP23xPS45 and 3xTg-AD). For glioblastoma models, 1x10^5 eGFP+ murine oMSC vs. eGFP+ sMSC were stereotactically injected contralaterally to tumor cells. Neural stem cells were infected with oncolytic adenovirus (200 MOI of Ad-Delo3-RGD) for oncolytic assays. Additionally, siRNA-mediated PDPN knockdown was applied to sMSC, and transient PDPN overexpression to oNSC and oMSC. The study focused on comparing the efficacy of selected/engineered cells versus original populations, with no other explicit dose-response comparisons reported.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study performed a comprehensive fine-mapping analysis of 150 breast cancer risk regions using dense genotype data from over 217,000 subjects (109,900 breast cancer cases, 88,937 controls of European ancestry). It identified 352 independent risk signals, containing 13,367 credible causal variants (CCVs), with 191-205 high-confidence signals and 191 likely target genes. The investigation revealed that CCVs were significantly over-represented in active gene regulatory regions, open chromatin, actively transcribed genes, and transcription factor binding sites. The study also found signals differentially associated with ER-positive and ER-negative breast cancer, and prioritized target genes through integrated computational approaches like PAINTOR and INQUISIT, collectively explaining up to 23.6% of the familial relative risk. Furthermore, it included eQTL analyses in normal and tumor breast tissue to link genetic variants with gene expression changes, and explored the enrichment of CCVs with various genomic features and their impact on specific biological pathways.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Genetic fine-mapping, risk profiling, and functional genomics analysis.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This study is a genetic association and fine-mapping analysis, not an interventional therapy. It utilized dense genotype data from over 217,000 subjects (109,900 breast cancer cases, 88,937 controls) of European ancestry, analyzing over 639,000 genetic variants (SNPs, deletion/insertions, CNVs with MAF ">= 0.1% or 0.005%") across 150-152 previously defined risk regions. Methodologies included stepwise multinomial logistic regression, Bayesian approaches (PAINTOR), and a gene prioritization pipeline (INQUSIT). Statistical thresholds like conditional p-values (< 10^-6 for strong evidence, < 10^-4 for moderate) and False Discovery Rate (FDR 5%) were applied. eQTL analyses involved linear regression with specific covariates, and functional characterization included enrichment analysis with histone marks and TFBS motifs (FIMO p-value threshold 10^-3). No dose-response comparisons for a therapeutic intervention were reported.

document_context_data.document_summary: The INVICTA study outlines its comprehensive methodology to assess the impact of repetitive subconcussive blast exposure (RSCBE) during military heavy weapons training on brain function and molecular changes. The study aims to identify acute and long-term effects, develop and validate a risk stratification system (RATING tool), and ensure uniform data collection for future comparisons and meta-analyses. It investigates relationships between blast exposure and various clinical, physiological, and neuroimaging outcomes, including specific blood biomarkers, to predict individual risk and inform military decision-making regarding performance readiness and return-to-duty.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Repetitive Subconcussive Blast Exposure (RSCBE) during Heavy Weapons Training (HWT)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants are exposed to blast overpressure during military Special Operations Heavy Weapons Training (HWT), involving firing weapons like the Carl Gustav recoilless rifle, Light Anti-Armor Weapon (LAAW), and AT-4 anti-tank rocket. Exposure is quantified using wearable blast sensors (e.g., Black Box Biometrics Gen 7 Blast Gauge System) mounted on helmets, shoulders, and chests, which record full waveforms for blast pressures exceeding ~6.9 kPa (1.0 psi) and define significant exposure at > ~27.6 kPa (4.0 psi). Incident peak overpressure and impulse are estimated using the FAST-CT algorithm. The study assesses naturally occurring exposure in RSOs conducting 6 training courses per year over a 2-year tour, with no controlled dose administration or explicit dose-response comparisons reported as findings, but aims to explore relationships between exposure extent and outcomes.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Elevations in blood levels observed in military Service Members (SMs) with blast exposure. Not specifically quantified in the provided text.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Linked to axonal injury (as a type of spectrin breakdown product).
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Blast exposure in military SMs.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Facilitates identification of axonal injury and elucidation of pathophysiological mechanisms related to brain trauma.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of 2-week hemp fiber (high and low doses) or placebo supplementation on post-exercise gut permeability and plasma metabolite shifts in healthy male and female cyclists after intensive cycling. While distinct metabolomic shifts were observed between the hemp fiber and placebo groups (R2Y = 0.987 and 0.995), no significant dose-response for gut permeability was reported.

Various machine learning models (e.g., univariate logistic regression, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator LR, random forest, neural network, support vector machine, and eXtreme gradient boost) with 10-fold cross-validation were used to analyze metabolomic data and clinical traits. Model performance was assessed by AUROC (>0.7 for inclusion), sensitivity, specificity, and F1 score. Vascular ultrasound was used for carotid/femoral intima-media thickness assessment of subclinical atherosclerosis. The study discusses the implications for guiding statin therapy or lifestyle modifications but does not directly test them, noting that standard statin prescriptions may be insufficient due to normal lipid ranges in SLE patients.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review systematically examines the therapeutic potential of gamma ("\u03b3") neuromodulation as a non-pharmacological strategy across a range of neurological and psychiatric disorders, including Alzheimer's Disease, Parkinson's Disease, epilepsy, Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder, schizophrenia, and depression. It investigates various neuromodulation techniques (such as rTMS, tACS, tDCS, neurofeedback, DBS, VNS, optogenetic stimulation, and rhythmic sensory stimulation) to regulate neuronal oscillations, particularly \u03b3 oscillations and cross-frequency coupling. The document highlights the role of \u03b3 neuromodulation in improving cognitive, emotional, and motor functions by addressing oscillatory imbalances, reducing pathology (e.g., amyloid-\"\u03b2" accumulation), improving seizure control, and sharpening executive functions, while also discussing the physiological mechanisms, intervention outcomes, and the need for further research into specific treatment strategies and precision medicine.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Various neuromodulation techniques are investigated, including gamma (\u03b3) neuromodulation, repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS), transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), neurofeedback (including EEG-neurofeedback and olfactory bulb-driven closed-loop neuromodulation), Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS - including responsive DBS and high-frequency DBS of the habenula, fornix, posterior cingulate cortex, subthalamic nucleus, and anterior nucleus of the thalamus), Vagus Nerve Stimulation (VNS), optogenetic neuromodulation, Rhythmic Sensory Stimulation (RSS), multisensory \u03b3 stimulation, \u03b3 Knife Surgery, \u03b3 Entrainment Using Sensory Stimulation (GENUS), and high-frequency modulation.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This review synthesizes existing literature and, as such, generally lacks specific dose-response data from new interventions. However, various dose details are mentioned for different neuromodulation techniques. Optogenetic stimulation increased cortical \u03b3 band oscillations (GBO) by entraining at approximately 40 Hz, with inhibition reducing GBO power. Multisensory \u03b3 stimulation was applied at 40 Hz, and 40 Hz \u03b3 entrainment via sensory stimulation (light flicker or sound) reduced amyloid plaques and tau pathology. rTMS is described as enhancing high-frequency oscillations (\u03b3, \u03b2) and reducing low-frequency rhythms (\u03b1, \u03b8, \u03b4), with low-frequency rTMS for epilepsy showing uncertain effectiveness. tACS synchronizes neuronal oscillations, directly entraining \u03b3 oscillations through phase-locked sinusoidal currents, sometimes targeting frontal areas. tDCS delivers low-level electrical currents to adjust cortical excitability. Neurofeedback (including EEG-neurofeedback and multisensory stimulation with operant conditioning) allowed for self-modulation of \u03b3-band synchronization, achieving up to 71% accuracy in enhancing neural synchronization in preclinical AD and older adults, with success rates for \u03b3 modulation varying (approximately 75%). DBS was applied to the fornix for AD, the posterior cingulate cortex for PD, the subthalamic nucleus (STN) for \u03b3 activity modulation, the subgenual cingulate or ventral striatum, and bilaterally to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus (ANT) for epilepsy, which reduced seizures by 40.5% at 3 months and 75.0% at 5 years. VNS aimed at desynchronizing epileptiform activity in the \u03b3 band. \u03b3 neuromodulation involved a rapid transition from an over-activated Cross-frequency coupling (CFC) pattern to an inhibited-activated state during stimulation, which remained significantly weakened post-stimulation. High-frequency modulation and high-frequency DBS of the habenula were also mentioned. The document notes a significant gap in research addressing specific, detailed treatment strategies with \u03b3 neuromodulations.

document_context_data.document_summary: This longitudinal study systematically investigated distinct host responses, cellular injury, and tissue damage in pediatric COVID-19 and Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children (MIS-C) through next-generation sequencing of plasma cell-free RNA (cfRNA), cell-free DNA (cfDNA), and whole-blood RNA (wbRNA) from 228 patients. It revealed unique molecular signatures distinguishing MIS-C from COVID-19, including increased multiorgan involvement and pyroptosis-related gene enrichment in MIS-C, alongside shared and distinct pro-inflammatory pathways. The analysis highlighted the complementary insights provided by cfRNA and wbRNA profiling, demonstrating varying biomarker trajectories, such as persistent immune dysregulation in COVID-19 compared to MIS-C resolution.

Samples were collected at acute, 1-month, and 3-month post-hospitalization time points. While some patients received intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg), it was not a tested intervention, and its administration was found not to significantly confound observed molecular differences. No therapeutic interventions or dose-response comparisons were conducted or reported.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated changes in cellular immune inflammation markers (NLR, PLR, SII), various blood cell counts (leucocytes and their subsets, platelets), and physical fitness parameters (VO2max, YYIRL1 performance, sprint, jump tests) in elite male soccer players over a 12-week period, including both uncongested and congested match play phases. It found that a congested match play period significantly altered immune cell counts and inflammation markers, leading to increased leucocyte, neutrophil, eosinophil, basophil, and monocyte counts, and higher NLR, PLR, and SII, with concurrent decreases in lymphocyte counts and aerobic physical fitness. These immune inflammation markers were negatively correlated with physical fitness (YYIRL1 performance, VO2max) and positively correlated with workload parameters, suggesting their utility for monitoring training intensity, competitive load, and aerobic physical fitness, and for preventing overtraining.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Elite Soccer Training and Congested Match Play
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Fifteen elite male soccer players were monitored for 12 weeks, comprising a 6-week uncongested match play period (30 training sessions, 45 hours training volume, 6 matches with 350±53.5 minutes average playing time) followed by a 6-week congested match play period (24 training sessions, 36 hours training volume, 10 matches with 629.6±133.9 minutes average playing time). Players typically trained five times per week and played one match per week, with the congested period exposing them to up to eight matches per month. Physical fitness tests (Squat Jump, Countermovement Jump, 20-meter sprint, Yo-Yo intermittent recovery test level 1) and blood samples were taken at T1 (week 1), T2 (week 7), and T3 (week 13). Workload parameters (Global load, Training load, Competitive load, Training volume, Session-Rating of Perceived Exertion) were recorded and compared. The congested period showed significantly increased total and competitive loads and decreased training load, training volume, and Session-RPE compared to the uncongested period. No explicit dose-response comparisons for varying levels of congestion beyond the two defined periods were reported.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of a 6-week, low-dose bovine colostrum (BC) or whey protein (WP) supplementation on exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD), inflammatory indices, hematological markers, and performance decline in soccer players following a Loughborough Intermittent Shuttle Test (LIST). The LIST protocol induced transient changes in immune cells, inflammatory markers, and declines in performance. BC supplementation demonstrated potential in mitigating some EIMD, improving recovery of muscle power (SQJ), and attenuating post-exercise increases in inflammatory markers (CRP, CK, IL-6) compared to pre-supplementation and/or whey protein, suggesting better maintenance of performance and reduced post-exercise EIMD.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Bovine Colostrum (BC) and Whey Protein (WP) supplementation in conjunction with a Loughborough Intermittent Shuttle Test (LIST) protocol.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: A low-dose of 3.2 g/day of either bovine colostrum (BC) or whey protein (WP) was administered for 6 weeks to soccer players. This consisted of 8 capsules x 400 mg per capsule. The LIST protocol was performed pre- and post-supplementation. No dose-response comparisons for the supplements were reported, as only one dose was used; however, comparisons were made between pre- and post-supplementation responses, and directly between the BC and WP groups.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Initially lower after LIST (7–9% decline at 24–48h post-LIST 1), but BC supplementation led to a faster recovery compared to pre-supplementation kinetics (trial × time: p = 0.001) and significantly higher iAUC in the BC group compared to WP [WP: -195.2 (-229.0 to -52.5) cm h, BC: -15.8 (-93.2 to 16.8) cm h, p = 0.034]. BC attenuated the decline in performance and improved recovery of SQJ.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study comprehensively investigated the functional implications of heterogeneity in human embryonic stem cells (hESCs), focusing on an endodermally biased pluripotent substate. Using a GATA6-GFP reporter line and single-cell functional/transcriptomic analyses, the research identified distinct, interconvertible hESC substates defined by differential expression of GATA6 and SSEA3. GATA6-positive hESCs, while retaining long-term self-renewal and pluripotency (often alongside OCT4 and SOX2 co-expression), exhibited a higher propensity and bias towards spontaneous endoderm and mesoderm differentiation, with downregulation of ectodermal genes. SOX17 was identified as a potential driver for this endoderm-biased substate.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Human Embryonic Stem Cell (hESC) Substate Characterization and Differentiation Study
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study utilized the Shef4 hESC line, which was genetically modified with a GATA6-GFP reporter via Zinc Finger Nuclease-mediated homologous recombination. Cells were cultured in KO/SR on MEF feeders or E8 medium. hESC substates, defined by differential GATA6 and SSEA3 expression (e.g., 3+/6-, 3+/6L, 3+/6H, 3-/6+), were isolated by Fluorescence Activated Cell Sorting (FACS). These sorted cells were subjected to single-cell cloning, gene expression analysis (qPCR, single-cell RNA sequencing), high-content clonogenic assays, and differentiation protocols, including a spin-embryoid body (EB) system, without external therapeutic interventions or dose-response comparisons for differentiation-inducing factors. The focus was on intrinsic marker expression and resultant lineage bias.

Lost most quickly upon differentiation compared to other surface markers. All clones after differentiation showed similar patterns to the unsorted stem cell line.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study describes a multi-round Delphi expert consensus process to identify and prioritize 14 key biomarkers of aging for use in human intervention studies. The identified biomarkers encompass physiological, inflammatory, functional, and genetic/epigenetic domains. The study outlines the methodology, discusses the suitability of biomarkers for different intervention durations, and identifies future research needs regarding biomarker standardization and early life application, concluding with a preference for composite biomarkers due to the complexity of aging.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Expert consensus methodology (Delphi method) for identifying biomarkers of aging for use in human intervention studies (nutritional, lifestyle, or pharmacological).
treatment_details.dose_specificity:
The study utilized a 3-round online Delphi method, starting with 116 experts in Round 1 and concluding with 60 experts in Round 3, out of 460 invited international panel members. Consensus for statements was defined as ">=70%" agreement, with "51-69%" indicating moderate agreement and "

	<=50%" leading to removal. Initially, 460 biomarkers were suggested, leading to 20 being appraised in detail. The consensus level for the 14 recommended biomarkers ranged from 70% to 98%. The identified biomarkers were deemed more suitable for medium- (3-6 months) and long-term (">=6 months") interventions, and less suitable for acute or short-term ("<3 months") interventions, as short-term changes are likely homeostatic responses with limited long-term significance for aging. No specific therapeutic doses or dose-response comparisons were investigated as this was a consensus-building study on biomarker utility.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Achieved ">=70%" agreement in expert panel consensus.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Evaluates postural control and stability, reflecting functional capacity within the functional domain.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Identified by expert consensus via Delphi method for use in human intervention studies on aging and for assessment of the aging process.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated brain and blood biomarker signatures in both rat models exposed to repetitive low-level blast and human veterans exposed to IED blasts, aiming to identify antemortem evidence of tauopathy and neuronal injury related to neurobehavioral syndromes. Key findings include chronic increases in hyperphosphorylated tau (p-tau) immunoreactivity and abnormal perivascular p-tau accumulation in specific brain regions of blast-exposed rats from 6 weeks to 12 months post-injury. In human veterans, a significant subset (50%) with multiple blast exposures exhibited excessive cortical [18F]AV1451 tau ligand retention, indicating tauopathy, which correlated with higher circulating plasma neurofilament light (NfL) levels, suggesting neuronal injury. The study also explored cortical diffusivity analysis and [18F]AV45 amyloid PET imaging, finding no significant amyloid pathology but identifying microstructural cortical disruption linked to tau pathology. Additionally, increases in stathmin 1 in the amygdala of blast-exposed animals were associated with increased anxiety. The findings collectively suggest a link between blast injury, tauopathy, neuronal injury, and associated neurobehavioral complaints, highlighting potential biomarkers for diagnosing long-term neuropsychiatric sequelae of mTBI.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Blast exposure (Mild Traumatic Brain Injury - mTBI)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Rats received three repetitive low-level blast exposures (74.5 kPa/10.8 psi, 4.8 ms duration, 175.8 kPa ms impulse) administered one per day for 3 consecutive days using a shock tube. Human veterans reported histories of multiple blast exposures from improvised explosive devices (IEDs), ranging from 1 to 50 or more, all associated with at least one mTBI. The study primarily focused on the effects of these exposures rather than varying doses, and no dose-response comparisons were reported. Diagnostic procedures included MRI (3-Tesla Siemens Biograph MR system) and PET imaging (370 MBq [18F]AV45 and 370 MBq [18F]AV1451 injected, with image acquisition approximately 60-80 min post-injection for 20 min durations).

document_context_data.document_summary: This study performed a comprehensive qualitative and quantitative proteomic analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) derived from different somatic origins (fibroblasts and peripheral blood CD34+ cells), comparing them to original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC) and human embryonic stem cells (hESC). Using ESI-MS e and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry, complemented by Western blot validation, the research aimed to characterize hiPSC proteomic profiles, identify known and novel pluripotency markers, and distinguish hiPSCs from their somatic precursors. Key findings include the identification of approximately 220 commonly up-regulated proteins in pluripotent stem cell lines, the development and confirmation of a 22-protein marker panel for hiPSC characterization, and the observation of coordinated up-regulation of proteins involved in protein synthesis, folding, RNA processing, DNA replication, DNA repair, and energy metabolism (including oxidative phosphorylation and lipogenesis) in hiPSCs. The study also identified somatic cell markers that were down-regulated upon reprogramming and highlighted specific proteomic differences between hiPSCs and hESCs, contributing to improved hiPSC quality control for therapeutic applications.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Proteomic characterization and comparative analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) and human embryonic stem cells (hESCs).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was a characterization study, not a therapeutic intervention, thus no 'dose' of therapy was administered. Quantitative and qualitative proteomic analyses were performed using electrospray ionization (ESI)-MS e (label-free quantification with internal reference standard) and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry. Two hiPSC lines (iNC-01 from CD34+ cells, SB5-MP1 from fibroblasts, both generated using loxP-flanked excisable polycistronic STEMCCA lentiviral vector) and one hESC line (H9) were analyzed at earlier and later passages. Comparisons were made against their respective original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC). Proteins were considered differentially expressed if expression changed by >=1.5-fold, with a maximum false discovery rate of 2% and >95% confidence. Western blot analysis was used for validation. The developed marker panel was further tested in 8-9 additional hiPSC lines or passages from different somatic origins and reprogramming techniques. Differentiation studies were conducted with embryoid bodies at 24 hours and 7 days to assess marker changes during spontaneous differentiation.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Consistently up-regulated in early and late passage cells of both hiPSC lines (by ESI-MS e) and confirmed by Western blot analysis. All selected proteins were confirmed to be up-regulated in hiPSC and hESC compared to somatic cells.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Proposed novel pluripotency marker identification and validation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Candidate novel pluripotency marker for hiPSCs/hESCs.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive observational study utilized plasma proteomics and machine learning to develop and validate a framework for measuring organ-specific biological aging, termed 'e-ageotypes', in humans. Analyzing 4,778 proteins from 5,676 adults across five independent cohorts, the research revealed that accelerated aging in specific organs (including heart, brain, kidney, muscle, liver, adipose, pancreas, lung, and immune system) is significantly associated with higher risks of all-cause mortality and various age-related diseases, such as heart failure, Alzheimer's disease, hypertension, diabetes, and cognitive decline. The study's methodology involved defining 'extreme agers' (individuals with highly accelerated organ aging), clustering them into distinct ageotypes, and identifying key protein biomarkers (e.g., REN, KL, NPPB, TNNT2, CPLX1/2) that contribute to these aging profiles and offer prognostic utility for disease risk and progression.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational Study on Biological Aging via Plasma Proteomics and Machine Learning
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This observational study involved the quantification of approximately 4,778 plasma proteins using SomaScan assays (v.4 and v.4.1) in 5,676 adults from five independent cohorts. Machine learning models (LASSO regression-based chronological age predictors) were developed and validated to estimate biological (organ-specific) age, referred to as 'age gaps' or 'e-ageotypes', for 11 major organs (adipose tissue, artery, brain, heart, immune tissue, intestine, kidney, liver, lung, muscle, and pancreas) and the whole organism. Models were trained on 1,398 healthy participants from the Knight-ADRC cohort and tested across the full cohort. Age gaps were calculated using local regression, z-scored per model and cohort, and adjusted for age and sex. Associations with various age-related phenotypes, future mortality, heart disease, clinical biochemistry markers, and cognitive decline were assessed using linear models or Cox proportional hazards models, with multiple testing correction (Benjamini-Hochberg method, 5% false discovery rate). No therapeutic intervention or dose comparison was performed.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased both the model age prediction accuracy and the age gap association with dementia severity (FIBA+). Showed a consistent pattern of decreases in AD brain tissue and increases in the blood with age and AD.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Involved in neurite outgrowth and axon growth cone collapse, crucial for neuronal health.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Alzheimer's disease, cognitive decline, brain aging mechanisms (as a component of CognitionBrain model).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of brain aging, cognitive decline, and AD. Increased blood levels may reflect loss or alteration in protein processing and subsequent shedding from the brain.

document_context_data.document_summary: This document provides comprehensive guidelines for establishing and managing immune monitoring programs in patients undergoing allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation and cellular therapies (TCT/HCT). It highlights the critical need for standardized protocols for assay, flow cytometric, and data analysis to ensure consistent, scalable, and comparable results across multiple centers. The aim is to enhance prognosis prediction, enable early relapse detection, and improve clinical decision-making by evaluating immune reconstitution and functional recovery, as well as by identifying predictive cellular and secreted biomarkers for complications like graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), infections, viral reactivation, and relapse.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Allogeneic Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation (HCT), Transplant and Cellular Therapy (TCT), and related immune effector cell (IEC) therapies, including Genetically Modified Hematopoietic Stem Cell Therapies (GMHSCT) and CAR T-cell therapy.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The document primarily focuses on immune monitoring protocols post-transplantation rather than specific therapeutic dose-response comparisons for HCT/TCT itself. It highlights the variability in transplant platforms (e.g., T-cell depletion techniques, add backs, T-replete) and conditioning regimens (e.g., lymphocyte ablation, total body irradiation). Monitoring thresholds are mentioned for specific immune cells, such as >50 CD4+ T cells/μL within 100 days and >150 NK cells/mL at day 30 post-HCT, to indicate timely immune recovery. Recommended longitudinal sampling schedules are provided (e.g., biweekly for 3 months, then monthly/quarterly) post-HCT/GMHSCT, along with typical blood volumes (8-20 mL), but lack specific dose details for primary therapies or dose-response observations.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the functional heterogeneity of mesenchymal and neural stem cells (MSC and NSC) to identify highly migrating subpopulations (sMSC and sNSC) and evaluate their therapeutic efficacy. The research found that sMSC and sNSC exhibited superior motility and migratory potential compared to their parental non-selected cells, with podoplanin (PDPN) identified as a major regulator of this enhanced migration. In mouse models, sMSC demonstrated improved targeted migration to glioblastoma tumor sites and significantly reduced Alzheimer's disease hallmarks, including amyloid-beta pathology, cortical hyperactivity, and memory deficits, while promoting neurogenesis, neuronal survival, and synaptic integrity. PDPN overexpression in NSC also enhanced oncolytic activity against glioblastoma cells. The findings suggest that stem cell motility and migration potential are key determinants of their therapeutic efficacy, with implications for developing customized cell-based therapies for neurodegenerative and oncological brain disorders.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Stem Cell Therapy (using Mesenchymal Stem Cells (MSC) and Neural Stem Cells (NSC) or their highly migrating subpopulations (sMSC, sNSC)), Gene Engineering (siRNA knockdown or overexpression of podoplanin (PDPN)), and Oncolytic Virotherapy (using Oncolytic Adenovirus Ad-Delo3-RGD).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Highly migrating subpopulations (sMSC and sNSC) were selected based on their superior intrinsic migration capacity. Treatments included intranasal administration (1x10^6 MSC in 40 µL PBS, applied on day 1 and 3 after pre-treatment with 100 U hyaluronidase) of oMSC or sMSC in transgenic Alzheimer's disease mouse models (APP23xPS45 and 3xTg-AD). For glioblastoma models, 1x10^5 eGFP+ murine oMSC vs. eGFP+ sMSC were stereotactically injected contralaterally to tumor cells. Neural stem cells were infected with oncolytic adenovirus (200 MOI of Ad-Delo3-RGD) for oncolytic assays. Additionally, siRNA-mediated PDPN knockdown was applied to sMSC, and transient PDPN overexpression to oNSC and oMSC. The study focused on comparing the efficacy of selected/engineered cells versus original populations, with no other explicit dose-response comparisons reported.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study comprehensively investigated the functional implications of heterogeneity in human embryonic stem cells (hESCs), focusing on an endodermally biased pluripotent substate. Using a GATA6-GFP reporter line and single-cell functional/transcriptomic analyses, the research identified distinct, interconvertible hESC substates defined by differential expression of GATA6 and SSEA3. GATA6-positive hESCs, while retaining long-term self-renewal and pluripotency (often alongside OCT4 and SOX2 co-expression), exhibited a higher propensity and bias towards spontaneous endoderm and mesoderm differentiation, with downregulation of ectodermal genes. SOX17 was identified as a potential driver for this endoderm-biased substate.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Human Embryonic Stem Cell (hESC) Substate Characterization and Differentiation Study
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study utilized the Shef4 hESC line, which was genetically modified with a GATA6-GFP reporter via Zinc Finger Nuclease-mediated homologous recombination. Cells were cultured in KO/SR on MEF feeders or E8 medium. hESC substates, defined by differential GATA6 and SSEA3 expression (e.g., 3+/6-, 3+/6L, 3+/6H, 3-/6+), were isolated by Fluorescence Activated Cell Sorting (FACS). These sorted cells were subjected to single-cell cloning, gene expression analysis (qPCR, single-cell RNA sequencing), high-content clonogenic assays, and differentiation protocols, including a spin-embryoid body (EB) system, without external therapeutic interventions or dose-response comparisons for differentiation-inducing factors. The focus was on intrinsic marker expression and resultant lineage bias.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: One cluster of stem cell-related genes was expressed in 3+/6- cells and downregulated in the 3-/6+ subset. GATA6 expression correlated with a reduction in these stem cell-associated genes. Gene expression for germ layer differentiation within all subclones was low and comparable to the unsorted line.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Gene expression differences between hESC substates; characterization of clonal lines derived from hESC substates.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Decreased expression indicates a shift away from a fully undifferentiated pluripotent state and a progression towards differentiation. Stable expression in clonal lines confirms their continued pluripotency and stem cell identity.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of 2-week hemp fiber (high and low doses) or placebo supplementation on post-exercise gut permeability and plasma metabolite shifts in healthy male and female cyclists after intensive cycling. While hemp fiber did not significantly alter post-exercise gut permeability (measured by urine sugar data), untargeted metabolomics revealed that the combination of hemp fiber intake and vigorous exercise increased beneficial gut-derived metabolites and influenced pathways related to tryptophan, primary bile acid, steroid, sphingolipid, alpha-linolenic acid, arginine and proline, lipid, and amino acid metabolism.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Dietary supplementation with hemp fiber (hemp hull powder) combined with intensive cycling exercise.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants received daily supplementation for 2 weeks with either a high dose (20 g/d) or low dose (5 g/d) of hemp hull powder, or a placebo (0 g/d). Each supplementation period concluded with a 2.25-hour intensive cycling bout performed at approximately 70% VO2max. While distinct metabolomic shifts were observed between the hemp fiber and placebo groups (R2Y = 0.987 and 0.995), no significant dose-response for gut permeability was reported.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the role of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) in traumatic brain injury (TBI)-induced neural damage in mice, employing a controlled cortical impact model and various pharmacological and genetic manipulations. The central finding was that inhibiting NETs with Cl-amidine ameliorated neuroinflammation, neuronal apoptosis, and neurological deficits by suppressing the STING-dependent IRE1α/ASK1/JNK signaling pathway. Specifically, Cl-amidine treatment reduced cerebral lesion volume, brain edema, and restored cerebral blood flow, while also attenuating blood-brain barrier disruption, inhibiting immune cell infiltration, alleviating neuronal death, and promoting a shift from pro-inflammatory to anti-inflammatory microglia/macrophage polarization. Conversely, STING activation by 2'3'-cGAMP abolished Cl-amidine's neuroprotection, and PAD4 overexpression aggravated neuroinflammation and neuronal death via the same pathway, effects that were successfully counteracted by STING or IRE1α inhibition. The study also detailed comprehensive methodologies for establishing the TBI model and assessing various molecular and cellular changes.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Controlled Cortical Impact (CCI) model for Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI); Pharmacological interventions including Neutrophil Extracellular Trap (NET) inhibition with Cl-amidine, STING activation with 2'3'-cGAMP, STING inhibition with C-176, and IRE1α inhibition with Kira6; Genetic manipulation via adenovirus-mediated overexpression of Peptidyl arginine deiminase 4 (PAD4).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: TBI was induced using a controlled cortical impactor (3-mm flat-tip, 5 m/s velocity, 200 ms dwelling time, 2.2 mm depth, 3.5 mm craniotomy). Cl-amidine was administered at 50 mg/kg intraperitoneally (i.p.) once daily for three days, starting 1 hour post-TBI. 2'3'-cGAMP was given at 1 mg/kg intravenously 10 minutes pre-TBI, then repeated at 24 and 48 hours post-TBI. C-176 was administered at 10 mg/kg i.p. 1 hour post-TBI, daily until sacrifice. Kira6 was given at 10 mg/kg i.p. 1 hour post-TBI, once daily for three days. Ad-PAD4 or Ad-con (control) adenoviruses were stereotactically injected (4 μL total at 0.5 μL/min across two cortical locations) 1 day before CCI to overexpress PAD4. PAD4 overexpression resulted in a 2.28-fold increase in PAD4 protein and 1.73-fold increase in H3Cit at 3 days post-TBI. Effects were analyzed at 1 and 3 days post-TBI. No explicit dose-response comparisons were reported for most agents, and potential inflammatory or cytotoxic effects of the adenovirus vector were not tested.

matched_biomarker_details.activity_type: Protein expression / Activation level / Cellular distribution

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher (after TBI), lower (with Cl-amidine), higher (with PAD4 overexpression/2'3'-cGAMP)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased significantly and time-dependently, peaking at 3 days post-TBI (p < 0.001). Significantly decreased by Cl-amidine treatment (p < 0.001). Its activation by 2'3'-cGAMP abolished Cl-amidine's neuroprotection. Mainly expressed in neurons (NeuN+) and microglia (Iba-1+) post-TBI; little co-localization with astrocytes, none with neutrophils or endothelial cells. PAD4 overexpression aggravated STING-dependent neuronal death and microglial activation.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: An adaptor protein located on the endoplasmic reticulum that mediates innate immune responses. It triggers proinflammatory cytokine pathways (like TBK1/IRF3/type I IFNs), is involved in ER stress and unfolded protein response, and acts as a bridge between NET formation and IRE1α activation.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI), particularly via the STING-dependent IRE1α/ASK1/JNK signaling pathway; modulated by NET inhibition (Cl-amidine), STING activation (2'3'-cGAMP), or PAD4 overexpression.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Its activation contributes to neuroinflammation and neuronal death, indicating its critical role in post-TBI pathology. Inhibition with C-176 abolished neurodestructive effects, and its reduced expression by Cl-amidine correlates with neuroprotection.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study protocol describes a 9-week randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind clinical trial investigating the ergogenic effects of a 6-week daily probiotic supplementation on high-intensity endurance running performance in healthy non-elite athletes (N=32). Primary objectives include assessing the impact on time-to-exhaustion, while secondary objectives involve evaluating perceived exertion, blood chemistry (glucose, lactate), immune and stress biomarkers (cortisol, alpha-amylase, sIgA), cold and flu symptoms, gastrointestinal health (symptoms, stool characteristics, microbiota composition), and body composition. The study hypothesizes increased running time-to-exhaustion and reduced gastrointestinal/cold/flu symptoms with probiotic intervention.

treatment_details.dose_specificity: A 6-week intervention period involves daily oral supplementation of 5 billion colony-forming units (CFU)/day of a specific probiotic capsule taken with a meal. The study is preceded by a 2-week pre-baseline and followed by a 1-week washout period. Participants are considered compliant if they take at least 80% of the supplement. Exercise testing includes a modified Bruce V̇O2 max treadmill test and a time-to-exhaustion treadmill endurance test conducted at 85% of V̇O2 max heart rate. No dose-response comparisons are reported in this study protocol.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the changes in biochemical markers of oxidative stress and muscle damage, along with psychomotor abilities (divided attention, handgrip strength, and strength differentiation), in 15 special unit soldiers undergoing a 48-hour military survival training program combined with sleep deprivation. The findings indicated that the training did not cause oxidative stress or muscle tissue damage, improved divided attention, but suggested a potential deterioration in motor control.

Measurements (biochemical markers, divided attention, maximal handgrip strength, and strength differentiation) were taken at baseline (P1), after 24 hours (P2), and after 48 hours (P3). No dose-response comparisons were reported.
