document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review identifies and recommends validated biomarkers for tracking health, performance, and recovery in athletes across multiple domains including nutritional status (macronutrients, micronutrients, food allergies), hydration, muscle status (damage, endocrine response), endurance, and injury risk (concussions, stress fractures, ACL). It advocates for a comprehensive, integrative, and individualized approach to biomarker analysis, emphasizing dynamic monitoring and contextual interpretation over single markers or universal thresholds to optimize training and minimize injury and overtraining risks.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Biomarker-guided monitoring and management of athletic training, nutrition, hydration, and injury recovery
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This review primarily focuses on the diagnostic and prognostic value of biomarkers rather than specific therapeutic doses. It emphasizes frequent, individualized monitoring (e.g., pre/post-exercise, daily, seasonally, after injury/competition) to establish personalized baseline ranges and track physiological changes in response to various training loads (e.g., acute bouts, heavy strength training, challenging training weeks). While specific nutritional intake recommendations are mentioned for protein (1.3–2.0 g/kg/day) and omega-3 fatty acids (≤3 g/day for average, 6–8 g/day for elite athletes), and iron supplementation at low-moderate doses, the document does not report dose-response comparisons for biomarker changes. Instead, it provides specific thresholds for identifying deficiencies (e.g., Vitamin D >50 ng/ml, Ferritin <12 µg/L), dehydration (e.g., >-2% body mass decrease, blood osmolality ≥295 mmol/kg, USG ≥1.020), insufficient recovery (30% decrease in T:C ratio), and overtraining (T:C ratio of 0.35 × 10⁻³). The overall approach prioritizes dynamic, contextualized assessment over universal thresholds for effective athlete management.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Reference range: 250–425 µg·dl⁻¹. Low daily variation (8–12%). Rises in iron deficiency as more free transferrin binding sites are available.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Reflects the total number of binding sites on the blood iron transporting peptide transferrin.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Iron deficiency; iron status assessment.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Valuable biomarker for determining iron status; reduces the likelihood of falsely detecting iron depleted states; rises in iron deficiency.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of 6-week cranberry (Vaccinium macrocarpon) extract supplementation on antioxidant capacity, inflammatory markers, and iron metabolism in rowers subjected to exhaustive exercise. Findings indicate that supplementation significantly strengthened antioxidant potential (TAC) and mitigated exercise-induced increases in pro-inflammatory markers (TNF-alpha), muscle damage indicators (myoglobin), and iron regulatory hormones (hepcidin) in the supplemented group. However, IL-6, ferritin, sTfR, iron, TIBC, and UIBC remained largely unaffected by supplementation or showed exercise-induced changes independent of it.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Cranberry (Vaccinium macrocarpon) extract supplementation combined with strenuous physical exercise
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Athletes received 720 mg of highly-concentrated large cranberry extract daily (two 360-mg capsules, containing 36 mg proanthocyanidins per capsule) for 6 weeks. The control group received dyed gelatin placebo capsules containing flour. Participants performed a 2000-m rowing ergometer test at maximal effort on day 1 (pre-supplementation) and at the end of the 6-week training camp (post-supplementation), with blood samples taken pre-exercise, 1 minute post-exercise, and after a 24-hour recovery. No dose-response comparisons for cranberry extract were reported within the study.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Statistically significant exercise-induced changes were observed at Trial II (main effect, p<0.001), but not at Trial I. Both parameters increased in response to physical exercise and then returned to their pre-exercise levels following the recovery period. Cranberry supplementation did not exert a significant effect on this parameter (main effect, p=0.219). Significant post-exercise increase at Trial II in both cranberry-supplemented and control groups.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Measures the maximum amount of iron that can be bound by proteins in the blood, primarily transferrin, reflecting iron transport capacity.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Strenuous physical exercise (post-exercise and recovery) at Trial II, with and without 6-week cranberry supplementation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Changes reflect dynamic iron transport and availability, which can be influenced by inflammation and iron status.

document_context_data.document_summary: This retrospective cohort study investigated the association between iron status and renal outcomes, specifically progression to End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD), in 111 pre-dialysis patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) and biopsy-proven Diabetic Nephropathy (DN). It found that reduced serum transferrin is an independent predictor of ESRD, and identified increased iron and transferrin deposition in renal tubular epithelial cells of DN patients, suggesting a pathological role for altered iron metabolism in disease progression.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study investigating the prognostic value of iron status and related biomarkers in Diabetic Nephropathy (DN) progression.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This retrospective observational cohort study analyzed baseline serum iron status markers (serum iron, ferritin, TIBC, transferrin, TSAT) and their association with progression to End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) in 111 Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) patients with biopsy-proven DN. Serum markers were measured using chemiluminescence immunoassay, immunoradiometric assay, and colorimetric methods. Additionally, histological analysis involved immunohistochemical staining for transferrin and Perl's blue staining for iron in kidney biopsy specimens from DN patients and healthy controls. No therapeutic interventions, dose comparisons, or active treatments were investigated; the study focused on correlation and predictive value.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Lower baseline concentrations in ESRD patients (median 35.4  5mol/L, IQR 29.32-42.2) compared to non-ESRD patients. The lowest quartile (Q1,  529.32  5mol/L) was significantly associated with increased ESRD risk (HR 3.88, 95% CI 1.14-13.25) compared to the highest quartile. Lower concentrations were observed in patients with lower serum transferrin quartiles. TIBC methods generally overestimate transferrin iron-binding capacity because iron binds to other plasma proteins.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Reflects the capacity of transferrin to bind iron, indicating iron status. Measures the total amount of iron that can be bound by proteins in the blood, primarily transferrin, reflecting the body's capacity to transport iron.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Progression to End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) in T2DM patients with Diabetic Nephropathy (DN); T2DM with biopsy-proven DN.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Lower levels are significantly associated with and predict an increased risk of ESRD. However, its utility for predicting ESRD in DN is limited due to overestimation and better predictive value of serum transferrin.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study aimed to establish comprehensive reference intervals for novel circulating biomarkers of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) and hepatic regeneration in healthy human volunteers. It investigated intra- and interindividual variability, as well as diurnal variation, to provide robust data for interpreting exploratory clinical DILI studies and assisting biomarker qualification by regulatory authorities.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study for establishing reference intervals of circulating biomarkers
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study involved serum sample collection from 227 healthy volunteers in a cross-sectional study (single sample). Additionally, 25 subjects underwent weekly serial sampling over 3 weeks, and 23 subjects had intensive 24-hour blood sampling every 3 hours after a 10-h overnight fast and standardized meals. No therapeutic interventions or dose comparisons were involved, as the focus was on establishing reference intervals and assessing natural variability in healthy subjects.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Reference intervals established; levels not significantly influenced by demographic factors in this study, but high variability across studies observed.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Reference intervals based on the 97.5% quantile (90% CI). No significant fixed effects of sex, age, height, weight, BMI, or ethnicity were observed. Intra-individual variability found to be non-significant. High variability in mean K18 levels across studies, suggesting influence of ubiquitous expression.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Establishing reference ranges in healthy human volunteers, characterizing natural variability, diurnal variation, and assessing its stability across demographic factors.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Identifies hepatocellular necrotic and/or apoptotic injury. document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the efficacy of a multimodal exercise countermeasure (including high-intensity interval training, low-intensity cycling, or strength exercises) in attenuating musculoskeletal deconditioning, cardiovascular fitness level reduction, and muscle strength loss during 14 days of head-down bed rest (HDBR) in healthy older adults. The research, conducted as a 2-arm randomized controlled trial, also examined the effects on body composition, vertical jump performance, tilt tolerance, and various blood parameters including hormones, inflammatory markers, and lipid profiles. While the exercise intervention helped maintain aerobic fitness (V̇O2peak) and resulted in a greater decrease in total body fat mass, it was largely ineffective in preventing reductions in total and leg lean mass, knee extension strength (isometric and isokinetic), and orthostatic intolerance. Both groups experienced significant reductions in several blood parameters (serum iron, total cholesterol, HDL-chol, LDL-chol, parathyroid hormone, testosterone) and increases in white blood cells and C-reactive protein. Alanine transaminase and cortisol showed differential responses, increasing in the exercise group while decreasing in controls.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Head-down bed rest (HDBR) with or without a multimodal exercise countermeasure
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants underwent 14 days of continuous 6-degree Head-Down Bed Rest (HDBR). The exercise countermeasure group performed 3 sessions per day, totaling 60-75 minutes of physical exercise daily, individually adjusted for intensity. This multimodal intervention included high-intensity interval training (HIIT), low-intensity cycling, or strength exercises for the lower and upper body. The control group received passive physiotherapy consisting of passive range-of-motion exercises. All exercises and activities were completed in a head-down tilt or horizontal position. No specific dose-response comparisons for varying exercise parameters were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Decreased in both groups following 14 days of HDBR, with no significant difference between groups.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Muscle mass and other fat-free tissues; crucial for strength and metabolic health.

document_context_data.document_summary: This systematic review aimed to synthesize and analyze scientific evidence on biomarkers used for monitoring chronic fatigue and physiological responses to training and competition loads in professional male team sport athletes. It synthesizes evidence across 28 studies, covering muscle damage markers, anabolic/catabolic hormones, inflammatory markers, immunological markers, and oxidative stress markers. The review concluded that professional team sports induce significant alterations in these biomarkers, reflecting physiological strain, muscle damage, oxidative stress, inflammation, and immunosuppression, with effects generally larger and more prolonged after official matches than training. It emphasizes that a comprehensive analysis of these biomarkers provides a holistic understanding crucial for managing athlete fatigue, optimizing performance, and mitigating risks of overtraining, injury, or disease. The review also highlights the importance of establishing sex-specific reference ranges and monitoring strategies for biomarkers.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Physiological loads from intensive training and competition in professional male team sports.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The systematic review analyzed responses to varying physiological loads experienced by professional male team sport athletes during official matches and training sessions across competitive seasons (e.g., 4-week intensive training, 6-month seasons, 12-week periods, consecutive matches over 1-week). Biomarker data was collected from sports including basketball, soccer, handball, futsal, rugby, Australian football, volleyball, netball, and water-polo. Responses were generally larger and more prolonged after official matches compared to training, with recovery times ranging from 24 hours to several days post-exercise. The review also considered the impact of congested fixture schedules, high-intensity efforts, and sports with high eccentric loads, noting variability based on playing position, game time, and specific sporting discipline, but did not provide specific quantitative doses for training or matches.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Correlated with player load. Specific direction or magnitude not quantified for total neopterin alone.

matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Associated with mucosal immune function and player load, contributing to strategies for athlete preparation and well-being management.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the impact of acute preexercise calcium intake on bone turnover markers and calcium homeostasis in elite male rowers during a day with multiple strenuous, non-weight-bearing training sessions. The findings indicate that consuming a calcium-rich meal before training stabilizes ionized calcium levels, reduces the postexercise parathyroid hormone response, and attenuates the increase in bone resorption markers (e.g., β-CTX-I) over a sustained 7-hour period, thereby supporting long-term bone health and reducing the risk of bone stress injuries.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Dietary calcium supplementation (via whole foods/meals) in conjunction with repeated, strenuous, non-weight-bearing rowing exercise.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Elite male rowers (n=16) participated in two trials, one week apart, each involving two 90-min rowing ergometer sessions (EX1, EX2) separated by 150 minutes. Before each trial, participants consumed either a high calcium meal (~1000 mg, CAL) or an isocaloric low calcium meal (<10 mg, CON). Each exercise session consisted of three 30-minute sets at 90-100% of individual 2 mmol·L−1 capillary blood lactate power (mean 255-260W). Calcium was provided acutely before training sessions. No dose-response comparisons were reported beyond the high versus low intake, nor for exercise intensity.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Unaffected by preexercise calcium intake. Decreased significantly after feeding (P < 0.0001), increased during EX2 (P < 0.001), and decreased during recovery from both sessions (P < 0.05 for EX1, P < 0.001 for EX2).

matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Reflects bone formation activity in response to exercise and feeding. Acute preexercise calcium intake did not significantly influence total osteocalcin levels, suggesting it's more influenced by energy/carbohydrate availability during exercise.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of total dietary antioxidant intake and capacity on body antioxidant mechanisms and exhaustive exercise-induced oxidative damage in ultra-endurance athletes. It examined physiological responses, including oxidative stress biomarkers (8-iso PGF2a, TOS, TAS, OSI) and lactate levels, during and after a combined cycling and treadmill exhaustive exercise protocol. Key findings indicated that higher dietary antioxidant intake was negatively correlated with pre-exercise total oxidant status and post-exercise increases in 8-iso PGF2a, while positively correlating with post-exercise increases in total antioxidant status and blood lactate concentrations. A higher dietary antioxidant capacity also positively influenced antioxidant defense and blood lactate removal (in both sexes) and running time to exhaustion (in males), but did not affect post-exercise heart rate recovery or perceived exertion.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Exhaustive Exercise and Dietary Antioxidant Intake Assessment
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Ultra-endurance athletes underwent an acute exhaustive exercise protocol comprising 45 minutes on a cycle ergometer at 65% VO2max, immediately followed by a treadmill test at 75% VO2max to volitional exhaustion (median running time ~26-27 min, RPE 19). Dietary antioxidant intake was assessed using the Ferric Reducing Ability of Plasma (FRAP) assay, with a median intake of 16.6-17.2 mmol/day, categorized as moderate-to-high. The study focused on correlation analysis between habitual dietary intake and exercise responses, rather than controlled dietary intervention or dose-response comparisons for exercise intensity.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effect of heart rate-matched (HR-matched) or work rate-matched (WR-matched) hypoxic interval exercise on post-exercise cardiac autonomic and cardiovascular responses compared to normoxic exercise in moderately trained men. Findings indicate that HR-matched hypoxic exercise mimicked post-exercise autonomic responses of normoxic exercise without inducing significant post-exercise hypotension (PEH) or impairing cardiac baroreflex sensitivity (cBRS). Conversely, WR-matched hypoxic exercise resulted in delayed cardiac autonomic recovery, a temporary decrease in cBRS, and prolonged PEH.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Hypoxic and Normoxic Interval Exercise
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants performed three interval-type exercise sessions (5x5-min work intervals; 1-min passive recovery) after a 5-min warm-up at 50% WR@VT1. Normoxic exercise (N) was at 80% of the work rate (WR) at the first ventilatory threshold (mean WR 183±19 W, mean HR 139±10 bpm, ~75%HRmax). Hypoxic exercise (FiO2 = 14.2%, simulating ~3000m altitude) was performed either at the same absolute WR as N (H-WR, WR-matched: mean WR 183±19 W, mean HR 154±11 bpm, ~83%HRmax) or at the same absolute HR as N (H-HR, HR-matched: mean WR 144±18 W, mean HR 138±9 bpm, ~75%HRmax). This resulted in a -21.1±9.3% reduction in WR for H-HR compared to N, and a higher HR (by ~15 bpm) for H-WR compared to N. Recovery was seated under normoxic conditions, with assessments at POST-15, POST-45, POST-60, and POST-90 minutes.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Decreased at POST-15 in H-WR (MD -0.16 mmHg s mL^-1, p = 0.009) and increased at POST-60 in H-HR (MD 0.18 mmHg s mL^-1, p = 0.003) compared to PRE. Reduced TPR was also generally mentioned to indirectly support post-exercise autonomic alterations contributing to longer PEH after WR-matched hypoxic exercise.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Post-exercise recovery at rest after HR-matched Hypoxic (H-HR) and WR-matched Hypoxic (H-WR) exercise sessions.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Decreases indicate vasodilation contributing to hypotension, while increases indicate vasoconstriction, both affecting blood pressure regulation and potentially tissue perfusion during recovery.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigates the metabolic reprogramming mechanisms underlying sorafenib activity and resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells and patients. It reveals that sorafenib impairs mitochondrial function, forcing a metabolic shift towards glycolysis, leading to D-lactate accumulation, which serves as a biomarker for treatment response. In resistant cells, adaptation involves rerouting dihydroxyacetone phosphate towards glycerol-3-phosphate synthesis, extensive phospholipid remodeling to evade ferroptosis, enhanced antioxidant capacity, and increased reliance on exogenous triglycerides, resulting in glycerol accumulation as a marker of resistance. The study identifies D-lactate and glycerol as potential plasma biomarkers for monitoring sorafenib efficacy and resistance in HCC patients.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Sorafenib
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The primary therapy investigated was Sorafenib, a multi-kinase inhibitor for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). In vitro studies used sorafenib at an IC50 of 8.5 µM for acute, 48-hour, or 7-day prolonged treatments, and 7 µM for sorafenib-resistant IR-Huh7 cells. Clinical treatment involved oral administration of 400 mg twice daily for HCC patients, with dose reductions permitted for adverse effects. Other interventions included adenoviral gene downregulation (50 MOI for Gpd1/1l, Gpd2; 20 MOI for Glo1) and supplementation with various fatty acids (SFAs, MUFAs, PUFAs) or lipoproteins (VLDL, LDL), and inhibition of Mgll with JZL184. No detailed dose-response comparisons were consistently reported for sorafenib, though Mgll inhibition showed dose-dependent effects.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated alterations in serum levels of tumor, cardiac, liver, and renal function markers, alongside the IL-18 rs1946518 polymorphism, in patients with breast, colorectal, and prostate cancers (BC, CRC, PCa), and myocardial infarction (MI), compared to healthy controls. It revealed significantly elevated tumor markers (CA 15-3, CA 19-9, CEA, TPSA) in cancer patients, which serve as efficient early detection biomarkers. Cardiac markers (hs-cTnT, CK-MB) were specific to MI and largely unchanged in cancer. Liver and renal markers (ALP, AST, ALT, urea, creatinine) showed varied elevations, particularly in CRC and PCa, suggesting their utility as alternative diagnostic indicators. The IL-18 -607 C/A polymorphism was identified as a risk factor for PCa (AA genotype and A allele), and also showed an Odds Ratio of 1.75 for BC, while A/C heterozygotes were linked to increased CRC risk and C allele homozygotes offered protection against CRC.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review identifies and recommends validated biomarkers for tracking health, performance, and recovery in athletes across multiple domains including nutritional status (macronutrients, micronutrients, food allergies), hydration, muscle status (damage, endocrine response), endurance, and injury risk (concussions, stress fractures, ACL). It advocates for a comprehensive, integrative, and individualized approach to biomarker analysis, emphasizing dynamic monitoring and contextual interpretation over single markers or universal thresholds to optimize training and minimize injury and overtraining risks.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Biomarker-guided monitoring and management of athletic training, nutrition, hydration, and injury recovery
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This review primarily focuses on the diagnostic and prognostic value of biomarkers rather than specific therapeutic doses. It emphasizes frequent, individualized monitoring (e.g., pre/post-exercise, daily, seasonally, after injury/competition) to establish personalized baseline ranges and track physiological changes in response to various training loads (e.g., acute bouts, heavy strength training, challenging training weeks). While specific nutritional intake recommendations are mentioned for protein (1.3–2.0 g/kg/day) and omega-3 fatty acids (≤3 g/day for average, 6–8 g/day for elite athletes), and iron supplementation at low-moderate doses, the document does not report dose-response comparisons for biomarker changes. Instead, it provides specific thresholds for identifying deficiencies (e.g., Vitamin D >50 ng/ml, Ferritin <12 µg/L), dehydration (e.g., >-2% body mass decrease, blood osmolality ≥295 mmol/kg, USG ≥1.020), insufficient recovery (30% decrease in T:C ratio), and overtraining (T:C ratio of 0.35 × 10⁻³). The overall approach prioritizes dynamic, contextualized assessment over universal thresholds for effective athlete management.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Protein deficiency, imbalance between dietary protein intake and needs
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Helps gauge protein status; low levels may indicate insufficient protein intake and potential lean muscle mass loss

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated whether pre-exercise ascorbic acid supplementation influenced antioxidant defenses, glucose metabolism, inflammation, and muscle damage in untrained healthy adults following a single bout of moderate-intensity cycling. Findings indicated that ascorbic acid supplementation reduced plasma Malondialdehyde (MDA) and increased Ferric Reducing Ability of Plasma (FRAP), while also modulating glucose levels and attenuating exercise-induced changes in albumin and total protein. While moderate-intensity cycling led to an increase in red blood cell Superoxide Dismutase (SOD) activity and low-grade muscle damage (Total Creatine Kinase), it did not induce systemic inflammation or lipid peroxidation. Ascorbic acid supplementation appeared to mitigate the exercise-induced increase in SOD activity but did not significantly prevent muscle damage or affect other inflammatory/damage markers such as hsCRP, LDH, CK-MB, GPx, or Catalase.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Oral ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) supplementation combined with a single bout of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Subjects received 1000 mg of ascorbic acid (or placebo) orally 5 minutes prior to a 30-minute indoor cycling session. Exercise intensity was set at 65–75% of maximum heart rate, which was predicted by an age-based equation. No dose-response comparisons were reported for either ascorbic acid or exercise intensity.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Higher immediately after exercise in placebo, returning to baseline by 30 minutes; no significant change with ascorbic acid supplementation
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Elevated immediately after exercise in placebo (P<0.05) and significantly (p=0.049) returned to baseline at 30 min post-exercise. This increase was not observed with ascorbic acid supplementation, indicating no difference between pre-, post-, and 30 min post-exercise.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Acute aerobic exercise (indoor cycling) in untrained healthy adults, with or without ascorbic acid supplementation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates acute physiological responses to exercise, potentially related to fluid shifts or metabolic demand. Ascorbic acid attenuated these changes, potentially promoting adequate hydration status.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of 80 mg/day oral iron supplementation on hematological parameters, muscle damage biomarkers (CK, LDH, Mb), and cortisol levels in elite male cyclists during a 3-week stage race (Vuelta a España). It concluded that iron supplementation effectively prevented declines in iron metabolism and hematological profiles (serum iron, ferritin, hemoglobin, hematocrit, TSI, TP, RBC), significantly reduced accumulated stress (cortisol), and significantly lowered Creatine Kinase (CK) levels within the supplemented group, thereby contributing to optimal recovery and performance.

The supplementation lasted for a 4-week period, starting one week before and continuing throughout the 3-week Vuelta a España stage race. No dose-response comparisons were reported, but a control group received no oral iron.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study utilized a sportomics approach to investigate the physiological, biochemical, hemodynamic, metabolic, and hydration parameters in elite athletes undergoing a 40-minute high-intensity functional Cross Combat (CCombat) exercise protocol. The main aim was to evaluate the effects of this intensive training on hydration and kidney function, ultimately suggesting albuminuria as a sensitive biomarker for assessing hydration status changes during strenuous activity and mitigating chronic renal impairment.

Sixteen elite-level professional male athletes were engaged in training sessions over a 96-hour protocol, with blood samples collected. The study was observational, and athletes had free access to hydration post-protocol. No specific dose-response comparisons were reported.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of short-term powdered Montmorency tart cherry supplementation on markers of muscle damage, inflammation, oxidative stress, and muscle soreness in aerobically trained individuals undergoing a half-marathon run. Findings indicate that supplementation attenuated muscle catabolism (creatinine, urea/BUN, total protein), reduced physiological stress (cortisol), lessened immune and inflammatory stress (IL-2, IL-6, IL-13), better maintained redox balance (antioxidant activity, TAS), and reduced muscle soreness, ultimately enhancing endurance performance and recovery.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Powdered Montmorency tart cherry supplementation and endurance running (half-marathon race)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Subjects ingested capsules containing 480 mg of powdered Montmorency tart cherries (CherryPURE®) once daily for 10 days (7 days pre-race, race day, and 2 days post-race), compared to a 480 mg rice flour placebo. This 480 mg supplement is equivalent to 51.3 mL (17.4 fl oz) of tart cherry juice, providing 991 mg of phenolic compounds and 66 mg of anthocyanins. The intervention was evaluated in the context of a stressful endurance challenge: a half-marathon run (21.1 km). No dose-response comparisons were reported, but the supplementation significantly affected physiological responses and race performance compared to placebo.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased 4% over pre-run values in placebo during recovery, and decreased 3% below pre-run in tart cherry group. Attenuations over time (p=0.081) and group differences (p=0.060), with significant elevations 60-min and 48-h post-run in placebo, but never increased above pre-run levels in tart cherry group over 48-h recovery.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: General indicator of hydration, nutrition, and metabolic state, as well as a marker of muscle catabolism.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Short-term powdered tart cherry supplementation surrounding a half-marathon run and 48-h recovery.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Suggests a tendency for reduced muscle catabolism, better protein balance, and attenuated physiological stress related to exercise.

The study aims to identify a new treatment strategy for mild COVID-19 and determine the number of days required to achieve a 50% or more improvement in clinical symptoms.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Clarithromycin
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Oral administration of clarithromycin is investigated in two dosage groups (800 mg/day, given as 400 mg twice daily, and 400 mg/day, given as 200 mg twice daily for 7 days) compared to a standard treatment control group. Patients are randomized in a 1:1:1 ratio, allowing for dose comparisons. Dose adjustment based on patient age, weight, and symptoms is possible. The doses are approved for other bacterial respiratory infections in Japan, and their safety is confirmed, but this is an exploratory trial as no prior dose-response data for COVID-19 pneumonia were available.

document_context_data.document_summary: This review provides updated guidelines and a consensus for standardizing pre-analytical variables in salivary biomarker studies for Alzheimer's disease (AD) research. It critically appraises current methodologies, identifies inconsistencies, and proposes a standardized protocol for saliva collection, processing, and storage to improve reliability for diagnostic biomarker detection and quantification. The document investigates various protein and metabolomic biomarkers in saliva, assessing their diagnostic potential for AD and Mild Cognitive Impairment, and highlights the importance of controlling factors like collection methods, centrifugation, and storage conditions for accurate measurement.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Salivary Biomarker Research and Standardization for Alzheimer's Disease Diagnosis
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This is a comprehensive review article focusing on standardizing pre-analytical variables for salivary Alzheimer's Disease (AD) biomarker studies, rather than a therapeutic intervention or dose-response investigation. It critically discusses how inconsistent methodologies and pre-analytical factors (e.g., collection kits like Salivette vs. passive drooling, acute food intake, physical activity, stress, diurnal variations, dental restorations, freezing/thawing protocols, centrifugation speeds) influence biomarker detection and quantification, leading to conflicting findings for analytes like Aβ42, Aβ40, and AChE activity. The document proposes a standardized pre-analytical protocol, including pre-collection instructions (e.g., abstinence from food, drinks, smoking, alcohol, exercise), passive drool collection (e.g., 2 mL after 5 min pooling), and post-collection processing (e.g., immediate freezing, visual inspection, two-step centrifugation, aliquoting 100-250 µL). Various analytical methods (ELISA, Western blot, SIMOA, MS-based methods, NMR) were discussed for diagnostic marker identification, emphasizing that a universal protocol might not suit all biomarkers due to their diverse physiological roles.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Differs between sexes. Significantly reduced in specimen when centrifugation speed is increased (>1000 x g). Can be increased by using centrifugal filter devices to concentrate low molecular mass analytes. Patients with AD had a higher salivary total protein concentration. Acid stimulation decreased total protein concentrations. Stimulated saliva collection also leads to decreased total protein due to dilution.

matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: General indicator of saliva composition; a critical pre-analytical variable. Higher levels associated with AD. document_context_data.document_summary: This pilot study comprehensively investigated differential cytokine profiles in matched serum and saliva samples from patients with Behçet’s disease (BD) with and without oral ulcers, recurrent aphthous stomatitis (RAS), and healthy controls (HCs). The study aimed to identify cytokine panels with diagnostic and therapeutic potential for BD, as well as to characterize the cytokine profile across different disease activity states and in response to immunosuppressive therapies. Key findings revealed that salivary cytokine levels were generally higher and more readily detectable than in serum. Specific elevated salivary cytokines, including IL-1β, IL-8, TNF-α, and IL-6, were identified in BD patients, both with and without oral ulcers, and during relapsed or quiet systemic episodes. The research also explored the impact of various immunosuppressive therapies on these cytokine concentrations and emphasized the importance of normalizing salivary cytokine levels to total protein due to altered salivary composition in BD patients. The study concluded that salivary cytokine profiling offers a less invasive and sensitive method for frequent monitoring of BD activity, progression, and treatment responses, with specific cytokine panels holding promise for differential diagnosis and predicting ulcer recurrence or systemic relapse.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Cytokine Profiling for Diagnostic Potential; Observational study comparing disease states and the influence of immunosuppressive therapies
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Concentrations of 12 cytokines (IL-1β, IL-2, IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IL-12p70, IL-17A, IFN-γ, TNF-α, TNF-β) were measured using the Human Th1/Th2 11-Plex FlowCytomix™ kit with IL-17A. Samples were matched serum and saliva from N=20 Behçet's disease (BD) patients, N=6 recurrent aphthous stomatitis (RAS) patients, and N=10 healthy controls (HCs), utilizing 25 µl sample volumes. BD patients received either single therapy (ST) (prednisolone, azathioprine, or colchicine, N=9) or a combination of therapies (CT) (prednisolone, azathioprine, colchicine, and/or Cyclosporin A, N=8), compared to patients not on any medication (N=3). Specific dosages for medications were not reported, and no dose-response comparisons for therapeutic interventions were conducted, as the primary focus was on biomarker expression and assay performance.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly lower in BD patients than in HCs (p=0.02). Varied between patients; significantly lower in Behçet's Disease patients compared to Healthy Controls.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: BD patients relative to HCs. Comparison between Behçet's Disease patients and Healthy Controls; normalization of salivary cytokine concentrations.

document_context_data.document_summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial investigated the effects of 12 weeks of daily protein supplementation on lean body mass, fat mass, muscle strength, physical performance, and various biochemical markers in physically active older adults with low habitual protein intake, who were also training for a 4-day walking event. The study found that protein supplementation resulted in a larger increase in relative lean body mass and a greater reduction in fat mass compared to placebo. While both the protein and placebo groups showed improvements in physical performance and cardiorespiratory fitness due to the walking exercise, no additional between-group differences were observed in muscle strength, muscle contractile properties, or physical performance from protein supplementation. Serum urea increased in the protein group, but no adverse effects on renal function or muscle damage markers were noted, indicating protein supplementation is a safe strategy for this population.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Protein supplementation combined with walking exercise
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Physically active older adults were randomized to receive either 31 g of milk protein concentrate daily (split into 15g at breakfast and 15g post-exercise/lunch) or an iso-caloric placebo for 12 weeks. This increased the protein group's total daily protein intake from 0.86 ± 0.23 g/kg/day upon enrollment to 1.29 ± 0.28 g/kg/day at 12 weeks. Both groups concurrently participated in walking exercise training for a 4-day walking event, covering an average of 338-391 km over 12 weeks. No dose-response comparisons for protein intake were reported, only the comparison between the protein and placebo groups.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant change was observed in both the protein and placebo group after the intervention.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the oxidative stress and genotoxicity in gas station refueling workers exposed to long-term, low levels of atmospheric BTEX in Nanning, China, comparing them to office workers. It found significantly higher BTEX levels in refueling areas, which, despite being generally below occupational limits, were associated with reduced antioxidant capacity (lower T-SOD and GSH) and increased oxidative stress (higher MDA and 8-OHdG) and DNA damage (higher micronucleus rate, tail moment, and Olive tail moment) in refueling workers.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Long-term occupational exposure to BTEX (Benzene, Toluene, Ethylbenzene, Xylenes) compounds in gas station refueling workers, compared to office workers
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Long-term occupational exposure to low levels of atmospheric BTEX, with refueling workers exposed for an average of 8.7 years. BTEX concentrations in refueling areas were significantly higher than in office areas (p < 0.001), with mean ambient air concentrations including Benzene (60.03 vs 16.86 µg/m3), Toluene (317.76 vs 89.93 µg/m3), Ethylbenzene (113.85 vs 12.09 µg/m3), m-xylene (40.91 vs 28.44 µg/m3), p-xylene (57.51 vs 10.62 µg/m3), and o-xylene (37.18 vs 15.67 µg/m3). These levels were generally below current occupational exposure limits, but fixed environmental monitoring may underestimate actual exposure. No specific dose-response analysis for individual BTEX compounds was reported in human subjects.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly lower in refueling workers compared to office workers (p < 0.001 to z = -6.303, p < 0.001); however, after controlling for confounding factors (age, gender, years of exposure, smoking, and drinking habits), T-SOD activity was significantly higher in refueling workers than in office workers.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review identifies and recommends validated biomarkers for tracking health, performance, and recovery in athletes across multiple domains including nutritional status (macronutrients, micronutrients, food allergies), hydration, muscle status (damage, endocrine response), endurance, and injury risk (concussions, stress fractures, ACL). It advocates for a comprehensive, integrative, and individualized approach to biomarker analysis, emphasizing dynamic monitoring and contextual interpretation over single markers or universal thresholds to optimize training and minimize injury and overtraining risks.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Biomarker-guided monitoring and management of athletic training, nutrition, hydration, and injury recovery
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This review primarily focuses on the diagnostic and prognostic value of biomarkers rather than specific therapeutic doses. It emphasizes frequent, individualized monitoring (e.g., pre/post-exercise, daily, seasonally, after injury/competition) to establish personalized baseline ranges and track physiological changes in response to various training loads (e.g., acute bouts, heavy strength training, challenging training weeks). While specific nutritional intake recommendations are mentioned for protein (1.3–2.0 g/kg/day) and omega-3 fatty acids (≤3 g/day for average, 6–8 g/day for elite athletes), and iron supplementation at low-moderate doses, the document does not report dose-response comparisons for biomarker changes. Instead, it provides specific thresholds for identifying deficiencies (e.g., Vitamin D >50 ng/ml, Ferritin <12 µg/L), dehydration (e.g., >-2% body mass decrease, blood osmolality ≥295 mmol/kg, USG ≥1.020), insufficient recovery (30% decrease in T:C ratio), and overtraining (T:C ratio of 0.35 × 10⁻³). The overall approach prioritizes dynamic, contextualized assessment over universal thresholds for effective athlete management.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Shown to be elevated in boxers after repeated punches to the head even without a knockout.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Marker of axonal damage in the central nervous system.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Concussion recovery, repeated punches to the head in boxing.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Detects and monitors changes in the central nervous system to objectively assess readiness for return to athletic pursuits after concussion.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study, part of the Concussion Assessment, Research, and Education (CARE) Consortium, investigated the utility of plasma biomarkers (total tau, GFAP, and Nf-L) for predicting return-to-sport (RTS) duration following sport-related concussion (SRC) in collegiate athletes. It aimed to differentiate athletes returning to sport in less than 14 days versus 14 days or more post-injury. The findings indicated that higher total tau concentrations at 24-48 hours post-injury and at symptom resolution, and lower GFAP concentrations acutely post-injury, were associated with a protracted RTS (>=14 days). Nf-L was not significantly associated with RTS duration in this cohort.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study of Sport-Related Concussion (SRC) recovery and return-to-sport (RTS) trajectories.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was an observational study involving 127 NCAA collegiate athletes who sustained an SRC. Plasma biomarker levels (total tau, GFAP, Nf-L) were measured at baseline, 0-21 hours, 24-48 hours post-injury, and at the time of symptom resolution. The study compared biomarker concentrations between athletes who returned to sport in less than 14 days versus those who took 14 days or more; no therapeutic interventions, specific doses, or dose-response comparisons were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: At 24-48 hours post-injury, mean plasma total tau was significantly higher in athletes with >=14 days RTS (-0.14 [0.14] pg/mL) compared to <14 days RTS (-0.65 [0.12] pg/mL) (P = .008). At symptom resolution, total tau showed acceptable discrimination power for RTS duration (AUC, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.63-0.86; P < .001). Baseline concentrations were not significantly different.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Post-Sport-Related Concussion (SRC) recovery monitoring in collegiate athletes, specifically measured at 24-48 hours post-injury and at the time of symptom resolution.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: May identify collegiate athletes who will require more time to Return-to-Sport (RTS) following SRC, indicating its utility in predicting longer recovery duration and tracking neuronal recovery.

document_context_data.document_summary: The study investigated the systemic innate immune response, specifically focusing on neutrophil phenotypes, as biomarkers to monitor exercise-induced immune changes during repetitive, prolonged walking over consecutive days (e.g., Nijmegen 4 Day Marches). It found that prolonged exercise leads to an initial systemic innate immune response, characterized by the mobilization and activation of various neutrophil phenotypes, followed by adaptation or partial normalization in subsequent days. Crucially, increased neutrophil activation, marked by high CD11b expression, was consistently associated with impaired physical feeling, slower walking speed, and a higher degree of physiological stress, suggesting its potential as a valuable marker for monitoring immune system changes and detecting overtraining.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Repetitive prolonged walking exercise
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants engaged in prolonged walking over 3 consecutive days as part of a public walking event (e.g., Nijmegen 4 Day Marches), covering 30, 40, or 50 km/day at a self-selected pace. Exercise intensity on day 1 averaged 65% of maximum heart rate. While the study involved varying distances, no explicit dose-response comparisons for immune markers were reported between different daily distances. However, increased neutrophil activation (high CD11b expression) was associated with slower walking speeds (approx. 4.1-4.2 km/h across days) and predominantly occurred in participants walking 30 km (66% of this group).

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated whether post-exercise branched chain amino acid and carbohydrate (BCAA-CHO) supplementation, compared to carbohydrate-only (CHO) supplementation, could mitigate performance decrements, muscle damage, and soreness, or alter immunological markers following three consecutive days of high-intensity resistance training (back squats) in resistance-trained males. The findings consistently indicated that BCAA-CHO did not significantly improve lower body strength, isometric/isokinetic torque, neuromuscular activation (EMG), perceived muscle soreness, or reduce levels of muscle damage markers like myoglobin, creatine kinase, and lactate dehydrogenase. However, BCAA-CHO supplementation did attenuate the exercise-induced increase in monocyte percentages, suggesting a modulated immune or inflammatory response.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Post-exercise nutritional supplementation (branched chain amino acids + carbohydrates vs. carbohydrates only) combined with a high-intensity, high-volume resistance training protocol.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Resistance training involved three consecutive days of 10 sets of 5 repetitions at 80% of 1RM barbell back squat, with a 5% weight reduction if repetitions could not be completed. Participants received two servings of either BCAA-CHO (3g L-leucine, 1g L-isoleucine, 2g L-valine, 2g non-sugar carbohydrates) or CHO (42g carbohydrates, predominantly sugars) immediately after each lifting bout and on a recovery day. Supplements were provided in 600 mL of tap water. The study compared these two supplementation types, reflecting a real-world application, but reported no further dose-response comparisons or standardization for overall carbohydrate or calorie content.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant main effect for time (p=0.37) or group*time interaction (p=0.15) for total WBC counts, indicating no differential alteration between or within groups due to supplementation.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: General indicator of immune system activity and systemic response to physiological stress or potential inflammation induced by strenuous exercise.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Following repeated strenuous resistance exercise and supplement consumption, over the duration of the study.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: No significant changes in general immune response, not differentially affected by BCAA-CHO or CHO supplementation.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigates the metabolic reprogramming mechanisms underlying sorafenib activity and resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells and patients. It reveals that sorafenib impairs mitochondrial function, forcing a metabolic shift towards glycolysis, leading to D-lactate accumulation, which serves as a biomarker for treatment response. In resistant cells, adaptation involves rerouting dihydroxyacetone phosphate towards glycerol-3-phosphate synthesis, extensive phospholipid remodeling to evade ferroptosis, enhanced antioxidant capacity, and increased reliance on exogenous triglycerides, resulting in glycerol accumulation as a marker of resistance. The study identifies D-lactate and glycerol as potential plasma biomarkers for monitoring sorafenib efficacy and resistance in HCC patients.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Sorafenib
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The primary therapy investigated was Sorafenib, a multi-kinase inhibitor for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). In vitro studies used sorafenib at an IC50 of 8.5 µM for acute, 48-hour, or 7-day prolonged treatments, and 7 µM for sorafenib-resistant IR-Huh7 cells. Clinical treatment involved oral administration of 400 mg twice daily for HCC patients, with dose reductions permitted for adverse effects. Other interventions included adenoviral gene downregulation (50 MOI for Gpd1/1l, Gpd2; 20 MOI for Glo1) and supplementation with various fatty acids (SFAs, MUFAs, PUFAs) or lipoproteins (VLDL, LDL), and inhibition of Mgll with JZL184. No detailed dose-response comparisons were consistently reported for sorafenib, though Mgll inhibition showed dose-dependent effects.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the impact of human bone donor age on the osteoinductive capacity of decellularized bone scaffolds and their conditioned media (DBCM), and their ability to promote osteogenic differentiation of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BM-MSCs). The main findings indicate that older donor bone scaffolds and their conditioned media exhibit superior osteoinductive capacity, enhancing osteogenic differentiation of BM-MSCs, which is potentially linked to reduced IGFBP1 bioavailability and increased porosity/altered trabecular architecture in aged bone.

treatment_details.therapy_type: In vitro assessment of human decellularized bone scaffolds and conditioned media for osteoinductive capacity
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study's primary variable was the age of the human bone donor (young: ≤50 years, range 34–49; old: ≥70 years, range 72–84). Decellularized bone cubes (1 cm³) were obtained from human femoral heads. Bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BM-MSCs) from both young (≤50 years, range 44–49) and old (≥70 years, range 72–81) donors were seeded onto these scaffolds (0.5x10^6 BM-MSCs per cube) or cultured in decellularized bone conditioned media (DBCM) for up to 28 days. The investigation focused on age-dependent differences in scaffold properties and their influence on BM-MSC osteogenic differentiation, rather than dose-response comparisons of a therapeutic agent.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant change in trabecular thickness between young and old donor decellularized bone samples.

document_context_data.document_summary: This case-control study investigated plasma levels of 16 trace elements and 27 AMD-associated genetic variants in 236 individuals with neovascular age-related macular degeneration (nAMD) and 236 age-matched controls. The primary findings revealed significantly elevated plasma levels of barium and cadmium, and reduced levels of chromium in nAMD patients, suggesting that an imbalance of these trace elements, influenced by environmental and lifestyle factors, may play a role in nAMD pathogenesis. No association was found between the AMD-associated genetic variants and trace element levels.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational biomarker association study
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Plasma levels of 16 trace elements (including arsenic, barium, calcium, cadmium, cobalt, chromium, copper, iron, magnesium, manganese, molybdenum, lead, antimony, selenium, vanadium, and zinc) were quantitatively measured using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) in 236 nAMD patients and 236 age-matched controls. Two additional elements (Al, Ni) were initially measured but excluded due to inadequate accuracy/reproducibility. This was a cross-sectional, observational study, and no therapeutic interventions or dose-response comparisons were reported or applicable. Patients with nAMD may have received past anti-angiogenic drug injections, but details regarding dose, intensity, or duration were not the focus of this study.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study developed and characterized a responsive human triple-culture model of the air-blood barrier, integrating distinct macrophage phenotypes (M1, M2 wound-healing, M2 regulatory) derived from THP-1 monocytes to mimic in vivo alveolar macrophage features. The research investigated their immunological impact, particularly on epithelial barrier function and inflammatory responses in both A549/ISO-HAS-1 and H441/ISO-HAS-1 co-culture systems. It demonstrated that the M1 macrophage model induced a severe inflammatory-like response, characterized by impaired epithelial barrier integrity and increased pro-inflammatory markers, making it suitable for modeling inflammatory lung diseases. Conversely, the M2 models (M2wh and M2reg) exhibited a non-inflammatory or pro-regenerative profile, maintaining barrier integrity and thus providing a foundation for establishing a quiescent, physiological air-blood barrier model. The study also detailed the specific biomarker profiles of these differentiated macrophage subtypes and their varied responses to Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) stimulation within the triple-culture system, highlighting cell line-specific differences in inflammatory outcomes.

treatment_details.therapy_type: In vitro differentiation of human monocytic leukemia cell line THP-1 into M1 (classically activated), M2wh (wound-healing), and M2reg (regulatory) macrophage phenotypes, followed by their integration into a human triple-culture air-blood barrier model. The model consisted of alveolar epithelial cells (A549 or NCI H441) and microvascular endothelial cells (ISO-HAS-1) cultured on Transwell filter membranes. Immunological impact was subsequently assessed via Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) stimulation.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: THP-1 cells were differentiated for 48h using specific cytokine cocktails: for M1 macrophages, 50 nM PMA, 100 ng/ml GM-CSF, and 25 ng/ml TNFα; for M2wh macrophages, 8 nM PMA, 100 ng/ml GM-CSF, 35 ng/ml IL-4, and 20 ng/ml IL-13; for M2reg macrophages, 8 nM PMA, 100 ng/ml GM-CSF, and 20 ng/ml IL-10. Dexamethasone (1 µM) was also used in some contexts. The differentiated macrophages were seeded onto the epithelial layer of the co-culture system. Cell culture media contained 10% Fetal Calf Serum (FCS), which was reduced to 5% for the triple cultures. The triple cultures were stimulated apically with 1 µg/ml LPS (end concentration) and incubated for 24h. No explicit dose-response comparisons for LPS or macrophage cell numbers were reported; the focus was on comparing responses across macrophage phenotypes and with/without LPS stimulation.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: decreased for M1; stable for M2wh and M2reg
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: M1 macrophages caused a significant decrease in TER (to 61 ± 37% compared to untreated co-culture, c) after 48h. In contrast, M2wh (103 ± 24% compared to c) and M2reg (108 ± 31% compared to c) maintained stable TER values after 48h. LPS stimulation did not significantly affect TER in any case.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Triple culture of H441/ISO-HAS-1 epithelial cells with differently stimulated macrophages (M1, M2wh, M2reg), with and without apical LPS stimulation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: M1 macrophages significantly impair epithelial barrier function, whereas M2wh and M2reg macrophages maintain it, indicating distinct roles in tissue integrity and inflammatory damage relevant to lung health.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study performed a comprehensive fine-mapping analysis of 150 breast cancer risk regions using dense genotype data from over 217,000 subjects (109,900 breast cancer cases, 88,937 controls of European ancestry). It identified 352 independent risk signals, containing 13,367 credible causal variants (CCVs), with 191-205 high-confidence signals and 191 likely target genes. The investigation revealed that CCVs were significantly over-represented in active gene regulatory regions, open chromatin, actively transcribed genes, and transcription factor binding sites. The study also found signals differentially associated with ER-positive and ER-negative breast cancer, and prioritized target genes through integrated computational approaches like PAINTOR and INQUISIT, collectively explaining up to 23.6% of the familial relative risk. Furthermore, it included eQTL analyses in normal and tumor breast tissue to link genetic variants with gene expression changes, and explored the enrichment of CCVs with various genomic features and their impact on specific biological pathways.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Genetic fine-mapping, risk profiling, and functional genomics analysis.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This study is a genetic association and fine-mapping analysis, not an interventional therapy. It utilized dense genotype data from over 217,000 subjects (109,900 breast cancer cases, 88,937 controls) of European ancestry, analyzing over 639,000 genetic variants (SNPs, deletion/insertions, CNVs with MAF ">= 0.1% or 0.005%") across 150-152 previously defined risk regions. Methodologies included stepwise multinomial logistic regression, Bayesian approaches (PAINTOR), and a gene prioritization pipeline (INQUSIT). Statistical thresholds like conditional p-values (< 10^-6 for strong evidence, < 10^-4 for moderate) and False Discovery Rate (FDR 5%) were applied. eQTL analyses involved linear regression with specific covariates, and functional characterization included enrichment analysis with histone marks and TFBS motifs (FIMO p-value threshold 10^-3). No dose-response comparisons for a therapeutic intervention were reported.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of 6-week cranberry (Vaccinium macrocarpon) extract supplementation on antioxidant capacity, inflammatory markers, and iron metabolism in rowers subjected to exhaustive exercise. Findings indicate that supplementation significantly strengthened antioxidant potential (TAC) and mitigated exercise-induced increases in pro-inflammatory markers (TNF-alpha), muscle damage indicators (myoglobin), and iron regulatory hormones (hepcidin) in the supplemented group. However, IL-6, ferritin, sTfR, iron, TIBC, and UIBC remained largely unaffected by supplementation or showed exercise-induced changes independent of it.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Cranberry (Vaccinium macrocarpon) extract supplementation combined with strenuous physical exercise
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Athletes received 720 mg of highly-concentrated large cranberry extract daily (two 360-mg capsules, containing 36 mg proanthocyanidins per capsule) for 6 weeks. The control group received dyed gelatin placebo capsules containing flour. Participants performed a 2000-m rowing ergometer test at maximal effort on day 1 (pre-supplementation) and at the end of the 6-week training camp (post-supplementation), with blood samples taken pre-exercise, 1 minute post-exercise, and after a 24-hour recovery. No dose-response comparisons for cranberry extract were reported within the study.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Neither cranberry supplementation nor physical exercise exerted statistically significant effects on this parameter (main effect, p=0.177).

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review identifies and recommends validated biomarkers for tracking health, performance, and recovery in athletes across multiple domains including nutritional status (macronutrients, micronutrients, food allergies), hydration, muscle status (damage, endocrine response), endurance, and injury risk (concussions, stress fractures, ACL). It advocates for a comprehensive, integrative, and individualized approach to biomarker analysis, emphasizing dynamic monitoring and contextual interpretation over single markers or universal thresholds to optimize training and minimize injury and overtraining risks.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Biomarker-guided monitoring and management of athletic training, nutrition, hydration, and injury recovery
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This review primarily focuses on the diagnostic and prognostic value of biomarkers rather than specific therapeutic doses. It emphasizes frequent, individualized monitoring (e.g., pre/post-exercise, daily, seasonally, after injury/competition) to establish personalized baseline ranges and track physiological changes in response to various training loads (e.g., acute bouts, heavy strength training, challenging training weeks). While specific nutritional intake recommendations are mentioned for protein (1.3–2.0 g/kg/day) and omega-3 fatty acids (≤3 g/day for average, 6–8 g/day for elite athletes), and iron supplementation at low-moderate doses, the document does not report dose-response comparisons for biomarker changes. Instead, it provides specific thresholds for identifying deficiencies (e.g., Vitamin D >50 ng/ml, Ferritin <12 µg/L), dehydration (e.g., >-2% body mass decrease, blood osmolality ≥295 mmol/kg, USG ≥1.020), insufficient recovery (30% decrease in T:C ratio), and overtraining (T:C ratio of 0.35 × 10⁻³). The overall approach prioritizes dynamic, contextualized assessment over universal thresholds for effective athlete management.

document_context_data.document_summary: This retrospective cohort study investigated the association between iron status and renal outcomes, specifically progression to End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD), in 111 pre-dialysis patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) and biopsy-proven Diabetic Nephropathy (DN). It found that reduced serum transferrin is an independent predictor of ESRD, and identified increased iron and transferrin deposition in renal tubular epithelial cells of DN patients, suggesting a pathological role for altered iron metabolism in disease progression.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study investigating the prognostic value of iron status and related biomarkers in Diabetic Nephropathy (DN) progression.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This retrospective observational cohort study analyzed baseline serum iron status markers (serum iron, ferritin, TIBC, transferrin, TSAT) and their association with progression to End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) in 111 Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) patients with biopsy-proven DN. Serum markers were measured using chemiluminescence immunoassay, immunoradiometric assay, and colorimetric methods. Additionally, histological analysis involved immunohistochemical staining for transferrin and Perl's blue staining for iron in kidney biopsy specimens from DN patients and healthy controls. No therapeutic interventions, dose comparisons, or active treatments were investigated; the study focused on correlation and predictive value.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Lower baseline serum concentrations in ESRD patients (median 1.38 g/L, IQR 1.15-1.65) compared to non-ESRD patients; lower serum levels incrementally associated with higher ESRD risk (e.g., Q1 HR 7.36, 95% CI 1.40-38.65 vs. Q4). It positively correlated with eGFR (r=0.21, P=0.03), hemoglobin (r=0.39, P<0.001), and albumin (r=0.69, P<0.001), and negatively correlated with proteinuria (r=-0.42, P<0.001). Lower levels, especially when combined with low eGFR, predicted a worse renal outcome.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Mediates iron transport and represents total iron-binding capacity. Most important molecule for transporting iron into cells, involved in iron transport across intestinal mucosa, intracellular iron transport, and chelating free iron for non-specific immunity. Also proposed to assess nutritional status. Dysregulation of iron homeostasis is a major factor in DN development.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Progression of Diabetic Nephropathy (DN) to End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) patients; T2DM with biopsy-proven DN.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Associated with progression to ESRD, indicating poor renal outcome; a strong independent predictor of ESRD with high diagnostic value. Indicates poor nutritional status and increased susceptibility to infection; more sensitive marker of early protein depletion than albumin. Higher serum levels are associated with better renal survival.

matched_biomarker_details.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Kidney Tissue (DN kidney biopsies, tubular epithelial cells and glomeruli)

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Higher / Absent in normal tissue, present in DN tissue
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Absent in normal kidney tissue. Positive staining observed in DN kidney biopsies, with strong positivity in tubular epithelial cells and less intense staining in glomeruli.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Iron transport and binding protein. Localized deposition can contribute to disease mechanisms. Transferrin-bound iron is potentially filtered by pathological glomerulus into the tubular lumen, leading to iron release and accumulation in tubular cells.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Diabetic Nephropathy (DN) progression, investigated in renal biopsy specimens from T2DM patients.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Suggested as a potential mechanism contributing to DN progression via tissue deposition. Indicates abnormal accumulation of transferrin and potentially iron in renal tissue, contributing to renal damage and disease progression.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study performed a comprehensive qualitative and quantitative proteomic analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) derived from different somatic origins (fibroblasts and peripheral blood CD34+ cells), comparing them to original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC) and human embryonic stem cells (hESC). Using ESI-MS e and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry, complemented by Western blot validation, the research aimed to characterize hiPSC proteomic profiles, identify known and novel pluripotency markers, and distinguish hiPSCs from their somatic precursors. Key findings include the identification of approximately 220 commonly up-regulated proteins in pluripotent stem cell lines, the development and confirmation of a 22-protein marker panel for hiPSC characterization, and the observation of coordinated up-regulation of proteins involved in protein synthesis, folding, RNA processing, DNA replication, DNA repair, and energy metabolism (including oxidative phosphorylation and lipogenesis) in hiPSCs. The study also identified somatic cell markers that were down-regulated upon reprogramming and highlighted specific proteomic differences between hiPSCs and hESCs, contributing to improved hiPSC quality control for therapeutic applications.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Proteomic characterization and comparative analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) and human embryonic stem cells (hESCs).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was a characterization study, not a therapeutic intervention, thus no 'dose' of therapy was administered. Quantitative and qualitative proteomic analyses were performed using electrospray ionization (ESI)-MS e (label-free quantification with internal reference standard) and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry. Two hiPSC lines (iNC-01 from CD34+ cells, SB5-MP1 from fibroblasts, both generated using loxP-flanked excisable polycistronic STEMCCA lentiviral vector) and one hESC line (H9) were analyzed at earlier and later passages. Comparisons were made against their respective original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC). Proteins were considered differentially expressed if expression changed by >=1.5-fold, with a maximum false discovery rate of 2% and >95% confidence. Western blot analysis was used for validation. The developed marker panel was further tested in 8-9 additional hiPSC lines or passages from different somatic origins and reprogramming techniques. Differentiation studies were conducted with embryoid bodies at 24 hours and 7 days to assess marker changes during spontaneous differentiation.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Included in the list of 982 proteins up-regulated by at least 1.5-fold in hiPSCs compared to parental somatic cells, identified with >95% confidence and a maximum false discovery rate of 2%.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Transferrin receptor protein 1; involved in iron uptake and cell proliferation; previously not used for hiPSC selection.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Comparison of proteomic profiles during reprogramming of somatic cells to hiPSCs and between hiPSCs and hESCs.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Potential candidate for hiPSC surface marker, indicating pluripotency and stem cell identity.

document_context_data.document_summary: This retrospective cohort study investigated the association between iron status and renal outcomes, specifically progression to End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD), in 111 pre-dialysis patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) and biopsy-proven Diabetic Nephropathy (DN). It found that reduced serum transferrin is an independent predictor of ESRD, and identified increased iron and transferrin deposition in renal tubular epithelial cells of DN patients, suggesting a pathological role for altered iron metabolism in disease progression.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study investigating the prognostic value of iron status and related biomarkers in Diabetic Nephropathy (DN) progression.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This retrospective observational cohort study analyzed baseline serum iron status markers (serum iron, ferritin, TIBC, transferrin, TSAT) and their association with progression to End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) in 111 Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) patients with biopsy-proven DN. Serum markers were measured using chemiluminescence immunoassay, immunoradiometric assay, and colorimetric methods. Additionally, histological analysis involved immunohistochemical staining for transferrin and Perl's blue staining for iron in kidney biopsy specimens from DN patients and healthy controls. No therapeutic interventions, dose comparisons, or active treatments were investigated; the study focused on correlation and predictive value.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Diabetic circumstance (T2DM with DN).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Increased expression favors tissue accumulation of transferrin and deposition of iron, contributing to iron overload and potential renal damage.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review identifies and recommends validated biomarkers for tracking health, performance, and recovery in athletes across multiple domains including nutritional status (macronutrients, micronutrients, food allergies), hydration, muscle status (damage, endocrine response), endurance, and injury risk (concussions, stress fractures, ACL). It advocates for a comprehensive, integrative, and individualized approach to biomarker analysis, emphasizing dynamic monitoring and contextual interpretation over single markers or universal thresholds to optimize training and minimize injury and overtraining risks.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Biomarker-guided monitoring and management of athletic training, nutrition, hydration, and injury recovery
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This review primarily focuses on the diagnostic and prognostic value of biomarkers rather than specific therapeutic doses. It emphasizes frequent, individualized monitoring (e.g., pre/post-exercise, daily, seasonally, after injury/competition) to establish personalized baseline ranges and track physiological changes in response to various training loads (e.g., acute bouts, heavy strength training, challenging training weeks). While specific nutritional intake recommendations are mentioned for protein (1.3–2.0 g/kg/day) and omega-3 fatty acids (≤3 g/day for average, 6–8 g/day for elite athletes), and iron supplementation at low-moderate doses, the document does not report dose-response comparisons for biomarker changes. Instead, it provides specific thresholds for identifying deficiencies (e.g., Vitamin D >50 ng/ml, Ferritin <12 µg/L), dehydration (e.g., >-2% body mass decrease, blood osmolality ≥295 mmol/kg, USG ≥1.020), insufficient recovery (30% decrease in T:C ratio), and overtraining (T:C ratio of 0.35 × 10⁻³). The overall approach prioritizes dynamic, contextualized assessment over universal thresholds for effective athlete management.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Reference range: 15–50%. Values under 15% consistent with iron deficiency. Functional iron deficiency defined as <16%.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Iron deficiency; iron status assessment.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates iron deficiency; valuable biomarker for determining iron status.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of 80 mg/day oral iron supplementation on hematological parameters, muscle damage biomarkers (CK, LDH, Mb), and cortisol levels in elite male cyclists during a 3-week stage race (Vuelta a España). It concluded that iron supplementation effectively prevented declines in iron metabolism and hematological profiles (serum iron, ferritin, hemoglobin, hematocrit, TSI, TP, RBC), significantly reduced accumulated stress (cortisol), and significantly lowered Creatine Kinase (CK) levels within the supplemented group, thereby contributing to optimal recovery and performance.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Oral Iron Supplementation
treatment_details.dose_specificity: 80 mg/day of oral iron (800 mg of iron protein succinylate, e.g., Ferplex 40®), administered as two 40 mg doses per day (during breakfast and dinner). The supplementation lasted for a 4-week period, starting one week before and continuing throughout the 3-week Vuelta a España stage race. No dose-response comparisons were reported, but a control group received no oral iron.

matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Reflects the adequacy of iron supply for erythropoiesis and overall iron status, crucial for oxygen transport and endurance performance.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated immune subphenotypes and biomarker differences in critically ill adult COVID-19 patients from the REMAP-CAP trial. It identified three distinct subphenotypes based on biomarker patterns, revealing differential treatment effects of ABO-compatible convalescent plasma therapy on hospital mortality and organ support free days (OSFD-21). Seronegative patients showed significantly higher hospital mortality, with specific biomarker profiles varying by serostatus within subphenotypes. The findings suggest that convalescent plasma therapy should be avoided in subphenotypes 2 and 3 and emphasize the importance of patient selection based on host immune response for COVID-19 immunotherapy.
