document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the safety and efficacy of human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cell (UC-MSC) transplantation in patients with severe COVID-19 and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), focusing on clinical outcomes, lung functional status, hematological parameters, cytokine levels, and miRNA expression profiles. The findings demonstrated that UC-MSC therapy was safe, improved lung lesions over a one-year follow-up by reducing fibrosis and markers of lung damage (CT score, Surfactant D, sRAGE), hastened lymphocyte recovery, and modulated inflammation (decreased ESR, CRP, banded neutrophils). The treatment also showed complex immunomodulatory effects, including altered levels of several cytokines (e.g., increased IP-10, MIP-1α, G-CSF, IL-10, while IL-6, MCP-1, and RAGE remained mostly unchanged in vivo but exhibited changes in vitro) and specific miRNAs, as well as influencing PBMC activation and proliferation in vitro.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Human Umbilical Cord Mesenchymal Stem Cell (UC-MSC) transplantation combined with conventional anti-viral treatment (antibiotic therapy, dexamethasone).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Triple intravenous infusion of UC-MSC at a concentration of 1 × 10^6 cells/kg, administered on days 0, 3, and 6. The average cell viability was 87.8% ± 5.1% before infusion. This was combined with conventional anti-viral treatment including dexamethasone and antibiotic therapy. No explicit dose-response comparisons were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant impact on relative expression levels (miR-221). Decreased on days 7 and 28 in both groups compared to baseline. Decreased more than threefold in the Control group but only twofold in the MSC group.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: MicroRNA involved in cell proliferation, apoptosis, and angiogenesis; implicated in tumor progression and immune regulation.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Severe COVID-19 patients after MSC transplantation.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Suggests modulation of cellular processes; MSCs might attenuate the decrease compared to control, potentially supporting tissue repair or immune cell function during recovery.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the safety and efficacy of human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cell (UC-MSC) transplantation in patients with severe COVID-19 and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), focusing on clinical outcomes, lung functional status, hematological parameters, cytokine levels, and miRNA expression profiles. The findings demonstrated that UC-MSC therapy was safe, improved lung lesions over a one-year follow-up by reducing fibrosis and markers of lung damage (CT score, Surfactant D, sRAGE), hastened lymphocyte recovery, and modulated inflammation (decreased ESR, CRP, banded neutrophils). The treatment also showed complex immunomodulatory effects, including altered levels of several cytokines (e.g., increased IP-10, MIP-1α, G-CSF, IL-10, while IL-6, MCP-1, and RAGE remained mostly unchanged in vivo but exhibited changes in vitro) and specific miRNAs, as well as influencing PBMC activation and proliferation in vitro.

The average cell viability was 87.8% ± 5.1% before infusion. This was combined with conventional anti-viral treatment including dexamethasone and antibiotic therapy. No explicit dose-response comparisons were reported.

document_context_data.document_summary: The study investigated the response of circulating miR-21, miR-378, and miR-940 to an acute exhaustive exercise in chronic heart failure (CHF) patients. document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated human blood-based target gene-miRNA associations in age-related hearing loss (ARHL) to identify potential protective mechanisms. Through transcriptome analysis of human blood samples (whole blood and PBMCs) from 12 ARHL patients and 12 normal hearing controls, and in vitro experiments on HEI-OC-1 cells, the study identified molecular changes. It confirmed the upregulation of IFNG in ARHL patients and demonstrated that miR-409-3p is significantly downregulated in ARHL and inversely correlates with IFNG. miR-409-3p was shown to downregulate both IFNG and p16 expression in vitro, a mechanism that promotes cell apoptosis and suppresses proliferation, suggesting a protective role for miR-409-3p in ARHL pathogenesis.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Investigation of molecular mechanisms in age-related hearing loss (ARHL), involving an observational comparison of ARHL patients and normal hearing controls, complemented by in vitro cell treatments.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study primarily involved an observational comparison between 12 ARHL patients and 12 normal hearing controls for gene and miRNA expression profiles. In vitro experiments on HEI-OC-1 cells included treatments with IFN-γ and miR-409-3p, but specific doses or dose-response comparisons for these cell treatments were not detailed. No specific therapeutic doses or durations were applied to human subjects, as the study focused on mechanistic analysis and target identification.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Lower when regulated by miR-409-3p; higher when induced by IFN-γ or with prolonged expression.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Expression decreased as miR-409-3p concentration increased, indicating miR-409-3p induced downregulation. IFN-γ treatment causes upregulation of p16 and p15 in most cell types, and prolonged p16 expression induces cellular senescence.

It is regulated by miR-409-3p.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Involved in age-related hearing loss (ARHL) and auditory dysfunction, acting as a senescence marker in HEI-OC-1 cells. Its expression is modulated by miR-409-3p and IFN-γ.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Its expression indicates cellular senescence and is associated with auditory dysfunction, including ARHL. Its regulation by miR-409-3p suggests involvement in ARHL mechanisms and the balance between tumor suppression and senescence.

document_context_data.document_summary: This scientific roadmap by the Heart Failure Association comprehensively addresses the complex and heterogeneous nature of fibrosis in heart failure, aiming to improve its definition, quantification, and treatment. It reviews mechanisms of myocardial fibrosis across various etiologies like pressure overload, aging, and cardiomyopathies, emphasizing the central role of TGF-β, collagen deposition, and myofibroblast activity. The document discusses challenges in detecting fibrosis using circulating biomarkers, proposing a framework for assessment and a roadmap for future research to identify individual fibrotic mechanisms, novel therapeutic targets, and diagnostic tools. It also evaluates diverse anti-fibrotic strategies, including pharmacological agents and non-coding RNA-based treatments, highlighting the need for targeted, multi-pathway approaches given the complexity of the fibrotic process.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Anti-fibrotic therapies for heart failure, including established drugs like angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, as well as specific anti-fibrotic agents like pirfenidone. Investigational strategies include targeting the TGF-β pathway (e.g., TGF-β inhibitors, CTGF inhibitors like FG-3019), MAPK pathways (e.g., ERK inhibitors), inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1α), neuregulin-1 administration, Matrix Metalloproteinase (MMP) inhibitors, Galectin-3 inhibitors, and non-coding RNA-based treatments (microRNA and long non-coding RNAs).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This is a review document, and as such, no specific therapeutic doses, intensities, or durations are consistently reported for any intervention, nor are dose-response comparisons detailed. While some agents like Pirfenidone and non-coding RNA modulators show utility in experimental models and clinical trials (e.g., microRNA-21 inhibitor in a Phase II trial), precise quantitative dosage or detailed treatment parameters are generally absent, reflecting a discussion of general approaches and their limitations, including a noted 'lack of precision' in current therapies. For example, MMP-12i was given 3h post-MI, but without specific dosage.

document_context_data.document_summary: This double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled study evaluated the effect of oral palmitoylethanolamide (PEA, Levagen+™) on recovery from muscle-damaging leg press exercise in 28 healthy young males. The study found that while PEA supplementation did not significantly reduce perceived muscle soreness, thigh circumference, or most inflammatory and phosphoprotein markers (Creatine Kinase, Lactate Dehydrogenase, IL-6, IL-10, hs-CRP, TNF-α, CREB, ERK1/2, JNK, NF-κB, p38 MAPK, S6K1, STAT3, STAT5), it did significantly reduce blood myoglobin and lactate concentrations. Furthermore, PEA increased Protein Kinase B phosphorylation immediately post-exercise, suggesting aid in muscle recovery through improved metabolic efficiency and activation of anabolic/repair signaling pathways from repeat bouts of exercise.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Oral Supplementation with Palmitoylethanolamide (Levagen+™) combined with Resistance Exercise
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants were randomized to consume either liquid PEA (167.5 mg Levagen+™ containing 150 mg PEA and 17.5 mg excipients, with 832.5 mg maltodextrin) or a matched placebo (1 g maltodextrin). Treatments were administered pre-exercise, immediately post-exercise, 24 h post-exercise, and 48 h post-exercise. The muscle-damaging exercise consisted of four sets of leg press at 80% of one-repetition maximum (1-RM) to volitional exhaustion, with 60s rest between sets, followed by a performance set at 70% 1-RM to maximal repetitions. No dose-response comparisons for PEA were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No main effects of time or treatment.

matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Leg press exercise to volitional exhaustion, with/without PEA supplementation.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study utilized genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screening in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) cells, primarily Nalm6 B-ALL, to elucidate the molecular mechanisms of panobinostat resistance and action. Key findings reveal mitochondrial activity as a driver of panobinostat resistance and SIRT1 expression as a critical determinant of sensitivity. Panobinostat treatment abrogates mitochondrial activity in ALL cells, contributing to resistance, while enhancing mitochondrial function (via rosiglitazone or SIRT1 overexpression) sensitizes ALL cells to panobinostat by activating the mitochondrial apoptosis pathway. The investigation identifies the SIRT1-mitochondria-PMAIP1 pathway as central to panobinostat response and suggests that higher SIRT1 expression or mitochondrial hyperactivity could indicate patient benefit from panobinostat therapy. The study also details various methods used, including cell culture, gene modulation techniques, drug sensitivity assays, RNA sequencing, Western blotting, and flow cytometry.

treatment_details.therapy_type: The study primarily investigated Panobinostat, a pan-histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor, often in combination with genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 knockout screening or SIRT1 modulation. Other HDAC inhibitors (chidamide, vorinostat) and conventional chemotherapeutic agents (l-asparaginase, cytarabine, 6-mecaptopurine, vincristine, dexamethasone, daunorubicin) were mentioned for comparative or contextual analysis. Rosiglitazone, a PPAR   γ activator, was used to stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis and enhance panobinostat sensitivity.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Panobinostat was frequently used at 10 nM for durations of 24 hours (for RNA sequencing, combination treatments) or 14 days (for CRISPR screening), leading to 60-80% cell death and significant proliferation inhibition in Nalm6 cells. Gradient concentrations were employed for drug sensitivity assays. Rosiglitazone was administered at 31.25 µM for 24 or 48 hours. Dose-response comparisons for panobinostat sensitivity were analyzed using Sanger GDSC1 IC50 data across 576 diverse cancer cell lines. No specific doses or dose-response comparisons were consistently reported for other HDAC inhibitors or conventional chemotherapeutic agents.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly enriched (P < .05; Figure 2B) in positively selected genes at day 14.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Cell signaling pathway involved in sensitivity to panobinostat.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: KEGG pathway analysis of genes positively selected during 14-day panobinostat treatment (10 nM) via CRISPR screening.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Defects in the p53 signaling pathway conferred panobinostat resistance.

document_context_data.document_summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover study investigated the ergogenic effects of acute pre-exercise homemade chicken broth (CB) ingestion, rich in histidine-containing dipeptides (HCDs) like carnosine and anserine, on high-intensity cycling performance in recreationally-trained men. The study found a significant 5.2% improvement in 8-minute time trial mean power and elevated plasma carnosine and anserine levels following CB supplementation. However, the ergogenic effect was not mediated by changes in acid-base balance or red blood cell glutathione status, indicating alternative mechanisms may be at play.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Acute pre-exercise nutritional supplementation (homemade chicken broth or placebo soup)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Subjects ingested either 8 mL/kg body weight of homemade chicken broth (CB), providing 46.4 mg/kg body weight of total histidine-containing dipeptides (HCDs) (specifically 15.6 mg/kg BW carnosine and 30.8 mg/kg BW anserine), or an equivalent volume of a placebo soup. The supplement was administered 25-40 minutes prior to an 8-minute high-intensity cycling time trial, following a warm-up. No dose-response comparisons were made, only CB versus placebo.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant effects of chicken broth supplementation were observed on blood pH. During the time-trial, pH naturally declined from 7.4 to 7.2.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Indicator of acid-base balance in the blood, essential for physiological processes and enzyme function.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: During an 8-min high-intensity cycling time-trial following acute pre-exercise chicken broth ingestion.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Unchanged pH indicates that the ergogenic effect of chicken broth is not mediated through improved extracellular pH buffering during high-intensity exercise.

document_context_data.document_summary: This document describes the protocol for an exploratory, multicenter, open-label, randomized controlled trial (CAME COVID-19 study) evaluating the efficacy of clarithromycin (400 mg/day or 800 mg/day) as an oral treatment for Japanese adult patients with mild COVID-19 pneumonia who do not require oxygen administration. The study aims to identify a new treatment strategy for mild COVID-19 and determine the number of days required to achieve a 50% or more improvement in clinical symptoms.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Clarithromycin
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Oral administration of clarithromycin is investigated in two dosage groups (800 mg/day, given as 400 mg twice daily, and 400 mg/day, given as 200 mg twice daily for 7 days) compared to a standard treatment control group. Patients are randomized in a 1:1:1 ratio, allowing for dose comparisons. Dose adjustment based on patient age, weight, and symptoms is possible. The doses are approved for other bacterial respiratory infections in Japan, and their safety is confirmed, but this is an exploratory trial as no prior dose-response data for COVID-19 pneumonia were available.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: To be determined by study outcomes; this is a protocol.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Not applicable as this is a study protocol outlining planned measurements; no results are reported.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Measure of acidity or alkalinity in the blood.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Clarithromycin treatment for mild COVID-19 pneumonia.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of acid-base balance in the body, which can be disrupted by severe illness.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study investigated the impact of extreme static apnea on blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity and neurovascular unit (NVU) protein exchange in ultra-elite breath-hold divers, aiming to distinguish between hypoxemic- and hypercapnic-induced stress. Findings revealed that hypoxemia, independently of hypercapnia, is a critical stimulus contributing to increased BBB permeability and neuronal-gliovascular reactivity, leading to a net cerebral output of NVU proteins. This suggests transient NVU dysfunction rather than structural damage, with evidence of active repair mechanisms and highlighting hemodynamic stress as a key factor in BBB disruption.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Maximal static apnea (voluntary asphyxia) and breath-hold diving
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Ten ultra-elite breath-hold divers performed two maximal dry apneas: Normoxic Normoventilation (NX) with an average apnea duration of 5m 6s (range: 3m 37s to 6m 49s), resulting in severe hypoxemia and hypercapnia; and Hyperoxic Hyperventilation (HX) with an average apnea duration of 15m 59s (range: 9m 39s to 21m 2s), preceded by 15 min of 100% O2 hyperventilation (targeting PET CO2 ~20 mmHg), which alleviated hypoxemia while compounding hypercapnia. Biomarker measurements were taken at baseline (pre-apnea) and at the apnea breakpoint, coinciding with the most severe hypoxemic-hypercapnic stress. NVU protein output was more pronounced in NX compared to HX (P < 0.05). Serial measurements for temporal dynamics and maximal rates of transcerebral protein flux were ethically constrained by blood volume loss, thus no specific dose-response comparisons were reported; however, biomarker output partially recovered post-NX, suggesting transient rather than sustained effects.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Reduced pH; during hyperoxic (HX) apnea, pH was 7.227 corresponding to PaCO2 of 68 mmHg.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Indicates acid-base balance in the blood.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Normoxic (NX) apnea and Hyperoxic (HX) apnea.
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates metabolic acidosis; participants became more acidotic at the end of HX apnea.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review investigates the potential of extracellular vesicle (EV)-enclosed non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs), including microRNAs (miRNAs), long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), piRNAs, circRNAs, and tsRNAs, along with N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA modifications, as stable, non-invasive diagnostic, prognostic, and monitoring biomarkers for a wide range of chronic liver diseases (CLDs). These include metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), metabolic-dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), Alcoholic Liver Disease (ALD), Autoimmune Hepatitis (AIH), Chronic Viral Hepatitis (HBV/HCV), cholestatic liver diseases, liver fibrosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), cholangiocarcinoma (CCA), and gallbladder carcinoma (GBC). The document also touches upon the therapeutic potential of engineered EVs for targeted cargo delivery in preclinical models to modulate inflammation and fibrosis pathways, highlighting their utility and associated challenges in clinical application.

treatment_details.therapy_type: This document primarily functions as a review investigating biomarkers for the diagnosis, prognosis, and monitoring of chronic liver diseases (CLDs). While the main focus is on biomarker identification, the review also touches upon the therapeutic potential of Extracellular Vesicle (EV) therapy, including engineered EVs for targeted cargo delivery, and mentions pharmacological inhibition of miR-34a as a potential therapeutic strategy.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study does not report specific therapeutic doses or dose-response comparisons for most interventions, as its primary focus is on biomarker evaluation. However, preclinical models utilized various EV-based interventions, such as native and engineered EVs derived from mesenchymal/stromal stem cells (MSCs) or human liver stem cells in models of liver fibrosis, NASH, and cancer, without detailed quantitative dosing. In biomarker contexts, some observations included a dose-dependent increase in serum miR-122 and miR-192 levels in induced liver injury mouse models. Disease states and exposures examined for biomarker changes included acute and chronic alcohol consumption, autoimmune inflammation, viral infections, cholestasis, CCl4-induced liver fibrosis, lipotoxic palmitic acid treatment of hepatocytes, arsenite-induced liver fibrosis, and various human liver conditions including biliary cholangitis, biliary atresia, liver fibrosis, HCC, CCA, and GBC.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Present at significantly higher levels in HCC samples compared to non-tumor controls. When combined with other piRNAs, it presented a superior AUROC for HCC detection.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Non-coding RNA, likely involved in gene regulation.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Diagnosis of Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Diagnostic biomarker for HCC, especially useful for detecting HCC with low tumor burden, with improved performance when used in combination.

document_context_data.document_summary: This comprehensive review investigates the potential of extracellular vesicle (EV)-enclosed non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs), including microRNAs (miRNAs), long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), piRNAs, circRNAs, and tsRNAs, along with N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA modifications, as stable, non-invasive diagnostic, prognostic, and monitoring biomarkers for a wide range of chronic liver diseases (CLDs). These include metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), metabolic-dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), Alcoholic Liver Disease (ALD), Autoimmune Hepatitis (AIH), Chronic Viral Hepatitis (HBV/HCV), cholestatic liver diseases, liver fibrosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), cholangiocarcinoma (CCA), and gallbladder carcinoma (GBC). The document also touches upon the therapeutic potential of engineered EVs for targeted cargo delivery in preclinical models to modulate inflammation and fibrosis pathways, highlighting their utility and associated challenges in clinical application.

treatment_details.therapy_type: This document primarily functions as a review investigating biomarkers for the diagnosis, prognosis, and monitoring of chronic liver diseases (CLDs). While the main focus is on biomarker identification, the review also touches upon the therapeutic potential of Extracellular Vesicle (EV) therapy, including engineered EVs for targeted cargo delivery, and mentions pharmacological inhibition of miR-34a as a potential therapeutic strategy.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study does not report specific therapeutic doses or dose-response comparisons for most interventions, as its primary focus is on biomarker evaluation. However, preclinical models utilized various EV-based interventions, such as native and engineered EVs derived from mesenchymal/stromal stem cells (MSCs) or human liver stem cells in models of liver fibrosis, NASH, and cancer, without detailed quantitative dosing. In biomarker contexts, some observations included a dose-dependent increase in serum miR-122 and miR-192 levels in induced liver injury mouse models. Disease states and exposures examined for biomarker changes included acute and chronic alcohol consumption, autoimmune inflammation, viral infections, cholestasis, CCl4-induced liver fibrosis, lipotoxic palmitic acid treatment of hepatocytes, arsenite-induced liver fibrosis, and various human liver conditions including biliary cholangitis, biliary atresia, liver fibrosis, HCC, CCA, and GBC.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Differentially expressed in CCA and GBC patients versus healthy controls; levels significantly decreased in circulating EVs of CCA and GBC patients 1 week after surgeries.

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Non-coding RNA, likely involved in gene regulation.
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Diagnosis and post-surgical monitoring of Cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) and Gallbladder Carcinoma (GBC).
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Promising candidate biomarker for diagnosing CCA and GBC, and for monitoring the efficacy of surgical intervention.

document_context_data.document_summary: This study performed a comprehensive qualitative and quantitative proteomic analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) derived from different somatic origins (fibroblasts and peripheral blood CD34+ cells), comparing them to original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC) and human embryonic stem cells (hESC). Using ESI-MS e and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry, complemented by Western blot validation, the research aimed to characterize hiPSC proteomic profiles, identify known and novel pluripotency markers, and distinguish hiPSCs from their somatic precursors. Key findings include the identification of approximately 220 commonly up-regulated proteins in pluripotent stem cell lines, the development and confirmation of a 22-protein marker panel for hiPSC characterization, and the observation of coordinated up-regulation of proteins involved in protein synthesis, folding, RNA processing, DNA replication, DNA repair, and energy metabolism (including oxidative phosphorylation and lipogenesis) in hiPSCs. The study also identified somatic cell markers that were down-regulated upon reprogramming and highlighted specific proteomic differences between hiPSCs and hESCs, contributing to improved hiPSC quality control for therapeutic applications.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Proteomic characterization and comparative analysis of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) and human embryonic stem cells (hESCs).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was a characterization study, not a therapeutic intervention, thus no 'dose' of therapy was administered. Quantitative and qualitative proteomic analyses were performed using electrospray ionization (ESI)-MS e (label-free quantification with internal reference standard) and MALDI-TOF/TOF mass spectrometry. Two hiPSC lines (iNC-01 from CD34+ cells, SB5-MP1 from fibroblasts, both generated using loxP-flanked excisable polycistronic STEMCCA lentiviral vector) and one hESC line (H9) were analyzed at earlier and later passages. Comparisons were made against their respective original somatic cells (fibroblasts, PBMC). Proteins were considered differentially expressed if expression changed by >=1.5-fold, with a maximum false discovery rate of 2% and >95% confidence. Western blot analysis was used for validation. The developed marker panel was further tested in 8-9 additional hiPSC lines or passages from different somatic origins and reprogramming techniques. Differentiation studies were conducted with embryoid bodies at 24 hours and 7 days to assess marker changes during spontaneous differentiation.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Coordinated up-regulation observed

matched_biomarker_details.core_biological_function: Aminoacylation of tRNAs for protein synthesis
matched_biomarker_details.relevant_activity_context: Cellular state of hiPSCs
matched_biomarker_details.performance_or_health_indicator: Underpins the high rate of protein synthesis in hiPSCs
